review_text: My second visit of the season to the Grand Opera House Belfast this time to see "Ghost" by the UOC. This musical, based on the original movie, has recently become available to amateur societies and I am sure it will become a favourite over the next few years. It has everything. Great chorus work, plenty of supporting roles, well known songs throughout the show, but also requiring some technical wizardry. The chorus worked their socks off, big dance numbers choreographed by Brooke Allen were all foot perfect and their singing and diction was terrific. A fine cast of supporting actors all played their parts, Tony Young (Hospital Ghost) sang in a most sublime relaxed manner in his rendition of that soul song "ball of wax". Sean Harkin (Carl) got the interpretation of his character perfectly. Smooth and charming at face value whilst underneath evil skulduggery. His intonation was very good but needed to tighten up the diction in his very wordy song "more". The comedy was led superbly by Kelly Brown (Oda Mae Brown). Her initial reaction to hearing Sam was delivered with wonderful precise timing and her reluctance, alter in the show, to give up the cheque was hilarious. Our two leading players Johanna Johnston (Molly) and Boyd Rodgers (Sam) worked together wonderfully and had a marvellous rapport. Ms Johnston sang with wonderful conviction in her performance and beautiful intonation. In "Three little words" her delivery and phrasing was marvellous. She sang "You" most wonderfully whilst sitting mournfully alone. When Sam died her abject despair and sorrow were acted most superbly. Mr Rodgers has wonderful control and super resonance in every pitch of his voice and he has marvellous control of his falsetto register which he used to great effect. To act on stage and not be part of a scene is a very difficult thing to do but Mr Rodgers achieved this wonderfully and his stage craft and movement were excellent. Director James Huish staged the show quite superbly with wonderful sets and scene changes that ran very smoothly. The technical side of the show was excellent with superb lighting to assist. The backdrop of video images of the city, the subway, the sidewalk cafe was brilliantly mixed and drew the audience into each scene. The orchestra, under Wilson Shields, supported the singers, but occasionally the brass section got a little carried away. The show climaxed when Molly was allowed to see Sam, through the medium Oda Mae, and when they had finished their last dance he walked through dry ice, brilliantly lit, to his final destination. Not a dry eye in the house. A most fitting end to a wonderful afternoon's entertainment.

A most wonderful setting in the Abymill Theatre in Fethard, Co Tipperary to where I ventured to see a first time production company in AIMS. JW Productions is a joint operation between Stefan J Doyle and Holly-Jean Williamson. Mr Doyle is credited with both direction and musical direction. His direction needed to be more precise particularly in the chorus scenes where not all appeared to be secure in their positions. The technical side needed a more definitive lighting plot as it never appeared to differentiate from any scene although sound was good and the dialogue was all clearly heard. I realise this is the company's first offering and perhaps budgets were very limited but the use of backing tracks throughout the whole show is not what is expected nor should it be acceptable. A musical requires musicians! The use of musicians to perform at a live stage production of a musical should be unquestionable. If you have a musical production then the emphasis should be on the music presentation. When a performer sings a musical number it is a collaboration between singer, musicians and conductor.

Ms Williamson played our female lead Morticia, dialogue delivered most crisply and she sang with a superb delivery of lyrics in a very laid back fashion. Kevin Fahey (Gomez) looked the part and sang with wonderful comedic timing. He had a tendency to speak too quickly which, allied with his accent, meant a lot of his dialogue, particularly the comedy, was lost on the audience, which was a shame as he gave the part full commitment. Jordan Freeman (Wednesday) attacked her brother with pleasure, bamboozled her father and then gave a wonderful display of love to Lucas. Her diction and accent were very good and her singing, whilst a bit rushed and regimented had good intonation.  David Hughes (Mal Beineke) was very secure in the delivery of all his dialogue although I would have liked him to have been a bit louder and brasher initially. Olwyn Grogan (Alice Beineke) gave a most assured display throughout. She played the "mumsie" part perfectly, then when she drank the potion at the dinner table Ms Grogan was superb. Brilliantly acted with no inhibitions with wonderful comedy portrayed both in her dialogue and her final slide across the table until she collapsed, marvellous. Killian Skorca (Lurch) had superb make-up and was the epitome of his character. A fine bass singing voice his lower range resonated around the theatre. The set, whilst well made, was extremely large for the stage and it impeded the players, particularly the chorus, on all their entrances and exits. The chorus themselves needed a bit more singing work and their dancing was more movement than dancing. Katy Wallace was the choreographer and whilst stage area was at a premium there should have been more energy throughout. The wardrobe department came up with some wonderful costumes the highlight being the ancestors who all looked marvellous.

This year there are a number of societies debuting in AIMS and my first journey was to Loughrea to see Bravo Theatre Group's production of Sweeney Todd. Bravo Theatre Group, under the guidance of Shane and Clodagh Farrell, have been producing shows for the younger members of their company and this was their first foray into an adult production. It was well worth the wait. Shane Farrell is well known in musical circles and he used all his contacts to assemble not only a superb front line but also a chorus, all of whom were up to the task. The chorus were magnificent. Diction and intonation are a standard requirement of a chorus but their attention to ensemble interaction was superb. This obviously was the work of Director Niall Heaney and Choreographer Aoife McClafferty. Whilst the stage did not allow for any expansive dance numbers, the chorus interaction and movement was marvellous. Mr Heaney allowed specific characterisation for his cast and his direction, particularly of the two handed scenes, was perfect. The story of Sweeney Todd requires your principal male to be capable of leading from the front, delivering all the nuances of his character whilst still keeping his feelings in the dark. Dave Langan is a very talented singer but his acting in this role was exemplary. With good stage presence, a swish of his blade and a gleam in his eye he held the audience in the palm of his hand. Katie Creaven (Mrs Lovett) matched Sweeney in every way. Her comedy timing was spot on and her singing was faultless. Sarah Corcoran (Johanna) and Louis Brennan (Anthony) sang most harmonically together, however a little bit more passion might have convinced us of their commitment. Ronan Lardner (Pirelli) gave us a super comedy performance and both his accents were excellent. His sidekick Kevin Murphy (Tobias) played the perfect straight man up to Pirelli's demise and then in Act 2 he gradually descended into a nervous wreck once he realised the truth of the pie ingredients, a super performance from Kevin. Declan Kelly (Judge Turpin) sang with a most resonant Baritone voice and delivered his dialogue most precisely. Michael Cooney (The Beadle) delivered his dialogue crisply and with a very good consistent accent, just needed a little bit more care with the lyrics. Sarah Griffin (Beggar Woman) acted perfectly deranged throughout. Her singing was excellent and her characterisation was brilliant. She used her actions and movement perfectly to match her dialogue or lyrics. The costumes were wonderful, lighting was never too dark to obscure facial features and the sound technician never missed a cue. Let me finish where I started, Shane Farrell had a 25 piece orchestra. They played like an orchestra should, supported throughout and not once did they overpower any singers. His downbeat and direction was absolutely first class. When you can sit and listen to an orchestra perform as wonderfully as Mr Farrell's orchestra did, it was a shame that the show had to end.

My second visit of the season to the GrBeing frisked by a member of the security forces upon entering a building is something I remember well from the days of my youth, and it was an appropriate way to start the evening in the Island Centre, Lisburn, and the Fusion Theatre production of "The Beautiful Game". The atmosphere of the era was immediately captured.

Director/Musical Director, Ian Milford, handled the emotional roller-coaster of this show extremely well, touching raw nerves in the dramatic scenes, but balancing nicely with the well accentuated humour of the piece. Musically, he was on top of his game, making the most of choral harmonies, and leading a well tuned and balanced orchestra. The girls chorus in particular, performed The Boys in the Photograph and God's Own Country with great emotion. This show does not have a wonderful score, but it was certainly wonderfully performed. This production was notable for its discipline, with well rehearsed performers comfortable both in voice and in action. It was also helpful to the production that the Youth were supplemented by a handful of adults, who added credibility to many scenes. The military presence was very good, except for the gun-toting soldier who heralded every scene change, a gimmick that became a little tiresome. The use of projected images, however, was quite excellent. The on-stage characters had been photographed (or magically superimposed into photographs) around the city of Belfast, John and Mary out on dates, a sequence of wedding photos. Excellent forward planning to create a superb effect.

The various levels of a simple but effective set were well used, and the props, particularly for the church, the pub and the Europa Hotel bedroom, were excellent. The funeral was very well staged, with grave diggers removing a section of the floor to become the grave. Stage Manager, Peter Kay, and his stage crew did sterling work to keep things running smoothly. As mentioned, the projection of albums on the back wall well very well planned. The lighting plot allowed the projections to be clearly seen, and created good atmospheres, with the important action always well accentuated. Apart from one moment of feedback during an emotional hug, the sound was well pitched, and cueing was excellent. The sniper who ran on to shoot Thomas was actually a distraction that elicited laughter from some of the audience. Had he been discretely lurking in advance, I feel this could have been avoided, or perhaps just the sound of the gunshot off-stage would have been sufficient to suggest Thomas's execution. Kudos to the Director for persuading Ulster television celebrity, Jackie Fullerton, to record a commentary for the kids' football final. I'm afraid, however, that I found the style and tone of the voice of the BBC Home Service more 1930/40's than 1960/70's.

Choreographer, Jillian Liggett, did a very good job of adding live and energy to a show that demands little choreography. The chorus and dancers were always energetic and disciplined in their movement, and strong pictures were created on the stage. The football match is a difficult challenge, and while the performers did all that was asked of them, including keeping the football on the stage, I feel perhaps that miming the ball, as was done in other scenes, might have given Gillian more scope and freedom to create a more adventurous routine. That said, movement throughout the rest of the show added significantly to the overall appeal of the production. Lucy Donnelly was delightful in the demanding role of Mary McGuire, growing in stature as the story progressed, and being totally convincing in the heart-wrenching final scenes. She has a beautiful voice, and a warmth of personality that make her instantly likeable as a heroine.

Michael Drake made a convincing and sympathetic John Kelly, full of fun and mischief in the early scenes, struggling to remain unaffected by the chaos of the ever-changing political climate, and ultimately finding the inner strength to turn his back on terrorism. His acting throughout was top notch. Vocally, the demands of long week of performance seemed to be slightly taking its toll on his upper range, but a good quality of voice was still evident.

Tierna McNally almost stole the show with her raunchy portrayal of Christine Warner. Here is a young lady with a very good sense of comedy, excellent stage presence and a fine voice. Very well performed.

The loathesome character of Thomas Malloy was grotesquely realised by Adam Williamson, managing to make me hate him, (a compliment) despite the fact that on occasions, his body language was a little gentle for the aggression of his dialogue. His finale scene, however, was excellent.

If Tierna McNally amused with her performance, (and she did!) Ethan Haddock positively grabbed us by the funny bone and forced us to laugh out loud at his comedic antics as the likeable rogue, Daniel Gillen. Excellent delivery of his lines, and his knee-capping scene was as brilliantly authentic as it was distressing.

There was a beautiful piece of casting placing Ian Simpson and Anna- Lee Corbett together as Ginger and Bernadette. They really did look and sound perfect together, capturing the hope and innocence of youth, and consequently breaking our hearts when Ginger meets an untimely end.

Rory Jeffers gave a valiant performance as the out of place Prod, Del Copeland, trying to bridge the sectarian divide, despite threats of personal injury. He was believable at every level, and a good companion to Christine.

Brian Devlin's experience shone through his performance as Fr. O'Donnell, making the most of his comedy, and adding gravitas to the more poignant moments of the show.

There were two delightful bigots, who doubled as the wives of two republican prisoners, who don't seem to have been acknowledged in the programme, but they made a strong impact, and a worthy contribution to the show.

As mentioned above, the adult performers gave great support to the young cast, giving the wedding and the funeral, in particular, a strong community feel. Perhaps a little less wailing at the funeral would have been desirable, but it was, regardless, an emotionally charged scene.

The chorus, throughout, performed with musicality, energy, enthusiasm, and most importantly, discipline, always backing up their principals with authentic and believable emotion.

Attention to detail was the trademark of the costume plot, from the military uniforms to the everyday clothing of the chorus and principals. There was good variety in the costuming of "God's Own Country". Hairstyles and make-up were always appropriate. As suggested earlier, there was great use of cast members as security forces on arrival at the theatre, and a very welcoming front of house staff. Particular thanks to Anne McCleary for her lovely hospitality. Fusion Theatre are a Youth group who set their standards very high, and inevitably manage to achieve them, through discipline, dedication and unbounded energy and enthusiasm. What a pleasure to have attended this wonderful production of "The Beautiful Game". Thank you for the great entertainment..

The greatest success of Greg Browne's direction in this show was a sense of wonderful people management and inclusivity. With well over 60 young performers on stage, so many were individually, or as part of a smaller group, given their opportunity to shine. From down-and-outs to servants, from the radio studio to the Cabinet office, dozens of cameo role performers made the most of their moments in the spotlight. The exuberance of youth is one of the most appealing delights to behold on any stage, and when it is combined with well rehearsed acting, singing and dancing, it is guaranteed to win a warm and positive response from an audience. Such was the case when Annie and her fellow orphans got this show off to a cracking start with a visually delightful and vocally delicious rendition of "It's a Hard Knock Life". While Stephanie Browne made an excellent job of the dancing throughout the show, her choreography of the orphan chorus was the sparkling feature of the night. All their routines were busy, energetic and brilliantly executed by the dancers. There was a rich blend of fancy footwork, good patterns, impressive gymnastics and clever comedy, with her young performers very obviously enjoying every moment on stage. Stage Manager, Brendan Manning, made a good job of manoeuvring a substantial set, which while being slightly cumbersome, was always effective visually. Scene changes could have been a little quicker. The main set, with its New York skylines, was well designed and well painted. Props throughout were appropriate to the era of the show, although it might have been nice to have a sofa or chaise longue in the Warbucks' mansion. The copy of the "Mona Lisa" was very good, but about three times too large. Lighting was adequate throughout the show, and if a principal missed their spotlight, they were quickly illuminated by the operator. Sound quality was well balanced, except for dialogue over music, which in the earlier scenes left many of the minor characters a little inaudible.

I would have to be honest and say that there were many moments of pathos lost due to the cracking pace at which the whole production was played. "Maybe", at the very start of the show, was rushed, and consequently not as emotional as it might have been, and similarly, several of the tender encounters between Annie and Daddy Warbucks were just begging to be slowed down to allow the sincerity of their relationship to be better realised. Pulling back on the reins would also have emphasised the good comedy between Miss Hannigan, Rooster and Lily and allow it to be further highlighted. Regardless of this, Musical Director, William Cullagh, had a very able orchestra under his control, and despite an occasional split note from the brass section, they made a good contribution to the show, although they could have been a little more p and a little less f when underscoring dialogue.

Megan Maher was most impressive in the role of little Orphan Annie, full of expression and energy, and with a vocal quality that befitted this demanding role. She was skilful in the execution of her dances, and while her acting was excellent throughout, her emotions would have benefitted from a slower pace to the more emotional scenes of the show.

Caroline Browne gave a feisty performance as Miss Hannigan, with a superb accent and wonderful facial expressions. She was vocally powerful, especially those final notes to "Little Girls", and her physical comedy was extremely good. Again, had the dialogue been slowed on occasions, the audience might have had more chances to enjoy her excellent reactions.

Eva McKeogh was an efficient and business-like Grace Farrell with a pleasant voice and good stage presence, and she functioned well beside Colin Dillon as her employer "Daddy" Warbucks. Given that the musical is based on cartoon-strip characters, the Warbucks bald head is as expected as the red wig on Annie, but having a full head of well coloured hair didn't detract from a strong performance from Conor. Anna Conway and Calvin O'Rourke worked well together as Lily and Rooster, making the most of their comedic caricatures, and establishing alternative personas as Ralph and Shirley Mudge. "Easy Street", alongside Miss Hannigan, was a well performed song and dance. Cathal Milner was a credible Bert Healy, and was given good support by Lara Smyth, Saoirse McGee and Rachel Browne as the Boylan Sisters. Luke O'Gorman was a severe but believable Roosevelt, and Milo McGee gave plenty of character to the role of Drake, the butler.

There were many, many smaller roles that were competently played, even if on occasions underscoring from the orchestra made lines difficult to make out.

Prince, in the role of Sandy, was adorable. The various choruses performed with great energy and musicality, rising to the demands of their production team with wonderful enthusiasm.

The costumes for the show were of good quality, especially the principals. There was a nice contrast between the impoverished Hooverville residents and the staff and household of Warbucks. There was perhaps a little too much variation in hem-lengths of the orphans final costumes, but the visual impact was still most effective. Hairstyles and make-up showed a good appreciation of the era, and there was some very appropriate ageing of the more mature characters.

The children of this youth production are lucky to have such a dedicated company and production team behind them, encouraging their effects, and steering them towards a high standard of presentation.

Long may they continue to strive and improve. Thank you for a most enjoyable evening.

Musical Director Shane Farrell had the most wonderful control over his orchestra which enabled him to give perfect direction to the players, and how well they followed him. A super downbeat, with tempi precise allowing the chorus to sing and dance so passionately. The dancing was light of foot, perfectly on the beat and choreographer Jay Molyneux's routines were performed so precisely. The 8 council members delivered every dance number in a most laid back relaxed manner. The chorus singing was led by the Dynamites whose harmonies were wonderful; they gave superb backing to Emma Brady (Motormouth) in "I know where I've been". Ms Brady gave us dialogue with an accent in a slow American drawl, always on cue and her stage presence was excellent. This show is all about Laura Charleton (Tracy). Her opening number typified her character and she portrayed this over the top, excitable young lady. Her dancing was rhythmic, her singing was super and when she first met Link I thought she would burst. Conor Walsh (Link) sang like a 60's crooner. His dialogue was precise and he gave Tracy great attention and support in all their scenes. Kevin Griffin (Edna) sang with super diction, he acted, especially with Wilbur, like a woman in love, but the highlight was his dancing. He was light of foot and he was step perfect, and he did all that in high heels, tremendous. Michael Cooney (Wilbur) got his dialogue and accent correct; he gave a most passionate display in his affections for Edna and did all this with a twitch of nervous excitement. If there are baddies in this show then the Von Tussles are guilty. Suzanne Garvey (Velma) strutted around the stage like a prize peahen, issuing orders and edicts, with a most haughty expression. Her singing was super and her rendition of "Velma's Revenge" a showstopper. Heather Doyle (Amber) was a chip of the same block; she gave a perfect mirror image of her mother. She was so full of self-importance; she looked down at all about her and her amazement when Link refused her was wonderful. Roisin Fowley (Penny) was Tracy's best friend. Her energy and passion was tremendous. Her jumping up and down, her nervous excitement and the twitching of her feet was a most marvellous characterisation. The costume department worked very hard and produced some wonderful 60's clothes for the ladies and a wonderful array of colourful suits for the men, particularly the dancers in the TV studio. A lot of bouffant hair do's were in place but some of the wigs needed more care attention especially Tracy's. Director Peter Kennedy had the company all delivering dialogue at a good bright pace, particularly the smaller characters who were all promptly on cue. His set was dressed very well and the studio scene, complete with camera, worked perfectly. Technically there were a few issues, the stage crew needed to quicken up the scene changes which were very laboured and interfered with the dancers and the lights technician needed to ensure that a musical number was finished before a blackout. This show is not that well known but it was a credit to the society that they managed to sell the show out for the run. A super musical evening in, once again, a very wet Galway.

Galway City two weeks before Christmas creates its own problems not especially parking. I made my way to the Black Box Theatre to see Twin Productions, another first timer to the family of AIMS, perform Oliver! Joint Directors Brian & Sean Power had procured a most wonderful adult cast to ably assist the young members of their performance academy. A full cast of over 120 performers on stage meant that the design of the stage was crucial to allow enough playing space for the show to run smoothly, and designed superbly it was. A most wonderful fixed set with two wonderful staircases and a bridge which would not have looked out of place in London itself. The chorus was moved in and out swiftly and on cue, their singing was passionate if not perfect, and their dancing was done with a smile on their faces and pure enjoyment. Ruairi O'Connor (Oliver) played the cherubic orphan, he had the most wonderful soprano voice and his singing of "Who will buy" was super. He was ably assisted by Keith Hanley (Dodger) who took him under his wing, sang a most excellent "Consider Yourself" and left him in the care of Declan J Gardiner (Fagin). Now whilst Fagin got his accent and actions perfectly some of his singing and dancing let his overall performance down a little. The comedy in this musical comes from lots of roles firstly the relationship between Neil Conway (Mr Bumble) and Hannah McCreanor (Widow Corney) was excellent. They got all the dialogue spot on, they teased and laughed their way into marriage and they sang most harmoniously together.  Mr Conway sang "Boy for sale" with wonderful control and his crescendo was superb. Comedy was also part of Karl O'Doherty's dual role (Mr Sowerberry & Dr Grimwig). He got all the nuances as the devilish undertaker and then his stuttering dialogue as the Doctor was perfectly played. Sean Hosty (Bill Sykes) acted with intimidation throughout and gave a most loud and forthright rendition of "My name". Katie Creaven (Nancy) stole the show though with a marvellous performance. Her dialogue was crisp and clean and her anger at Bill was vitriolic. Her attention to Oliver in his hour of need was played with wonderful care and then she sang with the most wonderful passion perfectly in tune and in keeping with her character. There were a few problems technically particularly the lighting plot which should have been much more on cue. The sound technician needed to balance a little better as the music overpowered the poor chorus constantly. There was also a decision made by the musical director to use backing tracks for this production, alas it did not work. There was no conductor, so the soloists and the chorus were left to fend for themselves on entrances and exits and this really took away from the overall production. The stage crew worked exceptionally hard and gave us the most perfectly swift scene changes which allowed the pace of the show never to drop. A full house two weeks before Christmas gave the cast a wonderful ovation and all left happily, humming and singing the well-known tunes.

This musical has a dark and sombre tone to it as it revolves around the death of a young girl. With music and lyrics by Jason Robert Brown he leads us through a tale of race relations and politics. Oisin Nolan (Leo Frank) plays the leading male role as the Jewish proprietor of a factory in a town that he cannot bear to be in. His stage craft and dialogue was especially precise and his voice soared around the auditorium. His relationship with his wife Lucille, played by Derry Keeling, was the focal point of the show. Ms Keeling was always trying to appease Leo and her acting was initially quiet and polite but then as her character blossomed so did she. Her acting was forthright and she played so passionately in her scenes of anger as she fought for her husband. She sang with the most wonderful melodic voice and her singing performance in her piece "Do it alone" was superb. The show had joint directors in James Bergin and Lorna Bailey, who was also the choreographer.. They gave wonderful direction keeping the pace tight, the dialogue all delivered with the same southern American accent, and they moved the chorus around the stage with consummate ease. Lorna Bailey did not have much scope in this musical drama but the dance in the Governors house was perfectly precise. Cormac Gleeson (Gov. John Slaton) gave us a character full of self-importance and was a typical American politician, and yet when he recanted at the end his dialogue was delivered in a wonderful tone of admission and regret. The show opened with a wonderful two hander between Stephen Carvill (Frankie) and Mary McGowan (Mary). Their dialogue was fraught with adventure as Frankie tried to entice Mary to the pictures. Their duet "The Picture Show" was sung with wonderful cadences and rhythms. Throughout the trial Jack Hanrahan (Judge Roan) ruled with a most imposing resonance of his baritone voice. Evidence given by Ause Braike (Jim Conley) and Rachel Adepoju (Minnie) needed to be more precise as emphasis appeared to be on the accent rather than the dialogue. The prosecutor was Colin Gilligan (Hugh Dorsey), his baritone had good resonance and his diction was excellent. His accent was precise, a smooth southern drawl which he used to great effect in holding onto the vowels making him sound even more obnoxious, if that was possible.  Other supporting actors were Malachy Conlon (Tom Watson) who played the bible thumping, god fearing preacher, Jack Carolan (Britt Craig) the alcoholic crime reporter and Anna Bergin (Mrs Phagan) who gave us despair at the funeral and outrage at the trial. The lighting plot was excellent, perfectly on cue with wonderful hues to set each scene and the sound technician knew all his cues. Roisin Heenan was chorus mistress and musical director. Her work with the chorus was terrific. The chorus sang most perfectly with raucous crescendos and wonderful precise diction throughout. She gave wonderful direction to her orchestra and whilst some of the balance was a little awry it never impeded on the overall accompaniment to the singers. The most melodic playing by the Violin and the percussionist was sublime. It was a wonderful evening of musical theatre.

Director, Kevin Kennedy, set this show at a cracking pace and really made the most of the shows comedy potential. Characters were well drawn and physical comedy was as well played as vocal delivery. Chorus were nicely integrated into the action and always had a sense of purpose. The set for the show was minimalist, with the only major moving piece being the balcony/ stairways, which were nicely employed, but not so nicely painted. Real potted palms would have been more effective than the painted ones. Lighting the top of the balcony also caused some problems, and indeed, throughout the show, lighting cues seemed a little patchy and insecure. Those few issues aside, this was a strongly directed show, displaying a good understanding of the material, and it was complemented by the choreography of Claire Kickham, who used every possible opportunity to put the chorus through their paces, with lively and inventive routines, capturing the mood and era of the show. There were good stage pictures and well- choreographed movement sequences, with a company who seemed secure in what they were doing. I loved the Oklahoma line dancing.

While I thought the orchestra were excellent, and captured the mood of the music, they were a little over-zealous in their accompaniment of the choral numbers, resulting in many of the vocal choruses being somewhat swamped. Possibly the sound desk might have been able to strike a better balance. Regardless of that, the show was very well musically prepared by Musical Director, Philip Kennedy, with audible harmonies sounding well-rehearsed, and the principal singers made a very positive impact on the show.

A tremendously strong front line was expertly led by a dynamic Ciarán Dunphy in the role of Laurence Jameson. Delightfully pompous, deliciously devious, and strong in stature, Laurence made the most of his comedy, and impressed with a fine voice and perfect diction, regardless of which accent he was employing.

Keith Flanagan was perfect for the role of Freddy Benson. His physical comedy was excellent, with wonderful timing and reactions to the torture he endured while restrained by a wheel chair. His Ruprecht was hilarious, and he made the most of all his vocals. An excellent performance. James Dobbs as Andre Thibault and Teresa Buckley as Muriel Eubanks together provided some of the most hilarious moments of the show with superb comic timing and their insatiable lust for each other, having both already established themselves individually as strong character players. Like Zis/Like Zat was brilliantly performed.

Ashley Doran gave an engaging performance as Christine Colgate, deviously passing herself off as delightfully dim and gullible, while she got the better of her two suitors. She had fine vocal quality and very expressive delivery of her lines. Her sassy return at the end of the show was a very good contrast.

Joanne McCabe gave a robust performance as the obsessive Oklahoma femme fatale, Jolene Oakes. Her Oklahoma number was performed with great character and energy, and her horror at meeting Ruprecht was palpable.

Several chorus members provided good back up in cameo roles, and the chorus generally were strong and supportive in their acting and reacting. When they could be heard, they produced fine harmonies and their movement was precise and well- rehearsed.

The main set successfully captured the atmosphere of the south of France, with good backdrops and a nicely painted interior, and the main moving piece, a double set of stairs with an effective balcony, was efficiently moved around the stage, a testament to the good organisation of Stage Manager Lizzy Heffernan and her team. . If the dressing of the stage seemed a little bare at times, it was due to the nicely selected props and furniture being placed around the periphery of the stage. This did, however leave plenty of free space for the chorus routines. As mentioned above, lighting the balcony did create some problems, and indeed there were occasions when principals seemed to miss their spots. Lights also seemed to 'bounce' in on occasions, when smooth transitions would have been more effective. The sound system allowed principals to be heard clearly throughout, but there was a balance issue between pit and stage, particularly during chorus numbers.

A very good job was done in costuming the show. Those who needed to look dapper certainly did, and there was an abundance of colourful attire. Hair and make-up were more than satisfactory throughout, in a very nicely presented show.

St Michael's have shown themselves, once again, to be ambitious and forward thinking in their show selection, and it's a gamble that paid off. With an abundance of excellent performers, comedy would appear to be their forte, and with this particular show, they have set a high standard for others to emulate, and I left St Michael's Theatre feeling thoroughly entertained and impressed by a dynamic company with a wonderful community spirit. Thank you so much for a most enjoyable night.

Carnew Musical Society was celebrating its 50th anniversary and chose this well known and much loved musical as its celebratory offering. An open stage with moveable houses gave us the basis for the village of Anatevka. The set design and stage management was quite excellent in this production, every scene moved smoothly, each set was specific to its purpose and the stage crew moved effortlessly through their tasks. Lighting cues in this production have to be precise. The plot gives numerous specific spots particularly on Tevye when he talks to God. The lighting technician, Ella Doran, at just 16 years of age, never missed a cue. Costumes were most correct and the props department provided an abundance of household goods for all as they were evicted. Director Michael Dunbar kept the pace of the show nice and tight, accents, with one exception, were all similar, and he made the most out of every piece of comedy. His clever use of a moving spot to symbolise the Fiddler was a novel idea which worked perfectly particularly at the end of the show. There are certain musical numbers in this show where the players on stage need specific direction from the conductor. Entrances and exits are so important in choral singing but Musical Director Lar Duffy was one of the instrumentalists in the pit and because of this there were a number of issues for both chorus and principals which was a shame, as in places the chorus singing was terrific. Jennifer Byrne (Golde) ruled the roost. The constant haranguing of her husband and her daughters was marvellous and she sang with the most wonderful control. The three eldest daughters sang "Matchmaker" with harmonies wonderfully. Catherine Stafford (Tzeitel) was precise in her acting and her enthusiasm when Motel proposed was super but she just needed to sing more through the notes. John Egan's (Motel) character was a busy body and his hesitant delivery of his dialogue with Tevye was very good. Eva Dempsey (Hodel) needed to work on her accent with her dialogue, her singing voice is very melodious but needed to ensure that phrases were delivered correctly. Anna Dillon (Chava) was extremely positive in all her actions, her dialogue was crisp, her singing was correct and her solo dancing was timed perfectly. Malcolm Byrne (Perchik) was very honest and forthright in the delivery of his dialogue and he upheld the character correctly, with good enunciation and good stage presence he carried off the portrayal. Timmy Connaughton (Fyedka) was positive in his actions, his dialogue with Chava was precise and he got all the nuances involved in his character. Fiddler on the Roof revolves around its leading man. Bill Stafford (Tevye) took on the role. He got all the subtleties in his character, from comedy with Lazar Wolfe, telling the story of the dream scene to his wife, to the private conversations with God. All delivered perfectly, sung with passion and fortitude but always with a little twinkle in his eye, it was a most wonderful performance. Per the front of house team, the show was a sell out for its complete run, which means that the society can continue to provide musical entertainment for its patrons and go on to succeed for another 50 years.

The show revolves around Annie. She must capture the audience's hearts by singing, dancing, being cheeky, small and feisty and Grace Killen (Annie) ticked all of those boxes. No sign of nerves or first night jitters, she hit every note, hit every line of dialogue, led from the front and had boundless energy which she carried through to the end of the show. A marvellous performance. Supporting Annie was a cast of orphans who all danced and sang with tremendous energy and they were all full on throughout the whole show. Jim Daly's (Warbucks) dialogue was secure with a good accent and wonderful timing. He had problems with the lyrics which then affected his intonation, and his dancing was a little laboured. Emma Kelly (Grace) has wonderful stage presence, her dialogue was delivered most perfectly and her singing was sublime. Nicola Brenchley (Ms Hannigan) gave a staggering performance of her slightly inebriated character. Her dialogue was delivered on cue, her actions were played perfectly over the top, and her revulsion of Annie was palpable throughout. Anthony Fitzpatrick's (Rooster) singing was excellent and his accent was most precise throughout the performance, there was, however, an issue with dance steps. Claire Costello's (Lily) dialogue was delivered in a high pitched, nasally American accent, typical to her character. Brendan Magee (Drake) was perfectly on cue, he gave us precise dialogue delivered in a very stately manner and even a little high kick whilst exiting. The set for the main house was plushly dressed although perhaps a bust or a vase of flowers on the plinths would have enhanced the scene. Costumes were dowdy and ragged for the orphans and suitable dirty for the Hooverville scene. The female chorus were excellent at both singing and dancing. Choreographer Lynn Gourley's routines for the orphans were full of big movements and used the acrobatic skills of some to full effect. The orchestra produced a nice sound in the quieter pieces but the use of the electronic keyboard instead of brass instruments didn't work. The show's opening notes are so well known that a lone trumpet was required. The electronic instruments overpowered the smaller instruments and the balance within the orchestra needed to be reviewed. The lighting cues improved as the show went on and there were issues with the sound technician who needed to improve his cueing.

Les Miserables is a musical that is sung from start to finish and the emphasis needs to be on the music. Whilst the keyboard playing of musical director Herta Kelly was first class and the balance within the orchestra was very good with controlled playing, unfortunately they chose not to have a conductor. This meant that entrances and endings were ragged, timings were off between soloists or chorus and orchestra and the wonderful togetherness required for this musical never materialised. Seimi Campbell's direction allowed the players plenty of room to give the characters scope to express themselves but just needed to tighten up on the smaller details and finer points of this musical. The two male leads fought a constant battle with each other to gain advantage and their confrontations were expertly played. Aodhan Gavigan (Valjean) gave us every emotion throughout his portrayal. Plenty of anger and guilt at the start through to melancholy at his demise. His singing was precise and "Bring him home" was performed quite superbly. Ryan Mulreaney's (Javert) stage presence was menacing and he sang with a very powerful voice, wonderful diction and enunciation. Kate Gurren (Fantine) sang "I Dreamed a Dream" with complete control and gave us a super crescendo, but she just needed to be more precise with her notes when she sang at her death. Aoife Breslin (Eponine) was dirty and tomboyish, she teased Marius to the full and her singing was wonderful. Bried-Marie Byrne (Cosette) has the most marvellous soprano register and her top notes were staccato perfect. Her diction was exact and in her acting she gave superb support to both Valjean and Marius. Oisin Joyce (Marius) gave a super acting performance, his embarrassment when he first spoke to Cosette was played marvellously and then his realisation at Eponine's death was filled with heartbreak. The comedy from the Thenardiers, Colm McGroarty and Alison Edwards was delivered in a very droll manner but they both needed to be more precise on the delivery of the punch lines. The chorus sang with passion and commitment and the big singing numbers were sung to the fullest. "At the end of the day" was sung with correct precise rhythms, and a rousing finale of "One Day More" in Act 1 raised the roof. Perhaps more attention to the choreography would have assisted some of the chorus movement as, on occasions, there were chances lost. The lighting plot was never too dark, but the technician needed to be aware when performers missed their mark. The use of a similar repeated set spot, dimmed down, for each death was very effective. The sound technician gave us thunderous sound effects which worked extremely well in conjunction with the lighting plot for the battle scene. A full house in Donegal town on a Saturday night ensures that musical theatre is alive and well and in very safe hands.

If you do as the writers of the musical suggest and "suspend disbelief" then Hairspray ticks all the boxes. It requires a young vibrant cast full of energy and the ability to sing and dance. The chorus in Boyle's production gave us just that. Energy in abundance ensured that there was no flagging in the big dance numbers choreographed by Vivianne Moran. Good rhythmic feet and hand movements enabled and encouraged the audience to fully immerse themselves. From Karen Gordon's (Tracy) opening number she led from the front in a most wonderful leading lady's performance. Super enunciation of dialogue and wonderful singing and her commitment to her leading man was marvellous. Darragh Beirne (Link) sang like an old fashioned crooner, with wonderful resonance and inflection in all his lyrics. Colette Noone (Penny) started off a little lacklustre but picked up in the second half and her work with Marc Egan (Seaweed) was terrific. Marc Egan delivered wonderful dialogue but just needed to perfect some of the dance steps. The von Tussles could have been sisters rather than mother and daughter. Niamh Noonan (Velma) gave a most assured display and sang with power and passion. Cliona Dowd (Amber) was a clone of her mother and played her part perfectly and her distaste for Tracy was evident for all to see. Diarmuid Beirne (Wilbur) never faltered in his display of affection for Edna and he played the dutiful and subdued husband, his dialogue was good but his singing and dancing needed a little more care. Stephen Tighe's (Edna) costume made him as broad as he was tall and he used his ample frame for wonderful comedy. His singing and dialogue was secure but his footwork needed more attention. Ronan Smith (Corny) was the epitome of the game show host, great smile, good precise diction and a very good singing voice. Director Vivienne Moran had the principals all cued perfectly without any delays in dialogue. The chorus were all aware of their responsibilities which all fed into the ethos of the pace of the show. Occasionally the orchestra got a bit carried away, whilst musical director Anne Kielty's keyboard playing is excellent occasionally the orchestra needed a more secure downbeat. The set design was super, rotating sets allowed scenes to be changed in a thrice. Stage crew all were perfectly prepared and their efficiency was superb. The ladies costume shades of bright pastel colours, the four lead male dancers had wonderful suits and superb white jackets and Edna's outfits were big and loud. The von Tussles wore beautiful, perfectly fitted outfits. Catherine Bolger (Motormouth) sang "I know where I've been". It was a collaboration of the chorus singing the most wonderful harmony, perfectly controlled and accompanied along with Ms Bolger singing with resonance and the most wonderful crescendo. It was a showstopper. The audience afforded the cast a suitable ovation at the end, well deserved for a wonderful evening's entertainment.

A change of venue always brings additional work for a society, in Castlebar's case it required a complete building of a stage in which to perform their 2016 production of South Pacific. The Breaffy House Hotel was their new venue and whilst it has a wonderful arena in which to perform the stage has to be constructed from scratch. To the societies credit the stage that they produced was magnificent and in addition they had a lighting rig which would have been most acceptable in many a theatre around the country. Director Alanna ni Mhiochain used the full expanse of the stage, producing a wonderful lighting plot giving us a backdrop of hues and colours. She allowed the show to move smoothly from scene to scene with a very cleverly designed set which the stage crew worked precisely. Alana ni Mhiochain also doubled up as choreographer, an onerous task doing both jobs, and whilst the smaller numbers were moved most precisely the larger chorus dance numbers needed a little more work. Deirdre Lee was Musical Director and whilst she kept a tight control of the 8 piece orchestra, because she was also playing Piano there were some issues with entrances and endings by the singers on stage. Ronan Egan (Emile) gave us a superb French accent which oozed gravitas and his performance of "Some Enchanted Evening" was terrific. He gave wonderful support to his leading lady Vivienne Lee (Nellie). Her character was full of bounce and frivolity, she exuded happiness and gave us a very precise accent. Her dialogue was delivered most assuredly but when singing she just needed to try and use the lyrics more specifically. South Pacific is an old fashioned musical and was written with certain comedy characters of the day in mind. Seamus Cafferky (Luther) was one of these. As a sailor out to make a buck any way he can he was the focal point of all of the male chorus work and he accomplished this superbly. His comedy timing and facial expressions were brilliant. His singing was clean and precise and he committed perfectly to his comedy dance in "Honey Bun". Deborah Kenny (Bloody Mary) was very confident in her portrayal and she had a wonderful accent which emphasised her dialogue, perhaps she could have adapted an even more high pitch for her shrieks of laughter. She was assisted by Stephanie Cassol (Liat) who glided around the stage so gracefully and in "Happy Talk" gave the most perfectly choreographed hand movements to accompany the song. Another player who has the most marvellous stage presence was John Byrne (Cable). His actions were sure and precise, his dialogue was delivered with a wonderful, almost natural, American accent, and his phrasing and control in his solo pieces was excellent. The supporting roles all delivered dialogue perfectly on cue and the chorus, particularly the females, worked extremely hard throughout. The costumes were suitable for the era, the sound technician never missed a cue and got all the radio transmissions spot on and the lighting technician, with the exception of the travelling spot, delivered a very well thought out lighting plot. Back in the 1980's this show used to be one of the most regularly produced shows in amateur theatre. It was wonderful to see it again in all its glory and the audience left humming all the well-known tunes.

Director/Choreographer, Suzanne O'Leary treated us to a very clean and efficiently executed production, which had all the signs of being well rehearsed. A cleverly designed set allowed virtually a full stage for all the production numbers, keeping them well spaced and uncluttered. Vibrant and energetic choreography was in abundance, with the Majorette number, Whipped into Shape and Legally Blonde being the stand out routines. Very good references to "Riverdance" made the Irish section most enjoyable. Indeed, the choreography throughout the show was of an excellent standard and helped to drive the pace of the production. Chorus were nicely integrated into the story, and the principal line was very impressive, although I would have liked Serena, Pilar and Margot, who were dynamic as a team, to show a bit more individual characteristics. One or two of the smaller characters could perhaps have been more exaggerated to make a bigger impact, but this was a very competent and disciplined cast.

What a lovely effect when the show began to see the girls of Delta Nu appearing at the windows, on two levels, of their sorority house. This heralded a clever set that was efficiently moved about the stage by a confident crew, under the direction of Stage Manager, Greg O'Leary. Props, and there were many, were appropriate, although the "Department Store" was a little sparse, and didn't quite have the "awe" effect to merit Emmett's amazement. But I do appreciate the limitations of the stage, and acknowledge that a vast amount was achieved on the space available. The lighting on the edges of the neutral stage flats was a good idea and allowed colour changes to equate to changes of location. The lighting generally was more satisfactory than spectacular, but cueing was very tidy, and the stage was always sufficiently lit to ensure that none of the action was missed. The use of projections on the back of the set was a good idea that needed a bit more attention, as often the images were virtually washed out by the stage lighting. With the exception of a couple of late cues, the sound were of good quality and well balanced.

Excellent sounds were emanating from the orchestra pit, under the precise guidance of Musical Director, Patrick Clancy. A good pace was maintained throughout the show, and the balance with those on stage was very good. As Chorus Master, Patrick got great work out of his singers, with harmonies being well realised, and even during the more energetic routines, vocal quality didn't diminish. Having pit-singers is a wise move in a show that is heavy on dance routines. Good work.

When you cut through the glitzy-ditziness of Legally Blonde, there are some really hard-hitting issues addressed by the story, none more obvious than the way women are mistreated by many members of the male species, and the one moment that really strikes a revolting chord is when Callahan, despite the realisation that Elle is actually an astute and intelligent intern, still feels he has a right to harass and humiliate her. And it was at exactly that moment that I realised that Sharon Clancy was an astute and intelligent actress, for it was the very real sense of humiliation and revulsion that she portrayed at that moment that made me believe in her character. It was remarkably poignant. Her singing and dancing were totally secure, and her comedy was always well timed and delivered, but it was her ability to bring moments of pathos and drama to an otherwise frivolous story that made her outstanding.

Gearóid McCauley was a relaxed and reassuring Emmet, capturing the shy, pleasantness of the early scenes, and allowing his romance with Elle to take it's time to develop. He was believably heroic in the final scenes. A nicely judged character, with a fine vocal quality.

Tom Joyce, as Warner, perhaps could have been even more conceited and full of swagger in the early scenes, but he grew in stature as he transformed into the whiney begrudger of the second half. Very good vocals during Time to Get Serious. As Vivienne, Yvette Walsh was a suitably toffee-nosed pain in the posterior at the start of the show, but she impressed me most in the sincerity of her willingness to admit that she had been wrong about Elle. Very nicely played. She also made the most of her few opportunities to shine vocally.

Majella Londra did absolutely nothing wrong in the role of Paulette, but I was left feeling that she could have exaggerated her character even more for comedic effect. That said, she was still delightful, and a good sense of comedy timing was in evidence. Ireland was very well performed. Neal O'Leary created a perfectly patronising Callahan, making a strong initial impact with his "Blood in the Water". His attempted seduction of Elle was nicely underplayed, with a Trump-like smugness which I found quite eerie.

Emma O'Leary managed to sing with gusto even as she skipped frantically into the role of Brooke. She had plenty of energy and looked like she had been following her own fitness regime.

I would have liked Caroline Horan to have been a tad brasher as Enid. She was almost two sweet, which weakened the impact of some of her comedy lines, but as with the rest of the cast, she performed with good confidence.

As a team, Catherine Devereux, Niamh Bolger and Emily Brazill, as Serena, Margo and Pilar, respectively, performed with an abundance of talent and energy, with all three having strong vocals and great moves. My only criticism is that they were too similar in character, and maybe could have been given more individual characteristics, i.e. ditzy, aloof, and gregarious. But that didn't detract from the fact that I loved their energy.

Tom O'Leary was a capable Kyle, who delivered his lines, and his packages, very efficiently. Again, though, I feel the "hunk of meat" aspect of his character could have been more emphasised for stronger comedy effect.

There was strong support given by Jane Kent, Mick Farrell, Dylan Walsh and Ryan Kavanagh, whose rap as Grand Master Chad was very impressive. Dara Cullen had a strong accent and good timing as Whitney, and a host of other cameo roles played their part in the overall success of the show.

The chorus contributed much to the atmosphere of their various scenes, always alert to the action, and reacting beautifully. Their vocal efforts were very commendable and their energy was abundant. Lulu as Bruiser and Hunk as Rufus were only brilliant!

Visually, the show was very pleasing to the eye, with costumes always suited to the character, and the chorus and dancers impressively dressed. With a modern setting, a wide range of hairstyles was more than acceptable, and everyone looked well turned out. Make-up appeared natural. The few wigs that were apparent were well worn.

Oyster Lane is blessed with a vibrant company, an abundance of talent, a very professional production team and a community spirit that was evident on the night. It was my very great pleasure to attend this fun filled evening of entertainment.

show_raw: How To Succeed In Business Without Really Trying
review_text:
In the hands of a superbly competent production team, "How To Succeed in Business" proved to be an offering high above the mediocrity that I had expected of this well-worn old chestnut of a show. There are still those endless scene changes that interrupted the flow of a clever and funny script, but in fairness they were expertly managed, largely due to the experience and expertise of stage manager Marie Cusack and her team, frequently assisted by a disciplined cast who moved much of their own furniture. The set itself was visually perfect, nicely painted and always appropriately dressed with well-selected props. Loved the urinals and revolving sink units. Sound was evenly balanced with secure cueing, and the narration voice-over was crystal clear and well-timed. Lighting was generally very atmospheric and contributed to the standard of the presentation, but on the final performance of the run, I was a little surprised to see principals frequently missing their spotlights, and unfortunately when this occurred, it wasn't always quickly remedied with back-up lights. On this very well designed set, we were never allowed to forget the location, thanks to a continuous flow of background activity, people using the elevator, moving from office to office, working at desks, etc. all of which excellently created the atmosphere of the World Wide Wickets building. The major key to the success of this production was meticulous rehearsal and attention to detail, combined with well- drawn and nicely exaggerated caricatures. Eoin Cannon attacked the script with a focus on playing it for every possible laugh, while ensuring that the pace was never allowed to flag. To enhance his efforts, Denise Donohoe similarly set the stage alight with imagination and precision routines that were as comical as they were electrifying. The choreography of "Coffee Break" was quirky and superb, closely followed by a terrific "Secretary is Not a Toy", a vibrant "Paris Original" and a show-stopping "Brotherhood of Man". She asked a lot of her dancers, and they delivered. This was excellent work.

Dermot O'Callaghan kept a tight rein on his orchestra in more ways than one. Not only did they perform the score with excellent balance, perfect timing and musical precision, but they did so in full view of the audience, perched high above the set, and not once did they distract or pull focus away from the on-stage activity. Equally impressive was the vocal quality of a disciplined and harmonious chorus, who achieved excellent harmony and diction even when engaging in furious choreographic activity.

Sean McMahon successfully carried the show on his shoulders in the role of J. Pierrepont Finch, with superb comedic timing, an assured voice and wonderful stage presence. In an excellent performance, he exuded confidence and dynamism.

Aoife Small was a syrupy sweet Rosemary, who seemed completely unfazed at playing a submissive sweetheart from another era. How the lyrics of "Happy To Keep His Dinner Warm" didn't stick in her throat is beyond my comprehension, but she carried it off convincingly, with an astute awareness of comic delivery and a very pleasant vocal quality.

Paul Laycock was a sturdy and believable J.B.Biggley, always in control of his underlings and impressively uncomfortable when attempting to deal with Hedy and his annoying nephew. This was a confident and concentrated performance.

Mark O'Looney played Bud Frump, the spoilt brat you love to hate, most convincingly, wallowing as the manipulative schemer and delightfully wimpy as the run-to-mummy cry-baby. A nicely portrayed role.

Ema Mae West was a formidable Hedy LaRue, particularly delightful in her attempts to seduce Finch. She was deliciously provocative amongst the men and perfectly captured a confused morality as she spoiled the treasure hunt presentation. She was well able to belt out her vocal contributions too.

At ease, relaxed, level-headed and astute, such was the persona created by Sharon Osborne in the role of Smitty, in a well- defined and stalwart performance. She was vocally and physically perfect for this role, and particularly impressive in weighing up the situation in "Been A Long Day".

The drawling, monotonous voice of Kelly- Marie Davy as Miss Jones was a superb device to establish her character, and she played it to a T. Excellent comedy caricature throughout, and a fine vocal contribution to "Brotherhood of Man". There were a host of solid, impressive and well-balanced performances from staff members, Mr Gatch (Robbie Keogh), Mr Bratt (Eoin Salley), Mr Tackaberry (James Place), Mr Ovington (Andrew Torsney), Miss Krumholtz (Julie Donnelly), Mr Jenkins (Stephen Fagan) and Mr Davis (Gavin O'Reilly), each with their own well- maintained idiosyncrasies…… and then there was Matthew Carpenter! Doubling as Wally Womper and Mr Twimble, this was a performance of immense stature, hilariously funny as Twimble and equally convincing as the Chairman of the Board. His rendition of "Company Way" was a show stealer! Excellent work.

Whether dancing the dynamic routines, vocalising in beautiful harmony, creating a background ambiance or moving furniture, the chorus never failed to impress throughout the show.

Costumes throughout were era appropriate and well worn. In an unglamorous show, I was a little surprised that the "Paris Original" dresses weren't a bit more dynamic. They were entirely appropriate, but colour-wise; a tad dull, but maybe that's just my taste. In all other respects, this was a good looking show, with good attention to hairstyles and make-up. From front of house staff to backstage crew, and the ridiculously talented number of creative and artistic people between them, thank you sincerely for another wonderful night of sheer entertainment.

The magnificent setting of the Grand Opera House in Belfast was this year's venue for BSPA's production, Les Miserables. My guest and I attended on the second Friday and witnessed a committed performance by a talented cast of teenagers. Leading the way was Valjean played by Matthew Quinn. He led from the front with a passionate performance, his acting matched his singing and we were left in no doubt as to who or what the show was about. He was pursued throughout by Tom O'Kelly as Javert. Tom has excellent stage presence although a bit more menace to his character would have been an advantage. Naomi Smyth gave us every emotion in her portrayal of Fantine, she sang most perfectly and died most graciously. Holly Ryan as Eponine was pivotal in every scene. Her rendition of "On My Own" brought the house down and at her demise she conveyed the most poignant emotion. Alexandra Dick played the adult Cosette and sang with a wonderful soprano voice and her relationship with Marius was acted most precisely. Ciaran McCormack led the students with passion and precision as Enjolras. He has a very good singing voice and he was most commanding in all of the scenes at the barricade. The comedy was delivered by the two Thenardiers, Malachy Conlon and Maebh Quinn. The emphasis was on the comedy, too much sometimes, leaving the words and notes not supported as well as they might have been. The highlight of the evening was Robert Kelly's portrayal of Marius. Every word, every note, every movement were all perfect. Not a foot wrong, not a word delivered incorrectly, not an emotion misplaced. When he climbed into Cosette's garden and met her for the first time, the awkward embarrassment was delivered superbly. Similarly when he realised that Eponine loved him but only at her death it was heartbreaking. It was a wonderful all round performance.

As for the technical side of this production, led by Director James Huish, it was not as slick as it could have been. Scene changes were laboured. Lighting was very good but every scene was too dark, daylight never appeared at all. Sound cues were very poor, a pity. The orchestra under Wilson Shields started at a most frantic pace and then got quicker! There also needed to be a little quieting of the brass section who overpowered all comers in the first act. The set design was very disappointing. A pre-requisite of a barricade is that it is taller than the members of the cast, this was not so. Players could clearly be seen behind the barricade awaiting their entrance. With the most marvellous facilities of a professional theatre a bit more thought in the technical side of this production would have assisted enormously. The chorus were note and word perfect and they sang with gusto and commitment. The opening convict's number was superb as was the female chorus in the factory. Well done to all concerned. Costumes were wonderful and correct to the time especially the prostitutes who were dressed most colourfully. The audience afforded the cast a standing ovation, well deserved for all their labours.

The town hall theatre in Claremorris, I am reliably advised, will soon be an 800 seat venue. The well-known professional musicians who are booked to perform there will have the pleasure of performing in a wonderfully appointed venue right in the heart of the town. Claremorris Musical Society performed their 11th production, Me and My Girl, to a packed theatre and how well they entertained their patrons. This show is a rarity in that the leading man is also the comedy lead. John Byrne (Bill) took on the challenge and played it quite superbly. His accent, dialogue and singing were marvellous but his forte was his dancing. He excelled in all his musical dance numbers and his tap was terrific. He was ably assisted by his leading lady Mary Dempsey (Sally). She took on his challenge and together they danced most sublimely. Her dialogue was enunciated perfectly and her singing of "Once you lose your heart" was beautifully melodic. Director and Choreographer Hazel McLynn kept the show moving at a wonderful pace, with the dialogue cues precise and she ensured that every last bit of comedy was garnered from the script to its fullest. Not only were the front two precise in their dance steps but Ms McLynn also had eight dancers who danced superbly in every number. Michael Goulding (Gerald) played the typical toffee nosed gent with a perfect high pitched accent and an air of despair each time his "true love" Lady Jacqueline rejected him. Vivienne Lee (Lady Jacqueline) played the femme fatale brilliantly, her scene on the couch with Bill left little to the imagination as she teased and tempted him. Her acting was marvellous and her singing was wonderful. Ciaran Kiely (Parchester) played the straight laced family solicitor, his dialogue was excellently delivered but we also saw him perform the comedy side of his character perfectly. The manor was ruled by Rosemary Noone (Duchess of Dene) who gave a most commanding performance. Her intonation was marvellous and she was in full control of her performance. Ms Noone gave us a typical, stereotype of an English Lady. Most formidable in her actions and her deportment, her dialogue was pronounced correctly and precisely. Seamus Cafferkey (Sir John) played extremely well in Act 1 as the Lord of the Manor although in the shadow of his wife the Duchess. His dialogue was precise as was his accent. He excelled in Act 2 and his duet with Bill took us back to the music hall where their rendition of "love makes the world go round" was a singing, dancing and comedy gem. The technical side of the show gave us perfect cueing from the sound technician and the lighting plot worked very well although a travel spot for some dances would have added to the visual. The set was well designed with the main three piece set swivelling for particular scenes and the interior scenes were very well dressed. The costumes were terrific, all fitting perfectly and very correct to the era. The orchestra led by Deirdre Lee accompanied with wonderful control and the tempi were perfect not only for the dance numbers but also for the quieter, melancholy number.

I am told that there is nothing unusual about a rainy Friday night in May in Galway. However the rain didn't stop me and a host of patrons and sponsors attending Corofin Musical Society's second musical offering. Hot Mikado is based on the Gilbert & Sullivan operetta with only a few modern adaptations to the music. It still requires a talented singing chorus and a raft of musical principals. Founder of the society Joey Power made his debut in directing and what a wonderful job of it he did too. He got the most out of his cast with special emphasis on the comedy, and his players all took up the challenge and never faltered.  Our wandering minstrel, Robert Reed (Nanki Poo) delivered his dialogue in a most crisp manner and never tired. He was a bly assisted by Alana Power (Yum Yum) whose dialogue was enunciated wonderfully. Their duet was sung most musically and the timing of the lyrics interspersed with the kisses was timed perfectly. The main comedy role fell to Stuart Barrows (Ko Ko), who gave us a wonderful character accent which he kept up throughout, his singing was delivered perfectly in tune and his comedy timing was exemplary. The arrival of Olibhia Donnelly (Katisha) was a show stopper in itself as she strode around the stage with a stare of displeasure... and then she sang. Her phrasing was sublime, her diction was perfect and she not only sang every note right in the middle but sang each note for its full value. Allied to her singing Ms Donnelly also gave us wonderful comedy with Ko Ko particularly in "tit willow". It is a very small stage in Corofin but the Power sisters, choreographers, managed to get the cast to move and dance and tap without any fear of mishap and they also got the chorus to get every bow and scrape timed perfectly when the Mikado spoke. Eoin Fahy (Mikado) made a grand entrance from the auditorium and spoke slowly and precisely asserting his authority throughout. The main principals were ably assisted by Elaine Hynes (Pitti Sing) and Roisin Broderick (Peep Bo) who along with Yum Yum gave us a wonderful musical trio and cameo of the Andrews Sisters, the harmonies were perfectly sung and perfectly balanced. It would be remiss of me not to mention Kevin Murphy (Pooh Bah) whose facial expressions were excellent, this assisted him in his many characters all of which he played with different accents and mannerisms, a most accomplished feat in itself. The set was simple and perfectly functional with a marvellous "fan" design at the back. The lighting complemented the set and in the opening of Act 2 gave us a most visual silhouette of the bride to be, Yum Yum. The sound technician knew his cues and his directions as he performed perfectly. The small orchestra under John Flatley's direction gave wonderful support to the performers, and Mr Flatley's accompaniment on the keyboards was terrific. The chorus mistress Martha O'Toole managed to get a wonderful sound from the chorus and they all sang with passion and gusto throughout. It was a wonderful night's entertainment to start the new season.

This show requires the chorus to hit the stage running and never stop, which is exactly what Fermoy Musical Society gave us. The male chorus was limited in numbers but they were positive in all their actions. The female chorus was marvellous. The energy that each gave was super. The choreographer Stephen Cullinane O'Regan had the chorus dancing and tapping their way through the show and the female chorus led by six dancers were terrific. The music from this show is based on the G & S "Mikado" but is adapted to give us a more, bluesy/jazzy accompaniment. Musical Director Deirdre Long led a very tight band of musicians. Three gentlemen who immersed themselves into the production also and their playing of trumpet, trombone and clarinet/saxophone was fantastic, and they even joined in on the ad libs where required. A small gripe was that the "electric" instruments were a little overpowering and the balance was a tad off. The sound technician had all his cues correct, the costumes were an abundance of colours, particularly the leading ladies whose dresses were fantastic. The six dancers in particular had wonderful matching outfits. The lighting plot had too similar back lighting which meant facial features in some scenes were not visually clear. Sarah Berry (Yum Yum) sang very positively, with good diction and good intonation. Her dialogue was precise and her commitment to Cian Daly (Nanki Pooh) was excellent. She just needed a little more precision in the dances. Aine Carroll (Pitti Sing) sang with a control and passion above her 17 years. Her phrasing and breath control were marvellous. Her dialogue was secure and she was very light on her feet. Gillian Fenton (Peep Bo) sang perfectly in the trio's with Yum Yum and Pitti Sing and held her line wonderfully, her dialogue was super and her acting whilst miming was hilarious. Colette Daly (Katisha) entered with a powerful voice which she controlled perfectly. Superb diction and intonation, she phrased all of her songs superbly. She performed the comedy scenes with Ko Ko in a relaxed manner. Cian Daly (Nanki Pooh) started off a little hesitantly but grew into both his singing and acting roles. Paul Finn (Pooh Bah) delivered his dialogue quite precisely with clean crisp enunciation. He has a most luxurious baritone voice with superb resonance and his lower register was velvety. Rory Ward (Pish Tush) has a superb upper register and carried the notes perfectly, just needs to enunciate a little better. His acting was always on cue and his attention to his fellow performers was excellent. Declan Woulfe (Koko) played the comedy role. The character requires boundless energy and Mr Woulfe gave us this. His characterisation appeared to be based on The Mask with his stance and facial expressions, and then his accent was mostly German, which sometimes interfered with the delivery of his dialogue. His singing was perfectly in pitch and his comedy dancing was good. Director Killian Collins kept the pace of the show nice and tight, his set was designed like an old time speak-easy with orchestra at the back and a flowing staircase u/s/r to allow prominent entrances of the principals. In 2024 the society will be 100 years old, and with a full house on a Tuesday night you can see that musical theatre is alive and well in Fermoy.

Guys & Dolls is one of those shows that require a mixture of performers. From the more established players who give us the back bone of the chorus through to the young female Hot Box dancers and a male chorus who need to be able to move rather than dance. The chorus, ably taught by Dave O'Connor, gave us good clean diction and the harmonies were precise when required. This show has some big dance numbers. For the men the movement in "lady luck" was a little too regimented, but the females, firstly the Hot Box singers danced and can- canned most precisely in "take back your mink" and then gave us wonderful slow suggestive dance moves in the Havana scene. The costumes for the ladies were beautiful in style and colour particularly the Havana scene with wonderful red, blue and gold dresses. Joanne Logue (Sarah Brown) has the most wonderful soprano voice, beautiful tone and vowel sounds and she sang in complete control of her voice. Her acting went from being strict and standoffish to being in Love with Sky and her committment to him was played perfectly. Kevin Hartnett (Sky Masterson) has the most wonderful stage presence. He strolled around each scene, delivering dialogue perfectly with a marvellous specific American accent. His singing has wonderful intonation and clean precise diction. The relationship between Sarah and Sky was played perfectly and their commitment to each other was terrific. Their voices blended marvellously in their duets with each giving marvellous support to the other. Terry Martin (Nathan Detroit) was the busiest man on stage, quick movements, super facial expressions relaying complete panic to the audience as everything he tried to achieve went pear shaped. His accent was precise, his dialogue was delivered quickly and his enunciation was excellent. Katy Nicholas' (Miss Adelaide) portrayal was spot on. Her nasally accent and shrill delivery of her dialogue, when talking to Nathan, was perfect. Her dancing was full of energy, her comedy timing was marvellous, and when she sang she had a most powerful voice perfectly in pitch and always well supported. All of the main players were well assisted by the supporting players. The opening musical trio sung by Chris O'Connor (Nicely Nicely), Kevin Macken (Benny) and Sean Button (Rusty) was wonderfully performed and they got all the rhythms spot on. There was also an excellent cameo performance by Aaron Tierney who played Harry the Horse. Helen McCann (director) managed to get the players dialogue delivered at a nice brisk pace, the sets were constructed and painted very well, the sound technician got all his cues correct, but the lighting plot was a little too repetitive. David (doc) O'Connor was the musical director and he gave a very good conducting beat to the orchestra and both hand and visual direction to the players on stage.

Chess is a musical that requires a large stage area to ensure that full respect is given to the wonderful chorus arrangements in this show. The Mercy School in Tuam has that space. The large open stage stretched across the entire width of the auditorium, wonderful painted chess pieces either side, the American and Russian offices down stage left and right, a marvellously lit chess board front and centre and to finish it off superb video screen shots that ran through the whole production. The musical director John Roe had a very tight and precise orchestra who, with the odd exception, played and accompanied wonderfully. Choreographer Ciara Kavanagh had some intricate dance steps which some of the chorus struggled with, but the corps de ballet who were used in the Chess games, were wonderful.
