A few more props would not have gone amiss either, but the advantage of keeping things minimal was the virtual invisibility of the stage manager and his team. As a further demonstration of dedication, that stage manager also happened to be the Director of the show, David O'Toole, who successfully managed to add some clever and original production touches to this well tried and tested piece of theatre. His use of human mannequins to dress Tony and Maria for their mock wedding in "One Hand, One Heart" was beautifully executed by the performers, and the use of torch starlight for "Tonight" was very effective. The appearance of a Maria double, eerily dressed in funereal garb, during "I Feel Pretty", hinting at the grim consequences of her relationship, was a gamble, but one that worked for me, because the rhythm pulled back almost to slow-motion, and Maria herself looked upon the mirage with a sense of foreboding. This was a nice touch, and rather Shakespearean in concept!

Technically, the show suffered from being back to back with the previous show, in so far as I suspect there was limited time to plot the lighting with much adventure, but at least the performers could always be seen clearly, and the sound quality throughout was good. Similarly, costumes were appropriate and well chosen, with the possible exception of Tony's yellow trousers.

Perhaps a more obvious distinction between the Jets and Sharks at the dance could have been achieved. In the safe hands of Musical Director, Dennis McKeever, an efficient orchestra stuttered only during the dance section of "Somewhere", but recovered quickly. There was a good balance between pit and stage, and the singers were well prepared in their harmonies. With so few boys available, it was a good idea to bolster some of the male numbers with the female chorus.

Linda Wright sensibly played to the strengths of her performers, keeping her routines simple but effective, with occasional displays of excellent talent from those of greater ability. As a result, the choreography was generally tidy and well-executed, with a nice creativity in the dream sequence. Perhaps the choreographed fight sequences could have been a tad more "hands on", but they didn't lack imagination. Bernardo led by example, making the most of his dance opportunities.

In any youth production, however, it is the energy and enthusiasm of the performers themselves that makes magic on the stage, and this group of talented individuals were not found wanting.

The quality of Ryan McNally's voice made him an appropriate choice for the role of Tony, at his best during his beautifully phrased solos and his duets with Maria, and his stature also added to the reality of him once being the gang leader of the Jets. Perhaps the intensity of his acting needs to catch up a little with his singing, but this is a talented young man with very great potential.

Niamh Donnelly, as Maria, was extremely likeable, if a little over-animated on occasions. Vocally, she was generally most effective in putting over the tone and sentiment of her songs, but perhaps needs to strengthen the bridge between her chest voice and her head voice. Her playing of the final scene was particularly impressive.

James Woods gave a lovely natural performance in the role of Riff, cocky and secure and with a good sense of the drama that surrounded him. He also moved well and had good control of his vocals.

Megan Henry displayed a mature and tuneful vocal quality in the role of Anita. Her concern for Maria and her flirtatious relationship with Bernardo were well realised, and her distress at losing her lover was very believable.

Understandably, Jordan Donnelly must have been selected to play Bernardo because of his dancing skills. He moved with ease and assurance, but was also very adept in the vocal department.

Cathal Mercer was a relaxed Action, and gave aggression and comedy to his role, especially to a nicely performed "Officer Krupke".

Michael Morrow was a suitably sulky Chino, who convinced in his scenes with Maria. Unaided by a less-than authentic gun-shot, he still managed to act out the killing of Tony with sensitivity.

Jessica Ashton made a very good impact as Anybody's, a real tomboy with an attitude problem. I'm not sure that she should have been at the dance in the gym dressed as a boy, but that aside, she played the role with conviction.

Nathan Riley as A-rab and Brendan Donnelly as Baby John contributed well to the Jets and to the general action of the gang scenes.

There was good support from Bláthnaid McCaughley as Consuela, Caoimhe Cullen as Rosalia and Ellie McLaughlin as Estella, and indeed the female chorus made a good overall contribution to the show.

Brian Devlin gave maturity and gravitas to the production as the grouchy and unsentimental Schrank, while Brendan Magee was a believable "walked-over" old-timer as Doc. Paul Magee was easily out-witted by the Jets in a splendid performance as Officer Krupke, and Thomas Larkham did all that was required to be the lame host of the dance, in the role of Gladhand.

The Jets and Sharks, though small in number, gave energy to every aspect of their performances, but perhaps the choreography of the fight scenes could have been more physical. Likewise, the various female supporting roles gave much enthusiasm to the action.

All in all, this was a very enjoyable night of entertainment from a delightfully industrious company. I wish you success in the future and thank you kindly for the wonderful hospitality.

show_raw: I Love You, You'Re Perfect, Now Change
review_text:
Just who do Newcastle Glees Musical Society think they are? Most us mere mortals need to spend absolutely thousands on lights, sets, two million costumes, an orchestra, a fancy venue and need a cast of fifty in order to balance the books and put on a great show. Not this crowd. Oh noooo. They had seven performers, three musicians, some cobweb-strewn lights (that turned on or off and nothing else), the odd pair of glasses or a hat to establish their character and a black box. And it was absolutely bloody brilliant. How dare they? Then how was it so good? Because the performers were outstandingly versatile and they were enabled by an endlessly inventive director.

Annesley Hall, situated where the mountains of Mourne sweep down to the sea, is the home of Newcastle Glees Musical Society. Rehearsals and performances take place in this old characterful building and it is even rented out for weddings. Presented through a series of vignettes connected more thematically than narratively, I Love You, You're Perfect, Now Change explores all facets of relationships from first dates to marriage to children. The original production used four actors, performing up to thirty roles. The number of performers can be fluid, however, and this production decided to use six people to play these roles. There was also an addition of a new character called Sign Man: a bonkers, mostly silent, comedian that introduced each vignette. This character enhanced the show entirely, by bringing extra dollops of comedy, but only because he was played by the super Jay Walsh. The other performers had a challenging, yet no doubt rewarding job and one they pulled off with style.

The cast was made up of Emma Nugent, Emma- Jane McKnight, Orla Russell, Gareth McGreevy, Jamie Johnston, Matt Dempster and Jay Walsh, each playing a multitude of roles. There were all equally as fabulous. They played one character after another, transforming themselves entirely with the use of voice and physical characteris ation. Each performer was hilarious and sang brilliantly. Between them and their director, they crafted every scene so that it never became boring or predictable. For example, if a character presented as confident, they would end up as a blubbering mess or if someone seemed bubbly and ridiculous, it turned out it was because they were hiding the pain of something tragic. The same intelligent structure was evident in the singing numbers, that never got stale, because they were always twisting and turning, through the dynamics of the singing and/or the emotional journeys the characters were on.

But the performers didn't do this alone. One of their castmates, a very hard working Gareth McGreevy, also acted as MD for this show. The singing throughout was excellent. Dynamics in the choral numbers enhanced the story telling e.g. the cast sang with an eerie monastic style when they appeared as monks and elsewhere we could hear the trepidation in their voices while they get ready as a group to go on a date. The cast knew their stuff really well, and while the musicians (piano, guitar and violin) were alone in the pit, they seemed comfortable in what they had to do. With only six radio mics in operation, balance throughout the whole show was great. My Fair Lady Rathmines & Rathgar Musical Society National Concert Hall 15/11/2017 to 19/11/2017 The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee The Odd Theatre Company The River Bank Theatre, Newbridge 10/11/2017 to 12/11/2017 9 to 5 Tullyvin Musical Society Tullyvin Community Hall 15/11/2017 to 18/11/2017 The Hired Man Harolds Cross Tallaght MS Civic Theatre, Tallaght 14/11/2017 to 18/11/2017 The Wizard of Oz S.O.N.G.)

An Tain Arts Centre, Dundalk 15/11/2017 to 19/11/2017 All Shook Up Coolmine Musical Society Draiocht, Blanchardstown 14/11/2017 to 18/11/2017 Rock of Ages Portlaoise Musical Society Dunamaise Arts Centre 18/11/2017 to 25/11/2107 A Celebration of Song Naas Musical Society The Moat Theatre, Naas 15/11/2017 to 16/11/2017 And finally, the man who took an okay piece of theatre and turned into something far more entertaining: Director Neil Keery managed to tease so much comedy out of this show. In partnership with Jay Walsh, he managed to have the audience in fits of laughter with the addition of these 'Sign Man' appearances. No doubt, he worked very well with the actors to craft their scenes so that each moment became an unpredictable journey through some facet of love. When the script called for honesty and pathos, the scenes were pitch perfect once again. The effect the director had on this piece was palpable. So despite the fact that Newcastle Glees Musical Society have some cheek to do so much on so little, I think there is a lesson to be learned here: That good story-telling doesn't necessarily need all the bells and whistles than can come with musical theatre. Maybe that's a good way for theatre-makers to measure how their shows are shaping up. Ask yourself, "If I stripped it all back, would it still be good?" It certainly was in Newcastle.

This was my first visit to An Tain Theatre, Dundalk, and was delighted by the intimacy of this lovely theatre, with a proscenium stage that was just perfect for the attractive set of "Me and My Girl". It was also a good size to cater for the large cast of chorus and dancers without ever looking over-crowded. This was also due to intelligent direction and choreography, with the creation of beautiful pictures and exciting dance routines.

Colin Hughes (Director) got the balance of this production just about perfect, giving all the performers an opportunity to display their talents to their best advantage. There was a good focus on characterisation, and good thought put into the comedy routines. The use of the servant staff to move most of the props throughout the show added strongly to the sense of continuity, and with the exception of needing to use the black drapes as a background on occasions, the settings were attractive and well dressed. Only the initial drawing room scene looked a little cramped, and the flow of the action might have benefitted from the furniture pieces being a little more spread out. The set itself was well-constructed and nicely painted, with good raised levels at the back which contributed to the action. Furniture and props, throughout, were very good, and the stage crew, under the management of Niall McCooey, did a very good job, assisted by a well-disciplined chorus of servants.

This was a very nicely costumed show, with good distinction between the different classes, and plenty of vibrant colour. Costumes were well worn, and hair-styles and make-up were always appropriate. With a large chorus on stage, Choreographer, Lea Carroll, wisely kept her patterns and movements simple and effective, but cleverly integrated her more energetic dancers into the action at the appropriate times. She played nicely to the capabilities of her dancers, ensuring that routines were precise and effectively performed. The several routines involving Bill and Sally were particularly clever, well- tailored and enjoyable. "The Sun Has Got His Hat On", "Leaning on a Lamppost" and "Lambeth Walk" were all colourful and full of fun. Very nice work.

Musical Director, Ronan Dennedy, took good control of his orchestra, combining his keyboard accompaniment with conducting, although I might have been inclined to pick the tempi up on occasions. A sprightly bounce would have added pep to "The Sun Has Got His Hat On", and "Take it on the Chin", and the beautifully sung "Once You Lose Your Heart" was just a tad too pulled back. A few distracting errors from the brass section were over-shadowed by some very fine playing from the strings and the reeds. Chorus Mistress, Ann McCabe, got very good results from her full choruses, with good strength and harmony, particularly from the ladies. The "Men of Hareford" seemed to go slightly astray, despite a powerful leading vocal from The Duchess. The opening of the show was balanced and secure, and "An English Gentleman" was vocally very impressive.

"Me and My Girl" needs a dynamic leading actor to carry the story and the comedy, and in this respect, Anthony Fitzpatrick (right) stepped up to the mark, with a relaxed and confident performance as Bill Snibson. His comedic timing was the outstanding feature of a very capable and competent overall performance. While he didn't strike me as a natural dancer, his body language was always excellent, and vocally, he was secure and pitch perfect. Equally enchanting was Orla Sheridan as Sally Smith. This role requires a comedienne who can also sing and dance, and in all disciplines, Orla made a very strong impact. The pace of "Once You Lose Your Heart" needed lifted slightly, but it was still performed with lovely emotion. Tim Ahern gave the role of Sir John Treymayne enough dignity to establish his class, and enough comedy to establish his roguish nature. This was a very fine and well-balanced performance, particularly in not over-doing the drunken scene. Very good work.

It's the relationship between Bill and The Duchess of Deane around which the plot really rotates, and Orlaith Crosbie played the Duchess to perfection, filled with a sense of superiority, and yet, susceptible to human emotion. She was stoic in her resolve, yet gracious in defeat, and when she opened up vocally, her voice soared throughout the auditorium.

Alan Doherty was a tad gentle in tone in the role of Gerald, but he physically and vocally maintained a sense of the ludicrous in his interpretation of an upper-class twit. He had a good grip on his comedy, and a pleasant voice.

Carol McCourt gave a brazen performance as the gold-digger, Lady Jacqueline, full of sass and sensuality, and well-played indignation when she was rejected by Bill. She was also vocally very secure.

Martin Gogarty as Parchester, was highly amusing in his delivery of "The Family Solicitor", and maintained a relaxed and reassuring character throughout the story. Gerry O'Hara was the most active Sir Jasper Tring I've ever seen, spending almost as much time out of his wheelchair as in it. The comedy with the suit of armour was very well played.

Strong support was given by Dominic Keating's hen-pecked Lord Battersby and his domineering wife, played beautifully by Karyn McCooey.

The deadpan attitude of Brian Halpin as Charles made his character believable and very amusing. Nicely played.

Olive Curran gave a sturdy performance as the nosy landlady, Mrs Brown, and Finn Conroy did all that was asked of him as Bob Barking.

James Brennan was an excellent pompous policeman, and the upper crust was well represented by Marie Meehan as Sophia Stainsley-Asherton, Jane Mehigan as Mrs Worthington-Worthington and Aisling McCormack as Lady Brighton.

A very talented group of chorus and dancers did all that was required to provide the perfect background to the action and to help create atmosphere. Lighting for the show was efficient, if more utilitarian than spectacular, but cueing was accurate, and nobody was ever lost in darkness. Sound quality was generally good, with perhaps an occasional boost needed for Gerald and Parchester to lift them above the chorus. There was a good balance between pit and stage.

There are occasions when directors and choreographers over-stretch or under- estimate the abilities of their charges, which can have detrimental consequences on a production, but on this occasion, the balance was just about perfect. Thank you to all concerned for a very enjoyable production of one of my favourite traditional musicals.

It is always heart-warming to see the "older" shows being presented in such a genuine and respectful manner. Hello, Dolly! stands strong after all these years, filled with witty dialogue, excellent comedy and beautiful music, and Pioneers have done it justice, with an intoxicating production that sent the audience home with smiles on their faces and music in their souls. Despite the attempts of Hurricane Ophelia to throw the production off course, depriving them of a technical rehearsal, there were no signs of un-readiness in this performance, and indeed, the technical quality of the show was quite exceptional, from the beautiful and complex set, to a very efficient and effective lighting plot, and generally very balanced sound. Out front, there was a lively and expressive orchestra, and between pit and set appeared a company who revelled in the frivolity of this wonderfully enjoyable show.

From the moment the curtain opened, the vibrancy of the colour schemes had an almost circus-like quality, but the visual display was ever-changing and always appealing. Not only was the set brilliantly constructed, but it was also manoeuvred with super-efficiency by stage manager, Joe Sinclair, and his crew. A vast array of appropriate props had been assembled and were well used throughout the show, even if it would have been nice to see a few more hats and hat-boxes in the Millinery shop, and maybe more bric-a- brac in the Hay and Feed store.

I would have liked to see more activity from the male chorus as customers in Vandergelder's Store, making their entrance into "It Takes A Woman" a bit more natural. Despite it being a wonderful performance, Vandergelder talking directly to the audience detracted from Dolly's monologues a little, and it might have been stronger to see him address his early speech to the male customers. Dolly, I feel, as virtually the narrator of the story, should really be the only character to breach the fourth wall. Regardless of that, Pat McElwain, as Director, got the tone and atmosphere of this show pretty much perfect, putting a strong emphasis on comedy and strength of character. Assisted by an extremely capable line-up, he made the most of every comedic opportunity, developing a great partnership between Cornelius and Barnaby, a sense of the ridiculous about Ermengarde and Ambrose, and delivering a sumptuous feast of laughs during the dining scenes at the Harmonia Gardens Restaurant. His direction made good use of the different levels on the set, and there was no awkwardness in positioning or movement. Coupled with a well organised stage crew, the overall effect was a fluid, well-paced production, uninterrupted by any lengthy scene changes. Similarly, Orla Savage's choreography was extremely well rehearsed and performed meticulously by her dancers. While all the routines were colourful and inventive, I did have a sense that she could have stretched the dances a little more, particularly in the waiters gallop. There was some fine acrobatics, and a marvellous uni-cyclist, in "Before The Parade" and a wonderful solo performance from one of the waiters, (Aisling Rountree, I believe), and the principal line-up also proved to be proficient in the terpsichorean art.

Yvonne McQuillan conducted with authority in front of a well-drilled and highly polished orchestra. Her reed section was particularly impressive. The balance between pit and stage was very good, and there was a beautifully modern, almost laid-back feel, to "Ribbons Down My Back", which was most appealing. Vocally, Yvonne was served well by her cast, making a good impression with their harmonies and their clarity. Principals were all very secure in their vocals. My only suggestion would be that perhaps the polka music in the Harmonia Gardens needed to be introduced under the preceding dialogue. Dolly was commenting on the dexterity of Ambrose even before he had started to dance. What I loved most about Jennifer McGann's performance as Dolly Levi was that she wasn't a fake Barbara Streisand. This was 100% Jennifer McGann, radiant in her portrayal of one of the strongest female leads in any musical. From right down in her boots came an earthy and endearing vocal quality, which soared to powerful levels during "Before the Parade" and "So Long Dearie". Alongside her delicious and delightful comedic delivery, there was a great sincerity in her monologues to her departed husband, making this performance a tour de force. John Furlong proved to be a great partner in performance as Horace Vandergelder, always alert and astute in his physical presentation, with wonderful facial reactions to the madness around him. His voice was appropriate to the role, with "It Takes a Woman" strongly interpreted. Stuart Pollock adopted an excellent character voice to give a sense of nervous energy to Cornelius Hackl, and he sustained it brilliantly throughout the show. This is a young man with strong stage awareness, a great feel for comedy, and a more than average vocal quality. He related brilliantly to Barnaby, and looked very comfortable with Irene, performing "It Only Takes a Moment" with warm sentimentality.

Oisín Nolan was so enjoyable in the role of Barnaby, and the perfect side-kick for Cornelius. Again, timing was what highlighted his comedic ability, and when he started to dance… wow! Filled with rhythm, precision and quirky energy, this was another perfectly portrayed character. The velvety smooth tones of Danielle Williamson made "Ribbons Down My Back" my favourite song of the evening, and in combination with beautiful acting and reacting, she gave quality and vibrancy to the role of Irene Molloy, convincingly mischievous yet believably romantic in her dealings with Cornelius. An exquisite performance.

Karen McCourt was quirky and quaint, giddy and garrulous, competent and confident in her interpretation of Minnie Fay. It was easy to understand why Barnaby was attracted to her, and she balanced beautifully with Irene in their scenes together.

Ríona Keogh deserves a medal for maintaining that irritating cry in the role of Ermengarde. She contrasted her "spoilt brat" whining with a very believable teenager-in-love persona that made her a strong choice for her role. She and Ambrose played very effectively together. Ben Hannigan as Ambrose was delightfully "artistic" in his attitude and delivery, playing the likeable nerd with conviction. With only a handful of lines, Emma Jane Reilly dominated the stage during her two brief appearances as the hilariously inappropriate Ernestina Money.

John Cryan was an authoritative and easily irritated Rudy, and Ian Rountree jumped effortlessly from a sprightly waiter to a greyed and whiskered Judge, adding a nice touch of character to the courtroom scene.

The chorus and dancers performed with zeal and energy, adding fine vocals and plenty of atmosphere to their scenes. Discipline and confidence were very evident.

With Dolly's Golden gown being the visual highlight of the show, costumes were very effective and well selected. The parade costumes were very good, although the majorettes could have been more glamorous, the waiters were tidy and well-presented, and all of the principal costumes looked splendid. The canary yellow of Ernestina was delightfully (and deliberately) tasteless, and very funny. Hair styles were totally appropriate to the era and wigs, make-up and facial hair, very well applied.

Lighting was beautifully atmospheric, skipping discreetly from colourful open settings to delicately lit moments of romance and reflection. Very good use of follow spots. Perhaps some of the solo work in the upstage area could have been more highlighted, but overall, the lighting was delightfully effective. The sound quality was very natural and never over- amplified. Cueing was, with one exception, excellent, and the balance was perfect. The Draiocht Theatre is a warm and comfortable venue, and the Front of House staff were friendly and efficient. Good direction, tidy choreography, fine musicianship and an abundance of talented performers combined to make this a very memorable show. Sincere thanks to the entire company for a thoroughly enjoyable experience.

First of all, congratulations to Director Karl O'Doherty on successfully presenting a show that ran without interruption, or any major disasters, from curtain up to curtain down, in this, his first ever production as a Director. There was much to be commended in the direction of principals in their dialogue and expression, but there was an issue, particularly with the less experienced performers, of them not knowing what to do when they weren't the centre of attention. This comes down to a need to direct their reactions as much as their action. With chorus, also, the more experienced performers had good facial expression, while others occasionally looked uncomfortable in their own skin. Karl wisely opted for a set that was uncomplicated and well tried and tested, which nicely framed the performers, and while there were some issues with lighting, the overall effect was colourful and quite pleasing. All in all, this was a good first outing for a new director, and should encourage him to move forward with a lot of positivity.

With the exception of my failing to understand why the dancers performed the entire opening number (Jail House Rock) with their backs to the audience, Declan Gardiner did a very good job, on a rather small stage, of injecting a strong sense of the Rock'n'Roll era into his choreography. The chorus seemed well rehearsed and generally tidy in their execution of routines, with "Devil in Disguise" being the only number that was disjointed. For the most part, routines were happy-clappy and fun, and contributed well to the overall production.

With a tuneful and very capable small band of 6 musicians, Musical Director, Ita Cunningham, did a fine job of keeping a good pace to the production. Principals seemed to have been well prepared musically, and there was evidence of good harmonies from the chorus, particularly in the bigger numbers. She also never allowed the band to overwhelm the on- stage singing.

The costumes were appropriate and effective, and it was a nice touch to have the peel-off drab skirts to reveal a more colourful set for many of the dancers when the Juke-box came to life. More attention needed to be given to footwear, particularly due to the frequent references to "Blue Suede Shoes". Hair and Make-up were fine throughout.

The set was good in design and was functional and well painted. Props were effective, especially the motorbike, and the staging, under the Management of Oisin O'Heartain, was tidy and efficient. Good work from the crew member who secured the motorbike when it looked like it was about to topple. Lighting was a mixed bag, with some very nice atmospheres created by good use of colour and backlight, but there were issues with the positioning of "specials", or perhaps with principals being unsure where they were positioned, which resulted in some soloists being in half-light, and occasionally in darkness. Sound quality was secure throughout, with good balance and good cueing. Cathal Ryan was a cool, cocky and confident Chad, winning over the audience as the cheesy-sleazy Roustabout. His songs were well performed, and his comedic delivery and facial expressions were extremely funny, especially when he realised his love for Ed.

Hannah McCreanor (above) gave a confident vocal performance in the role of Natalie, was secure in her tomboy characterisation, and made a credible and capable transition to the character of Ed. While she displayed emotions most ably, perhaps she just needed a touch more confidence to relax more into the role. Oisin Parslow delivered his lines effectively, and had the perfect look for the role of Dennis. His comedy could have been more exaggerated, but this is a young man with very good potential for the future.

Caroline Cradock had an appealing appearance, a well capable voice and good expression, but she did need more direction on maintaining the character of Sylvia through her reactions to the business going on around her.

Siofra Ni Chonluain virtually stole the show with a brazen, lusty performance as Miss Sandra. Her comic timing and delivery of punchlines was excellent, and she was vocally robust and always tuneful. A wonderfully strong and confident portrayal of this comedy character.

Karl O'Doherty gave the role of Jim a nice sentimental edge, and was relaxed on the stage. While his singing is not his strongest discipline, he was always tuneful and good in his timing.

An enthusiastic and encouraging performance was given by Laura Ni Cheallaigh in the role of Lorraine. She sang with confidence and achieved the sassy rebellious daughter characterisation. Caelan Smith, in the role of Dean, was a timid as a mouse, though certainly not lacking in ability or potential. With limited experience, he needed to be made more aware of body language and facial expression.

Elizabeth Cleary made a very good effort to characterise Mayor Matilda, with some fine moments of comedy, but she had a tendency to drop her voice to an intimate level, which caused several lines to be lost.

Feargal MacMeanmain was well cast in the role of Sheriff Earl, making the most of his few lines in Act Two, and with plenty of good visual expression during his muted first act. Nicely played.

With the exception of a few chorus players needing to use more facial expression, the chorus functioned very effectively, with good energy and good discipline. The main dancers gave a strong performance and danced with confidence.

I'm happy to report to your Director that he will probably never feel as much pressure as he did on this, his first outing. With every show, the chores become that bit easier, with growing knowledge and the ability to pre-empt problems. The only area that needed a greater directorial input was in regards to "off- focus" acting and reacting. This creates the difference between performing a character completely and just saying lines from a script. If performing AND directing (nothing wrong with that!) make sure you have a directorial assistant to watch out for the things that you might miss by being on-stage. With inexperienced principals, it does no harm to mark the stage with x's, to indicate important positions for lighting cues.

Musical Theatre is a wonderful medium, and is there to be enjoyed so find the fun in what you are doing, and you're well on your way. This was most certainly an efficient start and thank you to an enthusiastic young company for a very enjoyable night.

I headed for Siamsa Tíre in Tralee with great expectations of the LOST production of "West Side Story", mainly because of the wonderful standard of choreography that I had witnessed during their previous production of "Evita". Having enjoyed the work of their choreographer in a show with limited opportunities for dance, I felt sure that Katrina Galvin would relish an opportunity to bring life and energy to this superb Bernstein score, with its wide variety of rhythm and style. Suffice it to say, I did not come away disappointed. Katrina got the balance perfectly right, displaying sensuality and elegance with her females, and raw, acrobatic energy with the boy's routines. She was blessed with a very capable dance ensemble, who made the most of their opportunities to shine, with "Cool", "Dance at the Gym" and "America" being particularly impressive. The "Rumble" was energised and exciting, and while the brilliantly danced Dream scene started with a vague ballet section, it became powerful and more relevant when the atmosphere turned sinister. Choreography throughout was strong, focused and entirely appropriate.

With Musical Director, Anna Connolly on keyboards, and Aidan O'Carroll conducting, there was evidence of strong leadership in the orchestra pit, and the 13 piece orchestra handled the difficult score extremely well. Tempi and rhythms were strong and precise, and the balance between pit and stage was very good. The chorus were well drilled in their vocals, with the "Tonight" Ensemble being especially impressive.

Even if on occasions, the drama could have been more intensely realised, Director, Grainne O'Carroll presented a well-balanced and nicely paced show, which had believable actors who captured the essence of their characters with a relaxed confidence. The taunting of Anita established her intimidation but could have been a tad more physical and threatening, and while I believed in the love between Tony and Maria, they did play their romantic scenes a little too much to the audience rather than to each other. The relationship between Anita and Maria was particularly well established, and there was a strong sense of "belonging" between the members of the two gangs. Again though, during the war council at Doc's store, there could have been an edgier sense of a battle about to erupt. I did feel that perhaps more comedy could have been extracted from the "Officer Krupke" number, despite it being performed with confidence. The final scene of the show was emotionally very strong, but Shrank or Krupke really should have lifted the gun from the street. Stage manager, Des Hurley, and his team did a very good job of manoeuvring the trucked pieces about the stage in an inconspicuous manner. The set for the show was physically well designed with its pull-out bedroom, drug-store and dress shop, even if the general brick background was a bit monotonous. But the stage was well used, with multi-entrances, different levels at the sides, etc.

Doc's store looked very well, and the bedroom and dress shop had appropriate and effective props. The lighting plot was fairly simple but served its purpose in creating smaller pools of light to highlight the action, and in ensuring that nobody was left in darkness. Sound quality was secure throughout the performance. The principal line was effectively led by Eoin Foran, as a confident and likeable Tony, vocally strong, if a tad light on his falsetto, but extremely tuneful and melodic. He also acted convincingly, and was believably in love with Maria.

Sarah Cleary as Maria had a sincere youthful charm and innocence, and a very comfortable easy-listening voice. Maturity will see her upper range develop to another level of power and breath-control, but her performance was delightful.

Clodagh Harrington had a confident and alluring quality in the role of Anita. She showed maturity in her dealings with Maria, and sincere grief at the loss of her lover. Her "A Boy Like That" was a high- point of the show, full of expression and musical quality.

Dylan O'Sullivan was a live-wire as Riff, full of energy and passion, but could have afforded to slow his line delivery a tad. He performed his numbers very well.

Marcus Nolan was a smooth Bernardo, calm but intimidating, always in control of his gang, and very agile on his feet.

Cathal McLoughlin proved to be a composed and effective Chino, initially shy, and suitably bent on revenge when he realises that Maria has been seeing Tony. Kim Harris made a convincing tom-boy in the role of Anybody's, always feisty and confident, and well able for the taunting from the Jets.

Sean Atkinson had good confidence and aggression in the role of Action, and while "Officer Krupke" was a good number, it could have been more polished in its delivery.

Noel King, as Schrank, could have had a harder edge, but his sarcastic delivery still established him as a couldn't-be- bothered kind of cop.

Tim Landers was a convincingly walked- over Doc, and vented his frustration well in his final encounter with Tony.

Mark Moloney as Krupke and Alan McLoughlin as Gladhand did what was required of them, although both could have exaggerated their characters a little more.

The chorus of females were strongly led, both vocally and dramatically, by Caitriona Fitzmaurice as Consuela, Kay Barry as Rosalia, Katrina Galvin as Teresita and Tess Dowling as Francesca.

The boys in the gangs were all convincing and relaxed on stage, with Colm Atkinson as Baby John and Jamie Fitzgerald as A-rab being particularly worthy of note. The show was nicely costumed, with appropriate street clothes, and everyone dapper and well-dressed for the Dance. Hair-styles seemed tidy and appropriate, and make-up looked natural, resulting in an overall visually pleasing production. This youth group is blessed with a dedicated staff and production team, who seem willing to tackle challenging shows, and providing great opportunities for the youth of the area. Thank you for another most enjoyable visit to Tralee and a very engaging show.

There was plenty of fun and frolics aboard the SS.American, as Kilmainham Inchicore set sail with their production of the Cole Porter classic "Anything Goes". Director, Helen McCann, showed wisdom in playing this show in all its traditional glory, allowing the script and the music to take centre stage. For the most part, it was tidy and well-rehearsed, with a confident cast looking at ease on the stage. The set was well devised, with the decks of the ship being concealed by black drapes for the opening bar scene, and a very decent sparkle cloth for the ballroom. The upper deck of the ship could perhaps have been used more often, but when it was employed it was done effectively. There were one or two hesitant entrances, but the general pace of the show was very good. There was good characterisation of the main principals. During the crowd scenes, both on deck and in the ballroom, chorus could possibly have reacted with more certainty, particularly during the "I'm a Sinner" sequence, but they were nicely placed and when required, gave great energy to their musical numbers. A number of essential props and furniture pieces were quite efficiently moved around the stage by a very capable stage crew, under the management of Colum McDaid. Probably due to a limited number of lights on the front lighting bar, much of the stage was rather dimly lit during much of the first act, particularly near the front of the stage, but this did seem to improve as the show went on. There was a good use of colour for changes in mood, and the lighting of the cyc, behind the upper area, was effective and atmospheric. Sound was good, for those who were wearing radio mics, but as mentioned, quite a few solo speaking lines were lost for want of a microphone. Cueing was consistent, and balance was fine.

It's the majesty of Cole Porter's score that keeps this great show a firm favourite on the Musical circuit, for it's hard not to be captivated and nostalgic to the strains of "I Get A Kick out of you", "You're The Top", "Friendship", "It's De-lovely" and of course the title song. That score was given a fine rendition by Musical Director, Graham Walsh and his orchestra. The tone and tempi of the musical numbers was always consistent, and most pleasing. The numbers involving full chorus were very well sung, and while the men probably had the more frequent challenge of singing while moving, they still managed to spit their words out with confidence. Principals were very secure in their music.

Choreographer, Laura Macken-Posavitz, showed wisdom in going for good shapes and patterns, allowing her chorus to be presented to their best advantage. When Reno and the smaller dance groups were given the opportunity, however, they showed that they were well-able for the more adventurous routines. Choreography was tidy and well-rehearsed, with only a few of the men occasionally following a half-beat behind the ensemble.

Katy Nicholas, in the role of Reno, had class, comedy, charisma, vocal vivacity, disciplined dancing, assertive acting, and, in keeping with the alliterative praise, long, long legs! I don't mean to get personal, but I am implying that in every sense, she had the look and the demeanour of a glamorous leading lady. This was a wonderfully rounded performance, from a wonderfully gifted performer.

Adam McGealy gave a sympathetic portrayal of the love-sick, over-worked Billy Crocker, and displayed a good sense of mischief when deciding to follow his dream. He played comfortably beside both Reno and Hope, and his friendship with Moonface worked delightfully. He also has a very pleasant voice.

Freda Quinlan gave warmth to the role of Hope that sometimes gets lost in the blandness of her character. On this occasion, she was a believable ingénue, caught between the true love of her life and the requirements of maintaining family pride and finance. She had a feisty edge that made her very likeable, and a voice that made her delightful to listen to.

Can there be a worse fate than to be an unsuccessful public enemy? Terry Martin, in the character of Moonface Martin, proved that it can also be a lot of fun, playing his role with a strong sense of comedy and very good timing. Perhaps "Be Like The Bluebird" could have been a tad more ridiculous, but this was a very amusing performance.

Aaron Tierney gave a very sedate interpretation of Sir Evelyn Oakleigh, but nevertheless an extremely funny one, relying on a droll humour, where pantomime is often the alternative. I liked it very much, particularly "The Gypsy in Me", which was sublimely silly in its stiffness. In contrast, came a performance of pure pantomime, exaggerated incompetence, delirious drunkenness, and schmaltzy superiority from Frank Foley as Elisha Whitney. It was exactly what the character called for, and created much laughter in the auditorium.

Jackie Carroll was frightfully posh and pretentious as Evangeline Harcourt, contrasting nicely with her daughter, and setting herself up to become the partner of the suddenly affluent Elisha. Very nicely played.

There was a flirty, floozie quality to Sophia Daly's portrayal of the mischievous opportunist, Erma. With an exaggerated accent and swagger, she was the perfect moll to Moonface's gangster. "Buddie Beware" was well-performed.

There was good, competent support offered by Paul Johnston as The Captain, Sean Button as The Purser, Cormac McCarthy as the Minister, Laura Geoghegan as Luke, and particularly Graham Dunne with an uproariously inappropriate, non-pc send-up of the agitated Chinaman, John.

There were many minor roles that were more than capably performed, when they could be heard.

With the exception of one or two ill- fitting male costumes, most of the cast were suitable attired, with the dresses on Hope, Reno and Erma being particularly attractive. The "Blow Gabriel Blow" outfits were most effective, and it was good to see attention being given to hats and head bands. Hairstyles and make up were generally very good.

This was a society with a good age range represented on stage, which immediately suggested a great sense of community spirit, which in turn, transmitted to the audience and heightened their enjoyment. I appreciate the richness of such a palpable team spirit. They enjoyed what they were doing, which made me enjoy what they were doing. Thank you very much for a voyage that caused no sea- sickness, experienced no inclement weather, and was fair-sailing all the way.

'Spellbinding' is the word I would use to describe FACT School of Performing Arts' production of Cats. It was simply magical. The set, the costumes, the make-up, the lighting all contributed to a glorious spectacle. I expected a high standard of aesthetic with this production, but what I did not expect was an army of young performers who sang, danced and acted to a standard worthy of the West End. The entire cast were magnificent, enabled by a top-notch team of industry professionals. For those who cannot follow what is going on in Cats, a show based on the poetry of TS Elliot, you are not alone. Nonetheless, the direction must endeavour to provide as much clarity as possible and thankfully clear story-telling was successfully provided by the director.

Sean Gilligan's production of this show was incredible. He designed a set that used scaffolding, netting and old-school 'WANTED' posters of the Cats to create a world that truly felt as though it belonged to the feline inhabitants. The different platforms created lots of mysterious places for the Cats to hide and a central entrance gave drama to those who appeared through it. A large full moon and star-cloth framed this space, providing a celestial atmosphere. It was evident by the very good lighting, provided by Damo O'Connor, that there was a clear and focused vision shared between director and lighting designer. Lighting was meaningful and enhanced the drama of the score and the action on stage. Two mirror-balls were placed on either side of the stage, creating a glorious effect when lit. Costumes were of the highest quality, with no variation in standards whether a performer was playing a named Cat or not. Blocking, movement, staging, diction, feline movements, entrances, exits and aesthetic were all spot-on.

This aesthetic was enhanced considerably by the expert Hair and Make-Up provided by Ali Murphy and Sinéad Judd. Every face was painted excellently and each wig was as good as the next.

Killian Grumley Traynor was very impressive as Musical Director. He played keyboards, conducted nine musicians and provided excellent support to the performers on stage. The singing was top- notch and the harmonies were as good as any cast recording I have heard. I had goose bumps during the opening number and when the ensemble sang Grizabella into the Heaviside Layer. No doubt, the excellent sound, provided by Vinny Osborne, enabled all of this hard work to be heard so clearly.

Aoibheann Cooke and Emma Gannon provided choreography for this production that begged a belief. It was outstanding and it was executed to perfection by the cast of more than a hundred. A number of people told me that they wanted to jump out of their seats after the dance sequence leading towards the end of Act One. The precision, athleticism and talent of the cast was encouraged and utilised to a standard that was worthy of any professional stage. Sarah Hall as Stage Manager did some job at getting this clowder of cats on and off the stage. Thankfully, she had less to contend with in terms of scene changes with this primarily stand-alone set. Some magic tricks by Mr Mistoffelees were well executed.

All of this expertise would have fallen flat if the performers themselves had not been so fantastic. Anna Bergin's performance as Grizabella ground the show to a halt, as the crowd screamed in appreciation of her rendition of 'Memory'. Cian O' Sullivan embodied his Tom-Cat persona very well as Munkustrap and provided extremely clear narration (something which is very necessary if one is to make sense of this show). Callum Martin displayed all of the suaveness and bravado required to sock-it-to-'em as Rum Tum Tugger. Labhaoise McHugh as Jellylorum, Shona Carroll as Bombalurina and Rachel Galvin as Demeter all sang and acted brilliantly and were always very supportive of their fellow cast members. Colm Lombard had the difficult task of playing a character far more advanced in years than himself, but nonetheless had great presence and gentle authority as Old Deuteronomy. Emma O'Donoghue, as Jennyanydots, knocked her tap routine out of the park in her scene-stealing number. Daniel Sinclair had all the showmanship and trickery necessary to perform the role of the magical Mr Mistoffolees. Nathan Durkin was gentle and loveable as the old theatre-lovie Gus who regaled his tales of a better life in the theatre. Louise Kennedy was stunning as the white balletic cat Victoria. Katie Weir, as Jemima, performed an introductory version of 'Memory' with vocals that were as clear as a bell.

The magic did not stop there, however. It did not matter whether a performer played a named-Cat or not, the standard of performance throughout the entire 100+ ensemble was what truly made this production so spellbinding. There was not a weak-link on stage. Different dance troops slinked on and off in such a seamless manner that one never even noticed who was not there at any given moment. Each performer had perfected their feline characterisations and movements to a hypnotic effect. The execution of the choreography was extremely professional and singing throughout was gorgeous. The pictures created by the cast's excellent spacing were so memorable and the performers moved with military precision. They truly were 'feline, fearless, faithful and true'. This was all thanks, in no small measure, to the excellent production team assembled to provide the highest standard of training to this impressive troop. We were blessed to be in the presence of this 'mystical divinity of unashamed felinity'. It was a triumph.

With the superb music of George Gershwin to relish, Musical Director, Shane Farrell, and a wonderful orchestra, provided a flawless musical accompaniment to a show that was extremely high in musical quality.

With brass and woodwind sections that brilliantly captured the flavour of the era, from overture to finale, the sounds emanating from the pit were top notch. Happily, that musical standard was echoed by the vocalists on stage, with some extremely good choral work, with the Deadrock male chorus being especially noteworthy.

Directors, Enda Burke and Aoife McClafferty, presented a show that was performed with confidence, with good use of the available space, nice stage pictures and placement of choruses, and a cracking pace. There was much wonderful characterisation, particularly amongst the male cast of Deadrock hicks, and a confident and dedicated front line who did all that was asked of them, especially the two leading roles, but I did feel that some of the supporting cast could have had their comedy more emphatically pointed. The mock fight scenes were well orchestrated, as was the mirroring scene between Bobby and Zangler. Indeed, Aoife McClafferty's choreography throughout the show was vibrant and refreshing, and mostly very well executed by her dancers. There were lovely comedy steps for those crazy Deadrock guys, and the Follies girls were full of confidence. Bobby, in particular, exhibited some excellent tap dances, and his duets with Polly were beautifully moved.

Indeed, the only thing that interfered with a fast moving production was the overly-long scene changes, caused by an untidy set with too many cumbersome moving pieces. With a script that frequently references "glamour", the set, unfortunately, didn't live up to expectations. My sympathies lay with the hard-worked stage crew, under Stage Manager John Duggan, who did their absolute best to keep things moving. The best scene, visually, was the interior of the Bar room, with a fine assembly of props and furniture.

Although there were some beautifully romantic atmospheres created, especially for the duet dances, the lighting of the show suffered from not having enough solid surfaces to bounce off. There was a thoughtful use of colours in the design, and generally, the principals played or moved quickly into the highlighted spots and areas. Despite a few late cues, the balance of the sound was good throughout the performance, with some very good sound effects.

The all-singing, all-dancing, all-comedy, frequently romantic role of Bobby Child was played with comfort by a very versatile Alan Greaney. "They Can't Take That Away From Me" was a velvety vocal highlight of the show, but it was his energy in comedy and dance that made him a perfect performer for such a demanding role.

There was a delightful element of Tomboyish-ness to Emer Kelly's early scenes in the role of Polly, which gave way to a well-realised femininity when she fell in love. Her acting and reacting to every situation was achieved with great timing and expression, and her singing was quite beautiful, if a tad gentle on occasions. This was a beautifully balanced role by a very accomplished performer.

With an almost deadpan delivery, Steffen Knauer was very funny in the role of Zangler. His strongest scenes were those with Bobby and Polly, and perhaps his relationship with Tess needed to be more creatively explored for comedic impact. Regardless of this, his performance was most enjoyable.

Suzanne Garvey-Brennan gave a feisty rendition of Irene Roth, confident and controlling, and vamp-ish in her eventual attraction to Lank. She looked and sounded seductive in performing "Naughty Baby".

As Lank, Mike Flaherty showed his potential to handle a major role with confidence, making the character credible and believable. I do think he could have been pushed comfortably to inject more character comedy into the role, with both a more physically bullish appearance, and a more animalistic tone of voice.

Emma Brady transformed from the young thing that she is into a hunched, aged battle-axe of a Mother, in the role of Lottie. This was excellent characterisation, beautifully sustained throughout her performance.

John Mulrooney was a nicely befuddled old character in the role of Polly's father, Everett, consistently docile and nostalgic, and clear in his diction.

While acting, singing and dancing with confidence, I felt that Heather Doyle needed the role of Tess painted with stronger brush-strokes, and a heightened emphasis on comedy. Her relationship with Zangler had so much more comedic potential.

Norman Quinn as Eugene Fodor, and Emma Louise Harte as his companion, Patricia, both trotted onto the stage with confidence, and delightfully English accents, but perhaps needed a bit more comedic business to prevent them from seeming to fade a little into the background.

Martha O'Toole turned in a delightfully ditzy and dizzy performance as Patsy, demonstrating some very adept footwork along the way, and making the most of every opportunity to highlight her sublime simplicity.

Collectively, the townsmen, Cian Forde as Moose, Eoin Mullins as Mingo, Alan Kelly as Sam, Louis Brenna as Pete, Stuart Barrows as Wyatt, Declan Carroll as Custus, Shane McDonagh as Billy and Neal McHugh as Jimmy, played their goofy comedy with aplomb and presented some absolutely beautiful harmonies in their vocals, but they also managed to display strong individuality. This was excellent work.

The Follies girls, confidently led by a radiant and ever smiling Danielle Carroll as Mitzi, performed with energy and zeal throughout the show, and along with the remainder of the chorus, looked and sounded excellent in their big musical numbers.

The finale costumes were beautiful, and the Follies girls were generally very well attired. When the entire female chorus were on stage, the dancer's costumes put the others in the shade a little. Men looked decently costumed at all times. Make-up and hairstyles were appropriate, and the many wigs were generally well-worn. Good work in getting a strong match between Bobby and Zangler.

This was a most enjoyable presentation, and while some of the supporting roles perhaps needed a tad more production, no-one was lacking in energy or the sense of fun that kept the story rattling along at a very good pace.

Setting aside issues with the staging, this presentation scored extremely highly on musicality, and very highly on entertainment value. Thank you to all concerned for a truly enjoyable "Crazy For You".

Managing to put on half a dozen performances of a Musical and playing to "Sold Out" notices every night, it's a great measure of how efficient and successful a group really are. Newcastle West and their production of "Annie" could not have asked for a better acknowledgement of their dedication and their delivery of a highly enjoyable show.

Director, Tom Madigan, went about his task with energy and enthusiasm, not alone directing the show, but also designing and constructing the set, and featuring in the role of Franklin D. Roosevelt. As director, he instilled a confidence in his younger charges, and assured that each individual was secure in their characterisation. There was a good emphasis on comedy, and while some of the sentimental scenes were a tad rushed, the general pace of the production was very good.

There were some issues with technical aspects of the show. The set was possibly a bit too minimalistic, with stand-alone pieces as opposed to full sets, but what was there was efficiently used and was significant enough to suggest the various locations. The stage team, under stage manager Siobhán Hennessy, did a good job of keeping things running without slowing the pace of the production. There was a good selection of appropriate props throughout.

While no-one was ever left in darkness, the lighting tended to be block colours, and could have benefitted from a bit more variety. On a few occasions, some very warm atmospheres were created, but the fairly empty back wall tended to draw the eye with over-illuminated strong colours. With the exception of a couple of late cues, sound quality was very acceptable. Musical Director, Michael Young, managed remarkably well to keep his musicians together, given that they were constantly surrounded by children from the audience. There were some issues with balance in the pit, with the keyboards sometimes over-zealous with their accompaniment, and with no brass or woodwind, the overall sound was a little thin on occasions, but tempi and rhythms were always accurate and appropriate. Chorus Mistress, Susan Browne, did a very good job on drilling the choruses in harmony and diction, and the principals were well prepared vocally. Susan Browne was also the choreographer, and took full advantage of an energetic chorus to give life and excitement to her dance routines. The orphans in particular performed with zeal and enthusiasm, making the most of "Hard Knock Life" and "Never Fully Dressed", even including a smattering of tap. The choruses of servants, Hooverville residents and street folk were well disciplined and put great emotion into their routines.

Aideen Shanahan, as Annie, was a delight both to watch and to listen to, with a tuneful voice and very good expression. She acted her little heart out, making a particularly good impression in her emotional scenes. Her smile lit up the hall. I was unsure what accent Dave Wrenne was aiming at with Oliver Warbucks, but his delivery was good, and he injected a lot of fun into his character. His handling of a couple of forgotten lines was both hilarious and very efficient. "Something Was Missing" was sincere and mellow. Susan Browne (there she is again!) took to the role of Miss Hannigan like a frustrated parent (or possibly an over-worked chorus mistress!) filled with angst and a sense of hopelessness. Despite being a little too softly spoken on occasions, this was a nicely controlled character/comedy performance.

Jamie Herlihy gave a good account of himself as Rooster Hannigan, but I feel more comedy could have been made of his character change to become Ralph Mudge, but he was always secure and clear in his diction.

Molly Giltenane was a deliciously exaggerated character as Lily St Regis, making the most of limited opportunities to shine. Her deliberate over-acting as Shirley Mudge was spot on, adding much good comedy to her scenes. "Easy Street", with Rooster and Miss Hannigan, was a great number.

There was a warm and agreeable motherly quality about Mary Browne in the role of Grace Farrell, always comfortable, happy to be an obedient secretary to Warbucks, and sincere in her dealings with Annie. Her singing was quite delightful.

Liam Cronin, in the relatively minor role of Drake, the butler, managed to virtually steal the show, with a fabulously ridiculous cartoon-esque characterisation. His tone of voice and his body language was consistently hilarious from beginning to end.

Nicky Cotter added great eccentricity to the role of Bert Healy, sounding perfectly like a 1920's radio announcer. His added introduction to the show, (broadcasting from New York, directly to the listeners in CastleMaaaac-hon) was a clever and comical piece of direction.

Tom Madigan led his fellow performers by example, turning in a fine portrayal of Franklin D. Roosevelt, with good delivery and plenty of sentiment.

Robert Crawford was a suitable Mr Bundles, giving all that was required of his cameo role.

There were a host of other cameo servant, Hoverville and political roles, all of which were well handled, including a very nice soloist in "N.Y.C", and of course that lovely little dog, Shadow, who was word perfect in the role of Sandy.

The main orphans performed extremely confidently as a group and with great character as individuals, with Anna Doody as Molly making a particularly good impact.

The adult and orphan choruses gave everything to add to the overall strength of the show.

A few of the orphans were wearing leggings and tops that were out of keeping with the era of the show, and the same was also apparent with chorus costumes in the street scenes. A couple of the men wearing hats indoors seemed out of place, in an otherwise attractive set of servants costumes. Principals, especially the leading ladies were all nicely dressed. Hair and wigs looked well, and there were no problems with make-up.

When it comes to putting on any show, entertainment is of the essence, and there is no doubt whatsoever that Newcastle West provided their audience with a wonderful night of fun and energy. Thank you all so much for a thoroughly entertaining night of musical comedy.

It was with a sense of nostalgia that I entered the Theatre Royal, laden with so many happy memories of the Waterford Festival. It remains one of my favourite venues, and on this occasion, the welcome was warm and friendly.

The greatest story ever told, was told with intense passion and energy by the exceptionally talented South Eastern Theatre Group. Vocal quality was at a premium, acting was strong and always believable, and the ensemble danced with glee and precision, to make this show an absolute triumph.

With "I Don't Know How To Love Him" being the epitome of the sensitivity of Musical Director, David Hayes, his obvious love of this music was evident in the tone, the tempi and the interpretation of entire score. Rock sections were played with energy, while the appreciation of phrasing and in the more poignant moments of passion and drama was exceptional, allowing his singers to make the most of every opportunity. Assuming that he was also the Chorus Master, his handling of the vocals was superb, with secure and precise harmonies, and it was the tenderness of "Everything's Alright", "The Last Supper" and "Could We Start Again Please" that I found profoundly moving. This was excellent work.

The overall standard of the direction was so high, with Director, David Hennessy, putting so much thought and care into this presentation, enveloping his performers in an atmospheric blanket of technical and visual appeal. There was good attention to characterisation, and the dressing and pictures on stage were very impressive. On one or two occasions, the chorus departed a bit too abruptly, where it might have worked better to see them gradually disperse. The hanging of Judas was a huge artistic success, capturing the sense of the action without un-necessarily risking any accidents.

I would have liked to see Jesus contorting with slightly less physicality during his final scenes. Having endured the flogging, (brilliantly realised and superbly acted), I just feel that from then on, his torment turns from the body to the mind, and might have benefitted from a physically quieter contemplation of his fate. The only place where I felt the chorus could have been more effectively employed was as the Jewish community baying for the blood of Jesus. They were vocally aggressive, but a tad less physically threatening in their demeanour.

Raising Jesus on the cross was very well achieved, but I might have chosen to leave him there until curtain, as his release was slightly cumbersome. I'm aware that the suggestion of resurrection was being planted, but I felt that you could possibly have achieved that with a lighting effect and less physical effort.

The very fact, however, that the production gave me so much food for thought, is evidence, in itself, of the great strength of the direction.

Choreographer, Michelle Condon's work on this production was very good, not only in being filled with energy and creativity, but also for having her dancers so confidently prepared for opening night. The dancers were totally absorbed in the rhythms and the music of the show, and every dance sequence was a highlight. With the exception of feeling that there was a tad much physical gyration of Jesus in his latter scenes, there was an absolute powerhouse performance from Rob Vickers (above) in the titular role. He was completely at ease on the stage, a model of serenity at times, and equally passionate in his aggression at the follies of man, but it was the range, including astounding falsetto, and his superb vocal quality that delighted the audience.

Aisling Larkin's rendition of "I Don't Know How To Love Him" was possibly the best I've ever heard it sung, not to mention the similar sensitivity of her other musical numbers. She was a delightful Mary Magdalene, genuine in her acting and visually delightful in her reactions to the story unfolding around her.

Jamie Hennessy proved to be a performer of great stature, in the role of Judas Iscariot, well able to rock out the demanding vocals, and even more impressive in his acting abilities. As the Biblical villain of the piece, it pleased me greatly that humanity urged me to feel so much sympathy for his role.

Jack Fenton as Caiaphas and Ben Nolan as Annas, established their characters strongly and worked extremely well together, their respective voices proving totally appropriate to their roles. They were confidently and competently supported by Cathal Moran, Adam O'Neill and John Power as the other high priests.

Brian Tuohy sang/spoke/raged the vocals of Pontius Pilate with consummate ease, capturing the fear of "Pilates Dream" and the frustration and conflict of his encounters with Jesus. Very nicely interpreted.

There was more than a touch of the "theatrical" about Stephen Cody's King Herod, both in his attire and his delivery of the delightfully tongue-in-cheek "King Herod's Song". His in-your-face aggression at the end of the song was striking.

Excellent support was offered by Padraic Di Fusco as the enthusiastic Simon Zealots and Danny Brockie as the remorseful Peter. Both made a significant vocal contribution to the high standards of the show.

The chorus, in their various guises, were the backbone of this superb body of work, giving their all to their acting, singing and dancing.

A very attractively designed floor, including a sunken cross, served the production very well, and the material and columned abstract set was an effective background to the action. Furniture was minimal, and only essential, well selected props were used throughout the show, making for a comfortable ride for the stage crew, under the management of Brian Collins.

With the exception of the follow spots being a tad jerky in their movement, the standard of the lighting was very good and atmospheric. The candles filling the void created by the risen cross in the final scene were very effective.

Sound was nicely balanced, and given that some of the music is screeched in ear- shattering rock falsetto, volume control was excellent.

The visual presentation of the show was delightful, with the costumes being abstract, interesting and eye-catching, not quite traditional and not ultra-modern. The angelic costumes of the title song were very good, as was the attire of the High Priests and the outlandish attire of Herod. His make-up, and that of the High Priests, was very inventive. There was, perhaps, a touch too much fake blood applied to the body of Jesus before the whipping scene. It was the sensitivity of the musical accompaniment that made this production stand out, but in every department, thank you all for a beautiful and thought provoking night of top class entertainment.

With a strong production team, very capable performers and a lively and well- attired chorus, this was a very entertaining and visually delightful production of a fun-filled show. In the beautiful setting of The Great Hall, Downshire Estate, the audience hardly had time to breath between moments of comedy, the racy musical numbers and the very effective plants that form the backbone of the story. A wonderful set was constructed and painted to give a feeling of depth, which worked most effectively, and provided the perfect backdrop to a show that that was racy, comical and visually delightful, thanks to good realisation of characters, appropriately dingy costumes, and an abundance of energy from the performers. Director, Simon Pyper, presented a show that was as racy as a Formula One championship, and perhaps could have been pulled back just a little, particularly in some of the dialogue, but the director did an excellent job of animating his central characters. The plant was well-voiced and visually appealing, and the available space was very well used, with no serious over- crowding problems.

Technically, the show was well-co- ordinated, with lighting and sound effects all contributing to the overall tidiness of the whole package. While it might have been nice to have a way to cover the front of the open shop with a street cloth, the exterior pieces left and right and the space out front when the shop was rolled further upstage, adequately created the illusion of being outdoors. Props generally were very good, especially the plants, which functioned perfectly. It might have been funny to have some larger, more identifiable body parts of the dentist for feeding to the plant. The stage crew, under Cahal McKervey, were largely invisible, which is usually a sign of good organisation. Lighting was very effective, with good use of area specials, and a lovely blend of colours. The flower- like gobos were a tad distracting on occasions, but there were lovely surreal effects achieved when the plant was in sinister mode.

Matthew Campbell, as Musical Director, held the reins of the orchestra like a jockey determined to win the Gold Cup; such was the gallop from start to finish of the show. At times, the raciness of the score was electrifying and exciting, but I found myself wanting him to pull back a little in the wordier numbers, to allow the diction a little more clarity. That said, the music was of a very high standard, with a very capable orchestra, playing the revised score with great enthusiasm and accuracy. Singers were well prepared, with the three narrators achieving strong and beautiful harmonies, while the breathless principals managed to sound tuneful and secure, with very good diction, considering the speed of some numbers.

Choreographer, Alex McFarlane, managed to present some exciting work, both with the chorus and with comedic principal numbers such as "Mushnik and Son", which was excellent. Chorus involvement was limited enough, but when they were presented, they were tidy and enthusiastic in their movement, maintaining their characters throughout.

Ben McDaid was an extremely likeable nerd in the role of Seymour. He used his facial expressions to convey so much emotion, and his character voice was spot-on, with the one proviso that when he was over-excited, his diction became a tad garbled. Thankfully, this was a rare occurrence. There was a fine musicality to his voice, and he played his comedy with good timing and expression.

Courtney Burns captured the naivety of Audrey beautifully, both in appearance and personality. Her voice was just right for the role, and while her comedic timing was very good, I did feel that she could have been even more exaggerated in her simplicity. Nevertheless, this was a strong and secure performance.

Brian McElroy was a delightfully "Jewish" and comical Mr Mushnik, full of angry frustration and with a good ear for that tricky "Mushnik and Son". He sustained his accent and his character very well throughout the show.

Collectively, Laóise Carney as Chiffon, Lucy McIlwaine as Crystal and Melissa Poland as Ronnette, worked perfectly together as a team, and as individuals, they all had strong and distinctive voices, making the most of their solo lines, and then blending beautifully in their harmonies. While their acting was very acceptable, there were some occasions when they could have more overtly related their facial expressions to the words they were singing. They were, however, a strong and hard-working trio.

Performance of the night was a ridiculously outrageous Sean Harkin in the role of Orin Scrivello, the Dentist. There was a Christian Grey quality to his domination of Audrey, and an almost Trump-like narcissism to his self-adoration. As a comedian, he didn't miss a trick, squeezing every ounce of innuendo and irreverence out of his character. Brilliantly entertaining, with a powerful voice to boot. He was also highly entertaining in the quick change roles of Skip Snip, Mrs Luce and Bernstein.

Niall McLean was a good choice for the voice of Audrey 2, with a clear, expressive and resonant voice.

There was fine support given by James O'Neill as Patrick Martin, Mel Carney as the Customer and Adam Madine as the Radio Presenter, and many note-worthy contributors within the chorus.

The chorus and dancers looked and sounded appropriate, and made a very good contribution to the action and atmosphere of the show.

Sound was spot-on, with good balance between pit and stage and good use of sound effects. Audrey's radio mic was affected by a hug at one stage, but the problem was quickly and efficiently mended.

Chorus costumes were appropriately scruffy and low-key, giving a good sense of the seediness of skid row. Principals were all well-dressed, although I think an opportunity was missed to dress Crystal, Chiffon and Ronnette, (the neutral narrators/commentators of the blood- thirsty action) in something a bit flash or surreal for some of their numbers. There were no issues with hair or make-up. There was a good vibe from the whole company on stage, who obviously enjoyed every aspect of their performance, and that energy and enthusiasm came across the footlights to inspire the audience to relax and enjoy every minute of this most entertaining show. Thank you to all concerned for this mad-cap adventure.

The Tralee Musical Society Youth Company pulled out all the stops to present an "All Shook Up" that was musically delightful, technically secure, danced with energy, and sung and acted with confidence and assurance. With a deliciously funny script to work from, the performers really did stretch themselves to leave the audience rolling with laughter and singing along with the familiar music of Elvis. Oliver Hurley was blessed to have such a competent and capable cast of young performers at his disposal, when pulling together this production. The emphasis on the comedy of the book was well realised, although some lines were a little rushed, and on occasions, principals needed to give a little more time for audience reaction. One or two very funny lines were almost missed under the sound of laughter and applause. The visual presentation of the show was very good indeed, with entrances and exits having a natural flow, and there were rarely moments when the stage looked over-crowded.

A slick and energetic "Jail House Rock" opening to the show suggested that the Choreography would be fun, clean and tidy, and very well executed, and indeed, this proved to be the case. When the chorus and dancers weren't performing routines, they were well moved and positioned, so that the pictures on stage were effective and ever-changing.

Choral Director, Laura Crowley, did a wonderful job of creating a full and harmonious sound, particularly in "Falling in Love With You", "Heartbreak Hotel" and "Come on Everybody". Principals were mostly strong, secure and well-rehearsed in their vocals.

Dylan O'Sullivan was a cocky and confident Chad, who had all the moves of Elvis, and loads of charisma. He does have a tendency to rush his lines a little, but his diction was good, and his sense of comedy was excellent. "I Don't Want To" was hilarious, and possibly the best delivered song in the show.

Katie-Anne Harris was a gem of a performer, gorgeous and girly in the role of Natalie, and transforming with tomboy perfection to the person of Ed. With her comedic timing very sharp and her vocals delightful, she was well able for this demanding role.

Discipline was the quality that defined the performance of Barry Sugrue in the role of Dennis. This easy to overplay comedic role was finely judged and hilariously interpreted by a young man who has matured beyond belief over the four or five shows in which I have previously seen him. His timing and delivery were excellent. Sean McElligott, for all his youth, played the role of Jim with great maturity and sensitivity. He was a very believable father, mourning widower, and reluctant lover. His comedy was strong and his singing effortless.

Alongside him, Amy Roche was a no- nonsense mother-figure, capturing the essence of over-worked, under- appreciated hostess of the Diner. Her comedy was good, but she did have a tendency to rush the delivery of some of her punch lines. Vocally, she was a tad pitchy at the start of "Can't Help Falling", but her delivery of "There's Always Me" was warm and sincere.

Playing a highly sensual role in a youth production is never an easy task, but Aoife O'Mahony carried it off tastefully in her portrayal of Miss Sandra. Her disdain at the machismo of Chad was as comical and believable as her misguided affection for Ed, and she performed her numbers with raw passion.

Jamie Fitzgerald was a believably naïve and vulnerable Dean, transforming with confidence into the rebellious son, under the influence of the feisty Lorraine, delightfully portrayed by Dion Bauschlicher. This was a very nice pairing, with both characters capturing the essence of frustrated, parent-dominated teenagers. Both were also very vocally sound.

Kimberly Harris obviously enjoyed playing Mayor Matilda, wallowing in bitterness with which she controlled the lives of the townsfolk. Her stature and body-language were excellent, and her timing was very good. "Devil in Disguise" is tough song to stage effectively, but her delivery of the number was very secure.
