When he eventually got to speak, Cathal McLoughlin, as Sheriff Earl, got the desired reaction from the audience as he verbally rounded on the stubborn Matilda, but I did think that during his silence of Act One, his facial and body language could have been more comically exaggerated to emphasise his obvious frustration at being constantly silenced.

The chorus and dancers, throughout the show, gave an abundance of enthusiasm and atmosphere to all their scenes, which was complemented by their fine vocal quality and the energy of their dancing. Stage Manager, Des Hurley, had a disciplined team to ensure that the movement of props and set-pieces was efficient and unobtrusive. The stage itself was beautifully surrounded by a rough slatted wood effect that conjured up the sense of wooden town buildings and also the slats of the fairground rides. It was also a great surface for lighting effects. The set looked at its best during the very well projected fairground scenes, while the first act, with some very accurate projections, occasionally looked a tad sparse. Projections were used with great expertise, and combined skilfully with lighting effects to create beautiful atmospheres. Follow spots were tidy in their execution, but could have been used more often, to eliminate those few occasions when the projection/ lighting combination left a few principals in half-light. Sound quality was very good throughout, keeping the musical accompaniment at a perfect level to allow the on-stage voices to be heard to their best advantage.

The selection of costumes created a vibrant and colourful display, all appropriate to the era. Dancers were very well presented to give variety to several numbers, and the angel chorus behind "If I Can Dream" was beautifully attired. Hairdo's and make-up were similarly in keeping with the style and era of the show. The future on Musical Theatre in Tralee is in safe hands, judging from the standard of this youth production and an abundance of young talent. Thank you for another wonderful night of comedy, song and dance in Siamsa Tíre.

t can be difficult for an old codger like me to find his way around UCD, but once I found the Astra Hall I was very pleased to be whisked back to the post-war optimism of She Loves Me, staged with competence by the versatile UCD Musical Society. There have been many adaptions of the original Miklós László play, Parfumerie, including the 1998 Tom Hanks-Meg Ryan movie You've Got Mail. She Loves Me is a musical adaption and tells the story of shop workers Amalia and Georg who constantly clash at work, unaware that each one is the other's secret pen-pal, having made contact through a lonely- hearts column. By the end of Act One, it looks like these two are not going to get together, but after the usual Act Two of comedic fillers, often provided by the supporting cast, Amalia and Georg fin… wait, I won't ruin the ending.

The Astra Hall is not a purpose-built theatre and has limitations in terms of staging. For example, there are no wings so the actors enter/exit through the corridors along the teared seating. Nonetheless, director Jack Carolan provided us with an assured production with nice staging in a well-used space. There was some lovely decorative wall-paper on the back wall and efforts were made to add design to the floor. There were three excellently dressed glass counter-tops with corresponding stools, and a raised space on stage right that made an office look like a different room without the use of a wall. Additional furniture pieces were brought on and off to signify other spaces and this was done with a minimalistic quality, yet never felt scant. Most importantly, the staging of the performances was very good.

Musical Director, Ben Duffy, did a fine job at conducting an impressive thirteen musicians, all made up of college students - something which is to be highly commended. The band were positioned on the stage-left side of the room, meaning Ben was not always available if something went wrong on stage. This only happened once, however, and it was clear that the cast were well rehearsed for what they had to deliver musically.

There are slightly less choral numbers in She Loves Me than what I am used to seeing, so this show might not appeal to some societies. Nonetheless, the chorus of UCD Musical Society's chorus did a very good job when they were on. When they appeared as frenzied shoppers on Christmas Eve, they presented as manic and all over the place, yet each performer hit their marks when necessary, suggesting that the madness was actually well-rehearsed. This meant that Assistant Director Louise O'Connor's job as choreographer was not as full-on as normal. Nonetheless when the chorus moved, they did so with an intention that enhanced the story-telling.

Rory Sheehy gave an impressive performance as Georg Nowack, embodying his different relationships; whether he was foe, subordinate, friend or lover. His singing was very good, his accent spot on, and he had all the likeability necessary for this role. His stand-out moment came with the number 'Tonight at Eight' in which he frantically psyches himself up to finally meet his pen- friend. It is a manic number which requires intense concentration, energy and delivery and Rory pulled this off with style. It is no wonder his character collapses to the floor in the end.

Kate Lally performed the part of Amalia Balash beautifully. She has the voice of an angel and reminded me of Eliza Doolittle when she turns posh. Her performance of 'Ice-Cream' balanced impressive vocals with comedy.

Ilona Ritter was played by the hilarious Lauren McMahon and was the perfect foil to Amalia. I wanted this character to have her own spin-off show. It is a fab part and it was played excellently by Lauren, who is more than capable of belting those high notes.

Her partner in crime, Ladislav Sipos was played by Malachy Conlan who had the comedic prowess of Jim Carrey, taking some of his line-delivery beyond a sense of realism. He was the village idiot and played this role with commitment and conviction, providing plenty of laughs along the way.

In contrast to Malachy's heightened characterisation, Marco McVey as shop- owner Mr Maraczek gave us a portrayal that was low-mood, sometimes dark and very much grounded in the realism one might find in a play or a more serious musical.

Eoghan Walsh was adorable as Arpad Laszlo. His character's likeability ensured that we were rooting for him when he got his promotion. I look forward to seeing this talented actor in another role.

The character of Steven Kodaly is a baddie of sorts in so far as it appears he has more than more lady on the go. The sleaze and arrogance of the character was captured very well by Gavin Maloney, yet he still had enough likeability to be convincing as a heart-breaker.

Michael Tuohy's turn as the waiter in the restaurant was also a show highlight as he delivered his song with comedic effect. Costumes, Hair and Make-up and Props were untaken with aplomb by Aoife Barron and Rachel Murphy. Costumes were indicative of the era and were of high quality. There were numerous costume changes during a montage moment of time passing, but this was done cleverly so that an odd change to a costume provided enough to signify the passing of time. Hair and Make-Up was appropriately simplistic and lovely. Props were plentiful and to a high standard.

Stage Management by Laura Osbourne and Darragh McArdle was not too manic on the evening with most of the story taking place in the shop. Some stand- alone furniture was taken on and off with apparent ease to signify different places. These pieces were minimalistic but had enough detail to avoid feeling scant. Sound was good throughout.

Lighting designed by Camille Lombard did well at punctuating certain significant moments.

What struck me most about this show, first staged in 1963, was how very little has changed when it comes to affairs of the heart. Change letter writing to Tinder and this love-story is bang up to date. I applaud UCD Musical Society's decision to choose an old-school musical for the first show of the season. The choice contrasts excellently with their upcoming production of Spring Awakening. What a rich experience it must be to be a member of this society.

The group was set up by Seán McCarthy from Fermoy. He owns Take 2 Promotions and has a number of Irish dancing and music shows around the world. He wanted to set up a new show involving singing and dance, combining all of the best elements of other successful Irish shows.

He put out  advert online looking for four male singers, we applied and got the part. The group is made up of ten Irish dancers and four singer's; myself (Sean Kenny), Gavin Ryan, Conor McQuaid (all from Dunboyne) and Aaron Doyle from Monasterevin.

Having done musicals and pantos on the AIMS circuit for the past few years, it was really exciting to get to experience something completely different like this, and to get to travel abroad while doing it. We perform classic Irish songs, and some with a new pop twist. We were lucky enough to get to record an album with Sony music Germany in October, which was released just before Christmas. There are three songs on the album that are covers of a German group called Modern talking, a German pop duo whose lead singer Dieter Bohlen produced our album. He's the head judge on Das Supertalent, so that's where the idea came from to sing 9 Arches Musical Society, Claregalway JOSEPH AND HIS AMAZING TECHNICOLOR DREAMCOAT With Jay Molyneux taking on his first ever show as Director and Choreographer, Joseph proved to be the perfect vehicle to display his considerable talent. This was a real feel-good production with a cast of thousands… well, dozens anyway. Everyone on the stage seemed to be thoroughly enjoying themselves, his songs as Gaeilge.

Between producing an album and getting to perform for seven million people in the final of Das Supertalent, its been a pretty incredible few months. The album landed at number one on the German country charts, which is insane.

We are heading off on an 18 city tour of Germany now for the next four weeks, so we're all really looking forward to that. You can keep up to date on our upcoming shows and tours on Facebook: www.facebook.com/dulamanceltic/ Instagram: www.instagram.com/dulamanshow/ Website: www.dulamanshow.ie/ from the moment the show started to the end of the longest finale I have ever watched. It's a short enough show, so nobody minded a mash-up of all the songs, energetically danced while the company took their well-deserved bows. Jay certainly injected variety into his choreography, obviously enjoying the various styles that the musically score offers. An uncredited solo female dancer performed a very memorable tango with the brothers during "Those Caanan Days", and the dancers generally showed style and stamina throughout a show that rarely stopped moving. The Hoedown routine in the middle of "One More Angel in Heaven" was particularly impressive, and when the action moved to Egypt, there were quirky routines, performed with gestures and body shapes synonymous with the region. If anything, I'd have been inclined to cut back a tad on the busyness of some routines, such as Pharaoh's Song, where Pharaoh himself lost an amount of the lime-light amid the constant changing patterns of so many dance groups.

From a direction point of view, there were moments of awkwardness for some of the principals getting about the stage, due to the number of bodies to be negotiated, a moveable set of steps centre stage from the high level would have worked very well, as the side steps were constantly busy. The show ran at a very good pace and my only question mark was over the direction of the Narrator. While the rest of the show had very much an exaggerated comic book feel to it, one might have expected a funky, zany, hip narrator, rather than the gentle story-time teacher type that was adopted for this role.

The narrator is a demanding role, (often split and shared between a few performers) so fair play to Anne O'Donnell, who rarely left the stage, for her energy and commitment. She wasn't assisted by the strength of the orchestra early on, but she persisted and when the balance was right, she displayed a most pleasing and musical voice.

Despite reservations about his first costume, Conor Walsh gave a confident and endearing performance in the role of Joseph. He played the arrogant brother with great believability, and displayed a very good sense of comedy as his character grew in stature. His singing throughout was very good indeed. He also related well to the chorus of children. Michael Cooney made a good job of both Jacob and Potiphar, suitably miserable and heart-broken in the former, and flash and arrogant in the latter, although a bigger contrast between the two would have been aided by a better costume for Jacob. Michael generally sings well, but he does, still, have a tendency to mutter the final word or two of his sentences. David Alexander was a strong and convincing Reuben, really making the most of his opportunities to make an impact. "One More Angel in Heaven" was strongly led, and he established himself as the senior of the brothers.

Anthony Hughes gave a most affecting vibrato to "Those Canaan Days" in the role of Simeon, adding significantly to the French feel of the number. This was another highly notable performance. Likewise, there was a well-realised caricature from Mervyn Fahy in the role of Judah, demonstrating both good musicality and a fine sense of comedy in delivering the "Benjamin Calypso".

Dave Langan threw himself into the role of Pharaoh with a relaxed and confident nonchalance, and despite not putting a foot, or a note, wrong, his very amusing Elvis impression was almost swallowed up by an over-active stage.

Katie Bebbington was an effective, lust- filled, Mrs Potiphar, and there were good cameo performances from Alana Power as the Butler and Roisin Fowley as the Baker. The Brothers, as a collective, performed confidently together, and many displayed good individual characteristics. Michael Healy was a cute and quirky Benjamin during the Calypso.

The various chorus groups did all that was asked of them with bucket loads of enthusiasm. The children's chorus made a very worthy contribution to the show. With the orchestra under the stage, Musical Director, Shane Farrell had no problems at all in keeping stage and pit well co-ordinated, but the need for orchestra amplification led to sections of the accompaniment being somewhat over-powering, particularly over solo voices. The music was very well played, and by and large, well-sung. Both the male chorus and the children's chorus tended to be delivered more with enthusiasm than control, but they were impressive. The full company numbers were very nicely sung. The set was a good abstract backdrop, a raised back level with steps down either side, and a few free standing pieces. It was simple and quite effective, leaving the main stage free for the large routines, and the moving pieces caused no problems for Stage Manager, Chontelle Kenny and her team. Occasionally, when principals made entrances on the upper level, their flourish would have been stronger had there been a centre stage set of steps, rather than having to weave through the bodies on the side steps. Lighting throughout the show was good, and the operator displayed great industry in quickly highlighting principals who strayed outside designated specials. When a better balance between stage and orchestra was established, the sound quality was good, and cueing throughout was on point.

The costumes generally made a very strong impact, being trendy variations on the traditional styles, with Chorus and Dancer costumes being excellent throughout, vivid, colourful and nicely selected. There were, though, a few individual outfits that jarred in comparison to those around them. The narrator's opening costume was a bit bland and motherly, I didn't like Joseph's shorts and t-shirt, (not at all flattering), and I felt that Jacob was just a touch too casually dressed. Make up, hair and an abundance of wigs, were generally very good, and all- in-all the visual presentation of the show was most pleasing.

This was a well selected show from 9 Arches, and they are to be applauded for having the courage and vision to give Jay his first outing as a director. He certainly didn't let them down. Thank you to the cast, crew and committee for a delightfully enjoyable presentation of Joseph. .

'I like nonsense. It wakes up the brain cells. Fantasy is a necessary ingredient in living.' (Dr Seuss.) Perhaps we need to remember this quote before we dismiss Seussical the Musical as a frivolous blend of crazy narratives. But as Dr Seuss also said, 'Being Crazy isn't enough'. This is an overly-ambitious tale, where the writers seemed to shoe-horn all the thinks they could think into a story that borders on the slightly bonkers. That said, if clarity of story-telling is ensured, the show can be a success. Thankfully, Director Ian Milford, gave us a solid version of this work. Within a colourful aesthetic, that was inspired by the original illustrations of the Dr Seuss books, each character and their purpose were clearly introduced with helpful clarity. As the crowd filled in, the set was neither revealed to the audience nor simply hidden behind a curtain. Rather, there was enough on stage to create a lovely happy medium, without spoiling the reveal of the set: A mysterious tall, red and white striped hat sat downstage, tastefully lit and perfectly framed with rich red curtains and a blue backdrop. A puff of smoke and a blackout later and the young Jojo, played with great ability by Daire Downey, had appeared and was now staring at the hat which floated in mid-air. A second magic trick conjured the iconic Cat in the Hat, who prompted the boy towards a giant set of Dr Seuss books, each clearly showing an array of famous titles. This manifested a stream of thinks from Jojo's imagination, as one colourful character after another was introduced and the unusual story unfolded before our eyes.

There was a number of well-actualised gags: Horton the Elephant, played with some lovely moments of honesty and control by Ruairí McAlinden, cleaned himself with a fly swat in a tiny blow-up pool. The Cat in the Hat, played with competence and presence by Anthony Fitzpatrick, entered hilariously at one point on a piano-scooter. He also wore a muscle-suit to play an amorous pool- boy called José and he did a skit where he spoke in a Louis Armstrong voice. The final sequence leading into the interval, where the Cat in the Hat signals the passing of time by giving visuals to the various seasons, was very good: a water pistol was squirted for rain, leaves were comically tossed from a bucket to show autumn and Horton spoke with a blocked nose to signify winter. The Cat in the Hat appeared at the top of Act Two and mimed the various instruments along with the entr'acte with vim. This character was also equipped with a whip and trampoline, while he enacted the role of Ringmaster in the circus in which the kidnapped Horton has been forced to perform as an Elephant-clown.

Claire Costello, as Mayzie LaBird, was the perfect princess who exuded glamour. While she had lovely presence, she was at her best when she really sold the meaning of the lyrics she was singing. Jacqui Matthews, as Mrs Mayor, showed great vocal and physical comedy. She was perfectly partnered with a characterful Mr Mayor, played by Dennis Walsh. Through the power of his mighty imagination, Jojo had conjured a Mayor with a Northern Irish dialect in a cast that otherwise used American accents. But hey, anything's possible, right? Nonetheless, they were both very strong in their scenes.

Kyle Emerson played General Genghis Khan Schmitz. He had a perfectly deep, gravelly timbre to his voice for this role. I think he might have chewed up the scenery and thrown his weight around a little more, to intimidate his underlings. Maille Connolly, as The Sour Kangaroo, was full of sass and has an impressive set of pipes. She was equally matched by a brilliant Baby Kangaroo, played with style by Ellie Reynolds. Both kangaroos owned the stage every time they appeared, and they rocked it at the end of 'Biggest Blame Fool'.

Ronan Sharkey had a super speaking voice and line-delivery as The Grinch. He might have explored more ways to bring additional physicality to his characterisation, by bending into spooky poses or giving us more from those creepy green fingers.

A highlight for me was the performance of Emma Kelly as Gertrude McFuzz. She was adorable, sincere, honest and believable in her portrayal of a bird who becomes addicted to getting feather implants. She never wasted a single line, putting meaning and variety into everything she said. She sang very nicely too, while never breaking her ditzy character.

Given that Choreographer Lynn Gourley devised some slightly static, stand-on-the- spot-and-move-the-arms choreography, more synergy was required between direction and dance. Acting needed to be layered onto the singing to sell the meaning of the numbers. Execution, at times, was a little lacklustre, meaning that some of the numbers didn't bounce off the stage the way the music might suggest they should. Also, the animalistic nature of the entire chorus could have been explored to the same impressive degree that it was for the wonderful Wickersham brothers, played by Chrissy Corry, Adam Cooper and Ethan Haddock. Thankfully the simple movements for The Bird Girls', played by Niamh Walsh, Catherine McLoughlin and Anna-Maria Boyle, were executed with competence and in a hypnotic way that suggested the other-worldliness of a Greek chorus.

Musical Director, Dennis McKeever, kept the nine musicians very steady in the pit and was nicely low key in his conducting, supporting with subtlety that avoided massive gestures. An odd nod was all that was required, when necessary, suggesting that the cast must have been well-prepared for their singing. The beautiful 'Solla Sollew' number was sung very nicely by the company. 'The People Versus Horton the Elephant' has some very tricky timing aspects and, thankfully, appeared well-rehearsed.

The band were kept at a nice level by sound engineers Enda and Barry McCusker, never over-powering what was happening on stage. There were some children with additional needs there, so it was really nice to see an MD and a band who did not feel the need to blast the auditorium out of it. The opening number, for example, requires a lot of concentration to bring in all the various named parts. Thankfully, sound cues were on point, which is impressive for a show that has so many principal roles.

Visuals were gorgeous: The houses of Whoville that were flown in, the bathtub truck for Jojo, the jungle images on the flats, and Mayzie LaBird's impressive nest. A screen was lowered to show a video of fish swimming, better realised in this venue that it could have been anywhere else, I'd imagine. Lighting designed by Rodney Ellis, punctuated the special moments throughout giving atmosphere and, for the most part, clarity with the use of spotlights. A beautiful star effect was created with a mirror ball.

Props provided an excellent infant Elephant-Bird and an old-fashioned perambulator with cracked egg covered in foliage. Hair and make-up was very good throughout, most notably with the Cat in the Hat, the Wickersham Brothers and the Grinch. Mrs Mayor had a yellow wig that finished off her colour scheme perfectly and was great at establishing her as less traditional-human and more Who-like. Costumes, mainly from the company's own stock and managed by Chairperson Rosemary Kelly, were very good overall. Most characters were personifications of animals, presented primarily in human form, with simply a suggestion of animalistic quality. The Sour Kangaroo, for example, had a pocket in her dress that reminded us of this animal's pouch. Similarly, Mayzie LaBird looked like a showgirl, her feathers hinting that she was a bird. Unfortunately, I felt that Horton's more literal elephant ears pushed the animal imagery too far in comparison to the stylings of the other creatures. I think that those interpretations where Horton wears something like a hunter's hat, with furry ear muffs, is in better keeping with the overall vision. From the neck down, Horton looked fantastic. He wore a checked shirt and dungarees which worked well as elephant skin. The Cat in the Hat was perfect, with a Christmas decoration dickie-bow. The Grinch costume was awesome, and he wore lights on his head, symbolising his change of heart about Christmas. The Whos looked great in various yellow, white and blue costumes - all individual yet pulled together with the same colour palette. The costumes in the Circus McGurkus had such variety; there was a drummer, a muscle man, cheerleaders with their pompoms, gymnasts, a popcorn-seller, a tap dancer and many more.

Someone had a very good think when they decided to stage a musical in the IMC Movie Studios cinema of Banbridge! The venue was so comfortable and there wasn't a dodgy seat to be had. The stage had good width and depth, and set pieces could be flown in with ease - something that many societies cannot do on purpose-built stages. Stage Management was provided by Andy McKnight. Leaving the scene changes to the flies and to the conjuring Cat in the Hat, meant we never saw any 'humans' come on the stage (bar some kilted hunters) so the otherworldly illusion was nicely maintained.

The final verdict? Banbridge Musical society presented a beautiful and well- rehearsed version of Seussical the Musical with a very good front line of named parts, most notably Ruairí McAlinden, Anthony Fitzpatrick and Emma Kelly. The costumes, props and stunning pieces of scenery were fabulous overall. The chorus' contributions needed to go back into the oven for a few more minutes to ensure there was enough inventiveness, energy and acting in the ensemble moments. This recipe will be perfected for their upcoming production of Evita, I have no doubt.r

With Róisín Heenan at the helm as Auditor and Barry O'Donoghue as Producer (assisted by Laura Hinchliffe), UCD Musical society gave us their second production of the year, Spring Awakening. A tale about coming of age, cruelty and love, written for adults only.

A synergistic display of direction and choreography by Oisín Nolan provided a clear and focused vision, which left no amount of inventive stones unturned. The cast writhed around in frustration, lust and self-exploration; circling like tribespeople, connecting and disconnecting.

They smacked the floor and raised their arms in literal and symbolic movements that gave a pulse to the story-telling. Their positioning, whether in the church pews that framed the stage or as a Greek chorus consummating a relationship, whether back to back, face on, in or out of naturalism all meant something symbolic. Also, the chair dance in 'The Bitch of Living' needed to be seen to be believed. The set was symbolic in its dangerous green lighting that said "go!" to the metaphorical arcs and garlands of flowers in bloom, fertile and in their prime, like the principal characters of the show. An ominous, yet beautiful stained-glass window stood centre-stage, reminding us of all the beauty and understanding religion and education can bring, and perhaps some distorted views that might have been present in these institutions. The furniture hung on the stage, enabling the cast members to create spaces stylistically and with intention.

The costumes clad the younger girls in simple floral dresses, the young men in schoolboy outfits and short trousers, all coming of age but not quite there yet, all innocent but in danger.

Lighting was dynamic, bathing the space in atmosphere and emotion. An orange filled doorway was the gate way to the afterlife, not so much heaven not so much hell. A white oblong light on the ground was all that was needed to create a grave as the peaceful souls of the dead appeared to show up the frantic despair of the living.

Eight musicians, all conducted with clarity by MD, Barry Power, who never allowed the band to drown out the action on stage and who prepared his cast so well they didn't even need to see him. There will be no individual praise given for singing in this show as it was all excellent. Perhaps this is because the casts' well-nurtured talents were combined with a competent MD and a vocal director, Taylor Fewer, to enable finely tuned singing.

The cast were extraordinary.

Rory Sheehy was an awkward, tortured, lost soul who became so desperately overwhelmed by a sexual world he could not process or comprehend, unsupported by a father and teachers who could show him no empathy.

As the devastatingly handsome Melchior, Ruairí Nicholl was brave against authority, loyal towards his friends and honourable towards a girl who did not understand the world of the physical as he did. By the end he had sweated his soul onto the stage, thus was the emotional heights he managed to achieve.

We fell in love with Lisa Lyons as Wendla for her vulnerable yet powerful singing voice, her innocence, her poor judgement from an ignorance that she tried to escape and her unfair demise.

Cian Gallagher brought all the dry-wit and droll cynicism to the part of Hanschen, skilfully raising a laugh by his mere presence. He handled an over 18s act of self-exploration very well also. Together with his lover Ernst, played by Eoghan Walsh, they added exponentially to all of the ensemble pieces and Eoghan beautifully caught the wonderful nativity of being unlawfully in love.

These men were equally matched by Caoilfhionn Ní Dhulaing as Ilse and Leah Meagher as Martha, who brought beautiful introspection to their well- measured performances of equally lost girls, desperately trying the salve the horrors of their lives and the lives of their friends.

Supporting principals made up Meadhbh Flynn (as Thea), Niamh McGowan (as Anna), Aaron Clarke Maher (as Georg) and James Robertson (as Otto) were omni-present in their commitment to the success of the show. Their moves, their vocals, their intentions as they brought power, frustration, softness, despair and strength to an accomplished piece of work were super.

Aoife Barron as Frau Bergmann brought comedy in her initial scenes as Wendla's mother when she tragically dodges her daughter's request to learn about the birds and the bees. She brought the drama in equal measure when the consequence of this naivety was learned.

Frau Gabor, played by Adele Crilly, was elegant and charitable and three dimensional, bringing balance to an otherwise grotesque group of adult characters. Rory Geary had all the frustration and lack of empathy required as the stern and impatient school teacher, Herr Sonnenstitch. Richard Marek had the most beautiful speaking voice and brought composure and hardness to the part of Moritz's merciless father. Fraulein Grossenbustenhalter (Dickensian in its literalness) gave a no holds barred performance as the fantasy piano teacher. Caoimhe Bermingham and Malachy Conlon as Fraulein Knuppeldick and Herr Knochenbruch created surrealist baddie- style caricatures as the plotting teachers at the school.

Morgan Moore, Ruth Richardson, Robert Stubbs, Louise O' Connor, Tadhg Maloney and Áine Collier made up the rest of the ensemble. Their contribution cannot be underestimated as there was not a weak- link amongst them.

This production of Spring Awakening was the show that kept on giving in terms of inventiveness, talent and intelligence. It was emotional, visceral, tender and powerful, all wrapped up in a clever aesthetic. Oh and watch out world, there's a new up-and-coming director in town. I am very happy to say that, in terms of theatrical accomplishments, UCD Musical Society are most certainly not, as the song goes, "totally f%@ked".

9 to 5 can be a nightmare of a show for a technical team, with so many scene changes and various locations, but possibly the advantage of working on a small stage benefitted this production through the necessity of having to play much of the show in a neutral space. This simplification worked, and was a wise move on the part of Director, Chris Currid. There were sufficient props, well- selected, to give the sense of a busy office environment, and hats off to the stage team, under Gerry McCann, for their "no fuss" approach to the scene changes. Tidier art work would have enhanced the settings even more.

Lighting was simple but effective, using smaller pools to create special playing areas, and enough variation in colours to create different atmospheres. Sound was clear and well-cued throughout the show. The characters of the three leading ladies and their misogynist boss were very well established, and there was good attention given to the supporting roles by the Director. The pace throughout was good, and the emotion of each scene was well created. The placing of the screen for the projection of Dolly Parton was good, and the timing of dialogue was spot on.

Due to the need for so much office furniture, there is a limit to what can be achieved choreographically on such a tight stage, but Róisín Currid was inventive in including the desks and chairs as part of the office routines, which were pretty tidily executed. When an opportunity arose to use a clear stage, the routines were more adventurous, but sensibly stayed within the ability of the performers, and were all the better for that wisdom.

The band provided a balanced and considerate accompaniment to the action. The Musical Director, Vincent Tully, displayed a strong awareness of the need for balance between the stage and the pit. There was also evidence of a well prepared chorus, who added good vocals and harmony to the show. It was just a pity that one of the best vocal chorus pieces, "Joy to The Girls", had to be sung off-stage to facilitate a scene change. The one area that needs a slightly tighter control is the final note of some of the chorus pieces, to ensure that the singers and the musicians finish on the same secure beat.

Andrea Fitzpatrick was a delightful Violet Newstead, giving a good sense of the put- upon secretary who eventually snaps. Her feminism speech to Tinsworthy in the final scene was the peak of her performance, having already displayed a good sense of comedy, and an assured vocal quality. Doralee Rhodes was given a performance of stature and maturity by the 17 year old, Alanna Donohue, with a sense of comedy and stage presence well beyond her years. She had a wonderfully rich and appropriate voice, and used her femininity perfectly, as dictated by the script. It was hard to believe this was her first principal role.

Also stepping into the limelight for the first time was Pamela McCormack who, after a nervous start, gave energy, expression and a good vocal interpretation to the role of Judy. There was good comedy in her transition from mouse to mountain lion, and she worked well against the other ladies.

Paula McEntee displayed a timid and humble nature when she took her bow at the end of the show, but she really should have been joyous, for in the domineering yet fawningly sycophantic role of Roz Keith, she gave a debut performance of great stature and comedy, which only required a bit more self-belief.

I loved the smug, vulgar swagger of Tómas Glynn in the role of misogynist boss, Franklin Hart Jnr. His delivery of "Her For You" was delightfully tasteless and comical, and his facial expressions and body language throughout were very funny and well timed.

Conor Martin gave a shy and sympathetic portrayal of Joe, with a very nice delivery of "Let Love Grow". This was another performer who, with a tad more confidence, will develop in confidence and stature. His talent is already evident and considerable.

Seamus Smith gave a noteworthy performance as Tinsworthy, and was an obvious popular favourite with the local audience.

There were other notable performances from John Grogan as Dwayne, Eoin Martin as Josh, Aiden Fitzpatrick as Dick, Aoife Shalvey as Kathy, Orla Hannigan as Maria, Samantha Kelly as Missy, and a particularly good characterisation by Jackie McQuillan as the office lush, Margaret. Several chorus members gave good account of themselves in a variety of cameo roles.

As already stated, the chorus acquitted themselves admirably as actors, singers and dancers, to make a very worthy contribution to the show.

By and large, costumes were good and appropriate to the era, although opportunities were missed to add more colour and character in the dream sequence routines, and it would have created good comedy to have all the secretaries dressed the same as Roz for the "Heart to Hart" number. The leading ladies were perfectly dressed throughout, with their outfits appropriate to their character. Hair styles were generally good, and there were no issues with make-up. These are exciting times for Tullyvin Musical Society, so fresh and enthusiastic are they to grow and learn, and their abundant energy and sense of enjoyment will doubtless inspire others to come forward in their community, and help to build a strong and confident society. I wish the society well in continuing to grow and prosper, and thank them graciously for an inspirational and entertaining night at 9 to 5

Directors, Terese Dunne and Rosemary Winkless, summoned up a powerful collective imagination in their design and setting of this popular show, combining good performances with clever technical devices to keep the show lively and interesting from the get-go to the final curtain. Blessed with a very efficient cast of character actors, and an energetic chorus, the pace of the show rarely flagged, and there was good attention to diction and placement on the stage. When the chorus weren't dancing, they were always nicely presented in clean, clear pictures, and they reacted well to the focal point of the action.

The use of projections was superb, with brilliantly selected images and moving effects. It was almost a show in itself. Ranging from the stunning effect of the "twister" to images of the Wicked Witch engulfed in flames, to sublime backgrounds of the Kansas horizon, the projections took this show to another dimension. Details such as the shadows of the flying monkeys, and the ascending balloon were hallmarks of a thorough plotting, and the lighting designer complemented the projections without ever failing to keep the action well-illuminated. The stage was always awash with atmospheric tones, and cueing throughout was excellent. Props were plentiful and appropriate, and some, such as Prof Marvel's Crystal Ball, were stunning. The management of the props and set pieces was in the very safe hands of an efficient stage crew, under the direction of Moya Hodgers. There were no problems at all with the quality of sound. All in all, the technical aspects of this show were stunning.

Visually, too, with an excellent selection of costumes and wigs, and well managed hair-styles, the standard was very impressive. Nice work done by the make-up team, although the dark green of the Wicked Witch of the West, needed broken up with more highlighted features, as much of her facial expression was lost. Terese Dunne's choreography was always appropriate, and always within the capabilities of her performers, with some moments of terpsichorean delight from the more accomplished dancers. With large numbers to cater to, she kept her patterns and pictures tidy and effective, and the overall choreographic content nicely enhanced the whole production.

Lisa-Rose McMahon was a good choice for the role of Dorothy, and despite her youth, showed a wealth of emotion in her acting. Vocally, she was strong and tuneful, and always looked completely at ease on the stage.

Gavin Quigley had all the attributes to perfectly capture the essence of the Scarecrow. Physically adept, and almost like a rubber-man, his gesticulations were delightfully funny, and his voice was just ideal. There were a few occasions when he could have blended into the background a little, allowing the focal point to shift more effectively, but this was still a tremendously accomplished performance. Likewise, Brendan Cleary was perfectly cast as the Tin Man, with his gentler nature and warm sincerity. He maintained the stiffness required of a man of tin, without ever looking awkward, and he was vocally very secure.

The Lion is perhaps the cutest character in the story, and particularly so when given the comedic treatment of the highly talented Tom Doonan, who was not only hilarious in his characterisation, but also displayed an exceptionally high quality vocal capacity. "If I Were King of the Forest" was one of the musical highlights of the show.

Siobhan Jordan took on the dual role of the Wicked Witch and Mrs Gulch, with a most effective character voice, and a good air of smug superiority. This was particularly appropriate for Mrs Gulch, but I would have liked her to be more fiery and physically demonstrative as the Witch. Nevertheless, this was a very credible performance.

Kevin Stanley had the perfect befuddled look of the Wizard/Professor Marvel, and played the role with affable charm and confidence. His angry voice, combined with his distorted image "on-screen", had the desired effect on the children in the audience.

Leanne Toner was a delightful Glinda, beautifully attired and radiant in her persona. A warm and impressive vocal quality added much to a very accomplished performance, and it was nice that the revised score gave her more than usual opportunities to display that quality.

Richard Gamble was ideal as Uncle Henry, with his dry sense of humour, and he was ably supported by Sheena Duffy as a busy, yet sympathetic Aunt Em. Barry Dunne had good authority as the Mayor and a comical silliness as the Guard. Fine support was given by a number of cameo performers, all of whom made a good impact.

As mentioned above, the choruses were energetic and well integrated into the production, never giving less than total commitment to their allotted roles.

With several pieces of music I'd never heard before, this revised version of the musical score was given a fine interpretation by a small but very capable band, under the guidance of Musical Director, Patrick Dunne. They were never heavy-handed, allowing the vocals on- stage to come across clear and loud. Irene Dunne, as Chorus Mistress, elicited good vocal quality from her chorus, with clear diction and some effective harmonising. Principals were also well-prepared in their music. Musically, the show was delightful, but when time has elapsed, and I've travelled to more shows all over the country, it is the technical brilliance of this production that will stay clearly in my mind.

Thank you to all concerned for a show that was every bit as engaging as the Movie.

St Michael's Theatre, in the heart of New Ross, is such a fantastic resource. There was a great sense of occasion as the venue was clad with extremely impressive posters, balloons and other Harvard- esque paraphernalia. Legally Blonde is a great show, with really good principal and secondary roles, and with so much fun stuff for the chorus to do. There is no doubt about the hard work required to get such a production to the stage and I congratulate all of those involved for staging what is, deceptively perhaps, a mammoth show. The role of Elle Woods is a beast and I have nothing but respect for any actress who gets up there and does it. Her costume changes alone are a challenge, not to mention the vocals, lines, dance moves, characterisation and emotional journey she must go on. The chorus never get it easy either and have to deliver so much in terms of attack, energy, harmonies and movement. So SMTMS had a colossal job on their hands and, for the most part, did well. There were many successes I could attribute to this production and there are a number of aspects that were not as successful. Director, set-designer, programme- creator (and most likely doer of 2,000 other jobs) Kevin Kennedy, had a difficult task with this show. In Legally Blonde, the narrative moves from place to place so often and thus requires inventiveness in maintaining slick scene changes and consistent quality in terms of aesthetic. In this production, the Delta Nu house looked good with its nine windows and door, enabling that iconic opening to work very well. Elle's bedroom covered in Hello Kitty paraphernalia looked great. The best set piece was for Paulette's Salon. There were green head lamps, gaudy wallpaper, a nail-station, a reception desk which were all pulled together with a yellow, tan and green colour palette. There was a double- sided mirror that allowed people to appear from behind, which was inspired! Dewey's trailer was really effective also and there was extra detail, such as pizza boxes on the ground outside, which added texture to the overall aesthetic. Elsewhere, staging, in places, was somewhat sparse so more was required from lights to add colour and texture to some set pieces and the cyc at the back was left unlit too often. The finale of Act One saw the Delta Nus turn to reveal "Elle Woods" lettering on their hoodies which was cool. During a skipping routine, Brooke froze and her skipping rope froze in mid-air.

Stage Management was by Mark Hayden and a committed and hard-working crew. There are so many enormous changes in this show and it is never easy. Some suspect decisions were made in terms of when scene-changes took place. There are moments in this show that are specifically written to cover scene changes. One such moment is the line formed by the Harvard students as Elle fights her way through the crowd. While the writers do their best to make something of such moments, their function doubles up as a cover for a scene change. Therefore, it did not make sense to me to have stage hands bring the benches in for the lecture hall until the cast were masking them. Happily the benches came off at the perfect moment. The Hair Affair set was also struck in the reprise of 'Ireland', which is exactly right, and some chorus members covered the striking of the Department Store with some step/ touch moves which was also clever.

Lighting was by Paul Malone, Bobby Kavanagh and Colin Murphy. There were lighting strips on the wings, usually matching the colour coming from the lamps which was cool. Not enough was done with lighting to give texture and framing in the more sparsely furnished scenes. The cyc on the back wall could have been used to far greater effect as its limp grey presence reminded one of a cloudy day for 80% of the show. There was a green light when Kyle reveals that his middle name is Brendan which worked really well.

Musical Direction was by Philip Kennedy. This show is a complete roast and hats off to any MD who can get from the start to the end. The diction from the Delta Nus in the opening number was very clear. Drumming was very good in the cheerleading section of 'What You Want'. Enid's part of 'Harvard Variations' was sung at warp speed, leaving the band miles behind and became such a tongue twister that barely a word was comprehensible. 'Blood in the Water' appeared to be drastically under-taught. The band were late coming in and the timing was all over the place, as Callahan did his own thing, leaving the musicians desperately trying to make some sense of what was going on. 'So Much Better' fell apart at the end as Elle sped ahead causing a domino effect of problems for the band and the choral singers. Harmonies, when the sound- desk enabled them to be heard, were very good. Philip even played a part in the show, making the 'TV announcement' before the courtroom scene which was a nice surprise.

Choreography was by Claire Kickham. 'Whipped into Shape' is no easy feat and was successfully choreographed with well-executed rope-work. 'Bend and Snap' was the number of the night as the moves overall really matched the intention of the song. It was super slick and included Paulette just enough in the dance. The 'Legally Blonde' number was another highlight and the whole-company Riverdance moment was fabulous. These were the most slick and well-rehearsed numbers of the night and showed great commitment from the cast.

Any actress who takes on the part of Elle Woods deserves a medal. It is a monster- role and the sheer work that is required to learn all the lines, music and movements cannot be underestimated. So well done to Ashley Doran for all her hard work in carrying the entire show. That said, I felt that at times more honesty was required in terms of her characterisation and line- delivery, for example when Warner breaks up with her. It's not like it can't be funny, but it should feel real. There were too many moments were Elle delivered her lines out front to the audience. That said, she had some lovely vocals at times and her relationship with Emmett was lovely. I was not sure, from his first scene, if Keith Flanagan as Emmet Forrest was going to be successful in this role. He lacked presence as he addressed those in 'Harvard Variations' and did not inhabit the goofiness that is intended when he says lines like "represent". Thankfully, as the show went on, Keith's performance became one my favourites of the evening. His singing was super, especially during that "Little Miss Woods comma Elle" moment and his musical entrances were spot on. He connected well with Elle and played his part with warmth and style for the rest of the evening.

Trevor Kent as Warner looked great and sung very competently. More understated than other Warner's I have seen, I think he could have pushed the envelope a little with his arrogance during his first appearance. It was a performance that chose naturalism over comedy but he was convincing nonetheless.

Joanne McCabe's portrayal of Paulette was, for me, the performance of the evening. She was not as over-the-top as other Paulette's I have seen but she found a lovely balance between being full of character, while being honest and convincing. She maintained excellent diction through her rough accent and she told the story brilliantly in 'Ireland'. She really shone in the graduation scene. Since I first saw Kevin Reade perform, I have been a fan. He has such a beautifully rich low speaking voice that I could listen to all day, and his diction is second to none. The timing of one of this character's biggest moments, 'Blood in the Water', was suspect. I think Kevin might have chewed up the scenery a little more and really given those Harvard students something to be afraid of. More of that 'dorsal fin' he sings about was necessary, in my opinion.

Zoe Smith as Vivienne was at her more successful when she attacked Elle at the house party as there was real connection between herself and Elle. Her 'swore up and down you did not belong' vocalising was very good when she finally sided with Elle.

Another very good performance came from Claire O'Connor as Brooke. Her image was very suitable for the role. She was very convincing as she took no nonsense from her legal team. She socked the 'Whipped into Shape' number to the audience and sang very well in the later parts of the show. Her severe bun was a great hair-style choice. I'm glad it was not felt that Brooke needed to be blonde. Her hair was pragmatic for a personal trainer and high-powered enough to match her attitude, so well done to the Hair and Make-up team there.

Lizzy Heffernan as Enid caught the tough as nails attitude very well. She sang well too. She got too excited in 'Harvard Variations' and took off like a lightning bolt, but she performed all of her other material with competence. Seán O'Brien as Kyle had the audience in the palm of his hand from the moment he entered with a comic wiggling of his derriere and deserved his round of applause.

Fionn Murphy as Padamandan and Jack Ryan as Nikos both had very good accents. Bríd Moloney as Chutney Wyndam had very good physical comedy as she entered the courtroom, full of sass and unlikability. Lorcan Dunne, as Judge, had the most stunning speaking voice, indicative of an experienced Shakespearian actor.

The Harvard professors had a very good variety of ages, characterisations and accents. The Delta Nus were led by Kerrie Campbell (Margot), Caoimhe Kelly (Serena), Caoimhe Boyle (Pilar) and Claire Kickham (Kate) and they showed great commitment and enthusiasm to their roles. They were often joined by an additional group of Delta Nus, who had a huge amount to do in terms of singing, dancing and acting. They were full of character throughout. They had perfect energy and intention in their 'Positive' number and their armography was executed very well here. The seriousness at which the Delta Nus take the trickery of the shop assistant was not realised as they mainly giggled during this. The comedy lies in the fact that this is there whole world and I think they should have been comically horrified. 'Whipped into Shape' and 'Bend and Snap' were two highlights that were socked to the audience successfully. There was super energy from everyone in the final "Oh my Gods" at the end.

Wardrobe was by Gráinne Ryan, Lisa O'Connor, Sarah Treacy and Pauline O'Riordan. Costumes were excellent overall. However, the decision to put Callahan in corduroy and cheque was misguided. He owns a billionaire-dollar law firm and lecturing would be a drop in the ocean in his week. His suits would always be impeccable. He chastises Emmett for wearing ratty corduroy, resulting in him needing to go shopping with Elle and change his image to win his boss's favour, so Callahan's casual clothing jarred with me in the Harvard scenes.

The rest of the costumes were fabulous, however. The stuffy Harvard professors looked the part with their blazers, cheque shirts, chinos and mismatched ties. The cheerleader uniforms looked great, complete with their orange and blue pompoms (however, I think Elle should have been given pompoms to make sense of her moves). Elle looked gorgeous in her jeans, pink ankle boots and pink jacket. Her bunny costume was fab: The satin pink and white with matching ears, stand-alone collar and nude wedges. Her pink mac in the final scenes was lovely. Warner's first Harvard costume combined the student life with the ever-upright aristocrat with his bright blue shirt, blue jeans, brown belt and shoes and blue waistcoat. Paulette's image was spot on: her layered clothing full of gaudy textures and animal print, the green bracelet and hooped earrings, silver scrunchy and a high pony tail on her head. Her dungarees, blue top and tights in the graduation scene were great and set up a pregnancy gag well. Emmett was perfect in his open-collar shirt and t-shirt, brown satchel and chords. Dewey's belly hanging out of his white trash vest and checked shirt looked the part and was comic. The orange overalls in 'Whipped into Shape' looked super. The blue emblems on the ladies' black dresses - was that a nod to a tradition within the society? If so, then that was a special idea.

Overall, it was a mixed evening in New Ross, full of much to admire and things that did not necessarily work. The society have a clear vision with their three-year plan and will stage 9 to 5 next year. That show is, perhaps, a tamer beast and no doubt the society will do a very good job indeed.

A little episode with a couple of rather refined, old ladies, who decided to leave the show at the interval, indicated to me just how authentic the Portlaoise production of Rock of Ages really was. It was brash, loud, in your face, and yes, if you were of a certain frame of mind, offensive! But obviously I am NOT of that certain frame of mind, because I loved it. Ok, perhaps the number of times the F word was used, during this performance, left me wondering if perhaps Director Paul Norton had given his cast a tad too much free rein with their ad-libs, but in every other respect, any offence that may have been caused was the result of a very comical and authentic portrayal of the rock era. Visually, vocally, technically and musically, the show hit the mark in reviving memories of an era through which I very much enjoyed living. Rock is alive and well, and still dividing opinion as it did in its day.

Paul has a good eye and ear for comedy, and he took every opportunity to get as much fun as possible from the script and from his performers. There were one or two problems with diction, but visually the show bounced off the stage, and the pace was excellent. I particularly loved the opening, with many of the performers relaxing on the stage and enjoying an impromptu sing-song as the audience were filtering into the auditorium.

Opening the show with a wonderful lead guitar solo, an excellent band of rock musicians, under the leadership of Musical Director, Emer Hartnett, impressed throughout, and even managed to stay with Emer when a few extra bars seemed to sneak into "Every Rose Has its Thorn". Singers were well-prepared, with good vocal harmonies apparent throughout, and the pace and rhythms of the music were always as one would expect. It's easy for an on-stage band to over-power, but thankfully, this was never the case. Between them, Eoghan Fingleton as Drew and Aideen Leacy as Sherrie, provided the musical highlights of the show, with a super rendition of "Waiting For A Girl Like You" in Act One, and a show- stopping "High Enough" in Act Two. Both were vocally superb, and both had the acting ability to make their performances totally believable. The comedy in their faltering relationship was as well played as the romance, in two brilliantly realised characterisations.

Alex Cathcart was a confident Lonny, narrating the show with a fine sense of comedy and a comfort in playing with the audience. His singing was strong, and particularly in his scenes with Dennis he looked completely relaxed in the role. Jay Ritchie had an Andrew Strong quality to his vocals that suited the role of Dennis perfectly. He also had the perfect "stoned" look to add credibility to his performance. A few lines here and there were a tad too gravelly to be clearly understood, but generally, his characterisation was very good.

With the role of Stacee Jaxx, I had difficulty making out what Damien Keating was saying for a large part of his performance, as his diction tended to be lost in his growling tone. He looked right for the part, and sang much better than he spoke. His seduction of Sherrie in the Toilet cubicle was very funny.

Aishling Rohan gave great character and comedy to the role of Regina, enhancing her performance with a strong vocal quality. She was quirky and cute in equal measure, and was a robust leader of the demonstrators.

Pat Cullen turned in a strong comedic performance as Hertz, with a good accent, an arrogant nature and ultimately, a hilarious sensitivity in his love for his son. Sean O'Neill was physically very comical as hyper-sensitive Franz, but he was another performer whose lines tended to get swallowed by his accent and by being a little soft-spoken.

Angi McNulty, as Justice, could have been a tad more maternal and sympathetic to poor Sherrie, but she was a strong presence on the stage, and sang most impressively.

Dawn Kavanagh and Richard Finnegan did all that was required to convince as Sherries Mother and Father, and Rory Chadwick was a funny and believable money-grubbing Mayor, licking bank notes and betraying his community. There were several other fine cameo performances, most notably Barry Dunne as a leggy pole-dancing Candi, Paul Kenna as Joey Primo, Jayne Louise Kelly as Constance, Sonya Cuddy as Waitress #1, and a very competent performance from Derek McGinn as the Producer. Choreographer, Grace McGrath, summoned up her inner rocker to put together a series of routines that were perfectly in the style of the era, with lots of aggression and blatant sexuality. Her dancers performed with a sense of exhilaration and a relaxed ease, suggesting very good preparation and rehearsal. She never allowed the stage to look over-crowded, by using smaller groups and then replacing them, and only really bringing everyone together for the climax of the bigger numbers. Her chorus and Dancers performed with zeal, sex- appeal and exuberant energy throughout the show. Their vocal quality was also consistently good.

The show was played out on a well- constructed, well-painted and decorated set, with very good props on display throughout. Stage manager, Bob O'Kelly, and his crew, did a seamless job of controlling the few moving pieces on a set that required little attention. The lighting was very good and rarely missed the mark, giving much of the show a rock-concert atmosphere, and frequently melting down to an intimate state for those more romantic moments.

A major feature of this production was the quite superb sound quality. It went so much further than just ensuring that everyone was heard. The operator kept the band in check, boosted the lighter voices, and his use of reverb during certain sections was beyond impressive. Costumes were spot on, with a nice variety of outrageous rockers. The dancer's costumes were sleazy and appropriate, and wigs and hairstyles were generally very good. Candi blended in well with the girls, but would have been even more effective with a less obvious wig. There was a good display of wacky make-up. As a final comment, even with adult only shows, I'd be inclined to temper the level of potentially offensive language and gestures, because come the next show, you might want those two rather perplexed, little, old ladies to return to the fold. That said, congratulations on a really fabulous and extremely enjoyable Rock of Ages! Rock on!

The Hired Man does what a lot of good drama tends to do; it explores the human story against a large universal theme, in this case World War I. The inhabitants of a small mining village in Northern England have to deal with the perils of being both in and out of work, until the time comes for the local men to sign up. It is a tale of relationships between family, friends and lovers and the pain that can come with love and loss. HXT's version of the show did very well at exploring the complicated nature of the relationships between these characters, suggesting that Director Art McGauran has a keen eye for subtleties within a scene. And while it is a moving tale, some argue that the star of this show is the music, in particular the choral singing. Thankfully, the choral singing was a highlight, all the more impressive from a somewhat medium-sized ensemble. Dynamics, expertly actualised by MD Dermot O'Callaghan, gave nuance and texture to everything that was sung. The chorus, whispered, gossiped, warned and cursed the heroes of the piece with the power and effectiveness of on-point harmonies. Principal singing was securely rehearsed also. The band were hidden behind the stage and, while it is a small shame that they were not part of the whole theatrical aesthetic, the benefits were far more plentiful: Sound, by Vinny Osborne, was so balanced as a result, with lovely swells during playoffs etc. The Civic Theatre in Tallaght is a medium-sized space with no pit and there is chance that a band could drown out the action on stage. Thankfully, this issue was eradicated, something which is frustratingly rare. The set, designed and built by Stage Manager Marie Cusack, in co-operation with ProStaging, was a quality version of what one has come to expect for this show; a harsh rural, yet non-distinct, setting from a hundred years ago. The ramp of brick- work, subtly creating levels, had matching walls to frame the space with some other furniture appearing at times to punctuate the changes in place. Wooden boxes were also cleverly re-used to establish various moments throughout the show, most effectively when they became the barricades for the trenches of World War I. In addition to this, there were projections beamed onto the backdrop, made up of a series of atmospheric silhouettes that had thematic continuity, blending nicely with the set.

For the most part, changes from one scene to the next were stylised or worked into the action, adding to the mood, rather than delaying the narrative. It was slightly disappointing that this clever motif was not omnipresent, ergo the less slick stage-changes were somewhat jarring as a result. The chorus were struck from the stage to enable private conversations and then brought back on, which appeared somewhat clumsy and unnecessary. While the principal performances in the pub scene were great, the pub lacked atmosphere as the willing chorus were too quiet. There were also too many straight lines in the ensemble numbers. I understand the concept of a Greek chorus, but Greek choruses can be personified and individualised to give more naturalism to their contribution. In contrast, the number 'Day Follows Day' was sung, not out to the audience like the other numbers, but with a sense of naturalism that added physical characterisation to the lovely vocals. 'Warsong', the scene in which the men were in the war trenches, was an inventive highlight. Each time the lights came up on them they were in a different formation, showing the passing of time and the relentlessness of the war. A series of boxes moved cleverly, in slow motion, to their new place in a partial black-out and we had something new to appreciate each time they appeared. There was even a wonderful snow-machine effect to highlight the misery of their conditions. Choreography, by Erica Delaney Hayes, was simple with some synchronised tool movements in 'Worksong'. The highlight was the folk dancing which was inclusive of all ages and ability levels. This bounced off the stage, making sure we were as happy as could be before the sad bits, maximising their impact.

Kevin Fagan played our Everyman hero John. This somewhat timid character has to deal with learning of his wife's dalliance with another man and with a son who insists on going to war, only to meet disaster. It was a beautifully measured performance. While he was often understated, he never dismissed a moment as unimportant, always doing just enough to react to what was going on. He internalised his feelings rather than gesticulated every obvious emotion, making it all the more powerful when his feelings overflowed in private moments. The emotions seemed to surge from within, manifesting themselves into his voice and eyes in a way that was utterly convincing, truthful and honest. To top it off, his singing was professional, powerful and moving.

Like John, Emily is a massive part, with a huge amount to learn, and the role was in the competent hands of Kelly-Marie Davy. She was nice and affable and we were always on her side, which is important considering her betrayal of the faithful John. The scene in which Jackson wins her over was very well crafted; he would not take no for an answer and her lust for him dominated over her fear of sinning, leading to an inevitable and passionate kiss. Her reaction after the kiss was layered and fascinating: She trembled with lust, regret, fear and possibility. Seeing the complexity of the moment, we can stay on her side for the rest of the show. Her voice suited the lower part of the score best, but she emoted beautifully through song nonetheless. Her death was very touching, all the more because she had done enough things right to deserve the heartache of her loyal husband.

Damien Hurley's performance of Jackson made me wish that Jackson had a musical of his own, such was the subtle complexity of his interpretation. Does his darkness come from his overly-critical father or is his father right to be so harsh? Why does he want a married woman? How does he manage to win her over when she appears otherwise to be completely devoted to her lovely husband? (Getting the passionate nicey-nice treatment from a bad boy has won a few hearts in the past). How is he 15 years later? Slower, tamer, sadder but more settled. The war would have taken its toll, of course. All of this was measured very nicely by Damien, with just the right amount of ingredients, prompting more questions than answers, which is far more interesting.

Matthew Carpenter brought much-needed humour and energy in a characterful, persuasive and convincing performance of Isaac. His job was to bring vim, humour and strength to the very tame Tallentire household and he did this well. Such was his bravado that it was all the more painful when he broke down in tears, recalling the conditions of war that cost him dearly. It was completely convincing and avoided self-indulgence, which was great.

More drama was provided by Stephen Fagan as Seth. He had a more serious head on his shoulders than Isaac, bringing balance to their scenes. He was effective in the Miners' meeting. [Spoiler Alert] He added to the panic of Harry's youthful and misguided heroic attempt to flee the trenches to attack the other side and his embrace of the dead body was tense and moving. Charlene Masterson, as Sally, had great rapport with Emily and as such we saw more reason to like Emily throughout the show. Her discomfort at Jackson's arrival to Emily's house was cleverly acted and her singing of 'Who Will You Marry Then?' was very good.

Aoife Small, as May, had all the sass and confidence that her parents lacked, injecting energy and into the Tallentire household. She combined nice vocals with good story-telling ability in 'You Never See the Sun'. She was the perfect foil for her anxious brother. She took nonsense from nobody and, as such, was all the more effective when she became saddened in the later scenes.

In contrast, Jordan Bass as her brother Harry had all the nervous energy of an adolescent young man coming of age, looking for excitement and heroics. He was steadfast and persuasive as he told his mother that he lied about his age to join up, and his re-appearance at the end of the show was touching.

Eddie Brady showed his range as an actor by appearing as the criticising Pennington in the First Act, and the dithering and humorous clergyman later in the show. Paul Laycock was a pensive and committed Chairman of the Miners' meeting and added considerably wherever else he appeared. Julie Donnelly had great presence as the Landlady and established herself as the matriarchal boss of the proceedings in the pub.

Kevin Shirran was able to be funny or deadly serious depending on his function within a scene as Tom. Garrett Rogers, James Place and Robbie Keogh brought their experience to their roles of Bob, Joe Sharp and Ted Blacklock, ensuring that standards did not slip across the line of named parts.

Costumer, Andrew Reddy, has a great supply of costumes that are indicative of this time. Everyone was as cute as a button. I would argue that costumes could have been messier; with tears in the clothing, patches and grime that would make more of a suggestion towards the poverty and terrible working conditions of the mining families. The soldiers' uniforms looked great and those ladies of a higher caste stood out from the poorer women, such were their high-power rigouts. The use of modern-day spotlessly-clean overalls were neither suitable for the time period nor indicative of the awful working conditions of the men.

Couple this with a few too many Disney- like moments, where cast members pointed and gazed into the distance, all doe-eyed and dream-like, and I am not so sure that we got enough of the 'rugged' quality that Time Out magazine had once admired about The Hired Man.

Lighting was by Tomás Fitzgerald/Stage Lighting Centre who splayed some nice colours across the rocky wall of the set, giving atmosphere to various moments. The lighting of the mining scene where the men get trapped was too bright. This did not support the sense of position- cheating in the blocking or the sense of claustrophobia that was acted very well by those involved. There were some nice specials, such as when John had to deliver bad news to Emily from the Front. More specials might have clarified who was speaking in the opening sequence. They say that you have succeeded if you manage to split the audience and create debate in the aftermath of the show. Director Art McGauran managed this through his intelligent nurturing of scenes to explore the complexity of relationships. The audience may well have differed with each other about what actually happened, most notably with the kiss between Jackson and Emily. The final verdict of HXT's production of the Hired Man? Fantastic individual performances, overall, and superb choral singing, texturised with glorious dynamics. Scene changes were clever when stylised. But the chorus stood in too many straight lines. When I go to the theatre, I want to be moved to feel something; humour or sorrow or awe or elation. There were many tissues employed amongst the audience to wipe away a tear. This, in my book, means that the show induced such a catharsis and, as such, worked very well indeed.

I am reliably told that the Dun Mhuire Theatre in Wexford Town was once the third biggest theatre in Ireland. I would well believe it by the scope of this space that stretches far back to accommodate over 600 people. The large crowds this show pulled, despite the amount of other attractions in the town - such as the Opera Festival and the Spiegel Tent - was very impressive. Audience members were received with a relaxed, friendly yet effective manner by Box Office and Front of House personnel.

The official Footloose The Musical website describes the show as an "explosive rock 'n' roll musical sensation". I was expecting some fun, but I was not expecting so much substance in terms of drama. Little did I realise that this show is just as much about control and grief and eventual healing as it is about busting some moves. Dancing was banned in the town of Bomont after a group of young people died on their way home from a dance. Newcomer, Ren, whose job it was to help the townsfolk emerge from their grief, by re-establishing their love of dance, was undertaken by a very good actor and singer - Nathan Fitzpatrick. His abilities were equally matched by Niamh Bolger who played Ren's new-found love interest Ariel - a girl rebelling against her parents' grief. Niamh has great vocal range and sang brilliantly with sass or with softness as required. Ariel's father, the Reverend Moore (the man who banned dancing after his own son was killed), was played excellently by Greg Currid. He has a velvety yet booming voice that captured the authority and intention of the preacher-man. He could equally portray the vulnerability of a grieving father and he acted brilliantly through song. He and his wife Vi, played very well by Majella Londra, engaged in private arguments about how to heal from their past traumas and move forward for the sake of the youth in the town. These dramatic scenes, whether between husband and wife, father and tear-way daughter, or Reverend and advocate-of-dance Ren, were all excellently directed by Imelda McDonagh and had brilliantly varying emotional levels throughout. Additional tension to the piece was provided by Ren's struggling mother, Ethel, played with competence by a very good actor and singer, Caroline O'Connell. Poor Ethel is forced to take her son to live with his Uncle Wes (played by Andy Fanning with both comedy and crankiness) and his Aunt Lulu (played by Paula Malone Carty) who created the perfect foil for her uptight husband.

While these scenes brought more drama than I was expecting, there were still plenty of laughs too. James Dobbs played the slightly dim but very lovable protégé to Ren and provided some fantastic comedic moments in his portrayal as Willard, the honest hillbilly. More comedy was provided with a fine cameo from Marian O'Leary as Betty Blast, the owner of the local Burger Joint. This elder of the community took no nonsense as she sped dangerously around the diner with roller skates and Zimmer frame. Another competent cameo was provided by Neal O'Leary as Cowboy Bob who opened Act Two with a Country and Western number that inspired confidence. More colour was provided by town hunk Chuck Cranston who was played with all the bravado, cool and un-likeability necessary by Gary Stephens (who sang brilliantly with some nice falsetto moments). Such a baddie requires side-kicks of a lower status and these were provided with appropriate foolishness by the very good Luke Spellacy and Murt Murphy, who played the brain-dead Lyle and Travis respectively. More unlikeable characters emerged, making us fall in love more with our leads and their plights: The stricter- than-strict Principal Clark was played with great authority and presence by Donna Spellacy O'Leary and Dylan Walsh fulfilled the role of the revolting Coach Roger Dunbar with the right amount of pompous aggression. Ariel also needed some girly mates and received super support from Elaine Murphy as Rusty (who luckily enough finds love in the most unlikely places). Elaine joined Catherine Devereux as Urleen and Ceris Brown as Wendy Jo to form a competent trio of good singers with great accents.

These fine performances all took place on some very clever staging. Each set piece glided on and off with amazing ease and speed, thanks to stage manager Greg O'Leary and his team. The set pieces themselves, designed by Mark Redmond, were mainly presented as a series of trucks or stand-alone furniture that immediately and effectively defined the space and enhanced the narrative. Mark also provided lighting on the evening and he, with a clever cyc matching the colours present in the set pieces, created a synergy within the aesthetic.

While there was plenty of laughs and drama on stage, it is the case that the dancing in this show is a very important feature. With such belters as 'Holding out for a Hero' and 'Let's Hear it for the Boy', one expects this show, with its core message about the love of dance, to sock- it-to-'em in the dance numbers. This task, for the most part, was well realised by choreographer Suzanne O'Leary and her dance troupe. There were some central formations and V-shapes that seemed to work really well in a few of the numbers. Not all of the routines were as slick as one would have liked, such as the finale of Act One, but the finale of Act Two bounced off the stage and reminded everyone why dance can bring so much joy.

Singing throughout the show, by soloists in particular, was excellent and all the principal cast seemed to be very well prepared by Musical Director Patrick Clancy, who provided great support from the pit. Less successful was some of the group/choral work, particularly at the beginning of the show, which seemed to suffer from some gaffs from the sound desk. By the finale, however, the chorus belted out the famous 'Footloose' number and harmonies between the guys and girls were balanced here.

Director Imelda McDonagh has a talent for creating pictures; with each scene being so distinct from the previous one, while using a minimalistic and effective approach to staging. The clever structuring of the dramatic scenes, the individual performances, the solos, duets and small group numbers were, for me, the strength of the show. That said, it was also very uplifting when the entire company took to the stage for a final dance, leaving us with a feeling of healing and hope. Art imitated life and the more experienced 'cut loose' with the optimistic youth to celebrate the happiness music and dance can bring.
