As always, cues were on point and every word could be heard perfectly. Sound was very balanced throughout, the pit lending itself to the control in volume from the band. Choreographer Jillian Liggett created some lovely moments in the show when the choral numbers were highly structured and used formal choreography. Although the crowd scenes contained plenty of intention and reaction, they might have benefited by being more stylised, employing more moves that evoked the story and complemented acting. For example, the cross made by the chorus as they sat in formation was great, yet suitably unrealistic. It was cool the way Judas destructively knocked them down. This was all nicely symbolic.

Conor Taggart as King Herod ensured this fun moment bounced off the stage with his Elton John-esque interpretation of King Herod. He was hugely committed to this role, showing skills in singing, dancing and acting. What a showman! The way in which the four backing-builders swung Herod around the piano, allowing him to paddle on the "swimming pool" line was great, as was the way they held him by the legs as he tinkled the ivories. The kick- line, which included the stoic riot-police, was great. The tap-dancing was very good and, with Herod doing the same moves on the piano, it felt very complete. The backing-builders' finger-clicking and the riot-police's truncheon waving added to the comedy of the scene and meant there was much to admire in one number. At one point, Herod sang the line "Can You Feel the Love Tonight", which was suitably bonkers is this wonderfully over- the-top sequence. I think Elton would have loved the impressive pink grand piano and rainbow lighting on the ground. 'Superstar' was excellent, with the showmanship of Judas coupling with the contrasting groups of girls. The devils moved in double time, employing sass to their provocative moves. Those in white were more angelic and kept their moves mostly from the waist up. These two groups used the levels brilliantly, juxtaposed against the frantic crowds/ journalists and the live camera feed in the centre of the stage. The whole thing was feast for the senses. The number shows the abstract nature of this rock-album and I think this might have bled into the earlier crowd pieces. It might have been effective to have more interpretative dance moves in the leper sequence to compliment how they over-powered Jesus, for example. The ensemble overall was very good and there was not a weak link on stage anywhere. There was great energy and attack in 'Simon Zealotes'. Nathan Reilly as Simon Zealotes belted out his number, evoking the Svengali-like manager/ promoter of Jesus very well indeed. The Soul Girls with the sassy moves and the Angels with their safer moves added enormously to 'Herod's Song'. The Lepers' solos were excellently sung while evoking their suffering and desperation for help.

Daniel Marshall as Caiaphas and James Marsden as Annas captured the menace of these High Priests with great presence. Vocally they were very strong. Ian Simpson, as Peter, showed off a great voice and harmonised beautifully with Mary. His struggle at denying Jesus was very well displayed.

Rory Jeffers as Pilate captured all the unease the character felt after his prophetic dream. His low note on "blame" was beautifully sustained. He was suitably authoritative, blending aggression with arrogant dismissiveness, as he dealt with Jesus. He played the change after the realisation that this was the man from his dream very well. He growled and roared with power when he finally succumbed to the demands of the crowd and his inability to negotiate with Jesus.

Jessica Webb as Mary Magdalene had lovely presence on stage and the eye was drawn to her contributions. The score sat beautifully in her lovely pop-styled voice. She made sure that she acted, as well as sung, every moment of 'I Don't Know How to Love Him'. She evoked a caring nature towards Jesus, while dealing with her own introspection, and completed this talented trio perfectly.

Both leading men in their own right, the parts of Jesus and Judas were played by Stuart Anderson and Ethan Haddock respectively. The casting of these men and their characterisations contrasted brilliantly. Stuart was suitably composed as Jesus and captured the essence of a man who never asked for this job, struggling with his relationship with God. In contrast Judas could not contain his anger, frustration and bravado, wanting to argue about all that was imperfect about the situation. With Jesus' stillness, we had Judas' movement, as he climbed the scaffolding and chewed up the space. Stuart, with his cleanly-shaven face and fair hair, had a crystal clear angelic voice and impressive falsetto. The dark- featured bearded Ethan's vocals were angry, guttural and coarse. I am glad these men did not enter into that cringe-worthy falsetto-off. This can be like listening to two strangled cats and the lyrics are usually lost. Both of them delivered emotionally charged performances that were very well measured and believable. Jesus' suffering on the cross and Judas' suicide were both harrowing. They worked their socks off and their efforts are hugely appreciated. With Joseph and his Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat already in the pipeline, and bags full of talent, the future looks bright for Fusion Theatre.

In what was a very clean and tidy production by Director, Deigh Reid, the cast were well prepared in their roles, their characters were generally well defined and the chorus and dancers did all that was asked of them with energy and no small amount of talent.

There were occasions when the pace flagged a little, usually due to a slow scene change and the fact that there were less high energy numbers in the second half. Despite the neatness of the set, it could have done with a bit more variety in design, particularly in the 2nd Act Fairground scenes. Stage Manager, Christine Deane, and her team, did nothing wrong, but they did seem to amble through a few of the scene changes. Props were good and the 'bus' was excellent. Lighting was very atmospheric, creating colourful pictures on stage, and highlighting smaller playing areas. And thankfully, the 'disco' option was not overused in the livelier numbers. This was a well-selected show, giving, as it does, plenty of opportunity to bring on the younger talent within the company, and what a wealth of young talent there is. There was good depth of character to Riana Lynch's interpretation of Natalie, with a Tom-boyish insecurity in the earliest scenes, a natural shyness as she tries to embrace her girlie side, and a very good sense of comedy as she became "Ed". Her singing throughout was relaxed and easy to listen to, and at its best during "Fools Fall in Love".

Youthfulness didn't prevent Thorin Coffey from delivering the role of Chad with confidence and swagger. His voice was his biggest asset, giving strength and security to his vocal contributions. While he had an astute awareness of how to play comedy, he did have a tendency to rush his lines, and with so much natural ability, I don't think there was a need to make hip-swinging and groin-thrusting such a constant feature of his performance. An even more youthful Gregg Parkhill took the role of Dennis and impressed the audience with a characterisation that, while it was certainly confident, would have benefitted even more from slowing the dialogue and emphasising his dorkishness. He was vocally well able for the role.

Lorraine Roddy gave a strong and mature performance in the role of Sylvia, always looking at ease, and growing in breadth as her more emotional side became exposed. Her scenes with Jim were nicely sentimental, and she did a splendid job of "There's Always Me".

David Keown impressed as Jim Haller, the gentle widower who tries to reinvent himself, displaying, along the way, a very fine comedic ability. There was a sincerity in his performance that enhanced his relationships with both Sylvia and Natalie. Emer McCaffrey used her considerable experience to bring the character of Miss Sandra to life, with a good initial superiority, and an equally believable feistiness when she fell in love with Ed. Vocally very capable, her "Power of My Love" was her musical highlight.

Youthfulness again came to the fore in the pairing of Hannah Deane as Lorraine and Corey O'Connor as Dean Hyde, both of whom performed with confidence and showed their potential to become stars of the future.

Una Culkin had a lot of fun with the role of Mayor Matilda, delightfully superior and smug and yet capable as a bit of a rock chick in "Devil in Disguise". She delivered her lines with a fine awareness of their comedic impact.

Geoff Coke was an effective silent partner to the Mayor as Sheriff Earl, and when he eventually got the chance to break his silence, he made the most of his opportunity to assert his authority.

The chorus contributed good harmonies and fine energy and precision in their dances.

Musical Director, Peter Doherty, led the orchestra from the keyboard, and with the exception of a couple of slow starts, he did a very good job of keeping stage and pit together. Tempi were generally good, and the musicians had the right 'feel' for the style of music. The chorus were well rehearsed and harmonies were secure. Vanessa Chapman got the show off to a great start with a beautifully choreographed "Jailhouse Rock", full of energy and variety, and performed very well by a company who seemed well able for the steps. There were other moments of splendid movement and tidy execution, particularly "Come on Everybody" and "All Shook Up", but I did feel that the energy and inventiveness seemed to wane a little as the show progressed, and that another blockbuster on the scale of "Jailhouse Rock" would have elevated the second half of the show.

The show was effectively costumed and very colourful, with nice alternative outfits for the angels and devils. Principals looked as they should, although I wasn't mad about Natalie's oil-stained dress. Prisoner costumes in the opening number were very good. Hairstyles were acceptable and there were no problems with make- up.

The strength of any company lies not just in the hands of the young up-and- coming stars of the future, but also in the experience and encouragement of the "old hands", and it's always good to see company stalwarts, on stage, back-stage and front of house, doing their bit and supporting the next generation. This was a most enjoyable evening of entertainment, filled with foot-tapping songs and dances, very good comedy, and pervaded by a sense of community that should see the company enjoying a high level of success well into the future. Thank you to all concerned.

It has been almost three decades since I last saw Funny Girl on stage, and I'd have to be honest and say that it hasn't aged well. Not that Kilmacud didn't do everything in their power to perform the story with credibility, but the role of Fanny Brice, who in latter days may have been regarded as a strong women in the face of a selfish and thoughtless lover, comes across, in this day and age, as a weak and suppliant fool. Similarly, the role of Nick Arnstein may once have been worthy of some element of sympathy, but in the modern era, he is crass, manipulative and despicable. What mother nowadays would chastise her daughter for not sticking with such a husband in the manner that Mrs Brice did? I hasten to add that these are not criticisms of the cast, but ultimately, I left the theatre feeling that poor Fanny had been let down more by the script than by Nick Arnstein. I feel a certain sympathy for Director, Paul Fay, for he kept the show running at a decent pace in the right direction, with well-drawn characters, but by being faithful to the script and the tone of the piece, it inevitably drooped towards the conclusion, and I'm not sure that could have been prevented without a major re- write. Good use was made of the main stage area, with the somewhat sparse scenery pieces just about suggesting the various locations. Principals were well- rehearsed and disciplined, and relaxed, despite it being opening night, which, given the production delays due to the snow, was a great achievement.

I must, however, be honest and suggest that the set did little to add warmth or atmosphere to the show. Despite the brave efforts of Stage Manager, Aoife Ryan, and her team, there was little that could be done to enhance a set that was, at best, adequate, but lacked atmosphere and visual appeal. The upper level was too high, and it also created many problems for the lighting crew, resulting in principals singing, on occasions, in darkness as they tried to come down the stairs stage right. The lighting designer made a very good effort to enhance the surrounding with good use of colour, but there was little for him to bounce light off, which left the general lighting rather bland, but with some lovely atmospheres around special areas for soloists.

Having the band on-stage is perfectly okay if they are discreet or perform as a natural part of the story, but they were behind a totally translucent gauze, and Musical Director, Bryan Mullen, needed to be more aware of how visible he was to the audience. During dialogue and some emotional scenes, he needed to be still to not draw attention away from the action. The chorus and principals were well rehearsed, good at their harmonies and clear in their diction, but there needed to be more coordination between musicians and chorus on the endings of songs, which were occasionally scrappy.

Central to the story is the funny girl herself, Fanny Brice, and in the hands of Emma Coast, she was given as much humanity and sincerity as possible. Emma had the vocal ability to put over the songs, with "People" being beautifully performed, and "Don't Rain on My Parade" being full of energy and emotion. My heart went out to her when she was at her most vulnerable. Fergal D'Arcy was at his best when Nick Arnstein was at his worst. There was a very believable cold and angry sense of self-preservation as he used Fanny, allowing her to jeopardise her money, casual in his attitude to her dreams being destroyed. Fergal has a natural charisma, but it's more a kind of cheeky-chappie charisma, and perhaps needed to be more suave and sophisticated to truly capture the swagger of the early successful con- man/gambler. Vocally, thanks to his own determination, he continues to improve. Aisling Cuffe, although she looked a tad young to be Fanny's mother, gave a wonderful performance of a proud and pushy mother. I totally believed in her belief in Fanny, and while the script turned her into a less than attractive character, she continued to play it with credibility. Chris O'Connor as Eddie Ryan was the most natural character on the stage, a genuine grafter who accepted his lot, loved and lost, but never allowed it to drag him down. His was the only character who could be as likeable today as in the era of the writing of the show. Nicely played, and always comfortable in his music and movement.

Zarah Doyle gave good character and comedy to the role of Mrs Strakosh, with a very effective accent and mannerisms, and she had good support from Alison Gill as Mrs Meeker and Joyce Neary as a delightful Mrs O'Malley.

Billy Andrews needed a tad more authority and showbiz charisma to really make the most of the larger than life character of Florenz Ziegfeld. He made it a bit too easy for Fanny to walk all over him.

Lesley Cosgrave as Emma and Nóirín Sheridan as Jenny turned in fine light- hearted and note-worthy performances, and Ray Bissett made a good impact in the role of Mr Keeney.

There was good energy, discipline and fun from a chorus who sang and reacted well, making the most of their opportunities to contribute to the atmosphere of the show. Costumes were well-worn and appropriate to the era, with Fanny always beautifully attired and Nick looking suitably dapper. The costumes of the older characters gave good suggestion of their personalities. Hairstyles were good and there were no problems with make-up. I hate to reiterate the point, but the settings did little to enhance or surround the chorus outfits, which were, by and large, well selected. Sound quality was generally very good, with the exception of occasional crackles when principals were very close together. Sometimes there are good reasons why shows disappear from the circuit, and in the case of Funny Girl it is most definitely the script. It really does need a rewrite to make it more appealing to a modern audience, and to allow the very good musical score to continue to be appreciated. Despite that, I fully appreciated the hard graft, energy and enthusiasm with which the company on- stage accepted the challenge of this show, and I left this opening night presentation confident that Kilmacud would have a most enjoyable and rewarding week. Thank you to all concerned for your warm hospitality and your dedication.

Director Neil Keery gave us a production that poured a large dollop of slapstick comedy with equal amounts of pathos and sincerity and whisked it up to give us a nicely balanced treatment of Sister Act. This was my second opportunity to see Newcastle Glees this season but the landscape looked rather different this time round, with heavy snowfall threatening my trip northwards. Thankfully, with the success of their run, the society added a matinee, which helped save the day (and hopefully compensated slightly for a missed performance). There was a lovely buzz about the place as I shuffled in from the snow to the adorable Annesley Hall. This quaint space is not too unlike a church in its vibe and was a nice setting for this show. The bathrooms had pictures of nuns and priests to indicate the ladies and gents.

This was my fourth Sister Act to see this year and I love experiencing the different treatments of this show. Each time I see it, I hear something new or see an original possibility that I have not seen before. Newcastle Glees shaped excellent principal portrayals and, with very good musical direction by Gareth McGreevy and choreography by Timothy Bell, produced choral numbers to blow your socks off. Dancing was slick, harmonies were well- learned and the intention in which they were put across was perfect. I am so glad that I made it to this show.

Ciara Mackey as leading lady Deloris Van Cartier has all the aura of a star. She has an awesome singing voice, so well placed within the resonators of her face that we were confident she was going to nail every note and maintain her brilliant voice throughout. She also had good technique when it came to diction. She could do it all. She could move. She could be sincere when necessary (such as in 'Sister Act') or very funny (such as the scene where she witnesses the murder). She could show vulnerability without needing to compromise the beautiful singing. Absolutely excellent.

Emma Nugent as Mother Superior had some lovely moments of sincerity, particularly in 'Here Within These Walls'. "They are my sisters", she screamed later on, "and I will not allow them to come in harm's way". This gave me tingles. She also knew how to elicit great laughter from the audience and brought fun and seriousness in equal measure. She was suitably frantic towards the end of 'Haven't Got a Prayer' and showed a nice range of emotions throughout this number.

Jamie Johnston as Sweaty Eddie had a fascinating interpretation of this role. His characterisation was heightened, without the risk of becoming incredulous. The character's poor posture enhanced the uncool way he wore his costume. His speech impediment, very often caused by emotional disturbance, was a clever touch and became worse as he described the gun incident with his partner. He made every word count, finding meaning in all his material. 'I Could be that Guy' was like a monologue that was truly engaging and thought-provoking. Some actors choose to make a sudden change when the music changes gear, but Jamie chose to build the song more slowly, meaning it always had somewhere to go, and he still managed to bust some moves near the end. His transition out of the song was also gradual, as he bounced from the cool to the awkward. His singing to Deloris back at his place was heart-felt and meaningful too. A captivating performance.

Anna Moore, as Sister Mary Robert, captured her character's meekness and lack of confidence very well and I really bought into her bond with Deloris. She showed a very well measured transition when she stood up to the Mother Superior. She had some lovely acting-through-song in 'The Life I Never Led'. Boy did she nail those vocals, particularly the last note that left the audience whooping and hollering with appreciation.

Jay Walsh as the Monsignor O'Hara was a scream. He was 100% committed to his every moment on stage, pretty much stealing the show every time he appeared. There is no denying this man's ability to create a hilarious character and own the stage. However, if I were to play devil's advocate, I think the scene in which he reveals the sale of the church might have been played with a little more worry. The hyper, over-excitable nature of this character might have been more impactful had it been saved for the actual upswing of the storyline. Otherwise, the character appeared to be over-stimulated by every eventuality good or bad. This was highly entertaining, but the jury is out on how well this interpretation served the narrative. Orla Russell as the tough task-master Sister Mary Lazarus was another actor who unearthed meaning in this part, that I had not seen before. She appeared to be truly hurt during her 'ringer' monologue and I loved this because of course she would be. That said, when required, she could ramp up that comedy and have the audience in hysterics with her solo rap in 'Raise Your Voice' and her "You got the boogie". Very well done.

Emma-Jane McKnight had the voice to do this part justice, as Sister Mary Patrick is famously the soprano who can lift the roof. Her high range also gave those clunky earlier nun performances an extra level of hilarity. She was a beam of happiness on the stage, suitably jolly and excitable in all her scenes. Her repetition of "Where is your Jesus now" was very funny.

Andy Hill as Curtis had such an imposing presence on stage with his 10 feet tall stature and slicked back hair. He was really quite menacing in 'When I Find my Baby', as he relished his violent intentions towards Deloris. He vocalised this well, also. I wouldn't mess with this guy, and it made perfect sense that his henchmen would be so nervous around him.

Robert Annett as the chest-baring TJ showed some very good vocals in his musical ad-libs during the dialogue sequences. He appeared to be very comfortable with any movement given to him. He played a lovable version of this character, less afraid of his uncle than the rest of his cronies, bringing nice balance to the scenes he was in.

They say that good acting is about reacting and Paddy McGennity, who played Joey, is excellent at this. He listens carefully to every line as though it was the first time he was hearing it. They also say that one can never play the king, and that in such a scene, the rest of the actors need to react in such a way as to establish the King's effortless authority. Paddy's reactions to Curtis heightened this already imposing characterisation. And then there were those lustful moves on the floor. My goodness.

Josh Kelso as Pablo managed that Spanish motif well and deserves a round of applause for learning lines in another language. He completed a trio of individual stooges that filled the audience with glee. The chest wig was a scream.

Sheila Paolinelli as Sister Mary Martin- of-Tours and Aedin Hoey as Sister Mary Theresa evoked these aging senile nuns very well, adding lovely character to the scenes they were in. Suzanne Smyth and Caitlin McClurg, as Tina and Michelle respectively, provided comedy and accuracy in their backing vocals for 'Take Me to Heaven' and 'Fabulous, Baby!' There were some lovely moments of direction. Eddie's slapstick moments in the cop station were nicely fleshed out. This included an impressive stunt where he popped his feet on desk only for his chair to flip right over. The addition of a hard- drinking cigarette-smoking Mary Lazarus in the bar was comically revealed by Deloris turning her barstool at the perfect moment. The sincerity in the argument between Eddie and Deloris before 'I Could Be That Guy' had a nice level of tension to it. Mary Lazarus hilariously kicked Mary Martin-of-Tours, waking her up from her slumber at the piano. Having actual people walk in off the streets during 'Take Me to Heaven' was a great idea. The Mother Superior treating herself to a cigarette and the way she revelled in the long silence was very effective - done very much in private and not betraying her public persona. I wasn't well when those nuns started to say "take me", when the gun was pointing at Deloris, such was its touching impact.

Musical Director Gareth McCreevy's enthusiasm could be felt through the little gap at the top of the stage, where a slither of the band could be seen. He almost looked like he was dancing, such was the gusto with which he conducted his ten- piece band. I think MDs should remember that they are part of the aesthetic and atmosphere of the show and a grumpy all-about-business demeanour will not do. There was a super screen at the back of the hall, which fit so perfectly into its box that it looked as though it had been specially made. This meant that the band never overpowered the performers, yet we still got a hint that they were there, and the performers still got the support the they need also. This was the perfect combination for this petite venue.

It was clear that all principal and supporting cast were well prepared for their roles, as singing was delivered with confidence. The harmonies required from Tina and Michelle are all too-often butchered, so I am happy to report that these sounded really well here. Words were well-known, and diction was clear in 'Its' Good to be a Nun'. The choral numbers bounced off the stage, indicating thorough preparation. The backing vocals during the last bit of 'Here Within These Walls' were lovely. Nice high-pitched singing was elicited from the gangsters in 'When I Find My Baby' and 'Lady in the Long Black Dress'. The nuns' choral singing as the Mother Superior ordered them back to bed was gorgeous. The harmonies when Deloris was under attack were delivered in such a meaningful way. This was the first time I saw how empowering singing had become for them. Different productions choose to reprise different songs for the curtain call. I love the choice of 'Raise Your Voice' and the addition of the male voices gave it a communal feel.

Choreography was by Timothy Bell. The initial audition scene was nicely structured, with plenty of movement squeezed in here. There was also a very good amount of dancing in the all-male 'When I Find My Baby'. The nuns were very well prepared for their moves and the slickness in which they were executed is to be commended. 'It's Good to be a Nun' had some lovely formations around Deloris. Show choir choreography demands so much of that on-the-spot arm movement and it is difficult to be inventive here. Thankfully, Timothy was able to devise sequence after sequence that felt fresh and new and enabled the excellent choral singing to bounce off the stage. The gangsta moves on "Mathew, Mark, Luke and John" in 'Sunday Morning Fever' were gas. The 'Lady in the Long Black Dress', with all its sensual moves, involved much rolling around on the floor and pelvis thrusting. This was a howl and the audience were loving it. All the performers looked like they were having so much fun and we had fun as a result.

Stage Management was by Clare Donnelly and cleverly utilised the actors where possible. The nuns brought the benches on and off and were into business immediately.

Simultaneously, almost, the gangsters brought their own brick corner on, making it look as though the characters were creating their own sense of space.

The costumes were by Attracta Campbell and Janet Campbell, who also engaged Theatrical Costume Hire, Newry. Deloris' look - with her silver jacket, black top, teeny black shorts and high F.M. boots - combined style with tack, which I think is just right for this slightly lost character. The gangster costumes were a little showbiz (think Bee Gees/Abba etc) and I prefer it when they wear clothing more grounded in reality, less matchy-matchy and subtler - such as some nice leather bomber jackets etc. The dresses, fur coats and boots made the girls in the cop station look suitably skanky.

Eddie's costumes were suitably tragic, as he wore this baggy clothing far too high around his waist. There was some amount of sweat applied. When he finally goes in for the kiss with Deloris, he turned his back to reveal a heart shaped sweat mark on his back with the arrow cutting through which was inspired. The reveal during 'I Could be that Guy' was well executed. His red shirt and white waistcoat/trousers/ flares were nicely comic during this fantasy sequence.

There were a number of postulants in the convent, which was novel, and suitable considering their natural youthful appearance. The head-dresses and night- dresses on the nuns were well-sourced and looked the part. The silver material in 'Sunday Morning Fever' cleverly reflected the colours of the lights. The mis-match of 70's style onesies/catsuits on the fantasy dancers in the reprise of 'Fabulous, Baby!' looked great. The final silver robes with gold crosses looked wonderful. Deloris' final black and silver costumes, and a similar idea for Mother Superior, looked well and made them stand out.

I am not sure that the Mother Superior needed to be aged so much. In actual fact, many religious orders have a less- aged person at the helm. She cannot be too young, but she needs to have more wits about her than the senile elder members. The black lines on her face were not hugely convincing, unfortunately. That said, this was the first time I saw her remove the head piece of her habit, in a private moment, and I really liked the dimension this brought. Tina and Michelle sported similar enough hairstyles, evoking a sense of uniformity in their roles as backing singers, without being identical. Eddie's hair, with those greasy individual strips of hair glued down onto his forehead was so suitably gross. Curtis' was the only gangster who had hair that could be worked with. It's slicked-back nature was menacing. This is a common occurrence and I have seen productions that used wigs and glued side-burns etc. to evoke the 70s nature of the gangsters. The afros on the "gay guys" were a very good touch. Lighting and Sound was by Geoff Clarke. There was some nice use of gobos to give extra texture to the scenes and various swirling movers added energy. Spotlights were also used to good effect to punctuate solos and duets. Sound managed to create a lovely balance between the band and the performers. This was possible, most likely, by the positioning of the partially-visible band behind the stage, meaning they did not over-power in this small space.

Set design, by director Neil Keery and Seamus McGrady, used the space well. There were two folded pieces on either side of the stage that would open to reveal new spaces. The lectern, with its purple material and scripture book was subtly down on the floor, out of the way, ready to use when necessary. When I first saw the set for the church/convent, I thought "hmmmm that doesn't look great". But the joke was on me. Paint sheets were eventually stripped away to reveal organ pipes and the white windows were replaced with burst of colourful stained glass. The change in the aesthetic cleverly mirrored the success of the choir, and the funds they were raking in for the church, and it was worth the less-than-impressive original set-up. Eddie's comic book inspired Marvel duvet was a nice nod towards his less-than-cool nature.

These are examples of some lovely touches by director Neil Keery, always endeavouring to add additional clarity to the script and give extra detail to characterisation. He was part of a great production team that made sure that the show bounced off the stage. Add this to a cast of excellent performers and you have a recipe for success. It was such fun. After a long trek through the snow, Newcastle filled me with glee. Do you get it? Sorry.

It is difficult to believe that Top Hat, a musical based on the 1935 movie, was first staged in 2011. It is so lacking in cynicism or the modern obsession with misery, that it plays as though this stage version was written decades earlier. There was a lovely atmosphere in St Michael's Theatre, as I arrived at New Ross Musical Society's 50th Anniversary Production. The band looked very snazzy in their tuxes, and the welcome announcements were done in a suitably Broadway-style voice, both choices setting the tone nicely. This was a stage show that most would not have seen before and perhaps very few people knew what to expect. Nonetheless, the audience simultaneously jumped to their feet at the end, signalling that they had loved the show.

Not only did Derek Shannon direct this production, but he also gave us a star turn as Horace Hardwick. I sometimes get a little wary when members of the production team take on performance roles (or when a director MDs or plays piano or whatever). I become suspicious that, with their eyes off the stage, the polishing that will inevitably happen in the final rehearsals/first performances can be lost, resulting in a less than sheen finish to the show. Thankfully, you would never know that this director was double-jobbing, such was the gloss to this production. Plus; despite the fact the society were affected by that nasty Storm Emma, there was no evidence that this show was not audience-ready.

With a show that used a finely decorated and practical set, brought to life with suitably simple old-school lighting, with fine principal performances and an ensemble dressed beautifully, Derek gave us a delight of a show. The relationships between the characters were nicely explored. Horace and Madge had a very interesting dynamic, Bates the man- servant and his master had a comedic relationship, where the servant forever hilariously put down his 'superior'. Our leads' romance was a slow-burner. The way in which Dale's frosty attitude melted away, as she began to tolerate Jerry more in their dance routine at the bench, was a good moment of character development. Dale also took the higher status in their seduction number in Act Two. Perhaps there was a bit more girl power in this show than we might have seen in older similar stories. When the chorus appeared, they did so with intention such as when the maids entered to tidy the hotel room before joining in the dance.

The set was designed and constructed by Ben Hennessey. With this set, there was such a clever use and re-use of space. The wings jutted out in the shape of New York buildings. The pieces that came in front with the various doors were inspired. These partitions created a rich aesthetic in themselves and created lots of new playing spaces, while covering up the seamless scene changes going on behind. The rest of the set had beautifully rich furniture that gave the show a professional finish. The hotel, with its rounded desk, two spheres in the middle for seats and elevator worked very well. This desk area would easily transform into a bedroom, a balcony or a bar stocked with bottles. The panels in the wall were removable, making different pieces of artwork etc., effectively re-using the same stand-alone set, whilst creating different spaces within the narrative. Each scene was dressed to perfection with an impressive array of quality period props that added to the richness of the aesthetic.

This set was excellently manoeuvred by Stage Manager by Mark Hayden. This was in no small part thanks to the clever design that brought a series of walls/ doors in front of the main performance space, allowing the action to continue and enabling invisible scene changes to happen behind. That said, it was not always so easy and there were still some slick changes that took place before our eyes, as the set effectively moved into new versions of itself.

The set also use a screen at the back to great effect, managed on the evening by Production Manager and Lighting Designer, Paul Malone. The way in which half the screen was used to show the black and white moving street-scene behind a carriage ride was very clever. This gave us a different flavour here to when the full screen was used, showing invention in how the available set pieces were utilised. The old-fashioned image of the town in Milan was lovely and the waterside backdrop created great perspective and depth. So many shows nowadays are lighted like a Diversity concert. This production, however, had a lovely old school vibe which was very fitting, with pastel shades used to blend in with the set. That said, some of the numbers might have benefitted by a little extra punctuation to bring us into the number or in dance breaks. Follow spots were used to good effect to highlight the leads within group numbers. There was a moment or two when the image on the screen did not appear on time. This might be the result of double-jobbing by the lighting technician.

Musical Director Philip Kennedy appeared to be very much on top of things, showing spot-on control over the band. He had a clear conducting style, that was big when necessary and subtle when possible. The band motored along at a great pace and were tight throughout. There was a lovely old-school sound created, particularly enhanced by the brass section. He managed very well when additional scene-change time was required, by encouraging the band to continue playing until the right moment. The band were kept at a good level throughout, with all vocals and underscored dialogue clearly audible. That said, during the dance breaks etc. the band were let loose at little more and allowed to play with additional gusto. There was a lovely play-off at the end of Act One, before the house lights came up. The principal cast appeared very confident in their singing, suggesting that they were well-prepared. At times the female vocals were very dominant in choral numbers, particularly at the top of Act Two. I could see the male mouths moving but could hear nothing. This may have been more of an issue for the sound desk, in the charge of Abe Scheele of GS Audiovisual. This balance was better at the end of the show, however, and the full potential of the choral singing could be enjoyed. Sound was good in other areas in terms of cueing and use of sound effects. The gorgeous of-the-time choreography was by Anne-Marie Cooney. The first tap sequence was very good and the kick- line with canes brought that old-school magic, creating a stellar opening number that received massive cheers from the audience. The tap sequences throughout were lovely. The dancing after the curtain call combined simple but effective choreography, with the front-line doing a few more complicated moves, creating a lovely treat in the final moments. It is evident that a lot of work went into the choreography of this show, such was the slickness by which it was performed. There may have been scope, however, for the showgirls to really sell the routines with bigger brighter eyes and smiles, to ensure that they were really setting the tone of the numbers. Otherwise, this was very well done indeed.

Anne Marie's hard work was complemented by leading-man James Dobbs as Jerry Travers, who appeared to have worked very hard at perfecting his numerous dance routines. He must be very fit as his vocals never suffered during his highly energetic dancing. He has a lovely voice and performed his numbers in a relaxed and competent manner. He had a very good accent and was adorable in his partnership with Dale.

He was matched by a very good leading lady in Éilish Coady as Dale Tremont. She too executed her dance moves with precision. She could be feisty, funny, serious, flirtatious or stern when required. Pitching when singing on the balcony might have been a little suspect, which is surprising as the rest of her singing was good. Sometimes when we perform very close to the band, it can be a little hard to hear ourselves. Otherwise, this was a lovely portrayal.

Derek Shannon was hilarious as toff- producer Horace Hardwick. Speaking with lovely rhythms, he found that nice balance between heightened comedic characterisation and believability.

I completely believed that he was this character, such was his excellent accent and naturalism, despite the ridiculousness of his role. Horace faces a lot of funny stressors along the way, and Derek measured well how dishevelled and slightly unhinged his character became. He had a wonderful foil in his no non- sense wife, with Teresa Buckley as Madge Hardwick. She counter-acted all his ridiculousness with her dry personality. Her naturalism worked very well against his heightened lovie characterisation. She had some amazing one-line put-downs. Keith Flanagan was very good as the Italiano Alberto Beddini. His Italian accent was excellent, and he had all the suave necessary to fulfil the role of ladies-man. He was hilarious in his song. When he wrapped his leg around the flat… my goodness… and the audience showed an enormously positive reaction after this. He comically got famous English sayings incorrect such as "The penny has finally come home to roost", which were very funny.

Seán O'Brien made some hilarious cameos as the droll-witted man-servant Bates. Each time he appeared he was in another hilarious costume, having been previously up to no good somewhere. His relationship with his employer was well-observed, as he used some dry-wit to throw shade at Horace. His "cousin Fionnóla" or his "Great-Uncle Farooq" gags got a great reaction, making it a joy every time he appeared.

There was also a long list of cameos in this show, with each person committed to their roles and ensuring that the high standards never slipped. The hotel manager's reaction to the two men booking the honeymoon suite does deserve a special mention for being quite hilarious.

The chorus in this show were committed to their roles and the dancing from the showgirls etc. was particularly strong. There is no doubt about the work that went into learning the dance sequences. Everyone looked a million bucks also. It is important to keep a subtle but focused eye on the Musical Director during big choral sequences. While I could see Phillip very clearly bring the company off at the end of a word, such as those ending in "s", not everyone obeyed his commands. A few more of those obligatory plastered- on smiles were necessary from some to give that extra 5% of energy and to really connect with the audience during those show-stopper routines.

In general, the cast looked gorgeous. Horace's quaffed hair and styled beard was very effective at establishing his lovie persona. The stylised streaks of grey in Alberto's hair made him look very distinguished. I had to wonder about Dale's plaits in her hair - whether or not these were too modern and if some nice curled pieces would have been more fitting. Perhaps this was supposed to be a modern twist on a classic look.

No stone was left unturned, by Costume Co-ordinator Susan Synnott, with these fabulous costumes. When a society employs Utopia Costumes as their supplier, one is pretty much guaranteed a quality aesthetic in this department. This show was no exception, with the outstanding clothing on display. James managed some impressive quick changes and Éilish's appearance in her final fabulous white gown was impressively slick. They were simply gorgeous; with fabulous gowns, flapper dresses, coat- tails for the tap numbers with the shiny lapels, pompous cravats and loud jackets and shirts for Alberto, beautiful leisure wear and dressing gowns/pyjamas on the principals, burgundy uniforms on the hotel bell-boys and a green theme on the female employees, the maids, the ball dresses, all evoking the period beautifully. The use of pastels really evoked the time- period, linking in with colouring around the stage. Costumes, props, and set design all linked in with one another to ensure that certain colour schemes were used to pull the beautiful aesthetic together. What a gorgeous evening it was. New Ross Musical Society have a fine list of shows under their belt. They are not afraid to do new material or tried-and-tested favourites. They move from comedies to more serious pieces and back again. With the high standards evident in this show, from acting to aesthetic, no doubt whatever they choose next will be very good indeed. Congratulations to the society on their 50th anniversary and for staging the Irish premiere of Top Hat. I think we're going to see a lot more of it.

I seem to remember David Cunningham directing shows when I was only starting out on my theatrical career. I don't know how the man keeps going, but he does, and he does so with panache, as evidenced by the tidiness of this Newry Musical Society production of My Fair Lady. The snow was beginning to become a major nuisance as I made my way to Newry, a night earlier than originally intended, and it was a wise decision to change the date, as I might not have made it at all the following night. The one hour 20 minute journey North became a 3 hour 10 minute journey home, in the face of a blizzard, a rapid build-up of lying snow, and horrendously hazardous roads. But it was a journey worth making, combining a lot of nostalgia with a most enjoyable night of traditional musical theatre. From the well-designed and presented set, to the very good costume plot, and the excellent use of the stage, the show was more than pleasing to the senses, capturing the tone and atmosphere of the era and resulting in a nicely presented overall package.

There was just enough detail in the scenery to clearly indicate each setting. There was a plethora of good and appropriate props throughout, and furniture was good in detail. There was a lot of work for the stage team under Stage Manager, Leo Hayes, but at times it wasn't always coordinated, which caused a few long scene changes, but I did appreciate the industry involved in such a large show.

I did feel that closer attention needed to be paid, by a few of the principals, to the script. The show revolves around the "majesty and grandeur of the English language", and as such, the nuances of the script are vitally important. There were rather a lot of omissions and ad-libs that jarred slightly with an otherwise very fine production.

Choreographer, Donna King achieved a nice contrast between the refinement and elegance of Ascot and the Ball and the raucous busking of the cockney numbers, which were full of character and energy. Ascot was delightful and the Grand Waltz was well executed. The opening in Covent Garden leading into "Wouldn't It Be Loverly" was nicely delivered, and "Get Me To The Church" was the dancing high- light of the show. Chorus and dancers were well-disciplined and committed to their task.

Similarly, there was great commitment to the popular music of the show. From the start of the overture, there was an assuredness in the musical presentation, with Musical Director, Danny O'Neill, in good control of a very fine orchestra, who never over-powered the performers on- stage. Soloists were very well prepared, and the chorus made a strong impact in their opportunities to shine, with "Ascot Gavotte" and "Get Me To The Church" being the vocal highlights.

The confident and competent delivery of his songs was the out-standing feature of Fergal White's performance as Henry Higgins. Those lyrics are tongue-twisters and can often be lost, but his timing and his diction were excellent. He also displays a fine sense of comedy, but I did feel that he was a little over-animated/ agitated, on occasions, in his dialogue. His anger tended to verge on child-like temper tantrums, which lessened the self- assured, (some might say patronising) tone that one associates with the character. There were also several episodes of paraphrasing the script, which is so vital to the message of the show that it did slightly dilute his impact. That said, this is an extremely wordy and difficult role, and he did perform it with a good sense of authority.

Fiona Flynn seemed to really enjoy the role of Eliza, putting energy and emotion into her transition from flower girl to an elegant and very believable "lady". Her vocal quality was very good, with precise diction, which slightly highlighted the fact that her cockney accent slipped on occasions, but her character was strong and energetic. Once she became more sophisticated, her whole performance was more confident and highly commendable. Martin Morgan was a perfect Pickering, polite and dignified on all occasions, and with a very good delivery of that tricky "You Did It" solo. This was a lovely performance.

Ronan Sharkey had great confidence and stage presence in the role of Freddy Eynsford-Hill, and delivered "On The Street Where You Live" beautifully. My only concern was that he had a tad too much swagger early on to become the drooling, doting Freddy of the later scenes convincingly.

Damien Lavery thoroughly enjoyed the devil-may-care, wayward character of Alfred Doolittle, and injected a fine sense of comedy into his scenes. "Little Bit of Luck" and "Get Me To The Church" were strongly delivered.

He was ably supported by Sean Mullin and Paddy Heaney, who made the most of Jamie and Harry with good character and confidence.

Maille Connolly gave a good air of loyal yet indignant service to Henry Higgins, always obedient, yet not shy about airing her disapproval. A well-maintained characterisation.

Despite a script hiccup, Veronica Barr gave a robust and highly comical performance as Mrs Higgins, matching fine delivery with the most expressive facial expressions. Bravo.

With the exception of his beard and moustache being preposterously at odds with his natural hair colour, Jack McGowan established the sleazy character of Zoltan Karpathy most effectively.

Helena Hughes as Mrs Eynsford-Hill, and John Cookson and Judith Downey as Lord and Lady Boxington, added a sense of smug-superiority to the upper classes, with well-defined caricatures.

Anne-Marie Campbell as Mrs Hopkins and Jack McManus as the Bartender stood out among the plethora of cameo Cockney roles taken on by various chorus members.

And speaking of the chorus, they did themselves proud as singers, actors and dancers, adding ambience and atmosphere to all their scenes.

As with the choreography, there was a very good distinction between the classes in the wardrobe department. Cockney's were as scruffy as they should have been, and there was elegance in the presentation of the upper classes. Ascot was particularly attractive. Regardless of his tendency to shun the accepted dress code, Higgins most certainly should have been wearing white-tie and tails at the Embassy Ball, in the presence of Royalty. Hair and make-up were well-managed, with that exception of Karpathy's facial hair.

Lighting was more than sufficient in design, with good use of colours to create atmosphere and cueing was good. Sound was well-balanced and sound effects were spot-on.

There was a great sense of community pride about the whole evening, and your professional staff served you very well. Thank you to everyone involved for a night of warm entertainment that helped to thaw the chill of a very wintry conditions outside.

In a show that was musically very competent, technically acceptable and visually pleasing, it was helped along, in no small measure, by the tidy and traditional direction of Simon Pyper, who made good use of the talent available to him. There was a nice bit of scenery recycling involved in the set, which worked more than sufficiently, and other aspects of the technical presentation were well managed. What was once the Casa Rosada, converted most acceptably into the Golden Garter Saloon, and then to Fort Scully. Black drapes for "Black Hills of Dakota were a bit bland, but I appreciate the limitations of the stage.

Children were used to beef up the male chorus, which was a fine idea, but I think it might have been even more effective if they had been left as children, rather than made-up with stubble. However, I'm sure they enjoyed their experience, and they performed with good confidence.

Though small in size, the band, under Musical Director Matthew Campbell, had good balance and a good understanding of the score. While their pace and tempi were generally good, Higher Than A Hawk lost much of its charm by being rather rushed. I appreciate that the lack of a solid male chorus resulted in the lovely "Adelaide" harmonies being dropped. Vocally, the chorus were at their best during "Black Hills of Dakota" and "Windy City", with good clarity and harmony. Ashleigh Gault was a feisty Calamity Jane, completely comfortable with the vocal demands of the role, and displaying a good sense of comedic ability. She captured the frostiness of her relationship with Bill and was convincingly in love with Danny. "Secret Love" was delightfully rendered.

Courtney Burns was a pleasant and sincere Katie Brown, who performed with confidence, but could possibly have been more flamboyant and 'show-bizzy' in her revised rendition of "Keep It Under Your Hat". Her romance with Danny had a natural feel to it, and "Love You Dearly" was well delivered.

Aoife Barnes made the most of her opportunities to shine as Susan, evidently enamoured with Francis Fryer, and well able to stand up to her flustered employer. With such a brief involvement in the show, Cathy Curran could perhaps have played the role of Adelaide Adams with a more exaggerated smug superiority or bitchiness to really make a more lasting impact. That said, she did absolutely nothing wrong, and delivered "Harry I'm Planning to Marry" most competently. Brian McElroy brought a wealth of experience to his relaxed portrayal of Bill Hickock, exuding confidence and stage presence. I did however feel that, despite a very capable voice, "Higher than a Hawk" lost some of its tenderness by being rather rushed.

James O'Neill's Danny Gilmartin created a believable romance with Katie Brown, and played the antagonistic cabin scene with Bill with a strong sense of comedy.

Sean Harkin gave a strong performance of a fidgety and nervous Francis Fryer, using his comic ability to get the most from the role. I admire that he resisted the temptation to take the drag act too far over the top.

Extremely convincing also, was the high- blood-pressure portrayal of Henry Miller by Niall McLean. With a most amusing hyper-activity, he came across perfectly as the guy who is never quite sure if things are going to go right or wrong.

Good support was offered by Mel Carney as a very credible Doc Pierce, Len Fennell as Joe the Barman, and Jenny Long (yes, a female!) as Rattlesnake, the driver of the Stagecoach. I'm not entirely sure that a woman would have held such a position in such an era, but I appreciate that in the world of musicals, one often has to stretch boundaries based on availability.

The chorus, many of them very young, contributed well to the action, both vocally and visually.

This was a production that didn't focus too strongly on choreography, but the work that was done by Choreographer, Alex McFarlane was always tidy and appropriate. The chorus were well disciplined, and on those opportunities when the dancers came to the fore, there was a good level of competence. More could have been done comically with "Harry I'm Planning to Marry" and "Keep it Under Your Hat", but there was good movement for "A Woman's Touch" and an effective polka to start the Fort Scully scene. Good costumes helped to enhance the look of many routines, and there was attention given to hair and make-up, with my only reservation being the aforementioned stubble on the faces of the young lads. Try as they did, the make-up team couldn't prevent Francis Fryer from being a rather unattractive woman, but at least he DID look like a woman.

The general lighting was consistent and everyone who needed to be seen could be seen. There was good use of colours for atmosphere, even if, on occasions, smaller pools of light could have been used to focus attention on the principal action. Sound quality throughout was most satisfactory.

The combination of youth and experience worked well in this production, and in nurturing the musical talent of the future, the society can look forward to years ahead of presenting bright and entertaining shows. Thank you to all concerned for a most acceptable rendition of the popular "Calamity Jane".

Those of us of a certain generation learned all about harmony, diction, comedy and character from our close association with the wonderful operettas of Gilbert and Sullivan, and it's good to see that generation after generation still get immersed in the fun, the nonsense and the superb musicality of these masterpieces. Evidence that such old material can still generate excitement and talented performances was beautifully demonstrated by Tipperary Musical Society, whose production was as inventive and contemporary as it was rooted in tradition. Director Michael O'Donoghue had a field day putting together this highly amusing version of The Pirates of Penzance, infusing the traditional story and music with well-devised comedy and puns and jokes that even the great Mr Gilbert would doubtless have applauded. On a beautiful set, beautifully lit, a well- costumed presentation never flagged for a second, and produced some very fine performances. A hilariously clever "Sorry Her Lot" was added to the first act, sung by Ruth, and the "It really doesn't Matter" trio, purloined from Ruddigore, proved a great vehicle in Act Two for Frederick, Ruth and the Pirate King. "Fake News" found its way into the script, as did the long arm of the law and several other vocal and visual jokes, all of which enhanced the entertainment. A superbly funny Haka was performed by the Pirates before they went into battle, and was responded to by an equally funny Policemen's chorus of "Here we go gathering nuts in May." Indeed, the show was brim full of clever comedy which really tickled the funny bone.

The simple in design and nicely painted set gave no problems to Stage Manager, Brian English, and his team, and costumes throughout the show were of a very good standard. Pirates and Policemen were well attended to by the hair and make- up teams and the women were very well turned out.

From a music point of view, a fine orchestra, under the direction of Helen Colbert, provided a perfect accompaniment to the show, with good balance and secure tempi. On-stage, the choruses delivered well-rehearsed harmonies with energy and precision. "When the Foeman Bares His Steal" and "Hail Poetry" were the vocal highlights, but there were numbers a-plenty when good singing went hand in hand with comedic antics, without ever losing quality. Even during busy dance sequences, there was a good focus on ensuring that the music and lyrics were never sacrificed.

Emmet Donlan proved to be a dynamic and very capable Frederic, filled with righteous indignation at his lot, swash- buckling as a pirate and honourable when he left the pirate fold. His vocal quality was secure and very easy on the ear. He was well paired with Sinead O'Donovan as the delightfully flirtatious Mabel. Her confident voice was well able to cope with the demands of the role, and she enhanced her vocal performance with good timing and character acting. Her "Ah, leave me not to pine alone and desolate" duet with Frederic was very beautiful. John Murphy was a strong and dominant Pirate King, totally at home with the comedic aspects of the role, and quite superb in his vocal delivery. His diction, particularly in his patter numbers, was absolutely perfect.

The same must be said for Cathal O'Donoghue, whose very model of a modern Major General was exquisitely delivered. This was another performance that combined excellent vocals with a top notch understanding of comedy and a relaxed and confident stage presence. And not to be out-done by her male companions, Deirdre Ryan turned in a brilliant performance as Ruth, wallowing in the silliness of the first verse of the added "Sorry Her Lot" and displaying a sublime voice in the second verse. Her performance throughout was top quality. Aidan O'Connell not only impressed individually, but also led an excellent chorus of ridiculous Policemen, as the Sergeant of Police. His vocals were strong and his physical comedy was extremely funny.

Jack Sharpe was a disciplined and most effective Samuel, being both vocally secure and nicely individual as a character. Olwyn Grogan sang the role of Edith with a most impressive quality, and was a good natural leader of the daughters. She was well supported by Siobhan Scanlon as a delightful Kate, and Alma Quinn as a quirky Isobel.

Tipperary are lucky to have had a large and accomplished male chorus. Often, when the pirates and policemen split, the vocal quality of each group seems to lessen, but on this occasion, it remained strong and true. Similarly, there was good strength and ability in the chorus of daughters. The chorus contributed beautiful harmonies, lots of enthusiastic acting and reacting, and some very capable dancing and movement to the show.

It was her ability to choreograph strong comedy that established the talent of Choreographer, Miriam Ball. There was a lot of movement throughout the show, all of which suited the situation and enhanced the story, but the policemen's routines in particular really captured the imagination of the audience. Discipline was evident in every number, and Miriam, I'm sure, was grateful to have such energy and enthusiasm from her chorus.

Lighting was generally very good, with colourful atmospheres and nicely highlighted focal points when required. Sound quality was spot on.

It has been such a pleasure to attend Tipperary shows for the past three years and to see such a high standard of performance and presentation maintained. Thank you to all concerned for your sublime version of The Pirates of Penzance, filled with such energy and enthusiasm.

There was not a ticket to be had for Twin Productions' version of Sister Act, such was the draw to the Town Hall Theatre, Galway. This was my sixth version of this show to see this season and I am continuously surprised by how different it is each time I see it. The Town Hall Theatre has a cool vibe, with a nice foyer downstairs and an upstairs bar, providing a great night out for its customers. Inside the lovely theatre, there was a very impressive glittery Sister Act sign hanging on the stage and an atmospheric gobo on a gauze, that set the tone for the quality aesthetic that was to come. Indeed, the set and costumes were fabulous, baby. And then, Ladies and Gentlemen, there was Lucia Evans… It is no surprise that she was once on a TV show called You're a Star. This girl is amazing. Her believability in this role was second to none. Her interpretation unearthed all of the  comedic sass and character growth required for a scene- stealing turn as Deloris Van Cartier. Her accent was so convincing, her vocals were great (particularly gorgeous in the 'Sister Act' number), and she could body- pop with the best of them during the movement sequences. She was such a scream in the scene where she witnesses the murder, that she received a round of applause as she exited. What an incredible leading lady.

More unplanned applause was given after the scene where she and Róisín Egenton Lawless as the Mother Superior attempt to say grace together. This was a superb moment. Róisín has a lovely voice. She really spelled out the words of 'I Haven't Got a Prayer' with clarity, while getting many laughs during this number. Her riffing in the final moments with Deloris was a hoot, as was her repetition of the dance moves.

Mike Davenport as Eddie caught all the lack-of-cool required for this part with his slap-stick comedy in his first scene when he fell off his own chair. In fact, his first fall was so convincing that I wondered did he actually hurt himself. The fall looked very real and the dialogue that followed had issues, with Deloris prompting with made- up lines such as "I suppose you want to put me into hiding". I hope Mike was not hurt. Once he recovered from this scene, everything else he did was spot-on. He showed some lovely vibrato when he used his rich singing voice and he was cute and loveable when Deloris came to stay in his house.

Danielle McElroy was adorable as Sister Mary Robert. She is a lovely actress. She was nice and meek, such are the requirements of this characters, and has a sweet voice. She told her story very well in 'The Life I Never Led'.

Dave Langan had a super accent as Curtis and very clear vocalising when he sang. He is a man with strong presence, very convincing as the Mafia leader. His somewhat jolly singing contrasted cleverly with the lyrics he was singing (about disembowelling his girlfriend), something that delighted the audience.

Sarah Gilligan sported a brilliant old nasally voice as Sister Mary Lazarus. Her story-telling ability in 'How I Got the Calling' was very clear. She was highly comic in both of her scene-stealing raps. Ailbhe Slevin was suitably jolly as Sister Mary Patrick. She expertly evoked the same wonderful essence as Kathy Najimy in this highly convincing portrayal. She had excellent facial expressions. She was so cute, one just wanted to squeeze her cheeks. It is not the biggest role in musical theatre, but she played it with such mesmerising conviction. A lovely performance.

Mike Flaherty gave us a straight-laced Monsignor O'Hara. His glee, as he announced that the Pope would visit, was a hoot. Niamh O'Brien as Sister Mary Martin-of-Tours was super in this comic turns as she acted as though she was 2,000 years old. Linsey Cant was equally as good at the senile Sister Mary Theresa. Niamh McSweeney and Síofra Ní Chonluain played Tina and Michelle respectively. They are good actresses and movers, who gave excellent support to Deloris in these opening scenes. This singing is very challenging but was managed with aplomb.

Our trio of henchmen, Pablo, Joey and TJ were played by Marc O'Connor, Niall Conway and Cian Elwood respectively. They were suitably terrified of Curtis and their high-pitched vocals as they supported him in 'When I Find My Baby' were great. Niall as Joey proved that there are no small parts in his scene-stealing performance of 'Lady in the Long Black Dress'. He was hilarious, and I wanted him to have more material. He understands that comedy is about surprise and he knew how to spring a gag on the audience. His nipple action was something else. Similarly, Cian as TJ brought the house down with his thrusting. What he didn't do to that poor floor. My goodness. He also hit some nice high notes. Marc as Pablo gave the audience a great laugh with his falsetto singing here. Tuning in this number might have been a little suspect at the end, but no one cared, such was the enormity of the cheer they received when the song was over.

The title 'Twin Productions' comes from the two founding brothers Brian and Seán Power, who both directed this production. They provided a quality aesthetic throughout. Certain ecclesiastical set pieces were jaw-dropping. They ensured a pacy show. For example, it was a very good decision to cut the chase scene after Ernie's murder. This is never convincing or done well. At the end, the bows were ready to go after a quick curtain. There were some hilarious moments throughout. The show had to stop for applause when Deloris tried to ignore a dead body and when she and the Mother Superior said grace together. The nuns' awful singing in their first introduction was gas. The altar boys comically pointing to how much money was being raised was a great gag. Not all moments were played solely for laughs, however. Deloris was not afraid to fairly give it to Eddie in their row after she escaped the trio of gangsters in the bar. I love when the drama of this piece is given as much credence as the comedy. Sister Mary Robert also looked suitably lost in 'How I Got the Calling', indicating that all was not well with her. The blocking of the Mother Superior's 'I Haven't Got a Prayer' worked well, with her sincerely reaching for support from the table as she knelt down to beg God for help. The exit sequence from Deloris' bedroom, with the Mother Superior finding the bible and looking to the sky, was also very effective. I understand that directors are often faced with tough choices to make in terms of how many people from the greater ensemble to put into scenes. Having too many people on stage can result in a loss of structure to some moments, meaning that it can be difficult to isolate individual roles (particularly when they are all in identical habits). That said, I thought it was a slight shame that the core group of nuns appeared without the larger group of supporting nuns for some numbers. I think the songs had more punch when the larger group were used.

Elsewhere, Monsignor O'Hara should have been on before the "Job" gag, to make it look as though he was mid- sermon when lights came up. He and the Mother Superior might have been placed on the build-out at the cross-arch of stage left for the finale of Act One. She in particular would not have been so close to the nuns' performance. They needed to move aside here, and in the opening of Act Two also. The chase in the final scene used the space very well, but I am not sure if it always made sense. It might be an idea to seek some advice on stage combat to give a tad more realism to the attacks.

The lockers and presses of the cop station worked very well, decorated in wanted posters and a waste paper basket etc. The theme of blue was repeated around this set piece to pull the space together nicely. The diner sign with its devil's tail and flames looked great. This set was very well dressed - with its bar, beer bottles, stools, tables, assortment of old-style chairs and a very cool jukebox. Sliders were used to great effect, such as when the first convent scene was set up (complete with very cool gates) and when the down and outs were revealed for 'I Could Be That Guy'. The star-cloth also looked well for Eddies' number here. The mural of the Last Supper for the dining scene in the convent was outstanding. It was complemented by the tile work and the quality benched with beautiful swirl patterns on the legs. The backdrop used for 'Raise Your Voice' was awesome. The church scene, with its stained-glass windows, orb and image of Jesus, was just wow. The confessional boxes were really good. Curtis' den with was suitably dingy, with a pink bust and tassels on the nipples. The lamp, chair, mirror and TV all looked of-the-time. The blue walls, white skirting boards and brown door of Eddie's apartment worked very well. The red trimmed curtain that then appeared for the reprise of 'Fabulous, Baby!' was glorious. The series of brown doors with gold crosses was an example of how this was the set that just kept on giving. All of this was nicely finished off with quality props by Richard Brown.

The stage was managed by Kenneth McCarthy. The appearance of the stage crew might have been lessened by using the nuns and altar boys more to change some scenes. The tables and chairs brought on for the Mother Superior could have been placed by nuns working in the convent. The placing of these items was cumbersome and distracting and the crew were a little noisy in places. Otherwise, there were some fantastic reveals achieved, such as the murals etc. that were so impressive.

The lighting was designed by Paul Kelly. The sinister purple wash on the red- brick façade really helped create the idea of the alleyway of a nightclub in the scene in which Ernie is killed. The close lighting on the four gangsters in the final moments of 'When I Find My Baby' was clever as it covered the scene change behind them. The four movers and the ever-changing wash in 'I Could Be That Guy' gave nice energy to the number. The lighting change on the word "STOP!" in the 'Sister Act' number was very effective. The yellow movers within the purple wash (and smoke) at the end of the sequence in Eddie's apartment looked very cool. People were not always in the right places for the spotlights, or the spotlights were not always in the right places. More synchronising of this was required during tech rehearsals.

The first-class costumes were by Tara Killalea, Jenny Higgins and Creative Scene Productions. Deloris' first rig-out of purple boots, gold jacket and brown belt was complimented by the black and gold dresses on Tina and Michelle and the gold dresses on the four backing dancers. The suits on the gangsters were realistic and not costume-esque, like I have seen in some other productions. The skanks in the cop station looked the part in their leather skirts, revealing tops and fur coats. The cop uniforms also looked well, and Eddie had some suitably large sweat patches. Mother Superior's habit costume had some nice attention to detail, such as the brown beads she wore around her waist. Something went wrong with Eddie's reveal on the night, as his tie etc. had already fallen open long before the gag was to take place. I am sure this was better executed on other nights. Thankfully, the second part of the reveal was perfect and surprised the audience as intended. Mary Robert wore her Father Mulcahy boots at the end of the show! This was a very interesting little addition. The nightdress and headgear on the Mother Superior was just the ticket. This look was better than when some of the nuns wore pyjamas, which to me was too modern for a convent life in the 70s. The "gay boys" looked well in their dickie-bows and cummerbunds. Finally, the series of exciting nun costumes, as the choir grew in popularity and success, were gorgeous. The purple (with golden flame) looked very well in the finale of Act One and the reveal was awesome. Monsignor O'Hara's shiny purple costume for 'Sunday Morning Fever' was great fun. The silver and white nuns' costumes, with the doves, were fantastic. The darker silver on the principal nuns was a good idea. Deloris' gown in the finale was fabulous baby.

Wigs were provided by Ali Murphy and Pamela McGlynn. Tina and Michelle's wigs were different to each other, yet their brunette styling still pulled them together, meaning they were individualistic while still working as a pairing. The blonde wigs on the skanks in the cop station were effective. I am not sure how convincing the black lines were on Mary Lazarus' face. The cross-dresser in the bar scene might have looked a little more like Deloris, in terms of wig etc. to make more sense of the fact that the gangsters mistake him for her.

John O'Dea was Musical Director for this production, with Eoin O'Corcoran directing the choral and principal vocals. Eoin also gave very clear conduction on the evening. Principal vocal performances were top-notch. Deloris' sass in the counterpoint against the Mother Superior created a lovely contrast between the two voices and their delivery. The off-stage backing vocals in 'Here Within These Walls' were very nice, with some lovely low voices featured. The gangsters' high- pitched backing vocals, as they supported Curtis in 'When I Find My Baby' were great.

This was the most synthesised version of Sister Act I have heard, with the use of tracks instead of a full live band. This is an expensive show to stage as much is required (and was delivered in this production) in terms of set and costumes. Money certainly does not grow on trees, but I have to say the live instruments were missed. That said, certain moments such as the Country and Western style backing for Deloris' part in 'How I Got the Calling' was clever.

The chorus was made up of a committed group of ladies who worked hard to provide an entertaining evening for the audience. More projection was needed by some soloists in 'How I Got the Calling'. The microphone cannot do it all. Harmonies were subtle in places for some of the nuns' choral pieces, such as 'Sunday Morning Fever'. There appeared to be a lot of people singing the melody, while depending on a few to sing the harmonies. When this is the case, it may be necessary to work more dynamically with the sound desk, to ensure those more confident with harmony lines have more support from the mics. Eoin needs to make sure that everyone comes off the words at the same time, particularly those ending in "s". The jury is out on how much vocal impact there was in some of the choral pieces. Perhaps, there were sound/microphone issues that meant the sound did not carry as it might. That said, by the reprise of 'Raise Your Voice' at the curtain call, I thought some of the cast could take their own advice here. It is difficult to harmonise and do so much dancing, however. Sound was designed by Fintan Higgins. Cueing was very good throughout the evening. It was difficult to know whether more support from the sound desk was required to enhance the choral singing, or whether or not the nuns needed to give it more welly. The gunshot sound that killed Ernie did not sound like it came from the gun, unfortunately. The sound effects to illustrate the Convent gate opening, as Deloris first arrives to meet the Mother Superior, worked very well. The singing by the nuns in Deloris' bedroom was the best choral work of the evening, so well done for that.

The show was choreographed by Declan J. Gardiner. Tina and Michelle's involvement in 'Fabulous Baby!' combined moments of structured dance and moments where they sat and listened etc., nicely amalgamating musical performance with acting. The inclusion of the four backing dancers in Deloris' audition was a nice way to enhance performance opportunities for the rest of the cast and to utilise the talents of the group. The gangsters' finger-clicking and leg-pointing behind themselves were nicely comic, as they supported Curtis in 'When I Find My Baby'. The moves in 'I Could Be That Guy' were simple but effective.

While there were certainly some good moves in the finale of Act One, I would argue that there was the possibility for the exploration of more interesting formations to add variety. But if there were aspects in need of improvement in this show, they were made significantly better by Lucia Evans, who was simply fantastic as Deloris. Other positives about this show are primarily concerned with the quality aesthetic provided by Twin Productions in terms of the amazing set and gorgeous costumes. If other societies are thinking of doing this show next year, they would do very well to contact Twin Productions about where they got this set, because it was very special.

Something I find so appealing about Jesus Christ Superstar is that one never sees the same show twice. The script is really just a list of song lyrics. Those involved in telling this story must start from scratch, deciding the time in which the story is set, the relationships between the characters, what is actually happening during the songs, and which historical elements (if any) to include.
