Primarily, this version of Jesus Christ Superstar was set in biblical times, with nods to more contemporary issues appearing throughout.

The intimate, domestic, human story was fleshed out against the public lives of these characters. There were moments when twentieth century imagery was represented on stage, creating stark changes in the setting of the narrative. Was it a unique version of this show that endeavoured towards trying something new, daring, original and thought-provoking? Absolutely yes. Did it work? For the most part, yes.

The show began with the appearance of some contemporary young children dressed up as Nativity-play characters. The idea had super potential. This followed with a series of vignettes of crowds pulling lumps out of each other, creating a stark contrast to the innocence of the school play. There were some lovely nods to the stories of Jesus throughout, such as when he insisted that the children should come to him.

But there was much darkness also. The sound of Judas' bones breaking was harrowing, even more so by the accuracy at which the effects came in. The sound of the babies' cries was disturbing. More accuracy was evident during the 39 lashes, giving those an unsettling realism. The terrifying thunder and lightning sound effect nearly sent me into cardiac arrest, which I imagine was its purpose.

'Herod's Song' was unique. His wives appeared terrified of him and protective of their children, not surprising considering he took out a voodoo doll and killed the children by stabbing it, all while mincing about in teeny golden underwear.

This menace juxtaposed against the ridiculousness of his image, certainly doing something more interesting than the usual way this can be played for laughs. Herod was apparently crazy and that was certainly evoked, while ensuring that the dark and cruel tone of the story was not interrupted for a glitzy giggle-getting showstopper.

Musical Director Naoimh Penston enabled high-quality principal performances and ensured well-performed and dynamic choral singing. She had a fun energetic way of conducting her eight musicians and provided clear support to the cast on stage. She conducts with her whole body, almost like dancing, but with excellent clarity as she brought in various instruments and instructed the dynamics. The first piece of singing sounded like there was one soprano supported underneath by a handful of altos, giving it an eerie banshee-like feel, as she prophesied death. The 80s rock/techno vibe was sometimes replaced by a lovely folk-like sound from the real instruments being used, giving the score an authentic timeless feel in places. The electric guitar solo, added in to underscore that moment when the love/ loyalty triangle between the leads was given time to breathe, was very cool.

Dynamics were well considered, particularly during that male descant in the leper sequence, where their pain could really be heard. The all-female "Well done, Judas" was haunting in this moment. The tick-tocking of the drummer as Jesus contemplates ending his own life injected great tension into the moment. The band pounded away at full gusto and then, when they eventually died down, the "Well done, Judas" surfaced, which was really cool.

The choreography, by Martina Lynch, contained lots of highly energised moves that were slick and well-rehearsed. The direction really endeavoured to tell a detailed narrative and, as a result, I think that the best moments within the choreography involved story-telling or stylistic movement. There were a couple of times when that sock-it-to-the-audience out-front traditional idea of dancing in lines was used and, while there is no denying the performance quality, I suggest that these showbiz moments were a little jarring in the context of the overall vision of the production. In 'Simon Zealotes' for example, the circling around Jesus was a very good example of how this moment can be both entertaining and meaningful in the context of what is happening. Robert Vickers provided excellent clarity as Jesus. He was able to punctuate all his lyrics with a well-thought-out pentameter that ensured we caught his every intention. He knew when to slow down, speed up, take a pause, pull about the timing of numbers or speak a line when necessary to ensure that this was more than a concert. Thankfully, when using his falsetto, he still sounded like a man, avoiding those potential cringe- worthy moments that can sometimes be experienced when watching versions of this show. His final passion was so well acted. When the lights come up on the balcony, every second person was a blubbering mess, such was the way his suffering moved so many of the audience members.

Chris Currid was an emotional and musical tour-de-force as Judas. He never appeared for a second without the presence of an inner monologue going on. He acted every moment, extracting meaning with every second. This thought- process informed a highly convincing physicality, ensuring that there was no evidence of pre-rehearsed hand gestures or facial expressions. His technical ability when he sings is so impressive. His vocals were crystal-clear; we heard every word he sang, which is hugely impressive in this show that can often sound like a bag of scrapping cats. I think this is because he miraculously appeared to use his chest voice for the most part, while hitting those high notes in a powerful and masculine way, thanks to his impressive rock-tenor range. There was no cheating here. Just a lot of talent that made it all look effortless. Aly Coyne had a rough-around-the-edges style of singing as Mary Magdalene, which I liked. I sometimes wonder why Jesus and Judas sing in a rock-voice, yet Mary usually sings in a straight-up musical theatre style. She had an edge to her voice and a slight growl on the higher notes, evoking the idea that she is not simply some damsel in distress. Her singing of 'Could We Start Again, Please?' was particularly impressive. The love triangle that was suggested between herself and the two male leads was very well measured. She used her sensuality to pacify Judas, while remaining loyal to Jesus. She was the referee, but the jealousy Judas felt clearly fed into his dire decisions later on.

Éamonn Doyle as Annas was very good. I was so surprised to see how youthful Éamonn is from his biog photograph. His old-aged acting, forever bent over, was very convincing, This physicality really made him stand out and give variety and structure to these priestly scenes. He reminded me of Riff Raff from The Rocky Horror Picture Show, which I mean very much as a compliment.

Tomás Byrne was suitably authoritative as Caiaphas, injecting political tension into the narrative, bullying Jesus and Judas and ensuring their demise. He sang well also and himself and Éamonn made a great partnership.

Seán Hendley sang very well as Pontius Pilate. His 'Pilate's Dream' was nicely measured, and thankfully was not hysterical like some versions can be. He captured the authority of his character well, and nicely built the pressure and the unravelling of his situation in 'Trial by Pilate'.

Brian O'Gorman was excellent in his cameo appearance as King Herod. This role requires the actor to appear for one quick song, in which the characterisation, humour and cruelty have to be immediately established. We must be sucked in and given an unforgettable moment without a second to spare. This was all achieved and then some. Brian married humour and cruelty to give us a memorable performance of a mad king, half-naked with bejazzled chest and quaffed hair, treating Jesus like his play thing while killing babies through the use of a voodoo doll. This was a Herod I will not forget for a long time.

Pádraig D'Arcy was lovely as Peter. He has a very nice voice. He was suitably sorrowful in 'Could We Start Again, Please?' Gary Joyce was good as Simon Zealotes. I might argue that he is more of an actor than a singer, but he sold the song very well ensuring that the narrative was well maintained.

The cameo of Amy Penston as Pilate's wife was a joy. Not everyone would know the story of Pilate's wife's premonition and her role in impeaching her husband not to kill Jesus. I wish, in fact, this part of the story was included more in this short show. This extra stressor in Pilate's story was a lovely inclusion. Also, Amy has such presence and I wished that she had not left 'Trial by Pilate' so early.

All the inventive ideas conjured by Director Stephen Acton, the interesting choices and dynamics injected by Musical Director Naoimh Penston and all of the high energy dance moves made up by Choreographer Martina Lynch would mean nothing if they were not performed with competence and confidence. The ensemble of this production performed the material with style. Crowd scenes were highly atmospheric, with hissing and cackling all adding interesting layers to moments that could otherwise be played quite simply. A special mention to the quality of performance provided by the 'Superstar' dancers is warranted also. The costumes in the show suggested that the protagonists involved were dirt-poor, with Judas' coat in ribbons for example, evoking "People who are hungry/People who are starving". This enabled the higher-ups to wear more glamorous and highly structured rig-outs that separated them from the common crowd. The Priests contrasted starkly to the mismatch of the normal folk, with their highly uniform black robes, accessorised with dangerous blood-red material draped over the shoulders and around their waists. Their tall headwear, giving them extra prominence, was blinged-up to show the wealth within their garb. Pilate would appear in a fabulous dressing gown as he recounted his dream and later in a long purple leather mac.

Stylistically there were contradictions within the costuming, such as Judas' shoes that appeared a little modern and some women who appeared in trousers, which no doubt was all done on purpose to either blur the timeline or give a modern twist on a traditional look. Those in the temple also wore contemporary clothing, such as checked shirts. There was one woman going around with a statuette of Jesus and a crucifix, begging those having fun to stop sinning. Jesus arrived with the sound of a police siren to break all of this up. It begged the question: Who is this Jesus who arrives to a modern setting? Is he really there? Is he more a spiritual presence? Or are these protagonists all in some kind of cult, living out an alternative existence in their cave, against the modern day?

The lepers scene was quite interesting, as they were dressed iconically as people who would suffer in future years, such as soldiers from both World Wars or refugees currently risking their lives to cross the sea, pointing to the pressure on Jesus to heal the atrocities that happened long after his death. With these shifts in time, perhaps Stephen was suggesting that we have not come on much in two thousand years. I cannot say that the production, in its attempt to do all of this, did not present as a little muddled. I suggest that a world should be created and within that world, things should make sense. If there are too many worlds colliding, the truth might be sacrificed, in an anything-goes approach that could cause the audience to opt out of the narrative.

The chorus all appeared in black near the end, like Grim Reapers all here to signal Jesus' death. The 'Superstar' number, the one that traditionally looks at the narrative from another angle, featured angels in silver bodices with white wings, black feathered skirts and black wigs. Central to these women was a darker version, a black angel, played by Mary Magdalene, which was an interesting decision. Judas wore a grey suit with silver pockets and lapels to add to this statement moment on the phenomenon of celebrity.

I think that performance spaces, when presented in the abstract, should still have tone and atmosphere, shape and a sense of space. This was wonderfully achieved here. The walls appeared to be subtly decorated in scripture, Arabic I imagine, in a crimson colour that the walls of a sandy nation might take.

There was a stepped ramp swooping up and around the edges of the stage creating numerous levels on which the story would be staged. This cleverly enabled a sense of travelling in some moments while the performers could all remain in the space. There were two large entrances, shaped almost like the pages of a book on the upper level and the lower level. Other vignettes would be framed within these entrances also. There were two doorways on either side of the stage, beautifully lit in an amber candlelight at the top of the show. Under the ramps lay hidden another series of entrances and exits, giving the whole space the feeling as though tunnels were leading to an open cave space. I heard once that theatre is about a series of entrances and exits. This set-up enabled the cast to appear from all sorts of nooks and crannies, meaning we were always surprised by the next moment of action. Jesus Christ Superstar allows for bold choices and I am glad to report that Director Stephen Acton took the opportunity to make some such risks with this production. For that, I congratulate him. I believe that some of these choices created more questions than answers, which is perfectly fine. At times, it was as though Stephen created enough of a visual to get the mind racing without necessary resolving it for the audience in a logical way.

That said: I like soup and I like pizza and I like ice-cream. What I don't like is soup on top of a pizza on top of ice-cream on one plate. So, while each choice by Director Stephen Acton was interesting in its own right, the stylistic changes were somewhat problematic for me. A gourmet meal is thematic, with each course complementing the next. I am sure each moment readied us for the next, when random choices were made that bore little context to what had come before. For me, it's about creating a world that has rules and following those rules to ensure that everything that happens makes sense in the context of the world created. Harry Potter, Star Trek, Marvel Comics all have rules and we can buy into these worlds because they are honest in the context of their own narratives. My advice is to create one world, any world, and stick to it clearly, if we are to buy into its credibility. Sometimes we try to do too much.

Perhaps I am pulling the thing apart far too much. I find Lyn Garner, theatre critic for The Guardian, has something interesting to say about this: 'I sometimes wonder whether being too alert, too attuned to the cerebral rather than the emotional can actually hamper rather than help. Maybe there is a case for also feeling a play with your heart and not just seeing it with your eyes and hearing it with your ears, perhaps more in the way that you might experience a piece of music…. It is easy as a critic to fall into the unhelpful and self-defeating mindset that each play you see is some kind of exam and that you pass or fail on whether you "get it" or not. But of course there's no right or wrong; we'll all see different things.'

This production did not hold back with the passion of Jesus. The placing of the thorns on his head, as he screamed in pain, was very upsetting. His bloodied body was harrowing in its realism. The two Marys screaming at the foot of the crucifix, as Jesus writhed in agony, was harrowing. The house lights came up and every second person was a blubbering mess. Leaving Jesus on the cross as the audience filed out was so unsettling. His stillness made it look like an enormous crucifix over the altar of a church, as though frozen in time. This was highly emotional stuff in a production with quality leads, original directorial ideas, and dynamic choices from the pit. I don't think I have seen an audience moved in this way on my travels to date.

When it comes to writing, composing and directing your own musicals, I've been there, done that, worn the t-shirt and I know precisely how it feels to be totally absorbed by the project, so let me say without hesitation that in bringing Mr Carter the Musical to the stage, I appreciate the courage and determination of writer/composer/director and musical director, Stefan J. Doyle. Furthermore, he has demonstrated that he is a fine musician and a composer of some excellent songs. "Bang Bang Piano Man", "Sailor Man" and "Story of Us" were racy and exciting and filled with a the glitzy sense of show-biz, while "Mountain Top", "Wonder How The Moon Blinks Twice" and "Dreams" were melodic and romantic in tone and texture.

There were dramatic numbers too, like "Screw It", "Cry Over You" and "I Can't Hold You" that are potentially strong songs, even if I wasn't at all convinced that they fitted the show.

What Stefan successfully achieved, as a director, was to surround himself with some very gifted and talented young performers who gave 100% to making an impact on the stage. I'd have to be honest and say few of the cast looked totally relaxed in their roles, but I'm pretty sure that was due to the quality of the script and the lack of a coherent plot, for the show, as it stands, needs a lot of work to be a more cohesive piece of musical theatre.  It is not my place to adjudicate the show as a performance piece, but to review the production and performances, but it's impossible to review individual performances without referencing the script.

In its current state, nobody but the author could possibly direct this show, as I think the plot and the style of the production obviously make more sense in his own head than it does on paper or in performance. I mean this only as an observation that what the writer sees isn't necessarily what the audience perceive, and perhaps as Director, Stefan needed to step back more often to be sure that all of his thoughts translated into a cohesive story. There needed to be more meaningful interaction between husband and wife to set the scene initially. We also jumped into and out of the back stories of some of the supporting characters which had little relevance to the main story and served more as a distraction. Continuity was a problem, with unrelated scenes seeming to run together randomly, and the handling of the dialogue and the use of the curtains during the finale was repetitive and unimaginative. If the script was full of clichés (and it was), it was echoed by some inadvisable "dramatic" clichés that really should have been left on the shelf. A very drunk Darcy, dragging herself from the back to the front of the stage was as painful to the audience as it probably was to her. The basic problem with the direction was that the show was trying to be something that it wasn't. ie, high drama. In a world full of real life issues, the heartache of thespians wanting to be in the limelight comes across as extremely shallow and it's all been done so often. Such a story succeeds when it doesn't take itself too seriously, like the classic '42nd Street' or 'Crazy for You'. A show-business show like 'A Chorus Line' (which Mr Carter echoes quite a lot) works because the script gives powerful definition of characters and relationships. Unfortunately, that wasn't the case with 'Mr Carter'.

From a technical point of view, there were too many occasions when the back lights blinded the audience, and some of the solo spot lights were not always hitting their intended target. Played against a black box set, the show needed more imagination from the lighting desk to create atmosphere. As an on-stage rehearsal space, the black box was fine, but the script frequently refers to this becoming the greatest musical of the century, and the final "show-biz" numbers, all of which were very good, needed more glitz and dressing to reach a level suggested by the script. Stage Manager, Tadgh Magner, had little to do, but props were efficiently placed when needed. The sound engineer did a good job with balance and cueing, despite the band occasionally over- playing against soloists.

The high points of the show were the superbly drilled and executed tap routines, usually featuring "Bill" as the focal point, but brilliantly backed up by the supporting female cast. In conjunction with Holly-Jean Williamson, some of the other dance numbers were a tad bland, but with Robert Donnelly in control and up-front, a touch of choreographic class was brought to the production.

As mentioned, some of the music in the show was of a very high quality, but composer/ Musical Director, Stefan J. Doyle needs to be careful that his zeal on the keyboards doesn't overwhelm the performers on stage. The sweeping crescendos were frequently over-played and over-amplified, and on occasions, while the drummer was an excellent performer, it sounded like the keyboards and drums were competing for domination. The exaggerated crescendos at the end of several numbers also resulted in the singers finishing their performance several beats before the musicians reached their last note. While not doubting Stefan's talent as a musician, being Musical Director is all about keeping everyone together, and on a few occasions, Stefan the musician became a tad self-indulgent, at the expense of Stefan the MD.

Likeable though he was, there is little I can do but sympathise with David Cronin in the role of Mr Carter. His dialogue was stilted and repetitive, and there was minimal development of his character throughout the show. As the title character, he needed more action, more personality and more script to really make an impact.

Olwyn Grogan did everything in her power to make Mrs Carter a believable character, and if her monologues seemed to aimlessly meander on occasions, she at least managed to act out the sentiments dictated by the script. Her vocal ability was very well highlighted in "Dreams" and again in "Fools Forever in Love".

Holly-Jean Williamson played the role of Liddy much in the exaggerated style of the silent movie stars, except of course, that she wasn't silent, and I have to say that such a style works considerably better on screen than on stage, where it comes across as melodramatic and laboured. She wasn't helped by a fairly awful wig. Her vocal contributions showed a good ability to deliver a number, and she moved reasonably well throughout.

In every possible way, this production was "owned" by Robert Donnelly in the role of Bill Addams. He managed to make himself totally believable as a real person in a surreal setting, brimming with energy and confidence. His self-styled tap routines were beyond brilliant, performed with flair and finesse, and he was, without question, the adhesive that held the whole show together.  I have not seen better tapping in a long, long time, and would relish casting this young man in the lead roles in 'Me and My Girl', '42nd Street' or 'Crazy For You'. His training with the Billie Barry Stage School has paid dividends, and I confidently predict that, given the right environment, this young man will go very far in his theatrical career.

Olivia Parkinson made a very good impact in the role of vindictive but fragile show- girl, Darcy, and if her monologues and her torch song tended towards the over- dramatic, she at least whole-heartedly threw herself into them with conviction. Susan Akintomide, despite being given some very strange direction, and a script that was a clichéd commentary on the issue of race, gave a stunning performance as Aby, the highlight of which was a super fabulous rendition of "Mountain Top" exhibiting a powerful vocal quality that made this, vocally, the outstanding number of the show.

Convincing too was Chelsea O'Toole as Eva, in a role that allowed her to be sassy and flirtatious, a chain smoker, and frequently sick and coughing, which she did very convincingly, even though it didn't seem at all relevant to her character or the plot. She was also a very accomplished hoofer, as were all the girls.

Tom Doonan gave a very credible performance as Eddie the technician with a heart, and ultimately as an old man looking back at his fond memories of show-business and lost opportunities in love. With a re-write, this should be the character who narrates the story, looking from the outside in. There wasn't enough of him in this version.

Shelley Calvin as Sally, Carla Silver as Mavis and Matilda Magner as Annie, similarly worked well to create believable characters and shone as energetic and accomplished singer/dancers in the show- biz numbers. The cast was completed by nice cheeky performances from young Grace Egan as Letty and I believe it was Elicia Dalton that I saw in the shared role of Sarah. Two young ladies with good dancing feet and plenty of attitude, who will doubtless be stars of the future. There was no chorus in the show, but all of the above became the all-singing all-dancing ensemble, and the moments when they performed their excellent routines were among the best moments of the show.

The costumes for the show were generally very good, and the dancers' costumes were excellent. Even more impressive were the quick changes that the girls performed between the finale numbers. Wigs and hairstyles, with the exception of Liddy's wig, were a good observation of the era, and make-up seemed accurate and appropriate. There was good ageing of Eddie for the final scene.

It is always a pleasure to visit an original show, and to be there at the launch of something new, but along with that pleasure comes an obligation to be as honest and helpful as possible to try to help the show on to further heights. It would be remiss of me not to suggest that perhaps Stefan J. Doyle needed to step back from this production a few paces and view it as a punter, or even to appoint a neutral observer to say this works and this doesn't work so well. The strength of this piece was the music, which given a better frame work, would make an even more powerful impact, and while the choreography was remarkable enough to hold the audience attention, there were swathes of script and monologues that were either superfluous to the story, or over-dramatic for their own sake, rather than to benefit the plot. It was this lack of a cohesive script that left me somewhat unsure of the whole production, despite there being a very talented cast working hard to keep it going.

Finally, if this review seems harsh, I trust it will be accepted in the spirit in which it is intended, that is, as a warning that if, as referred to in the show programme, there is an intention to "announce it's UK Premier in none other than the West End London later in the year", it will need a lot of rewriting to prevent it being torn apart by professional critics whose honest brutality would make my observations look like a rave review. I know from my own experience that it's easy for the Author/ Composer to become too deeply involved to actually see when things are going wrong, and it's a good lesson to learn to delegate, and to allow others to contribute to the process. I'm grateful to have had the opportunity to view the show and to meet the very charming and impressive cast members, and I wish you well in the future.

The Hired Man is a well-meant, beautifully scored, but somewhat flawed piece. Like all good plays, it explores the domestic against the backdrop of greater events, such as war. It has all the ingredients; love, sexual misconduct, the people revolting against the system, and death. I might argue that it tries to do a little too much and achieves slightly less as a result. The love triangle at the centre of the show is set up very well but is conveniently disposed of, causing some drama with a rather tidy resolution. After everything that happens, there is no real harm done. The themes of the war and the miners' working conditions battle it out for supremacy within the plot, with the war winning out. The miners' stuff involves one argumentative union meeting and a father worried that his son wants to take it up. The mining accident results in everyone being okay, which misses the opportunity to show the full harrowing existence of these workers' reality. However, the fact that John served his country and has no choice but to return to these conditions is tragic, ensuring that the show has something to say. The music is a firm- favourite for so many musical theatre lovers, the characters are well-drawn and their story is an emotive one. My job is not to assess the writing of the show, but how well the society managed it and I am glad to report that Galway Musical Society staged a gorgeous production of The Hired Man.

John Wright's beautiful set created a striking hill of rock and plant-life. The ground was covered in soil, which was a lovely addition to this space, with the audience was raised looking down on the stage. There was a proper waterfall in the rocks, which created such aesthetic and aural atmosphere. The kitchen set was gorgeous; with its redbrick, and rich three- dimensional grey stone texture, believable without needing to be a full set-piece. The later kitchen set-up was lovely, adding a cupboard, showing the passing of time. Three pieces of trench-like set pieces came on for the war scene, filled with logs and sandbags. The flashing red lights on the cyc to indicate explosions, coupled with the smoke spewing from the rocks was memorable.

Ronan Kenny of Roken Lighting ensured that lighting was simplistic, just like the people's lives in the story. There were no Diversity Concert style laser beams of lighting here, thankfully. There was a lovely sunset on the cyc, as the stage sat there in all its glory as the audience filed in. There were clever lights hidden behind some texturising material on the flats, enabling them to light up, which was very cool. The explosions during the war were very well done. The lighting was tasteful and tame, like the story itself. How the rock lifted up to reveal the mine underneath was a fantastic surprise, with blue light creating the dark atmosphere below. This worked great as the audience were looking down upon them, creating the illusion as though they were really low down. Another surprise came with the flats revealing themselves as a gauze, housing the images of those who had died. Wonderful.

Stage Manager Chontelle Kenny, assisted by Jacqlyn Cronin, ensured that the cast were well rehearsed in their scene- changing tasks, resulting in there being no need for stage crew to appear. The setting up of the pub was subtle, as it was happening while dialogue took place on the opposite side of the stage (something that works well when one uses a wide stage like this). This pub set had been left on for quite a while, but we never noticed because of how the rest of the scenes were staged and lit. This was far better than trying to take it on and off every five minutes. The final mining accident was very well executed, as the rocks lifted to show the actors below.

Naturalism. That is the word that mostly resonates with me as I reflect on this production. The set looked like real rock and was decorated with proper plants, foliage and soil. The chorus never mugged any of their material, but were utterly convincing in their acting. I believed all the lead characters, none of whom tried too hard to "show" us anything, but rather they engaged in natural rhythms that made their dialogue flow with brilliant understated sincerity.

Director Paul Norton must have been responsible for this natural and sincere tone, as it was uniformly actualised by the entire cast. The opening number achieved clarity by giving the employers boxes to stand on. Our heroes were nicely connected in their duets, not performative or Disney-like. The inclusion of a real infant was special. I was on the edge of my seat as Jackson dramatically rows with Emily in the kitchen, resulting in their kiss. The actors here allowed the melody to take second place over the emotion, which captured their passion expertly. They almost couldn't sing because of their heightened emotional state. John's return from his trip created some brilliantly complicated reactions from Emily. The fighting was superb; exciting, well- staged and realistic, not at all cringey like some stage combat can be. John battered Jackson and threw Emily to the ground, allowing her to start her song on the floor, which was moving. There was definitely something in my eye when that older gentleman hugged the youngest soldier before going to war. Harry's death, complete with blood exploding from his mouth was highly impactful and John's recount of this, with the girls sobbing at the table, was moving. There was a nice change in mood for John and Emily's final duet after the folk dancing. This was lovely and simple, intimate and realistic, not showbiz-like or overly performative, all beautifully performed against the trickling of the waterfall. The accident in the mine was very well staged and acted. The scene between Seth and John at the end was touching.

I am not sure if the levels in the Jackson/ May/Harry scene at the top of Act Two were fully explored. To me, this is a complicated moment and where he (and we) wonder for a second if he could be Harry's father. I did not see this complication, with Jackson walking off rather jovially at the end. I might argue that the trench scenes were the tiniest bit repetitive; some moving of the trench pieces and more switching up of the formations/activities of the actors might have enhanced these moments. Given the simplicity of the lives of these village folk, little was required in the Hair and Make-Up department. Jackson was the only one with a bit of hair-oil, setting him apart from the others as the local stud muffin bad-boy. For those who do not know the story, the jump in the second act is confusing. There was little suggestion that I could see that Jackson had aged. I think it is important to push this here, as his appearance functions as Exposition 101 and ageing make- up would have helped everyone get up to speed a little better. There was some good ageing of John by the end, however and Emily's illness seemed to appear gradually. Tara Killilea and Jenny Higgins of Creative Scene Productions ensured quality costuming throughout. The cast sported caps, waistcoats, aprons and shawls, appropriately creased, with the odd tear or hole, (without taking that concept too far) while ensuring they were not too polished. Issac's severed leg was achieved by placing some black material behind it, creating a clever illusion, giving it a pointy quality that looked very realistic. Musical Director Shane Farrell conducted his nine musicians with clarity, ensuring the music was lovely overall. Placed to the stage-right of the theatre, his image was beamed to a screen at the back of the audience. Principals appeared very confident with their singing, nailing all their entrances. Transitions from the underscored dialogue to the choral singing were also seamless. Some of the underscoring was done with just the piano, ensuring that it was never over-powering and we could hear every word. I cannot say that I could fully make out the lyrics of the opening number and I would suggest that diction could have been enhanced here. The trumpet was a little loud in places. Dynamics were good after the brawling, where the chorus sang with a lovely low quality. All of those "hahs" in the holiday pub were slick and impactful. The trio 'If I Could' was fabulously sung; staged simply, it was very moving. Attention to dynamics in the finale of Act One was very good, as the chorus began softy, hitting full belt by "step by step". The entr'acte was nice and short, just enough to settle us back into the zone. The counterpoint from the opposing sides was very good the Miners' Union row. The men signing against the women in the finale worked very well as they began softly and allowed the number to grow. Derek Recks was on Sound, ensuring that the band never overpowered the performers. Cueing was spot-on throughout the evening and everything was crystal clear. The birds tweeting at the top of Act Two opened this soon-to-be-bleak Act with some cheery optimism on this bright summer's day. The war sound effects were excellent, adding to this dramatic moment, as was the sound of the lift going down into the mines.

Choreography was by Jay Molyneaux. It must be frustrating to a be a choreographer for a show that has very few opportunities for dance in the traditional sense. Jay endeavoured to do as much as he could with the little material available to him. What I particularly hate about this job is when I am negative about an aspect of a show, when it is clear that an extraordinary amount of work went into it. That said, I think that the opening number was one move away from being over-cooked. It was stylised in a way that never occurred again, meaning that while the movement was representational of the narrative, it was jarring from a tonal point of view. 'Work Song' was overly-stylised also with endless formations, trying to achieve too much. The second sequence was more successful here as it employed more of those movements with the tools etc, albeit overly uniform. Jay might consider teaching the moves but encourage the chorus to make their own expression of them, merging structure with naturalism. The chorus seemed very well-rehearsed, however, suggesting that a lot of hard work went into these sequences. The ribbons on sticks was a nice moment, with the school children led by their teacher. The folk-dancing was excellent, with the men lifting up the ladies and circling, putting us on a high before the sombre ending. After all, we need to be brought up to come back down. So well done to Jay on such hard work overall. I look forward to seeing more of his work in the future in a show that begs for more dance.

David Langan was excellent as John, understated, natural and completely believable. He has a lovely singing voice. His solo after returning from holiday was gorgeous, sweetly moving, as he figured something was up with Emily. He did a lovely job on 'What Would You Say to Your Son?', which was impactful without him needing to even leave the chair. The way he did everything in his power not to cry at the end was exactly the way to do it, always far more moving than someone bawling their eyes out. "I best be on me way", he said, and we were allowed to do the crying for him.

Anne O' Donnell as Emily had the same natural quiet disposition as John, making them well-matched as a pair. She has an absolutely gorgeous voice, with rich vowel sounds. She had such a range of emotions to play; hopeful, affronted, lustful, regretful, worried, and sorrowful and she hit every mark without ever needing to be overly- obvious. She measured her deterioration very well, ensuring that it was gradual and convincing. Another great performance. Alan Greaney continued this quality of acting and singing as Jackson. He was everything that John was not; confident, cool, boisterous, oozing with bad-boy machismo. "Fancy yourself?" she says to him, and she was not wrong, as he captured all the confident lothario nature of this big fish in a small pond. He acted really well through song also. I wish he had more to sing, so we could listen to him for longer. He completed this trio perfectly. Nicky Lawless was wonderfully characterful as Isaac, injecting humour and energy into the rather tame Tallentire household. He showed off some great vocalising as he moved from the kitchen to the pub. He was a beacon of light in this sombre piece, never losing the jovial essence of himself, even when the war had cost him so dearly. Very well done indeed.

Frank "Jay" Hall as Seth showed off a gorgeous rich bass voice. His acting in the union meeting was strong and persuasive. While there was some small musical glitch in the Miners' meeting, Frank was still excellent in this scene, ensuring that the drama and agro of the moment bounced off the stage. He was much-changed after the war, with his nervous repetitive shake showing us the toll the events had taken and his final scene with John was touching.

Emily Macken was lovely as May. She and her brother were both entertaining in their first scene, as they captured the youthful fun of a summer's day. She combined being something of an innocent cherub with being a bit of a bauld strap. Her song 'You Never See the Sun' was performed very well. She captured our hearts as she squealed with delight when Jackson said that Harry could try out his gun and moved us when she was worried about her brother heading off to war and when she and her Mother received bad news from the Front.

This brother/sister duo was perfectly rounded off with Keith Hanley as Harry. He captured all the wide-eyed enthusiasm of the teenaged boy, overly enamoured by the concept of a gun. He was afraid of nothing, wanting to get a job in the mine and by insisting he must do his duty and go to war, lying about his age. We cared very much for this young man and were devastated when he was killed. Very well done.

Gráinne Curtain was very nice as Sally. She matched Anne O'Donnell's gorgeous voice in the 'Who Will You Marry Then' duet, easily reaching some lovely high notes. They were confident in their harmonies here and delivered them in a fun manner, like two women enjoying a sing-song while at work. She brought some light-heartedness to the piece, and effectively presented as far more grown up at the end.

Kenneth Kennedy played the parts of Pennington and Blacklock. He gave us a stern father figure to the messy Jackson and was very good in adding to the tensions in the Miners' Union meeting. Kevin Griffin as Joe, Mervyn Fahy as Dan, Daniel Broderick as Tom, Paul Hughes as Bob, Cian O'Ceallaigh as Josh/Alex and Mike Flaherty as Farmer 5 all acted convincingly in their material in the pub and in the Miner's Union meeting, ensuring the high standard never waned, even with the smaller roles. Michael Cooney played the dual part of Union Chairman/Vicar. He was authoritative as the chairperson, roaring at times, adding effectively to the tension and agro here. As the vicar, he had a nice energy, slightly comic and upbeat, helping to take us "out of ourselves" as John put it. Martha O'Toole as Landlady has all the confidence and presence required as the Mistress of the House. Kori Kilduff sang beautifully and with emotion as the Female Soloist.

The chorus had great facial expressions and clear intentions, while ensuring that sense of naturalism at all times. It felt as though there were always smaller narratives going on within the chorus, not just cringey reactions, while never becoming distracting either. Their dialogue got some genuine laughs as well.

The hardest thing to do is to rehearse something ad nauseum so that it is slickly performed, then make it sound like this was the first time it was being said. That was achieved by everyone on stage in Galway Musical Society. It was a beautifully touching, emotive show, all staged on an aesthetic that was as tenderly nurtured as the performances upon it. It was a simply lovely. Naturally.

The University Concert Hall in Limerick is a fine space which holds somewhere between six and seven hundred people and was abuzz on the night we arrived. Entering the premises would have been impressive enough, but the set that stood waiting for us immediately established the tone for a show that would have excellent aesthetic value throughout. The show had fine principal performances and a highly energised committed chorus, providing us with a thoroughly entertaining production, as the dance routines hopped off the stage. Set firmly in a modern context, with very good direction by Des Henn that used the space well, while nicely exploring the phenomenon of celebrity against the personal stories of the characters within. Judas began the show by walking forward towards the well-lit crown of thorns, initiating a series of images and videos on screens, showing today's violence and working right back to the beginning of time. Riot police appeared at the top of the show, banging their truncheons off their Perspex shields to the rhythm of the music. This undercurrent of violence was well developed throughout, with the handing out of guns in 'What's the buzz?' motivating Jesus' line "Why are you obsessed with fighting?" The crowd appeared to cheer on Jesus in 'Hosanna', creating an interesting sinister turn as they shook their fists in slow motion, a troubled Jesus and Mary realising that the crowd were asking "would you die for me?" A troubled Pilate appeared slowly under Jesus' singing of 'Poor Jerusalem', to recount his dream, with a bottle of Jameson in hand. Interestingly, Jesus stayed for a while to create a moment with Pilate, both looking at each other as though we could see what was happening in Pilate's head. The setting up of the Temple scene was a moment in itself; involving sultry women dressed in red bodices and suspenders dropping large pieces of red material from the balcony to give structure to the moment, as flames appeared on the screens, one of the priests making a connection with another male here.

Caiaphas poured the money on top of Judas as he shopped in Jesus, as the ensemble appeared all in black, with torches under their chins to sing "Well done, Judas" at the end of Act One, creating an eerie moment. Act Two picked up exactly where were left off, providing a nice moment of continuity. Judas' suicide involved him whipping out a gun and shooting himself in the head, shocking the audience with the speed of this moment. The hanging sequence rarely works, and with the modernisation of this production, this was a dramatically impactful choice. The stage was covered in a red wash of light, the ensemble repeating "Poor Old Judas", as the men carried out his dead body. The hanging usually requires some kind of instant blackout, meaning Judas is gone without a by your leave. It was very interesting to see how much of a moment was made in the aftermath of his on-stage death.

Niamh Twomey devised entertaining choreography. She was assisted by Dance Captain Pamela Cotter. The appearance of the riot police during the brass introduction of 'Simon Zealotes' began a thoroughly engaging number, with differentiated dance moves happening all over the stage. The seven people on the upper level had different moves to those two groups bopping on each side of the cross on the ground. The eight people who moved into a machine-gun yielding formation behind Simon was impactful. 'Herod's Song' was a showstopper with their swapping of places in a scissor-like fashion and with three or four groups doing different things. 'Superstar' was energetic and entertaining, jam-packed with armography and the crowd adored it. I would argue that too much Judas' first song was played out to the audience; with lines such as "Listen Jesus to the warning I give" not directed at the man himself. I would suggest that this number was at its most successful and meaningful when Judas engaged with the action on stage. That said, I cannot say for certain that I fully understood all of the action going on in this opening sequence either. Also, I would argue that Jesus was not dishevelled enough by the time he was put on trial, considering how much he had been beaten and how panicked Judas had been about the violence inflicted on him up to now.

The contemporary costumes had a link to the past by using pale and muted colours. This contrasted nicely with the five uniform baddie priests in fully black attire; long coats, turtlenecks, waistcoats, trousers and shoes. Jesus changed throughout the evening, sporting more and more flowy white clothing, casting off the grey parts to his attire, perhaps charting his journey from man to god. Mary's long orange Grecian dress and golden tresses made her image look ancient and modern all in one. The lepers wore grey coverings on their heads and their bandages were made of the same material, combining realism with something more stylised. Herod's flapper-style show girls were suitably colourful and blinged-up, him nicely over-the-top in a blue/purple embellished suit, sequined turtle neck and cummerbund. Judas did 'Superstar' in a purple suit, showing the change from realism to abstract, his backing dancers sporting either red or white.

A huge amount of work by a large team of people went into this impressive set, overseen by Construction Manager Tom Lynch and well-managed on the night by Michael O'Regan. It was an expanse of two levels with pillars, the steps covered with ancient lines of scripture. Other iconography was painted on the floor and gorgeous stonework married an ancient setting with the contemporary images of the actors. The floor sported a giant cross that would be used in parts such as the Last Supper. There were three archways on the lower section that would house the angry mobs who were baying for Jesus' persecution. Projections of Renaissance artwork was displayed on the screen, contrasting with the modern vibe, and mirroring the action/characters on stage e.g. Mary kneeling at the lap of Jesus during 'I Don't Know How to Love Him' or Judas kissing Jesus in the Garden of Gethsemane. The metallic chairs and tables covered in silver material finished off the Temple Scene in style.

The red wash of light on the stage, with two white spots on Jesus and Mary as she wiped his forehead in the opening scenes mixed intimacy with danger and ensured clarity. A white special appeared on the downstage steps as two other girls bathed Jesus, with everyone else chilling, heads in each other's shoulders, in a blue wash that effectively suggested twilight. Atmospheric candles also appeared for the "Everything's alright…" section here and again later for the Last Supper Scene. Circles of light on the ground during "Neither you Simon nor the fifty thousand…" created a lovely change in tone that matched the slower tempo of this section. The seven purple spots on Pilate were spooky as he recounted his dream, seeing Jesus passing in front of him, to then turn white and spread out in a cloud of atmospheric smoke. White sprinkles of light on the cross on the ground were really cool, as the five priests made various still and stoic formations around the stage, bullying Judas into betraying Jesus. There was a gorgeous celestial white light on Jesus for 'Gethsemane'. Red light on Jesus' first encounter with Pilate invoked the danger of the situation and again in the crucifixion.

The truncheons and shields were well- sourced by props personnel Jane Finnegan and Eoin McCann.

The posters of Jesus in 'Hosanna' effectively established his celebrity status in the modern context. The goblet in the Last Supper was nice and big, ensuring the large audience would see it clearly. There was a silver bowl on a brown wooden table on stage-left for Pilate to wash his hands after condemning Jesus.

Máire Keary-Scanlon was Musical Director for the show, leading nine musicians. As the band were hidden behind the set, her image was beamed onto a screen behind the audience. The "everything's alright" sung by the males as a counterpoint to the female's "close your eyes" was cool. The band were a little low for the first part of 'I Don't Know How to Love Him', but were at a great level by the time the instrumental section kicked in. Harmony in the final "Superstaaaaar" in 'Hosanna' was very good. The descant in the lepers' sequence and the 'The Arrest' scene was searing, as the pressure built in these moments. Pilate's theme music was effectively repeated before 'Superstar' to allow for the cross-section of the crucifix to be tied to Jesus.

There were issues with the volume of the band being backstage and I was wondering why the pit in front was not used. The presence of a live band can be a great visual thrill at a musical (as well as aural) and some societies would kill to have a pit, so I wonder is the potential there to revisit this decision. There were some opening night jitters with some tricky entrances less-polished than we would have liked, but those gremlins are often present in a first performance. There was a slight effect on Pilate's voice during the dramatic face-off between him and Jesus in 'Pilate's Dream'. There was also an echo on the lepers' voices, as they sang their pained solos, enhancing the symbolism of the moment, as though it was all representational of what was happening in Jesus' head. The reverb on Judas' voice as he tells the priests about the Garden of Gethsemane sounded as though he was singing in a cathedral or a mosque. The hammering noises during the crucifixion were harrowing.

Kevin Prout showed off an excellent voice in his lower register as Jesus. Some of the rock-tenor moments were a little challenging, such as "If your slate is clean" and it might have been an idea to reimagine the score here and work more with the more impressive section of the voice. There were some nice moments of falsetto, however, such as when he sang "When you're gooooone" and "Get out" (in the Temple scene). The end of 'Gethsemane' was moving as he became sad and overwhelmed by the task ahead of him. The passion of the crucifixion was very well acted.

Paul Shesgreen as Judas was impactful in his remorseful panic, vigorously attacking the priests for how badly they had beaten Jesus. He was moving in his version of 'I Don't Know How to Love Him'. Not everyone of those nasty high notes were nailed e.g. "feet and haaaair", and I suggest that choices should be made that sit best in the voice of the actor. He really came into his stride in the 'Superstar' number, however, knocking that one out of the park.

Kim Burke showed off a very good voice as Mary Magdalene, sometimes rolling her notes nicely, while acting well through song during her introspective 'I Don't Know How to Love Him' and her emotionally still 'Could We Start Again, Please'. She displayed a special connection with Jesus, while showing us her ability to pacify Judas also. Well done. Ger Treacy as Caiaphas had an awesome bass voice, suitably stoic and authoritative, as he and his fellow priests (played very well and with presence by Pa Woulfe and Radim Zedka) owned the stage, plotting menacingly against this threat to their power. James Malone showed off a super voice as Annas, able to sing the material at pitch without sounding silly. The use of this quality performer in the bit with Peter at the well was an inspired idea and added danger to the moment.

Aidan O'Connell was fierce, aggressive and intimidating as Pilate. His burnt-out private persona, as he knocked back his late-night glass of whiskey, gave an interesting glimpse to his non-public life also. He measured that tricky 'Trial by Pilate' well, by beginning with great attack, realising that Jesus was the figure from his dream, becoming overwhelmed by the pressure from the crowd and re-taking charge of the situation, by blaming Jesus for his own downfall and condemning him to death.

Nigel Dugdale gave us a fierce, camp, just on the right side of panto baddie as Herod. With psychotic eyes, he danced like a lunatic, sending the audience wild with delight. This is a cameo role, with one quick appearance to do a stand-alone song, yet it was highly memorable because of Nigel's heightened characterisation and no-holds-barred attack to the number. Very well done indeed.

Jason Hannon as Simon showed that he is a great mover, giving super energy in the 'Simon Zealotes' number, vibrating with delight with the thoughts of "the power and the glory". He opted for some lower choices in the notes he sang, which is exactly the right thing to do. This score should be built around the voices of the performers, not the other way around. Christian Tan as Peter captured all of the panic and remorse his character felt when denying Jesus three times at the well. His singing with in 'Could We Start Again, Please?' was lovely as he harmonised with Mary. The woman at the well was very intimidating and provided a good vocal here.

It does not matter how many ideas a director has, how inventive a choreographer is, or how musically talented a musical director is, if the ensemble of the show does not have the talent or put in the hard work to pull it all off. Thankfully, the chorus did great work throughout, ensuring a highly entertaining evening. They appeared to understand their role and intention in each moment i.e. whether they were chilling out, sad or angry.

The ending was memorable. The crown of thorns had some built-in special effect that made blood gush down Jesus' face in a horrifying manner as it was placed on his head. The torturing of Jesus was done by the ensemble dipping their hands in small pots of red paint and running by Jesus, smearing his body in blood. Two chains came down from the ceiling and attached the wood already on Jesus' back to the scaffolding, creating a memorable crucifixion scene. Plumes of smoke gushed from the ground around a red-lit cross, raised high in the air against dramatic music and lightning effect. The video on the screen as lighting struck around the animated Jesus, the dementors bursting through him, was awesome. It is rare for a crucifixion in a contemporary production to be moving, but it certainly was here, evident by the standing ovation from the audience against the stillness of the cast in their non-bowed curtain call. This was dramatic stuff; a combination of set design, direction, musical direction, choreography, costuming, lighting, sound and very good acting.

It was unfortunate for Naas Musical Society that they had to cancel their first two performances due to the snow brought by Storm Emma. That said, there was little sign that preparations had been disturbed by the time I got to see their second successful performance. It was a great example of how a community can pull together. The principals did a conference call to run lines. The hair people gave tutorials on Facebook. Videos of the dance routines were shared in the Whatsapp group, all to ensure that momentum was not grounded to a halt and that the show must go on. As the show states, "there is a special kind of people known as show people" and the company of Naas Musical Society proved that with their production of Curtains. Thankfully, the panic was gone by the time I reached the theatre, having parked my car on a mound of stubborn snow. Front of House was managed by Rosemarie O'Dowd and an impressive list of volunteers. The lovely displays mixed current photos with posters of past productions. Some of the past AIMS trophies were on display, celebrating the achievements of the society. Cheese, chocolate, crisps and wine were on every table, making the environment very inviting.

Director Philippa Alford gave us a solid show that whizzed along with a good sense of pace. She enabled believable and naturalistic performances and gave us a good balance between comedy and pathos. Set design was very clever, with the sliders at the back creating new places in seconds. The scene changes (with simultaneous flat-turning etc.)

were well-planned. The use of the given environment of the venue, such as the door on the stage-left side of the theatre and the balcony (for the flies) was very good. The chemistry between Frank and Nikki was particularly well-realised. The staging of 'The Man is Dead' was very good, with each set of hung sheets comically opening one after the other and then all together. The last ten minutes were when the show was at its most impactful for me. We got a happy ending that managed not to be sickly sweet or cheesy. "Bravo the great director"/ "Bravo the great detective" was nicely touching, as was the scene between Carmen and Frank in front of the curtain.

Philippa also designed the set, with Tina O'Kelly, Claire O'Reilly and Stage Manager Bob O'Kelly. This design worked very well in enabling very slick and prompt scene changes. The sliders at the back worked great. The set pieces for the show-within- a-show were suitably two-dimensional. There were numerous Robin Hood sets: such as the one depicting the Saloon and General Store and the one with the posters saying "5c Hot Bath/Clean Water Extra" and "Cowboys leave your guns at the bar". The lamps, painted bottles and buffalo head were lovely here too. The use of that balcony space on the side of the audience as the flies, effectively covered in thick pieces of rope, was inspired. Furniture was well positioned around the stage and the choice of red table-cloths was good. The cast were utilised to bring furniture on and off. Closing the main curtain, while the dialogue continued in front of it, was a very good idea, enabling scene changes to happen behind.

The choral performances were very good, with the ensemble producing lovely rich vowel sounds, singing with power. The dominant soprano line, with the rest of the chorus responding, in 'The Woman's Dead' was very impactful. The final "DEAD" was fabulous here. Georgia, Nikki and Bambi's harmonies in 'In the Same Boat' were really tight. The moment when life imitated art and the cast sang the three different versions of 'The Same Boat' was awesome. The final "tough act to follow" was very nicely sung by the chorus. Choreography, by Trisha McDermott, was simple but effective and suitable for the group. The moves in Robin Hood, the swinging and kicks, were suitably cheesy for this Country and Western context. The use of lines and sharp head movements in 'The Woman's Dead' worked very well. The number was nicely built-up, piece by piece, and by adding extra people in as it progressed. This culminated in an awesome kick-line that finished off an excellent number. The chair dancing was very good, creating three sections for the girls to dance in. The final formations in 'Thataway' were lovely and the girls on the floor, kicking their legs in the air at the end, was fun and evoked that saloon- style madness. The use of torches in a night time scene was super and the final moment, when they were covered by the performers' hands, was slick. The dance- off between the village girls and the Native American girls in 'Wide Open Spaces' was exciting.

Lieutenant Frank Cioffi was played by Craig Regan. This is a mammoth role with an extraordinary amount of dialogue and it was very clear how much work Craig had put into this, ensuring that his speeches flowed competently. He had a great accent, a very clear speaking voice and sang very well. His relationship with Nikki was lovely and he delivered those moments where his character appeared more concerned with the show than the murders in a nicely comic way.

Siobhán Clifford played the youthful Nikki Harris with competence. Her ditzy acting was effective and her chemistry with Frank was convincing. Her harmonies with the other ladies were tight and her dancing was very good.

Maggs Jacobs had great presence as Carmen Bernstein. She had a lovely, confident and rich singing voice. She was well-able to get the laughs when necessary, such as with her line "If one of you is the killer, would you please take her next". She was very convincing as the strict mother, making it all the more impactful when Frank revealed how she really wanted the best for her daughter. After a tough-cookie performance, and many laughs, she played her final conversation with Frank in an honest and sincere way.

Julie Donnelly was naturalistic and convincing as Georgia Hendricks. She used that alto-voice of hers to great effect. She found a nice balance between pretending she was not interested in Aaron with vulnerability about their relationship. There was a nice sense of catharsis when the couple were reunited.

Aaron Fox was played by Carthaigh Quill. He has a gorgeous voice, like velvet chocolate. He was every bit the leading love interest, as he sat intensely at the piano, bow tie open, trying to write music without the love of his life/song-writing partner.

Bobby Pepper was played with competence by James Place, who had all the performance skills necessary to play the leading man in the show-within- the -show. His singing was great, and he danced very well indeed.

Martin Fahy showed off an excellent accent as Christopher Belling. He found a lovely balance in his character: He was a dramatic toff-like lovey, without going so over the top that he became unconvincing. The comedy was subtle, but enjoyable and he added considerably to the show. Bambi Bernét was played by Sarah O' Driscoll. She has a lovely voice. Her arguments with her mother struck that nice balance between comedy and tragedy. We selfishly enjoyed the shade thrown by her often-comic mother, while still feeling sorry for Bambi who just wanted a little recognition. She did very well in her dance "audition".

Oscar Shapiro was played by Paul Dicker. He was a good side-kick to Carmen and his lighter personality balanced out the scenes he was in with the brooding Aaron. Johnny Harmon was played with all the authority and man-about-business style, that is required from stressed out stage managers, by Patrick Brian Gallagher. He had good presence when he came on stage and injected pace with his orders to the company.

Daryl Grady was played by Conor Clear. The boo the audience gave him during his bow was testament to his very good performance. His accent was great, and he was very good at being psychotic in the final moments.

John Dooley had an imposing presence as the tough-guy producer Sidney Bernstein. He owned the stage whenever he appeared and was so suitably unlikeable that we were inevitably on Carmen's side when he was killed.

Jessica Cranshaw was played by Áine Coe. She was brilliant at being crap. Another performer who served the narrative by embracing the comic unlikability of her character. Another death that didn't bother us in the slightest. Stephen Fagan had specific responsibilities as highly featured member of the ensemble Randy Dexter and performed his material with competence and confidence.

There have been many compliments listed above about the Direction and  Choreography. None of those compliments would be possible without the talent and hard work of this chorus. Harmonies were well-learned and sung with power. The routines bounced off the stage and the reactions in the crowd scenes were excellent throughout.

June Young from That Looks Good and Claire O'Reilly were in charge of costumes. The country and western dresses and the male cowboy costumes in Robin Hood looked very well. Aaron's open bow tie, in comparison to how smartly dressed the other producers were, gave him a look, that evoked the emotional state of his character. Georgia's floral dressing gown was lovely. Darryl needed a coat, to illustrate that he had come from the outside. Carmen's mourning dress was suitably sexy and accessorised with a purple flower, showing that she wasn't that aggrieved (or going to sacrifice her sense of style) for a dead husband whom she could not stand. Pyjamas throughout were classic and evoked the old-style effectively (This is an area that can easily go wrong, and societies sometimes scrimp here, so well done). The Kansas dresses were gorgeous. The tanned Native American female costumes with brown frill and the yellow feather in the head-pieces (but red for Bambi) looked nice and theatrical.

Make-up was by Catherine Coventry and Hair was by Leona O'Neill. Wigs were excellent throughout, transforming some of these ladies' natural looks, and ensuring that the leads looked very much part of the period in question. Darryl's hair was somewhat modern in style and might have benefited by a little more slicking- down.

Lighting, designed and supplied by Stagelights.ie., was used well to punctuate the beginnings and the endings of songs and to add to the energy during the numbers. The eerie green lighting in 'The Woman's Dead' worked very well. The spotlight on the piano for 'I Miss the Music' was very nice for this sincerely performed ballad. The red wash to punctuate Aaron's "thinking of you" was very effective.

The play-within-the play calls for "Light Cue 5" to be shone on Georgia as she reluctantly performs one of her own songs. I think she needed her own spotlight to phase out a little of the business around her, rather than simply shining pink on the backdrop. I found some of the well- intentioned reactions from the crowd a little distracting after a while. I think she needed to be framed in her own intimate space for this, so that the chorus reactions were more subliminal.

Sound was by Vinny Osborne of The Sound and Music Company. There were numerous solos in 'The Woman's Dead' and each one was perfectly cued. There was a little bit of feedback caused by the chair dance, which I am sure was sorted as the week went on. Everywhere else, the balance between the band and the performers was excellent, thanks in part to the positioning of the band behind the performers and thanks to the sound desk, of course.

Philippa Alford directed a show that gave us sincere performances and believable relationships, presented in a very good aesthetic. The principals and chorus alike gave us impressive vocal performances. Trisha McDermott devised inventive numbers that bounced off the stage. This was all possible thanks to a talented cast and a committed chorus. Thankfully the impact of Storm Emma did not mean it was curtains for Curtains. "The show must go on" is a lyric repeated in this score. And the show did go on. And it was very good indeed.

Rush Musical Society stage their show each year in their local Millbank Theatre, a gorgeous intimate venue. With tiered seating, there is not a bad view in the house. They do a nine-night run, which deserves a round of applause in itself - no small ask for the leads of Jesus Christ Superstar. This show is never done the same way twice, something I enjoy about it. That said, sometimes versions can be a little overcooked, cramming as much in as possible, losing the run of itself in the process. This version was lovely and simple, easy to follow and clear in its interpretation, visual representation and style. There was many a red eye when the house lights came up, showing that it was an emotive night for some.

Director Barry Kavanagh chose to set the show in biblical times, unmuddled by too much referencing to modern day motifs. With no script and only a list of lyrics to go by, there is no end to the directions this show can take. However, with no boundaries, productions of this show can aim to do too much and as a result achieve too little. I appreciated the straight-forward simplicity of this version. We got biblical versions of the characters exploring the phenomenon on celebrity, leadership, politics and religion in the context of 2,000 years ago. Like all versions, the rule book is thrown out for the final 'Superstar' number, which reverted to modern showbiz pizazz, drawing parallels with modern superstardom.

The set was comprised of a triad of two- tiered playing areas of wooden scaffolding, that were connected when necessary. The middle area could move up and down stage and turn to become something else, and this was slickly executed by Stage Manager John Foley and his team. The crucifix would be attached to this section also. The low table for the Last Supper was about a foot off the ground, meaning that the Apostles could sit on the ground and the action never felt blocked. In the context of the traditional setting, the wood worked beautifully, and the various levels provided so many mini-performance spaces onto which moments could be staged and pictures created. Light could fall in these areas effectively also.

Lighting, by Colm Eaton, effectively created atmosphere and framed the narrative throughout. There was a dim red light on the top of the central steps and subtle gobos on the floor to bathe the sleeping stage as we filed in. The yellow light for the lepers was suitably eerie. Reds and purples evoked the menace of Pilate's layer. The crowd in green and the soldiers in red during 'Trial by Pilate' enhanced the danger of the moment. Jesus being backlit for the lashes was very effective. The celestial light on Jesus as he was on the cross was lovely.

Slow-motion montages during the 'Heaven on Their Minds' opening, walked us through a series of recognisable bible stories, summarising Jesus' ministry, thus bringing us up to the point that the narrative begins in earnest. The High Priests created an omnipresence within the show, forever observing from a height with defensive folded arms, not just appearing for their solo moments. These heights were also used effectively to allow Jesus to preach. There were some nice moments of sinful behaviour in the Temple, such as a Belly Dancer who was walked around on a lead. There was an interesting dynamic in 'I Don't Know How to Love Him', as the sleeping Jesus clung to Mary and she fobbed him off in her confusion. It can often be portrayed with her being all over him, so this role reversal was enjoyable and interesting.

Including the women as servers gave an extra dimension to the Last Supper and Jesus washing the feet of the Apostles was a nice touch also. Thankfully the Apostles did not fall asleep in one quick movement as though gassed. The crowd taking over from Pilate in the counting of the lashes was a clever way to signify how he had lost control of the situation. The slow-motion crowd movements during his "Where are you from, Jesus…" created an effective change in tone. Direction ensured that from the crucifixion straight through to the end was particularly successful and well-structured. Placing Jesus on the white sheet after the crucifixion was lovely.

In terms of the performers' image, the Biblical setting of this show was nicely actualised throughout the evening.

The coverings on the female heads were particularly important, I thought. Noticeably, Mary did not wear a head scarf, which set her apart and suggested a certain defiance or rejection of modesty in the context of the setting. Judas wore a red shirt with black waistcoat, two dangerous colours that pointed to the darkness of his character. The Priests were nicely uniform in their gold and black tunics. I might argue that some of the chainmail/ armour was a little unconvincing. Perhaps there was a tone of theatricality that was slightly lost on me. Either way, this contrasted with the realism of the rest of the costumes. That said, Herod's version of this was convincing, complimented by his purple cloak and broach. Pilate's gold chainmail over his wine costume established his authority, complete with a crown of golden leaves.

Hair and make-up designed by Ali Murphy was kept suitably simple throughout. Jesus' real-life image was dramatically transformed to create the iconic look we have come to associate with this man. The High Priests wore stylised eye make- up with thematic black strips in their white beards (the opposite with Caiaphas' beard). Herod's make-up enhanced his bonkers persona.

Musical direction was provided by Dave (Doc) O'Connor. In the context of this small theatre, it was not surprising that the band was in another room behind the stage. There were two small monitors on either side of downstage for the actors to see the MD. They were quite subtle, and I almost did not spot them.

Those infamous opening "aaawwwws" at the top of the show were performed onstage by the ensemble, which was really nice. The sopranos were particularly impressive in the "Superstaaaaaaaar" finish of 'Hosanna'. The bass-voice drone on the "well done, Judas" at the end of Act One was impactful. It was cool the way the ladies gave the "pool of wine" response during the Last Supper as they served the men. The harmony by the Apostles, after Jesus and Judas left this scene was lovely. "I wonder how he knew" was beautifully harmonised by Peter and Mary and I have not heard it done like that before. Their harmonies in 'Could We Start Again, Please?' were lovely also.

Unfortunately, the show was a bit loud. The band were behind the stage, which usually solves the problem of the music being over-powering. This was not to be the case, however. To counteract this volume, the mics appeared to be up sky-high, meaning that the top of the show was a tad deafening. The groups singing the "Tell me Christ…" bits after Gethsemane were hit and miss, with some groups containing people with mics and others who did not. It appeared to me that all mics were up here and it was pot-luck whether a group were heard or not.

There were a number of times when entrances were not secure e.g. Mary's initial entrance before the 'I Don't Know How to Love Him Scene' (I didn't get the impression it was her fault), the start of 'Hosanna' was a beat off and the entrance into the Temple singing was tentative and took a while to establish itself securely. It took a handful of confident people to get a verse going before everyone else knew they were to come in. Perhaps this was because the band were in another room and everyone was relying on technology to sync what was happening on stage with the band.

Choreographer Sinéad Lightley ensured that her cast were well-prepared in plenty of high energy entertaining dance routines. The opening number was very interesting. There was something hypnotic about it. It appeared to mix what looked like sign language with slow, quirky folk dancing that seemed unique and unlike much of what I have seen before. The crowd surfing in 'Hosanna' was awesome, really capturing the meaning of the number. The six dancers in 'Herod's Song' were great and their reaction to his entrance, as though irritated by him, was funny. It was clear that a lot of work went into the rest of the numbers. The cast had clearly been well-rehearsed by Sinéad and they executed the routines with energy and commitment, ensuring some highly entertaining up-tempo numbers.

Adam McGealy as Jesus had a cool, almost hippie vibe, as he moved hypnotically in some of the slow-motion scenes. He had all the warmth and likeability required for the role. It is often the case that Jesus is very angry and argumentative, and while some of the score and lyrics asks for this, I think that Jesus should have a calming, ultimately forgiving nature that contrasts with Judas' anger. I don't see how Jesus can spread the message of love and be constantly at war. Even in the betrayal and the passion, there is an apparent inevitability to it all. The death needs to happen, and perhaps Judas is being asked to play his part in it. Happily, Adam's interpretation found a lovely balance between a man who is made of flesh and bone, who has relationships, who is afraid, with a man who wants to inspire those around him. He has a lovely voice, with a bit of a rocker growl to it. That said, I am not convinced the right choices were always made in rehearsals. By far, my favourite rendition of 'Gethsemane' is by Michael Crawford, who steers clear of all of those hyper- falsetto moments. While Adam nailed some of them, such as his "Why should I die", others were not as natural to him such as the "get out" in the Last Supper. I think the natural voice of the actor should be the starting point when devising the vocals for this show. Do it simple and well, rather than reaching for an ideal that is not within the natural timbre of the voice. But hey. What do I know? The audience went wild after 'Gethsemane', indicating that there was much to be admired here (in particular how he sustained the word "mind" at the end).

In contrast to Jesus' balance, Jim Walsh as Judas gave us a man on the edge, both physically and emotionally. So much on the outskirts of the Jesus phenomenon, he could not reconcile with much of the hype surrounding his leader.
