The oil stain on Natalie's orange dress was in keeping with her character, as was the green hat and fur coat on the Mayor. Dennis looked particularly comic with his hair split into curtains and sleeveless jumper with gaudy diamond pattern and beige trousers - too short and thus showing his striped socks. The lipstick smeared all over the snogging Dean and Lorraine was a scream. Rightfully, Sandra's dresses were always more demure than the local small-town girls, whose dresses were pretty but not as daring. The blue suede shoes, blue denim jeans on those in the 'Blue Suede Shoes' number gave a nice change to what we had seen before. The moving statues looked super in their white satin, pink/purple material off the shoulders and their gold-leaf headpieces. Bodiced female angels wore wings and guys in black sported glittering horns for 'Devil in Disguise'. Natalie's white jacket contrasted nicely with Chad's black in the final scene. For all of the compliments paid to Lea Carroll's choreography and Alan Recks' wonderful work on the vocals, none of this would have been possible without this high-energy talented and committed ensemble, who ensured every scene was full of life and every number bounced off the stage. Superb work all round here, with one impressive number after another. How lovely is the ending of this show? While it is almost panto-esque in its conclusion; with everyone pairing off in both likely and unlikely partnerships (even the baddie turns good and falls for someone), it all completely re-affirms one's belief in love.

Vibration: to hum, quiver, shake, quaver, quake, tremble, tremor, judder, shiver, shudder, oscillate, vacillate, reverberate, resonant, pulse, beat, drum, throb, thump, pound, palpitate, buzz, rumble.

Synergy: the combined power of a group of things when they are working together that is greater than the total power achieved by each working separately.

Example: Leixlip Musical and Variety Group's West Side Story was synergistic in its direction, musical direction, choreography, cast performances, lighting, set and costumes to create a vibrational experience that will not be soon forgotten. Director Claire Tighe was no doubt responsible for this synergy, bringing together all the production elements into one unforgettable experience. With a firm decision to be utterly inventive, she was not afraid to take risks. With a contemporary essence to the production, she appealed to our current sensibilities, styling the performers with an ultra- modern sexy look and ensuring that they moved with the same visceral vibrational attack. Attack was the only form of defence in this world and this was invoked in every tiny movement.

The modern look evoked the gangland culture that still very much exists today, capturing some of the essence of how Baz Luhrmann modernised Romeo and Juliet. If one was shown different period dramas from the BBC, one could always tell in which decade it was filmed, by the hairstyles etc. Period pieces are usually given a modern twist, so people don't look too ridiculous. We can take them seriously because their styling draws on historical elements, while appealing to our modern sensibilities. The theatrical license taken with the costuming of this show was brilliantly actualised by Rita Tighe and Bern Dawson. The skin-tight miniskirts and the barely-there bandage dresses appealed to our contemporary understanding of youthful gangland personas and sexy girls dressed up to the nines, rather than being ornately stuck in the past. While the motif used to distinguish the Sharks from the Jets was deliberate, it was not overly theatrical or obvious. The Sharks wore reds and blacks, evoking a Latin flavour, while the Jets contrasted in more All- American denims and greys (not white - that would have been too squeaky-clean). The angelic Maria appeared in white on several occasions, supporting her cherub- like persona. Bern ensured that the Puerto Rican males were covered in tattoos, shaved heads and manbuns, something we might associate with today's Mexican cartels.

That said, there was a timelessness to the piece (there were no mobile phones etc. to be seen, which might have impacted too much on the plot points). Therefore, like the story itself, it was a meeting of two worlds. The old and the new, side by side. But unlike Luhrmann's Romeo and Juliet, the language is not as impressive as Shakespeare's and some of the group dialogue moments might have presented as a little corny in comparison to the credible danger of the choreography. But what is the alternative? Slow all the talking down and make it moodier, more sinister and laboured, adding ten minutes onto the show? No. So some of the dialogue ran with the energy and enthusiasm that was originally intended, clashing slightly with the dark intensity of the dancing. The pay- off of those unforgettable dance routines made the clashing of these two worlds well worthwhile.

With Jennifer Dawson assisting with choreography, there were so many twists and turns in the opening number that I cannot even describe the awesome dancing here. The lads in 'Jet Song' were like mutant monkeys as they jumped around the set, clinging onto bars, ensuring there was never a dull moment in this committed performance that did not allow for a single breath.

The dance at the gym began with an abstract suggestion towards a haunting masquerade ball, the cast covered in ghostly masks, temporarily removing all identity and race, before a divisive event in which racial tensions were palpable. There was a fierceness to the aggressive dance- off, in which the attack and sharpness of the moves gave us something memorable to behold. In contrast, the meeting of Tony and Maria was stylised as they stood on heights, their eyes meeting against the slow-motion of the dancing couples. There was lovely energy and rhythms in the dialogue and singing in the Balcony Scene as Tony and Maria gripped the scaffolding and each other, flirting, playing lustfully in their impassioned attraction. Yet when she called "Tony!", she immediately looked back to check had she been heard by those indoors, acknowledging the danger of the situation. "I love you" he said awkwardly, acknowledging the cringe- worthiness of the first time he said it. But their confidence grew and the 'Te Adoro' was more direct. Sometimes it is easier to say it the second time, and in another language.

Girl power was in full force during 'America'. Those closed formations were incredible, as they socked the number to the audience, each girl Beyoncé-like in her attack. The moody blue and green lights of 'Cool' felt like an underwater scene, complementing the inner-monologue of the suffocating Jets. This was visceral, as they appeared to beat as one pulsating heart, performing with a whisper quality that made me wonderfully uncomfortable. The pressure built and built in the rumble with slurs such as "chicken" thrown at Riff by the Puerto Ricans, his own Jets roaring at him not to "just stand there". The fight scenes co-ordinated by professional stuntman Stephen Ryan were realistic in parts, and stylised elsewhere. Much work must have gone in here to ensure that the moves fit perfectly with the percussion of the score. One would think the crescendo would climax at the killing of Bernardo, but not here. Tony, not able to move from the spot, sat over the dead body, screaming 'Maria' and our nerves were gone because the police siren was getting closer and closer.

Tony and Maria's 'Somewhere' was nicely complicated, as she embraced him then pushed him away, shaking her head, praying at the bedside that they'd "find a way of forgiving". As Officer Krupke exited in a flurry, his hat was cleverly knocked off his head, something that would then be effectively used as a clarifying prop through the number. The stunt where the lads flipped over while being attached to another was unbelievable, driving the audience insane with delight.

Set Design, by Director Claire Tighe, Aidan Mannion and Eileen Fagan, utilised every square inch of space to create so many nooks and crannies in an uninviting aesthetic that was drenched in ominous lighting. Three moveable separate pieces of railing would glide along a pole on top, giving varied texture to the different spaces.

Windows contained only a suggestion of the bars, which looked more like spikes, enhancing the dangerous tone of the set. There were so many impressive details, such as the vents and piping. The more time one spent looking at the set, the more one noticed. Balconies on either side were framed with excellent brickwork. The "DOC'S" sign created a nice sense of space, cleverly lighting up as Tony repaired it. A window would ingeniously pull out of the flat and turn to create the interior of Maria's bedroom. Another add- on created the wedding shop, with purples in the tux and bridesmaid's dress matching each other, linking with the purple wash and two splays of white light in a scene full of sexual tension.

This is a tiny space, particularly backstage and Stage Manager Mary Purcell was blessed to have a stand-alone set to work with. Cleverly, Consuela pushed the railings in a boozy stumble and Tony pushed it in utter frustration, cleverly working this necessity into the action of the scene in a meaningful way. The lights strewn across the top of the gym scene appeared like magic (from where, I do not know). The spirits of Bernardo and Riff manoeuvred Maria and Tony's love bed, ensuring that we were not solely swept away by their romance, reminding us of how complicated their union was. Louise Kenny, Séamus Kenny and Peter Flynn were in charge of props that included modern beer bottles, knives and guns. The use of these props often gave meaning to the action, such as when Tony was carrying the tray, or helping Doc to stack the chairs, or when the girls were boozing. Two stands for a tuxedo and a bridesmaid dress were all that was needed to effectively create this space.

Lighting Designer Darren Kelleher shone a spotlight on MD David Hayes at the top of the show. There was an instant lighting change as the first dramatic note of the overture kicked in and lighting punctuated the various changes in this introduction. The moving gobos on the side also added energy and the moving green spotlights built suspense. The lighting successfully established mood and identity throughout the show: There were red washes when the Sharks sang and Blue for the Jets (linking in nicely with their costuming), with green being the product when the two mixed. The spotlight on Tony during 'Maria', with the pink shadows, on the rest of the stage, along with purple backlighting that then added red to denote the danger of his seemingly innocent thoughts, all worked very well with the music and blocking. Lighting was often energised in the scene changes, ensuring that (with this awesome band) the transitions never felt boring. Blue light blinded us as the casts magically changed from the girls in 'America' to the Jets in the drugstore. David Hayes ensured such quality in terms of musical direction that the overture was like a night out in itself. The strings for the 'Tonight' motif were gorgeous, as was the brass section that played "There's a place for us". The drumming was a visual and aural treat in the Mambo section here. He gave crystal-clear signalling throughout, passionately conducting with his whole body. He knew how to bring it down, like in the romantic 'One Hand, One Heart', only to bring it pounding back in again for the 'Tonight Quintet'. Underscoring simmered nicely underneath the dialogue but was allowed to soar at the end of scenes as they segued into the next part. Principal vocals were always excellent, but acting the lyrics was considered just as important as singing them. Ensemble vocals had great attack. The male versus the female line for "There's a place for us" was lovely, as the cast stepped aside to reveal the five leads drenched in red light. Sound Designer Jason Fallon ensured that transparent Perspex shields surrounded the band to help reduce the volume. If I were to have one criticism of the show, it was how the relationship with Doc and the rest of the hoodlums was explored. Essentially all stories are the same. Doc is the Senex of the piece, the Dumbledore, the Gandalf, the Obi Wan Kenobi. As the moral compass in the writing, his lines, such as "You make the world lousy", have sent shivers down my spine in the past. But not this time, as they seemed a little too hastily washed-over, never truly capturing his relationship with the youngsters and the frustration he feels as he pleads with them to wise up.

Brian Dalton as Action showed that he was always ready for a fight as one of the most hot-tempered members of the Jets. Fionn O'Dwyer as A-Rab presented as slightly less quick-tempered than Action. His close companion, Baby John was played with sensitivity by Cillian Hogan, who got beaten in the opening fight sequence. There was not a weak-link to be found amongst these Jet and Sharks and those without named parts were just as incredible as everyone else.

Seán Duffy as Officer Krupke captured all of the fuss-pot nature of his character, busy in his interactions with the hoodlums, contrasting nicely with the darker more burnt-out Shrank. Ciarán Austin was a hoot as the nerdy Glad Hand - the poor unfortunate organiser of the gym dance, desperately trying to create an opportunity to ease the divide between the two gangs. Lauren Dooley was full of tough-girl attitude as Anybody's. She was the one who always seemed to have the inside scoop or could come up with a plan in a crisis. Behind every man (or group of hoodlums) there is a great woman.

Avril Doyle was very good as Rosalia, competently delivering half the lead vocals in 'America'. She was joined by Orla Jennings as Consuela and Aoife Masterson as Francisca in a quartet of 'I Feel Pretty' - expertly harmonised, full of naturalism, giggling under the vocals, as the girls lowered back bottles of beer and rolled around on the bed half-pissed. They had some official moves here but expertly gave their own expression of them.

Bert Carruthers, as Doc, maintained hints of his Irish brogue, which worked perfectly fine in the context of immigrant America. It was harrowing as he screamed "Stop!" when interjecting in the assault on Anita. Jordan Donnelly as Chino created an interesting character; shaking with nerves as he stood at the entrance to the wedding shop and clearly broken after killing Tony. He arrived at Maria's house stressed and out of breath, covered in cuts and bruises, giving context to immediacy of the situation. His incomprehension at Maria's ill-placed concerns forced him to play against the drama and whisper the line "He killed your brother". Very tastefully done.

Pat McElwain gave us a dark Detective Shrank, with a speaking voice that one wouldn't mess with. There was no good versus evil here. Just another shade of grey, danger in another guise. Angry at the youngsters, and clearly no time to eat a proper meal, he threw a chip at one of the lads. "I got the badge, you got the skin" he reminded them, no shying away from his own racist intentions and/or manipulations. He presented as another sinister element (victim?) of the story. "I want to help you get rid of them", he states, before taking a sip from his hipflask, "You try keeping hoodlums in check and see what it does to you". Cleverly, he had softened when he visited the girls, combining respect with business, as he insists he must question them no matter how upset they may be. Ian Tighe, as Bernardo, had excellent presence and showcased a super accent. His characterisation was perfect; dark, domineering and aggressive, the angry underdog wanting to carve out status for himself in an uninviting world.

Ross Murray as Riff was an excellent foil to Tony. All too eager to rumble, he would not take no for an answer from Tony when it came to the rumble. This youthful but misguided enthusiasm contrasted nicely with Tony's quiet, mature disinterest. His vocalising at the start of 'Jet Song' was very good.

Jacqueline Brunton was wonderful as Anita. A no-nonsense sultry broad, she gave us powerful singing that oozed the accent. She was fierce as she passed Velma in the gym. Her duet with Maria was a tense screaming match, yet she was able to portray an intense stillness on the bed; frozen with grief, disbelief, and how numbingly complicated it now was with Maria. She was, of course, traumatised after the assault in the drug store. With her, we could not "see" the acting. She had the ability to "be" the character, which is the holy grail for all good actors.

Gavin Ryan was less preppy and polished than other Tonys can be. More interesting in his silence, he was understated, convincing, naturalistic, laddish, masculine, introverted with Riff and less- so with Maria, just like young lads might be around males and females. He really acted his sung material, finding meaning in every word. We did not get squeaky clean perfectionistic concert versions of this music, but guttural and edgy renditions that punctuated the vocals to show clear thought-processes. His physicality was always interesting as he hung out of the bars of the set, taking ownership of the space to embody his characterisation. Sorcha Fenlon was simply gorgeous as Maria. She has a lovely voice and used it well, ensuring that we fell in love with her. Her singing was as clear as a bell in 'One Hand, One Heart'. Her partnership with Tony was cute and passionate all in one, as they invoked young excitable love and optimism. Angelic in nature, we could not bear for anything bad to happen to her, ensuring that her heartbreak at the end was moving.

The final moment was heart-breaking as always; the cop standing beside the murdering Chino enhancing the tragedy of the act. There were no winners. Except for the triumph of the production itself. It won every heart in the place, such was the amazing reaction it got from the crowd. Vibrational synergy? Synergistic vibration? Whatever it was, it was unforgettable.

The strength of this production was in its visual impact, with nicely selected costumes, well-worn by the cast, and in the positioning of chorus and principals on the stage. As I've come to expect from Director, Wilfie Pyper, there was a natural feel about the placings, and plenty of background business going on when the chorus were contributing to various scenes. The show was extremely well cast, and the performances were generally strong, although I did feel that much comedy was lost as a result of the dialogue frequently belting along with few breaks or pauses for comedic effect. Given the limitations of the venue, the set design was fairly straight-forward and adequate for its purpose, although much more needed to be done to effectively light the upstage raised walkway, as it was frequently employed for dramatic exits. During Act One, dialogue was seriously over-amplified, but the problem was amended by Act Two.

I do appreciate the need to pace My Fair Lady very well to prevent it from running to 3 hours, and no doubt that was the reason for the omission of "You Did It" and "Show Me", and as the former merely repeats what has already been shown during the ballroom scene, it was a good natural cut, but I did miss "Show Me", which can be a powerhouse number for Eliza.

A bigger concern was the pace at which much of the dialogue was taken. I did feel that comedy suffered from being passed over at such a speed, and on occasions, sentiment was also diminished, particularly in the Eliza/Higgins scenes. At such a pace, the audience will follow without really having time to consider the emotions being expressed.

The show was, nevertheless, delightfully presented, and my only other criticisms would be of minutiae, like Higgins wearing his hat indoors on several occasions. The functional set was well painted and just about complex enough to define the various scenes of the show, it was also efficiently, if not always speedily, manoeuvred around the stage by Andy Bell and his team. Some of the props and furniture were very good, but the chaise longue looked a tad thrown together. The slightly raised level at the back was impractical due to the inability to light it effectively, and unfortunately some dramatic exits and entrances were performed in half light. The lighting, generally, was atmospheric, but too often soloists were lost in the shadows created by the gobo effects. There was good use of colour, and cueing was good. Sound cueing throughout was quite satisfactory, but the whole first act was over-amplified, which, combined with the frantic pace of some of the dialogue, gave several scenes a sense of un-necessary aggression. In Act Two, the balance became much more satisfactory, and the sound plot included appropriate ambient sound effects on several occasions.

Costumes were of a very good quality, with good attention to detail and accessories. The traditional black and white for Ascot was most pleasing, and the ball gowns were good. Perhaps the couple of street entertainers in the opening number could have been made to stand-out more. The principals were perfectly dressed, with Eliza radiant in her ball gown and her Ascot attire.

Hairstyles were appropriate and well- managed, and make-up presented no problems.

Wilson Shields is, thankfully, one of those Musical Directors who can play and conduct at the same time, giving perfect leadership to his musicians but still ensuring that the chorus and principals come off their final note on the correct beat. This was evident from well-drilled choral contributions throughout the show, with a good concentration on harmonies. The pace of the music was spot on, and this allowed sentiment and emotion to be better expressed in song than in the dialogue. The musical quality of the principals was remarkably good. Overall, the show was a musical delight.

Oprah Devitt's choreography throughout the show was relatively simple but universally effective, playing to the ability of her performers and presenting extremely tidy routines. A nice soft shoe routine blended well into a scene of well- organised movement at the start of the show, while Eliza and the dancers added a nice flow to "Wouldn't It Be Loverly". The "With a Little Bit of Luck" reprise was nicely moved and "Get Me To The Church", while somewhat truncated, was the dance number of the show. Ascot and the Grand Waltz at the Ballroom were both tidy and pleasing to the eye.

In the demanding role of Eliza Doolittle, Karen Hawthorne was at her best as the less than eloquent flower girl of the opening scenes. She was feisty and extremely expressive, and her anger and frustration during her formal training were palpable, as was her comedic timing. She remained strong and resolute as she became more refined, but a tendency for the pace of the script to be delivered at almost break-neck speed did lessen the dramatic impact of some of her scenes. What it didn't impact at all was her remarkable vocal performance, as she delivered her songs with quality, precision and wonderful diction.

Tim Pentland cut a strong and commanding figure as Henry Higgins, precise with his language and condescending with his attitude. Unfortunately, he too suffered from the speed of the dialogue, resulting in some scenes being good when they might have been excellent. He combined the common procedure of speaking much of his songs with some very confident singing, and got the balance just right. In probably the wordiest role in Musical Theatre, he was pretty much word perfect, a highly commendable accomplishment. A little bit like myself, Billy Rea has reached the stage of slotting comfortably into the more laid-back and mature character roles, and he was the perfect choice for Col. Pickering, bringing a wealth of experience and excellent timing to the role. Always the perfect gentleman, he was a natural as the role model for Eliza. A good accent and a high level of impropriety were the hallmarks of a fine performance from Andrew Scott as Alfred Doolittle. Looking every bit the unrefined dustman, he performed his musical numbers with great energy and a tuneful voice. His fine sense of comedy was highlighted in the Study scene with Higgins and Pickering. He was very ably assisted in his shenanigans by Colin Gregg as Harry and Jack Cranston as Jamie.

It seems that a show isn't a show in Northern Ireland unless Sean Harkin is involved in some way, and on this occasion, he pops up as the somewhat effete suitor, Freddy Eynsford Hill. This was a nicely interpreted role, displaying a very good vocal quality for the ever-popular "On The Street Where You Live".

Heather Campbell gave a motherly quality to Mrs Pearce, trying to keep an element of civility and decorum in the Higgins household. This was delightfully portrayed. Vivian Shepherd played the actual mother of Henry with a quirky and highly effective upper-class-twitishness, which gave way to a more heart-warming appreciation of Eliza as a strong and independent woman. Very nice comedy.

From a long list of supporting characters, there were stand out performances from Claire Cranston as a very able Mrs Hopkins and a lovely cameo from Simon Pyper as the ridiculous Hungarian, Zoltan Karpathy. I always knew there was something Regal about Ann Ekin, who was appropriately cast as the Queen of Transylvania. Liz Boyd, Shane Johnston, David Mehaffey, Liz Johnston, Drew Reid, Victor Berry, Desi Martin, Ben Armstrong, Naomi Lloyd and Tracey Patterson all contributed as well to the chorus as they did in their cameo roles. I'm delighted to see that Lisnagarvey continue to provide their audiences with a high standard of entertainment. Thank you for a most enjoyable (and nostalgic) night of good old traditional musical theatre.

Kilkenny Musical Society stage their show in the lovely Watergate Theatre. There is not a bad seat in the house, with its nice wide stage and pit for the orchestra. There was a large circular screen in the middle of John O'Donoghue-designed stage, like an orbed stained-glass window, that contained the Sister Act logo. An abstract representation of Philadelphia buildings jutted up towards this screen, giving the aesthetic energy and exciting shape. On this lovely aesthetic, we would be treated to super lead performances and great choral numbers.

The set was constructed by Harry Harris. There was a screen at the back which shone the Sister Act logo as the audience filed in, which suitably re-appeared for the bows, bringing the show full-circle. Some of these wings etc. were cleverly re-used for the bar across the street from the convent. This set-piece also flew in posters and artwork in addition to a bar decorated in a record motif (that was repeated on the screen), as well as a juke box and some bar stools. These flats would be used once again for Deloris' 'Fabulous, Baby!' fantasy sequence.

The projections added to each set-up. For example, a golden mirror-ball was shown for Deloris' audition and fantasy sequence in Eddie's house.

The Philadelphia Police emblem for the cop station, or the street scene outside the convent added additional clarity.

A simple desk (nicely dressed by Props Mistress Sheila Lynch) and a flown-in cage was all that was needed to establish the cop station. A Philadelphia skyline gave perspective to the back wall when necessary. Deloris' shiny audition curtain cleverly turned to become the red-bricked graffiti-clad back-alley of Curtis' club, where poor Ernie would meet his untimely end. This was coupled with a slide of an alleyway for further clarity. Some side- sections opened out to give us those texturised gothic walls on either side of the stage looked fantastic. The confessional boxes were of good quality. The Mother Superior's desk was nicely dressed; with its old phone, bible, teeny crucifix and pen stand.

Director David Hennessey ensured a show that knew when to be funny and when to take itself more seriously, using the space well to frame moments. The gunshots during the chase scene after Ernie's death added excitement to the moment (and were a good distraction as the cop station scene was being set up behind). The crap singing when we first meet the nuns was really given time to breathe, which I think is important. Getting Deloris to interrupt a silent prayer in the dining room with her "Bless You" was a nice idea, clearly demonstrating her disruptive presence in the convent. Mary Robert took her time when deciding if she would follow Deloris to the bar, which worked dramatically while enabling more time for the cop station to be set up. Deloris cueing the nuns to laugh after Mary Lazarus made her little joke showed how they were a little intimidated by the strict chorus mistress and how Deloris was getting them on side. It was gas how the altar boys were bopping along in 'Sunday Morning Fever' as the fundraising thermometer was brought on and off. The audience loved the moment in which the nuns seduced TJ with a wiggle of their knee in the chase scene. It was quite moving as the nuns said "Take Me" to Curtis to protect Deloris. The bows were done in character; as the gangsters did the Charlie's Angels pose, then dismissed by Curtis who was then blessed by Monsignor O'Hara.

There were lots of good moments when the lighting punctuated the ending of songs, such as the purple wash after 'Fabulous Baby' near the beginning of the show and at the end of 'How I Got the Calling' and 'Sunday Morning Fever'. Yellow and blue movers in 'Fabulous, Baby' added energy to the number. Celestial white light at the beginning of 'Here Within These Walls' was effective. The white light on Mother Superior and the dimmer wash on Deloris worked well here during their counterpoint moment to show the differences between them. The disco-ball lighting used in the bar scene was nicely atmospheric as it spilled out into the audience. The light got warmer as Mary Robert stood up to Mother Superior in her 'Life I Never Led' reprise. Musical Director Emer Hartnett ensured top-notch principal vocals and choral numbers that bounced off the stage. There were nice moments concerning dynamics, such as the whispered "sexual tension" in 'How I Got the Calling'. The slow bit at the beginning of the nuns' version of 'Fabulous, Baby' was gorgeous. The harmonies were so clear in 'Sunday Morning Fever', such as on the phrase "double jointed". The nuns knew to keep a keen eye on the MD, as they very nicely held hands at the end of 'Bless Our Show', to ensure they came off in sync at exactly the right moment. The high-pitched backing vocals from the gangsters in 'When I Find My Baby' were good.

The drum beat at the beginning of the first 'Fabulous, Baby' almost gave me a heart attack, such was the loud sharp crack it created. The man in front of me nearly jumped out of this skin so I don't think I was alone there. The band, made up of ten musicians overpowered the vocals, particularly in the beginning, which is a shame considering the use of a pit usually supports this rampant issue that is happening around the country. No doubt Sound Man Terry Hanlon did his best, as this seemed to settle as the show went on. Choreography was by Nicole McDonald (with Roisin Currid assisting). 'How I Got the Calling' built nicely, by adding more and more nuns in as the number grew. The nuns' headbanging during Mary Lazarus' rap was comic in 'Raise Your Voice'. The raising of the hymn books and slamming them shut at the end of this number worked very well also. There are certain moves that these show-choir numbers beg for and they were all in there in abundance, slickly performed by the super cast of nuns. The spinning crucifix formation in the nuns' 'Take Me to Heaven' was awesome. The fantasy dancer sequence was a visual treat, circling Deloris to mount pressure on her, with a semi-circle of nuns behind, all effectively messing with her head. Pulling Mother Superior and Monsignor O'Hara into 'Sunday Morning Fever' was funny and the kick-line at the end was great. The diagonal line created to bring Deloris on for the final number worked really well and it was nice how this number included the altar boys. The nuns' circling to get into lines for the bows was slick.

Stage Management was by Séamus Reade. The crew were dressed as priests to bring in the desk, chairs and coat rack in the middle of 'Here Within These Walls'. A lot of work had to go into the setting up of the dining scene, such was the enormity of the tables etc., but all the fuss was worth it when the lights came up on the picture of the million nuns present. The lighted cross to measure the church fundraising was nicely flown in. The gangsters were given a little business after 'Lady in the Long Black Dress' to cover the scene change. Using the gangsters to drag Ernie's body off was a good idea - instead of bringing on the crew to do this (or having the actor walk off in a blackout).

Costume co-ordinators Ailín Dunphy and Claire Gibbs ensured that everyone looked smashing. Monsignor O'Hara's black habit with red belt and buttons and priestly hat was great at establishing his station in the historical context. Deloris sported a head of curls and wore a leopard print top, golden blinged belt, black leather skirt and those infamous purple Father Mulcahy boots. The red and gold on Tina and Michelle, whose hair looked like Farah Fawcett just out of the bed, linked nicely with the colours within the set. The gangsters wore various attire (thankfully not uniform) that evoked the 70s, with Curtis looking the most dapper of course. Joey had a brown-check suit, black leather coat, green shirt and navy flares. A very tanned and moustached Pablo had the chest out with on open shiny green shirt and purple suit. His medallion shot searing beams of light around the theatre. The three skanks in the cop station looked suitably trashy. The winter coats and hats on the down- and-outs looked just right. Eddie's sweat patches were well-realised. I will admit that I have seen more successful reveals for 'I Could be That Guy', as Eddie's sleeves, feet and askew tie gave the gag away slightly. Then again, perhaps I was looking far more closely than the audience were. The gold tunics with red hearts were lovely for the nuns' first public performance. How they turned their backs to the audience to ensure an effective reveal gave the audience a great surprise. The various coloured tunics with matching headgear in 'Sunday Morning Fever' were fabulous, showing how much the nuns' act had grown. Mary Lazarus was a scream here in her matching sports jersey, sunglasses and blinged-up cap for her rap sequence. The pyjamas were at their best when pastel in colour with an old-school vibe. The platinum blonde wigs (with headscarves) on the fantasy dancers were super. Each time Monsignor O'Hara appeared, he was more fabulous than the last. The nuns' sequined habits with gold embroidered cross looked super at the end. The gangsters appeared as blinged- up altar boys for the finale. Deloris' dream came true and she got to wear her white fur in the end.

Carol Knox created such a memorable character for her portrayal of protagonist Deloris Van Cartier. With her initial arrival at the convent, we got a cool rough- around-the-edges broad, with a dollop of ridiculousness. Her character grew throughout, however, and we were left with a woman who was a little wiser, more self-aware, who had developed more meaningful relationships. She had a very good accent. She gave us a lovely rendition of 'Sister Act'. I might have spotted a tear at the end, and if so, I hope they were tears of pride, moved by the amazing reaction that she got.

Sarah Brennan gave us a (mostly) serious Mother Superior, strict in her running of the convent, suitably panicked by Deloris' arrival and firm in her dealings with the new addition. She took no nonsense as she stormed across the stage to strike Deloris' bowl, declaring a fast. She had a great R.P. accent. She sang some gorgeous high notes; classical, nun-like. Her 'I Haven't Got a Prayer' was moving at times in its sadness, yet comic in places also. She was hilarious when she hit that high note when copying Deloris' riffing at the end.

Eoghan Fingleton had a very good accent as the poor unfortunate Sweaty Eddie. He portrayed enough of Eddie's goofball personality, yet we could still see why Deloris would fall for him. His 'I Could be that Guy' got a great reaction from the audience. He was adorable with Deloris in his apartment, as he encouraged her, telling her that she was going to be a star. Amy Mulholland captured all the meekness as the gentle Sister Mary Robert. She showed some lovely acting in 'The Life I Never Led' and had very good belt on the final note of this song. She was great when she stood up to the Mother Superior at the end, portraying her character's growth nicely.

Cathal O'Donoghue as Monsignor O'Hara provided a very funny warm-up act for the show, working the safety announcements into the act. He shone here as a natural comedian with lovely rhythms and an off-beat delivery that was hilarious in its naturalism. He was a hoot as he bopped along to the nuns' first public performance and when he guiltily blessed himself before saying "I adore this music" in the confessional scene.

David Doyle gave us a sleazy letch as Curtis, showcasing a great speaking voice. His character was cool and suave (as well as being a bit of a pig), and he also showed that he is quite the mover in his 'When I Find My Baby'.

Marian Gaffney took no nonsense as Sister Mary Lazarus. This character gets some cracking material in the form of raps etc. during the nuns' numbers, and Maria was funny performing these.

Edwina Cummins was suitable jolly as the ever-smiling Sister Mary Patrick who brought joy and positivity to each scene she was in. Her moment in 'Fabulous, Baby!' was funny, as was her repetition of Pablo's Spanish threats.

There was not a weak-link in the great trio of actors that made up Curtis' foolish henchmen. Kevin Reade as TJ, Aidan O' Dwyer as Joey and Trevor O' Neil as Pablo committed to their roles, injecting a lot of comedy into the show. The wiggling of their hips and their seductive moves in 'Lady in the Long Black Dress' were a scream. Joey's body-spray gag was great. Maeve Tierney and Nicola Brennan as Tina and Michelle respectfully were sassy but dumb, full of attitude yet hilarious. This is the first time I have seen so much physical comedy worked into their routines; their hands pointing towards Deloris in admiration made me chuckle. David Brybone gave us two good cameos as Ernie and the Cab Driver.

The very good choreography, the nice harmony lines and the fun direction from the production team would not mean a thing if these people did not have a committed ensemble to execute all these nice ideas with precision. The chorus of this show were great, ensuring that the nuns' numbers had impact on the audience.

Kilkenny Musical Society know how to stage a hit. And I am not just talking about the gangsters. The 'Raise Your Voice' reprise included the whole cast, providing so much excitement and energy. The audience were sent out the door, buzzing after a fantastic evening of song, dance and comedy in a production that knew when to play the thing for laughs, and when to give time to the more moving moments of character development.

The Little Theatre ain't so little; it's a fine space with lovely red walls and seats that swoop right down to the red curtain of the wide stage. There was a lovely atmosphere in the venue as people arrived, with the help of a wonderfully dressed Ozian man in the foyer, setting the tone nicely. Full disclosure. When I learned that I was to adjudicate The Wizard of Oz, I was not bursting with excitement. It is a story that we all know so well, and as it is so familiar, it is unusual to be enthralled by it. I have seen this show where I felt as though the thing was going through the motions; aimed primarily at children who do not know the story that well or who are excited to see their favourite characters in the flesh (or tin, or straw). I was pleasantly surprised by how entertaining this production was; full of engaging principal performances and exciting ensemble moments, all wrapped up in an impressive aesthetic. Each time 'We're off the see the Wizard' kicked in, a riot would break out in the audience, as they clapped, whooped and hollered enthusiastically, indicative of the fun they were having.

The set, designed by Gabrielle Brickley and constructed by Paul Doran, Frank Byrne and Michael Kinsella, was very impressive. The Kansas set-up was a simple affair to illustrate the simple lives of the characters. There was the corner of a house, beside bunker doors, that would rattle and shake and move about when the tornado came. There was a small chicken coop and turn table that would spin Dorothy back on when she returned home. This was coupled with a projection of a dull cloudy sky that would become significantly jollier when Dorothy arrived in Oz. The cart with the missing wheel was great. I might argue that the Kansas set-up was a little sparse for the width of the stage, but on the other hand this bleakness contrasted nicely with the excitement of the Oz scenery.

The backdrops in Oz were gorgeous; indicative of a Hobbit village crossed with Dr Seuss illustrations. The crushed feet under the house worked well. The Scarecrow set-up was lovely; the hills on the backdrop matched the rainbow colours in the wings, a ramp at the back formed the yellow-brick road all nicely framed with fantastic ears of corn. The Spooky Forest was a visual treat with scary faces carved into the trees, with one branch actually forming the word "boo". The sparkling gate of Oz would cleverly reflect any colour light shone onto it and the bell looked cool. A lot of work went into the backdrop for the Emerald City, made up of a skyline of turrets and pyramids on top of a marble wall. I might suggest that more green could have gone into this backdrop to evoke the idea of an Emerald City, but the Dublin colours were appreciated nonetheless! An enormous head with searing red eyes, surrounded by billowing flames, making up the Wizard's chamber, was amazing and impressively turned again to become the gates of the Emerald City.

Mary Morris was in charge of props and responsible for some striking items such as the lights in the Witch's broom and the fantastically giant lollipops for the Lollipop Guild. Props were great in the grooming scene, such as the enormous scissors. The snowy branches were a lovely touch in the Poppy scene. The Scarecrow's rifle, the Tinman's axe and the comically passive fishing net for the Lion added comedy in the scene where they go to get the Witch.

Mark Redmond's lighting added nicely to the story-telling. The swirling gobos on the floor added to the drama of the tornado. The green light, flash and smoke created a dramatic moment for the entrance of the Wicked Witch of the West, and this green motif was repeated during her voice- overs also. A red and green wash gave a magical, mystical, slightly dangerous environment for the poppy field, matching and enhancing the colours within the costumes here. The gobo of bars looked very well in Dorothy's prison.

Paul Doran's stage management was admirable. Scene changes were performed in a jiffy. Perhaps this is because the Stage Manager was linked to the creation of the set. The set pieces for the tornado did not just come on and off but they shook violently with the doors slamming etc., creating lots of drama. Dancers were also utilised as part of the tornado to remove and replace set-pieces. The gates of the Emerald City cleverly turned to become the talking head façade of the Wizard. Slick work here.

Theresa Donegan, Mary Spellman and Adrienne Casey were responsible for the costumes which, overall, were superb. The Kansas folk looked perfect in their various shirts, dungarees, waistcoats and straw hats etc. Dorothy wore the classic gingham. Miss Gulch wore a black and red motif that would be cleverly repeated when she appeared as the Wicked Witch of the West. Glinda's crown, staff and gorgeous pink sequined dress were all suitably fabulous. Our three heroes looked just perfect and the Lion's mane was fabulous. Gorey Institute of Make-Up did a great job in creating these fantastical characters. Glinda's long blonde hair was lovely, magically transforming her from the dowdy Aunt Em. The Scarecrow, Tin Man and the Lion face-paint was perfect. If I were to be very picky, I could point out that no actual straw fell out of the Scarecrow's costume when he fell, as the dialogue suggested. The Crows wore bird-beak masks and black and orange striped tights. The apple-throwing trees looked so cool with their long brown gowns and tall hats. Out of these hats, they would take their soft material apples to fling at our heroes. There was great variety of green attire in Oz. The Emerald City guard looked fab in his green and gold. There was great attention to detail with the Winkie costumes - made up of Russian hats, staffs, green tunics with crests on the chests and red cloaks. The black and gold Jitterbug costumes were varied, while maintaining a thematic uniformity.

The Munchkins sported a blue and white motif full of checked clothing, gingham, dungarees and bonnets. For me, this motif did not really create the otherworldliness we might associate with these characters. There is no denying the quality of the costumes here, but I think a burst of colour with clothing that was a bit more out- there in terms of shape, cut, design etc. might have transformed the Munchkins into something a little more alternative to normal humans. They looked more like Kansas folk than quirky characters from a mystical land. There was, however, good clarity achieved in the costuming of those named Munchkins, indicating their professions, with the Coroner all in black for example.

With direction by Michael Dunbar, the audience laughed their way through the evening. Simple phrases, such as when the Tin Man said "oil can", or when he began to move his mouth, got great laughs. This is an example of how comedy was teased out in a way that could be over- looked in other productions of this show. The primary characters were very well drawn. There was such clear line delivery from all the cast, including the very young performers, suggesting that a lot of effort was spent assuring quality throughout. The tornado was nicely actualised, with mysterious dancers moving the furniture, along with the banging of the doors on the set, all slowing down nicely as Oz was revealed. The slipper-swap from the flattened Witch to Dorothy was well executed - I never noticed it happening. The snow-drops and snow creatures were a nice surprise, ridding the field of those nasty poppies. Ensemble crowd reactions in the Emerald City were great. Necessity is the mother of all invention and the use of glitter, instead of water, to melt the Witch combined with well-designed lights, smoke and cool sound effects to create a memorable moment.

Musical Director Conor McCarthy conducted the band of eight with clarity and played keyboards on the night. Principal vocal performances were spot-on throughout. The underscoring in the first scene in Oz created a lovely atmosphere, while never interfering with the crystal- clear dialogue from Dorothy and Glinda. Kelli-Ann Masterson did a wonderful job as Choral Mistress on this show. The 'Somewhere Over the Rainbow' motif sung to 'Ah', as Oz was revealed, was gorgeous. The "ah's" in the poppy field were glorious, nicely supported by those off-stage also, I imagine. Our four leads sang very well in harmony in the Jitterbug sequence. This work was supported by the excellent sound by i-Tech Productions. Underscoring during dialogue moments was perfectly balanced. The scary noises in the spooky forest were effective, nicely establishing the context during the blackout, as were the effects when the Wizard head appeared.

Choreography by Clodagh Leacy provided exciting and well-executed numbers. The tornado characters combined moves with functionality, as they moved furniture around. The Munchkins had great dance moves, full of attack and energy (the hand-slapping was cool). The trees posed so elegantly and moved so gracefully, as though blowing in the breeze. The poppies dance was split into two dynamic groups; each with their own moves, one group on their backs on the ground. The laughing, dancing and jolly belly-holding by the Citizens of the Emerald City, as they sung their "huh ho hos" really captured the fun of the number. While the Jitterbug dance moves worked really well with the music (and the leads were super joining in with the routine), I might argue that at least the first half of this number might have invoked a scarier intention. It was a little bit of a show-dance and did not have enough heightened menace for me. Each number was very well rehearsed, however, full of enthusiasm, enhancing the enjoyability of the evening.

Grace Kehoe gave us a high energy performance in the demanding role of Dorothy. She had a lovely voice, evoking a similar quality to Judy Garland and she produced very nice vowel sounds. The ending of 'Somewhere Over the Rainbow' was particularly memorable. This is such a mammoth role with so many lyrics, lines, harmonies and dance routines to learn all while being emotional throughout and Grace made it all look very easy indeed. Our three Ozian heroes were full of character in their appearance in the Kansas scenes at the start of the show. Sometimes people are too understated in these opening scenes, saving the enjoyable characterisation for the scenes in Oz. I am glad to say that they were entertaining from the get-go, helping those sometimes-dull Kansas scenes spring to life. Tomás Byrne as Hunk/Scarecrow was lovely and warm, with bundles of likeability. His physicality as the straw man was very good and he sang and danced with panache. Brendan Kenny as Hickory/Tin Man gave us good metallic physical movements. His timing was just right, meaning he could elicit a laugh in places I have never heard laughs before. His terrified screaming in the Jitterbug sequence was hilarious. Malcolm Byrne produced plenty of laughs as Lion/Zeke, comically cowardly and cute as a button in his braver moments. This is a character that really grows throughout the show and Malcolm charted this development very well. All three men nailed their parts and I doubt anyone who wanted to see their favourite characters come to life was disappointed in these portrayals.

Ciara Spellman as Almira Gulch/Wicked Witch of the West was nice and eeeeviiiil in her portrayals of both characters. Both appearances require an actress with presence and energy, who can own the stage playing one of musical theatre's most famous characters. I am glad to say that Ciara did not disappoint.

Aunt Em/Glinda was played by Genevieve Molloy. She gave us a realistic simplistic woman as Aunt Em. She showed a great change in characterisation when she appeared as an upbeat, ditzy high energy Glinda, surprising us with her range as an actress.

George Percival played Uncle Henry/ Emerald City Guard. Like Aunt Em, there was a simplicity to his characterisation as Uncle Henry, meaning he was unrecognisable as the characterful guard. His funny walk as he was over-listening to the conversation by our four heroes was a hoot.

Mark Ivory's portrayal of Professor Marvel/ The Wizard of Oz was characterful and entertaining.

These characters must establish themselves instantly when they appear on stage as they are not given a slow introduction. Mark had good presence and naturalism and managed this task nicely. He captured the balance between Professor Marvel as the chancer and as the wise man very well.

With the greatest respect, I have to say that sometimes when very young performers appear on stage, they can lack a certain polish, energy and volume, sometimes creating a lull in a show. Not with this superb troop of young stars! Clearly the ensemble had put a huge amount of work into their performances. The energy from the Munchkins was amazing. Their movement was so slick. Dressed as ballerinas, the Lullaby League gave us some brilliant ballet dancing. The solo lines in the Munchkin scenes had super energy and clarity. The Citizens of Oz had superb reactions. The Flying Monkeys (with a very good Katie Cunningham as Nico) had well- developed animal physicality. The Poppies and Snow People created a magical moment and the Jitterbugs gave us a show stopping routine. All of this added to the lovely principal performances, in a show that looked great and ran like clockwork. There was nothing boring about this version of this classic tale. It was super fun.

In this somewhat stylised production, the staging difficulties normally associated with "Sweet Charity" were significantly alleviated, which worked very well, although it did put an added pressure on the lighting designer to be highly inventive, and the lack of a structured set did, on occasions, lead to a slight lack of atmosphere. The set was minimal with only occasional free standing pieces that were essential for comedic business. The wardrobe in Vittorio's bedroom and the lift both worked well, even if more could have been done to give the illusion of the lift moving or rising before it jammed.  These pieces, plus furniture and props, were efficiently put in place by Stage Manager, Amy McCarthy and her team.

While there was plenty of colour and variety to the lighting plot, with moving heads and attractive effects on the cyc, I rarely had the feeling that the colourful display was particularly relevant to the action. The most effective states occurred when smaller areas were being focused on and there was less activity. While the recorded opening dialogue probably took pressure off the sound engineer, it did also detract from some very funny dialogue, as the audience were more concerned with trying to grasp what was going on. Apart from that, the sound quality throughout was very satisfactory. Where Director, Kevin Hynes, scored highly was in his drawing of the characteristics of the various individuals on-stage. This was a thoroughly well-rehearsed cast, each of whom had a definite and individual identity. It was easy to be sympathetic to Charity with her quirky naivety, and to see through the transparency of most of the male characters.

While she sang very well and moved with ease and comfort, it was the sincerity of her acting that made Gail McGrath so acceptable in the role of Charity. There was an almost self-effacing quirkiness to her humour, which made her a delightfully sympathetic character. Vocally, she was well up to the challenge of the role.

There was a good contrast between Sophia Daly as Nikki and Róisin Ryan as Helene, Sophia with a seen-it-all, done- it-all acceptance of her lot, coupled with a brash sense of humour, and Róisin the more reluctant and frustrated hostess, with a drier, bitter view of their station in life. Both were consistent and extremely capable in their portrayals, displaying great rhythm and vocal ability, with Sophia having that extra dimension of being a sincere, if somewhat misguided, mother hen figure. The two worked extremely well together and with Charity.

Chris O'Connor gave a stalwart performance as their seedy boss, Herman, always comfortable on the stage, albeit in a loathsome kind of way. This was an enjoyable performance, coupled with a very good delivery of "I Love to Cry at Weddings". Chris also doubled as "Daddy" to perform "The Rhythm of Life", which he did with panache, although I would have liked to see him visually more outrageous or flamboyant.

Peter O'Brien handled the claustrophobic comedy of Oscar with talent and very good timing, establishing his character from the outset. He had an infectious likeability as the quirky would-be lover, and it's a testament to his acting ability that when he suddenly refused to accept Charity's circumstances, the audience, quite vocally, turned against him. This was a well-acted and well sung role.

Aaron Tierney brought an unexpected kind of bedraggled, youthful exuberance to the role of Vittorio Vidal, with a mixture of fame induced arrogance and naïve insecurity. It did work very nicely, although I did feel that more comedy could have been squeezed out of the bedroom scene. Alicia O'Connor was suitably pouty and pretentious in the role of Ursula, full of tantrums and shallow affection.

The principal line was completed by a very worthy Laura Walsh as the not so innocent new-comer, Rosie.

The chorus performed with great credibility throughout the show, adding atmosphere and character to all their scenes, and the feeling of inclusiveness was beautifully highlighted by the performances of Alice McGrath and Mark Claffey, who made their presence felt in a most delightful manner.

In the very secure hands of Musical Director, Caitriona Ni Threasaigh, there was little to criticise in the delivery of the musical content of the show. Tempi were always on point, and the effervescence of the livelier numbers was balanced by a sympathetic rendition of the more mellow and emotional pieces. Principals were vocally well-disciplined in numbers which are rhythmically quite challenging, and the chorus performed "Rhythm of Life" and "I Love to Cry at Weddings" particularly well. There were beautiful tributes to Bob Fosse in Nicole McDonald's choreography, which was always stylish and appropriate to the show and the music. Her chorus and dancers made a very good job of executing the Frug and Rhythm of Life in particular, and she had good dancers in the principal roles, who were able to give life and energy to "Something Better Than This", and "If My Friends Could See Me Now". The small hand movements of "Big Spender" work better on camera (with close ups) than they do on stage, but this still developed into a good routine.

Costumes were of a good standard, with the dance hostesses always suitably attired. Outfits for the Frug were very good, and principals were appropriately dressed. There was good attention to hair styles and make-up, giving the overall effect of the era of the show.

I'm delighted that Glencullen took a chance on this piece of musical theatre, and did so with conviction. The 'studio' style of the production was interesting and imaginative, but perhaps because of the need for certain set pieces to give comedic effect, it did seem to fall somewhere between an abstract concept and a fully staged show. Thanks, however, to a very committed cast and some very good direction and choreography, it was still a highly entertaining night of musical theatre.

In the safe hands of the experienced Justin Parkes, I expected to see a well-drilled, thorough and entertaining production of this classic, and that's precisely what I got. While it may have been more traditional than innovative, it had polish and commitment from all on stage, and was marked by a beautifully natural sense of community, through the involvement of children in the crowd scenes. While Dunboyne weren't able to use all the pieces of their hired set exactly as designed, due to stage limitations, they very cleverly crafted the pieces they could use into an excellent background to the action. It was well painted and functional, with the smoke house being particularly impressive. Just as important as it looking good was the fact that it was seamlessly manoeuvred around the stage by Stage Managers, Elaine McLoughlin and Sean Keany, and their team. There was good flow and pace to all of the action, and very good attention to the development of characters.

The strength of Aishling Rountree's choreography in this production was that it carried through on the director's sense of inclusivity, so that instead of a stand- alone dancers routine for "Farmer and the Cowman" we got the whole community dancing as you might expect at a box- social. There were kids doing their own (choreographed) thing, oblivious to the adults around them, and there were people dancing in their own little groups and circulating to dance with others, an occasional bit of tension between a farmer and a cowboy, and there were cowboys showing off their steps and girls trying to flirt and dance with them, and it all just worked brilliantly. I'm well aware that such organised chaos is much harder to perfect than a straightforward routine. In "Kansas City" too, there was plenty of step work, but it was played with Will Parker teaching the others their steps, at which they gradually improved until they were all dancing joyfully in unison. Very clever work. The Ballet was excellent, with Jud, Curly and Laurey fronting it with some very nifty dancing. Overall, the choreography thoroughly superbly enhanced the quality of the production.

Kevin Hartnett and Keila-Ana Whelan developed an almost symbiotic relationship in the roles of Curly and Laurey, feeding off each other in the comedy of their teasing, and totally believable in their developing romance. Their voices blended beautifully together and they flowed gracefully in the execution of their dances. Individually, they created strong and believable characters and interacted very well with the rest of the cast. Keila-Ana's loathing of Jud was as convincing as her love for Curly, and both were beautifully acted.

Monica Hannigan (above) was a secure and homely Aunt Eller, well able for the antics of the men around her, and delightfully sympathetic towards her niece. She steered the auction scene with good authority and contributed well to the vocals of "The Farmer and the Cowman". Eoin O'Reilly was an animated Will Parker, enjoying his opportunities to display his dancing ability, and comfortable in his comedic encounters with Ado Annie. He made a very good job of "Kansas City". Meaghan Ebbs was a quirky and robust Ado Annie, making the most of her silliness, and putting good comedy and energy into "I Cain't Say No".

There was almost a sympathetic simplicity about the loneliness of Shane Fox's Jud Fry, until the turning point when Curly exposes the inner soul of an unsettling psychotic personality during the smoke- house scene. From then on, he was scary. This was an excellent performance, both in character development, and in the execution of his songs and dances.

Eoin Kenny sustained a very interesting accent throughout his performance, and used it to good comedic effect, playing the role of Ali Hakim with great character, confidence and comedy.

Grace McEntee's laugh was obnoxious! (That's a compliment.) She presented a good character and got plenty of fun out of the supporting role of Gertie Cummins. If I met Gerry Hannigan with a shotgun, I'd run the other way, so grumpy and gruff was he when he stepped out as Andrew Carnes, but he balanced that scariness with a fine sense of comedy, and developed into a very likeable old character. Good work in "The Farmer and The Cowman".

There was good dependable support from Ian McColgan as Ike Skidmore, Ben Hannigan as Slim, Cyril Green as Fred and Colm Woods as Mike, while Sean Whelan gave a good smug self-righteousness to Cord Elam in the ad hoc court scene. The chorus were particularly well integrated into their scenes, always having a sense of purpose and reacting to the focal point. Their vocal contributions were secure and they dance and movement were lively and well-executed.

Musical Director, Paul Strachan, led an impressive orchestra securely through the score, with good tempi and good volume control. The chorus were well-rehearsed in their music and lyrics, with well-realised harmonies and clear diction. Principals were musically very secure. The musical quality of the show was most impressive. There were no issues with the fairly traditional costuming of the show, with chorus and principals alike very well turned out. Jud looked sweaty and filthy, which I credit to a good make-up artist, and the rest of the cast looked as they should, both from a hair and make-up point of view. The lighting of the show was delightful, with the frequent beautiful blending of lavender and amber gels. The ballet gave a well-taken opportunity to be a bit inventive and artistic. It was atmospheric, picturesque and cueing was very good. Sound quality was very satisfactory with good cueing and some lovely ambient background effects.

Dunboyne Musical Society did themselves credit and were well served by their production and technical teams. Thank you for a very enjoyable evening and a very nice presentation of a popular classic.

The Backstage Theatre in Longford is a super resource, with comfortable tiered seating and a fine stage, creating the perfect setting to put on a show. This was my eighth time to adjudicate Sister Act, yet there is something about it that always seems fresh and new. It never fails to delight, and this version was no exception. With strong performers in the leading roles, supported by a great chorus of nuns, the production provided a great night's entertainment for all.

Director Seán Power gave us a solid version of this show that used the space very well. The way the nuns appeared live on stage for their backing vocals in 'Here Within These Walls' was cool (they often do these off stage) and it meant they were ready to go for the dining scene. The prayer before meals built very nicely. Mary Robert was very clearly blocked in isolation during 'How I Got the Calling'. I loved how Deloris brought the cheesesteak back from the bar and how the Mother Superior snatched it out of her hands. The business given to the bums, such as searching the bins for bottles, gave context to their appearance. The two altar boys pointing to the fundraiser thermometer was a hoot and the five altar boys wearing sunglasses on the balcony was gas.

The 'Fabulous, Baby!' reprise, in which Deloris wrestles with her conscience, was very well staged with the nuns up on the balcony with their backs to the audience, looking over their shoulders when it was their turn to interject. Mother Superior hyperventilating into a paper bag was a hoot. The moment Deloris leaves the convent was lovely; sad, sombre and touching. The moment when she told Mary Robert to "stay or go" was very nicely measured.

The chase scene combined humour and danger well. The cross-dresser came back for a cameo! The fighting in the chase scene never looked real, however. It is possible to look like contact is made between two people, without hurting anyone. The bump on the head was not in time with the music either. My friend was crying when the nuns starting to say "Take Me", which is a testament to how touching the moment was.

Set design was by Robert Belton and Stage Manager Eddie Kiernan. The lovely wings, each with its own lancet stained- glass window, stayed on for the whole show, framing the stage nicely. A series of trucks were wheeled on to form a sense of space behind the actors, such as a backdrop for Curtis' Bar and the entrance to the convent with a statue of Mary. The bar across the street from the convent looked cool with its silver bar top, dartboard, shelves with proper 3D bottles, red and white tiles on the floor, jukebox and disco-ball.

The convent set was fantastic with its series of doors, circular windows with clover-like stained glass decoration and balcony finished off with organ pipes. The working doors utilised in the chase scene were excellent and it seemed a shame that they were not used more. When Mary Patrick was eavesdropping on Mary Robert and Deloris, she might have used one of the doors, for example.

The confessional boxes looked really well. The crew were cleverly hiding behind the confessional boxes all the while so they could magically wheel themselves off at the end of that scene. This also happened behind the entrance truck with statue of Mary as it glided off like magic before the final scene. The curtains on the side solved a problem that most other societies were not able to overcome. The sofa and T.V. were all that were needed to establish Curtis' gaff. Deloris' room was nicely framed with a small backdrop with crucifix and her old school blanket and tartan bedspread on her little brown wooden bed looked the part. Eddie's dingy apartment was effectively established with the covered sofa and small set of flats behind it, framed by the Philadelphia skyline, creating a nice sense of space. The big red staircase gave great structure to the final number.

Lighting was designed by Paschal Gough. There was a nice white special on Mother Superior in the opening of Act Two when she tells God he is killing them with "the cure". The special on stage-left to cover at the top of the 'Fabulous, Baby!' reprise in Eddie's house was helpful at covering the scene change, nicely revealing the convent when it was set-up. The flickering light coming from the TV was cool. The 'Sister Act' number was great, with the slow disco-ball at the beginning, followed by a lovely rainbow effect on the floor and a final blackout, with the stained-glass windows left on.

Musical Director Alan Recks gave clear conduction to his seven musicians, while two keyboards sat in front of him also. Sound by Jody Trehy was perfectly balanced, ensuring that the seven musicians never overpowered the performers on stage, which is always an impressive achievement when the band are in the room, without a pit etc. Principal and choral vocals were all very good. The final three sentences of 'How I Got the Calling' contained noticeably well- delivered harmony lines. The high-pitched backing vocals from the three gangsters were good. The final "Heaven" in the reprise of 'Take Me to Heaven' was sung with power. The counter-point from Mother Superior and Eddie in 'Sunday Morning Fever' was clearer than I have ever heard it. The backing vocals from the bums were good. Mary Robert stayed down the octave for the ending to 'The Life I Never Led' which was the right choice. It is far better to do something simple and do it well. The 'Benedicta Tu' choral singing from the nuns and Mother Superior, after Deloris suddenly leaves them, was gorgeous. The 'Raise Your Voice' reprise bounced off the stage, sending everyone off on a high.

Choreographer Emer O'Brien impressively crammed the moves in 'When I Find my Baby', showcasing that a lot of work went into this number. All that sideways marching on the tiptoes looked great. There was a lovely organic feel to the 'Raise Your Voice' rehearsal as Deloris worked in small groups and the nuns filed in gradually. Bringing the nuns out of their pews for the final bit of 'Raise Your Voice' was impactful and while the Bible moves at the end was excellent in theory, the final 'Your Voice' was a little off, as though the nuns were slightly distracted. The choreography for the nuns' 'Take Me to Heaven' was well-rehearsed, slick, inventive, varied, never boring and never ending. 'Lady in the Long Black Dress' contained some cool moves and got a great reaction from the audience. 'Bless Our Show' was lovely as the nuns innocently danced circles around Deloris, "wooing" as they moved in and out. Their hand holding as they raised their arms at the end was lovely, showing their solidarity before Deloris has to suddenly leave. Including the Mother Superior in the movement of the final moments was gas. The bows were a moment in themselves, with Deloris coming down the impressive red staircase.  The moves for the curtain call were simple, but hugely effective when done in such a fantastic formation. Janice Gibney as Deloris was full of attitude in her opening scenes and rough around the edges when first introduced to the convent. Her facial expressions were hilarious. She was funny when she saw Ernie being shot. She showed good character development as she wrestled with her conscience in the 'Fabulous, Baby!' reprise, was bitter-sweet in her introspection during 'Sister Act' and when she defiantly stood up to Curtis in the final scenes.

Valerie Nolan was very good as Mother Superior. While dry and droll in her characterisation, she was capable of being funny also, such as her line "I take it back" when the Monsignor reminded her of her vows. She had a lovely voice, perfect for the role. She was lovely and quiet and sad in her little reprise of 'Here Within These Walls'. She was nice and sincere as she simply proclaimed that she was frightened when talking to God in her study. Her lyrics for 'I Haven't Got a Prayer' were so clear and she showed impressive soprano on her powerful high notes here. She also showed off some impressive vocals when comically repeating Deloris in the final scene.

Maryann Lynch as Sister Mary Robert was meek and shy at the beginning, barely able to talk or make eye contact. She grew in confidence nicely and acted through song very well indeed during 'The Life I Never Led', really getting to show off her singing voice in the first section of that song. Anthony Heavey was very good as Eddie. While I think he could have let go a little more in his 'I Could Be That Guy', this routine got a great reaction from the crowd. It was very cute when he sang to Deloris in his apartment, and his assurances to her that she would be a star were nicely convincing.

Dearbhaile Barrins as Sister Mary Patrick captured all the sunshine and jolliness of the character. She was very funny as she continued to interrupt Mary Robert in 'How I Got the Calling'. Michelle Kelly Conlon was good as Sister Mary Lazarus, with her no-nonsense Bronx-style accent. Her "ringer" speech was good as she accused the Mother Superior of holding a grudge of a past folk-mass. She performed her raps well.

Paul Hennessey was suitably slimy and had a great accent and scary growly voice as Curtis. He was comic in the heights of his aggression about Deloris in 'When I Find my Baby'. Lorcan O'Brien as Pablo, Dylan Murray as T.J. and Cormac Göbl as Joey formed an entertaining trio of goofball gangsters. Their moves were slick in 'When I Find my Baby' and it was clear that a lot of work had gone into the movement of this number. Their high- pitched backing vocals were good here too. Joey was gas in his solo for 'Lady in the Long Black Dress', as he rolled on the ground or his legs open towards the audience. T.J. showed off some impressive snake hips as he comically wriggled around the stage. Pablo got a great laugh with his high-pitched singing, as he rolled his r's brilliantly.

John Kelly did very well as Monsignor O'Hara. He was brilliantly excitable in his scene where he reports the news that the Pope is coming to visit.

Niamh O'Brien and Sinéad Mullally played Tina and Michelle respectively. They matched Deloris in their attitude, taking no nonsense for the deluded wannabe diva. They managed those difficult backing vocals in the opening number with aplomb and performed some sassy dance moves too. Eimear Reynolds as Sister Mary Martin of Tours was very good, with eyes that really captured the otherworldliness of the character. It was gas the way she was splayed out on the piano asleep and her quotation of Isaiah 55:12 was genuinely touching. Ríona Lynch as Mary Theresa gave us some very good old-aged acting as the nun who was apparently old enough to have known Jesus personally. Daire O'Muire as Ernie and Aaron Nelson as Cop/Taxi Driver provided quality cameo appearances.

June Belton and Yvonne Bennett headed up the costumes, which were hired by Sparkle Costumes, Dublin. Deloris wore her signature animal-print dress with a hint of a pink bra popping out and her infamous Father Mulcahy purple boots. Tina and Michelle wore spray-on psychedelic flared catsuits. The backing dancers all wore gold sequined dresses with black trim. I can't say for certain that Eddie's strip worked as well as it might have, with his sleeves already half open and the second cop uniform exposed by the low red neck. His white suit gave us a laugh, however. The gold tunics with red hearts looked super on the nuns' 'Take Me to Heaven' and the reveal was well- executed. The multicoloured robes for 'Sunday Morning Fever' were fun. Mary Lazarus' sunglasses, chains and blinged- up cap were hilarious. The head-caps and white night dresses were perfect, and always better than when productions use pyjamas. The silver and white robes on the ensemble nuns in the finale looked great as the primary nuns wore black sequined versions. The altar boys were dripping in bling here also. Deloris' dream came true, with her fabulous gown and white fur for her final appearance.

With this show, everything hangs on the chorus. Their numbers are what makes it so special. I am glad to report that we had a committed group of nuns who worked hard to learn their harmonies and ensured that the dance moves bounced off the stage. By the final number, the audience were buzzing leaving the venue.

Congratulations to St Mel's Musical Society on their 40th Anniversary (including John Kelly who has appeared in all forty productions!) and for putting on a very good show.

society_raw: St Patrick's Hall Mus. Soc., Strabane
review_text:
You can always spot when the Director of a show is also a Drama School Teacher, for they have that ability and desire to encourage as much involvement as possible from all the participants in the show. That was clearly evident here, with the chorus and dancers being integrated at every possibility into the action and the musical numbers, and what a huge and talented bunch they were. The real talent of Director, Leah McCay, was that even with so many involved, the stage rarely looked over-crowded. There was good attention to characterisation, and even though there are sections of the script that are a bit tame and poorly written, everyone maintained their character very effectively. Some of the scenes could have been better highlighted with more specific lighting, but stage positions were good, and the show kept a good pace from start to finish. There was good emphasis on comedy throughout, yet very good sincerity from the leading players. Corey O'Connor (pictured with other cast members below in  rehearsal) proved himself to be the perfect choice for the role of Ren, full of angst and fire, song and dance ability, and yet, sensitive enough to become the more considerate and thoughtful Ren of the last few scenes. While he was dynamic and constantly on the verge of breaking into a dance, perhaps he could have become a bit more calm, physically, as his mind become more focused, but that's a minor criticism. This was a very well sung, danced and acted role.

Ariel, the vicar's daughter with a bit of a reputation, was charmingly played by Shonagh Forbes, with a precocious nature that never stepped over the mark, and was equally full of heart. She had a relaxed pop-style voice that suited the role, and a great rhythm and style. Her acting was very believable.

Cahir O'Neill is a young comedian/song and dance man to watch out for in the future. There was a great goofiness to his character, and a very good sense of timing about his comedy, making him perfect for the role of Willard. The scene where he admits his inability to dance, and then transforms into a dance champion, was pure gold, and his rendition of "Mama Says", backed by all the boys, was the comedic and musical highlight of the show.

Naoimh Long was a cute, quirky and radiant Rusty, with a sense of comedy that was matched by her strong vocal ability. "Let's Hear it For The Boys" highlighted her all-round ability and made her a popular favourite with the audience. Very well played.
