Jamie-Lee Gallagher took on the least likeable character in the show, Chuck, a bully and a thug, and did a very convincing job of making him loathsome. It's harder to play the bad guy than the good guy, so this was a very good achievement, and he also showed his fine vocal quality in "The Girl Gets Around".

Wendy Jo and Urleen, Ariel's pals, were charmingly played by Maria Carlin and Darci Wilders, respectively, both making the most of their comedy and their song and dance support. They had some lovely moments with Lyle and Travis, two wannabes, effectively played by Matthew McLaughlin and Oran Curley.

Fronting the adult roles was Joe Harley as the Reverend Shaw Moore, the misguided vicar who couldn't let go of his past misfortunes. While Joe acted well and sang with good emotion, I had a feeling that he was not always comfortable with some of the rather contrived dialogue that was given to this lost father figure, which was almost certainly a problem with the script, rather than the performer.

Judy Duddy as Vi, his wife, had better material and a more rational character to portray and did so very admirably. If her singing sounded slightly forced, it was none-the-less performed with good emotion.

Ann Coyle, the abandoned mother of Ren, gave a solid performance, never allowing her own circumstances to distract from her concern for her son.

Stephen Bradley showed good vocal quality and a confident character at the Bar-B-Que, as Cowboy Bob. Wes and Lulu Warnicker proved themselves to be the Uncle and Aunt from hell, or at least from Bomont, and were nicely characterised by Martin McGurk and Andrea Porter. Of the many other smaller roles, Andrew McDaid was an wonderfully obnoxious Coach Roger Dunbar and fine performances were turned in by Janice McCay as Eleanor, Evan McCrea as Jeter, Tom McLaughlin as Garvin, Mark McLaughlin as Bickle, Clare Dunbar as Betty Blast, Mary-Claire McDaid as the unyielding School Principal and Jamie Bonner as the Cop.

The chorus throughout the show were filled with youthful energy, wonderful dance ability, and a good quality of vocal ability.

Emmet Stewart's choreography was funky, it was fresh and it was varied and he did wonderful work with a highly capable dance team and chorus. It was as much about creating atmosphere as it was about doing the steps right. There was also a very good awareness of the need to extend the comedy into the dance routines.

Ryan Quinn led an extremely efficient band from the keyboard, and got under the skin of this energetic and fun musical score. The tempi throughout were very good with as much sensitivity in the slower numbers as there was attack in the rock numbers. The on-stage singers didn't always finish on exactly the same beat as the band, but they were generally good at their harmonies, and sang with great enthusiasm. "Footloose", "I Need A Hero", "Let's Hear it for the Boy" were all very strong numbers, but the absolute show-stopper was the amalgamation of comedy, harmony and musicality that was "Mama Says".

The composite set, with its bridge at the rear, if not a work of art, was at least functional and practical, and with a good amount of well-sourced props and furniture, was sufficient to suggest the locations of the various scenes, and stage manager, Marie Brown, kept things going at a good pace with efficient scene changes. The members of the cast also contributed well to carry bits and pieces on and off the stage.

While the lighting was always colourful, and with some nice disco effects, it really did need to be a bit more specific with cueing. It was somewhat random, and some of the more emotional scenes would have benefitted from having smaller areas, atmospherically lit. The sound quality was very acceptable, with all lyrics clearly audible over the rock score. Costumes were well-selected, with a good distinction between Ren and the country bumpkins, and a lovely display of checked shirts and country dresses at the Bar-B-Que/Barn Dance. The adults were all suitably attired, and the change in Ariel from obedient church-goes to party girl was excellent. Hair-styles were funky and appropriate and make-up was fine throughout.

It's always nice to welcome a new Musical Society under the umbrella of AIMS, joining the 120+ societies who are bound together through a mutual love of Musical Theatre. With this production, by St Patrick's Hall Musical Society, Strabane, the positives heavily out-numbered the negatives, and I am absolutely certain that AIMS will be all the richer in the future for the involvement of this vibrant and exciting young company. Thank you so much for a very enjoyable experience, and I wish you great success with your future projects.

With so many ultra-modern productions of this show tending to be the trend, it was refreshing that Director, Liam Butler, chose to go down the more traditional route, and it was a good decision. With the costumes of the era, there was a much elevated sense of the history of the biblical epic. Played against a quite stunning set, I felt that much more could have been done, particularly in the more dramatic second act, to enhance the set with dynamic lighting, which was initially very good and atmospheric, but seemed to wain as the show progressed. With a very good cast at his disposal, Liam achieved some very strong moments of drama, but there were times when the involvement of the chorus seemed somewhat pedestrian. There wasn't enough joy and celebration as Jesus entered the square amid a profusion of palms, and the market place, despite some excellent work from the ribboned dancers, lacked a feeling of debauchery and corruption. Jesus' interruption of that scene needed much more drama and ferocity. The crowd also needed to be much more threatening to Pilate as he tried to determine how to deal with Jesus. More imagination was needed when carting Jesus from Caiaphas to Pilate to Herod and back to Pilate and when he was being beaten by the guards in slow motion, a more emphatic lighting effect would have enhanced the drama.

When the dancers were given their (all too rare) opportunities to shine, they proved themselves to be well-disciplined and energetic, and they did justice to some very effective choreography from Aisling Rountree. "Jesus Christ Superstar" was the highlight of the terpsichorean display, but there was good work too in Herod's Song and in the Market Place. I'd have liked the good tempos of "What's The Buzz" and "Christ, you know I love you" to be given a bit more expression through movement, as they tended to be a tad "stand around and mingle", but as stated, what choreography was permitted, was most attractive.

Aiden McCluskey cut a fine figure in the role of Jesus, and despite it being his first major on-stage role, he used his concert and band experience to exude a certain confidence and charisma in his acting. Vocally, there was very good quality in his lower range, but much of the score sat above his comfort zone, which resulted in several optional lower notes, and occasionally a falsetto that sounded a tad shrill and strained.

Sinead Butler brought a fine vocal quality and a warmth of character to the role of Mary Magdalene. "I Don't Know How To Love Him" was full of emotion, and the "Could We Start Again Please" duet with Peter was particularly moving.

In the narrative role of Judas, Kevin Fagan dominated the stage from the first moment to the last, relaxed and comfortable with the demands of the role, both dramatically and especially vocally. Here was a voice that is full of sublime musicality, a superb range, an amazing falsetto and capable of expressing the widest range of emotion in song. This was an outstanding performance.

Sean Flanagan had a beautiful calm in his expression of "Pilate's Dream", and then displayed a commanding presence in his early encounter with Jesus. The performance was rounded off with a very believable reluctance and lack of understanding as he eventually washed his hands of Jesus. Nicely played.

The casual, flippancy of Herod was very effectively captured by Colin Flynn, who made a strong impact with "Herod's Song" without having to resort to high camp or over-theatrical devices. Very well delivered.

There was a good superiority about Ian Rountree's Caiaphas, which balanced very well beside the more snide and aggressive nastiness of John Husband's Annas. The two worked very well together, and were ably supported by Barry Murray and Vincent Russell as the other high priests. The four performed their vocals with comfort and confidence.

Ultan Ó Cinnéide, as Peter, gave a nice vocal tone and quality to the "Could We Start Again Please" duet, and was believably frightened when confronted as an acquaintance of Jesus. Craig Regan, as Simon, led the vocal to "Poor Jerusalem" with confidence.

The chorus generally functioned very well, adding ambience to their scenes, but I did feel that they needed to be more fiery and vitriolic in the trial scenes.

Both principals and chorus were secure and well-rehearsed in their music, and well done to Chorus Director, Helen McHugh for the clear harmonies and diction. But as with the occasional pedestrian pace of the production, I felt that this was more of a "Middle-of-the-road" opera than a "Rock" opera, as the orchestra, under Musical Director, Paul Byrne, seemed a little too laid back to give the show its strong, pulsating, rock feel. There were no wrong notes and no lack of musicianship from Paul or his players, and the pace was fine for most of the songs, but the 'feel' just seemed to lack energy.

The set for the show was absolutely beautiful, both in construction and in visual impact, capturing the location perfectly. I therefore found it somewhat frustrating that technically, it was let down by a lighting plot that showed so much promise in the early scenes and then seemed to run out of steam in the most dramatic scenes. There was good use of colour and good focus to the smaller areas in act one, and the lightening flash effect in the whipping scene was quite inventive, but the hanging of Judas and the crucifixion of Jesus were underwhelming and somewhat bland. The standstill finale wasn't specific enough to work effectively. There was little for stage manager, Tracy Fitzsimons, to be concerned about as there were very few moving pieces, but the cast members who erected the cross were obviously well tutored and rehearsed. There were just enough appropriate props to meet the needs of the production. There were no problems with sound quality.

In a very traditional style, the show was beautifully costumed, and when required, there was a nice flamboyance about the "special" costumes, i.e. for Herod's Song and particularly the excellent and unusual black costumes for "Jesus Christ Superstar". Hairstyles, facial hair and make-up were all very good and appropriate.

A strong production team and a dedicated company have resulted in a production that, while I felt it needed an injection of energy at times, was nevertheless beautifully presented and most competently delivered. Thank you too all concerned for a very enjoyable night.

The Riverbank Arts Centre in Newbridge was the perfect venue for The Odd Theatre Company's production of Rent. The venue has an intimate quality which really added to the enjoyment of the production. This is a show which is set in New York in the late 1980s and is overshadowed by the HIV/AIDS epidemic that was ravaging the city at the time. It is loosely based on La Boheme and revolves around the loves and losses of a group of artistic friends living in East Village, Manhattan. The show has a rollercoaster of emotions involved in it as there is much humour in the lyrics but there are also moments of tragic loss and sadness. Both aspects must appear genuine or the audience loses the impact of the story. Direction was in the hands of Cian O'Dowd who also performed in the show and was stage manager! Quite an undertaking for such a young director. The direction was taken at quite a pace but there were moments when we paused and enjoyed some beautiful singing such as 'Seasons of Love', 'Light My Candle' and 'Will I?'

Cian chose to use one set for the show. This comprised a graffitied wall at the back of the stage and a set of steps onto a platform stage right. There were two rather large tables which dominated the stage slightly and multi-coloured chairs which could be moved to create different venues. At times I felt that the furniture slightly got in the way of the action on stage.

Cian gathered together a very talented and mostly experienced cast. He obviously inspired them, as they all worked together extremely well and supported each other on stage.

One thing he could have a look at in future is how individual numbers are finished on stage. I feel that each one should have punctuation at the end so the audience knows that moment is now over. This was generally a sound and moving piece of direction, well done Cian.

Niall Mulpeter was the musical director for the show and showed a great ability to control the orchestra and balance the sound from the pit with the singing from the stage. This has been a gripe of mine for a while as in this particular show the story is told in song and to miss any words would be to miss the story. I did not miss a syllable in the show. This was very refreshing. As it turned out from further inspection the orchestra consisted of four players who were positioned backstage and linked up with the cast by video projection. This seemed to work really well for the show and the cueing and tempi of the songs was very good throughout. There were times when the accompaniment was very minimal. It was nice to have that contrast with the rock moments which really blasted and brought the house down.

Although there is very little formal dancing in the show I was looking also at the general movement that was involved. Choreographer Áine Foley gave a very naturalistic touch to the choreography. It seemed that at times the cast had been given free rein to be inventive with their own movements. This created a spontaneous feel to the show. I did like all the set pieces including the wonderful 'Tango Maureen'. The cast moved well and used the acting areas effectively. There was a lovely bit of 'tableography' for the 'La Vie Boheme' number, which was very clever and performed with such accuracy by the cast. This was when they were sitting at the table and were doing moves such as slapping the table, linking arms, putting their hands above their heads but all done at a great speed and with perfect timing.

Daniel Ryan played Mark Cohen. He is an up-and-coming filmmaker and his use of the camera pin points the events of the story, giving his audience a focus. Daniel has a beautiful tone to his singing voice and his acting was good too. He worked well with Roger and they seemed very comfortable together on stage. Chris Corroon played Roger who is the rock star with, as he put it, baggage. He is HIV positive and his girlfriend has committed suicide when she finds out that she was also. He begins a love affair with the beautiful young Mimi. There are some wonderful moments of tenderness between the two and also moments of extreme frustration when Roger can't quite tell her all about himself and how he feels about her. He is trying to protect her but in doing so chases her away. Chris made this part his own. He has a beautiful singing voice: rocky and emotional. He looked the part and he acted the part. This was a very moving portrayal. Mimi played by Seana Stenson worked really well with Roger. Seana is a beautiful mover on stage and we were always fascinated by her. She was exotic; she was frightened, she was angry. She portrayed all these emotions beautifully. When we thought she had died in the second act, we were all devastated and there were people crying in the auditorium. She sang with conviction and I particularly liked the moments of gentleness that she had when singing duets with Roger. Tom Collins is a gay activist in the show and was played by John Conroy with great conviction and style. He meets and falls in love with the transvestite, Angel, who helps him when he has been attacked. It is an unlikely match, but such is life. The initial attraction between them was electrifying. John played the part really well especially when Angel was being consumed by AIDS and he was attending to his lover in his final hours. This was very moving. John has a beautiful rich singing voice which he used to great effect throughout the show. Gerard Lyons had the difficult task of playing Angel who is the transvestite in the story. We meet Angel first of all in the guise of a man and then meet her again in the persona of the female Angel. Gerard seemed more comfortable in the former role rather than the latter role. I was impressed by the potential that Gerard has for musical theatre. He has a most unusual, stunning tone to his singing voice which was used to best effect in the number 'Contact'. When his confidence grows and he begins to relate a little more to his audience I am sure he will be a great asset to any musical theatre company. Maureen is a fascinating character for any actor to play and it was played brilliantly by Jessica Adamson. She was able to create the wacky stand-up character very well and we were all blown away by her rendition of 'Over the Moon' which was so physical, so funny and so successful. She has a great ability to relate to her audience and she has a wonderful singing voice. Those eyes were just so involving. Her partner Joanne was played by Keelin Kilduff. Keelin has a fantastic singing voice and she could reach heights that other singers might dream of. Again, she related well to the audience and we instantly became involved with her life. This was a good all-round performance. Cian O'Dowd not only directed, stage managed but also played the part of Benjamin in the show. He is the ambitious friend who owns the building in which the story is set. He also is in love with Mimi and at one stage tries to buy her love. This was a solid performance. Cian has a very pleasant singing voice and the voices of the three men blended very well together. Other players were not just chorus members each person had a part to play in the show and each person played it extremely well. I particularly liked Emma Kilduff as Alexi. Her sense of comic timing was brilliant.

The show's setting was adequate, with a graffitied wall covered in rock posters to give us the idea of Roger's profession, a functioning doorway and a platform raised at the back of the stage with a staircase leading up to it. As I have said before, there were two large tables on stage. These were at times used well as they became a bed, a sofa, and the tables in the restaurant but maybe smaller ones would have sufficed. I walked the stage after the show and there was very little space so hats off cast for how well you moved around it. The lighting was generally a little dull for my liking and that was a pity because there were wonderful moments on stage which would have benefited from a stronger pool of light to give focus to what was going on. The sound was well-balanced and each person's words could be heard loud and clear. Well done Connor Wilkins for that. The properties were of the correct time and all looked authentic. Make-up and hair were fine but it would have been nice to see a little more of a nod to the late 1980s in design. The costumes too were adequate but again it might have been nice to try and create the 1980s look. Either that or do the whole thing in just black t-shirts and black trousers.

Overall this was a good production which was thoroughly enjoyed by the full house on Saturday night, so much so that there was an instant standing ovation which went on for several minutes. This was thoroughly deserved as the heart of the show was extremely good and moved us to the core. It is hard to believe that what was then seen as the 'gay plague' has now been tamed but it is important to know what journey we had to come through to get to that point and remember those who didn't make that journey.

Many thanks to all at the Riverbank Arts Centre for your warm welcome.

show_raw: The 25Th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee
review_text:
Written in 2005, 'The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee' is a musical comedy in one act. A diverse group of six geeky adolescents, all played by adults, compete for the Putnam County spelling championship. They spell their way through a series of words, hoping never to hear the "ding" of the bell that signals a spelling mistake. But, hey, at least the losers get a juice box!

As we entered the Astra Hall, which was decked out like an American High School Gymnasium, we were greeted by Rona Lisa Peretti (Anna Bergin) - moderator of the Bee. So, straight away the fourth wall was broken and we were endowed with a collective character, that of spectators of the Bee and not audience to a musical. This was a clever device that worked really well later on.

The band, set at stage left, was tuning up and there was a palpable sense of excitement in the audience. This was the second performance of the show for UCD Musical Society and it was a packed house. The audience consisted of 80% students, with a few proud Moms and Dads and younger siblings of the actors in attendance.

To kick things off, each character came on and introduced themselves in song. Anna Bergin, as moderator Rona, immediately impressed with a fine soprano voice. We met Chip Tolentino (Morgan Moore) last year's winner, dressed as a boy scout, Logainne Schwartzandgrubenierre (Louise O'Connor), the youngest competitor with Pippi Longstocking pigtails and irritatingly high voice, Leaf Coneybear (Peter Richardson) with Superman cape and dungarees, William Barfée (James Bergin), whose name is mispronounced constantly during the show, Marcy Park (Lauren Dooley), who has just transferred from another school and Olive Ostrovsky (Niamh McGowan) with her massive glasses.

Each performer sang well in the opening number 'The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee' and we got a sense of their characters. They all played considerably younger (12 - 14yrs), it was written for adults to play children, but this did grate a bit during the show as sometimes they played it too young.

However, that was not all of the contestants, Rona called out four names to the audience. Turned out these were real audience members and they were invited up on stage to participate. Strangely, she only chose men on the night I attended, however I'm informed that it varies considerably from performance to performance. The four were suitably game and when called up to spell, they initially got easy words. The words became progressively more difficult in order to clear the stage of the non-actors.

We then met Vice Principal Douglas Panch (Malachy Conlon) who had a sinister past he would not discuss. Panch called out the words and when asked to place them in a sentence created very funny juxtapositions "Spell phylactery." "Can you put that in a sentence?" "Billy put down that phylactery - we're Episcopalian." The final character was Mitch Mahoney (Pádraic O'Brolcáin), the school counselor.

The band led by Musical Director, William Le Bas, consisted of Piano, Synth, Flute Alto Sax and Clarinet, Cello, Drums & Percussion. They were very tight but the balance was a bit too much to the audience right as that was where they were placed. Sound design and engineering was un- credited and whilst the cast was well mic'ed and sounded great the band was at times overwhelming.

Choreography by Mairead Bond, was simple as befitting the style of the show and mostly culled from other productions. There was a great slo-mo section, which worked very well, mostly thanks to Malachy Conlon's accompanying slowed down vocal.

Lighting design by Camille Lombard, was a bit hit and miss, the cross fades were a bit sudden and operation seemed to be improvised. The three par cans utilised as house lights were too bright and flattened the visuals. Set was simple, some steps, a table and a few pennants and flags attached to a red tab. A nice touch was the pyramid of large kindergarten style lettered building blocks up stage left, some of which were internally lit.

Stage management by Eoghan Walsh was relatively easy on this show, I suspect as once it starts it doesn't really stop as we are in the same location and it's mostly in real time. However all actors seemed to have everything they needed when they needed it. Costumes and props by Kelly Nic Chumascaigh, were perfect for the characters and added to their 'youth'. The props were functional and suitable.

Anna Bergin as Rona, is a fabulous vocalist, her work on all of the numbers was splendid. She controlled the whole show like a cross between a presenter and a judge. Her delivery of seemingly improvised comments on the audience spellers was perfectly insouciant. She also played Olive's mother with great internal emotion.

Malachy Conlon played V.P. Douglas Panch with an exquisite inner energy. His deadpan delivery of the words and their meanings was perfect and his comic timing excellent.

As Mitch Mahoney, Pádraic O'Brolcáin was well cast. Looking like an undercover cop, his looming presence was counterpointed by his character's obvious care for the contestants, hugging and kissing them when they failed. He also played Olive's Dad and at one point, a highly irreverent but hilarious Jesus tied to a huge cross. The six contestants were very individual. Clearly, much work went into their characterisations. Director, Ruairi Nicholl, ensured that his cast was constantly alert, in character and responding to every situation.

Morgan Moore played Chip Tolentino, a boy scout who won last year's Bee. Mr Moore played him as a nervous but likable lothario as he fantasises about Leaf's sister, Marigold who is presumably in the audience. His song 'My Unfortunate Erection' during the 'Snack Break' is a highlight of the show. He also played one of Logainne's Dads in a delightful vingnette.

Logainne Schwartzandgrubenierre as played by Louise O'Connor, the youngest competitor and spoke with a superbly delivered lisp. Her vocal was strangely off key at times, but I suspect it was deliberate. Ms O'Connor was perfectly cast in the role.

Leaf Coneybear was played by Peter Richardson and he stole the audience's hearts with a beautiful performance full of childlike vulnerability.  His vocal was patchy at times but full of character. Mr Richardson also hilariously played the other of Logainne's Dads.

James Bergin played William Barfée as a repulsive, nose picking, irritatingly clever, know all. (That's a compliment!). His characterisation was brilliant. From the 'interesting' choreography with his 'Magic Foot' to his sweet puppy love scene with Olive, Mr Bergin embodied William Barfée. Marcy Park, who speaks six languages, was well played by Lauren Dooley. Ms Dooley played the piano at one point and her scene with Jesus was skilfully timed. Her portrayal of Marcy, the poster child of the Over Achievers was excellent, particularly when she decided to purposely fail.

Niamh McGowan delivered a near perfect performance as Olive Ostrovsky. She was the youngest looking actor and she radiated youth and a shy energy. Ms McGowan depicted Olive's journey from introverted, over looked child to self- reliant teen remarkably well. Her singing on 'The I love You Song', was the finest vocal of the evening. Outstanding work. "The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee" is a quirky little musical. It's funny, has a few good songs, a great script and was a perfect choice for the Society who gave it a very 'syzygy' production. UCD Musical Society is a group who know who their audience is and what they want and are experienced and talented enough to give it to them, and more.

This lively and energetic musical is not all hairspray and bubble gum. Underneath its glossy coiffed exterior there are themes of fat-shaming, racism and discrimination. It is a show full of the joy of life but the sadness of being not accepted. It therefore needs to be handled with care on both these levels. Set in 1960s Baltimore our hero Tracy Turnblad takes us through her own personal journey of acceptance and reveals other discrimination, especially at the local TV station where black people are not allowed on the show except on the monthly 'Negro Day'. Tracy rallies her friends to protest and change how they are treated.

I was made most welcome at the Scouts' Hall in Nenagh and was so pleased to meet the team who created such a good production of Hairspray.

Stephanie Browne directed the show and choreographed it too, with style and great attention to detail. The young cast were obviously very well-rehearsed and also enjoyed every moment on stage.

Stephanie chose an excellent cast of leading players who were backed up by an enthusiastic and talented chorus. They were always involved in the action on stage.

She created, with the help of producer Greg Browne, an interesting and innovative setting for the show with two stage extensions which were used to good effect throughout the show.

I had concerns as to how the Afro Americans would be portrayed in the show. Stephanie decided that she would use a darker base for their make-up and added touches such as black tights and black shoes. This created the difference between the two groups without being offensive. The show had a great sense of energy and pace throughout, giving us as the audience a roller-coaster of fun and reflection.

The musical director William Cullagh created some wonderful moments with his nine-piece orchestra. There was a great sense of the era in the playing. The sound cues were all very good and the pace of the show musically was excellent. The individual singers sang with confidence and emotion throughout the show and there were some amazing voices on the stage. Occasionally the sound of the orchestra was a little loud and we could not hear all the words sung by the principals which was a pity.

Stephanie's choreography was slick and reflected the time in which the show was set. All the cast and chorus looked comfortable with their movements and the routines were delivered with verve and gusto. There were some very talented dancers on the stage who were supported by a well-rehearsed chorus. Nice to see boy dancers who can really dance and can work with their partners to produce beautiful patterns and routines. The duets and group numbers were moved very well throughout the show. The 'You Can't Stop the Beat' number as a real show-stopper with the audience clapping along and most of us wanting to join in.

Jayde Ryan was an excellent Tracy Turnblad. She looked right, she sounded right and she moved and acted the part excellently. The audience liked her from our first meeting in 'Good Morning Baltimore'. Edna, her mother, played by Colin Dillon was a real source of humour throughout the show. Although not feminised too much, Colin played the part with excellent comic timing and his 'Timeless to Me' duet caused great hilarity. Lara Smyth played Velma, the scheming TV producer, with all the charm of a rattlesnake which was perfect for the role. She appeared older than her years, sang well and moved elegantly round the stage. The smarmy ever popular TV presenter Corny was played by Shane Killilea-Curran with the style of the stars of the time. One of the highlights of the show was the performance of Caroline Browne as Motormouth Maybelle. She had real stage presence, a wonderful singing voice and knew how to move around a stage to perfection. Her 'Big Blonde and Beautiful' number got a huge round of applause from the audience. Calvin Coleman charmed us with his performance as Link. He was always in character and made a lot out of his role. Tracy's friend Penny is a part which is sometimes not made the most of. Not so in this show as Joanne McDonnell was able to get every laugh out of the script. This was an intelligent and endearing performance. Velma's daughter Amber was played by Megan Maher. She is the ambitious over-indulged child who is determined to win her slot on the TV programme. Megan gave us a really good portrayal of this role. Wilbur who is Tracy's father was gently played by Jack McGrath. It was not until his big number with Edna that we realised what comic ability Jack had. He and Edna worked together so well and gave us so many laughs. Justin Heaney who played Seaweed gave us just the right amount of swagger and attitude. He moved well, always keeping the Afro-American feel in his movements. There were lots of other roles in the show such as Rachel Brown as Prudy Pingleton who gave us a frightening mother to Penny. Other roles such as Little Inez was played by Indya Higgins with style and commitment. Ciara Sherlock was the prison matron who really rattled our cages. Dillon Noonan-Kelly was beautifully dressed as Mr Pinky and Liam Daly was a cut throat business man as Harriman F Spritzer. The Dynamites were wonderful to look at in their purple sparkly dresses and they danced and sang with real Supremes' charm.

I was very impressed by the chorus in the show as they had a large part to play in its success. They sang and danced well but they also were able to listen to what was going on around them, which focused our attention onto the main action on stage. The set itself was a bit of a masterpiece. As I have said there was use of LED lighting around the proscenium arch but on stage there were banks of television sets. Each one had a colour changing screen so that the atmosphere on stage could be altered at the press of a button. This was very effective. At the back of the stage projections such as rooms, walls and patterns were shown, creating scenes very quickly. Larger pieces of scenery were wheeled into place by a very experienced stage team. These were items which were well made and well painted, such as the Har de Har shop counter and the large can of hairspray which had smoke coming out from the nozzle. The lighting on stage was usually of a very good standard with very few dead areas and was excellently cued. The microphones worked very well and on most occasions the sound was excellent with a well-balanced tone, though at times it was difficult to make out the words being sung during some of the songs as the orchestra appeared to be a little loud. The show looked beautiful and one of the reasons was the wonderful costumes on stage. These were well chosen, beautiful colours and all fitted the cast very well. I was impressed by the attention to detail, for example in the choice of shoes: the boys all wore black patent shoes when they wore their white and black suits. The girls' shoes were all the same type and matched their costumes which were beautiful. There was a range of pastel colours used for both the boys and the girls. Mr Pinky's outfit was stunning as were the outfits worn by the Dynamites, who wowed us with their purple sparkly outfits. The makeup was right for the era and the Afro-American cast who had a darker base make-up had darkened eyebrows and heavier eyeliner. This looked effective without being offensive. The wigs were generally very good though I still think that we could have had even more exaggerated beehives.

There were a great many people helping with the show. There was a team of very enthusiastic folk working in front of house. They made everyone so welcome and helped to create the real buzz before the show began. Nenagh Choral Society Ltd is a very family friendly group and it is obvious that the older members really want to support the up-and-coming younger members. This is a wonderful ethos and in no small way a reason why this show was such a success.

The Helix is a wonderful modern theatre in leafy Dublin City University. It has a large front of house area with a bar and coffee shop and tucked away in a corner, a small tuck-shop. Having directed and lit a show there a few years ago, I can attest to the excellence of the staff and the facilities. I arrived to see 'Legally Blonde', which I had seen a number of years earlier on the West End, and was greeted by the venue's manager and the company's Front of House Manager. Both made me feel most welcome.

The original 'Legally Blonde - The Musical' has been described as "high- energy, empty-calories, and expensive- looking hymn to the glories of girlishness", an "ingratiating trifle" and "it should be entitled 'Irredeemably Bland'". It is true that the plot is not exactly Shakespearean in its' complexity (girl loves boy, girl loses boy, boy wants girl back, girl has moved on) nor are the characters anything more than two-dimensional. However, one knows this in advance of attending and indeed, I would argue that this is part of its charm.

Based on the book and MGM film, 'Legally Blonde' is about the lovelorn Elle Woods whose boyfriend, Warner, dumps her and attends Harvard. Elle follows him to college and whilst there grows up, gets an education and ultimately finds her true vocation whilst staying true to herself. She also falls in love again.

Sean Gilligan's production was fairly slick. The set, designed by Mr Gilligan, was cleverly rendered through projections of images, designs, text and colour onto various drapes, which were flown in and a solid twin stair-cased platform set upstage. A door truck was on and off for various scenes and served as a great entrance and exit for different locations. Unfortunately, on the night I saw the production, opening night, the cast and crew seemed to be still getting to grips with the scene changes, but this didn't take from the overall pace of the piece. This was all lit well by Damo O'Connor, there were a few glitches but nothing serious. The house light preset included two very bright lanterns, with pink beams, shining into the audience. The tab warmers were in the shape of a heart. All very appropriate, given the nature of the show. The crisp and clear sound was by Vinny Osborne, again very professionally done, a little bit of feedback and mic drops here and there but nothing to spoil the night.

Superb Musical Direction by David Hayes who conducted a reasonably large orchestra, strangely there was no band credits in the programme so I can't comment on individuals, and a large chorus from the pit. His direction was precise and on-target, eliciting impressive harmonies particularly from the 'Delta Nu' ensemble on 'Omigod You Guys' and the Greek Chorus on 'So Much Better', which opened and closed the first act. The choreography, credits were shared by Aoibheann Cooke and Sean Gilligan assisted by Rebekah Byrne, varied from huge high-stepping parade like numbers like 'What You Want' to concise routines like 'Gay or European' was suitably Broadway in its scale as it should be as it is predominantly a dance-driven show. The dancers were well drilled, effortlessly segueing from one style to another, hip-hop to dance exercise videos to Riverdance, but again it was the 'Delta Nu' ensemble who really excelled here, their characters shining out through the complicated routines. 'Bend and Snap' was particularly memorable as was 'Positive', where they really gelled as an ensemble.

Hair and Make-up by Ali Murphy and Sinead Judd was suitable and varied enough to show individual character. Costuming by Sparkle Costumes was absolutely perfect; from the Harvard preppy look right up to the heavenly Greek Chorus ensemble. It was flashy, full of sequins and with, of course, lots of pink. Stage management by Sarah Hall, seemed smooth enough but I would have liked the stagehands/arms dressed in black.

The success of 'Legally Blonde' rests firmly on the casting of Elle Woods. She has to be blonde, feisty, be a superb singer, good dancer and a great actor. Elle's journey from Marilyn M to Jackie O is peppered with cringy dialogue and cartoonish characters, so she must rise above this to make us care about her. Ciara Lyons was Elle Woods. She sang and danced faultlessly and delivered the somewhat silly dialogue with just the right amount of dramatic irony. Her voice was crystal clear, her range impressive and she displayed an inner energy and vivaciousness that burst out when required.

Her 'Delta Nu' ensemble, who were mostly her Greek Chorus, complemented her talents. Hannah Brady as Margot, Aly Coyne as Serena, Shona Carroll as Pilar and Caoimhe Donnelly as Chutney lit up the stage at each visitation. They had a wonderful grasp of their roles with impeccable singing, sensational dancing and a delicious tongue in cheek humour. Less assured was Kevin Hartnett who played Warner, he sang well on 'Serious', but struggled with the character I felt. James Deegan's Emmett was an excellent dramatic performance full of poignancy and nuance. His singing on 'Chip On My Shoulder 'was heartfelt, although the higher notes were a strain on his range. Inga Bourke Mullaney acted Vivienne to a tee. Her spat with Elle at the party scene was hilarious. Her accent and singing were a bit patchy, but she did redeem herself during the 'Legally Blonde: Remix' in the second act.

Professor Callahan was played by Sean Hendley, a confident solid performance with just the right amount of imperious sleaziness. A special mention must go to Conor Clear who played four different characters; Prof Winthrop, Carlos, Elle's Dad and the slovenly Dewey. Mr Clear's performance was a textbook example of multi-characterisation, he was funny and totally owned every scene he was in with his stage presence.

Sarah Gordon excelled as Paulette. Her characterisation, her singing, her dance and her sub-text and comic timing were a joy to watch. Marco McVey played Kyle with a beautiful swagger, which had the audience wolf-whistling. Brooke Wyndham was played by Serena Salmon. A confident assured performance, her dancing was superb, her rope skipping excellent. Of the two dogs featured, sadly we only saw Elle's dog, 'Bruiser', happily relaxed in her handbag. Paulette's dog got stage fright and refused to exit his trailer. This was a very entertaining evening; the sets, costumes, sound and performers gelled together to create a very good Legally Blonde. The absolute star of the show was Ciara Lyons, her entire performance consolidated the show under Sean Gilligan's first-class direction.

The Belvoir Studio Theatre is a 200-seat venue tucked away behind a Community Activity Centre in Belfast. A small foyer leads to a traditional end on auditorium with raked seating. This was my first visit and it took some time to find, as it was poorly signposted. Belfast Music and Drama Society (BMDS), the Society staging this outing of 'The Producers', was formed in 2015 and has produced a rake of shows, both traditional and contemporary in the last three years. They have garnered a good number of nominations and wins thus far from AIMS and have a very busy schedule for this and next year.

Mel Brook's 'The Producers', is one of my favourite musicals. The story of Max Bialystock and his quest to produce the worst show on Broadway, aided by his reluctant OCD accountant Leo Bloom, in order to keep all of the investor's money, was originally a very successful film made by Brooks in 1967. In 2001, he wrote a stage musical version, which also became a big hit. The plot is simple, the songs are catchy and the show is risqué but very, very funny.

Once inside, I joined the small audience and was treated to the 8-piece band soundchecking. They were located at audience left beside us in the auditorium. The front tabs were drawn, concealing the show to come. We could hear cast running around and whispering behind the tabs, which was quite amusing for the audience. I suspect, however, it was not intentional noise. Over the PA system, there was a selection of show tunes (Les Mis, Moulin Rouge etc.) playing as house music. I kept my coat on as the building was freezing. There were less than 50 in the audience, so we couldn't generate much warmth.

Finally the house lights dimmed and the small orchestra went into the Overture. I immediately realised that there was going to be sound issues as the balance of the music was mostly to the left, which was to be expected, as that was where they were sited. However, I assumed the front of house mix would have addressed this, but sadly it didn't. But that was just the start of the evening's audio problems. Four usherettes; Chloe Bell, Amy Blackshaw, Cherelle Hinds and Sarah McFarlane, opened the show with 'Opening Night', setting the Broadwayesque tone of the show to come. They sang and danced well, dressed in tails and tights but were dreadfully under lit. Paddy McGennity as Max sang 'The King of Broadway' well, but was let down by loud sound issues and again was in and out of shadow. The ensemble backed him up and sang really well, with complementing harmonies and, despite the small stage, good movement. The staging of the show was somewhat hampered by a very solid set, designed by Vincent Vyce, upstage consisting of two small staircases leading up to a platform, whilst downstage left and right we had two doorways which were trucked on and off. As the main set was so unyielding, it had to remain for all of the show. This compromised not only subsequent scenes but reduced the playing area available to the choreographer and ultimately the actors. The set remained dressed as Max's office throughout.

The choreography, by Alex McFarlane was good, with some lovely sequences executed by a well-rehearsed cast. It was great to see some good tap routines and these were relished by the dancers and appreciated by the audience.

Costuming was un-credited but was very germane where needed; the Third Reich brown shirts and swastika armbands gave a real sense of menace, whilst Roger DeBris's dress was very becoming! I missed the opulence and couture of the Broadway the show was lampooning though, it would have been delightful to see some glitz and glamour. Hair and make up was un-credited but worked well given the intimacy of the venue.

Sadly, much of the show was under lit by Robbie Irwin and Gary Redpath. The LED pars on stage and four or five generic profiles out front were insufficient to light what is essentially a large scale musical. A followspot was used once, that I could see, on Max as he was singing 'Along Came Bialy', but I think this was to try and isolate him as ASM's moved set, rather than as an artistic decision. There was no big difference in the look of the show once we got to the Broadway staging of 'Springtime For Hitler', which was a pity as the sumptuousness of the musical within a musical is an important plot point in the main show. That said, some of the blue states were effective. Stage Management by Andy McKnight was reasonably well achieved but we could see ASM's behind the flats, holding doors shut from the audience's gaze.

Sound by Diarmuid Rankin was not perfect by any means. To be fair to the Society, the Director, Jordan Walsh, informed me prior to the show that their Sound Engineer was taken ill and they had to hire a replacement at short notice. But I can only judge on what I heard, or didn't hear. There was a very unbalanced front mix, which meant that most of the sound came from stage right. Sometimes mics were left on when actors exited into the wings, so we could hear them speaking to each other or stage management. There were many incidents of loud electrical buzzes and crackles and pops. Ulla's mic cut out during When You Got It, Flaunt It. On the bigger ensemble numbers, it was very hard to actually hear what the cast were singing as the mix was so cacophonous.

Musical Direction was by Wilson Shields. Mr Shield's players were well rehearsed but let down by the poor sound quality. The brass were strident and had a nice big band quality at times, the violin was gentle and always present, drums and bass kept everyone in line and the reeds were earthy and subtle.  However, the sound mix did mean that the band were overwhelming at times, particularly during solos.

Max played by Paddy McGennity was an interesting casting choice, as he seemed a little young for the role. His Max was full of nervous tics and peculiar facial expressions. He had a great energy and put every ounce into his performance, and while not note perfect his singing was full of emotion, exasperation and character. Timothy Bell played Leo as an OCD ridden, lovelorn Mammy's Boy. His comic timing was excellent, his singing very good and his dancing superb. Mr Bell stole every scene he was in with subtlety and attention to character detail.

Both Karl Dawson as Roger DeBris and Matthew Watson as his live in lover, Carmen were brilliantly portrayed. Their singing was flawless and their onstage relationship hilarious.

Mr Dawson's depiction of Adolf Hitler during 'Springtime For Hitler' was sublime and a highlight of the show.

Simon Pyper as Franz and Kathryn O'Neill as Ulla did wonders with their roles and whilst neither sang brilliantly their acting was first class. Sean Harkin, who sang the opening of 'Springtime For Hitler', has a beautiful tenor voice and was another stand out. The ensemble worked very hard with multiple costume changes, difficult choreography and tricky choral work, their youth and energy drove the show.

As directed by Jordan Walsh, this production clearly lacked budget, suffered from poor production values and was possibly not a great choice of show for the society. However, the cast saved it. Their commitment, talent and sheer doggedness made it an entertaining evening. I look forward to visiting with them again.

Originally written as a stage play based on real life events in 1924 by Maurine Dallas Watkins, Chicago was turned into a musical by Bob Fosse, John Kander and Fred Ebb in the early 1970s. It has been revived many times since and became a very successful film in 2002.

Bravo Theatre Group's production was staged in a provincial hall in a small town outside of Galway, but on entering the venue we were transported back to 1920s Chicago. Set dressing was extended right out into the auditorium, where the orchestra was set up around a grand piano. Haze in place of cigarette smoke hung in the air and there was a tangible sense of seedy intemperance in the Temperance Hall.

The show opened with a charmingly played overture by the seventeen-piece orchestra under the assured musical direction of Shane Farrell. The band was confidant, vibrant and perfectly in accord. Mr Farrell conducted from the grand piano and his arrangements of the score were suitably sleazy, with the trumpets muted and the percussion hopping.

Since the film, many non-professional productions strive to imitate the look of that movie by casting Zeta Jones and Zellweger lookalikes, and Bravo's production was no exception.

Velma, played by Emily Lohan looked exactly like Catherine Zeta Jones, with her dark bobbed hair and red slash of lippy; Roxie, played by Hannah Wright was a dead ringer for Rene Zellweger with her blonde locks and surprised facial expressions. However, both actors played their parts so well, that one forgot about the movie stars and became transported away with their interpretation of the characters.

However, this lookalike casting didn't extend to Mama Morton (Jessica Bray), Billy Flynn (Michael Coen) or Amos Harte (Chris Coroon). All three performers were exceptionally well rehearsed in terms of their acting and singing and created unique interpretations of their characters. Jessica Bray had a fine commanding presence and a great jazzy vocal, her duet with Velma, 'Class', was, well… class. Michael Coen's portrayal of the shyster lawyer, Billy Flynn, was one of the best I've seen. His true phoniness was revealed brilliantly in 'All I Care About' and his duet with Roxie, 'We Both Reached for the Gun' was a stand out moment in the show. Poor Amos Hart, the true victim of the scheming shenanigans of Roxie and Flynn, was poignantly played by Chris Coroon, his 'Mister Cellophane' was charming in its simplicity.

The director, Aoife McClafferty, also choreographed the show, and whilst the ideas behind the choreography were sound enough, I'm afraid the execution left a lot to be desired. Bob Fosse, the original choreographer, created a style of dance, which is evident in Cabaret, Sweet Charity and many films of the 50s, 60s and 70s. His style, famously 'adapted' by Michael Jackson, was all about insolence, attitude and perfectly executed meticulous movements. The choreography in this production, rightly attempted to recreate some of the routines created by Fosse, but sadly, failed to live up to the exactness required. That said, some of the individual dancers did impress, notably the (un- credited) lead male in 'All That Jazz' and 'Cell Block Tango'. The choreography of the 'jury' in the courtroom scene was, whilst not sharp enough, very creative. Overall, the choreography in Chicago is all about the technique, the attitude of the performers/characters and the precision of the moves. It didn't really have that Burlesque decadence that it should. I feel that the dancers did let the choreographer and the show down a little by their lack of finesse.

Some of the choral work on this show by Shane Farrell was superb, his work on the duets was particularly fine as noted above. However, we did miss the power of choral voices from the stage. The ensemble was not punchy enough in their vocal. As I was watching 'Cell Block Tango' I was waiting for the big vocal on the chorus, but it was sadly fairly weak. I don't think this was a PA problem as the sound by Derek Recks was near perfect throughout. The same issue arose with 'We Both Reached for the Gun', a lack of power from the vocal ensemble. These numbers are meant to pretty much nail you to your seat with their intensity and intention, but they didn't. Set, props and lighting worked perfectly in harmony on this production. Paul Kelly's sparse but effective lighting design, with festoons and little LED's everywhere and his clever footlights during the trial and vaudeville ventriloquist scenes, worked really well. Aoife McClafferty and John Wright's set was very simple; the main set piece a hydraulic bridge spanning the width of the upstage was used very ingeniously to create different playing levels. The jail cell doors on castors worked well, but were a bit cumbersome and probably not really needed. However, I really like the festoon-rigged frame that angled upstage during the trail scene. The bentwood chairs were perfectly in era and the mocked-up newspapers were a nice touch. Hair and Make up were good and costumes by Utopia Costumes were also on point.

Of course, the real success of Chicago rests firmly on the casting of the two female leads. Emily Lohan's interpretation of Velma Kelly was a delight. Her singing was near flawless, her dancing very impressive. She seemed to run out of steam a little toward the end of the show but her characterisation of the murderess was striking. Her vocal work on 'Nowadays' with Roxie and 'Class' with Mama Morton was lovely.

However, as good as Ms Lohan was as Velma Kelly (and she was very good), she was totally eclipsed by the performance of Hannah Wright as Roxie Hart.  This was an outstanding performance from an accomplished actor, singer and dancer. For one so young (she's twenty- one), her command of her craft was very impressive. Her accent was perfect, not just in terms of location but in terms of the era (or what we know of it). She played the innocent equally as well as she played the hard-nosed vixen, effortlessly switching between the two sides of Roxie. Her dancing was super, her comic timing superb and her singing, particularly on 'Roxie' and 'Nowadays', impeccable. Her portrayal of the ventriloquist puppet on 'We Both Reached for the Gun' was perfect.

Direction by Aoife McClafferty was excellent. It was obvious that she exerted total control over all of her departments, drawing them all together to service her vision of the piece. Her work with the leads created super living and breathing characters, most of whom we cared about. Ms McClafferty's attention to detail on the setting of the show, involved us in the audience, completely and for a couple of hours on a rainy September evening in County Galway we were transported back to the roaring twenties of Chicago.

'Pajama Game' was based on the 1953 novel '7 ½ Cents.' With music and lyrics by Richard Adler and Jerry Ross this is the story of workers in the Sleep Tite pyjama factory who campaign for a seven and half cent pay rise. Love blossoms along the way between Sid and Babe. The show opened on Broadway in 1954 and there have been numerous revivals since. The score is glorious with some classics of the musical theatre genre, such as 'I'm Not In Love At All' and 'Hernando's Hideaway'. The show was directed with pace and energy by Philippa Alford. Philippa chose to use an adaptable set with a range of large pieces brought on as appropriate. There was clever use of lighting at times to make acting spaces more intimate and to create atmosphere. The characters of the cast were broadly painted and well defined. In shows such as this there is a tendency to go slightly 'over the top', this was not the case here as we really felt we knew these people. The movement around the acting areas was good throughout, though there were a few times when masking of players occurred. A solid piece of direction which brought out the humour of the piece.

Barry Power created a lovely balanced sound with his twelve-piece orchestra. There was always a steady tempo to the music and a great balance of the instruments. The cast were very comfortable in all their singing roles and the ladies' chorus in particular were outstanding, giving us that fifties sound. There were good harmonies throughout. A couple of characters however did just push their voices at times into a pop range which didn't quite work. Cueing was generally sound and the balance between voice and pit was very good. The 'There Once was a Man' number was a highlight of the show.

Laura Macken-Posavitz's choreography was very much in the style of the show. There were many memorable dance moments such as 'Steam Heat', with the girls in their sparkly dresses. I loved the clock like movements used in 'Think of the Time I Save' and my favourite was the joyful 'Once A Year Day'. There was a good use of the whole stage area and the changing moods and patterns added so much to our enjoyment. It might have been nice to see a little more movement in the duets and solos which could have added to the fun.

Philippa had gathered a very strong cast for this production. Sophia Daly gave us a feisty performance as Babe. This is the union woman who fights for the increase in pay. She sang really well though at times added a wee pop element to her voice which didn't really fit. I loved her singing of 'Hey There' which was a magical moment. Her acting was good and she reacted well to most of the players on stage. This was a strong performance. Her love interest was Sid Sorokin played by Kevin Macken. Kevin seemed a little nervous to begin with but soon settled into the part and gave us a nice portrayal of Sid. Kevin has a glorious singing voice which soared at the end of each number. He became a very likeable and watchable character. Aaron Tierney was Hines. This was a great performance which gave us plenty of laughs along the way. I loved his 'drunk man' act which was very realistic. He also had to do a knife throwing act which was very convincing. He moved around the stage so well with very fluid movements. His partner was Freda Quinlan as Gladys. Gladys is the dipsy secretary of boss Mr Hasler. Freda created a wonderfully rounded character from the way she walked to her screeching Bronx accent. Freda has a great sense of comic timing and we were in hysterics at her antics at times. She is also an excellent mover which she really showed us in 'Steam Heat' and 'Hernando's Hideaway'.

Prez who is the factory's lothario was played by Brian Dennison. He tries to work his way round all the girls in the factory who can't resist his charm. He played this role well. He looked the part and acted it well too. His singing voice became stronger as the show progressed. His rendition of 'Seven and a Half Years' was great. Jackie Carroll was the long- suffering secretary with attitude. Where Gladys was always in a turmoil, Mabel was just the opposite, she had seen it all before. This was a nicely characterised role, though just watch the pace.

Terry Martin played the frazzled boss Mr Hasler. The hall echoed when he shouted, 'Gladys!' and poor Gladys came scurrying on after him. He was all bluster and shouting which was perfect for this role. He looked so ill at ease in his casual checked shirt, rather than his usual suit, at the picnic which was very convincing. Yvonne Coyne gave a really strong performance as Mae. She looked as if she had stepped straight out of a 1950s movie. I loved the tone of her speaking and singing voice. At one point she was talking about potato salad and she even made that sound sexy! Brenda was played with real style and charm by Laura Geoghegan, Jen Keane made a lovely Virginia and Nikki Johnson was a most convincing Poopsie. What I liked most about these three players was that they worked selflessly as a team. They sang really well individually and as a group and really supported Babe in her big numbers.

Darragh Carroll was a handsome and at time panic-stricken Max. As the boss's aide he discovers that the pyjamas have been tampered with, with hilarious consequences. Daire Kelly has the most glorious tenor voice. I hope we hear more of it in the next show. Pop was played by Paul Johnston who captured the hardworking man so well.

The chorus in this show added so much to its success. They never stopped acting and reacting on stage. They sang well together and those with individual lines to say or sing did so with great clarity. The harmonies were good too. Well done chorus.

The stage had a raised platform at the back and above this there were the factory windows. This was clever as with a lighting change they became lit panels in Hernando's Hideaway. They were covered over for the picnic with panels painted with trees. The rail of the raised area was used to hang a union badge, festooned material etc. Pieces were brought onto the stage such as desks, chairs and the sewing machine stations. This was all very slickly executed and didn't interrupt the flow. The lighting was good, creating moods and more intimate areas. I loved the red moody light used in the night club. The properties were well chosen and looked correct for the period, adding much to the feel of the production. I would have loved a filing cabinet in the office which would have given a wee bit of business for the secretaries to do and would have made the scene with Mabel less static. That box file with the lock was wonderful, we were all dying to know what secrets were stashed in there!

The costumes were generally in the correct style for the era. The wide skirts worn by some, complete with layers of underskirts, Gladys' tight and tailored look. The men in their rolled-up sleeves, bowling shirts even the orange dungarees, all looked correct. Babe had quite a range of dresses. I liked the purple spotted one and some of the darker floral ones. This actress really seemed to suit the stronger colours. Make-up and hair were appropriate for the time and place with nice bright red lips and matt foundations. The girls had a consistent look. Their hair looked good too, though some of the men might have needed a wee trim to make their look more period.

I was made most welcome and I loved the fact that the front of house staff were wearing little 1950s neckties made from colourful material. The pyjama bunting in the foyer was most effective.

This was a great night's entertainment and fun. It is now very obvious why this show has been revived so many times. Well done Philippa and team for choosing this classic and bringing it to life for us to enjoy.

The fictitious household created by cartoonist Charles Addams is a satirical version of the ideal 20th century American family. They are a clan who delight in the macabre and seem to be unaware or don't care that other people find them frightening. Following on from the television series and the movies comes The Addams Family Musical. The An Táin Arts Centre in Dundalk was the venue for the show produced by Dundalk Musical Society. A show such as this needs a perfect sense of comic timing and excellent lead players. We had both in this production and we had a wonderful chorus who worked so hard during the whole show adding much to our enjoyment. Director Bernard Lynch managed to bring out the humour of the show very well. The audience of all ages enjoyed the humour throughout the production.

Bernard chose to use beautifully painted cloths as the setting for the show with a feature sweeping staircase. The show was well paced and scene changes were planned to not interrupt the flow of the show. The musical director was Ronan Dennedy who gathered a strong team of players for his orchestra. The tempo of the show was excellent throughout as was the cueing of the cast and the balance between stage and orchestra was as it should be. The cast were all very capable singers and thanks must go to Ann McCabe for her efforts as chorus mistress as we were treated to some great musical moments. There was some inventive choreography from Lea Carroll who had obviously worked extremely hard rehearsing the group as there was great attention to detail in the movement. I particularly liked the scene at the table when we had bit of 'handography' which was well timed and extremely funny. Paudie Breen as Gomez gave us a charming South American characterisation. We loved his eccentric nature and enjoyed his beautiful rich singing voice. He pointed his comedy lines extremely well to get the most laughter from them. His wife Morticia was played with scary charm and elegance by Carol McCourt. She was the epitome of our image of the character. She could act, dance and sing. What more could we have asked for as our Morticia? Wednesday was played by Hannah Mullen in a tomboyish and slightly frightening style. She shocked us when she crushed the budgie and fed it to the cat but we could see there was a softer side underneath especially in her romance with Lucas. Her brother Pugsley was played by E.J. Dunne. Although only eleven years old E.J. gave us a great comedy performance with some lovely nuances throughout the show. He looked appropriate and sang really well. Wednesday's love interest was played by Alan Doherty as Lucas Beineke. He and Wednesday made a good on- stage couple and he sang and acted the role very well. His mother Alice Beineke was played by Karyn McCooey. This was a standout performance with comic timing at its best. Karen never stopped acting on stage and we got to see two or more sides of her personality. The audience were in stitches at her 'Full Disclosure' at the red table. This was a hilarious and memorable performance. Her husband was played by Brian Halpin. Mal starts off as quite a boring businessman but revisits his youth in the 'Greater Than You' number which was a memorable part of the show. Grandma played by Marie McSorley was a great little character, so self-contained and quirky. Uncle Fester was in the capable hands of Gerry O'Hara. This was a wonderful comic performance. Gerry looked, moved and acted so well, always in character and always entertaining. His love affair with the moon was intriguing for us all and the final picture of him hugging the moon was a fitting farewell to his character. Andrew Sansom as Lurch gave us a very strong and controlled performance. It was a delight at the end to see him come to life and sing with such a rich, dark tone.

The chorus (pictured right in a pre-show pose) in this show played a very important role. They were on stage for most of the production, watching, listening and focusing the audience's attention on the action. They never distracted, they always added to the production. They sang well, they moved well and their costumes were wonderful looking. They all had individual personalities and it was obvious that they had worked out exactly what character they were meant to be and what period they were from.

The lighting in the show was an important part of its success. There was a complicated lighting plot with all sorts of gobos; including trees, moon etc. There were specials which created beautiful pools of light on the stage and there were lights behind scrims which magically revealed their secrets. There were functioning candles on the staircase and even some suspended above it. I was impressed how smoothly the lighting plot ran during the production. Praise indeed must go to Peter McDonnell.

The sets in this show were mostly beautifully painted cloths which could be flown in or pulled across the stage. This added quite a professional touch to the show. The feature staircase was solid and looked stunning on the stage. I walked over the stage after the show and the staircase hardly moved when my considerable weight climbed up it. It was painted in black with rich red curtains. The properties in the show were also of a very high standard. We had big props such as the torture rack, the stocks, a huge throne like chair, dressing tables, a cart laden with bottles of potions. There was quite an array of properties evocative of the period and they all looked in keeping with the feel of the show. Overall the costumes in the show were excellent. The chorus who appeared from the family crypt were all dressed in the same cream toned costumes. This gave unity to the group. What was nice was that the costumes were all of different eras but the material colour palette was the same, very uniting. The principal costumes were either colourful (like Alice's yellow dress) or monochrome. Either way the costumes were a very good fit and completed with the correct footwear on all occasions. The costumes were finished off with a set of excellent wigs. The chorus ones were all shades of grey and the principal ones were a variety of styles such as Wednesday's plaits. They all looked correct, they all looked professional. The make-up also was carefully planned and executed and always in character with the production. I commend the hair, makeup and costume teams who must have worked together so closely to produce the look of the show which worked so well.

Overall this was a most entertaining evening. There was much laughter, maybe a couple of tears in places but what impressed me most was the team work on stage and around the stage. It was obvious that the cast were all having a ball and because of that we enjoyed every moment of The Addams Family. Well done Dundalk Musical Society.

There was a real buzz of expectancy around the St George's Hall in Tuam for the Irish premiere of the musical Made in Dagenham. This charts the struggle that the female workers supported by their male counterparts had in the late 1960s when their status was reduced and hence their wages cut. It is set in the Ford car factory in Dagenham. The said ladies are on the conveyor belt making the leather upholstery for the cars. What was quite interesting was during the show a new exciting car is being premiered, it was a Ford Cortina. Frighteningly I remember the first Cortinas so well.

As we entered the hall there was a large and interesting display of Ford memorabilia such as dungarees, car tyres and press cuttings from the time. I, like most of the audience that night, had really never seen the show in its entirety before. I had googled a few numbers to familiarise myself but the evening's entertainment was a complete surprise and a very enjoyable one at that. The hall is a good size with a raised platform midway so that there is a good view of the staging. There was no curtain and the stage was open displaying an interesting blue light. An extension had been added to the stage which gave a large acting area and two more intimate spaces in front of the proscenium arch on either side.

The show, directed by Enda Burke and assisted by Aoife McClafferty, moved very well. The dialogue on most occasions was slick and the pace of dialogue was good, particularly with the female cast. There was great attention to detail shown with the staging of this show. Upstage right we had a room which was one of the worker's homes. It was the usual chaos of a kitchen with a young family. There was washing, table, chairs etc. which were all in keeping with the era. Even the wallpaper felt authentic.

The directors had established individual characters for the workers in the car factory and they had an expert touch at bringing out the humour in the show which was hilarious at times. When the story was being told it was hard to believe that women were treated in such a poor way in the workplace and interestingly enough still are as there is still not always parity of salary in every job. The main acting area was the shop floor of the factory and we saw the cleverly made sewing machines of the workers with conveyor belt for their finished products moving in the background which was very authentic looking. Various pieces of furniture including tables, coat-stands and benches were brought on in a very organised manner so that the flow of the show never faltered. Properties used were authentic and all were in good condition such as the beautiful decanter and sherry glasses that the ladies tried to sip from as they visited Barbara Castle in Westminster. We even had the epitome of 1960s chic, a fondue set in the boss's house which was so appropriate.

Shane Farrell who modestly praised his team of players in the orchestra, but took no praise himself, played keyboard throughout the show but led the orchestra from his seat. There was nice playing from the orchestra throughout with reeds, trumpet, guitars, bass, drums all blending so well and adding so much to the production. The instruments never overpowered the actors as we could hear every word of every song. The sound team from Dervan Sound, Loughrea did a great job on the show as there were many body microphones used, the dialogue was clear and cues were accurate.

As I said earlier there were interesting lighting effects created with coloured lighting but there were also moments where we had intimate lighting areas which created a great atmosphere for the scene. A well-lit show Indigo Lighting. The cast were excellent throughout. Suzanne Garvey-Brennan was excellent in the role of Rita O'Grady. We watch Rita develop from the under-pressure mother trying to keep all the balls in the air, including her job at the factory, looking after two children, wife to Eddie O'Grady played by real life husband Louis Brennan. She takes on the fight that Connie Riley begins and ends up speaking at the Trade Union Conference, which was quite a moment in her life. She sang well, she moved well and she was very convincing particularly in her relationships with her fellow workers, Connie and of course her husband. This was a well-studied and three-dimensional performance, well done Suzanne. Her husband Eddie fitted with her like a glove. We could see his frustration when the women were on strike and he had to move away with his two children for his own peace of mind, this was a very moving performance. Trade Union leader Connie was played by Frieda McGrath with a sincerity and honesty. Frieda was able to capture the strength of character of the real person. There were some beautifully touching moments which were gently played. Martha O'Toole had us in stitches as Beryl with her strong language and strong emotions. She created a wonderful character on stage. Emer Kelly was Clare who was a slightly eccentric character and give us lots of laughs along the way. Mary Newell as Sandra was a breath of fresh air with her wonderful singing and dancing, particularly in the Cortina number. She also acted very well her uncertainties as she is tempted off the strike to take part in a bit of advertising.

Lisa Hopkins was played by Clodagh Ruane. This is the rather posh wife of the boss of the Ford factory. It seemed that she was worlds apart from Rita but in actual fact they were able to strike up a wonderful friendship which was a very heart-warming thing to see.

Alisha Garvey was appearing on stage with her mother and stepfather as Cass and she did them both proud, as she moved, danced and acted extremely well through the whole show. Norman Quinn's Harold Wilson was absolutely wonderful. He took the stage by storm and his wacky interpretation of the part. It was so funny, we laughed out loud on so many occasions. This was a real tour de force of comic genius. Well done Norman! Beside him was Barbara Castle played by Eileen Newell with great dignity. Barbara Castle was a tough politician in the 1960s and Eileen captured the essence of her quite well. Stuart Barrows was jetted in as Mr Tooley who came from America to sort out the dispute. He was all chat and all bluster and reminded us of some modern American politicians!

Patrick Cummins played this sexist supervisor in the factory and it was interesting just to see how his approach then compared to what it would actually be now. Mr Hopkins was played by Declan Carroll. He achieved the feel of the period in his relationships with his workers and also his long-suffering wife. The rest of the male players worked hard to give us balance in the show. They all had the correct look and acted the part of factory workers very well. They all had the required 'blokishness'. The Cortina man was played by Owen Mullins in a 1960s pop star way which was just right for his 'Cortina' number. This was well choreographed and well portrayed.

The two children in the show Jack Blake Cleary and Taillte O'Callaghan as Graham and Sharon did a great job. They were under her feet when she and her husband were getting ready to go to work in the morning but they also showed great attachment to their mother when she was going off and leaving them.

The look of the show was achieved well with particular attention to hair and make- up, though the old-fashioned drawing on of lines to age people didn't really work for me and I think wasn't necessary. There was also great attention to detail with the costumes and I'm not sure where they got all those overalls from but they all looked like authentic Ford factory outfits. The girls' dresses were all in keeping with the period and the American cheerleader costumes sparkled and they added pizzazz to the number. The silver outfits which were used in 'Cortina' added more sparkle particularly with the shocking bright pink gloves which floated around the stage. The costumes were a good fit and they looked as if they had actually been bought by the people wearing them, they seemed to match their personality. On the whole this was a really memorable performance of the Irish premier of Made in Dagenham. There was a serious story to be told but it was told in a very fun and interesting way. This was a wonderful night's entertainment and we all left St Jarlath's Hall feeling we really had had a great night out. Thank you to The Marian Choral Society for a night of fun.

Originally written in 1971 as a gritty, violent slice of life about working-class Chicago youngsters in William Taft High School, Grease has been sanitised down through the years from a raw adult show into a the pasteurised, PG version we all know and love today.
