The Ulster Operatic Company, who staged the show in the Grand Opera House in Belfast, has been around for about 108 years and has a huge number of productions in their canon. Following on from last year's Spamalot, they returned to a fan favourite, Grease and were rewarded by seven sold out shows.

This year is the fortieth anniversary of the hit 1978 film, which starred, a 23 year- old, John Travolta and, the then more established, Olivia Newton-John. In the Ulster Operatic Company's programme for the show, they dedicate a whole page to trivia from that film, so we could see the massive influence that movie has had on the creation of this version of Grease, from the costumes to the choreography and even the casting to a degree. But it's de rigueur now to try and emulate the 'movie versions' because that's what the audience want and expect.

The show opened with a unique and refreshing version of 'Alma Mater' by the Musical Director, Wilson Shields. No stranger to the Belfast stage, Mr Shields' interpretation of the score; his sterling work with the singers and his deft touch with his nine piece band brought a joie de vivre to the show.

The large ensemble on this production was admirable; their voices blended beautifully and exuded a palpable energy. They female voices particularly shone on 'Beauty School Dropout' with delicacy whilst the male voices on 'Greased Lightnin' were muscular and energetic. Of the male characters one stood head and shoulders above the rest vocally; Matthew Campbell's Doody was note perfect and commanded the stage like a young Ed Sheeran. His duet with Roger, played extremely well by Jordan Walsh (who soldiered on with his arm in a sling), 'Rock and Roll Party Queen' was effortlessly performed. They both shone over the other T-Birds in their sense of comic timing and general consistency of character. With 'Those Magic Changes', Mr Campbell gave us a masterclass in pitch, tempo and faultless delivery. He's definitely a performer to watch out for in the future. Joel Johnston's Kenickie rocked out well on 'Greased Lightnin'' as did Sonny as played by Rory Jeffers. Laura Livingstone's Jan and Rachel McAdam's Marty were also excellent as were Jordan Rosborough's Patty and Courtney Burns' Frenchy. But Ciara Mackey stole hearts with her rendition of 'There Are Worse Things I Could Do'. Her pathos in delivery and her emotional investment in her characterisation of Rizzo were superb. She really made the character her own. The stand out comedic performance on the night was Laura Kerr's Miss Lynch. Like a 1950's Bette Midler, her sense of timing was superb and her delivery spot on. A close runner-up was Jay Walsh's Vince Fontaine, his characterisation of the sleazy radio jockey was suitably cringeworthy as he oiled around the stage. Johnny Casino was brilliantly played by Vijay Sharma. His singing on 'Born to Hand Jive' was reminiscent of Prince in his heyday.

Vocal performance of the night was by Matthew Cavan who played Teen Angel, Frenchy's guardian angel. His drag performance of 'Beauty School Dropout' was perfection. His range was very impressive and he had a thrilling 'growl' in his voice, which he used to great effect. He also looked fabulous, with his big hair, skin-tight dress and huge heels. This scene was brilliantly directed. It looked like a colourised 1930s Hollywood movie scene, all smoke and sharp lighting and a vampy Guardian Angel striding up and down a staircase to convince the hapless Frenchy to go back to High School.

Jamie Johnston was cast as Danny and his vocal was quite good, and though his singing of 'Sandy' lacked a bit of emotion, he got through it. Caitlin McClurg as Sandy however, brought the house down with 'Hopelessly Devoted to You'. This was faultless as was her reprise of 'Look at Me, I'm Sandra Dee'.

Sadly, the dynamic between Jamie Johnston's Danny and Caitlin McClurg's Sandy wasn't as electrifying as I would have expected. They just didn't gel on the night I attended. The scene at the drive- in didn't land at all. There didn't seem to be any real chemistry between them. Mr Johnston's Danny was presented as a wise cracking class clown, full of tics and stutters. He didn't portray the charisma needed to be leader of the pack and mugged a lot at the audience. Ms McClurg, in the admittedly underwritten role of Sandy, didn't convince in her scenes with Danny but worked well in her scenes with the Pink Ladies. As the T-Birds were presented as so incompetent and frankly harmless, one wondered why Sandy would be attracted to their lifestyle or to Danny, who was played as being quite low status within the gang.

The staging was splendid; the set by Scenic Projects was a big help here as the design made for quick transitions between scenes. Production Manager, Gareth Maxwell, did a good job on keeping all of the elements working together as did Director, Neil Kerry. His work with the ensemble was commendable, as they seemed fully invested in the piece.

Timmy Bell's choreography was of high quality. Two memorable routines were 'We Go Together', where the entire ensemble was on stage in perfect sync and 'Born To Hand Jive' for his innovation. Overall the standard of choreography and the execution was very good. His integration of 1950s classic dances into the routines was clever and implemented well by the ensemble.

His work on 'Greased Lightnin' with the male ensemble was superb, their timing and physicality was frantic and rousing. But it was Beauty School Dropout where his work really shone. The quasi-1930s fashioning and feel on this number, really worked well. Teen Angel and her dancers (angels) evoked a past era but yet, also a 1970s Diana Ross like styling, it was a standout moment in the production.

Stage Management by Andy McKnight and his crew was good. The transitions were clearly well rehearsed, props by Valerie Greenlees and Ann Browne, were of the era (I liked the album covers, nice touch) and seemed solid.

The sound by Geoff Clarke was quite full and well balanced throughout the show, with little or no feedback and a good harmony between band and singers. There were some lovely evocative lighting states by Declan Anthony; the drive-in (the restrained use of the star cloth was pretty) and Teen Angel, come to mind.

The costumes by Jennifer Johnston, Martine Vitty and Margaret McAlister were just about perfect. They were totally authentic and evoked the era very well. The colours were vibrant and popped out at us. Teen Angel's dress and the silver capes of her entourage were suitably ethereal and otherworldly and a direct contrast to Frenchy's drab costume during the scene.

On the night I attended, the audience became part of the show. Singing along and clapping with the more popular numbers. I think this threw the cast somewhat, although they behaved impeccably throughout these interruptions, didn't reference them, and strove on bravely. This was a superbly entertaining production by Ulster Operatic, showcasing some fine new and established talent and adding new ideas, musically and in terms of production, to a tired, at this stage, formulaic musical. Their injection of energy, innovation and sheer fun into the show made us see and hear it anew. On the way out of the theatre I overheard one of the audience exclaim; "That was better than the film!" I totally agree.

It was a pleasure to attend the opening night of Jesus Christ Superstar in The Feohanagh, Castlemahon Community Hall.

This production marked the company's tenth anniversary and it was obvious that they are going from strength to strength.

There was a very family feel to the evening with a wide range of ages involved on and off stage. I was royally welcomed by the Chairperson and found out a lot about the history of the society.

The show was directed by Susan Browne who has worked tirelessly to train the cast for a polished first night performance. Susan was also the choreographer of the show and appeared on stage too. I commend Susan for all she does voluntarily for this young society. She chose a simple but quite effective stage setting with feature moving scenery pieces. There was a raised area front right which was occasionally used as Caiaphas's base. There was a television screen which showed us names of characters, settings, plot details through the show. I wasn't too sure about this initially but it did work well. The pace of the show was good with prompt scene changes and a good pacing of music and action. Susan had gathered a cast with a range of experience and it was good to see some of the less experienced rising to the challenge that this difficult show provides. Generally, there was good positioning of the principals throughout the show with limited masking of characters. There was a good flow to the production and I was impressed how well the story- telling was managed.

Choreography was a bit restricted due to the size of the stage and the huge cast involved. It would have been nice to see more patterns being created with movements which would have added more interest for the audience. The hand and arm movements were well rehearsed and executed. The chorus were always actively involved in all their routines. They moved on and off the stage with ease and I was very surprised to see the limited area they had in the wings.

Michael Young was Musical Director and made a well-rounded sound from a fairly small orchestra. The principals showed a wide range of talent and coped really well with this demanding piece. The tempo of the show was steady throughout and Michael showed great control over the players in the pit. The rendition of 'Herod's Song' was lively and 'I Don't Know How to love Him' was gently accompanied and created a memorable moment.

Jesus was played with passion by Jamie Herlihy. He coped well with the demanding score. He related well to the cast on stage but I would have liked him to angle his body a bit more towards the audience so we were included in his emotions. He moved with ease around the acting area and with his slightly retro flower power image we were transported back to the late 1960s which worked really well. He has some explosive moments particularly with Judas which he handled well. He also has to show a complicated love of Mary Magdalene which he carried through convincingly. A solid performance Jamie. Shane Walshe gave a strong portrayal of Judas. His frustrations were clear and the decision to betray Jesus was not taken lightly, this turmoil was very well acted. His singing was strong, particularly in his lower and mid vocal range.

Mary was performed by Grainne Aherne with genuine warmth. We were convinced by her feelings toward Jesus and her uncertainty of what those feelings really meant. Her singing was beautiful and 'I Don't Know How to Love Him' was a beautiful moment. Grainne was extremely watchable and moved elegantly around the acting areas. Dave Wrenne wowed us with his deep, rich voice. He created a menacing role as Caiaphas. He looked good in his dark robes and showed great stage presence. Annas played by Padraig O'Shea was a good second in command, a character to listen and comment on the action. He added much to the scenes he appeared in. Young Robbie Moriarty gave us a focused and committed younger priest and he shows potential for the future. Peter was sensitively played by Diarmuid Curtin and he gave a super rendition of 'Peter's Denial.' Shane Prior was a believable Simon who wowed us with his singing throughout the show. Tom Madigan was a slightly camp Herod. He sang and danced his way through a great rendition of 'Herod's Song'. This was poignant and hilarious at the same time. The dancing in this number with Tom and the glamorous girls was great and it was one of the highlights of the show. As I said earlier there was a huge cast of all ages, in fact there was a chorus of nearly sixty. They all acted and sang their socks off and contributed so much to the success of the evening.

Siobhan Hennessy and her extensive stage team who created, built and moved the set did a great job throughout the show. We had a pair of huge triangular trucks which when revolved lit up to show intricate designs. There was a suspended Star of David which shone down on proceedings from the back of the stage. Large blocks of polystyrene rocks were quickly moved into place as the base for our pole dancers outside the temple. A wall of greenery and potted trees might not really have been needed to create the Garden of Gethsemane as a lighting change would have been more effective. The lighting through the show supported the action most of the time and there were some very pleasing touches. It might be good in future productions to investigate how to create intimate scenes with lighting effects. There were limited properties used in this production but those used added to the intended style of the piece.

Hair was mostly in a hippy chic style and looked appropriate. I didn't particularly like Jesus' wig as in Act Two it hid his face from us. I really loved his white flowing top which gave a nod to the Middle East. Judas looked great as the rocker and the rest of the principals had simple costumes which had a real feel of the desert setting. Herod and his harem were in red sparkly outfits which added a perfect incongruous touch. The chorus looked great in a complete mixture of costumes adding a hippy commune look their numbers. This was a very sincere and honest interpretation of the script. The story telling was excellent throughout and the audience were captivated throughout the show. There was a well-deserved standing ovation at the end. I wish the society happy anniversary and good luck for the next ten years and beyond. Susan you should be proud of all you have achieved with such a large and talented cast.

I have looked forward to seeing this new musical conceived and written by the late Bryan Flynn. It is a great legacy to leave the world of Irish amateur theatre and a wonderful symbol of Bryan's passion for the stage. I was not disappointed by the moving and detailed production of the show performed by Oyster Lane Theatre Group. There was a buzz around Wexford and in the foyer of the Dún Mhuire Theatre on the final night of the show. The theatre which had been a cinema was a good setting for the musical. The tiered balcony seating gave a great view of the stage and the acoustics for the most part were very good.

The open stage was beautifully lit to reveal a raised platform, ramparts and intimate areas in front of the proscenium. The set seemed well painted with images of the Custom House on either side of the acting area. I was later to discover that this represented the fragmentation of British imperialism making way for the resurgence of the Irish Nation. An image of 'The Big Fellow' was projected onto the cyc. A hazer helped to create shafts of light on this scene. It was evident from the start that there would be great attention to detail and indeed there was.

Director Imelda McDonagh and Choreographer Suzanne O'Leary gave us exquisite movement of cast and chorus throughout the show. From that first moment when Mother Ireland opened her cape to give birth to a new Ireland right through to the end of the show, there were stunning tableaux, gentle choreography such as the waltzing when Kitty first meets Collins and strong aggressive positioning of the men at Frongoch. The show was a delight to the eye and a challenge to the senses.

There is a play within a play as throughout the musical we revert back to the Abbey Theatre's production of WB Yeats' 'Kathleen Ní Houlihan'. The extremely well-chosen cast carried this off to perfection, right down to the slightly over staged voices they used when in the play. The character of Mother Ireland was used to weave through the story giving a poignancy to each scene. There was careful thought given to every detail of this production and it showed. I loved the way Imelda teased every last meaning from the text which in the hands of our admirable cast came to life with a natural realism. The movement of the large chorus was great too and scenes were speedily changed using the cast to bring on chairs etc. This was a thoughtful and slick piece of direction.

The music was in the most capable hands of Patrick Clancy. He controlled the eight musicians in the pit as well as leading the cast and chorus, pit singers and pre- production Celtic ensemble. The sound was glorious with some very rousing music which reminded me of current West End shows. The tempo of the music was nicely judged throughout the show. There were lovely quiet moments when the orchestra almost vanished and rousing patriotic numbers which moved the soul. Our MD and our orchestra coped wonderfully with this complex score.

Of course, to even contemplate this show you must have a leading man of the highest calibre. A man who can act, convincing us of his passion for his country, he must show the fire in his belly and the gentler love in his heart for Kitty. We had this in Chris Currid who gave us a stunning performance as Michael Collins. Chris must have worked hard to find the very essence of the character. How he thought, how he moved, how he acted and reacted. Chris also has a superb singing voice. This part demands a singer with a wide vocal range and this we had in the effortless singing of Chris. He looked, sang and acted superbly well. Denise Brennan was equally as good as Kitty Kiernan. She shone out from the rest of the cast with her striking looks, stage presence, perfect diction and beautiful singing. This was a very convincing performance. Completing the love triangle was James McDermott's Harry Boland. This character not only helps to create a domestic conflict with Kitty and Collins but also becomes a political commentator and hence some of the show revolves around his political aspirations. This was a well-balanced portrayal of a complex character.

De Valera is a very difficult role to play. He is probably a personality in Irish politics which some of us can remember as he was third president of Ireland until 1973. Sean Hendley not only looked like him but also captured his mannerisms, giving us the soul of the man. Sean created some wonderful moments such as his stay in gaol which gave us another gentler facet of his personality. This was a well-rounded and well sung characterisation.

Joe Emmett was played by James Hobbs. James gave us an energetic and optimistic interpretation. He moved well around the acting areas and became a good sounding board for the rest of the cast. Mother Ireland was expertly portrayed by Louise Dillon. From that first moment with the cape, we were intrigued by the strange, mysterious woman. She came to life in the Abbey Theatre play. A chilling performance Louise. The rest of the Abbey Theatre troupe were extremely believable. The interplay between this group was excellent. Well done Yvette, Neal, Niamh and Gearoid you were all wonderful, as were Brian Kelly and Andy Fanning who played Cathal Brugha and Arthur Griffith. These were strong political leaders, and you gave them a voice, well done both of you. Eilish Coady, Dara Cullen and April Roche-Kelly you all played Kitty's sisters with style. You all danced beautifully too. Jonathan Blake gave us a very upset young soldier and Greg Currid was just perfect as the British Viceroy.

The chorus were the very backbone of the show. They created such memorable moments of such deep meaning. The unforgettable image of 'The Killings' when indiscriminate killings were carried out. It was the sound of the gun and the thud when each character hit the floor, this was so thought provoking. There really was not very much wing space but the chorus never showed the limitations as they dragged their executed countrymen off stage.

The staging of this show added much to its success. The stage as described earlier was solidly constructed and well painted. The were also hidden surprises such as the gangplank which lowered so poignantly indicating the leaving and returning to the native land and the door of the gaol which pulled out of the scenery stage left. The painting of the set and of course the stunning lighting plot which included historical back projections created a very professional look. Throughout the show the lighting was used to great effect to create atmospheric moments and was adapted as the show progressed to create a continuous flow on stage. Expertly done Mark Redmond. The sound was also very well managed as cueing was perfect and effects such as gunfire were always well- timed. A good job I -Tech Productions. Personal props were always of the correct period and I was impressed to see an array of different chairs appear on stage depending on the scene. Nice touches Clara McDonald.

Costumes, hair and makeup were all natural looking and with the odd exception costumes fitted and were of the correct era. The black, white, grey palette unified the look of clothes on stage. There was real attention to detail throughout.

This was an extremely moving show which was particularly successful in the First Act. The performances were all of an extremely high standard and the essence of the story came through loud and clear. There was great attention to detail throughout the whole show and I absolutely loved how groupings of people were placed. Imelda and team you produced a memorable evening of amateur theatre.

The foyer of St Patrick's Comprehensive School in Shannon was decorated as a New York subway station, complete with hairdressing salon, ticket desk and buskers, to create the atmosphere for Muse Productions interpretation of In the Heights. The audience were brought in through a side door past posters of the New York underground system, so we really felt that we had gone on a journey to get into the auditorium. The show is set in 2008 and deals with three days in the life of a Latin American community in New York, struggling from day to day with that ever-present desire to return to their homeland.

We were greeted by an open stage with a stunning set created by Ted Germaine and his wonderful team. This was a New York street scene with hairdresser, car rental shop, the bodega and in the distance, there was the Washington Bridge which was accurately created and was lit in many different ways during the show. The set which was solid and looked as if it has been built out of bricks extended from the stage into the auditorium. It was aligned at a sharp angle which gave an illusion of depth to the stage making it appear much bigger than it actually was. In a show such as this the characterisation is actually more important than the storyline itself. Director Martin McNelis had obviously worked hard with the cast to investigate the characters in the show with very pleasing results. Martin also expertly created different moods for different events and also for different times of day. So clever was this that we really felt that we were on a journey with the cast of this show. The pace of the production was very good with rattling dialogue and then pauses to appreciate more tender moments.

Martin was supported by a wonderful team of choreographers: Pamela McGlynn and Edina Erdei. There were all sorts of dance routines in the show from Latin American jive, salsa and mambo to hip-hop. These were all carried out with great conviction by the cast who moved effortlessly around the stage giving us wonderful patterns and dance moments. I particularly liked the moment in the club when we were treated to some wonderful cha-cha-cha dancing. One of the highlights for me was the 'Carnaval del Barrio' which nearly brought the house down. This number started slowly and then build up to a frenzy. The music was from an orchestra of ten pieces with Mary Rose McNally playing keyboard and conducting.

For the most part this was a very tight sound with wonderful Latin American rhythms and brassy touches. The rap moments were well attempted but sometimes difficult to make out the words due to a lack of balance between the pit and the stage. There were some glorious harmonies in the show with the singing of such numbers as 'No Me Diga' with Carla, Nina, Vanessa and Daniela. There were some lovely tender moments of song too such as Kevin's 'Atención', Claudia and Usnavi's 'Hundreds of Stories'. The orchestra provided such wonderful energy for Pamela and Edina's stunning dance routines, which were carried out with such vigour by this young and enthusiastic cast.

Usnavi was portrayed by Eoghan Rice. He is the central character in the show and narrates the events going on in street. So called as his father named him after the first ship he saw when entering New York, unfortunately for him it was a US Navy ship!! He runs the bodega which is the focus for the social life of the area. We see his frustration at being away from his home and the tragedies that befall him during these few short days. Much of Eoghan's singing was in the form of rap which is a difficult thing to master and he did a great job at doing so. Eoghan showed great emotion in his relationship with Abuela Claudia and his relationship with Vanessa played by Lauren Rice. Lauren created a three-dimensional character as Vanessa, we could see her frustrations in her relationship with Usnavi and her desire to move away from The Heights and yet there was something holding her there. Clíodhna McNelis played Nina with an easy charm and showed wonderful interpretation of the script and the music. She has a super stage presence and singing voice. She really made the character of Nina her own. Her love interest is Benny played by Tom Barrett. Tom is a gentle character in the show who falls in love with Nina and much to their parents' disgust, begin a relationship together. Aodan Fox played Kevin who was Nina's father and Camilla who was her mother was played by Anna Marie Barrett. These two worked together brilliantly to create a convincing married couple. There were highs and lows, there were fights and reconciliations, there was tenderness. A very well-rounded performance from both. Sonny played by Cillian Fahy had a love of life which was contagious. Sonny is Usnavi's cousin and someone who hasn't really settled down to the responsibilities of life. This was an energetic and fun-loving portrayal. The part of Graffiti Pete was played by Conor McNelis. He gave us a character for Sonny and Usnavi to bounce off but also creates a memorable moment with his graffiti for Abuela at the end of the show.

Daniela who runs the hairdressers was played by Clare McNelis (this is really a family affair). She looked stunning on stage and created a wonderful rounded character. Daniella is moving from the street to somewhere she considers better, closing her hairdressing salon and leaving the street behind. It was a very emotional and charming performance. I also liked how she sang in her various songs such as the beginning of 'Carnaval del Barrio'. Working in the shop is Carla who is played by Hazel Park. Carla is the junior in the hairdressers. This was well-acted and her innocence was very endearing. I really enjoyed the performance by Edel McFadden as Abuela Claudia. This is someone who knows how a stage works. She really knows how to relate to the audience. She knew how to use the light so that it glistened in her eyes. She could sing to perfection in this role. She knew how to get us on her side, this was a most memorable performance, well done Edel. The Piragua guy was played by Ronan Mitchell who appears pushing his cart selling his shaved ices. He looked well and acted his part well too. Chorus members were super with really good male and female dancers. Nice to see men on stage who can really dance too and a few characters who really brought a warm smile to our faces as they were so involved in all the action. I would like to thank Cormac for his lovely portrayal of assistant to the Piragua Man.

Everyone looked right on stage for the part they were playing and right for the period in which the show was set. The costumes were varied and ranged from Claudia's crossover house coats, to the street wear and baseball hats of the chorus. I particularly liked Usnavi's bowling shirt which really added a New York feel to the stage but all the costumes worked really well. They moved well and they did not inhibit movement round stage. Properties such as chairs, tables, various cans, litter, hairdressing supplies, hairdressing stools were all in keeping and correct with the period of the show.

The lighting was stunning as supplied by Star Systems Thurles. There were beautiful moments of sunrises and sunsets. There were mood making moments like the light in the club and the bridge at the back was often delightfully highlighted by coloured light. I particularly liked the scene after Abuela Claudia had died and the cast came on with various candles creating a magical tribute to her. The sound was good except for that little problem with the balance during the rap numbers, the rest of it was spot on. The cast make-up and hair were appropriate to the time and were often accompanied by the correct baseball hats and other accessories of the time.

This was a very interesting show, one that I had not seen before but I am delighted that I have now seen it in its entirety. It is a very emotional and a very funny piece of musical theatre too. Our evening in Shannon with Muse Productions was most enjoyable. A huge thank you to all the cast and crew for inviting me to your show and for the faultless hospitality I received when I was there.

Does somebody need a hug?

One of the most popular Christmas films in recent years is Jon Favreau's Elf starring Will Ferrell. It's a perfect family film, with goofiness for the kids and hilarious innuendo aimed at Mum and Dad. The musical loses some of the wicked humour, but has a few very good songs and is narrated by none other than Santa Claus. Staging a show aimed at an audience of children is somewhat daunting as you have to keep their attention through spectacle, energy and a kind of magical realism. Unfortunately, Belfast Operatic Company decided to stage Elf - The Musical in the vast Waterfront Hall but didn't size the production to fit the venue, so whilst the Hall is spectacular and the cast had great energy, the magic was just not there. Except for Buddy.

Playing Buddy the Elf of the title was Paddy McGennity. His energy onstage as Buddy was intensely maniacal and he had great comic timing. His portrayal of the man-child was very good and more reminiscent of Tom Hanks in Big rather than a direct copy of Will Ferrell in the film version of Elf. This was a good decision by him and his director, Wilfie Pyper, as he made the part his own and not an impersonation. Complete with elf suit and afro wig, Mr McGennity bounced around the stage like a small child on Christmas morning. His singing was quite sweet and at times emotional. Mr McGennity was especially moving on the 'World's Greatest Dad' where he imagines what his actual father may be like. Buddy's duet with Jovie, his love interest, on 'A Christmas Song', where he convinced her to sing, was really heart-warming.

As the underwritten Jovie, Aideen Fox, did well and was quite believable. I preferred her early scenes when she was a bit grouchy as her comic timing was very good. She had a wonderful musical theatre voice and a good range. Her solo song in Act Two, the jazzy 'Never Fall in Love With An Elf' was touching and one of the best performances of the evening. However, the best vocal performance of the evening was by 12-year-old Andrew Montgomery who played Michael Hobbs, Buddy's half brother. His two duets with his onstage Mom, Emily Hobbs played by Laura Kerr, were impressive. His voice was amazingly controlled for one so young and he handled all of his songs like a true professional. He soared to impressive heights whilst retaining the emotions and intentions of the songs. He had good comic timing and he played him as a likeable kid influenced by his kind mother rather than his often-absent father. Laura Kerr had a marvellous warm tone to her voice and she also excelled when she sang with Mr Montgomery on 'I'll Believe in You' and again on 'There is a Santa Clause'. She exuded a sincere maternal nature and her scenes with her onstage son were very realistic. As Buddy's father, Walter, Colin Boyd played him perfectly, a workaholic businessman rather than a bad guy. His performance was consistent and he sang rather well too. As Santa Claus, Eric Miller definitely looked the part but he changed accents at the start of Act Two, which kind of worked for the local references but was in danger of straying into Panto territory, however he got it back towards the end of the show.

A special mention must go to Shirley Adair who played Deb and sang superbly on 'In The Way' and 'Just Like Him'. She told a hilarious story of Polko, the one legged Hungarian boy, who got a leg for Christmas. Her comic delivery was perfect and her New York accent was spot on. Keith Pyper as the Store Manager was also very good as was Kerry Cooper as Mrs Claus. The evil Mr Greenaway was played with confident assurance by Jeff Manning. Gary Redpath and Ian McMaster played Chadwick and Matthews, two office workers, with glee and fine comedy. Josh Kelso and Alice Johnston played Charlie and Shawanda very well as did Liz Boyd as Charlotte Dennon the T.V. Reporter. Colin Scott was Musical Director on this show and his arrangements and interpretation of the score was quite faithful. Mr Scott also conducted the medium sized orchestra and acted as Chorus Master on the show. A twelve- piece band gave us a big tinselled full sound. The band's tempo and pace were just right and their tone and balance were superb. I loved the percussion, especially the sleigh bells!

Choreographer Timothy Bell created some great routines for this show. Christmastime with Buddy and the elves was very well executed, and despite the elves being on their knees, it was full of energy and dynamism. The scene when Buddy gets to New York during 'World's Greatest Dad' and is amongst the commuters was also very good, each actor had moves specific to their situation, waiting for a cab, on the subway and so on.

In 'Sparklejollytwinklejingley' the Store Manager and his staff along with Buddy did a great routine involving Christmas presents and decorations. Again they had a great energy, unison and connected well together. The scene with the ice skates (actually roller blades) was also well choreographed.

The sound by McCusker Audio was well- balanced and filled the vast auditorium well. There was a good mix between band and singers and it was a nice full sound. Lighting by ACK Productions was well- designed and operated with a good use of two follow spots allowing for some nice saturated states on stage. The lights on the Christmas trees should have been dimmable as they just snapped on and off during crossfades. But generally it was a brightly lit show and we could see everything we were meant to see.

Set design was accredited to Alan Marshall and he produced a good array of Christmas trees. All of the specific areas and locations were created by furniture and by projecting images onto the BP Screen. There was very little in the way of traditional flats or set dressing apart from Christmas decorations. The company used a snow machine at one point but it was very noisy and only produced a small amount of 'snow'.

Projection design was by Paul Young Scenery Projection and was very sharp and bright. Some of the animations looked a little laggy and some of the images didn't really convey location well enough. But generally it was good of quality.

The costumes were bright and colourful and seemed to fit well. Buddy's elf costume was perfect and the office workers all had red ties or scarves, which showed a good uniformity. The department store elves had lovely, festive sparkly costumes during 'Sparklejollytwinklejingley' and the scene with all of the fake Santas, 'Nobody Cares About Santa' was resplendent with Santa suits. I liked all of the white costumes at the 'Finale' too. Hair and Make-Up were unaccredited in the programme but looked fine.

Stage Management by Marie Cusack and her team was a bit slow on the setting but quite quick on the strikes. Props were a bit sparse for a show that's set in the Elves Workshop, a Department Store, an Office and other locations, but what was there worked fine. I liked that Santa's Book of Names was an iPad.

The pacing on the show was very staccato. The transitions between scenes seemed to take longer than they should have, as there wasn't much to bring on or strike. The pacing within scenes was better as most of them were driven by the high energy Buddy.

It wasn't a bad interpretation by director, Wilfie Pyper, but I did feel the whole show was too small for the venue. The pieces of set looked tiny on the big Waterfront Hall stage, the actor's energy did help fill it out a bit, but ultimately they looked a bit lost. Too much focus was placed on the projection screen images, which I think distanced the audience more from the live action and so we lost that 'liveness' and immediacy that is essential for the audience to empathise with the characters.

The whole show was driven by the frenetic performance of Paddy McGennity. His Buddy elevated the production. He had great presence and his energy and commitment to character was admirable. Clearly fuelled by the four main food groups: candy, candy canes, candy corns and syrup, Mr McGennity was magical.

A smiling dummy nun at the roadside welcomed us to the Tullyvin Community Centre. Tullyvin Musical Society were to perform their version of Sister Act. Tullyvin is a small society which has only formed within the last few years but seems to be going from strength to strength. The foyer of the hall was decorated with church candles and the smell of incense burning. It created the atmosphere of the show. The hall itself is a good size and seats around 300 on two separate levels. The stage was open as I entered and the set looked solid with a large extension built to the front of the stage which created a huge acting area. In the centre of the stage there was an altar with a candle burning and a cross, this was lit by very strong white beams which you could see in the shafts of light created by a hazer. The walls of the stage were very convincingly made to look like brick and had a three-dimensional quality about them.

I was interested to see that the musical direction was by Barry Power whom I had seen the previous week in Dublin. This time Barry was dressed as Bishop Power which was a very effective beginning to the show and the chaos he created going up and down the aisle made a diversion so the set could be changed to the nightclub. Barry gathered a strong team of players and there were some nice moments such as the balance in 'I Haven't Got A Prayer' which was enhanced by beautiful clarinet playing. The show started with a real bang musically but settled down to a more rounded sound as the show went on. The show was directed by Paul Norton who gave us a thoughtful well-paced production. From the opening with the clever use of Monsignor O'Hara as the announcer of fire regulations there were wonderful entertaining moments through the show. The cast was made up of so many well-developed characters, who gave us much fun throughout the evening. Each one of the nuns had an individual charm and personality. Each one even funnier than the one before!

Paul had chosen to have the back panels of the stage revolve to change scene and also a fold out panel stage left which turned into the police station. This was very effective and did not detract too much from the pace of the show. The set created by Brian Feerick and team looked great and worked well. Large pieces were brought onto the stage to create a scene such as chairs and even a jukebox. These items were usually well-managed. Properties were all very much in keeping such as the lectern, guns etc. The lighting added much to the show with some nice touches. I particularly liked the roving blue and red spots which were teamed with the police siren, very effective. It might have been nice to have a few atmospheric gobos, maybe of church windows, casting interesting shadows.

There were a few things in the setting of the piece which jarred with me. Nearly all the solos and a few duets were played downstage centre. They also tended to be static. This worked for some such as the magical Sister Mary Robert solo, but to be honest it became a little too static for some of the other numbers. I really enjoyed the joy that the cast showed when moving but I would have loved to see more changing patterns in the choreography rather than the excellent but usually static 'armography' on stage. We need to be visually challenged when watching a show so changing patterns are essential. The moves on stage were in keeping with the 1970's and all the cast managed to carry them out really well with huge smiles on their faces.

Andrea Fitzpatrick headed the female cast as the soul singing diva Deloris. This was a good performance and Andrea grew in confidence as the show progressed. She created a believable character whom the audience supported throughout. The lady can sing too! She really blew us away in those big numbers such as 'Raise Your Voice'.

Mother Superior was played with just the right amount of severity by Fiona Lynch. She captured the inflexible head nun beautifully. There were lovely moments of comedy brought out in the performance too especially with those confidential chats to God. Tomasina McGinnity, who also choreographed the show, played Sister Mary Robert with such realism we were totally convinced. Her character grew from the timid postulant to the strong woman at the end of the show. Her singing was wonderful throughout. A great performance. Sister Mary Patrick was played hilariously by Sandra McCormack. She had such an expressive face and captured those outbursts so well.

The reluctant policeman who comes up trumps in the end was played by Jack Carolan. Poor Sweaty Eddie as he was known has a fear of guns which he manages to overcome at the end of the show. This was a lovely performance by Jack who looked so natural in the role. He coped well with his big number while doing a speedy costume change, quite a feat!

Sister Mary Lazarus was a delight as played by Pamela McCormack. She had this booming voice and wore heavy dark rimmed spectacles which gave her such a comedic appearance. Seamus Smith was a sparkly and enthusiastic Monsignor O'Hara. From that first announcement we knew we were going to love the character and we really did. He was such fun in all those glittery costumes. He also dealt well with the more serious moments he had with Mother Superior too. His two altar boys Odhrán and Donnchadh were great wee characters too and added to the scenes in which they appeared.

Liam Wallace was a very threatening Curtis. He sported a gun which had a horrible clunk and when he actually pulled that trigger at the start of the show it put the fear of God into all of us. Liam really played the controlling psycho so well. He can also sing well and performed 'When I Find My Baby 'really well. The rest of the gang comprised John Grogan as TJ, the gangly sidekick who kept getting it wrong and getting in trouble with the boss, Eddie Hall as the man of few words Pablo, who was always threatening and Joey played by Dermot Carragher. Dermot looked a bit like a seventies pop star in his long wig. The audience loved their sexy moves in 'Lady in The Long Black Dress'. Sister Mary Martin of Tours was a brilliant cameo performance by Finuala Duffy who really made the part her own. She was just an 'over the top 'character we couldn't help loving. Jackie McQuillan really aged up to be a convincing Sister Mary Theresa with hilarious moves and a great delivery of her lines. His Holiness who appeared in his push along Popemobile gave us all a great moment.

Other smaller roles, which are too numerous to mention were well performed. The chorus in this show worked their socks off and assisted by the pit singers they produced some very nice singing with beautiful harmonies at times.

Gemma and Claire looked great in those Farrah Fawcett wigs as Deloris' backing singers. The hair and makeup were pleasing, on the whole, and a good effort had been made to capture the feel of 1970's, even with the men's hair. The costumes were at times stunning, especially those glittery nuns' habits. Most of the costumes were a good fit and the cast appeared comfortable in them. Sister Mary Robert those boots were something else! How you were able to walk in them, I will never know. The transformation costumes were good too.

There was a wonderful community feel about this show. It was obvious that several generations of a family were taking part and everyone was having a ball. That's what our wonderful hobby is all about, us having a great time while making others happy too. This was a great effort by Tullyvin Musical Society who gave us an evening of such enjoyment. Well done everyone.

Back Of The Net!

Now I'll be the first to admit that I never understood the attraction of soccer. In school, I'd always be last to be picked for teams and I don't understand the offside rule. However, having seen South Eastern Theatre Group's version of 'The Beautiful Game' in the beautiful Theatre Royal in Waterford, I'm almost convinced to watch a match or two.

Written by Ben Elton, one of the stars of '80's 'alternative' T.V. comedy, and with music by Andrew Lloyd Webber, this thinly veiled allegorical tale of two halves is set in Belfast in 1969 and follows the trials and tribulations of a local football team. Using the troubles as a backdrop, quite literally as we see projections of war-torn Belfast quite frequently, the story revolves around the team members, their love lives and paramilitary groups vying for the hearts and minds of the citizens. This was a bit of a departure for Lloyd Webber as the whole show is rooted in naturalism, but when Elton approached him with a treatment of the script, he immediately set to work.

The music, helmed by the ubiquitous David Hayes, was a mixture of rousing anthems, sweet mournful ballads and even included a glorious fife and drum band. His arrangements of the score were first class and he added charming little 'celtic' touches. He clearly worked hard with the ensemble as they were dynamic, harmonious and robust in their delivery of the, sometimes rousing, choruses. His work with the fife and drum band was excellent and they clicked seamlessly into the production.

The orchestra of nine was cloistered under the stage with a trap open for Mr Hayes to conduct both the singers and the band. Apart from the keys, the flute and percussion really sparkled in this production. There was an exquisite warm tone achieved for some of the softer numbers and great attack on the more energetic songs. During the funeral scene at the end of Act One, we had an evocatively effective solo drummer, Johnny Farrell Doyle, playing on stage. This was a wonderful arrangement by the MD and a poignant way to end the Act. The ensemble sang well on the choral numbers. I was particularly impressed by their impassioned work on The Beautiful Game, The Final and The Craic. Their harmonies on The Happiest Day were beautiful and I really liked the power of the male ensemble on Dead Zone. They could also dance quite well.

Working with untrained dancers is always difficult for a choreographer, however Michelle Condon did wonders with her young ensemble and created some brilliant football inspired routines. During the main match the players circled each other, going through a series of choreographed swerves, skids, deflections, fouls and mimed goal scoring in slow motion. This was very effective and was helped by the swirling lighting. Other routines consisted of much simultaneous movement by the ensemble, mimicking supporters loudly cheering on their teams. Sound by 'All Around Sound' was reasonable. A full range was achieved with no feedback or signal drops to the many mics during the songs and band numbers. However, I felt that the pure dialogue sections were badly equalised and many actors sounded muffled; especially John and Ginger. Also, all of the dialogue came from all of the speakers rather than being panned to left or right depending on where the actor was on the stage. This resulted in a very artificial sound, as these sections were also quite unnaturally loud. But the music and singers were blended quite well and a nice balance was restored during the songs and musical interludes.

The show featured some of the best lighting I've seen in quite a while. It was pin sharp with a great use of movers, which mixed well with the generics. The prison scene was very effective as was the football match and the training scenes. Designer Eoin Sheridan also lit the set very well and created a tense dangerous mood during the rioting scenes. Full points to him for a sympathetic, considered and faultless design and plot.

Set design by Dermot Quinn was very good with many flats and set pieces trucked on and off. The corrugated look was very striking as was the brick effect on the side flats. Sadly, we could barely see the projections from where I was seated, which was a shame as they looked interesting and clearly added context to the show. The locker room and football stands were very authentic looking, as were the house interiors with de rigueur Sacred Heart pictures. Hair and make-up by Christine Hennessy was expertly applied and well researched, as was costume by Avril Musgrave and Elaine Tighe.

Mary, played by Phoebe Dipple, sang well on the duet God's Own Country but it was Niamh Fennessy as the Protestant Girl who really excelled here. Her voice had a beautiful ethereal quality on the song and we wanted to hear more from her. However, Ms Dipple really came into her own on the highly emotional If This Is What We Are Fighting For and the memorable Our Kind Of Love. She had a fabulous sensitive voice, full of character and empathy and sang and played Mary exceedingly well. Mary's beau, John, as played by Adam O'Brien, sang well throughout the show. He didn't have a lot of power in his voice, but his tuning was good and he sang with passion. His acting was very believable and he had a good dynamic with Ms Dipple.

Thomas, John's friend and later enemy, played by Danny Brockie, had a very strong vocal. His singing of I'd Rather Die On My Feet Than Live On My Knees was full of anger and frustration and really encapsulated the feelings of those under duress. His was a multi-layered performance, and he played the sub-text splendidly. Fr O'Donnell, the genial man of God and part-time football trainer, was played by Paul Corcoran. He was quite charismatic, in a Spencer Tracy - Father Flanagan way, and played it well.

The camaraderie of the team was very palpable, they had clearly worked hard with their director and he built up a fine, credible ensemble. Both Daniel, played by Cathal Moran and Gregory 'Ginger' as played by Ben Nolan were particularly effective and portrayed their close friendship very well. Mr Nolan played Bernadette's (Carrie Mullane) new lover who reached a sticky end and his duet with her was sweet. Ms Mullane had an exquisite tone, delicate and full of sorrow when she sang a short reprise of Let Us Love In Peace.

Padraic Di Fusco's, Del, the protestant team member who was dropped from the team, was sublimely played as an intelligent young man who saw the writing on the wall for what it was and escaped to the USA with Christine, his Catholic girlfriend played by Aisling Larkin. She brought the audience to their feet mid- show when she sang the main parts of Let Us Love In Peace. Her performance of that song in particular made us remember we were at a Lloyd Webber musical. She had a brilliant range, with her soaring top notes and her emotional investment in the song was intense.  Ms Larkin was definitely the stand out performer, vocally, of the evening.

This was a great production full of youthful energy and edgy emotion. Some scenes were extremely well produced. I loved the funeral scene where sections of the stage were removed to create a grave and the coffin was lowered into it, accompanied by a solo drummer and a video rain effect. The pacing of each scene was perfect, with the exception of the wedding night scene, which dragged a bit. The prison section was also cleverly staged with a flown in fence and sharp lighting. It was a very good interpretation by director, David Hennessy, which certainly ranked high in terms of emotional intensity and production values. Now, what time is the match on?

society_raw: St Michael's Theatre MS, New Ross
review_text:
St Michael's Theatre was the interesting venue for this production of the Dolly Parton musical '9 to 5'. Interesting in that the once church building now doubles as a cinema and theatre. It is a pleasant auditorium with a good feel from the stage of the tiered space below. There is a pit for the orchestra which in my book creates a better more balanced sound for any production. It is ambitious for the company to maintain and run this great facility which also has a little restaurant which can provide pre-theatre meals. Dolly Parton herself introduces the show by video projection. The setting for the show was a slightly abstractly painted set on moveable trucks. This was clever as the trucks were quickly moved and scene changes were pretty slick throughout. It would have been nice if these flats had been a bit sharper in their construction and painting which didn't quite work for me. There were however some effective touches on the set and the bathroom scene was well appointed with taps and sink. Great effort had also gone into making the rear of the car (pictured above) where poor Hart was flung. The desks and all the props thereon looked very authentic. These were speedily carried into place. The boss's desk was on a wheeled truck. There was an unusual peachy/orange colour palette used for the scenery and the city skyscraper backcloth.

Director Kevin Kennedy used the available space quite well adding in some action on an extension stage left and also a room in the stage right area. The direction was neat and the production moved at a steady pace throughout. The movement of a large chorus is quite a daunting thing to choreograph and the general office scenes could have had more passing through movement with chorus entering and exiting the space for some logical reason otherwise we have slightly distracting action behind the principals. The clip boards were great in one of the dance routines but were a bit overused at other times. Kevin chose his cast very well and everyone seemed most suited to their role. He must have worked hard to develop the individual characters and the various American accents were sustained well by the cast. He managed to tease out all the humour from this quite straightforward script. I would however have liked Hart's sexy moves to have been toned down as I think it might have been more in keeping with the character and would have led to more laughs. Overall a competent, slick production.

Musical Director Philip Kennedy created a very rounded and usually balanced sound from the ten-piece orchestra. There was the lovely brassy sound which the show demands as well as that Country and Western lilt. There were a few times in the big Country numbers when the singers on stage were overwhelmed by the sound of the accompaniment. The cast were well rehearsed and, on most occasions, sang really well, in character. There were some beautiful harmonies with the chorus and the three principal ladies made a gorgeous sound together. The choreographer Claire Kickham created some wonderfully memorable moments. I particularly loved Roz and her lookalikes' 'Heart to Hart'. This was an hilarious routine which really used the words of the number to create the moves. 'The Dance of Death', 'Cowgirl's Revenge' and 'Potion Notion' were all such well-constructed and executed routines. I would have liked to see a bit more interpretation of the words of some of the big group numbers, which though well danced were a little static and didn't push the story telling along.

Violet who is the divorced, hard-working mother was played superbly by Teresa Buckley. She has wonderful comic timing and delivered all her lines with great punch. She captured that 'Bronx' feel very well with her sharp movements and impeccable accent. She sang really well and I particularly loved her emotional duet with Joe, 'Let Love Grow'. Doralee was played by Jennifer White. She really looked the part in her beautiful blonde wig and fitted costumes. She had a nice Country tone to her voice when delivering dialogue and sang quite well. This is a difficult sing as the part builds to the end of the big musical numbers and the singer has to compete with a building accompaniment. Judy was delightfully portrayed by Ashley Doran who first appears in an oversized hat. Ashley was perfect for this role and we were carried along on her journey from a shy 'I will not cry!' novice in the office to the beautiful and confident business woman at the end of the show. She moved elegantly around the acting areas. What a delightful tone Ashley has to her singing voice too. The womanising boss, Franklin Hart Jr was played with great swagger by Keith Flanagan. He really got the audience to dislike his wicked ways. He moved and sang well and was able to deliver his lines with aplomb. He was too easily tied up and didn't seem to mind being hoisted in that harness either!! Joe was gently played by Michael Benson. This is Violet's accountant suitor. Michael created a really lovely character which was in complete contrast to his lecherous boss. He sang his duet with Violet very emotionally. Roz was the wonderful creation of Julie Kinsella. This was a fantastic performance which had the whole theatre in hysterics. Her love for Franklin was almost tangible. She slightly underplayed the role which was a great idea but Julie was never afraid to let herself go and her moves in her solo with the 'mini me's ' were absolutely brilliant. Dwayne was nicely played by Phil Erskine. He is Doralee's supportive husband. Phil gave the role a sincerity and old world charm. Owen Cullinan was Dick in the production. He played the angst- ridden estranged husband of Judy with a sense of awkwardness, no doubt regretful having walked out on his beautiful wife. Edward O'Dowd was violet's son Josh. Edward created a great rapport with Teresa on stage. We were totally convinced by his portrayal. There were a few great moments of comedy from the drinking antics of Margaret played by Bríd Maloney. We were so surprised to see the reformed Margaret at the end of the show, who was almost like a different person. A nice wee character performance Bríd. The Chairman of the Board Mr Tinsworthy was played with great style by Lorcan Dunne. He injected a bit of energy into the plot towards the end of the show. This was a small but memorable performance. Hart's wife Missy was portrayed by Caoimhe Doyle who really captured this tortured but at the same time defiant woman. She added much to the scenes in which she appeared. Other parts were well played and contributed much to the show's success. The chorus were of all ages from office lads to more senior staff members. Everyone on stage created a wee character of their own and shared that with us the audience. I just wish the chorus ad lib moves had been choreographed, as at times it did look like they were moving in circles with no set purpose. The chorus sang and danced well and were always reacting to everything happening on stage.

One problem I had with this show was the rather dull lighting. Looking around, I could see a huge array of lights but at times feet were being brightly lit while faces were shadowed. It didn't help that there were overhead stage lights which shone directly down plunging faces into semi darkness. We were always told, 'If they can't see you, they can't hear you!' this might be old hat but at times this was true as we were not focussed on who we should look at. There was possibly a technical glitch on the night I attended and I hope it was resolved. There were however some nice lighting moments such as the spotlight at end of 'Here For You'. The sound was generally well executed and sound cues were accurately carried through. There was a slightly tinny feel to the sound for some of the characters. I loved most of the properties used on stage, the desks with their painted panels worked well, I loved the typewriters, very in keeping with the show, the desk phones, all the smaller details such as the revolving phone book. I think though that flashy Franklin might have had a trendy new desk. Overall good attention to detail with the props.

This was a huge costume plot and I congratulate the team for a job well done. The chorus women had a great mixture of appropriate styles and colours of dresses and two pieces. Our principal women were carefully differentiated by very different clothes which quickly helped us to recognise them. I loved all of Judy's outfits, most of Violet's and all of Doralee's, especially the lovely red blouse. Killer heels were in evidence, just not sure how anyone can walk, let alone dance in those. The hospital uniforms were authentic. I loved those purple blouses in Roz's big number though I thought identical skirts would have been better. Roz appeared back from her French lessons in great style, red scarf, beret and shoes. She looked wonderful.

Hair and makeup were all fine. Jennifer's nice Dolly wig was stunning.

The hairstyles all looked very much of the era. A few characters might have needed a wee touch more make-up. The eighties were times of excess and the clothes, hair and makeup created that effectively in this production.

To sum up, this was a most entertaining show with some great performances. There were a few things to do with the presentation of the show on stage which could be easily resolved. Thank you to everyone who greeted us so warmly to St Michael'sTheatre, I hope the rest of the run went well.

Released on Broadway in 1997, coincidently the same year as James Cameron's blockbuster film, 'Titanic - The Musical' won public and critical acclaim garnering five Tony awards.

The well-documented, ill-fated Titanic, pride of the White Star Line, sadly sank during its maiden voyage in 1912. On board were over two thousand, two hundred and twenty-seven people. To maximise space in the first class areas of the ship, which was where the lifeboats were stored, there were only enough lifeboats for half that number. During the pandemonium of evacuation, none of these lifeboats were at capacity. Only seven hundred were saved. Most of these were first and second-class passengers. The majority of the drowned were from third class.

Titanic - The Musical was quite a political piece, focusing on the class divide, the well healed embarking on a holiday experience and the poorer hoping to seek their fortune in America, where the streets were paved with gold. It also highlighted the greed of the owner and pride of the designer. It also called into question the professionalism of the Captain and crew. Dunamaise Arts Centre, whilst a fabulous and well-regarded community resource, doesn't have a very large stage. So, when I arrived I wondered how they would stage such a huge piece of contemporary theatre. Although Titanic - The Musical is not a traditional popular musical, and there have been chamber versions done in the past, it has a huge score, is mostly sung through and requires a large ensemble to do the choral pieces justice. Massive challenges for cast and creatives and how daring for Portlaoise Musical Society and director Paul Norton for attempting it. The Dunamaise foyer was awash with Titanic memorabilia and an exhibition mounted on the walls by local schoolchildren. A children's string quartet was playing live as background music and a huge poster detailing the names of all who were on board the ship was hung on one of the walls, as was done on the original Broadway production. When we received our tickets we were also given a small piece of paper with a passenger name and encouraged to see if our person lived or died. A bit ghoulish, but it did provoke us to read through the big list. Sadly, my passenger never made it.

The set, designed by the reputable John Wright was basically a representation of an area of the ship. It was beautifully finished, with clean lines, portholes, two levels and side flats dressed as bulkheads. Two doors were set upstage under the bridge and they became cabin doors, a cleverly pulled out radio room and access to the third-class decks. A small boat was suspended from the setting line bar and information such as location, date and time was regularly projected onto its surface. Later in the piece, the boat was flown in and some of the survivors boarded it to escape the sinking vessel. During the final moments of the production the upstage platform started to list quite effectively and passengers and crew could be seen to slide off it into the abyss. During the scenes in the boiler room, the actors lifted four traps in the stage, which vividly represented the engine room, lit in an intense red. This was an absolutely brilliant set, the attention to detail, the cleverness of multi-function and the pristine look of it all was marvellous. To cap it off they even had a small hydraulic platform dressed as a crow's nest from which Crewman Fleet first spotted the iceberg.

Lighting by Nick Anton was very atmospheric, with good use of haze and dry ice. Some lovely tight focusing on the portholes, a range of blues, a practical chandelier and effective use of floor lights blended well into the production. Vinny Osborne's sound was perfectly balanced; the singers were crystal clear and the band powerful. His sound effects were also very good, the sound of the sea and waves were evocative and the sound of the ship hitting the iceberg at the end of Act One was terrifyingly deeply effective as was the groaning and metal rending of a ship falling apart. Bob O'Kelly and his team handled stage management very efficiently and successfully on such a huge show.

Costuming by the Theatrical Costume Company was perfect. Showing the class differences between the passengers through dress was well done and the crew uniforms were simple yet accurate. Make up and wigs by Maria Corcoran was elaborate where needed and inconspicuously subtle given how close the audience was to the stage. Props by Eva Fairbrother were very authentic. I really liked the large scale of the ships blueprints and the maritime paraphernalia and a brilliant touch was the blankets the survivors were wrapped in. They were printed with the word Carpathia, which was the name of the rescue ship.

Musical director/Chorus Mistress and Conductor on this show was Emer Hartnett. Her work with the ensemble was impressive. Their harmonies, pace and timing were perfect and very powerfully emotional. Ms Hartnett's band of ten sounded much larger than their number. The lush orchestral sound really did justice to the swirling symphonic score. Some of the music is written as swells, peaks and troughs mimicking the sea and Ms Hartnett's arrangements captured this perfectly.

This is not a conventional production in that there is no central love story, no boy meets girl, loses girl, gets girl back kind of plot. Instead it centres on two issues; mankind's technological aspirations and mankind's aspiration to better themselves socially or in the case of the Upper Class, retain their status. This and the quality of the score is what separates it from many recent 'jukebox musicals'. It also has a huge cast of characters.

Some of the actors were preset on stage when we entered the auditorium, the projection told us we were in the iconic Harland and Wolff Shipyard and here we met the ship's designer, Thomas Andrews, wonderfully played by Eoghan Fingleton. He sang In Every Age and played the character of the designer with a naive simplicity, believing global transportation is the future for all of mankind. Later, as the ship is going down he remained, obsessing as to how he could redesign it in Mr Andrew's Vision. He had a wonderful duet with Ismay, The Blame, where they argued over whose fault it was that the ship was sinking. The ship's owner, J. Bruce Ismay was portrayed by Alex Cathcart. Written as the only antagonist in the piece, Mr Cathcart played him as a highly strung, cowardly bully, ordering the Captain to go faster to enhance the ship's reputation despite being advised by Andrews and Smith that it would be unwise. Captain E.J. Smith was sympathetically played by Paul Spencer. He exuded a commanding presence but also showed a distinct vulnerability. All three sang The Largest Floating Object In The World, where they had superb complementary voices and really delivered the excitement they felt of being a part of history.

Gradually we were introduced to more crew, Daniel Whelan as the young radio officer Harold Bride really impressed with his characterisation and sang well on a number of songs most notably The Proposal/The Night Was Alive which he shared with Barrett perfectly played by Shane Kelly who also excelled on How Did They Build Titanic and Barrett's Song (The Screws Are Turning). Similarly, David Walshe as Frederick Fleet was impressive particularly on No Moon, where he is in the Crow's Nest and sees the iceberg looming. Mr Walshe has a wonderful rich voice, which cut through the intense Finale in Act One. Cian Mac Gearailt as 1st Officer Murdoch, who was at the helm when the ship crashed played his mind-numbing guilt brilliantly and Donal Brennan as 2nd Officer Lightoller performed well as did Sean O'Neill who played two characters; Quartermaster Hitchens and Bandsman Bricoux. Colm O'Toole also skilfully played two characters; 3rd Officer Pitman and the cantankerous, long-winded Major, one of the few comic characters in the piece. Further crew members included a lovely delicate performance from Charlene Duff as the Bellboy, an emotional and stoic performance from Jason O'Reilly as the Steward who really cares about the passengers, particularly the older ones. The Stevedore was strongly played by Jamie O'Callahan, who sang well on There She Is and John Coss portrayed a wonderfully camp but officious Harry Etches and sang well on What A Remarkable Age This Is. Paul Kenna also played two characters; Bandmaster Wallace Hartley, who sang Autumn quite well and Chief Engineer Joseph Bell. The three Irish girls, all named Kate, who meet for the first time in line to board the ship were all excellently portrayed, they embodied the hopes and dreams of the poor Europeans wishing to better themselves in the New World. Aishling Rohan, who played the pregnant Kate McGowan, sets her sights on Jim Farrell, solidly played by J.J. Tynan, as a potential father for her child. Their scene during the long Finale of Act One was very touching. The two other Kate's, Zeta O'Reilly as Murphy and Jayne Louise Kelly as Mullins, also did wonderfully well particularly during Lady's Maid.

Ida and Isidor Strauss, the older couple, were played movingly by Dawn Kavanagh and Aidan Delaney. Their duet Still, where Ida decided to stay with her husband rather than taking to the lifeboats brought a tear to many an eye in the audience. Michael Lillis played the millionaire Astor who, with his pregnant young bride, Madeleine played with child-like vulnerability by Aishling Kelly, epitomised the privilege of the Upper Class as did Frank Egan as Guggenheim and Julia Cahill as Madame Aubert. Hilary Treacy as Edith Corse Evans and Joan White as Charlotte Cardoza were very believable in their portrayals as was Angi McNulty and John Lynch as the well- off Widener couple whose stage son was unaccredited on the programme. Brian Rohan played J.H. Rogers, the swindler very satisfactorily. Conor Harte and Teresa Lynch as the Thayers performed well as did Claire Carroll.

In second class the piece focused on two couples specifically. Charles Clarke played by David Wrest and Caroline Neville played by Suzanne Lillis as the eloping couple, off to find a new life away from family influence. They played it elegantly, their relationship finely honed and quite sweet. Alice and Edgar Beane were brilliantly played by Louise Moore and Rory Chadwick. Their comic timing was faultless as were their accents. Ms Moore sang wonderfully, she has a beautiful voice and amazing articulation particularly evident on The First Class Roster. A special mention must go the wonderful child performers featured in this production, many of them played 3rd Class passengers trapped during the sinking which had a devastating effect on the audience, others played more well- heeled passengers of privilege with gusto. Choreography on the production was by Grace McGrath. Her work on the traditional 'Irish' dances in third class was uplifting and her choreography on the upper-class deck ball was elegant. However, it was her innovative addition of three white clad superb contemporary dancers during the finale of Act One that was a standout moment of this production for me. Representing the iceberg, the three wraith-like dancers interwove around all of the passengers during the lead up to the crash, contacting with each and every passenger and crew member. Their dance became more and more frenetic and emotional as the ship came closer to disaster, almost as if nature itself was trying to intervene and halt the course of fate. A wonderfully evocative end to a first act as ever I've seen.

Director Paul Norton created a fabulous production, his attention to detail and mentorship of his cast was exemplary. His artistic vision for the piece was lucidly delivered to the other creatives and he clearly inspired all involved to produce their best work. This production was a fitting tribute, not just to the writers of the show, but to those brave souls who lost their lives and to those who survived. Portlaoise Musical Society is to be lauded for creating a truly civic production, the involvement of the wider community of crafts people and in particular children and young people, onstage and offstage, created not just a local show but an exceptional event to remember by all involved and those who were lucky enough to see it.

society_raw: Harold's Cross and Tallaght Mus. Soc.
review_text:
What a way to make a living!

Dolly Parton (on video) opened this show by Harold's Cross and Tallaght Musical Society at the Civic Theatre by telling the audience it was watching a musical set back when there was no cell phones and when women couldn't be promoted to positions of power. She popped up again at the end wishing us well and singing a bar or two of the titular number. The audience lapped it up but I must admit I found this very odd and couldn't see Mr Lloyd-Webber doing it. But this is an odd show, written in 2009 and based on a film made and set in the late '70s/ early '80s about office politics and a misogynist boss (Franklin Hart Jnr.) vs his rebelling staff (Violet, Judy and Doralee). It is an engagingly old-fashioned, simple story full of Dolly songs and lewd slapstick, with a Scooby Doo thin plot and, in this version, some wonderful performances.

It started out with the ensemble asleep on the stage floor under blankets and duvets. I think beds would have been more appropriate as it looked like a teenager's sleepover, but the Civic stage is not that big, so perhaps they ditched the beds in favour of a bigger ensemble being onstage. They all woke up to and sang the opening number '9 to 5' and quite literally performed the actions of the song. This segued into a very well- choreographed, by Lea Carroll, dance routine. Ms Carroll's work on the show was very accomplished, particularly on the fantasy sequences; 'Dance of Death', 'Cowgirl's Revenge' (pictured overleaf) and 'Potion Notion' where three different styles of choreography were on show. However, her work with Violet and the Male Ensemble on 'One of The Boys' in Act Two was outstanding. Reminiscent of a Busby Berkeley musical of the '30s, Violet and the boys danced some very complex and decorative patterns that would challenge some professional dancers.

In the opening scene, most of the cast were under lit or not lit at all. This continued into the show, with some states so dark that we could not discern who was on stage. It did settle after a while and I suspect that some of the front of house was tweaked in and out manually. That said there was the most exciting use of movers, by designer Darren Kelleher, I've seen in a while, swirling with the music on some numbers and they came into their own during Judy's fantasy sequence 'Dance of Death'.

Musical direction on this shown was by Dermot O'Callahan. His musical arrangements added a certain home- spun country and western feel to the majority of the show, not surprising as all the tunes were written by Dolly. His work with the offstage chorus in particular shone through. There were a couple of musical genres explored in the score, from jazz to hoedown to big brassy Broadway numbers, but Mr O'Callaghan worked well with his band to authentically deliver each style. As the Civic does not have a pit, the band was sequestered way upstage but out of sight. I have no idea how many were in the band as there was no band credits in the programme. But I liked the guitar work and the percussion was resonant. As mentioned, I thought the ensemble was top notch on this show. They had some lovely harmonies on 'Nine to Five Finale' and 'Shine Like the Sun' and provided powerful backing to some of the other numbers.

A very clever set design by Marie Cusack, who also stage managed, saw the office desks connected to the chairs on castors, making scene changes very easy. A large cut out skyline upstage showed the city. Hart's office was beautifully finished, with bookshelves, a large desk and chairs. His bedroom was also very well done, with him being trussed and trucked on and off very effectively. The hospital scene was well represented by hospital screens on castors, and the bathroom scene with the two toilets worked quite well.

Costumes by Martina Foreman, Joan Kelly, Rosaleen Nolan and Martin Heffernan were suitable for the era and well fitted. I particularly liked Judy's fantasy scene dress, sparkly and form fitting and Violet's 'One of the Boys' costume. Doralee's country and western outfits were great as was Hart's suit. Wigs by Ali Murphy were super and looked real and make-up by Catherine Coventry was well applied and suited the characters.

Damien Hurley as Franklin Hart Jnr, really grasped his role with both hands in this production. He relished every scenery chewing, cartoonish moment, with his Tom Selleck mustache and a fierce misogyny, he epitomised male privilege in business with gusto. His comic timing was excellent as was his physicality in the more slapstick moments. Vocally he was super too, his 'Here for You' is probably the most sexist song ever written and he hammed it up perfectly.

As Violet Newstead, Julie Donnelly commanded the stage in every scene she was in. Playing the hard-working widow, she was totally believable. Her scenes with the younger office worker, Joe - nicely played by Stephen Fagan, were tender and they had a good chemistry.
