Similarly, her scenes with her stage son, Josh well played by Jordan Bass, were believable and conveyed her sweet maternal nature. Ms Donnelly's stand out moment was on 'One of the Boys', where she sang and danced brilliantly with the male ensemble. Serena Salmon performed Doralee Rhodes with an exuberant good ol' girl energy. Ms Salmon played her sub-text very well and really projected the character's life-long problem of being misunderstood with a fine touch. Her singing was particularly memorable on 'Cowgirl's Revenge' and 'Backwoods Barbie'. James Pierce as her husband, Dwayne with his ever-present bandana, gave a solid performance as the supporting partner.

As Roz Keith, Kelly-Marie Davy really radiated competence and bitchiness in equal measure. Her love for Hart, although bizarre as he was such a monster, was well played and surprisingly convincing. She performed a wonderful '5 to 9', showcasing a fabulous voice coupled with an amazing energy.

Gavin O'Reilly as Dick, Judy's ex, did what he could with a drastically underwritten role but he didn't have much to work with. Stand out performance on the night was Jaqueline Brunton as Judy Bernly. Ms Brunton's comic timing was excellent, she played the character as physically awkward and innocent, Judy's reactions were always a second later than everyone else. Her pathos was also brilliantly executed, we genuinely felt sorry for her and were willing her to succeed. Her performance of 'Get Out and Stay Out', brought the house down. Ms Brunton's masterful control and emotional investment during this song was stunning. In this fluffy, feel-good, yet divisive show, her performance of the song brought the whole show to another, higher, level. Her characterisation of Judy was peerless. Director Art McGauran did a good job on this show. Yes, it is hammy and creaky and out of date already, but he had such a light touch with the comedy, it worked. The staging was quite good in places; the fantasy sequences were well handled and the office scenes were well rendered. The pacing of the production was quite fast as it should be, and there were some lovely set pieces.

His casting of the principals was excellent, particularly Mr Hurley and Ms Brunton and his work with the ensemble, together with the MD and choreographer, raised the show to a higher level. However, the Dolly videos brought it all back down to a crassness he was clearly trying to conquer! But, I suspect one has to show them as part of the licence. Which is a shame as the production was better than that.

Every Heart Awaken Michael Collins - A Musical Drama, was a real labour of love for its' creator Bryan Flynn. Many years in the making in collaboration with different venues and numerous creatives, the show centres on the years and activists during and following the Easter Rising in 1916. Like a cross between Les Miserables and Evita with a W.B. Yeats play at its centre, this is a complex piece of theatre that requires many talents and abilities to do it justice. Coolmine Musical Society has been in operation for a long time and have won many accolades for their productions, so when I made my way to Draíocht, I knew that they would certainly have the experience to stage it well, but would they have the passion that's required to deliver the pathos.

I need not have been concerned as from the outset, with the Players preparing for their roles in simple mimic gesture on the apron in front of a black gauze, I knew we were in for a treat. Opening with such mesmerising theatricality, whilst the audience were still entering the auditorium was a superb device that set the stage for what was to come.

High production values by Coolmine ensured that this biographical show where we followed the life and times and eventual martyrdom of Cork's most famous son was given the respect it deserved.

Collins was played by Kevin Fagan and whilst smaller in stature than the Big Fella, he delivered a very fine performance. His acting was nuanced and strong, his rock tenor singing was well modulated, dramatic and articulate. His stand out songs were; 'Survival of the Fittest and his duet with De Valera 'Confrontation'.

Kitty Kiernan, the woman at the centre of the love triangle involving Collins and Harry Boland, was played by Nicole Lamb. She had a wonderful musical theatre voice, her belt was exceptionally smooth and she poured great emotion into her singing. I particularly liked her work with Harry on 'For Nothing Else I Cared' and her duet with Collins 'Our Love Will Never End'. Her performance was imbued with an elegant delicacy and she was an excellent casting choice. Equally, Liam Egan as Harry Boland was very well cast. Showing a naked vulnerability beneath the fervour, he played the role with self- possession and a fine balance. He sang well throughout but especially well on 'Not That Man', where he held that last note perfectly for its' duration.

De Valera was played by Seamus Sullivan. His singing was strong and his parlando was good. His characterisation of Dev was however a trifle strange. He played him as very stiff and wooden and whilst De Valera was a formal character, I felt that Mr Sullivan's interpretation of this stoicism was too villainous.

I was very taken with Colin Flynn's performance as Joe Emmet (pictured top right surrounded by "the players"), from the first scene he radiated a youthful warmth and eager intensity to help Collins. His character's journey from innocence to terrorism was subtly executed and on point.

The Players were outstanding in their character(s). Bouncing from Greek Chorus to the Abbey Players, they spanned genres effortlessly. Kathy Kelly and Jim Walsh as the older Players exuded experienced stagecraft and morphed from poor rural peasants to the higher status of narrators with ease. Matthew Williams and Orla Walsh as the younger Players, had a tangible vitality and were equally adept at this dual characterisation. As Player5/Mother Ireland, the relatively young Niamh Carroll convinced as a much older character and her sean nós singing was eerily memorable. Her stillness and presence were fascinating to watch. With the exception of Collins, this quartet had the lion's share of singing in the musical as they narrate, perform characters in the play within the play and sing with most of the principals. Their precision, unity and individual distinctive voices were a most welcome and elegant respite from the sometimes full-on emotional expressiveness of the ensemble.

Other notable mentions were, Michael Flynn as Arthur Griffith and Ciaran Lenehan as Cathal Brugha, both showed great musical timing in 'Treaty Debates'. Despite Mr Flynn's mic not working, he projected brilliantly and we didn't miss a word.

Michael Collins is obviously not a Broadway dance show and doesn't have many routines or dance numbers for a choreographer to get their teeth into. However I'm sure choreographer Nicole McDonald was an enormous help with the fight, group and battle scenes as they looked very well-rehearsed and more importantly, safe. The use of freezes and slow-motion was very effective too. The prison scene, where the male chorus sang 'Frongoch Prison Song', was very well staged with the choreography physicalising their powerlessness.

The opening scene with the Isadora Duncan'esque scarves dance was quite ethereal and worked well.

This set was quite sympathetically designed. Upstage we had a platform, mostly used by Mother Ireland, flanked by sections of two story houses. The Abbey stage was cleverly built in two sections and trucked in from left and right to join at centre. Some scenes were created by simply bringing on furniture and there was great use of the downstage left and right pros by the Players and to isolate characters. During the street battle scenes a barricade was trucked on where the actors could hide behind and this was particularly effective.

Clearly a lot of imagination went into this set by designer Dave Benson and the build quality was very good. It really captured the mood of the piece as most of the set dressing was distressed, looking like a war zone or at times an area suffering great deprivation. Collin's mobile podium was trucked on and off and even used by Dev at one point. It could spin 360 degrees and looked perfectly in period. The flying in of the tattered tricolour was cleverly divisive and the downstage black gauze was used very well, particularly at the start of the show.

Projections by Donal Cantwell were splendidly designed and constructed, showing newspaper headlines and time and place, reducing the need for exposition.

Lighting by Denis Twomey was quite good, however I felt the sound was a tad too loud and we missed some of the lyrics on the bigger numbers as they became quite muddy. Costumes by Nomac were of the era and hair and make-up by Ali Murphy was very good, particularly the ageing make up on Mother Ireland.

The eight-piece band, lined up across the front of the stage on the auditorium floor, was comprised of violin, two keyboards, clarinet, French horn, drums & percussion, guitar and electric bass. They played accurately, were tight and their tempo was good. Musical Direction by Dave McGauran was excellent. His mastery and clear admiration of the music enhanced the delivery, by a committed band, of this emotional production. Mr McGauran's excellent work as Chorus Master ensured that even the weaker singers, and there weren't many of them, blended well. The tracking was very effective too, particularly the uilleann pipes and additional percussion. The live band blended well with the tracks and we couldn't discern any joints.

This was a very good show, the Director, Pat McElwain, did a fine job in bringing the story and all of the themes and passion to the stage. The pace was perfect, it never lagged, which is quite good for such a long show. The settings were professionally rendered and expertly placed, the blocking of the actors was natural and the sheer emotion rolling off the stage was palpable. Mr McElwain clearly infected the cast with his passion and enthusiasm for the work and it showed in their performances and their tears during the curtain call. A well-deserved standing ovation by an emotionally wrung out audience, told Coolmine that yes, they did awaken our hearts and definitely projected the pathos and also that terrible beauty of a turbulent era in Irish history.

The Siamsa Tíre in Tralee is quite an imposing sight, set back from the road just a short walk away from the bustling town centre. The foyer is a wonderful space with curved stone wall, pleasant sitting area and bar. We were warmly greeted by the beautifully attired Ena, who was a great help throughout the evening. The auditorium has wide curved and tiered seating areas and the most comfortable seats.

There was a scrim about midway across an open stage, through this we got the impression of the staging behind. There were illuminated fairground signs which set the scene and created interest. The side flats were of a slightly three- dimensional quality which lit well during the show, adding texture to the panel. There was no music playing which was a pity, as I think this adds a bit of a buzz and gives an opportunity for the audience to be familiarised with an unknown score. This production was accompanied by a recorded track which was a good sound quality and created a nice balance between singing and music throughout. The settings for this show were produced by John Hurley. WOW! This was a touch of genius. The settings were projected onto the flats on stage creating wonderful surrealistic scenes which were ever- changing. The time, effort and expertise that John showed in his design were quite staggering. We had butterflies flying, a stunning Emerald City scene, balloons taking off - you name it. The stage became alive with all this movement and wonderful colourful. I would have one criticism about this effect. Because it was projected from the back of the auditorium and not from above the acting area as it is usually done, the images also projected on our cast. Due to this we at times lost the clarity of these figures on stage, and most importantly facial expressions. This needed to be counter-balanced by some more front lighting on the cast. This was a very exciting and innovative way of creating scenery, not one that would suit every show, but in the Oz fantasy world it was stunning.

There was a huge cast of enthusiastic and talented young people involved in this show. You can't force a genuine sparkle from the eyes of everyone on stage unless they are all really having a great time. This group showed us that they were enjoying every moment. A huge part of this must be the excellent way in which they were directed by Oliver Hurley. Oliver grabbed every opportunity to involve as many of the cast into the production as possible. He created a 'waistcoated' backing group who appeared from time to time throughout the production, adding visual and vocal backing to many of the big musical numbers. The Munchkins were played by the youngest members of the troupe, who were all so involved in the production. There were huge dance sequences.

These were so neatly executed by the team. There were great arm movements with super extension to the tips of fingers. The routines involving Dorothy and 'the boys' were slick and fun. The 'Tornado Ballet' was a riot of twirling moves in some very voluminous costumes. The show was moved well and dance routines seamlessly segued from dialogue.

Oliver had gathered together a very talented cast of principals for this show. Originally a vehicle for the vocal talents of Michael Jackson and Diana Ross, there are some difficult 'RnB' songs for the leading players, demanding a lot vocally from this young group. They managed superbly with the challenge, Laura Crowley had obviously worked hard with the cast, especially the principals. Clodagh Harrington blew us away with the opening number 'The Feeling We Once Had'. Sarah Cleary sang powerfully throughout. I loved Matthew Dineen's tone, especially in 'I Was Born On The Day Before Yesterday'. Padraig Harrington gave us a really soulful 'Slide Some Oil On Me' and Marcus Nolan had touches of Barry White in 'Mean Ole Lion'. Laura created some lovely harmonies between the principals such as in 'Be A Lion' when the two voices blended delightfully. The chorus also created some harmonious moments when singing on stage or in the wings.

The sound system was in the capable hands of Murt Whelan Sound Ltd. The backing track was always on cue and there was good balance between the accompaniment and the singers on stage - and thanks too for those occasional sound effects such as the dog barking at the beginning of the show.

The cast worked their socks off throughout the show, always keeping in character, always convincing in their various roles and maintaining their accents so well. Dorothy was played with so much fire by Sarah Cleary. Not only could Sarah deliver some of these very difficult songs, but she acted through the whole range of emotions in this show. She built up very believable relationships with 'the boys'. This was a nicely judged and acted performance. 'The boys' in question made a great on stage team. Matthew Dineen surprised us all with his rich deep southern tones. He captured the essence of Scarecrow with his floppy body moves and turning, twisting and falling at the drop of a hat. Matthew entertained us with the characterisation from his first appearance on the helter-skelter to the end of the show. Padraig Harrington was a great Tinman. He moved so well on his first appearance, slowly coming to life limb by limb. He too acted and sang in a style which fitted the part so well. Lion was portrayed with so much macho charm by Marcus Nolan. His rich voice and great movements using the whole stage area created a wonderful persona. He really provided so much humour in his performance with his easy delivery of lines. Pierse O'Brien was very mature in his performance as The Wiz. He managed to capture the overpowering 'Great Wiz' and also the discovered 'fake' equally as well. He moved around the stage with great 'watchability'. Aunt Em was beautifully sung and sympathetically acted by Clodagh Harrington. She gave the role the maturity which it needed and we were convinced that she was much older than Dorothy. Katie-Anne Harris made Addaperle into a wonderfully colourful comedic character with real 'attitude', very in the style of 'Legally Blonde'. Aoife O'Mahony gave us a powerful and strong rock chick performance as the nasty Evillene. She blasted her way through her dialogue and belted out her musical numbers with great venom. I felt sorry for Dominick Hurley as Monkey, Eoin Griffin as Lord Underling and particularly Jordan Tearle as Messenger, who all caught the terror of Evillene. Well played boys for your portrayals of these smaller yet important roles. I feel I have to mention Sorcha Ringland as Glinda. She entered in semi-darkness sitting on a carousel horse which was lit by fairy lights. The horse miraculously rose and fell as it galloped across the stage. The effect was wonderful. Also wonderful was the singing of the rider. This was such a magical moment when vocal, performance and staging combined to produce one special and unforgettable picture on stage.

The chorus of 'The Wiz' made a huge contribution to the show's success. They were always there supporting the action, listening, focusing our attention. They all sang out, there wasn't one person who wasn't committed on stage, not one who wasn't giving their all in their singing and dance routines. The future of musical theatre is safe, keep acting and singing everyone!

The look of the show was enhanced by great costumes. With the number of cast involved on stage, this was a huge costuming challenge, so well done to the costume team who obviously went that extra mile. Some of the creations on stage were extraordinary, such as the wonderful 'space invaders' costume in 'Kalidah Battle'.

The principals' costumes all worked really well. Dorothy in her red checked short skirt, T-shirt with touches of gingham, leather jacket and sneakers (later to be replaced by a beautiful pair of glittery silver court shoes) The Witches all had a different identity due to some wonderful fantasy outfits. Addaperle's dress was particularly extraordinary with a sort of crinoline effect. I loved the simplicity but effectiveness of the Munchkins' costumes. Pastel colours of T-shirts teamed with matching jeans and trainers looked very striking on stage. The principal men in their interpretation of the original Scarecrow costume, in this case a pinstripe suit with patches, a leather look silver Tinman's suit and glorious Lion costume, completed by a stunning Rasta wig. The wigs throughout, such as Evillene's black and red creation, were wonderful. The make-up was appropriate. The principal men had character make- up which was beautifully applied. The rest of the make-up for chorus was quite naturalistic but consistent.

The staging was not just created by the use of projections, there were also moving trucked panels which became the onstage screens for the projections. These were moved seemingly effortlessly into place by a well-drilled stage team. There were also big pieces such as the fairground helter-skelter which later became the hillside on which we discover Scarecrow, a roller-coaster car which appeared carrying Lion into the scene, and of course that magical bobbing horse which was cleverly operated with a bit of brute force but looked so entrancing on stage. Smaller props were few but were in character with the show such as the green Ozian sunglasses.

This was a polished and visually stunning show, with great commitment shown by everyone on stage and a huge support given to the Tralee Musical Society's Youth by the more senior members of the company. I know that many of The Wiz's cast will be leading players in the adult society. I wish them all future success.

Lime Tree Theatre in Mary Immaculate College in Limerick is a most interesting space. It obviously doubles as a lecture hall during the day but can be used as an excellent theatre space in the evenings. The steeply tiered auditorium gives each seat an excellent view of the stage and creates an excellent acoustic from the stage area. From my seat in row G I had a perfect view of the action. The rich velvet curtains were drawn at the beginning of the show and the sound of Michael Young's Orchestra tuning up could be heard. Michael had gathered together a group of ten musicians who worked excellently together to interpret this tricky fast paced score. This was musical direction and playing to the highest level. There was a wonderful blend of sound and the tempo of all the musical numbers was excellent throughout. The balance between stage and orchestra was perfect and we could hear every word of every song which is so important in this show as there is so much humour in each musical piece. The cast all sang their parts excellently and had all clearly been rehearsed extremely thoroughly. There was an unfortunate glitch in the microphone system in the second half of the show which was sorted quite quickly but did cause a lack of pace at one point.

The director of this production was Des Henn who added wonderful nuances into the production. The humour of the piece was extracted to perfection and delivered so well by a most talented cast. The movement of principles and chorus was excellent throughout the show. Everyone was so well chosen for the role they played and they played it very convincingly maintaining the correct accent throughout in most cases. The choreographer of this show was Barbara Meany who created some stunning and inventive choreography for the show. From the beginning with the four usherettes whose detailed movements were perfectly in time with each other, to the huge finale, this was a delightfully choreographed production and one of which Barbara should be most proud. She was working with a fantastic team of dancers and a strong chorus. One number that I particularly enjoyed was 'I Wanna Be A Producer' which had a team of girls in smart silver dresses creating all sorts of patterns on stage. Barbara's choreography rose to crescendos paused and then rose again, this really is to me what good choreography is it all about. She also used the words of the songs so well to create storytelling through her dance movements. A job well done Barbara.

There was a very talented cast in the show who played each role so extraordinarily well. Dickie Donnelly made a great Max Bialystock. His adventures with the older women were hilarious and he managed to get a wonderful mix of panic and humour into his portrayal. Dickie has a great singing voice and the tone of his voice really suited the character he was playing. Leo Bloom was played beautifully by Jason Ronan. We loved watching Jason hugging his little blue blankie. I loved his optimism about the world, willing him to leave his job in the boring office to become a Broadway producer. He has a very pleasing singing voice and showed it off to good effect in all of his musical numbers. Wow! Tara Downes was a wonderful Ulla. She looked the part, she acted the part and she sang the part, always in character. She had us all entranced with her Swedish accent and her impeccable comic timing. This is an actress who can move extraordinarily well around the stage using the whole stage area to create memorable dance moments. Well done Tara.

James Malone was an over the top Carmen and his on-stage partner Roger played by Brian Henry were both great creators of sublimely hilarious moments. There was no shortage of camping it up for these two. I loved the bitter sweet relationship they had together. They delivered their rendition of 'Springtime For Hitler' with great style, producing a great wee moment of musical theatre. 'Keep It Gay' was another highlight with the gathering of all sorts of artsy characters. Franz Liebkind was played well with a lack of Germanic charm by Barry Danaher. Barry created a totally wacky Nazi-loving character. He sang well and moved well around the stage, always in character. We all loved his dancing pigeons and those lederhosen!

There was a wonderful group of dancers and chorus who for me really added the professional gloss to this production. They showed commitment to every scene they were in and those brilliant, expressive faces always added just the right amount of showbiz in their smiling eyes that gave the show a real class. There were so many beautifully played cameo roles in this show. Well done Hold Me, Touch Me played by Clíodhna de Paor and Lick Me, Bite Me portrayed by Gráinne Hartnett, hilarious. Roger's Team gave us a real mix of brilliant characters of all shapes and sizes! Other parts, mostly played by Glen Carr, contributed much to the success of the evening.

The staging of the show, cleverly managed by Ray Burke, was fascinating. There was a pair of box-like trucks which could be moved and opened to reveal different scenes. We had nicely painted and functioning doors of the theatre, the stage walls and doors for the auditioning scene, then the panels opened to reveal a detailed office scene with windows, functioning doors, painted wainscot and book shelves. The whole thing revolved again to become Roger's apartment. This was a substantial piece of scenery and it did take a little while to set up but we were captivated as to what was going to happen next so it didn't really distract from the flow of this production. Everyone quite obviously had their job to do so scene changes were sharp. The props used to finish the sets were all in keeping and looked authentic, such as the step ladder, adding machines and work stations. I was however disappointed with the lighting in the show. At times this was excellent and created wonderful effects such as when the posters at the sides of the stage were correctly lit, either from behind or with bulbs encircling them. The general lighting was quite dull at times which slightly cut us off from the action. Cues were a bit tardy at times. There was also a roving lighting effect which really had no place in this production. This was just confusing and really made no sense. Overall the sound plot was well managed and there was a good sound quality with a nice balance between stage and pit. A pity we had a wee blip with a microphone in Act Two, it happens.

The costumes throughout were stunning with great attention to detail. The principals' costumes were all great fitting, especially Ulla's which looked as though she had been sewn into them, a perfect fit. The chorus costumes were many and varied. I loved the red usherette costumes, the silver show girls' outfits, the wonderful 'Springtime For Hitler' set of costumes. The old lady dresses and hats were great. Where appropriate there were matching shoes though I would ask that sets, such has these should be double checked in future as a wee difference in shoes or socks doesn't seem important but it really catches the audience's eye on stage. The make-up was very cleverly applied in the show as it was strong enough, especially the girls' eyes and lips, to appear to be show makeup from a different era. The hairs were all in appropriate styles and the wigs were well set. There was an almost 1950's style created. This worked well with the overall feel of the show which didn't really have a set time zone.

This was a wonderful evening of Broadway glamour and just great fun. It was a slickly directed show which was very well cast. The choreography was intricate and well- rehearsed. We had a great team of dancers and chorus. Musically it was a delight. This was a good show from a great team. Well done The Cecilian Musical Society.

Based on the true story of the Von Trapp family, 'The Sound of Music' is undoubtedly the epitome of the classic stage and movie musical. Based on the blossoming love affair of Georg Von Trapp and Maria, the origins of the Anschluss in Austria and the family's exit to a brighter life in the United States. Obviously, there was a bit of poetic licence in the final Broadway production which opened in 1959 with the then forty-six-year-old Mary Martin as Maria. It was an instant hit and is still popular with audiences today. It was a pleasure to be back in Galway's Town Hall Theatre to see 9 Arch Claregalway Musical Society's production of the show. I attended on the opening night of the society's short four performance run. There were a few wee first night nerves which I am sure were sorted out during the rest of the run.

The show was gently directed by Jay Molyneux who explored the script to tease out as much humour as possible from it. There were some lovely touches in the direction such as how certain lines were delivered, how and when pauses were taken to maximum effect and some of the disapproving facial expressions were great. There were a few wee pieces which I would have directed differently and would have held a moment a little longer for dramatic effect. This is an important story which really shows how Hitler was able to manipulate minds such as Rolf and Franz, turning neighbour against neighbour and family against themselves. The horror of what was to come after the family left Austria should always be at the back of our minds.

Jay was also choreographer of this show. Although there is not much dancing as such in the show the stage movement was on the whole well thought through and executed, though there were opportunities for even more movement in the production. There was obviously a wide range of talent which I am sure could have risen to further challenges.

Shane Farrell conducted the nine-piece orchestra. This was a beautifully melodic interpretation of the score. The singing throughout the show was of a high standard. The chorus, particularly the huge chorus of nuns, at times created a wonderful depth of sound. The principals and those with just one or two lines in the show sang with conviction in a very tuneful and pleasing manner. The children had all great voices which made a beautiful blend together and sounded very good in their individual roles. Maria and the Captain's voices sounded very strong individually and harmonised well together.

Maria was beautifully played by Megan Lohan.

There was a well-scrubbed innocence in this portrayal. Megan looked the part, sang with a gorgeous tone and acted so well too. There were some lovely moments such as her confrontation with Von Trapp, the first meeting with the children and her subsequent winning them over and a nice scene in the bedroom with Frau Schmidt. She related well to the Captain and their love affair seemed very natural. Alan Greaney (above) gave us a slightly wittier Captain than usual, with a natural flair for comedy shown in some excellent delivery of his lines. He too had a beautiful tone to his singing voice and gave us a pleasing 'Edelweiss'.

Elsa was played with class by Anne O'Donnell. She moved so elegantly around the stage creating beautiful poses as she went. Her acting throughout was in keeping with the part and she has a stunning singing voice. Max who looked a bit like Georg's brother with the same body type, hair and beard differentiated himself with great comedy timing and a convincing American accent. This was a gentle and nicely paced performance. Annette Cavanagh who played the Mother Abbess did so with a great deal of dignity and gave us a wonderful version of 'Climb Every Mountain'.

Cian O Ceallaigh as Rolf and Saoirse McCarthy as Liesl worked well together as the ill-fated young lovers. Cian created a character who grew from a nervous young man to a determined Nazi who almost betrays the family. Cian moved round the stage well and I think I would have stretched his dancing skills much more than in the slightly lack lustre routine for 'Sixteen Going On Seventeen'. Liesl too looked as if she could have risen too much more of a challenge. As the eldest child in the family, Saoirse was most convincing, particularly in her growing friendship with Maria. This was a great performance with Saoirse showing a lovely maternal quality towards the other children. She sang well in all her musical numbers.

Franz, played by Michael Cooney, made an efficient butler who really can't be trusted. He was always there in a scene bringing information and pushing the story on. Olibhia Donnelly played a warm Frau Schmidt and I really didn't mind her using her own accent. David Alexander was a threatening Herr Zeller. Feargal Cavanagh played the Admiral von Schreiber with an experience and menace in his voice. The three principal nuns: Sister Bertha (Sonja Stevens), Sister Margaretta (Eve Garavan) and Sister Sophia (Katie Bebbington) were all excellent in their very individual roles. Each one created a particular stage character but they all worked so well together. The singing was great and we had a lovely version of 'Maria'. I particularly liked some of the looks of disgust poor Maria was given. The team of children did a great job right through the show. This is quite a long show and they never seemed to tire as the night progressed. Friedrich was the young man of the group. He delivered his lines really well, moved well round the stage and sang with a rich but very tuneful tone. Well done Keith Hanley for your interpretation of Friedrich and thanks for the laughs you gave us in 'Lonely Goatherd'. Louisa played by Alana Mullins had wonderful posture on stage. Her accent was impeccable and she managed to maintain it throughout the show. She sang gloriously and moved with such ease around the acting areas. Cameron Heneghan created a very believable Kurt. I loved his dancing with Maria at the ball. He sang brilliantly, how can we ever forget that last note in 'So Long Farewell'. Katie Larkin gave us quite a few belly laughs as the slightly outspoken Brigitta. Her delivery of lines was faultless. She too sang strongly and moved well also. Lucy Keenan made a lovely Marta. She had a wonderful stance on stage and she lit up the auditorium with that radiant smile. The youngest member of the family was Faye Greaney as little Gretl. Well done Faye you played your part so well. There were lovely moments with this character, like when she steps forward to bow but doesn't, Faye played this with such great comic timing. She also sang her solo line in 'So Long Farewell' so beautifully.

The setting of the show caused all sorts of problems which I hope were resolved after the opening night. The society had decided to use a series of painted cloths, some of which were beautifully painted. Cloths of this type then set a standard for all the properties, furniture etc which appears in front of them. I was very disappointed in the look that was created and also by the impracticality of giving so much of the stage area to a permanent hillside which was really only used at the start and end of the show.

This caused great congestion on the stage which was a big area and problems of this type with more creative planning just wouldn't have happened. I have seen quite a few shows recently which have used rotating trucks to give a seamless change, maybe an idea for next time. I would also advise that the stage team should constantly check that that black tabs are positioned so that they cover activity in the wings, unfortunately this was not the case in this show. The props were a mixed bag with some nice pieces of furniture, tea set etc. I really missed the tombstones or grille in the penultimate scene which was a bit flat with the family hiding behind one lectern.

The stage was quite well lit through the show, though I think a few tree gobos would have added a lot to the evening scenes. The penultimate scene in the Abbey really didn't work as the stage light was too bright and Rolf's torch was too tiny. Pity as this can be one of the most dramatic moments in the production. The final picture however was absolutely stunning with the nuns silhouetted and the family at a height behind them. The quality of the sound was great throughout the show. A lovely tone was created and the stage/pit balance was perfect.

The costumes were generally of a pleasing standard but a few modern shoes and a selection of coloured stockings on the nuns did jar a little. The children looked pristine in their beautiful costumes and Maria had a good range of outfits. The nuns' habits were all very authentic looking. Hair and make-up were generally sound but I would aim for less colour on the nuns whose makeup should be very nondescript. There were nice touches with hairstyles at the ball.

The huge chorus in this show added much to the production. This is a bit of a thankless task for the chorus who aren't on stage too much but this cast gave heart and soul when they were on. Well done.

There were some fine performances in this production of 'The Sound Of Music'. The bones were here for a great show. I would hope that in future this company would think about the show's staging, as sets, props etc should enhance a show and not detract from it.

This was a hugely entertaining night of a heartfelt production which was lyrical, witty and at times poignant. Well done to all involved in 9 Arch Claregalway Musical Society's The Sound of Music.

Carrigaline Musical Society is a community-based project which involves a wide range of ages and talents from the local area just outside Cork city. It produces a musical each year, this year they chose the classic Oliver! Based, of course, on the novel Oliver Twist by Charles Dickens this show is jam packed with memorable tunes. There are of course many children's parts in the show so it is a firm favourite with groups such as this. There was a real buzz around Carrigaline Community Complex for the Sunday afternoon matinee of the show. The hall is a good size though to stage this performance a stage had to be created at the front which did take up quite a sizeable space. An orchestra of just six players was placed in front of the stage under the musical direction of Denise Crowley, who created a very pleasant sound throughout the show with this limited orchestra. There was beautiful violin playing especially in 'Reviewing the Situation'. The casts' singing had obviously been rehearsed well and the chorus also created a good sound on stage with some pleasant harmonies at times. Nancy's 'Oom-Pah-Pah' was one of the show's many musical highlights. The director, Jacinta McBride chose an adaptable set and used trucked on pieces to create changes of scene. A black curtain was also pulled across and was acted in front of and at times this covered scene changes though I would advise a better-looking cloth for future shows. The cast of young and not so young players were totally committed to performing to their very best standard in their production of Oliver! One could feel the pride they all had in working together as a team. Jacinta moved the cast well around the stage and there were some nice moments of tension and humour created through the whole show such as Bill's chilling arrival at the bar. The Cockney accents had obviously been drilled well into most of the cast and the majority of the performances were very convincing. There were just a few moments of people being masked on stage especially when there were entrances at the back of the stage. Overall a steady piece of direction.

Choreographer Tara O'Connor set her choreography within the limits of the cast and created some interesting pictures and movements for some of the set pieces such as 'Food Glorious Food' and the shortened version of 'Who Will Buy?' Tara used marching movements which were very effective with the children. There was a lovely moment with white umbrellas in Fagin's Den. The movement was neat and of the period.

The set was very interesting and looked very realistic. Rough wood and brick effect had been used to create a multi- purpose stage which would change from Fagin's lair to the street, to the bridge. The brickwork was well painted and the addition of practical candles added a very Victorian touch to the show. Properties also were realistic looking and of the time. There was a beautiful metal bed brought on for Mr Brownlow's house. There were tables and benches which looked appropriate for the pub, there were bottles mugs etc which were in keeping. Shay Gilley played Oliver with a gentle and thoughtful style. He sang really well and acted well too especially in his scene in the undertaker's where he has a real fight with Noah. He worked well with Fagin and he and Dodger were very believable as a couple of unlikely friends. Sam Tanner played the part of Dodger with just the right amount of swagger and charm. He worked well with Nancy and the rest of the boys in Fagin's lair. Ava Costin looked and sounded great as Nancy. She broke down the fourth wall, challenged us as the audience and brought us into her world. We could see the pain in her soul as she sings 'As Long as He Needs Me' and knew that she really loved Bill Sykes and though she shouldn't she just can't help herself. This was a very strong performance. Bill Sykes was played with much menace by Dec Kiely. He threatened the cast and was even threatening to us as an audience as he prowled the stage. He had a very gravelly voice which was perfect for the part. Surprisingly Fagin was played by a female, in this case the wonderful Lorna Hughes. I was sceptical that this would work when I read the program but was instantly caught up in Lorna's performance and forgot all about gender. Lorna weaved her way in and out of the story with such style and captured the essence of the character brilliantly. She also sang very well too and though some of the music may have to have been transposed, most of it she was able to perform as written. I particularly enjoyed her rendition of 'Reviewing the Situation' which was one of the highlights of the show.

Laura Reddy played Nancy's sister Bet. This was a very polished performance as she sang, moved and acted really well. She and Nancy had a great relationship together on stage. The idea that they were sisters was very convincing. Mr Bumble was played by Kevin O'Keefe in an energetic way. This Mr Bumble moved well around the stage and danced about with ease. He and Widow Corney, Angela Tanner worked well together as a couple and sang and acted their song 'I Could Scream' with great style.

Mr Brownlow and Mr Sowerberry were played by Aidan Hurley who give us a gently paced performance. Possibly a little more pace was needed in the scene with Dr Grimwig who was played by Brian O'Keeffe. Brian looked well on stage but needs to watch his pace of dialogue. This is not how quickly you say the lines but the lack of gaps between people speaking. We naturally slightly overlap or come straight in when we are chatting to a friend, it is really the same on stage. Mrs Sowerberry, Mary O'Sullivan, was a nice fussy character with a voice which would have cut corn as she entered the stage. Liz Hesse-O'Sullivan was on stage as the old woman in a wheelchair. We didn't actually see her face but she told her story well.

Charlotte was played by Clodagh Tanner and Noah by Fionn Mehigan. Again, they were well developed characters and made us not like them too much, as they were so nasty to Oliver. Mrs Bedwin, the nurse was played by Helen Hunter and she had a lovely moment with Oliver in the bedroom where he is sick in bed. The chorus in the show worked very hard, both adults and children, particularly in the first half of the show when they were involved in so much of the action. They were all committed and they all sang very well. They moved well too and everyone seemed to be able to remember the tricky choreography that they were given - well done!

The costumes were a bit of a mix in the show there were some beautifully made costumes which were right for the era, though many of the costumes were just too clean for Victorian London. I particularly liked Bill Sykes' costume which was very authentic, right from the top of his perfectly fitting top hat to the bottom of his perfectly chosen boots. Nancy looked good too and her red dress with lace-up boots, nice new lace-up boots, but in some cases more attention to detail could have been made to the costumes as there was a bit of a mixture of particularly footwear which can be distracting whenever you are looking at a period piece such as this. The hair, in particular the girls' long hair, was caught back into ribbons occasionally and looked very good. There were some hair styles of the ladies which were too short for the period and I would suggest that in future you should be able to gather up some wigs and hair pieces for these ladies. Eye make-up too should be in character with the time so I would avoid coloured eyeshadows like greens and blues and instead use a brown and cream palette which would be more in keeping with the period.

Overall this was a great afternoon's entertainment. The hall was filled with an audience of all ages and as I entered, quite a few of the children were on iPads and phones but from the second the show started these were put away and they never appeared again, which goes to show how involved the children were with the show. They were watching and living it. This is what it is all about!

Well done Carrigaline for a great effort. There are a few things which are small details with costumes etc which could be worked on for next time but your young society has the heart and soul to produce a great show. Well done everyone involved. P.S. I am sorry I didn't see the other group of players perform too, (some parts had alternating cast) time would never allow me to do that, but I am sure they all did a great job too.

The Hawk's Well Theatre in Sligo was the venue for Sligo Fun Company's production of Sister Act. The intimate theatre was packed with an audience of various ages. There was quite a buzz of expectancy before the show and we weren't disappointed. Based on the movie starring Whoopie Goldberg, Sister Act is a feel-good show which revolves around the cabaret singer Deloris, originally Doris, and her escape for protection into a struggling convent. There is a wonderful sense of fun throughout the show and it is a great vehicle for a company with a large number of women in the cast.

The characters have all to be well-formed and the pace at times needs to really rattle along. There are also other moments of tenderness and self-doubt which have to be brought out too. Mary MacDonagh was the Director and Choreographer for this busy show. There were some wonderful pieces of direction on stage backed by glorious dance moments. The show moved at a great pace with quick changes of scene. Steffen Jorgensen created two large revolving pieces which had three different scenes on each one. These, with the exception of one which I didn't like the painting of, were very effective, especially the convent scene which had a three- dimensional quality.

Mary took a few risks with the casting of the show and chose several principals who hadn't played a major role before. Well done, this really did work as everyone on stage was excellent. She also managed to really bring out a great performance in each player and created some wonderful on-stage personalities. Mary's eye for detail was wonderful, especially in the placing and moving of the cast. There was wonderful grouping of cast on stage. Clever reactions with each other like poor old TJ being constantly hit on the head. There were good relationships shown between the cast such as the gang and how well they all worked together and also between the nuns and Deloris. I particularly liked the friendship between Mother Superior and Deloris at the end. The movement during acting scenes was well thought through and always made sense with the dialogue. The movement during the dance routines was just my kind of thing. There were constantly changing patterns, building up to a crescendo, holding and building again. This always left us as an audience wanting more. The solos were nicely moved too, in a way that did not take away from the feel of the moment. She even had Deloris dance with her bottom to us in 'twerky' fashion and it was fantastic! This was an interesting, ever changing piece of choreography. I loved the way the six altar boys were incorporated into the final number, they had a ball.

Musical Director Niamh Crowley gave us a wonderfully energetic and balanced sound from the pit. What was interesting to see was the variety of ages playing, from more experienced to teenagers. There was a glorious accompaniment throughout and I particularly enjoyed the delicacy of the playing for solos and duets. The cast had been very well rehearsed musically and everyone was singing strongly within their own vocal range. Diction in the singing was excellent and every syllable was as clear as a bell.

Niamh and Mary did have a wonderful cast to work with of course. Sinéad Conway made a great Deloris Van Cartier. That first 'Take Me to Heaven' number nearly blew us away and at times Sinéad's singing was so good, it felt that we were watching her in concert. (She was backed by the wonderfully dressed backing singers played by Holly and Kerry - well done ladies). Sinéad's acting became stronger as the show developed and she managed to get great moments of humour out of the role. This was a great first major part in a musical. Well done! Her love interest Eddie was played by Kieran Cunnane. Poor mocked Sweaty Eddie begins as the gun-shy cop and becomes the hero. This was a nicely judged performance. He carried off the instant costume change into John Travolta very well. The other bad boy, that Deloris had a thing for, Curtis was played with comedic menace by Franny Curley. He looked good in his leather jacket, with the gangster swagger. This was a frightening performance at times but he was able to have humorous moments especially in his dealings with his gang. He sang well and gave a great rendition of 'When I Find My Baby'.

The characters of the nuns were all different and all brilliantly portrayed. Mother Superior was played by Angela McGuire with just the right amount of coolness and yet showing a great heart at the end of the show. Angela brought out humour in the lines I hadn't even thought of before. She has a soaring voice and gave an emotional but witty 'Here Within These Walls'. Fiona Hiney played Sister Mary Robert and took us on a journey with the character from a timid postulant to a forceful woman. Fiona sang beautifully and her solo was a lovely moment.

Sister Mary Patrick was portrayed wonderfully by Rebecca McGillen.

Rebecca was just so involved in all that was going on on stage. She was a great listener and those facial expressions were super. Pam Lindey was Sister Mary Lazarus, whose gruff exterior hid a really comic side, especially in the rap number. Sister Mary Martin of Tours was a statuesque and commanding nun, as played by Maureen Howley, with some great well delivered comic lines. Siobhan Terry gave us a prickly Sister Mary Theresa who added a spark to all the scenes she was in.

Curtis' three henchmen were hilarious; there was TJ who was constantly battered for his stupidity played by Luke Devaney, Pablo (Brian McGauran) who was a silent but deadly type and Joey played with great style by Micki Murray. These three had us in hysterics, especially in their 'Long Black Dress' number. They gave us their best pumping and grinding moves and created a magical comedy moment. Robert Fitzpatrick was a wonderfully fussy Monsignor O'Hara. He related well to both Mother Superior and Deloris. He was like a breath of fresh air each time he entered. He kept the story telling rolling along by telling how 'the two antique dealers' were progressing with their negotiations. Other roles were captured well by Mark, Darren, Killian, Lloyd and Hugh. Hugh you were a very humble Pope to join us in the stalls! The chorus very so involved and everyone knew exactly what they were doing in all those complicated dance routines.

The lighting in this show was pleasing throughout with some lovely gobos being used. There were nice effects made with coloured lights, particularly against the back arches. Intimacy was achieved by giving us pools of light as appropriate. I must say increasingly I like the 'shaft of light' effect a hazer can produce in a show. We had some smoke when Deloris was in the confessional (those confessionals were stunning props with their red velvet curtains) this smoke gave a great atmosphere on stage. I hope the problems with the sound system were resolved. The costumes all looked in keeping with the feel of the show. They were a good fit and appeared to represent the 1970s very well. The sudden change costumes worked well. I loved the white and silver finale costumes. The sparkly coloured habits were quite nice but could have been even more over the top. I loved Curtis' leather jacket and the boys' flared trousers took me back! The nuns' basic habits were a good fit. Our drag queen was a treat in that great outfit. The Pope looked wonderful as he entered and sat among us.

The women's wigs were well presented and I thought the men's wigs gave a nice 1970 touch. Make up was subtle for the nuns. I did love Kerry and Holly's makeup which was stunning. Deloris' wig moved really well but I am glad to say never covered her face, it looked pretty realistic. This was a great night of comedy musical theatre. It was a thoughtfully directed show which teased out all the comedy of the writing. The music was a glorious balance between voice and instrument. The choreography interpreted not only the music but also the words of each song. This was an evening we just didn't want to end. Congratulations to all the cast and crew for a job well done.

Despite countless requests, George Bernard Shaw resisted releasing the rights of his most famous play Pygmalion to be turned into a musical, a genre Shaw believed to be frivolous. However after his death in 1950, Alan Jay Lerner and Frederick Loewe embarked on the long journey to turn it into a musical. Despite many rewrites, as they felt the story didn't follow the conventions of the 'musical' at the time in that there is no central love story, they managed to create the immensely popular My Fair Lady.

One of the most prominent reasons for the musical's popularity lies in the retelling of the Greek myth of Pygmalion, the sculptor who created a statue of Galatea, the perfect woman, brought to life for him by Aphrodite. In Pygmalion, Higgins is the sculptor and Eliza the clay which he moulds from a simple lower-class flower girl into a Lady. However, the Eliza of My Fair Lady takes a more active role in her own transformation and at play's end becomes a necessity for Higgins, who has "grown accustomed to her face." Shaw didn't want a romantic ending to Pygmalion. He said in a postscript to Pygmalion in later editions, "She will, if she marries either of them, marry Freddy…" Lerner and Loewe retained an ambiguity in their script and it could be argued that Eliza had nowhere else to go because even though her speech had improved, she didn't have the wherewithal to improve her station or class. In Shaw's revised play, Pickering helps her and Freddy open a flower shop and they both live happily ever after. In the musical we are left wondering what her role will be in the Higgins household.

Carnew Musical Society under the assured direction of Michael Dunbar presented a mostly traditional telling of this joyful musical. In the foyer, the staff were dressed in Edwardian costumes and in the auditorium the company had affixed silhouetted scenes from the show to the walls, in particular Ascot, which immediately gave a sense of place. The stage was open with a set of side flats fashioned to resemble old hardback book spines, akin to a giant's library. A stage wide platform upstage was also dressed as books stacked on their sides. A wraparound cyclorama on the back wall doubled as a projection screen. A very well stocked flower barrow was set centre stage and lit in preset.

The twelve piece orchestra were situated in front of the stage and screened from the audience. The Overture was sumptuously full, the viola, violins, cello and bass giving that lush string sound with the woodwind and brass cutting through backed by the drums and percussion. The keyboard added another pleasing layer to the resonance. Musical director and conductor Lar Duffy conducted with deftness and his timing and pace with the band was perfect. Mr Duffy also doubled as Chorus Master and his work with the ensemble was excellent, producing lovely tones and wonderfully, powerful and joyous harmonies.

Eliza as played by Joanne Logue, looked and sounded a lot older than the traditional portrayal of the character, her physicality and throaty cackle was more akin to an older woman. During her initial scene with Pickering and Higgins, she was less the waif like urchin and more an older hard- bitten Dickensian Nancy in Oliver Twist, had she lived. Ms Logue's singing however was superb, her soprano was crystal clear and note perfect. When she sang "I Could Have Danced All Night", we knew we were in the presence of a first-class soprano. As she became educated, we started to see her character's intelligence shine through, her speech whilst not quite received pronunciation, did convince. Interestingly her posture did not change. She still carried the world weary furtiveness, which was odd as one would have expected her to have the aloofness and bearing of one to the manor born needed to convince, yet it somehow worked and was quite realistic. Ms Logue's scene with Higgins when she asks what is to become of her, now she has won him his wager was quite heartbreaking. Her portrayal of anger and helplessness brought a sense of tragedy to the story, which was very refreshing as it is not often played as realism.

As Professor Higgins, Rory Robinson channeled the voice of Rex Harrison, his cadence was uncannily similar, particularly during his singing/parlando. However his physicality was much more energetic. His performance was a highlight of the show, he became Higgins. Mr Robinson played the privileged misogynist extremely well and his insouciance towards Eliza gleefully incensed the audience.

Colonel Pickering, with whom Higgins makes the wager to turn Eliza into a lady within three months, was played by Sean Hallahan. The Colonel was also a linguist, having spent some time in India and Mr Hallahan played him as a genial gentleman. He was more attuned to Eliza's plight and tried to soften Higgins more outlandish demands. As Freddy, the young man who was besotted with Eliza, Padraig D'Arcy sang "On The Street Where You Live" rather well and was quite believable as the simpering Mummy's boy. One could never see Eliza being in any way attracted to him and she practically tells him so during "Show Me".

John Young played Eliza's father with a cheeky cockney charm. Mr Young was a very physical Alfred Doolittle, animated and dynamic - particularly when being repeatedly thrown out of the Pub. His sidekicks, Jamie played by Jimmy Spellacy and Harry played by Paul Doran were perfectly cast and all three sang "With A Little Bit of Luck" with great energy and zeal. His "Get Me to the Church on Time" showed off his clowning prowess and his fine baritone.

Higgins Housekeeper, Mrs Pearce was played by Mandie O'Keefe. Although written as an English servant, Ms O'Keefe retained her own accent, which was a good decision as it gave her a softer edge, particularly when dealing with the distraught Eliza. A kindly portrayal, her Mrs Pearce was quite endearing. Also present in the Higgins household were the servants; played by Anna Furlong, Cathy Tighe, Catherine Stafford, Ellen Kinsella, Paul Doran and Richard O'Toole. Their choral work was top notch, particularly on the quite difficult harmonies.

As Higgins' Mother, Jennifer Byrne excelled at playing the subtext. Although concerned with propriety, Ms Byrne played her as quite feisty and ultimately benevolent.

Eileen McCabe, as Freddy's mother Mrs Eynsford-Hill, played her well. She perfectly embodied the upper-class sense of entitlement Shaw despised. Professor Zoltan Karpathy, who Eliza must convince that she is a Lady at the Embassy Ball, was played with a delightful over the top performance by Malcolm Byrne. Mr Byrne, complete with incredibly coiffed facial hair and impeccable Hungarian accent, flounced around the stage in a welcome cameo performance.

Choreography on the show was looked after by Frances Ryan and she did a great job. Stand out routines were the broomstick work in "Wouldn't It Be Lovely", the slapstick of "With a Little Bit of Luck" and the fabulous synchronicity of the "Ascot Gavotte". The Embassy Ball was well staged and the group energy of "Get Me to the Church on Time" leaped off the stage.

The set by Tony Barry worked well, basic trucked flats and furniture against a white Cyc and the stylised book end flats and platforms. There was some projection on the cyc, but it was underpowered and frankly looked badly skewed. Ultimately it was not required, as it did not add anything in terms of setting, location or time. Props by Grace Dunbar, Lar Duffy and Cathy Tighe were very authentic and well sourced.

Costume was mostly supplied by Nomac in Waterford and was of the Edwardian period. The Ball gowns looked great and I liked the smoking jackets and the men's attire. Make-up and hair was looked after by a team of eight and looked well.

Lighting was by Kevin McEvoy and was perfectly fine, mostly general washes with little specials and some practicals as befitting the show. But the LED lights didn't fade smoothly with the generics, so the cross fades were bit jerky. Sound by Joe Murphy, Itec Productions was full and well balanced but Higgins mic didn't work in the first scene, his "Why Can't The English" was a bit lost against the full band, but he managed to keep getting close to other actors and used their mics, which sporadically worked. Stage management by Tommy Kavanagh and his crew was very good. Transitions were swift with the cast doing some of the work.

Director Michael Dunbar produced a fairly traditional take on what is now known as 'the perfect musical' but he also added a great deal of pathos to the playing, particularly of the role of Eliza, which is not often done.

As a revisionist viewing through a contemporary lens, My Fair Lady could be seen as a celebration of sexism and misogyny. Directing this musical today, one must be aware of how far society has progressed in terms of equality and the class system. Mr Dunbar clearly addressed these issues in this production by highlighting Eliza's plight at being used as an experiment in social conditioning. Joanne Logue as Eliza brought a modern sensitivity to her playing and an innate sadness in that she had to return to her creator, as she had nowhere else to go. Interestingly, the casting of a seemingly older Eliza does make the relationship between her and Higgins more viable, although Mr Shaw would I imagine vehemently disagree!

This production took risks, and whilst playing it as a light comedy it did not shy away from the conflicts and the injustices that women experienced in Edwardian England and are still experiencing today. Well played Carnew, well played.

There was a warm welcome on a cold winter's night in Claremorris Town Hall which had been decorated with a balloon archway to greet an enthusiastic Friday night audience. BIG THE MUSICAL was a new experience for me and apart from the research I had made online I really was open-minded about the show. I had seen the movie starring Tom Hanks in the late eighties and I was looking forward to seeing how the story transferred to the stage as a musical.

Director Donna Ruane had taken on this show at relatively short notice and in doing so took on a show that involved a cast of various ages. The basic premise for the show is that young Josh who gets tongue- tied when he meets the love of his life, visits a fair and at the 'I Grant Your Wish' machine he wishes to be suddenly 'big'. His wish is granted with some hilarious consequences, as he has the heart and mind of young Josh captured inside Adult Josh's body. He comes to realise that being a grown-up isn't all he thought it would be, as with age comes baggage and responsibility. So, he eventually finds the machine and reverses the wish/ curse. To be very honest there are some nice musical moments in the show with a couple of lively dance numbers and a few beautiful ballads but the script could be wittier. That being said Donna made a good job of directing the show and the story was nicely told. The production was set at a good pace but there were pauses for the more poignant moments too. Donna and the stage team used an open set for the show with raised platforms at the back of the stage. This was topped with a cut out of the city skyline which was detailed and looked effective. Behind this was a black syce which later during the 'Stars' song sparkled with stars. The side flats were on a rotational pivot and on one side there was a realistic brick wall while the reverse had a collage of photographs of various toys and games. The two front stage extensions housed the boys' bedrooms. These were detailed in their dressing but were not utilised very much during the show which was a shame. The audience will always look for that big floor piano moment. The keyboard had been created at the front of the stage and it lit up effectively when Josh and George danced out 'Chopsticks' on it. This was a difficult thing to time properly and to synchronise movement with lights, it nearly worked. The large pieces of scenery such as the wonderful Zoltar's cabinet were quickly moved into place, though a couple of things did take more time as the crew were working in a very confined wing space. David Keane, I don't envy your job trying to make a set of bunk beds disappear in this limited space. Most scenery was nicely painted though the style and quality of these was not always consistent.

There was a pleasant blended sound from the orchestra under the direction of Deirdre Lee. Deirdre directed with great control and precision from behind the keyboard. There was a good balance between the singers and the accompaniment so we could hear every word. There were pleasant harmonies and the ladies' chorus really created a powerful sound. Principals were secure with their songs though the vocal range of some of the numbers did prove quite challenging.

The choreography from Jay Molyneux was in character with the general era and added to the feel of the show. There were some good lively numbers for the younger cast when they could show real 'attitude' by moving sharply from one pose to another. Arm movements were big, extended well, in time and in sync with each other. I would have liked to see more changing patterns on stage to add further interest. I did however love the angles and move of the smartly dressed secretaries in 'Coffee Break'. The ballet with young and adult Josh, Susan and Cynthia was very moving. Everyone looked like they knew exactly what they were doing and most important everyone was having a ball. Young Josh was played by Jack Mannix. He gave us a sensitive performance as the boy who struggles to express his feelings to Cynthia. The older Josh of Cairán Hennelly was most convincing. He managed to maintain that wide eyed innocence of youth throughout and gave us some humorous moments.

Josh's pal Billy Kopecki was intelligently played by James Fletcher who showed great comic timing for a young man. Josh's mum was portrayed by Karen Ronane. She emoted well from nagging mother to heartbroken parent. She sang well too and her wee moment at the table singing 'Stop Time' was beautifully done. Sonja Stevens was Susan Lawrence. Sonja has one of those show voices which can really affect the listener. The 'Little Susan Lawrence' number was a wonderful moment. I also enjoyed her awkwardness when having to sit on those huge bean bags.

Ronan Egan made a strong boss of the toy shop, George MacMillan. He moved easily around the stage and acted with conviction. Ronan showed us what a strong, rich singing voice he has. His office manager was the highly efficient Miss Watson played by Aishling Costello. She moved round the acting areas with great style and her frustrations at Josh's ideas and demands were clearly shown in her facial expressions. Michael Goulding was the upwardly mobile Paul Seymour who tries to control Susan and hates the boss's new favourite. We believed in this character and I am sure many of us have worked with a Paul who would climb over everyone to get to the top.

Cairán Kelly was busy as Zoltar and also as the BMW owning sophisticate in the roof top apartment scene. He played both roles very well and created the magic required for the wish-granting automaton. The pairing of Abigail (Vivienne Lee) and Diane (Mary Dempsey) was wonderful. They added a well needed burst of energy and sang really well together giving us great harmonies. I loved the sophistication these two added - two polished and experienced performers. Mrs Kopecki had just the right blend of bossiness and frustration that all parents of thirteen-year olds have. Nicely acted Tara Niland. Young Josh's love interest Cynthia was played by Ciara Farrell. She was just right in the role and the support she got on stage from her group of friends was effective.

The chorus contributed much to the production. I would ask that in future any 'business' the chorus have to do is thought out a bit more. I always feel that their movements in the background should be 'choreographed' too as sometimes when less experienced chorus are left to their own devices, they are just not too sure how to improvise in character. The freezes in the show were held very well.

Some of the costumes, particularly the ladies' costumes gave us a real sense of 1980's. Hairstyles were sometimes in keeping with the era. The make-up was a little restrained and could have been stronger on the ladies. Small personal props were in good condition and appropriate to the period.

The sound was excellent in this show. The tone and cueing were exemplary. The smoke machine was a bit heavy handed and left such a cloud during the following scene that we couldn't see the action which spoiled the momentum. Lighting created different moods throughout and the team were not afraid to give us good bright light on the stage. (One of my pet hates is unnecessary dullness on stage unless for a special effect). The light up piano was effective though difficult to co-ordinate the foot stamp to the flash of light. There were some nice pools of light which gave intimate moments.

In summary, this was a competent show. One which cast and audience thoroughly enjoyed. A really good night out.

When we think of the portfolio of songs made famous by the wonderful Elvis Presley, it is hard to imagine why a show such as 'All Shook Up' didn't happen much sooner. This story tells of a roustabout Chad who gets out of jail and comes to town. His hip-swinging ways make him popular with the women of the town. A comedy of errors follows against the musical backing of the songs of Elvis. This is a clever and funny script which needs good comic timing and breakneck pace. We had this in spades in the production staged by Birr Stage Guild. The red velvet stage curtains were closed at the beginning of the show in Marian Hall when we entered and found our seats. These opened to reveal a desert landscape, painted cloth (I think it might actually have been painted onto the back wall) with neck and headstocks of guitars as telegraph poles disappearing into the distance. This effect created an illusion of depth to the stage. The guitar theme was carried out to the proscenium arch where there were two huge guitar cut outs mounted.

The opening scene had free standing cell bars for the first number 'Jailhouse Rock'. As the show continued various items such as the bar, complete with quite an array of bottles and props were wheeled on. Tables and chairs appeared and disappeared quickly. A petrol pump and sign represented the garage, the motor bike providing an authentic touch. Human exhibits represented statues standing on box plinths in the museum. There was a detailed and well-painted Tunnel of Love car. Props and set worked together well and one of the highlights of the show was the Greyhound bus which miraculously revealed itself when suitcases carried on by the passengers opened and placed side by side formed the side of the bus, very clever and very effective.

The orchestra was under the direction of Enda O'Connor. I was initially puzzled that I couldn't actually see the orchestra in the auditorium. It turned out that they were in a side room and their sound was played out over speakers into the hall. There was a video link with the MD to screens which were on either side of the stage. It worked perfectly and we had a glorious balanced sound between the stage and the orchestra. This is a lively show with some real rock 'n roll belters such as 'C'mon Everybody' and melodic ballads such as 'There's Always Me'. Both genres were played well. The orchestration never overpowered and cues were excellent throughout.

Every ounce of humour was brought out of the script by experienced director Paul Norton. He added those magical nuances which make a simple, though witty script into a rollercoaster of laughter.

There were clever moves, gestures, facial expressions, moments held, breakneck pace, all the ingredients of great comic timing. His choice of set which was followed through by the work of an excellent stage team meant that the show never stopped rolling, carrying the audience along with it. Paul's choice of cast was so important too as they not only rose to his challenge of attention to detail and timing but they all looked like they were having a great time on stage. The characterisations were broadly drawn but also nicely developed as the show continued. We felt real empathy for every principal character and really willed there to be a happy ending for each one.

The casting of this show really came in pairs and each of the pairings in this production worked well, with a natural connection established between them. David Sheils who played Chad had a bit of the Elvis swagger but also an innocence of youth. He sang well throughout the show and his pumping and grinding brought colour to one or two cheeks in the audience! He worked with the many characters he built up relationships with but we all loved watching his on-stage relationship flourish (with twists and turns of course) with the stunning Sarahgene Loughnane who played Natalie, or was it Ed? In both roles Sarahgene gave her heart and soul. Her blokeish moves and sound effects (how did she burp on cue?) were great and when she, as Ed, and Chad kiss we are quite shocked. There is a great deal of comedy in the writing of these two parts and these two got as many laughs from the script as they could.

Jim (Natalie's father and owner of the garage) was played by Patrick Byrne. We were in stitches when Jim tries to tell Sandra that he fancies her, we were willing him on from the auditorium. Jim's character develops as the show progresses and Patrick did a great job throughout. We had great humour but some tender moments such as when Jim comments on Natalie's red dress. He gradually falls in love with Sylvia and we could see this love blossom before our eyes. Barbara Hanamy was the hard-working bar owner Sylvia. She tries to be dogmatic with her daughter but realises she has to let go and leave her to follow her dreams with Dean. Barbara has a beautiful tone to her singing voice. We were delighted when she and Jim finally did get together.

We couldn't take our eyes off the attractive Miss Sandra (Bríd Delaney). We loved seeing her transformation from museum manager to vamp. She played both roles very well. She made great use of the side flats as a place to gyrate and her stage exits were always fascinating. We weren't sure who Miss Sandra was going to end up with but we wouldn't have guessed the geeky Dennis played by Patrick Kelly would have stood a chance. When Patrick appeared initially, I thought I wasn't going to like the performance. He had an exaggerated voice and movements, but after the first scene I was bowled over by his total commitment to the part. This is an actor who has that something you really can't teach, perfect comic timing. He can make a word or a line funny by timing, facial expression and delivery. The man can sing too and he is not a bad mover either! Well done Patrick you gave us so much joy as Dennis.

Sylvia's daughter Lorraine (Robyn Luttrell) is the feisty young woman who meets GI Dean played by Gerry Clarke. Their love affair is the most straight-forward and sweet pairing in the show. They worked well together and the 'It's Now or Never' number was a real blockbuster moment. Both players were convincing in their roles.

Heather Colohan as Mayor Matilda I enjoyed your tough no nonsense character. Again, Heather has wonderful comic timing and I loved how she asked poor Earl (Kevin Murphy) a question but never gave him a chance to answer it. That walk was wonderful. Many actors begin building a character from the feet up and I got the impression that is what Heather had done. A great piece of comic theatre. Earl was the lap dog who appeared to follow her everywhere, never objecting but adding little gestures to others as he left the stage. What a joy to see Earl stand up for himself and to wow Matilda not with aggression but with love. There is a lesson for men here in how he managed to re-establish a relationship in the nicest possible way. This was a great on-stage partnership.

The chorus backed up the principal cast well. They sang strongly and moved with great co-ordination during the big dance numbers. Nice to see a wee troupe of dancers. Aideen Leacy, the choreographer had ten ladies who moved really well throughout the show. They first appeared coming down the aisle for the opening number and appeared regularly during the show. I always look at feet, body extensions and faces. Faces are so important and the joy from these dancers was so obvious. The routines were tight, neatly carried out with sharp arm movements.

Though space was limited when chorus and dancers were on together, I would have liked to see more changing of patterns and pictures on stage. The use of torches was a lovely touch in one of the numbers and created a magical effect. The movement of couples and small groups was gentle and at times added to the story telling.

The quality of the sound was very good and the tone of the orchestra and voice were well blended. I would have liked a bit brighter stage lighting at times but there were some nice moments when 'specials' created great atmosphere.

Well done stage team for moving the scenery on and off with so little room in the wings. The scenery was on the whole nicely painted and looked effective. The costumes were smart and sets of costumes such as the striped prison outfits worked very well. Neckties etc gave a 1950's feel. The blue suede shoes were smart and the court shoe version on Sylvia were great. The red and white spotted dresses were very effective. The hairstyles gave a nod to the period, with pigtails and of course Miss Sandra's flowing Marilyn Monroe golden locks.
