There was a light touch at times too, such as in 'Me and My Baby' when Roxie and two girl dancers in bowler hats gave us a delightful soft shoe type routine. Nice period moves and patterns. 'All I Care About' was good, though it would have been nice to see something new in the staging of this number. 'Razzle Dazzle' was nicely set and the last few moments of the whole show with the full cast were stunning. This was a competent and intelligent piece of stage choreography.

There were fifteen in the orchestra, again all students. This created a glorious rounded sound. We had lovely touches of jazz and ragtime with a rich brassy sound. The cueing was a bit problematic at times but when that was sorted, Molly Burke had a good control over the orchestra and there were good tempi in most of the numbers. Emily Hogarty had obviously trained the cast well and I enjoyed the harmonies between two players. ('Class' with Mama and Velma was particularly good). Again, at times the cast were not always too sure when to come in with the music, but I am sure this improved as the run continued.

Before I move on to individual performances one thing I would advise as a general rule, be careful with shouting on stage. If you let yourself go to a scream too soon you have nowhere else to go but higher and more hysterical. We lose diction and to be honest it becomes unreal (just something to watch, sometimes held back and quiet can be more effective). Wow what a strong line up of principals we had for this show. Really there are just six principal players who have to totally convince us and carry the show. Rua Barron made a great Roxie with a nod to 1920's hairstyle she looked right for the role, sang really well, giving us great moments of comedy in her singing. She acted her role well too and moved well in all her dance numbers. Rachel Galvin built a great character as Velma and the on/off friendship with Roxie was nicely told. She has a real belter of a voice but also can hold an audience in those softer, gentle moments too. She commanded the stage in in her many solos and her dancing had the right amount of vaudeville feel. There were lovely harmonies created between the two leading ladies who both told the story very eloquently. The smooth-talking Billy Flynn was played by Joshua Hurley. He did a great job with the part (though I wanted to see him in a beautiful suit and Oxford shoes). He sang really well and his ending notes of 'All I Care About' and 'We Both Reached for The Gun' were excellent. He had the right stature for the part but might have needed signs of his success such as nice gold cufflinks, tie- clip etc. A good performance Joshua. Joseph Ó Baoill played poor Amos really well. He gave us a heartfelt performance of 'Mr Cellophane' and showed at the end what a rich and beautiful tone he has to his singing voice. Máirín Hayes was a very glamorous and striking figure as Mama Morton. Máirín was very at ease in the role. She moved well around the stage convincing us that we were in her world. She sang well too, giving us a great solo, 'When You're Good To Mama' and a lovely duet with Velma in 'Class'. She managed to capture the money-grabbing prison warder without giving the part the usual sexual undertone. Jenny Kearns did a great job as Mary Sunshine. I think when you cast a woman in this role that the actor has to work twice as hard to develop the character. I loved the way Jenny at times used her voice. On those occasions when we thought her voice was going to keep soaring, she would drop an octave or two! Very funny portrayal of the part.

The girls of 'Cell Block Tango' were all so different and so talented. They carried out their song with great style, super singing and brilliantly choreographed moves. A very slick moment of theatre. I also loved the male dancer being added in to do the tango of life and death with each girl, this was very effective. Well done Ina Caul, Katie Clarke, Jill Montgomery, Sarah McAleer and Lainey O'Sullivan. Oh, and Jill that walk to the gallows was so very moving. Dave Quane made a convincing Fred Casely. I particularly loved the interplay with Roxie in the courtroom scene. Sean Cassidy and Jack Farrell, I was keeping a careful eye on you as I had played the Master of Ceremonies a million years ago. It is a nice wee role and fun to do, you both gave it real gusto. Pity the lighting cues weren't on your side each time you appeared. Well done too Matthew Coalter as Officer Fogarty and Sarah Curran as the Socialite Kitty.

That huge chorus was a wonderful team of enthusiastic and committed players. There was obviously great teamwork and rapport between the group. Each person knew their own moves and carried them out really well. The individual pieces came together so well to complete the intricate jig saw.

One thing I wasn't too keen on was the lighting for the show. There were some nice moments when we had a pool of light and in particular, I loved the way 'Class' was set and lit. However, there were far too many times when cues were late and the overall feel of the lighting was just dull. The old adage. 'If you can't see them you can't hear them,' still holds true for me. To be honest there were times when we lost characters on stage. Maybe think about having light coming onto the stage from off stage 'rooms', or creating pools of light on stage, or possibly follow-spot more. Maybe the lighting was mostly from directly above the stage which of course will tend to plunge a face into shadow, hard to work around that but it does need to be addressed. I hope the lighting of the show improves as the week progresses. The twenty-four microphones gave our characters a great sound and we could hear everyone very well above the sound of the orchestra.

The costumes were a mixed bag for me, some nice black gear, with the black leotards and touches of lace, men in black waistcoats, see-through shirts. There were black trousers and white shirts for the reporters. I liked the grey overshirts for the prison girls. The 'Cell Block Tango' outfits were great. I thought Billy needed a much better cut suit, maybe a dark suit with a broad pinstripe. We should see Billy as a sharp dresser. I know the effect that the over-large jacket was meant to have on Amos but not sure it worked for me. The Roxie and Velma outfits at the end of the show added the sparkle we needed. Hairs were generally in the cast's own style though the up-pinning of Roxie's own hair gave it a 1920's feel. Velma's wig was a good shape and moved well. It would have been nice to see more of a nod to the period with touches such as waves and kiss curls for the girls' hair. Make up was quite restrained, very nicely applied but I would have gone for a lighter base and really accentuated the eyes, darker greys for eyeshadow and an even heavier colour on the lips, maybe a mulberry colour. The make up was however very consistent and looked for the most part in period. Overall, props were in the style of the piece with simple black tables and chairs, good 'Cell Block' cell bars etc. It is worthwhile to copy the originals of newspapers of the time as modern papers tend to have colour pictures which stick out a mile. In conclusion this was a very competent and entertaining show. There was good attention to detail in the direction, though I would have liked a little more 'razzle and dazzle' in some of the presentation. Some super performances and theatrical moments. Well-done all in Trinity Musical Theatre and good luck to those with their finals this year.

It's a Hard Cold Tumble Of A Journey Urinetown is a hidden gem of a satirical musical written by Mark Hollmann and Greg Kotis in 2001. It is set in a weird future where water shortages are the norm and the government has restricted human urination to public toilets controlled by the UGC (Urine Good Company). The musical satirises politics, capitalism, bureaucracy, justice and social responsibility. It is also a parody of other musicals such as Les Mis, The Threepenny Opera and cleverly the musical form itself as well as certain films and even Shakespeare. Urinetown is one of those shows that seems light and easy enough to stage but it is very demanding of its cast, both vocally and physically. Oh, and of course it's a comedy, so it has to be funny.

Trim Musical Society, engaged Liam Butler to direct the piece and it was staged in Scoil Mhuire during the mid-term break. The venue was a school hall, where the society had to bring everything in. As a venue, it was limited in its facilities and the society had to work hard to stage the show. But it really paid off and we were treated to a tight, hilarious, beautifully theatrical piece of work.

The set, designed by Liam Butler, was really clever, with two staircases leading up to a platform upstage and a series of louvred flats stage left and right on the apron and upstage. Lights were built into the flattage and gave a three dimensional feel to the set. The set was glowing when we entered the auditorium and we watched the band, in front of the raised stage, tune up.

The entire show is narrated by a policeman Officer Lockstock assisted by a young girl, Little Sally. These two characters would pop out and speak with the audience, telling us what was going on, what was going to happen and what we should feel about certain characters in a lovely parody on Brecht's Epic Theatre conventions. The Brecht link continues into the orchestra where, like in his Threepenny Opera (which is itself a socialist critique of capitalism), musicians double and triple up on instruments. Urinetown's band, conducted by the Musical Director Dermot O'Callaghan, had five musicians playing about eleven instruments. Mr O'Callaghan's musical direction was very faithful to the original score and he managed to get a great big sound from relatively few players. I must mention the two horn and wind players, who expertly played many instruments between them throughout the piece. Helen McHugh as Chorus Mistress did a wonderful job with the ensemble, their harmonies rang out and the solos were perfect.

Choreographer, Aisling Rountree clearly worked very hard on this show. The ensemble were all very well drilled and it seemed relatively effortless for them. I really liked the intricate choreography on 'Cop Song' and the slo-mo sequences were very well handled. Ms Rountree put great humour into the routines too; 'Don't Be A Bunny' and the title song were hilarious.

Every story needs a hero or a heroine and the hero of this piece was the dashing Bobby Strong, played by James Branagan. Mr Branagan sang really well on 'Follow Your Heart', a duet with Hope and on 'Look At The Sky' with the poor people of the town. His voice was sweet and gentle but full of character. He played Bobby as an innocent happy go lucky kind of guy until his father, Old Man Strong played with red-faced earnestness by Sean Fox, gets sent to Urinetown. Urinetown is a place where folk get banished to for breaking the rules and Old Man Strong broke the rules because he urinated in the street as he couldn't afford the fee to pee in Public Amenity #9. Bobby leads a revolution and falls in love with Hope Caldwell, the daughter of the President of the evil UGC. Mr Branagan's timing and physicality was spot-on and he had a lovely energy in the role.

Public Amenity #9 was overseen by Penelope Pennywise, played by Helen McHugh. Ms McHugh had a super range and handled the very demanding 'It's a Privilege To Pee' with great vocal dexterity. Her comic timing was also excellent and her duet with Caldwell, 'I'm Not Sorry (Reprise)' was heartfelt. As Caldwell, the exploiter of the poor and Head of UGC, Ian Rountree played him with a cold callousness. Like a cross between a certain US President and Will Ferrell's Mr Mugatu, he embodied the evil capitalist with cartoon-like glee. His singing was also rather good, particularly on 'Mr Caldwell', 'Don't Be A Bunny' and the 'Act One Finale'. Caldwell's side-kick (all villains have side-kicks!), was the delightfully camp Mr. McQueen, a self- serving sycophant brilliantly played by Sean Brown. His physicality, mimicking Caldwell's every action, was sublime. Shane Fox played a crooked Senator Fipp as a cigar chewing Texan, who just wants to fly to Rio. Mr Fox was excellent in the role, his lasciviousness towards Caldwell's daughter, many years his junior, was cringe worthy.

Bobby fell in love with Hope Caldwell, the baddie's daughter, who having just returned from the Most Expensive University in the World to learn the family business, eventually joins Bobby as part of the Revolution. Played beautifully by Megan Pottinger, she exuded a delicate innocence and naïveté that was very funny. Her voice was lovely as she sang 'Follow Your Heart' with Bobby and later the reprise, solo.

Officer Lockstock, the narrator, was played by Ronan Walsh and he absolutely nailed the role. His timing, choreography and singing were near perfect. Mr Walsh's presence and stage craft was superb, reminiscent of Jim Carrey in his early films, he totally immersed himself in the role. His rap style duet, 'Cop Song' with his foil, Officer Barrell - played wonderfully by Eoin Kenny, was laugh out loud funny. Little Sally, Lockstock's co-narrator who constantly questions the validity of the show, was played by Áine Fox. She sang quite well on 'Too Much Exposition' with Lockstock and on 'Tell Her I Love Her' with Bobby and Co. But it was her comic timing and precociousness that made her shine for me. She was cheeky and mocking but with a tongue-in-cheek knowing intelligence that belied her years. Sally's friends, who joined the revolution were played by an ensemble that was well-rehearsed, vocally excellent and showed great movement and attention to detail. Little Becky Two Shoes, a girl with a leg-brace, was wonderfully played by Jenny Seery; Colin Flynn played the unhinged Two Blades Harry, who really shone on 'Snuff That Girl'; as one of the bigger actors on the stage it was only fitting that Paddy O'Sullivan played Tiny Tom; Gwen Bagnall really impressed with her playing of Bobby's mother Josephine, one of the few characters allowed to play the pathos of the piece, she was perfectly cast. The ensemble really seemed to 'get' this piece, they relished every scene, knew when to pull back and when to go full on and generally just enjoyed being in it! Costumes by Miriam Donnelly were perfectly pitched, Les Mis rags for the poor and sharp suits for the rich. Make-up by Ali Murphy also suited the characters, I really liked Mr McQueen's overall styling and Fipp's aged make-up. Lighting was by Denis Twomey and was just right for the show, naturalistic and not flashy and everyone was perfectly lit. Sound by Alan White was just the right mix for the hall, good balance between band and singers and a lovely warm tone was achieved. Stage management by Frank Connolly assisted by Elaine McLoughlin, was slick and timely. Transitions were quick and accurate and the show didn't lag at all. Director Liam Butler did a marvellous job on this show. He wrung all of the classical and contemporary references and jokes out of the script and gifted them to his actors. His pacing of the piece was just right, his comic timing of the set pieces was perfect. Mr Butler clearly has a well- developed sense of humour as a director would need this to stage Urinetown. It is a piece of musical theatre in the Absurd tradition, it could have been written by Ionesco or Beckett, and Mr Butler's instinct and intuitive direction absolutely captured the nature of the absurdity. He shared and developed it with his actors and creatives and we in the audience were lucky to have borne witness to this wonderful production.

Where's the Buzz?

Like Chess and Evita, Jesus Christ Superstar, started out as a concept album, ostensibly to raise the funds to stage it as a show and to generate interest in the notion in 1970. It opened on Broadway a year later to mixed reviews and some controversy as did Stephen Schwartz's Godspell, which opened the same year. They both have similar themes but whereas Godspell focuses on the effects of the teachings of Jesus, Superstar spotlights Jesus and his disciples, especially Judas. The controversy was that neither musical concentrated on the resurrection, and in the case of Superstar, that the character of Judas was written sympathetically. Over the years, the controversy died down and there have been many different styles of production staged of Superstar; ultra- modern, futuristic, contemporary and so on and also versions rooted in the time Jesus is said to have walked the Earth. Which is what director, Bill Stafford and Tipperary Musical Society decided to do in the Excel Theatre in Tipperary in February.

Using an open staging with no tabs drawn, the audience were immediately treated to a massive set, impressively designed by Ben Hennessy, based on a Syrian landscape with a large hill-like structure and what appeared to be caves cut into the pink sun-drenched rock and built- in mesas. At the base there was a large fabric sheet with an image taken from the Turin Shroud. At rise this was removed to show a wooden trunk, which initially looked incongruous, but once a bunch of children in modern-day costumes entered (eventually followed by some of the show's characters) to the overture and started to play hide and seek, it made sense as it contained accessories for these characters. The children offered the accessories, in a ritual, to the players and the show began with 'Heaven On Their Minds' wonderfully sung by Judas.

From here on in it was quite a traditional version of the musical. As most audience members already know the story, exposition and dialogue was seen by the writers as superfluous, so all words were written to be sung. Relying on non-verbal communication and the score only, this show needs very skilled actors/singers to pull it off.

Musical direction was by Helen Colbert who was also chorus mistress and conducted an orchestra of twelve players. The three keyboards and two guitars were very present in the score, as one would expect in a rock musical. The brass and woodwind section allowed a more organic sound and integrated well with the electric instruments. Ms Colbert's work with the large male and female chorus was very good, harmonies were melodic and there was a great big choral sound in some numbers, particularly; 'Hosanna', 'Damned For All/Blood Money' and 'The Arrest'.

Choreography was by Miriam Ball and whilst the show is not a typical song and dance Broadway musical, she managed to create some very interesting routines. I really liked the Marionettes on 'King Herod's Song' and the choreography on 'Superstar' was superb.

Thomas Grogan gave a good performance as Jesus but his characterisation was quite internal. Dressed in white, to stand out from others, he gave us a very subdued Jesus throughout, apart from smashing through the moneylenders in 'The Temple' and in his altercation with Judas during 'The Last Supper'. Of course, Lloyd Webber and Rice did write Jesus as an angst-ridden prophet so it's rather difficult to portray him as a charismatic Superstar who enthrals all at this point in his story. But Mr Grogan's singing was pleasing, particularly on the melancholic 'Gethsemane' and the lead in 'Everything's Alright'. His voice really suited the role and his falsetto was very good, however, we never really got any flash of his magnetism in this production. It is an aphorism that the baddies get all the good lines and Superstar is no exception. Judas the betrayer was played by Emmet Donlan with a scenery-chewing intensity. His performance was very good, if a little over overplayed at times. 'Judas' Death' was very melodramatic and badly paced, the emotion hit its peak too early and he had nowhere to go for some time, despite this he certainly convinced for the most part due to his marvellous singing and brooding inner tension and presence. Mr Donlan had a wonderfully expressive voice and he controlled it very effectively. On 'Heaven On Their Minds' where he voices his doubt that Jesus is the Son of God, he displayed a fine rock vocal and on 'Superstar' he excelled.

As Mary Magdalene, one of Jesus' followers who was considered a prostitute, Deirdre Ryan was also quite good. She played Magdalene as an infatuated believer, in love with Jesus as revealed in her very good rendition of 'I Don't Know How To Love Him'. Dressed down with head covered, Ms Ryan underplayed the role but her performance did suit this production's portrayal of Jesus in that she emanated a quiet devout belief in him and matched his internal characterisation. Her duet with the disciple Peter, the pop ballad 'Could We Start Again Please?' was really well-sung by both and the ensemble and she really stood out vocally on 'Everything's Alright'.

Jack Sharpe as Peter gave a fine performance, he portrayed Peter, the denier, exceptionally well.

From an excited, exuberant larger-than-life character to a self-loathing coward; his journey through the show was carefully plotted. The other featured apostle in the show was Simon, effectively played by Alan Kennedy. Mr Kennedy had just the right amount of pathos for the role. Both actors sang strongly too.

As Caiaphas, the high priest who regards Jesus as a revolutionary, Derek Ryan played him with very high status, his remarkable bass voice resounded around the auditorium. His acolyte, Annas, played by James O'Donovan also acquitted himself well, his voice an imposing contrast to Caiaphas. Liam Hunter and David Hughes, both as High Priests, completed this impressive quartet of conspiring clergy. All sang 'This Jesus Must Die' with conviction and brevity, and working with Judas, had Jesus arrested and brought before Pilate.

Pontius Pilate, capably portrayed by Aidan O'Connell, sang the prophetic 'Pilate's Dream' about how he will be complicit in Jesus' death thus heralding the rise of Christianity. Mr O'Connell sang extremely well on this and on 'Pilate and Christ', where he showed his exasperation with Jesus' failure to defend himself. He played the subtext with finesse as he sent Jesus to Herod and, fulfilling his own prophecy, ultimately to his death. Mr O'Connell gave a very powerful performance and I look forward to seeing his next role.

'King Herod's Song' was written in a camp Ragtime style, as a sarcastic mocking of Jesus by Herod, here played by Martin Cosgrave. However, Mr Cosgrave, whilst embodying the regal power of Herod, practically shouted his way through the song and lost the satire by hitting it too hard.

The ensemble sang exceptionally well on this show, the large male and female chorus were very powerful and I heard some harmonies here I'd not heard in previous versions of Superstar.

Stage management on the show was well controlled by Denis Fitzgerald, who had a very large cast to manage. Costume design was unaccredited but was provided by a range of costume hire shops. I liked the High Priest's robes, Herod's sparkles and the apostles were clad in earthy colours as a contrast to the whites of Jesus' costume, which worked well.

Make-up and hair were very well done by a team of six. I liked the eye make- up on the High Priests, this was very effective and quite scary. Unfortunately, Jesus's wig came off during the arrest, but thankfully divinely reappeared in the next scene. Sound by Star Systems was perfectly balanced and full range, I would have liked a touch more reverb on all the lead vocals to give more presence. Lighting by Paul Browne was good with some nice sculpting of the set (particularly the crucifix) and efficient use of the follow spot, though the show could have done with two spots. Cuing was a little lazy on some states though, Judas death by hanging scene was a fraction late, which spoilt the pathos.

Director, Bill Stafford produced a fairly solid, uncontroversial traditional staging of Superstar. He didn't re-imagine it or stress any one specific theme, nor did he really add any superfluous events or scenes. Some scenes were very powerful; the flogging where Jesus was held by ropes from the pros, whilst a soldier whipped him relentlessly; the actual crucifixion scene was quite emotionally staged and the High Priests were frighteningly dominant. It was a simple re-telling, where the music was front and centre against a splendid set, populated by a good cast and a fabulous ensemble and chorus.

Tomorrow Belongs To Them There is such a thing as a perfect storm in theatre, it happens when all of the elements that make up a show are perfectly aligned. It doesn't happen very often, but when it does it stays with you for a long time. It happened on the night I attended UCD Musical Society's Cabaret, the audience were enthralled from start to finish with the inventiveness, uniqueness and sheer virtuosity of their production. Most people know Cabaret from the Bob Fosse directed film starring Liza Minnelli made in 1972. It's based on Christopher Isherwood's 1939 book, Farewell To Berlin, a sort of biographical novel about his time spent in Berlin in the 1930's, a time when the decadence of the Weimar Republic was transitioning to Hitler's Germany. The plot is about an aspiring young American writer who arrives in Berlin and meets a young English Cabaret artist, Sally Bowles. They fall in love but outside forces tear them apart.

UCD's Astra Hall is on campus and is a very flexible space. For this show, directed by Cian Gallagher, they constructed a large raised stage with three solid doors and a pair of staircases leading up to two platforms upstage, over which a sign reading 'Kit Kat Klub' was placed. Around the stage they placed festoon lights and furniture and props were brought on and off to denote locations. Set design was clever and designers, Kellie Comerford and Kieran Sheehy did well to create the seedy club atmosphere.

1930's German music was playing in the pre-set and when the show started, a young man, bruised and in rags entered through the middle upstage door and switched on a pre-set gramophone. The song "Tomorrow Belongs To Me" played, after a while he switched it off and exited. Then the Emcee, a wonderful Ruairí Nicholl, entered with the Kit Kat Klub dancers and playfully sang "Wilkommen", complete with ad-libbing and improv with the audience. This playfulness continued into all of his songs with the exception of "I Don't Care Much", where he sang it straight and very well. His singing on "Money", "Two Ladies" and "If You Could See Her" was sublime. He played the Emcee as an androgynous libertine, salacious with his fellow characters and in his repartee with the audience, but he also projected pain. Mr Nicholl's performance was layered and exquisite with a delicious topping of sleaze. He was present in most scenes, lurking, watching. This show had some very competent actors, oozing talent and commitment to the piece. Caoilfhionn Ní Dhúlaing's portrayal of Sally Bowles was nuanced, at times brash and bold, other times thoughtful and desperate. She developed this 'thousand yard stare', an unfocused gaze to inoculate or distance herself from the impending horrors of what was starting to happen and also to distance herself from her own life and what it had become. Ms Ní Dhúlaing gave an extraordinary performance and captured the essence of the character. She sang Sally Bowles' songs perfectly. More Jane Horrocks than Liza Minnelli, which was the right choice of character as Sally was a young English girl out of her depth in Berlin. Her singing went from seductive and alluring to audacious and at times wasted. On "Mein Herr", she had a lovely command of her vocal and on "Cabaret", which was slowed right down at the beginning, she paced the song beautifully. She was note perfect and imbued each number with intention.

As Cliff, Andrew Murray only had a couple of songs - his duet with Sally, "Perfectly Marvellous" and on the "Finale". Mr Murray had a nice voice and sang well. Playing him as a genial, sensitive artist who falls head over heels for the ingenue Sally, his performance was finely pitched. He transmitted Cliff's sexual curiosity well in his brave scenes with Bobby and Victor and the audience really empathised with him.

Ernst Ludwig, who befriends Cliff on the way to Berlin was very well played by Colin Gilligan. He handled his sub-text really expertly and gave us affability masking his fervent dedication to the National Socialist German Workers' Party. When he revealed his swastika armband, the audience were quite shocked.

As an actor, it's very difficult to portray a character that is decades older than yourself and generally a director will always cast an actor closer in age to the character. But in a student society such as UCD's, that is not always possible. Thankfully this show was served with two superb performances by actors, who on paper, are for too young to effectively play the septuagenarians; Fraulein Schneider and Herr Schultz. As the convivial Jewish Herr Schultz, Pádraic Ó Brolcháin used his physicality and voice to great effect to create the older character. What I liked is that he didn't give us a stereotypical playing, but played him as a quiet gentleman, who prides himself on being a German. Similarly, Taylor Fewer played Schultz's love interest, Fraulein Schneider in a non-traditional manner. Her gestures and lower voice gave her the age she needed to convince. Ms Fewer played the character's anguish very well and we really felt for her.

Cliff moved into Fraulein Schneider's boarding house and eventually Sally moved in with him. Fraulein Kost, a prostitute who lives in the house was comically played initially by Eimear Finnegan, however she gradually revealed Kost's dark side as she sang "Tomorrow Belongs To Me" a Nazi anthem with Herr Ludwig. As Sally's employer at the Club, Max was played with menace and repressed violence by John Felton.

Like all of Kander and Ebb's work, particularly when Bob Fosse was involved, dance and choreography is another character and must be performed well. Using the Bob Fosse style throughout, choreographer Leah Meagher's work with the cast was fantastic. Each routine became more daring and adventurous. Sexy, confident and very on point, the dancers were shameless and gave off tons of attitude to complement their superb dance work.

Whilst, the early numbers "Wilkommen", "Mein Herr", "Don't Tell Mama", "Two Ladies" (where she added another six dancers) and 'Money" were perfectly choreographed and executed, it was the "Entr'acte" / "Kickline"  that opened Act Two that really showcased her talents. This section featured a series of very well- choreographed dance sequences, led for the most part by the Emcee, and lasted about ten minutes. The final kickline was perfectly done and the audience were on their feet at the end of it. There was also a really funny dance sequence between the Emcee and the Gorilla during "If You Could See Her".

Musical direction was by Ben Duffy with chorus work being looked after by Hilary Murnane. Mr Duffy's vision for the music was clearly an intermingling of the popular of the time with the classical and he amassed a fairly large band of fourteen players. His interpretation of the score was faithful to the original but he added some additional flourishes by adjusting the tempo of some of the music to suit the action on stage. Hilary Murnane's work with the chorus was excellent, the singers were all very well-rehearsed, harmonious and perfectly pitched. The ensemble were very tight, but yet left room for improvisation as did the principal singers. On the bigger numbers; "Mein Herr", "Wilkommen" and "Money" there was a great attack, but yet they were full of harmony. On "Tomorrow Belongs To Me", which closed the first act, they were rigid and militaristic and very powerful. Stage management was looked after by John Higgins and Luke Corish assisted by the fabulously named Praise Titus. Transitions were, whilst not necessarily fast throughout, totally in keeping with the pace of the show. Laura Deignan and Seán Hayes are accredited as Costume Managers and they did a super job. The Kit Kat Girls were perfectly, if sparsely clad. The Emcee's leather coat and shirt- front was totally in character for him as was Sally's 'posh' coat and Cliff's suit and bow tie. The older characters were also well-costumed as befitting the characters ages. A really clever touch was the Emcee having an exact copy of Sally's dress. The 'striped pyjamas' at the end was a chilling touch. The wigs and make up were managed by Elsa Joyce and was well applied and sourced. I really loved the bruising on the Kit Kat Girls and Boys and the Emcee's series of different looks. I was particularly impressed with the matching running eye make-up on the Emcee and Sally toward the end. Great attention to detail.

Lighting by Henry Cahill was suitable for the production. His use of LED Pars and movers was perfectly discreet, particularly given the time the show is set. The follow spot was very well used during the club scenes and they made a feature of it. A remarkable sound plot was operated flawlessly. Having such a large band, who were sited to the audience right, and so many ensemble mics was not going to be an easy mix. But the uncredited sound designer did a remarkable job in getting such an even balance and mix.

The pace of the production was perfect, at times breakneck at other times slow and languid. Cian Gallagher's interpretation was clearly influenced by the Sam Mendes version rather than the film, which was good as it is a more contemporary take on the Isherwood stories. I liked how the production highlighted the political and didn't shy away from the decadence of the club and the licentiousness of that time in Berlin. The staging was first-rate and the audience interaction was a great idea, which served to make the piece immersive due in no small part to the tables set up around the edge of the stage.

This production was superb in every way and the audience left the auditorium buzzing and humming the songs. If this is an indication of how good the younger generation of musical theatre makers are, then tomorrow definitely belongs to them and musical theatre in Ireland is in good hands.

Auf wiedersehen! A bientot! Good night?

There was a great buzz around the Millennium Forum in The Maiden City for the beginning of Londonderry Musical Society's presentation of Guys And Dolls. This classic musical by Frank Loesser, Jo Swerling and Abe Burrows isn't perhaps performed as often nowadays as it should be. Based on the characters of New York created by Damon Runyon, the musical traces the ups and downs of love in the shady world of 1940s gamblers. The script is sharp and witty, the music very tuneful and the story optimistic. One of Broadway's perfect musicals.

The Millennium Forum would be a great challenge to many societies as it seats over eight hundred on tiered seating which is quite a lot of seats to fill for each performance. I was welcomed by Valerie who showed us and Noda representative, Sheelagh Hobart, great hospitality. As we entered the auditorium the stage curtains were opened to reveal a beautifully painted cloth with tumbling dice. There was a large sign advertising the name of the show suspended in front of it. The orchestra was tuning up but no taped music to get us into the mood of the era. The orchestra for the show were positioned in the pit. I have seen orchestras of three and four players but in this case there were eighteen for musical director Peter Doherty to guide, this he did extremely well once the show got up and running. With such a huge orchestra there was a wonderful rounded accompaniment to the show. The lively numbers such as 'Bushel and a Peck', 'Take Back Your Mink' and of course legendary 'Luck Be a Lady' sounded wonderful with the huge brass section, nicely supported by the other members of the orchestra. Michael Kielty ensured that the on-stage voices were never dominated by the orchestra and we had a beautiful balanced sound throughout.

I was sitting in the balcony and from there we had a great view of the stage. This is a huge acting space to fill for any company. The scenery was brought on in the form of trucks which had buildings nicely painted on top of them. These created a sense of perspective to the stage. The movement on and off with these pieces was very neatly done. The interior of the mission looked solid, well painted and even had functioning doors. Occasionally the front cloth would be lowered from the tower to cover changes behind it. This is quite an old-fashioned way of doing it but it works. The interior of the store for the crap shooters had been touched up with UV paint which gives it a luminescence at the start of the scene which is very effective. I commend Lee Thomas and his team for a huge job very well done. This was scenery in the traditional sense of the word but it really established the location and era of the show. The properties used to fill the space such as tables chairs etc. were all very in keeping and looked authentic and well maintained.

Of course, this huge area had to be filled with a wonderful cast and chorus. This was down to the director Michael Poole and choreographer Venessa Chapman. Venessa was blessed with a huge chorus of young performers, particularly girls who really could dance. They looked like a professional dance troupe not only in their movements but in their presentation, as their hair, make-up and costumes all combined to give a truly West End look. The choreography was neatly set and performed with nice changing patterns throughout the show. This was a group who could actually dance rather than just do set movements. Venessa was also fortunate in the fact that she had a good principal cast who could also move. Sarah gave us a lovely routine for 'If I Was a Bell' and the boys worked their socks off in 'Luck Be a Lady'. One of the highlights of the show was 'Sit Down You're Rocking the Boat' which was well moved and enthusiastically sung. Overall a well-conceived and polished piece of choreography.

The cast was well mentored by Michael Poole. This was a young cast but a very talented one which will ensure the future of this society. The dialogue was taken at a steady pace though there was good pausing for laughter and comedy moments were mostly teased out and played well to the audience, though this is something that could have been further extended with further pauses before punchlines. The characterisations were very strong and must have been discussed in great detail before the show, for example we had a most unusual version of what is normally a nondescript part of Lieutenant Brannigan. Michael and Jonny Everett created a Columbo type eccentric for this part which added great humour especially with each exit line. The two young ladies who played the leads were very strong in their characterisations and nicely complimented each other. Their counterparts Warren McCook as Skye and Eoin Callaghan as Nathan gave us some wonderful moments of stagecraft. This was a lively and detailed piece of direction with some nice touches throughout. I had seen Ashton Murphy before, at the end of the past summer and was impressed by her then. I am even more impressed by her now. Not only has she a stunning singing voice, but she is also capable of being a fine actress too, particularly in the comedy role. Sarah Brown has to appear slightly drunk. This is a difficult thing for an actress to do realistically, particularly such a young actress. Ashton did it brilliantly without going too far. Her singing voice is so adaptable; she can sing operatically and then can change to a comedy stage musical voice. This is a real gift and one which we all appreciated. Her love interest was the handsome and charming Sky Masterson played by Warren McCook who happens also to be handsome and charming. This was a very polished performance and a mature one for such a young performer. He moved well around the stage, sang well and he also convinced us that he was the character he was portrayed. The appearance in the stage box wearing just an apron was quite a moment though not sure it was in the style of the show! I found it hard to believe that the 'engaged for fourteen years' Adelaide is only eighteen as Hannah Dean played the part with great mature humour and made us really sympathise with her. She also sang well and looked right in the middle of the dancers for her two big dance numbers.

Eoin Callaghan captured the 'hard done by, always in a fluster' Nathan Detroit very well. He had a very strong delivery of his lines, always thought through to get best comic effect. He sang well and moved well too. It is obvious that Eoin would be adaptable to many other stage roles. Nicely Nicely always seemed to be appearing stuffing his face with sandwiches etc. The character created by David Keown was nicely constructed and added much to the humour of the piece. Of course, David had the huge 'Sit Down You're Rocking the Boat' to sing at the end of the show and he blew us away with that number. Well done David.

Judith O'Hare made a very convincing General Cartwright, initially turning up to close the mission and eventually falling under the charm of Sky as well. A nicely rounded character, Judith. Donald Hill was Arvide Abernathy. My goodness this is a man who can really sing. I found the tone of his voice totally hypnotising and very emotional. What in my book makes a great voice is that ability for the singer to touch my heart and soul and in this show that happened more than once. Thank you, Donald for sharing your God given gift with us. 'What More Will I Give You' was a beautiful moment in the show. Nice to see younger members of the cast taking leading roles such as Conor Pooley as Benny Southstreet. He worked well with Jamie Clements as Rusty Charlie. The opening of the show is a very difficult three hander which the boys managed well but I would advise that they would keep their heads up over the newspapers and connect more with the audience. Well done Amy Smith who played Mimi looking for her earring and squealing on for Nathan who started the crap game again. Big Jule was played by Greg Doherty. He looked interesting in the role which is normally played by a particularly tall person but he was big when it came to his personality. Geoff Coke made a scheming Harry the Horse, who was always there to complain about the lack of a game. Kim Porter made a nice Agatha who was a good sounding block for the scenes in the mission. As I said earlier, we had Johnny Everett as Lieutenant Brannigan. I loved the character which was drawn for this part as it added much humour to the show particularly with that little sound as he left the stage.

Of course, there was a huge cast of chorus members of all different ages and we had a great dancing team particularly of girls but well done also boys who made a great effort to master their moves. The mission group looked smart though possibly everyone should have had the same shoes ladies. Then the gangsters who looked well though I would have liked to see a little more care taken with their costumes throughout the show, we needed a bit more colour and the braces on stage looked good though more would have been effective.

On the whole this was a very stylish and enjoyable show, with good performances from the principal players. It was wonderful to see so many younger members involved and I hope they all will stay on in the company and take part in future shows. Thank you for a most enjoyable and nostalgic evening.

What an incredible effort had been made to turn the Dean Crowe Theatre into a 1920s speakeasy for the Athlone Musical Society production of Chicago. There were huge cut outs of the Cell Block Tango girls silhouetted against coloured windows above the entrance to the theatre. There was a red carpet with glowing lanterns on either side leading into the foyer which had been decorated with red and black material and many, many ostrich feathers, including an archway of ostrich feather fans making an entrance into the auditorium something very special. The bar in the theatre had also been given the Chicago makeover treatment, covered tables, more feathers and there were framed posters showing scenes from the show we were about to enjoy that evening. The team who must have spent hours creating this pre-theatre world did a wonderful job and I really appreciated all the effort.

As we entered the auditorium there was an open house curtain to reveal a well- constructed staging comprising a raised platform with three doorways and below the platform a further three doorways. Two curving staircases swept to the upper area. In the centre of the stage there was a grand piano with brightly flickering candles in a simple candelabra. There were nicely positioned tables and chairs to finish off the first scene.

The orchestra for this production was led by Musical Director Ger Madden who conducted the orchestra from behind the piano in the orchestra pit. I do like the sound that comes from an orchestra in a pit as it tends to soften and round the overall sound and this was no exception. The show was started by the MC Tomás Glynn who played the initial trumpet sound (or appeared to do so) sitting at the table on the platform. The playing of the orchestra throughout the show was of a very high standard giving a wonderful 1920s jazz sound throughout. The tempi of the musical numbers were lively which really added sparkle to the evening. The principal line up had obviously been well trained in their singing and each delivered an effortless musical performance. Nice also to hear a great volume from a huge number of chorus members who created some very pleasant harmonies throughout the show. Overall this was a very slick and well-rehearsed piece of musical direction. The director of the show, Alfie Kilduff, set a cracking pace for the show which was carried through by speedy scene changes which did not hamper the action. All the characters in the show were clearly defined and particularly in the on-stage pairings, each pair worked together very well bouncing off each other in a very natural way. The chorus and cast moved with ease around the acting area and I liked the way acting areas were separated from the main stage by the lighting, creating a room by just well-defined lighting.

The lighting through the show was excellent and there was an ever-changing colour on the back wall. Excellent lighting underneath the platform from a bank of LED lights worked well. Even the scene in the stand-up bed was well lit so we could see exactly what was going on. A follow spot was used during the show and once it was on target it was effective and quite in period for the production. Always a little bit difficult to get that initial spot targeted. The sound was good throughout the show as well and there was an excellent balance between the sound of the orchestra and the singing of the cast.

Normally this show is done with a relatively small cast, this time we had a huge number on stage particularly the ladies chorus. All of these ladies were immaculately dressed for the part and all had been well trained in their dancing by Lea Carol. There were nods to the Charleston era with twists and arm movements and I was impressed by the pictures formed during the choreography on stage. The 'show off' numbers for Velma had just the right amount of Vaudeville feel and the final sequence with the canes was well executed.

Some of the costumes were outstanding, for example the girls' white fringed dresses at the end of the show and of course the magnificent Razzle Dazzle costumes. Billy Flynn looked very smart in a well- cut dinner suit and black tie throughout the show and Amos had a nondescript colour of suit which was very in keeping with his character. The Cell Block ladies and the costumes worn by the rest of the female chorus had been devised by each person and I give them all great credit for the effort that they made, nice attention to detail ladies. It was a clever touch just to add a hat or a pair of glasses to make the costume change into a reporter. Of course, Velma and Roxie looked great throughout and Mama Morton's trouser suit gave her a standout look, especially with that basque underneath.

Hairs and make-up followed through the style of the era and although most people adapted their own hair rather than use wigs, they had gone to the effort of putting finger waves etc in to look the part.

The principal cast were well chosen and each player was well suited to their individual role. Heather Doyle looked wonderful as Velma Kelly and acted the part really well. From the spoilt b**** at the start of the show and then her act of desperation later in the show when she realised that she wasn't Queen Bee anymore. She moved well, she sang well with a real blasting musical theatre voice and her acting moments with Mama Morton and Roxie were nicely judged. Roxie played by Kori Kilduff took us on a real journey through murder, prison, pregnancy, acquittal and finally to Vaudeville. Kori played the part of the feisty Roxie with ease and I was impressed by her singing and movement particularly in the number 'Roxie' which to me was one of the highlights of the show. Both Roxie and Velma gave us a great finishing number to the show with marvellous energy in 'Nowadays'. The two killer dillers worked together well as sworn enemies and also as an unlikely partnership, well done.

Petrova Mulvey gave a strong performance as Matron Mama Morton. I particularly liked her rendition of 'When You're Good To Mama'. She acted the conniving, money grabbing prison wardress very well.

Billy Flynn was played by dashingly handsome Kieran Kilduff who gave us quite a gentlemanly performance as Billy. He looked very smart in his dinner suit throughout the show and he moved around the stage with great presence. His singing was excellent and the way he finished some of the musical numbers was quite outstanding, especially that huge long note that he held at the end of his first number. Mr Cellophane himself, Amos was played by Joe Steiner. This was a very sensitive interpretation of the role for which he earned great sympathy from the audience. His 'Mr Cellophane' number was delivered really well and his scenes with Billy Flynn were well played, giving us some nice moments of humour.

Mary Sunshine was played by Edel Moriarty. I have seen quite a few shows recently where this character was played by a woman which is fine but the line 'things are not always what they seem' always feel a little bit flat. Not in this production as when it came to that point Edel took off her coat to reveal that underneath she was dressed the same way as the prison girls with basque, suspenders and fishnet stockings. I felt that this made sense and worked really well in the show. Edel sang her 'Little Bit of Good' very well with a lovely tone to her singing voice. She also focused us onto the action at times, was a good foil for Billy Flynn and pushed the story-telling along too. Tomás Glynn was the Announcer/MC. He introduced the first number while playing the grand piano which was a nice touch, then appeared throughout the show with great style and polish, announcing the next scene.

As I have said before, the chorus of very many women and some men worked really hard throughout the show and added so much to the success of it. The Cell Block Murderesses played by Amy Kelly, Laura Hannon, Róisín Carey, Sarah- Jane Mangan and Cherise O'Moore did a brilliant rendition of the 'Cell Block Tango' with great energy and forcefulness in their delivery.

The properties used in the show all looked of the right period for example Billy Flynn's desk was covered in the correct bits and pieces of a successful lawyer of the time even down to the paper of the time.

I was delighted to be asked to attend Athlone Musical Society's production of Chicago. It was a slick, well-rehearsed and fun evening of entertainment. The attention to detail throughout the show starting from the decoration on the outside of the building through to the last minute of the production was incredible and much appreciated. Thank you for making me feel so welcome and particularly to Michael who looked after me all night and even walked me to my car.

Cabaret is one of the most thought- provoking musicals. Set against the decadent lifestyle of the inhabitants of the Kit Kat Club the piece shows how the good doing nothing helped accept the growth of Nazism. How friends were turned against each other, families shattered and lovers separated. It was the worst possible of times for Jews, homosexuals, travelling community and anyone Hitler saw as a threat. At first huge graves were dug and the naked and kneeling prisoners were shot to fall in on top of all those bodies below. Then the 'Final Solution' of a conveyor belt system of genocide with the use of poisonous gas in what appeared to be showers. So, this time of horror should be very much in our mind as we watch this show. There should be moments when we are lulled into a false sense of security only to be shocked by either the acting or end of a musical number, such as 'If You Could See Her'.

Tim Vos directed this student only production at very short notice, only taking over the task of director in mid-January. I commend him for his efforts and I am sure there were many rehearsals late into the night as the cast seemed very at ease on the acting area throughout the show. It was performed with the audience sitting on three sides of a rectangle. This is a very difficult thing to direct and movements have to be well thought through to avoid the masking of characters for a prolonged period. This rarely happened in the show and this young cast moved quite naturally around the area on most occasions. The characters had been quite well thought through and the cast gave us some strong performances with some moving moments and good singing. I feel that overall the main theme of the show wasn't as pointed as it could have been and those spine-chilling moments such as the 'Reprise of Tomorrow Belongs To Me' fell a little flat. There was only one swastika arm band on stage, think of the impact if through that number each member of the chorus had revealed their armband and Emcee had unfurled two huge flags from the lighting gantry! That would have been the impact we needed. Also, there was a missed moment when Herr Schultz had the window of the fruit shop smashed. We needed a sound effect (dropping knives and forks into a biscuit tin off stage sounds realistic) and something visual, maybe a gobo of a smashed window against the back wall to really point the moment. The very talented cast I am sure would have been up to further challenges.

Aiden Fitzgerald gave us an eerie Emcee. Always observing the action and cleverly appearing in every scene pushing our attention on the scene. Sometimes he appeared on the lighting gantry, sometimes on a little platform stage right. Aiden related really well to the audience and his lead-ins to those big show numbers were nicely played. He moved well in the dance numbers such as 'Two Ladies' and his singing was strong throughout the show. We felt that he was very much in charge of the action and in a strange way I found the character he created endearing. The final exit should reflect the final exit of so many into the gas chambers, I am not sure this moment worked and a simpler final pose and blackout might have been better than the exit through a tricky doorway.

Sally Bowles was played with a wonderful thirties flourish by Aisling Crotty. I was pleased that she tried to create her own interpretation of Sally, rather than copy a version of what has gone before. I liked her appearance in the part with an untidy but in the style of the era wig and a couple of good costumes. She acted the part well and there were times when we could see the inner conflict of the character, for example when she aborted the child. Aisling has a powerful and emotional singing voice which was at its best in the title number. Cliff was gently played by Diarmuid Curtin. As the central character in the show we trace his journey to Berlin and some sort of enlightenment. He falls in love then Sally aborts his child and the harshness of real life under the regime kicks in. The fight scene with the two dancers turning on him was well played. Just watch a few wee nervous habits on stage as they could be distracting. Diarmuid sang well and his 'Perfectly Marvellous' number sounded good.

Fraulein Schneider was very sensitively played by Izzy Ronan. This is the older landlady of the boarding house who just wants to bury her head in the sand and make a living from her rooms. She does however fall in love with Jewish Herr Schultz who owns the greengrocers. This was a bitter sweet relationship, ill-fated by the regime and pressure of those around her to fail. Izzy sang and acted the part well creating the look, movements and tone of a woman in the last bloom of youth. 'It Couldn't Please Me More' or 'The Pineapple Song' as I call it was a gloriously touching moment of love between two older characters and 'What Would You Do?' was a magical moment. I think we needed to see a few more moments of self-doubt before she made her only decision to break off the engagement but overall a well-controlled performance. Joe Kerbey gave us a gentle portrayal of Herr Schultz. He didn't overplay the 'ever so humble' older man which can happen in this roll but he was most believable in the part. He managed to get the gentle comedy from 'The Pineapple Song' and 'Married' was emotionally sung.

Conor Birkett was a very straight-laced Ernst Ludwig. Working for the Nazi party, smuggling information from France we are instantly suspicious of him but he almost convinces us that it doesn't really matter. I would have liked a bit more chilling response to Cliff's protestations before he sets the guys on him to beat him up. The entertainer of the German fleet Fraulein Kost wears her heart on her sleeve in her dealings with all her cousins. This character and her relationship with her landlady pinpoints how the country became a 'if it doesn't affect us directly it doesn't matter' society. Katie O'Neill gave us some tension relieving moments of comedy in this role. She also led the singing at the party with great gusto. The chorus were busy through the show. They have a variety of big musical and dance numbers to perform which they did with great energy and commitment. Their choreography was designed by Erin Hayden and Gráinne Fleming. There were good changing patterns in the musical numbers with a feel of the period injected into some of the routines. 'Mein Liebe Herr' was traditionally staged in the Fosse style with the bentwood chairs and was nicely set and performed. Some of the duets and groups were well moved but a couple of times we just needed an edge more such as the little dance in 'It Couldn't Please Me More'. Overall very well done ladies. What did puzzle me was the very low volumes of the backing track. In this setting with very limited finances the use of a backing track is fine (though there is nothing like the energy and sound from a live band). The voices seemed at times very hollow and unsupported, with the result the cast didn't 'up their game' to sing with the music but at times one felt that they held back a bit. It was a nicely played track and the talent of the singers on stage was undeniable but the overall feel of the show was a little restrained. However, the body mics were all sounding great and the cueing was good.

The scene changes were in the form of pieces being brought on and off the stage area. This was very slickly done by a competent stage team. I had a few issues with the selection of the props used in the show which I have gone through in more detail in my private report. An experimental approach to this show is worth considering, having no props and just carefully miming their existence is a possibility. If it is really well done the audience will believe it.

The styling of the performers was quite effective. Emcee's make up was extraordinary and his costumes created a good effect. The other costumes created a nod to the period. I did love Fraulein Schneider's thick practical tights. The Kit Kat Club costumes were a good mix. I would have liked a pair of 'lacey pants' for Sally in 'Don't Tell Mama'. Make up and hair was in character in most cases and I particularly liked Sally's eye make-up. So overall a really strong cast and crew giving us a very earnest production of Cabaret. This is not the usual boy meets girl musical and there are many underlying themes which really take time to develop fully. Thank you all for having me to your show and please keep acting and singing when you leave university, we need your talent in the amateur theatre world.

Bryan Flynn, the creator of Michael Collins, was a most tenacious and talented man. He spent many years and worked with many other creatives to produce his magnum opus. The show focuses on the Civil War, and specifically Michael Collins, during and following the Easter Rising. Heavily influenced by Les Misérables and Evita in structure, with a play-within-a- play (Yeats' Cathleen Ni Houlihan) as an allegorical nucleus and four narrators; it's an intricate piece of theatre that requires a talented group of theatre makers to do it justice.

Thurles Musical Society took on the challenge of staging this iconic musical in March at the Premier Hall. The society has been in operation since the early fifties, when they burst onto the scene with a rake of Gilbert & Sullivan light operas and just last year, they staged Ragtime, which was awarded runner - up for Best Overall Show.

The society were lucky to have access to the hall for some weeks before opening night and used the time wisely to construct an elaborate and hugely impressive set, designed by Oliver Hurley and Tommy Sweeney. High platforms leading to Georgian houses out on the apron stage left and right and an upstage hydraulic platform, a flown in bridge, mobile steps and trucked in flats with a working downstage trap, it certainly looked dramatic and expensive. In the hall, posters and framed prints of Collins, de Valera et al, were affixed to the pillars and on the walls, which gave the audience a sense of the history of the era of the show.

Unfortunately, Keith Dwyer-Greene's passionate Michael Collins was suffering from throat issues on the night and this did mar his performance somewhat as he had the majority of the vocals in the show. Nonetheless, Mr. Dwyer-Greene's portrayal was spirited, and he really embodied the fearless but flawed Collins. His energy was especially palpable in his scenes with de Valera, here played with an assured confidence by Cathal O'Donoghue. As Dev, Mr O'Donoghue sang well on most of his numbers, but it was his characterisation of the cunning statesman that most impressed. His was a deeply nuanced portrayal, quite austere and cold natured in smaller groups yet dramatic and fervent during his oration scenes. Beautiful work from Mr O'Donoghue.

Collin's love interest, Kitty, was played with a wistful sensitivity by Marie-Therese Kirby. Her vocal matched her portrayal and was full of emotional intention, particularly when she sang the duet, 'Our Love Will Never End' with Collins. Ms Kirby's scenes with Collins were quite moving but her scenes with Harry Boland, the third player in this love triangle, were deliciously intense. Harry was played by John Hayes and whilst vocally he clearly struggled with some of the songs during the show, he sang 'Not that Man' and 'Fly the Flag' quite well. His performance was animated and earnest as he played the rejected suitor and betrayed friend with a fiery intent. Joe Emmet, a young acolyte of Collins, was played by Peter Donnelly. His performance was quite lively, and although his vocal was a little weak for some of the songs, he had a nice energy. The show is essentially about these five characters and their interactions against the backdrop of the Civil War. During the Treaty Debates, we were introduced to another two of Ireland's famous rebellious statesmen; Cathal Brugha and Arthur Griffith. As Brugha, Jonathan Gleeson was marvelous, his passionate speech and vocal was so excellent, it was a pity he was only on for a small amount of time. As Griffith, John Butler also gave a fine performance, feuding Brugha in the debates. The historically accurate love triangle between Harry, Kitty and Collins served to enrich their characters, but it is largely a political piece and really works best when alluding to the almost Machiavellian actions of the main characters, which director Oliver Hurley rightly focused on.

The entire show was narrated by four players, unseen by the main characters, who also acted in the Yeats play. In addition, we also had the personification of Éire in the form of Mother Ireland, played by Deirdre Hayes, who also was unseen by the main characters. Ms Hayes was a looming presence in the show, at times standing unmoving on an upstage platform at other times weaving in and out of the action. She had a great stillness and a fine Sean Nós voice. The four players were played by Nina Scott, Frank Tuohy, Linda Ryan and Damien Sweeney. All four were superb as the Abbey Players and really brought the Yeats play to life with solid characterisations. As the narrators they were ethereal and quite stealthy, we never knew where they were until they sang. Their singing was good too, and they had pleasant harmonies.

Musically directed by Mary Rose McNally, who also conducted with brio an excellent seven-piece band, the big choral songs sounded fabulous with well- defined harmonies and powerful voices. Choreography by director Oliver Hurley and dance captain Michelle O'Connell, was interesting. We had the contemporary represented in the five dancers who physicallised some of the conflict and then the traditional waltz in London where Collins went to sign the treaty and the syncopated movement of the ensemble in some scenes.

Lighting was by Gerry Taylor and his use of pars was great, going with an orange and green palette which was quite apt. Sound by Star Systems was superb, crisp and clear with plenty of bottom end for the explosions. Costumes by June Young were perfect for the era and I particularly liked the British Army costume and Collin's uniform. The show was stage managed by Tommy Sweeney and stage directed by Rita Dempsey. They did a wonderful job as the transitions were swift and accurate and the hydraulics well-timed.

Director Oliver Hurley did well to helm such a huge production, gathering all of the elements into a cohesive whole. The pace of the production was quite good and I think his interpretation was quite faithful to Mr Flynn's original concept. It was well-rehearsed and beautifully staged. Well done.

Viva Evita!

Claire Tighe directed this elegant production of one of Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice's finest collaborations for Teachers' Musical Society in Dublin City University's auditorium in early April this year. Teachers was established nineteen years ago, when a small group of primary school teachers decided to put on Fiddler On The Roof in DCU. Since then, they have staged many productions and won a plethora of awards from AIMS. The society has gone from strength to strength and now embraces teachers from primary, second and third levels in their annual production. This year they staged Evita with Dermot O'Callaghan as musical director, chorus master and conductor whilst Serena Salmon looked after all things choreographic.

Evita charts the rags-to-riches rise of the First Lady of Argentina, who won the hearts of the people after marrying soldier-turned-president Juan Perón. Set in Buenos Aires from the late 30s to the early 50s, the show follows Eva Duarte on her journey from rebellious teen to ambitious actress to the most powerful woman in Latin America and, eventually, to a saint-like figure after her death from cancer at age 33. The events in Evita's life are presented and contextualised by the show's cynical narrator, Ché, who is quite aggressively critical but does fall for her charms. It was initially rejected by Lloyd Webber when Tim Rice presented the concept, as he couldn't see anyone being interested. But Rice persisted and they eventually released it as a concept album in 1976 and a full production hit the West End in 1978 and Broadway a year later. Worldwide success followed and in 1996 Alan Parker directed a film adaptation starring Madonna and Antonio Banderas. It's a big sung-through musical with over twenty-five songs and it employs an eclectic range of styles; classical, choral, rhythmic Latin, ballads and rock where most of the singing is done by Eva and Ché. So, it was imperative that the casting on this show was as perfect as possible. Yasmine Missaoui played Eva Perón, her voice was certainly up to the task and her singing was most effective on the more ballad-like and slower songs, where we could hear the colourful tones and intonations of her vocal. The most famous song in the show, 'Don't Cry for Me Argentina' was beautifully performed as was 'I'd Be Surprisingly Good for You' with Perón. 'You Must Love Me' was hauntingly delicate and 'Eva's Last Broadcast' full of pathos and poignancy. Ms Missaoui's character's journey was finely charted and her acting was admirable. She had a Grace Kelly-like quality, a lovely stillness and presence, where every move was calculated and full of intention which captured the shrewd and conniving nature Eva Perón was said to have had.

Kevin Fagan embodied the part of Ché, the narrator, his delivery and timing was excellent. Mr Fagan's singing and recitative was clear, full of feeling and intention. On 'Oh What a Circus', he really captured the bitter-sweetness of Eva's funeral and played the comedy of 'Goodnight and Thank You' brilliantly. As the show's Greek Chorus, he was nicely subjective in his reporting, a wink and a shrug to the audience punctuating the text. Kevin Fagan had a great presence on stage, his energy and total immersion in the role was tangible.

As Juan Perón, Carthaigh Quill had wonderful gravitas and bearing for the role. He sang Perón sublimely, a rich-timbred baritone imbuing the songs with authority and power. 'On the Balcony of the Casa Rosada', which opened the second act really showed how Perón could command respect. The lighter number 'She Is a Diamond', showcased his timing and articulation. Mr Quill was a perfect casting choice for the part, he exuded presidential control and dominance but also a gentle devotion to his Eva.

Augustín Magaldi, Eva's first love who leads her to Buenos Aires, was played by Kevin Hartnett. He sang 'On This Night of a Thousand Stars' very well, and was great on 'Eva and Magaldi'. His scenes with Ché were very well timed and he definitely elicited empathy from the audience.

In the most underwritten role was Fiona Hiney as Perón's Mistress. She only had the one song, but it is a great song. 'Another Suitcase in Another Hall' was charmingly sung by Ms Hiney. She played her as a character with dignity and poise and these characteristics suffused her singing. The large ensemble, played many different characters from soldiers to peasants. Their singing was glorious on 'Requiem' and 'Montage' and powerful on 'Oh What A Circus' and 'A New Argentina'. They were clearly very well-rehearsed and had amazingly modulated choral voices and superb dance skills.

Serena Salmon's choreography was very commendable on the show. Her ' Buenos Aires' was full of life and colour, it was a great big production number worthy of the West End. On 'The Art of the Possible', there was some great chair work from the male ensemble, quite complicated but well performed.

Dermot O'Callaghan not only shaped the musical direction of the show but also conducted and was chorus master. His interpretation was uplifting, exciting and very faithful to the original. The music is a fusion of Latin American tangos, soft rock and lush symphonic ballads plus instrumental passages and underscores as the musical is sung-through. A marvellous tight band supported his work with the principals and ensemble who were excellent, wonderful harmonies and power.

The show was played out against a cleverly adaptable set, designed by Ben Hennessy, which consisted of large classical pillars that were moved around to create different locations. A balcony scene opened the second act, with the Perón's making a public appearance to the cheers of the crowd. Stirring stuff, with flags waving in slo-mo as the band launched into the opening strains of 'Don't Cry For Me Argentina'. Stage manager, Gerry McCann and his crew effortlessly moved these giant pillars around the stage, adding props and furniture to create new locations.

Lighting was designed by Denis Twomey, and was very sympathetic to the show. Everyone was very well lit throughout and he had a great range of colours, which complimented the costumes. 'Buenos Aires' was particularly vibrant, with the lights matching the rhythm of the music. Sound by Jason Fallon was near perfect, great big orchestral sound and clear vocals.

Eva's costumes were resplendent; haute couture, furs, elegant gowns all co-ordinated by Andrew Reddy. It was interesting that Ché, didn't wear army surplus as is often done, but I think it was the right choice. His costume was that of an ordinary man, as the writers suggested he was in later interviews, and not the revolutionary Ché Guevara. Make-up and hair was designed by Ali Murphy. Ché's facial hair was very distinctive and really set him apart from others at a glance. Eva's blonde wig was quite singular as was Magaldi's slicked-down look. The make-up was also quite distinctive on these characters, setting them apart from others.

Claire Tighe did a wonderful job on this perfectly cast show. Her vision was very precise and she certainly realised it on stage with the help of her talented creatives and performers. The pace of the show was very even and her staging was clever. It was a fine interpretation of this very difficult musical and the audience were emotionally wrung out at the end!

Something Good There's something charming about The Sound Of Music that lassos one's emotions and no matter how many times you see it, it still retains the power to captivate. St Agnes' Choral Society, under the assured direction of Laura Kerr, produced Rogers and Hammerstein's most famous collaboration in Belfast's Grand Opera House for six sold-out performances in late March of this year. St Agnes' Choral Society have been around since 1959 and have staged everything from The Mikado to the more contemporary 9 To 5 and Hairspray down through the years, winning many awards and accolades along the way. This is their second staging of The Sound Of Music, having produced it just six years ago. But that's the power of this show, once a society do it once, they feel compelled to do it again because it really is the perfect musical.

A young nun, Maria Rainer, leaves her convent and becomes the nanny for a widowed Austrian Captain, Georg Von Trapp, who has seven regimented children. She wins their hearts and eventually their father's as well. Meanwhile the Nazis are taking control of their homeland through their Anschluss programme of invasion. A tale of adventure based on fact with nuns and religion, a love story, cute motherless children, a beautiful score… and Nazis. What's not to like?

Well, very little as it turned out. This was a sumptuous, detailed production that grabbed us from its opening scene, an Austrian village complete with fountain and Nationalist Party members recruiting young people whilst the villagers went about their daily business all to the strains of Musical Director Colin Scott's wonderful arrangement of the overture. Mr Scott gave us a remarkable interpretation of the score, his choral work was particularly good, the strings were lavish and the brass and woodwind gorgeous. His pacing of the songs was just right and the show bounced along.

Maria, played by Michelle Hannaway portrayed the wide-eyed innocent very well and was quite boisterous with the children, which was a delight. Her scenes with Georg really worked and their relationship was very natural. Her singing was also first class; 'The Sound Of Music' was clear and full of elation, 'I Have Confidence' was feisty and her songs with the children were full of fun and gaiety, particularly 'My Favourite Things' and 'The Lonely Goatherd', where we were cleverly taken back to the village of the prologue.

Tony Young was a warm, fatherly Georg. His scenes with the children were so natural. When he first sang with them on 'The Sound of Music Reprise', there wasn't a dry eye in the house. He showed a lovely camaraderie with Max, his friend and his relationship with Elsa, his fiancé (until he met Maria that is) was quite believable. His scenes with Maria were also superb, his exasperation turning into love. Mr Young sang well with Maria on 'Something Good' but he brought the house down on 'Edelweiss' and had the audience joining in with him. A fine, considered performance that brought a freshness to the character I felt, an unconditional paternal love coupled with a fierce nationalism for his homeland. Michael McDowell was an avuncular Max, who was Georg's friend. He had a twinkle in his eye and his comic timing was spot on. I particularly enjoyed his scenes with Georg, they had a jocular relationship, clearly showing their intense friendship. He also sang well on 'How Can Love Survive?' and his compering of the concert was quite funny.

Lucy Williams played Elsa, the rejected fiancé as quite an emotional woman, cut throat and self-serving in business but very warm with Georg. When she made the decision to leave him, she projected a sadness bordering on bereavement, which was palpable. Her singing on 'How Can Love Survive?' with Max was good too.

As Georg's servants, Pat Smyth gave a good performance as the butler in this underwritten but important role. When, half way through the show he arrived wearing a Swastika armband, it was a shock for the audience. As Frau Schmidt, the housekeeper, Ditanya McKinty had a great dynamic with Frantz, her scene with Maria, where she was quite candid about the Captain was very truthful.

As Liesl, the oldest of Georg's children, Aideen Fox was great. Her voice on 'Sixteen Going on Seventeen' was full of fun and curiosity with a hint of innocent flirting. Her songs with her onstage siblings were controlled and she had a delightful relationship with them. She played the emotion of her devastation at Rolf's party leanings very convincingly too. As Rolf, Joshua Clarke played him with earnestness, his adherence to the Nazi ideal was very well played as was his scene in the Abbey towards the end. Whilst his voice was a tad eclipsed by Liesl's on 'Sixteen Going on Seventeen', he did have a lovely lilt to his singing. The other von Trapp children were very well rehearsed and drilled in their characters and their singing.

They were a joy to watch and I enjoyed their performances enormously. Each one had developed a very specific character and they interacted extremely well. Their singing blended beautifully and they did well to handle the quite tricky harmonies. As the Mother Abbess, who initially sends Maria to the Von Trapps to 'find herself', Fiona Keegan gave a wonderfully controlled performance, she projected warmth and understanding towards Maria and had a superb voice.
