His relationship with his love interest, Truly, was quite believable and they sang well together on the title song and on the 'Doll on A Music Box/Truly Scrumptious' number.

As Truly Scrumptious, Janna Foley was impressive. Her accent and diction were very BBC c.1950 and her singing was heavenly. Her eponymous song, 'Truly Scrumptious' with Jeremy and Jemima was delicate and they blended well together. 'Lovely, Lonely Man', her declaration of love for Potts simply soared powerfully around the theatre. Her robotic movement on 'Doll on a Music Box' was exceptionally well done as was her dance throughout. Ms Foley gave us quite a chipper and plucky Truly, who kept calm and carried on!

Jeremy and Jemima were played with a great controlled energy by David Lynch and Fiona O'Connor. Their singing was perfect on all of their numbers, especially 'Truly Scrumptious' and 'You Two' and they harmonised wonderfully on the title song and its' numerous reprises. They had a great onstage relationship with Potts and Truly and were a pleasure to watch. As Grandpa Potts, Tim Moran gave quite a relaxed performance. His Grandpa was not the normal loud brash colonial Sergeant Major type but more congenial, which worked in his scenes with Potts but not as much on the song 'Posh!' with Jeremy and Jemima. However, he was great with the inventors on 'The Roses of Success' where he became a lot more energised.

In Vulgaria, where all the baddies lived, we met the Baron and Baroness. As the Baron, Tim Landers played him as a big child. He sang well on 'Chu-Chi Face' but he never really came across as a serious bad guy, easily distracted by toys or sweets! The Baroness was played by Jackie O'Mahoney who portrayed her as quite a sensual despot. She struggled a bit vocally with 'The Bombie Samba' but danced it well. Strangely, a group of ladies in the audience whooped repeatedly whenever she entered, which was odd as it was a kid's show and it must have thrown her a bit, but she remained unruffled and ignored the catcalls.

The Baron and Baroness's henchmen, Boris and Goran were played with great comic timing by Marcus Nolan and Matthew Dineen. As a pair of incompetent spies tasked with kidnapping Caratacus Potts for the Baron so he could enslave him and force him to build him a car, they played it as a Vaudevillian double-act. Both sang 'Act English' very well and quite inventively appeared when we least expected them. Of course, they snatched the wrong Potts, attaching the outhouse where Grandpa was ensconced to a zeppelin and flying it to Vulgaria. Hence the rescue mission by his family and Truly. Also, in Vulgaria we met The Toymaker, who makes children's toys in his shop, not for children but for the Baron as children have been banished from the Kingdom. Played with a gentleness by Aaron Mclarnon, the Toymaker hid the children in the sewers of Vulgaria, away from the Baron and Baroness. Mr Mclarnon had a delicacy to his playing that really worked, and he sang well on 'Teamwork'. The other henchman of the Royal duo was The Child Catcher, a hideous long-nosed, black clad monster, played with lovely malice by Padraig Harrington. His scenes were quite scary, especially when he lured Jeremy and Jemima into a mobile cage to be taken away and imprisoned for the crime of being young.

The show started well with the children in the old car and the ensemble behind a gauze singing the 'Prologue' and the film and sound effects were very good here. However, once we opened out into Goggin's Garage and then into the Potts house the energy seemed to flag a bit and the pace was very slow. It did start to flow better once the restored Chitty arrived on the scene and picked up from there to the finish line.

The music in Chitty Chitty Bang Bang is quite good in places and musical director Aine Murray gave us some lovely arrangements of the score. Her work with the principals was excellent, particularly the children. Kudos must go to Choral Director, Laura Crowley for the fine harmonies in some of the songs, particularly the reprises of the title song, 'Teamwork' and 'The Roses of Success'. The orchestra impressed throughout, with super percussion and bass on 'The Bombie Samba' and gorgeous piano and violin on 'Hushabye Mountain'.

Mr Hurley's choreography was also quite inventive, I liked the South American dances on 'The Bombie Samba' which were very tight and filled the stage with movement and colour. Truly's doll-like movement was very well directed and executed and the children in 'Teamwork' were perfectly drilled. 'Me Ol'Bamboo' was also good, frenetic and accurately achieved.

Polymath, Mr Hurley also designed the set, which was excellently rendered and utilised. It was quite an industrial/ steampunk design with cogs and gears on the pros framing the action on the stage. Potts' inventions were also quite quirky, and he made great use of projections. The props were all good too, Truly's bike was very realistic and I liked the house set. But the star of the show was the Chitty car, which the society built themselves. It drove around the stage, apparently floated and when it rose up and banked it really looked like it was flying. Costumes were designed and created locally too by a large team and looked great, the 'Toot Sweet' costumes were colourful and bright and the Vulgarian traditional costumes looked quite Austrian, which was perfect for the Teutonic state. The Child Catcher's layered look added to his menace. Make- up and hair were looked after by Emma Quirke Hair and Una Sheehy and was totally suitable for the era.

Lighting and Projection design was done by John Hurley and worked very well. Mr Hurley's use of colour and follow spots was fabulous and he lit the set equally as well as the cast. The projections were of high quality, were sharp, bright and cleverly designed. Sound by Murt Whelan was suitably loud and sharp and the sound effects by Nicola O'Flynn were of good quality and very well cued. Stage manager, Des Hurley kept everyone and everything in line and his transitions were smooth.

This was a great show by Oliver Hurley and Tralee Musical Society, there was lots of colour, great sets, good acting, super singing and it really delivered the magic for the children and their adults and we truly did believe that that car actually flew!

Why do we love going to the theatre and why do we love musical comedies? Escapism, for a few hours the mundane is forgotten and we get transported off into a different world. We meet new friends and see their struggles, celebrate their successes. This was definitely the fact when I went to see the phoenix arise from the ashes in Carlow. This was the first full length musical to be performed by the town in over twenty years. A huge effort had gone into making this show the joyous night out it surely was. Well done to the enthusiastic team who worked so hard to re-establish this form of entertainment in Carlow.

The centre for Contemporary Art and George Bernard Shaw Theatre certainly lives up to the grandeur of its name. This is striking modern building in the midst of striking ancient buildings so was the perfect location for Striking Productions to perform the show.

The set was cleverly designed with a raised area at the back of the stage accessed on either side by a set of steps. This was used well through the show, particularly by the nuns. There were flats of stained glass on each side and some realistically painted stonework. A huge circular window dominated the back wall with two other arched windows which unfortunately didn't let light shine through. The props brought on added to the scenes. Changes were usually pretty slick and didn't interrupt the flow too much. Lighting created some very pleasing effects though a set of moving lights, such as at the start of the show, benefits from having a steady beam on faces as we lose focus. I hope the glitterball worked better later in the week as it is such a magical moment in the script.

Under the raised area at stage level was the quite large orchestra who were facing towards Musical Director Joan Butler located stage left. This very much in the central location didn't actually detract from the unravelling story as I thought it might. Joan led the players very well creating a lively and interesting accompaniment. This of course is a great sing for the ladies in a company with not quite as much for the men. What a great sing it was too with a wonderful leading player Deloris, Kayla Kehoe. Her voice really just soared. It had that wee bit extra too, that ability to touch and move you. The nuns all sang well in their individual roles and collectively they were great. Of course, 'Raise Your Voice' was a real showstopper! The men tried very hard to compete. The accompaniment was just that and never overwhelmed the singers on stage. Good idea to have some off- stage voices which gave a depth to some of the numbers. I also liked the fact that the nuns appeared in a dream like manner on the raised area when Deloris is tormented as to pursue stardom or friendship and love in 'Fabulous Baby reprise', as this punched their voices out at the same level as the dancers. The sound team balanced the instruments with the voices to create a harmonious whole.

The show was directed and choreographed by Robert O'Neill who should be very proud of all he achieved for the company. Dialogue was generally good with plenty of humour brought out of the script. The pace was sound on the whole, though a couple of the characters seemed a little nervous and the odd line was fluffed which added a hiccup. There were some pleasant groupings of cast especially the nuns who appeared nicely grouped when practising their singing. One thing I loved was that each of the nuns seemed to have very much their own wee character. This really made the show come to life for me. The men's characters were quite good though I am afraid the talent around them did outshine.

The main dance routines were quite well set and the choreography on the whole was well synchronised. Michelle McMahon and Tracey Rea gave the show an authentic and energetic start as the two backing singers. The boys did a good job with 'Lady in The Long Black Dress'. There were a few numbers which were using the upper body only without moving position on stage. These worked quite well with good movements of arms. Others used changing stage patterns and were much more interesting for the eye. This show must have a strong Deloris. Kayla Kehoe acted and sang this role brilliantly. She has that ability to affect you. We could see what the character was thinking rather just have someone deliver lines very well. Her singing was stunning, exciting and touching. She delivered the comedy lines with a great sense of comic timing. This was a very real and genuine Deloris. Can I take this opportunity to wish Audrey Cooper who played Mother Superior a speedy recovery. I believe that she took ill later in the run and at very short notice Sarah Brennan stepped into the part with no rehearsal. Sarah you are a star for doing that, I am sure the society will be singing your praises for years to come, another AIMS hero. Audrey did a great job as the strong and unshakable Mother Superior. Her diction was great both with dialogue and when singing. She gave us a heartfelt 'Here Within These Walls'. It was great to see the reconciliation with Deloris and her acceptance of change, well a little change. Get well soon Audrey.

Curtis had the 1970/80 attitude and appearance in those wonderful suits. This was Riccardo Tavolieri's first acting part and he made a good first effort. I am sure he learned a lot from the experience. Barry Harmon was kind and good-natured Eddie. He seemed a bit nervous initially but began to settle into the role as the show continued.

Sr Mary Patrick was brought to life by Cathriona Kelly. She glowed with the joy of life and brought a huge energy to the scenes she was in. Nicely sung too. Sr Mary Robert was played by Siobhán Kavanagh, the postulant who has been virtually reared in the convent. This was a moving portrayal. 'The Life I Never Led' was sung with emotion. Mary O'Driscoll was the edgy Sr Mary Lazarus. A hugely entertaining and funny portrayal. Sr Mary Martin of Tours was hugely funny as the eccentric who came out with thoughts out of the blue, as played by Aoife Doyle. Ursula Hayden created a wonderfully crotchety Sr Mary Theresa.

Paddy Behan you are one of Ireland's treasures. This is a man who is so at ease on stage. His acting makes it look easy, which it isn't. We totally believed in him as the Monsignor O'Hara. His 'getting down' delivery of lines was hilarious. The gang comprised: TJ played by Seán Óg Ferry, Joey (Scott Cooper) and Jack Lawlor as Pablo. This is probably the youngest group in these parts I have seen. They worked together well and had a great rapport. The dressing up as nuns followed by that Brian Rix farce (younger readers - Google it!) moment of the chase was hilarious.

The nuns' habits looked smart. The 'outside' clothes indicated the era very well. Those purple boots were great. I loved Curtis' clothes; I hate to admit it but they are what I would have worn back in the day! The cream suit looked marvellous. The bar clothes looked good. The nuns' sparkly accessories such as the tabards added glitter to the occasion.

I loved Deloris' eye make-up sparkly and different from everyone else. Some of the nuns who doubled up roles might have needed less make-up around the eyes. This was a great wee show with the story well told. There were wonderful moments of singing, comedy and movement. I hope this will be the first of many more shows to come. I would advise the company to keep reading 'Show Times' as there are ideas for new shows and even older shows revived. This is a great theatrical community which helps each other out so that we all benefit, as was proved recently to this company at a time of need. I wish them continued success.

The 1957 musical which was made into a movie in 1961 is to get a new lease of life as Stephen Spielberg will be directing a new version of this classic. The magical score by Leonard Bernstein and words by Stephen Sondheim give this modern interpretation of the Romeo and Juliet story an edgy view of post war urban life. This is a very dramatic and at times violent show which has many themes of intolerance and prejudice which I hope this young cast never have to face in their lives. So, it is quite a challenge to take on this difficult show. It must be moved well and some of the songs need to be quite operatically sung. St Patrick's Hall Musical Society rose well to this challenge and gave us a dramatic and moving version. As I entered the hall, I was impressed by the wonderful set created by John McGuinness. On either side of the stage were two pretty solid looking buildings which were wrapped in scaffolding. A ladder gave access from stage level to what would be the balcony in the love scene. Cleverly hidden behind the blinds on one side was the orchestra and on the other the drummer. Each building had graffiti of the relevant gang, meaning that the stage in between became the battle ground. The addition of the wire fence upstage gave the hemmed in, trapped nature of these young people's plight. The lighting added much to the feel of the piece with an intricate lighting plot. The back cyc was flooded with an array of colours during the show. There were sharp 'specials' which really pinpointed the action. Throughout the production the lighting was used to enhance the production. I would however have liked a more night-time feel for the dance scene which was a bit too bright.

The show was confidently directed by Leah McCay. The pace was steady though a few scene changes did pause the rhythm. She had obviously put in a lot of work with each group as there was a unity between each gang member. I would have liked to see a bit more individual characterisations shining through. Some of the cast had really thought who they were as an individual and they appeared very real on stage. In most scenes the positioning of the cast worked well. I would advise that unless for dramatic effect cast shouldn't be forced to look upstage to talk as it weakens their position. The scene in Doc's with Anita was uncomfortable to watch as it should have been. This is a particularly difficult scene. Well done for hiding the action and leaving our minds to do the rest.

Ryan Quinn was Musical Director. He had assembled an orchestra of fourteen players to bring us this glorious score. This was a beautiful sound which had great depth. With this score we can't have half measures and indeed we didn't here. I was impressed by the welling of huge orchestral sound and the delicacy of some other moments. Of course MK Audio gave us a well-balanced sound throughout. A delightful range of beautifully sung moments, especially 'Somewhere'.

The choreography plot was brought to us by Emmet Stewart. This was an energetic and demanding set of dance routines which very much paid homage to some of the moves in the original movie. There were many innovative movements added which though challenging, the young cast carried off very well. There was real athleticism from the boys and elegance from the girls. There were some good lifts, but this is something I think could be developed further. The clever, comic story-telling in 'Officer Krupke' worked brilliantly and was a real highlight of the show.

The ill-fated lovers were played by Shane Farrell as Tony and Niamh Long as Maria. Shane looked well in the role and sang those memorable songs with a beautiful tone to his singing voice. He moved around the stage well and created a very real character. Niamh gave us a very emotional Maria. She showed the joy of love and the devastation of loss. She sang really well and her duets with Tony were heavenly. Shonagh Forbes gave a strong and feisty Anita. I loved her rendition of 'America' but she really blew us away with her singing of 'A Boy Like That'. As I said earlier, she handled that disturbing scene in the Drug Store really well. Jamie Lee Gallagher was Riff. This was played in a very sincere and realistic way which worked well. The fight scene was quite convincing. He had great energy on stage which set him up as the gang leader. Bernardo was played by Ryan McGinn. He stood out as being a bit more worldly wise that the others. The accent was well maintained through the show. I really liked how much commitment Cahir O'Neill gave to his role of Action. We could see the emotional damage which had been done to the character and how this manifested itself in violent outbursts.

Matthew McLaughlin was an involved A-Rab. Diesel was played well by Mark McLaughlin. Roisin Moore was great as Anybodys who was always trying to get into the gang. Her denial of Anita when she was being attacked was quite disturbing.

This core cast were really well supported by a great team of other actors and dancers, too numerous to mention here. Suffice to say this was very much a team effort and each part of the team did a great job. The more mature members of the cast added a depth to the feel of the show. Andrew McDaid was a forceful Lt Shrank who showed us his frustration with the kids. Officer Krupke was given the right amount of incompetence by Marty McGurk. Doc was nicely portrayed by Joe Harley and Mary Claire McDaid was a frustrated Glad Hand at the dance in the gym.

The show was well costumed with a differentiation made between the two groups, particularly in the girls' dresses. All looked right for the period though some of the footwear wasn't appropriate which was a shame. The men's jeans were a good shape and t-shirts were correct. The girls' hair was mostly a styling of their own hair with a few wigs. Some of these looked realistic while the blonde one looked very artificial. Long hair on the boys would have been rare but a touch more Brylcreem would have helped unify the look a bit more. Make-up looked quite natural with nicely outlined girls' eyes. Properties were few but they were in good condition and mostly added to the feel of the show. The dummies in the shop were good though if they had been on casters it might have made them less awkward to move into place and return them afterwards. More stage dressing for the dance might have helped create the atmosphere.

The audience really loved St Patrick's Hall Musical Society's West Side Story. I was speaking to one lady who had returned to see the show several times. There is such a positive buzz about this group which comes from a wonderful, driven core of committee and producers. The young people in this show had a superb opportunity to take part in one of the world's greatest musicals supported by a fantastic team. Well done everyone.

Heaven Can Wait Andrew Lloyd Webber's Whistle Down The Wind, directed by Simon Pyper, was staged by St Patrick's Choral Society in the Great Hall theatre space in Downshire Hospital, Downpatrick in March this year for four performances. The Society was founded in 1962 and has been consistently producing stage works since then, garnering many AIMS awards in the process.

The venue was a first visit for me and it was quite a historic building with an interesting history. Founded in 1869, it was previously called Down County Mental Hospital and frequently housed over a thousand patients. The auditorium, boasting an original vaulted ceiling, was originally the dining hall of the hospital and the building has all been sympathetically renovated. A raised platform stage with very little wing space was at one end of the hall, draped with red tabs. A raised seating bank took up most of the room with some floor level seating in front of the stage. The band were lined up across the front of the stage.

Whistle Down The Wind was written by Lloyd Webber and Jim Steinman with additional book by Patricia Knop and Gale Edwards, in 1998 and is based on the 1961 film starring Hayley Mills which in turn, was based on the novel of the same title written in 1959 by Mills' mother Mary Hayley Bell and set in rural Lancashire. The musical setting had been moved from England to rural Louisiana in 1959. Three sisters; Swallow, Brat and Poor Baby who have just lost their mother, discover a man in their barn. He is injured and before he passes out, they ask his name: 'Jesus Christ' he says, and they believe him and so decide to hide him. In fact, he is an escaped prisoner, convicted of killing his wife. Swallow wants him to be Jesus in the hope he can bring her dead mother back to life and together with many of the local children, secretly feed and care for him. But a secret shared is a secret revealed, especially in small towns and a mob gathers to capture the man.

A tale of children's innocent faith is contrasted with the evils of the world in this well-directed production by Simon Pyper. Featuring a cast of some adults and many children, there was a lovely energy on stage with finely honed musical direction by Matthew Campbell and supportive choreography by Alex McFarlane.

The structure of the show is a bit odd in that the 'Overture' is played after the first song, 'The Vaults Of Heaven', which was sung by almost the entire cast and set in the Town Church. Lloyd Webber's score is a bit of a challenge for a musical director as it veers between opera, rock, Country & Western and pop with a bit of Christian folk music thrown in. Musical Director Matthew Campbell did well to somehow wrangle the disparate tunes into a cohesive whole. His choral work with the ensemble was fine on 'Vaults Of Heaven' and 'No Matter What' at the end of the first act.

The Children's ensemble were great, with some fine voices on display. Their timing and harmonies were well-rehearsed and quite strong. They seemed to rejoice in singing 'When Children Rule The World' and 'No Matter What' as they shone out with brightness during these numbers. Individually, the three sisters were good too with Swallow taking the lead in most of their numbers.

Talented fifteen year old Olivia Davidson (pictured above)  sang Swallow quite well. Her voice had a purity and a power quite striking for one so young. She controlled the jaunty 'I Never Get What I Pray For' with her siblings well and her duets with The Man, 'If Only' and 'Try Not To Be Afraid' were powerful. 'Nature Of The Beast' also with The Man, was emotionally compelling. Swallow is quite a difficult character to play as she is written as fourteen or fifteen but yet has the gullibility of a nine or ten year old. To make sense of this anomaly, Ms Davidson and the director managed to highlight Swallow's grief over the loss of her mother and grasped at the slight chance that The Man actually was 'Jesus' and that he would resurrect her mother. Swallow's relationship with Brat and Poor Baby was nicely defined, despite their physical differences and she had a strong chemistry with The Man. Their relationship was quite complex, she became his disciple but yet the relationship often veered into romance but she played this internal conflict extremely well. Ms Davidson gave an exquisite performance in this show. Ellen Taylor's Brat, the middle sister, was perfectly performed. Ms Taylor had a lovely gentle quality to her performance and she had a very strong presence on stage. She also had a beautiful voice which she used delicately and skilfully. Olivia Pyper's Poor Baby, the youngest sister, was delightful in her tomboyish characterisation and her comic timing was superb. Her voice was full of mischief and sass, befitting her character. As The Man, Sean Harkin handled the songs with ease being a Lloyd Webber veteran. He paced 'Annie Christmas' well and his songs with Swallow were strong, particularly 'Nature Of The Beast'. He played the character's desperation at being trapped through injury effectively. When he was mistaken for Jesus by Swallow and revered by the children, he initially played along in order to remain hidden and to get food. But Mr Harkin's Man gradually became chastened by the innocence and devotion of the children and by Swallow in particular. He convincingly showed The Man's anguish at being cornered and his volatility but yet we never believed that the children were in danger from him. A fine performance. Matthew Campbell's Amos was quite a hideously mixed up character. He perversely hankered after under-age Swallow yet was aiming to elope with the more mature Candy. Mr Campbell's portrayal was good, he had great energy and projected that James Dean bad boy image very well. He sang 'Tire Tracks and Broken Hearts' with Candy, played by Naomi Smyth and their voices blended well together. He also sang with The Man and Swallow on 'A Kiss is a Terrible Thing to Waste', all three sang powerfully on this rather melodramatic number. Naomi Smyth's character, Candy was the one character that stood out in the town in that she had ambition and was prepared to do anything to follow her dreams. Spurned by Amos, her boyfriend, she turned Judas and vengefully told the secret. Ms Smyth played her very well, her physicality and stage presence was perfect for the role. She had a fabulous voice on 'Off Ramp Exit To Paradise' and was impressive and emotionally connected to all she sang. The girl's Father, Boone was played by Niall McLean. He sang 'It Just Doesn't Get Any Better Than This' and the title track and its Reprise with emotion. He pitched the character as an ordinary man, trying to be mother and father to his three children, he developed a believable relationship with the girls and his home- spun philosophy was endearing. James O'Neill's Ed, sang 'Cold' with good ol' boy, country and western charm and was quite amusing. Andrew Devonshire's bullying Sheriff and Vijay Sharma's Earl were well-conceived but Tomás Harkin's Snake Preacher was at times quite scary, wrangling with the real snakes. They all contributed expressive vocals to the production, particularly Mr Harkin.

There was an impressive cohesion between all of the performers on stage in this show and they all looked like they belonged in the world created by the writers and the director. Choreographer Alex McFarlane, devised some interesting stage pictures, particularly when the ensemble were all on stage. The opening song 'The Vaults Of Heaven' was nicely moved although it had to be all upper body as it was big ensemble on a small stage. Set Design was by Danny Doherty and worked quite well. A platform was installed upstage that was cleverly used for a variety of locations; a bridge, a railway track etc. But the main set was the Barn with doors trucked in from stage left and right to enclose the playing area. There was some projection on the cyc; the moon, a sunset, a road etc., which added depth to the world. Lighting by Danny Doherty with Kathryn- Anne Simpson, utilised earthy colours and a subtle follow-spot. Sandy McCallister designed the sound and did a pretty good job except that the underscore was too loud at times so we couldn't hear some of the dialogue. This happened early on in the show and it did improve considerably as the production progressed. Cathal McKervey did a great job in managing this production as there was no wing space and the performers had to be sequestered elsewhere when not on. Alex McFarlane's costumes mostly adhered to a muted colour palette and make-up and hair styles were of the era.

The production was well-paced by director Simon Pyper and his interpretation of the book and music was quite faithful. Whilst I don't feel he brought anything new to the material, he did highlight the provincialism and pragmatism of adults and the innocent faith of the children. Mr Pyper's staging of the production was quite clever as it was a big show on a small stage with limited facilities.

Easter Camp Oliver!

Sean Gilligan Performing Arts presented a production of Lionel Bart's Oliver! at the end of April. The show involved adult actors alongside a large cast of children at the Helix in Dublin's DCU. Directed by Brian and Sean Gilligan with choreography by Aoibheann Cooke and musical direction by Sean Gilligan, this was a unusual version of Oliver! , which strayed into pantomime territory at times. However, the choreography and musical direction were good as were some of the performances.

Lionel Bart's musical is based on Dicken's Oliver Twist , a novel published in serial form from 1837-39 about the trials and tribulations of an orphan boy growing up in Victorian London. The musical premiered in 1960 and went on to be adapted into a very successful film in 1968, directed by Carol Reid, which won six Academy Awards.

Oliver, a malnourished orphan in a workhouse, becomes the apprentice of an undertaker, who he beats up for insulting his late mother. Oliver escapes and meets Dodger, a young pickpocket who lives with a group of thieving children under the care of old Fagin, a fence for stolen goods. When Oliver is captured for a theft that he did not commit, the victim, Mr Brownlow takes him in. Fearing for his livelihood if Oliver talks, Fagin employs the malevolent Bill Sykes and his girlfriend Nancy to get him back, however things don't go according to plan; Sykes kills Nancy and is in turn shot by the police and Oliver is returned to Brownlow, who through a series of 'Dickensian' coincidences, happens to be his Grandfather. Fagin and Dodger flee together and most likely set up business in another Borough.

The show opened on a bare stage, but for four big tables and a cyc screen on which was projected the programme image of the word Oliver against a cloudy sky. Eventually about forty dirty-faced children entered all dressed in very clean tunics and trousers and nice shoes. In the middle of these was Oliver. It was dinner time in the orphanage and the children lined up with shiny metal bowls to get gruel, whilst singing 'Food, Glorious Food'. Oliver had the temerity to ask for more and was ridiculed by his peers and the orphanage management, Mr Bumble and the Widow Corney, who decided to sell him. So began the story of Oliver Twist and although it was a big opening, it was all a bit sterile and clean for a Victorian Workhouse, but the singing was great on 'Food, Glorious Food' and on 'Oliver' by the children's ensemble.

Mr Bumble was played by Brian Gilligan with a quiet confidence. His Bumble was cruel and pompous, full of his own importance, yet totally dominated by the Widow Corney, whom he marries during the show. He sang 'I Shall Scream' with the widow quite well in a wonderfully directed 'mating ritual' scene. 'Boy for Sale' was also well-performed as he tried to sell Oliver on the streets of London. The Widow Corney was also well played by Emma O'Donohoe and she performed 'I Shall Scream' with Bumble hilariously. Their scenes were a highlight of the show, they had a very good chemistry and great comic timing together.

Oliver was played by Fionn Vigors, who had a lovely unbroken voice. He sang 'Where is Love?' very well and on 'I'd do Anything' with Dodger and Fagin's gang. Fionn also further demonstrated his vocal prowess on 'Who will Buy?' with the vendors and sellers set up outside Brownlow's house. He was befriended by Dodger, played by Michael Corr on the production I attended. Michael had a super Cockney accent and a great energy in the role. He sang wonderfully on 'Consider Yourself' and 'I'd Do Anything' and with Fagin on 'Be Back Soon', he also danced very well on the many dance numbers involving Fagin's gang that accompanied these numbers.

Fagin was played by Conor Clear, dressed in a long green coat with long grey hair and he certainly looked the part. His singing was accomplished as was his accent. On 'You've Got to Pick a Pocket or Two', a huge number involving all of the gang, he excelled and really sold the song; on 'Be Back Soon', another big number, he demonstrated a fine voice and some good footwork. His scenes with Bill Sykes (James Deegan) and Nancy (Shona Carroll) were quite successful and he fully engaged with them and played the scenes naturalistically. The song 'Reviewing the Situation', Fagin's solo in Act Two, became a little pantomimic as Mr Clear went out of character and interacted with the Musical Director and the audience. But he sang it very well and recapped the entire show up to that point, which was very funny.

Bill Sykes is one of Dicken's most famous bad guys and here he was played with menace by James Deegan. Mr Deegan gave an excellent performance as the malevolent miscreant. He prowled the stage like a caged lion, scowling at everyone and being beastly to his lover, Nancy. Mr Deegan showed a wonderful inner tension in the role and was captivating to watch.

Shona Carroll played Nancy as a grown- up street urchin, not far removed in age from Dodger and the other children, she still had the spark of youth but yet showed the ravages of experience. Her singing was beautifully emotive on 'As Long as He Needs Me' and rousing on 'Oom-Pah-Pah'. Ms Carroll had a superb stage presence and was successful in showing the maternal side of Nancy with the children as well as playing the fear of Sykes and, at times, the lightness of her character. A multi-layered performance of some skill.

Musical direction by Sean Gilligan was rather good. He created some great arrangements of the score with a relatively small band. The ensemble voices were very clear and powerful and quite harmonious at times. The smaller choruses were also quite good, particularly the street vendors on 'Who Will Buy' with Oliver. Some of the band's work was exceptional; I liked the synth on 'Boy for Sale' and the violin and piano on 'Where is Love'; the brass on 'Consider Yourself' and percussion and on-stage fiddle player on 'Oom-Pah-Pah'. Choreography was looked after by Aoibheann Cooke assisted by Rebekah Byrne. The choreographers did sterling work on this show. The scenes involving the children 'Food Glorious Food', 'Consider Yourself', 'Got to Pick a Pocket or Two' and 'Be Back Soon' were superbly directed and executed. 'Oom-Pah-Pah' was also well moved and used the whole stage, there was a nice use of the boxes and tables to give other levels and on 'Who Will Buy', the circus-style choreography at the top of the song was excellent.

Set, by Sean Gilligan, was quite simple as it had to be as there were so many performers! Printed drape legs, stage left and right and upstage framed a cyc for projections, a really well-made fireplace truck for the Bumble/Widow scene and simple furniture and a great bridge set for the final scenes and four street lamps. Lighting by Damien O'Connor was suitable for the show, LED pars on stage with a nice bright front of house wash and a follow spot. The lighting perches were also lit for the vendor scene. Sound by Derek Nangle was very full, voices were clear, and the band sounded well. Costumes by Sparkle Costume Hire worked well for the show, but everything looked too clean! Hair and make-up design by Ali Murphy, was suitable for the era and there were some great wigs on show. Sarah Hall wonderfully stage managed the show, the transitions and cast wrangling were super-efficient.

Overall it was a good show in parts, some scenes didn't interlock as well as they should and sometimes it seemed like a song cycle rather than a book musical, but there was some lovely choral work from the ensemble of children and adults. Nice work.

Little Shop of Surprises more like! This show rattled along with very gentle and authentic story-telling and then!!!……. more details later!

Portmarnock Musical and Dramatic Society performed their show in Malahide Community School. The hall doesn't have the glamour of some of the venues I have visited but there was a real buzz of expectancy from the Thursday night audience. OK the hall was a bit bright as there are no blackout blinds, maybe the acoustic is not the greatest but somehow as the story unravelled on stage those things paled into insignificance as we were carried into a different world.

The set comprised of three main pieces. There was a doorway and steps downstage right, a stairway stage left leading to a small balcony and rotating central piece which provided the interior and exterior of the flower shop. This had the window and door marked with the Mushnik name. There was a pull-down blind on the window which was used when the dentist was being fed to the plant, creating a fantastic moment with a change of lighting. There was a real city feel to the set aided by a smoky hazer. The only criticism I would have were the three wall panels which were brought on for the Dentist's initial entrance which seemed a bit awkward.

The Orchestra under the direction of Marian Mullen was set on floor level in front of the stage. There was a really rocky accompaniment of course with that wee 1960s twist. The final number was quite extra-ordinary but there were wonderful musical moments throughout the show. The four girls in the singing group did a great job. Each one of these ladies can really sing out this music individually but they sounded even better together with lovely touches of harmony. The chorus for the most part sang out though one or two did seem a little shy on stage. However, it was the line up of principals in this show that really set it apart. All had powerful and very tuneful voices. Not everyone is suited to this sort of music, this band of talented actors were in spades! Of course, I have a few favourite moments and 'Somewhere That's Green' is such a beautifully constructed song which was delivered fantastically by Danielle Williamson. I also loved 'Da-Doo', which the ladies sang so well. I could go on, as this was principal singing at its very best.

The show was joint directed and choreographed by Aisling Breen and Gavin Quigley. Not sure how that worked in rehearsals but the finished product worked well. The show had some moments I haven't seen before but which added so much to the story-telling. The addition of the young Seymour was a great bit of character-building so we could see his back story. The characters were thought through and what impressed me about the acting in this show was that we could actually see what the main players were thinking before they spoke. This was very considered direction and carefully executed delivery.

So, what was the surprise? It was of course the creation of Audrey 2. We had the first plant on the desk worked by someone under the desk, looked good. We had the second plant, a bigger pot held in Seymour's arms, looked fairly good too. Then imagine my disappointment when the fully-grown plant appears and to be honest looked like a leftover Christmas table decoration with spiky leaves jutting from it. Then up rose the creation of this man/woman/creature/plant. The idea was amazing but could have fallen flat if it had not been followed through fully and followed through it definitely was by the amazing Kevin Fagan. The movements he gave for the plant, which never ceased, remarkable. His stillness when not the focus of the scene. Just when we were getting used to him, the front of the plant base opened and out strode the plant in green glittery leotard, fishnets and impossibly high red platform boots. This was an image which blew us all away, that strutting aggressive Audrey 2. A similar idea had been used in Regents Park Open Air Theatre last summer but this pushed that idea on even further. Excellent moments of theatre. The choreography had been good up to that point, from then on it went to another dimension. Well done all.

The central cast really made this into a great show. As I said earlier, we had a quartet for the backing singers' group. Very much functioning as a group but individually excellent too. We had Louise Steele as Chiffon, Sinéad Walshe as Crystal, Orla Sheridan as Ronnette and Amy Taffee As Rachelle. They had all the right attitude and moves for the roles. This time their styling was of a more contemporary nature with camouflage trousers giving a city feel. The shop owner was beautifully played, so much so that I didn't actually recognise Ciarán Mooney as Mr Mushnik. Played very much in the Bronx, Jewish idiom Ciarán gave us a well-acted and moved role. Occasionally there are musical numbers in which we lose ourselves, when everything around us vanishes, (dear reader I hope you understand what I mean by that) I had one of those moments when Mushnik and Seymour sang and moved 'Mushnik and Son'. Sean McMahon gave us a freshness and huge energy as Seymour. He really added pace to his scenes. He used the acting areas extremely well. The songs were all perfectly in his range and he sang the duets well with Mushnik, Audrey and Audrey 2.

Audrey was brought to life by Danielle Williamson.

This was a delightful performance. We had just the right amount of dottiness, acceptance and charm in the role. Danielle is such an intelligent actor, as she was able to show us what she was thinking in the part, a rare gift. Some beautiful moments of singing too with a very passionate 'Suddenly Seymour'. Orin Scrivello, the Dentist was courtesy of Fergal D'Arcy. He gave a mad-cap edge to this demanding part. There were some great moments of comedy, especially when we were willing him to die and he kept rising back up again. He reappeared again as a whole variety of parts, so was kept busy after his stage death!

Now Kevin Fagan, that was quite astonishing. I always asked people to commit to a part or don't do it, by Jove you committed to the part for every second you were on stage. That crazy persona was never dropped. At one stage I looked to see the audience's reaction. Half of them were sitting opened mouthed as we had never seen anything quite like it before. Kevin acted from his very soul to the tips of those pointed leaf fingers. He is an astonishing physical specimen too which gave that wonderful juxtapositioning of pretty/ugly,male/female. The styling and make-up added to the finished look. And he can sing too! Well done Kevin.

The chorus gave a good vocal sound each time they were on and looked good as the poor in 'Skid Row'. Boy did they enjoy that last number when they could really let themselves go! The costumes throughout had a modern feel but interestingly they added a little touch of fluorescent yellow/ green which slightly gave a nod to the outer space origin of the plant. The principals were all appropriately dressed though a bit more girliness for Audrey would have worked. The black and green finale costumes were a wonderful and colourful surprise.

Audrey 2 had stunning make up and the rest of the cast looked consistent with well defined eyes. The four girls had great sparkle.

The central stage area which cleverly revolved to create different scenes was well presented with props. Good phones, plants etc and that bunch of $100 roses was hilarious. The spray can was a clever touch for the gas, though I am sure the front row were nearly knocked out by the smell of cheap deodorant!

The stage lighting created some good moments. I loved the way those shafts of brilliant white light were used. Some nice moods created with colours such as the demise of the Dentist with greens turning to red as the roller blind was lowered, we knew what was going on without having to see it. The sound balance was a little instrument heavy at the very beginning of the show but it settled quickly and we had a good rounded sound for the rest of the show.

So 'Surprise' is the operative word for this show. Some surprising effects, ideas, portrayals. Well done to everyone in Portmarnock Musical and Dramatic Society.

I was really intrigued to find out about Phoenix Performing Arts College, I had heard about the college but didn't realise that in fact it is a full-time college with students able to extend their learning right up to A Level. There are full time classes in Dance, Drama, Acting Through Song, English Literature, Business, German, Philosophy, Anatomy and Audition Technique. Of course, actual performance is a vital part of any young actor's training and to this end the group had chosen to perform the hilarious The Addams Family. The venue being the Liberty Hall Theatre on Eden Quay in Dublin which is a most interesting performance space in the heart of the city.

The auditorium of gently tiered seating is wide, as is the stage. The stage was open. Beside the small orchestra situated downstage right at floor level there was a set of steps leading onto the stage. This is a good-sized acting area. The staging for this production was very limited which was such a shame as the cast were working so hard in the actual show. I would suggest that stage management is one area which this group really do need to address, I am sure someone from other groups would be pleased to pass on their experiences to these young adults who are obviously so keen to learn.

Our cast were great. We had a happy go lucky Gomez as played by Nathan Everett Patterson. There were some good moments of comedy in this portrayal though occasionally the rich South American accent was just a little too rich and diction suffered. He sang well throughout the show. There was a very believable relationship between him and the ice cold Morticia played by Shelley Gibson Parkinson. Her willowy stature really added to the role and she seemed to glide from place to place. Her movements were wonderful with every gesture perfectly placed. Shelley demonstrated good timing with her delivery of comic lines giving many laughs along the way. There was an expressive tango with Gomez.

Inga Bourke Mullaney was Wednesday, the feisty daughter. She was dressed immaculately (as were all the cast actually - more later on costumes) and dominated the scenes in which she appeared. She seemed to get a bit too nice too soon and we missed the brother torturing character. Good delivery of lines Inga and well sung too. Her brother was Colin Redmond. I had the pleasure of sitting beside his father who rightly was very proud of his son. There is a real rock star voice in there bursting to come out. Acting wise, he very much underplayed the role which was a novel approach.

Wednesday's love interest Lucas was played by Darren Dixon. This can be a little bit of a thankless role as it is the straight man amid the chaos. Darren acted well and built good on-stage rapport with both Wednesday and his two equally mad parents. The role of Alice Beineke must be a joy to play as there is that wonderful 'Full Disclosure' scene. Georgia Gaffney did a great job in the role and brought howls of laughter from the audience. Husband Mal who has a great moment of self- rediscovery was portrayed by Ben Collins who looked and acted slightly older than the others on stage.

The other Addams Family members were Ross McHugh as Uncle Fester who didn't make the ultimate sacrifice of shaving his head as others playing the role have but had quite a good bald wig. The love affair with the moon was nicely acted. It took me a little while to realise that the beautiful ballet dancer (sorry I have no name for the dancer) represented the crescent moon. A lovely touch from Choreographer Mark Kennedy. We all loved Uncle Fester. Oisín Dunne managed to maintain the straight- faced character of Lurch right up to when he surprised us by singing at the end of the show. The Grandma was created by Jessica Conway McLoughlin. She appeared to be made of rubber as she bent herself into all sorts of contortions. This was a really off the wall wee character. All the cast were appropriately dressed. As I go around shows the same sets of costumes keep reappearing I notice, but the audiences wouldn't. However not in this show as these costumes were all tailormade for this cast. The ancestors in particular were simply stunning. All fitting perfectly. So inventive, so beautifully made. A triumph Therese Rooney and Stefanie Lynch. All the eras of the family's history were represented and made in a limited colour palette which worked brilliantly. Footwear was good too and I particularly loved Wednesday's bright yellow Doc Martens.

The show was directed and musically directed by Lauryn Gaffney. This is a huge amount for one person to do and if it was me, I would feel very under pressure. Generally, the direction of the acting and movement around the stage worked well though there were a few moments when cast were forced to talk upstage which is fine if it is done for effect but it just looked a bit awkward at times here. There were quite a few straight lines right across the stage which I would have broken up to create interesting groups. That being said the pace was mostly good and the characters were well constructed. The ancestors were used well as observers through the production.

The music sounded good from this limited orchestra and the singing was at times impressive. It would have been good to soften the scene change silences with just a little music. The first dance number 'When You're An Addams' was a fantastic start to the show with some very clever and well synchronised arm movements.

The choreography through the show courtesy of Mark Kennedy was interesting with ever changing patterns and a good use of the rhythms of the music and words sung. The tango with Gomez, Morticia and a few other couples was nicely handled.

Make up was fabulous. When I see the wonderful Ali Murphy's name on a programme, I know we are in for a treat and of course this show is the perfect vehicle for her talents. I am sure that the cast have learned much from this expert. The cast all looked wonderful.

Props were limited and maybe this is an area too which needs consideration in the future. I did love that wall at the start with the magic picture through which the finger clicking arm appeared.

Granny had a nice array of bottles in her trolley. I wanted to see more appropriate furniture such as chairs and tables of an older style.

One thing I must comment on is the announcement at the beginning of the show.  I have felt very strongly, coming from a teaching background, that there should be no photography of the show. It really spoils it for those sitting around, and under child protection legislation as was pointed out it is not legal. This was a strong message, beautifully spelled out, and no 'phones were out during the show. Thank you for this no-nonsense approach. In conclusion well done everyone who performed in this show, you all shone. I hope the staging in future shows is given more thought as it let down the overall look of what was good show, nicely acted, sung and danced.

A Malthusian Catastrophe 'Nothing can kill a show like too much exposition. Or bad subject matter. Or a bad title.' And with that admission from Officer Lockstock (Cian O'Dowd) and Little Sally (Jodie Moran), Urinetown was off and irreverently deconstructing the musical form at Newbridge College Theatre in April of this year. Produced by Newbridge Musical Society, as their thirty-ninth show, and directed by Sharon McNamara with musical direction by Dave McGauran and choreography by Julianne McNamara. This was a fast-paced romp which took pot-shots at capitalism, politics, the Malthusian trap and the very form that contained it - Musical Theatre. Set in a dystopian future where draught has crippled society, toilets have been privatised and everyone must pay to use the lavatory or risk being carted off to Urinetown, an ambiguous punishment that no one ever comes back from. This micro- cosmic world is run by the Urine Good Company (UGC), headed up by Caldwell B. Cladwell (Philip Emmett) a nasty corrupt capitalist. The story twists when an Assistant Public Amenity Custodian, Bobby Strong (Cormac Malone) organises a revolution at the inadvertent command of his new love Hope Cladwell (Keelin Kilduff), the daughter of the head of the UGC, that he follow his heart.

There was a great energy on stage from the ensemble and their singing, characters and dance was first-class. With a show like this, the director and cast must get the humour to apply it effectively, and director Sharon McNamara and the cast got it. Tongue in cheek all the way, the cast pushed the silliness to make the crazy concept of the show work. It's not as easy as it seems, but they made it look that way. The essence of every drama is conflict and here the battle was between the haves and have nots. The protagonist was reluctant hero, Booby Strong, played by Cormac Malone.

Mr Malone had a wonderful energy and a great grasp of his character. His singing was marvellous especially on 'Follow Your Heart' with Hope and on 'Run Freedom Run' where he conducted the ensemble in an a cappella section, much to the annoyance of the Musical Director, who threw the score at him! He expertly commanded the rousing 'Look at The Sky' and was very prominent in the 'Act One Finale'. Cormac Malone performed Bobby as a reluctant hero, who when his father is carted off to Urinetown, finally snaps and starts a revolution. His timing and 'heroic' posturing were very funny, and he had a great physicality for the role. His scenes with Hope were also quite sweet in a 'boy meets girl' kind of way.

Hope was played as a ditsy but principled character by Keelin Kilduff. Her comic timing was excellent, and she played her character's inner tension very well. Ms Kilduff sang beautifully on 'Follow Your Dreams' with Booby where she unwittingly encouraged him to rebel and on 'Mr Cladwell' her voice soared over the ensemble on her very funny lyrics. She demonstrated a fine contemporary voice on 'I See a River' where she sang ironically about unity and justice, as her character went from Cosette to Éponine.

Hope's father and the antagonist of this anti-musical, Caldwell B. Cladwell, was played by Philip Emmett with a competent assurance as he oozed menace and tried to squash the rebellion. He sang well on 'Don't Be the Bunny' an allegorical song about stepping on the little guy and on 'I'm Not Sorry' the unapologetic number where he duetted nicely with Ms Pennywise. A good performance from Mr Emmett. Cladwell's assistant, Mr McQueen was played by Rory Dignam with a cheerful but snide campness. His posture was great, with lovely little hand gestures and he sang well on 'Mr Cladwell' and 'Don't be the Bunny'. The corrupt Senator Fripp, who is in Cladwell's pocket, was portrayed as a cowardly, lascivious creep by Conor Kilduff, perving after Cladwell's daughter whilst dreaming of escaping to Rio with a bag of cash.

As Ms Pennywise, employee of the UGC who runs Public Amenity #9 and Bobby's boss, Helena Begley seized the character and made it her own. She had a fabulous voice and sang the tricky 'It's a Privilege to Pee' with great gusto and accuracy. On 'I'm not Sorry' with Cladwell, her vocal was gentle and imbued with loss. Ms Begley played Ms Pennywise with a repressed sensuality, clearly fancying Bobby and yet knowing she shouldn't, she was impressive.

The narrator of this Brechtian tale of greed was Officer Lockstock played brilliantly by Cian O'Dowd. He continually told us that this is a musical, and so anything goes, and any kind of emotional identification would be unwise. This turned out to be particularly the case with Lockstock himself, as later the genial officer/narrator turned out to be not what he seemed. Mr O'Dowd impressed with his timing and his song/dance scene 'Cop Song' was hilarious. His side-kick Officer Barrell was admirably played by Andrew Dancey, who seeped childish menace from every pore as he abused his position of power over the poor.

As the poor, a rag tag assortment of steampunk clad misfits, the ensemble was very focused. Little Sally, a waif-like urchin who constantly questioned the veracity of the show and irritated Lockstock by interrupting his narration. Superbly played by Jodie Moran with Harley Quinn styling, Ms Moran also sang well on the hilarious 'Tell Her I Love Her', with the mortally injured Bobby. Little Becky Two Shoes, an unhinged pregnant rebel was played by Clodagh Donnelly in a scary scenery chewing performance and Hot Blades Harry, a psychopathic rebel was played by Daniel Ryan who sang lead very well on 'Snuff that Girl' a pastiche straight out of West Side Story, complete with Sharks and Jets choreography. Emma Kilduff played Soupy Sue as a more well-adjusted character than the rest of the rebel poor, being quite gentle and she danced really well.

Choreography by Julianne McNamara shamelessly re-appropriated other musicals; the marching dance from Les Miserables on 'Look at the Sky', complete with giant red flag, the West Side Story homage on 'Snuff That Girl' and Cats, Oklahoma! and others. But it worked as the enjoyment of the show is partially dependant on the recognition factor. Musical Direction by Dave McGauran was great too, a small band in the style of The Threepenny Opera of multi-instrumentalists played his clever arrangements with aplomb. Mr McGauran's work with the ensemble was masterful, the chorus work on 'Look at the Sky', the 'Act One Finale', 'Why Did I Listen To That Man' and 'I See a River' was excellent and the a cappella section of 'Run Freedom, Run' was exquisite. Stage Management by Tom Kavanagh and his crew was sharp and the transitions quick. The quirky set was constructed by Darren Tierney and was quite simple, wooden clad walls and side flats with steps leading upstage to a tunnel like structure, detritus was liberally strewn around and made for convenient seats etc. It all looked suitably grimy and distressed. Costumes were co-ordinated and designed by Andrew Reddy, with the poor in rags and the rich in nice suits. Make-up was looked after by Kirstie Duggan, Robyn Campbell and Debbie Trundle and worked a treat. The Stage Lighting Centre designed and operated the lighting which took yellow and green as the primary look for the show and worked wonderfully. Sound by Jody Trehy was sharp and full, with great sound effects on the death scenes.

Director Sharon McNamara produced a tight, well-staged funny show for Newbridge. It never took itself too seriously, a cheeky parody, a knowing cast, a fun night out!

Ziegfeld's Girl Funny Girl is a, partially fictionalised, biography of Vaudeville performer Fanny Brice. She was a stage, radio and film performer in the US in the 30s, 40s and early 50s. Fanny Brice was an arch feminist, long before it was fashionable to be so and her writing, for theatre and radio, was quite risqué. Like Groucho Marx, she revelled in writing innuendo into her sketches, the most famous at the time being the Baby Snooks radio programmes, where she played an inquisitive child who asked embarrassing questions.

Nick Arnstein, her husband, and father to her children, was basically a suave gangster, implicated in many heists and jailed for bond theft. Brice spent a lot of money on his defence and when he was released after three years jail time, he disappeared from Brice's life and that of his children. Funny Girl, somewhat romanticises their relationship and focuses on her time spent with the Ziegfeld Follies. Written in 1963, the musical was also made into a film in 1968 starring Barbra Streisand.

New Ross Musical Society staged the show in St Michael's Theatre under the direction of Derek Shannon with musical direction by Philip Kennedy and choreography by Ann-Marie Cooney. The proscenium arch of the theatre was clad in a blue painted design reminiscent of the art deco theatres of the past and on an upstage screen was projected a photograph of a large auditorium, taken from the stage. Projections were used throughout the show to show locations such as a street, dressing room, kitchen etc. and worked quite well.

As the funny girl, Fanny Brice, Yvette Walsh's voice was impressive. Each of her numbers were saturated with excellent phrasing and intention. Her vocal was powerful on 'Don't Rain On My Parade' which closed the first and second act and on 'I'm The Greatest Star' and 'The Music That Makes Me Dance'. She was gentle on 'People' and really made it her own. Her duets with Nick 'I Want To Be Seen With You Tonight' and 'You Are Woman' demonstrated a delicate complementary vocal from both. She was quirky, had good comic timing and was well cast in the role.

Nick, Fanny's husband, here played by Keith Flanagan had a smooth baritone and sang well and his vocals blended elegantly with Ms Walsh. Nick's gangster roots were downplayed and he came across as less of a cad and more a suave man-about-town, but I feel an element of danger could have been hinted at through more detailed characterisation as the role is quite one dimensional as written. Although the scene where he seduced Fanny was very well timed and hilarious. James Dobbs played Eddie Ryan, a dancer Fanny befriended early in her career. His singing was super in the duet with Fanny's mother, 'Who Taught Her Everything?'. Clearly in love with Fanny, the character was quite complex. He had a stand out scene with Fanny where they effortlessly chatted and danced simultaneously.

His was the only character to show real distrust in Nick, and his characterisation was terrific. Ms Walsh and Mr Dobbs had a great stage chemistry, they bounced well off each other and their scenes together were super.

Mrs Brice, Fanny's Mom, here played by Teresa Buckley channelled the stage 'Jewish mama' stereotype. Her timing was good, she came across strongly. She sang well on 'If a Girl Isn't Pretty' with her neighbours and with Eddie on 'Who Taught Her Everything'. Her cattish neighbour Mrs Strakosh, played by Carmel Rowe, had great comic timing and a strong characterisation. Catherine French's Mrs Meeker and Phyllis Smith's Mrs O'Malley encapsulated the older nosey but kind neighbours very well. All sang spiritedly, despite some issues with the higher notes, on 'If a Girl Isn't Pretty'. Trevor Kent demonstrated a good voice as the Ziegfeld Tenor on 'His Love Makes Me Beautiful' and doubled-up playing Mr Renaldi, a business man.

Florentz Ziegfeld, played here by Edward Hayden with a David Lynch hairdo, came across as quite a pushover and was played as quite low status rather than the scary, successful impresario Ziegfeld actually was at that time. This was a little disappointing as his text would have supported a more august and less avuncular characterisation I feel. Tom Keeney played by Seán O'Brien, was a good gruff characterisation of a harried producer trying to deal with the 'difficult' Fanny. His scene with Nick, when Nick hoodwinks him into raising Fanny's fee was very well played. John, the stage manager, played by Thomas Crowdle, with his ever present clipboard had a nice presence. Emma, Fanny's long-suffering assistant was quite good as played by Niamh Murphy. Jenny, a dancer friend of Fanny's was wonderfully played by Niamh Cullen and came across as one of the most natural characters on stage. Her focus was extraordinary and she exuded confidence and superb dance skills. Musical Director, Philip Kennedy, who was also Chorus Master and conductor, got that big Broadway sound from his orchestra on this show, particularly on 'Don't Rain On My Parade' and the Reprise. His arrangements and interpretation of the score were satisfyingly authentic and his conducting authoritative. Ensemble and chorus harmonies were bright and melodious and the singers had a great power.

Choreographer Ann-Marie Cooney did a fabulous job on this show. The dancers were well-drilled and some of her sequences were splendid. There were some great tap routines, particularly from James Dobbs - a true triple threat. 'Henry Street' was a great example of every performer being on the same page, choreographically. The reveal of the pregnancy bump in 'His Love Makes Me Beautiful' was brilliantly integrated into the dance. On 'Rat-Tat-Tat-Tat', the military precision was commendable and the dancers focus was excellent and I liked the nod to Fosse on the Burlesque dance with bentwood chairs. The pas de deux between Eddie and Mrs Brice was like an old MGM musical in its choreography and execution, lovely stuff!

Set design by Derek Shannon, Ray Shannon and Paul Malone served the production quite well. The projections on the cyc were effective for the most part and did give a sense of place. The flown in elements, such as the white drape and the garland worked in showing the glitz of Ziegfeld's shows. The lighting in this show, designed by Paul Malone, was sharp, clever and very well programmed. His use of colour was excellent and his use of movers was subtle. Sound by Abe Scheele c/o GS Audiovisual was full range and the volume was perfectly suited to the auditorium. There was a great balance between singers and orchestra and vocals were crisp and clear.

Production management by Paul Malone was excellent on this production, all of the elements worked so well together. Stage Manager Mark Hayden and his team, wrangled cast and set competently. Assistant Stage Managers were dressed in period costumes as they moved set and props, which was a fine touch. Costume by Utopia was perfect. The red and black basques and the feathered costumes were opulent. The army uniforms and gold lame worked a treat. Make-up and hair was good for the era, although some of the make-up was a little heavy at times. Director Derek Shannon paced this show superbly and it all flowed beautifully. His interpretation of the source material was quite good, but I would have liked more work on some of the characters. His staging was excellent, a very good use of the space. There was a lovely evenness from all of his performers, which showed Mr Shannon's control of the world of the show. Nobody was too modern and the cast had a great focus. It was a very enjoyable production and the audience gave it a well-deserved standing ovation.

The timeless classic Oklahoma! was the first collaboration between Richard Rodgers and Oscar Hammerstein II. Having originally worked with other partners, they opened the show as 'Away We Go' of which producer Mike Todd said 'No legs, no jokes, no chance!'. The creators restructured it, added in the 'Oklahoma' number, renamed it and really the rest is history. It is one of the first 'book' musicals in that the story telling continues during the songs. It won all sorts of awards along the way and is still regarded as the foundation stone for the modern American musical. Appearing at a time of war and conflict, its themes gave hope for a brighter future.

I was delighted to see that Lisnagarvey Operatic & Dramatic Society had decided to perform this sometimes-forgotten show as I think it is a great vehicle for the many talents of the society. I have seen productions of the show in the past which get too bogged down with settings which take time to change and really slow the pace of the show, not here, Director Wilfie Pyper MBE (congratulations again Wilfie on this well-deserved accolade) moved the show on at a great rate of knots drawing us into the story and involving us in the lives of the characters. I will probably overuse the word 'pace' in this critique but it was something which really stood out particularly in that very difficult auction scene, which if not done correctly can really drag the second half down. All the individual lines and the drive of a great Aunt Eller meant that this did not happen. There were however some beautifully paused moments when we were given the gentle romanticism of the piece. I particularly loved the 'Surrey With A Fringe On Top', just that wee moment when Laurey's head fell 'kerplop' on his shoulder was delightful. There were some lovely nuances in Wilfie's direction, the wool winding with Aunt Eller and Curly, the business with folding the bed cover etc all adding to the realism of the moment. He had worked hard with the principals in establishing their individual characters. Some of these were slightly different from the norm but they all really grew on me. The positioning of the cast was good though one or two of the cast did have a tendency to angle away from us which blocked us out of their world at times. Nice moments of freeze were used to good effect. I would have liked to have seen more realistic fight sequences, possibly slow motion would have been more successful, as the death of Jud didn't really work.

Wilson Shields did a great job with a talented team in the orchestra. We really need this larger orchestra to give the sound for this show. There was a lovely balance from the pit (I love a pit, always think it softens and blends the instruments together). Nice steady tempi in all the numbers. What really fascinated me was how effortlessly some of the leading players flowed from dialogue seamlessly into a song, it was a wonderful effect and one I have not seen as well done before. There was good singing from all the cast including those with just one or two lines, such wonderful voices. The chorus too really rose to the challenge and sounded so strong in their rousing numbers such as 'The Farmer and the Cowman'. A job well done Wilson.

The choreography throughout the show worked very well. The style that Oprah Devitt created was very in keeping with the era and setting of the piece. The duets were nicely handled and gently but effectively moved. The big company numbers were full of life and the cast put their hearts and souls into these dance numbers. Individuals and groups danced beautifully such as the dancers at the beginning of the Dream Sequence and Ballet and the show girls in the number. I think we could have made that number even more eerie with more angular moves, that being said it brought the first act to a dramatic climax.

The production team were blessed with a very strong and can I say young cast. Aideen Fox (pictured above) made a very natural Laurey Williams. I was impressed by how she related to all the different characters around her. This was a very poised and controlled performance. She moved well around the acting areas with ease and she sang beautifully, her voice harmonising nicely with Curly. This role was played by Joshua Martin. Again, this character seemed very real. As an audience we felt that we were eaves dropping rather than watching two young people acting. He moved nicely from dialogue into song and he has the most delicious speaking voice and a very pleasant singing tone. He quickly became a pivotal performer on stage to whom our eyes were always drawn.

Gillian McQuade gave us a forceful Aunt Eller. Gillian worked so hard during that auction scene to push on the dialogue, well done for that alone. There were however gentler moments when we could see the love she had for her niece and the wonderful rapport she had with Curly. This was a convincing portrayal. Ashleigh Gault just burst onto the stage as Ado Annie. The stage sparkled with her vitality in the role. She engaged with us as the audience by talking out a lot to us which is so right for her role. She milked every drop of humour from the part and I loved how she reacted to others when she wasn't the main focus of a scene. She gave a passionate delivery of her songs. One of the men in her life was Will Parker played by Jordan Walsh. This was a slightly different approach to the part and to be honest I wasn't too sure I liked it at the start. Very soon I 'got it' and wow I really enjoyed him in the role. He made a sincere and very funny character especially focussing on how Will moved around the stage, always at top speed. Well done Jordan I loved what you did. The part of Jud Fry is one which up to now I have never seen played by someone I envisage as Jud. Up to now. Colin Boyd was a handsome but troubled Jud. If we were to psychoanalyse the character, we would find that some big set back in his life had twisted him and pushed him off in the wrong direction. If Jud had been a different personality Laurey would have been attracted to him physically. Colin gave the part a moody intensity but I wanted him to look out at us a bit more so we could see what he was thinking. That said, this was a super portrayal of a dark character. How great to see Sean Harkin playing a more comedic role. This was a real tour de force of musical comedy acting. The pointing and timing of lines were excellent. His movements around the stage, facial expressions and maintaining that difficult 'Perrrrsian' accent - brilliant. Well done Sean you gave us some wonderful moments.

Andrew Scott Snr gave a strong portrayal of rifle totting Andrew Carnes. He was a great support to the other players around him, always gruff and always commanding on stage. Bryony Randall I can still hear that laugh echoing in my ears. Giggling Gertie is a real challenge for any young actor and you did a great job. Other roles with not quite so much to say were well handled by a group who stepped up from their chorus involvement. All as clear as a bell.

Talking of which the sound in this show worked really well. There were quite a few body mics on stage, they all sounded good and were well cued. Well done Geoff Clarke. The lighting was good at times but I wanted to see a bit more sparkle and more of a feeling of time of day. I have seen quite a few shows with moving lights and in most cases, they only detract from October 2019 The Addams Family Nenagh Choral Society Ltd The Scouts' Hall 02/10/2019 to 06/10/2019 September 2019 Chitty Chitty Bang Bang Fusion Theatre Group Island Hall, Lisburn 04/09/2019 to 07/09/2019 An evening of musical hits Gorey Musical Society Ashdown Park Hotel 05/10/2019 to 05/10/2019 the show unless they are appropriate with the mood of the moment.

Costumes were generally quite good but there were some details such as colour of footwear, patterns of the colours of dresses on stage etc which might need to be tightened up in future shows. Same applied to hair and makeup. There were some good-looking wigs but some not so good, some had made a great effort to restyle their own hair, others hadn't and the result was inconsistent, losing a sense of time and place. In a show like this we really didn't need the false eyelashes and heavy makeup. Though the girls in the basques needed to be more made up with period rouge and smoky, smudged eyes to set them apart.

The set was simple and worked quite well though a cyc which could have been interestingly lit would have been preferable than the rather crudely painted field and sky. The interior of the smoke house though not too smoky looking was fantastically dressed. I would have liked to see more bits and pieces on the porch which looked a bit flat. Properties such as the rocking chair, bench etc looked appropriate.

This was a great evening of good old- fashioned musical theatre. It was slick, well-acted, well sung and full of joy. Thank you, Lisnagarvey Operatic & Dramatic Society, for your production of Oklahoma!

show_raw: Joseph And The Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat
review_text:
What's not to love about Joseph? It has great music, an array of character roles, plenty of opportunities for dance and interpretation, a good smattering of comedy… and it's short! On a wintry night, with a long drive ahead of me after the show, it was great to be on the road at 10.15pm, thoroughly entertained, humming the familiar songs and remembering the key moments of a delightfully uplifting production.

This was a very tidy, by-the-book production by Director, Kevin Kennedy, enhanced by some lovely comedy touches, and nicely directed principal action. The simple but effective set meant few delays throughout, and the selection of props and furniture added greatly to the fun. The pace throughout was very good, and the principals had well-established character. There was good attention to atmospheric lighting, and sound quality allowed for every line to be clearly heard. Perhaps the Narrator could have had a change of costume for the second act but costuming throughout was very good. My only niggle was that on a few occasions, when Joseph and the narrator were dancing with the chorus, they were the only ones not singing, and while the Narrator was strong and secure, I did feel she needed a confidence boost to be more exaggerated in some of her comedy. These are, however, minor criticisms of an otherwise very strong and secure production.

Choreographer, James Dobbs, kept the pace and action on stage varied, creative and well-disciplined. The wives and brothers performed their routines with panache, and the bigger chorus numbers were alive with energy and enthusiasm. There were nice comedic touches too, with a fun routine during Those Canaan Days, and maybe a slightly less successful dance for Mrs. Potiphar, but the overall choreographic contribution to the show was extremely positive.

Definitely a highlight of the show was the quality of the music, both from the pit, under the leadership of Musical Director, Phillip Kennedy, and from the stage. All of the singing principals made a strong impact, but it was the chorus, and particularly the male chorus, that really lifted the show. The band of Brothers achieved great harmony and character in all their songs, and when they combined with the ladies, the harmonies were excellent, and the vocal strength was awesome.

Timmy Moloney had a relaxed, easy- listening vocal quality and chanted his way through the central role of Joseph with confidence. His acting was commendable throughout, growing in stature as the story progressed. I did feel that his modelling of the Technicolored coat in the finale became a tad exaggerated and flamboyant, nevertheless, this was a very well-played role.

Sophie Blaney Parslow carried the exhausting role of The Narrator with a most genial manner. Her vocals were extremely secure with a good, rounded tone, occasionally giving vent to a bit of quality belting.
