While many of her facial expressions captured the comedy of her situations, there were a few times when she looked a little bit self-conscious, but given her obvious talent, she should have more self-belief. She is a lovely performer. David Burke was a convincing Jacob, who beautifully over-acted his sadness, wailing almost in tune, and when he sang, he displayed a strong and articulate baritone voice. A nice balanced performance.Keith Flanagan played Pharaoh with secure comedic timing and a lot of swagger. Clearly, he enjoyed the freedom of milking the comedy of the Song of the King, and the audiences thoroughly enjoyed his antics. His singing was in keeping with the Elvis styled number.

James Dobbs, not contented with doing the choreography for the show, popped up not only as a very convincing Naphtali, with a splendidly pigeon-French rendition of Those Canaan Days, but also as the delightfully comical, high-camp Butler to Pharoah. He played each part with individuality and aplomb. Anthony Finn, as Asher, did a very good job of leading the brothers in One More Angel in Heaven, and Phil Erskine gave a flamboyant charm to the Benjamin Calypso. Individually, and as a group, the brothers were a strong and secure presence throughout the show. Martin Conway and Brid Moloney worked nicely together and fulfilled the roles of Potiphar and Mrs. Potiphar most credibly, and Ger O'Riordan did all that was required of him as the unfortunate Baker.

The Brothers, The Wives, Maid-Servants, Hairy Ishmaelites, Guards and Dancers all contributed to the overall success of the show with committed performances, displaying good acting, great movement, some inspired dancing and above all, a very strong vocal ability. When the full chorus were on the stage, not just the volume but also the quality of the singing was of the highest order. And then of course there were the children, who looked and sounded so good, and if some of them couldn't resist spotting and waving to their parents in the audience, well, it only added to their cuteness and my enjoyment. Very well done, kids.

The stage was very nicely designed, with colourful, neutral flats and very effective set and furniture pieces, like the well that doubled as Mrs. Potiphar's bed. Palms added a nice atmosphere, and the Sphynx was excellent, as was the Chariot of Gold in the final scene, and the prison bars were very good. The stage crew, under Stage Manager Lizzy Heffernan, kept things moving at a brisk and efficient pace.

Lighting was well-plotted to enhance the action, and created beautiful atmospheres, most notably when Joseph was imprisoned. Not a word was lost, thanks to a very good and well-operated sound system.

This was a vivid and colourful production that benefitted strongly from well-selected costumes and good accessories. Wigs and beards were very good, Joseph's coat was very effective and the final effect of the coat taking over the whole stage at the end was wonderful. But it was the attention to detail that added so much to the show, like the very realistic goat that got torn limb from limb, the 'very last sheep', the comical glove-puppet snake, and top marks go to the amazing nodding, singing, fur-coated camel which almost stole the show. There was always something interesting and comical or colourful to draw one's attention and to add another level to the visual impact of the production. There was an abundance of wigs and beards and they all looked very effective, as was the standard of make-up.

Having recently directed Joseph myself, it was a humbling experience to see how different, and creative and beautiful the show can be, in the hands of a different director, and from one Mr Kennedy to two other Mr Kennedys, congratulations on achieving such a wonderful standard with this highly entertaining production.

Thankfully, as it seems to be extremely popular of late, All Shook Up is one of those shows that I don't mind sitting through several times in a season. It has a good comedic book, a plethora of zany and identifiable characters and above all else, the wonderful music of Elvis. For an old guy who grew up in awe of "The King", such a musical tribute is always a pleasure to savour, and when it is presented with such striking choreography and such a high standard of direction, production and performance, there aren't really many better ways to spend an evening.

Director Stephanie Browne ensured that her production of this show was vibrant and fast-paced, colourful and creative in design, and captured the essence of the rock and roll era. With a very strongly cast show, the direction and movement throughout made sense and her cast always looked comfortable on the stage. Characters were all very clearly established, and with the exception of a few laugh lines being skipped over, and an occasional over-the-top comedic reaction, all gave believable and commendable performances. But it was her choreographic achievements for which Stephanie deserves the greatest plaudits. The energy level was ultra-high throughout, and the dance routines varied from graceful and genteel, to raucous and outrageous, with smatterings of gymnastics, acrobatics and jazz-hot gyrations. She was, of course, assisted in her task by a very fine and dedicated troupe of dancers who seemed to enjoy every second of their performances. Excellent work.

Congratulations to the production and technical team for creating a show that was so colourful and varied, visually, that one was scared to blink for fear of missing something. The lighting was generally top-notch, with great use of special effects, including a projection screen which created some beautiful effects, although in some of the gentler moments of the show, it was a tad distracting. Good atmospheres were created with strong use of colour and moving lights, but the down-stage right and left areas did have a couple of dark spots. Stage managers, Rachel Browne and Máire Long and their team executed the scene changes efficiently, preventing the excellent pace of the production from being interrupted. Sound quality was generally very good, with the minor faux pas of a mic being kept alive on one of the off-stage performers. Well done, also, to the props team, for a wonderful array of appropriate and well- selected items to enhance the ambience and period of the piece.

Musical Director, Laura Kearney, got good results from her chorus and principals, with well-rehearsed harmonies and an abundance of vocal talent on display. The orchestra were tuneful, rhythmic and energetic, if on occasions, a tad over- exuberant. The chorus, singing while executing quite intricate dance routines, were once or twice slightly over-powered by the pit. Nevertheless, this was a production with a high-quality musical accompaniment.

Gráinne Scullane brought a good balance of femininity and tom-boyish comedy to the role of Natalie, especially amusing in her assumed role of Ed. Here is a young lady with good vocal quality, fine stage presence and a very capable sense of comedic timing. This was a well-judged performance.

Joe Keyes had all the swagger and bravado required for the role of Chad, enjoying the hip-swivelling and outrageous flirting and cutting a fine figure on the stage. If not the most powerful singer, he certainly had a secure vocal quality and enough charisma to carry off the Elvis numbers with confidence.

As Miss Sandra, Caroline Browne dominated the stage from the outset, oozing confidence, sexuality and excellent comedy and combining it with powerful vocals. This was a wonderful piece of casting and a most note-worthy performance from a very talented actress. Dylan Noonan made a very convincing Dennis, almost pantomimic in his nerdiness, and very secure vocally throughout. He was believable in his love for Natalie and provided a good contrast to Chad in their scenes together. I did feel that he was a tad over-zealous in the delivery of some of his comedy, and perhaps pulling back a little would have made him even more sympathetic.

There was a very good sense of maturity about the performance of Conal Daly as Jim, achieving a believable father- daughter relationship with Natalie, and delightfully awkward in his attempts to impress Miss Sandra. He handled his romance with Sylvia very sincerely, and also displayed a most pleasant vocal quality.

Caroline Kennedy, similarly, achieved the maturity required of Sylvia, delightfully cynical about love, and yet beautifully sincere in her affection for Jim. There's Always Me was very nicely delivered. Lorraine was confidently played with an appropriate feisty attitude by Megan Maher, always secure in her vocals and her sense of comedy. She was also perfectly cast opposite young Jayden Guillfoyle, as Dean. With an overload of cuteness and a bucket-full of ability, Jayden won over the audience as easily as he won friendships at last season's AIMS Youth Summer Camp. It's so good to see these young performers growing in talent and in confidence.

Cleo Griffin brought the right amount of pretentious piety and pomposity to the role of Mayor Matilda, maintaining a comical severity right up to the point where she melts under the affection of Sheriff Earl. She delivered Devil in Disguise very comfortably. As her eventual sweetheart, Earl, Adam Carroll convincingly mimed three-quarters of his performance with good, if occasionally over-stated, comedic effect, and his eventual vocal outburst was met with the desired hilarity by a very appreciative audience.

The chorus and dancers were exemplary in the execution of their involvement in the show, whether in their actions and reactions or in performing their varied and energetic routines.

They were vocally secure and well-rehearsed in their harmonies.

Visually, the show was stunning. From curtain up to the finale, the colour, the styles and the variety in scenery and effects made this a most absorbing assault on the senses. Both chorus and principal costumes were well-selected, appropriate in style and well-worn. The variety and flamboyance of the dancers' costumes was most note-worthy and added so much to the atmosphere of the various scenes. They even managed to change their hairstyles between routines. But it was the combination of all the various visual elements of the show that made it a captivating production.

My only suggestion, and not really a criticism, would be that perhaps on occasions, less can achieve more, particularly with the use of projections. There is a fine line between their ability to enhance and their ability to distract from the focal point of the action. While technically and visually, this production exploded off the stage, it did walk that line on one or two occasions. However, I can afford to nit-pick only because the overall standard of this show was so high. Director/Choreographer, Stephanie Browne has certainly established herself as a force to be reckoned with.

The foyer of the Nenagh Scouts Hall was delightfully adorned with memorabilia from past company productions, and a warm and welcoming front of house staff ensured that patrons were comfortable in their surroundings. Hospitality before and during the show was sumptuous and greatly appreciated, and I am indebted to all concerned for a really wonderful night of entertainment.

I'm not quite sure what my expectations were as I headed north to visit the Letterkenny Music and Drama Group production of Calendar Girls the Musical. All I knew about it was a vague memory of the movie, involving members of the Women's Institute making a rather saucy calendar to raise funds for charity, and as it was billed as being appropriate for a 12+ age group, I reckoned there was the possibility of a bit of on-stage nudity. Well, I've never been one to shy away from nudity, but the prospect of observing it in such a public setting had me intrigued, to say the least. So, was it worth all the speculation and curiosity? You'd better believe it, and it was nothing to do with the nudity! No matter how easy the leading ladies were on the eye, it was the effect they had on my heart that made this a night to remember. It was the combination of beautifully played comedy and the most heart-wrenching emotional drama that had me spell-bound by this quite brilliant production. Any show that can make you cry and then raise your spirits to convulsions of laughter has got to be note-worthy, and this show did it all. Empathy is the word that comes to mind when considering Director, Pluincéad Ó Fearraigh's handling of this material. There was so much tenderness in the scenes involving Annie and John, not a gushing outpouring of emotion, but a delicate and respectful handling of the heart-breaking subject matter.

Such empathy also accompanied the scenes involving the hapless Ruth and the struggling single mother, Chris, and yet the intertwining of the social dramas with the comical characterisations of these women was perfectly balanced, and the setting of the scene for the eventual calendar shoot was comedy gold, and courageously handled by the ladies, who threw caution, and their clothing, to the wind, all in the name of charity. The upshot of this wonderful production was that the cast did actually produce an amazing calendar, which is now raising much needed funds for Donegal Hospice and Cancer Care West. What made it all the more poignant was that members of this company were not just acting but were putting into their performances the very real heartache of personal experiences, having been touched, as so many of us are at some time, by the cold reality of cancer. This show was a tribute to souls who have departed and to those who still live and cope with this horrible disease, and I am in awe of these calendar girls. It was the laying bare of their souls, not their bodies, that made this an extraordinary production.

This visual presentation of the show was absolutely perfect in its simplicity, capturing the essence of ordinary people going about their ordinary lives. Costuming was natural and delightful without ever pulling focus with outrageous or flamboyant outfits. Even while glamour girl, Celia, looked a cut above the others in style, she still blended perfectly with her surroundings. Hair and make-up were natural and individual to each character, but the real visual strength of the show was the combination and coordination of costumes, settings, lighting and the superb array of beautiful props. It all created something akin to the nostalgically beautiful sense that I get when watching an episode of the Last of the Summer Wine or The Darling Buds of May.

In the leading role of Annie, Ciara Gallagher quite simply melted my heart with the most tender and moving performance of a woman coming to terms with losing her husband to cancer. She had a most beautiful and affecting vocal quality and a wonderful grip on the comedic side of her character, but her handling of the most poignant and heart-wrenching moments of the show was indescribably superb. It was one of those moments when you forgot that this was an actress playing a role, for she had become the person she was portraying. A stunning performance. With a range of talent that ran from perfectly timed comedy, to emotionally charged drama and moments of fiery passion, Rachel Akkoc's portrayal of Chris was filled with energy, compassion and the most outrageous joie de vivre. Hers was the struggle between being a good role model as a mother and casting convention to the wind to become a role model not just for those affected by cancer, but for women in general. Throw in a very secure vocal quality and this was another truly amazing and empathetic performance.

It will be a long time before I forget the vision of Mary Lane, as Cora, sitting stark naked (with her back to the audience) at the piano. The courage that it must have taken to appear thus, was shared by every one of the fabulous Calendar girls, and Mary epitomised the sense of fun and determination that made this such a terrific show. Her comedy and her spirit were top-notch, and she led the unorthodox Christmas sing-along with strength and passion. Then there was the 'surgically enhanced' dolly bird, Celia, played with a beautifully comical mixture of vanity and vulnerability by Maire McGinley. I will never be able to look at Cherry Bakewell's without thinking of her again. She gave a strong and confident rendition of the, So I've Had a Little Work Done song, which epitomised her spirit and her strength as a performer.

Mary Harte hid her natural good looks under aged make-up and wig to play the stuffy but comical schoolteacher, Jessie most convincingly. Before I saw her youthful photo in the programme, I thought, "My God, they're not going to get that old granny to strip off her clothes, are they?" But just like the others, she bared all (discreetly covered in balls of wool) and played her part delightfully.

And then there was the extremely comical Ruth, the rather frumpy and industrious do-gooder who devotes her time to making scones and being the unsung hero of the WI, all as an escape from the sadness of a joyless marriage. Geraldine Galligan inhabited this role superbly, with wonderful self-effacing humour that caused us all the more to celebrate her vodka-inspired transformation into a strong and independent (and proudly naked) woman. Her 'My Russian Friend and I' was brilliantly performed, as was her hilarious unveiling for the calendar photo-shoot. Wonderful comedy.

Angela Gallagher played Marie, the stoic and unyielding leader of the local WI, with the right amount of self-righteousness but also enough heart to eventually accept the changing times around her. She was a good strong contrast to her daughter Jenny, played with vim and attitude by the talented Siobhan Sweeney, who added a youthful perspective to the telling of the tale, and took a typically edgy path towards teen romance with a very nicely portrayed Danny, by Caolan Kelly. Danny and Tommo, played comically by Ciaran Ó Gallchóir, provided a nice little side story of two young men highly concerned about the daunting prospect of losing their virginity.

The female line up was completed by competent and confident performances from Tina Higgins as Miss Wilson with the strategically placed Teapot, Sheila Brown as Miss Wilson with the dignity-saving Coffeepot, Kerry O'Donnell as Brenda Hulse and Kate Doherty judging the bake- sale as Lady Cravenshire.

The men in this production were led by Martin Gallen, who gave a touching performance as the unfortunate John, whose demise during Act One inspires the desire to create a calendar. His tender scenes with Ciara were most affecting. Martin Towey gave a delightfully uncomfortable and comical performance as Lawrence, the amateur photographer who agrees to shoot the calendar photos. The husbands trying to come to terms with the outrageous behaviour of their women folk were well captured by Martin Anderson as Colin, Bill Vaughan as Denis and Rodney McKeague as Rod, each creating a well-defined individuality.

The chorus, who were few in number, added enthusiastic support in the crowd scenes, integrating well into the action and flavour of the show, and making a good solid vocal contribution.

Apart from the early over-exuberance of the band, Musical Director, Denise Roper had good control of a fine sounding group of musicians, who played the music of the show with steady tempi and tone. The score has hints of The Hired Man, with featured trumpet solos, which were nicely played. Vocally, principals and chorus alike were well-rehearsed and very confident in delivery of their pieces. The more emotional pieces were delicately handled and yet, when required, a good full sound was achieved.

Sound quality presented a few problems, with one or two mics requiring a bit of boosting or the band needing to reduce their output a little. The difficulty is that when strong regional accents are being used, as they were, quite superbly, articulation is of the utmost importance, and the imbalance in sound did require the audience to struggle, initially, with making out some of the lines. Thankfully, the problem seemed to resolve, fairly swiftly. The show was presented on an artistically beautiful set, depicting the Yorkshire hills and dales, with a clever opening section that became the interior of the local WI. Other locations were created with the excellent use of pools and areas of special lighting which cut out the need for elaborate scene changes and assisted in a very smooth flowing action sequence. Lighting generally was most effective, enhancing the beautiful artwork and adding poignant atmosphere to so many of the scenes. Stage Manager, Fiona McDaid, as well as keeping everything moving like clockwork, also led the team that amassed an amazing array of props, with trucks and barrows, a piano, stalls and the massive collection of food items, blossoms, pots and pans, etc., that were utilised in providing 'modesty' during the calendar shoot. Excellent work.

I won't lie, it's a show that takes a while to get going, maybe because the expectation was a comical romp, but when you suddenly realise that you are in the middle of a most dramatic scenario, involving very real people and a story strewn with real heartache, it quickly becomes an absorbing, compelling and truly astonishing piece of theatre. There were, perhaps, some areas where a tad more creative choreography might have enhanced the scenes, and the inclusion of air hostesses in one scene was a bit superfluous to the action, but the general shape and pattern of the piece was so very well realised, and I can only congratulate Pluncáid on his crafted and sensitive direction of a show that really does require an understanding of human nature and the importance of focus and balance. I am indebted to the entire company, and most specifically, to the dedication and courage of the Calendar Girls themselves, for this most thought-provoking and totally satisfying night of sheer entertainment.

For those unfamiliar with the story of Spring Awakening, it is a multi- layered exposé of a society corrupted by religious indoctrination, misguided parental ineptitude and teenage angst and confusion around matters of a sexual nature. That a show, written as a play before the start of the 20th century, still resonates with the audience of today, is an indication of how little we have advanced as a species and how astute the playwright, Frank Wedekind, actually was. In modern terms, it attempts to look at both physical and mental abuse, mental health issues and non- conformity, as viewed through the eyes of its victims. What makes this particular production quite outstanding is the total fusion of music, dance and drama into an immersive theatrical experience that verges on modern ballet.

Director, Niamh McGowan, Musical Director, Roisin Heenan and Choreographer, Leah Meagher have pooled their thoughts and visions to create a seamless display of integrated theatre that is all about the whole experience.

Musicians walk through the story, furniture is danced into place, emotions are expressed as much through song and movement as through the spoken word, and it works because every person on board believes in the project and contributes on so many levels.

Using the simple symbolism of the Biblical apple to represent temptation, and the tree of knowledge as the most prominent set piece, Niamh McGowan displayed the central theme of the story in a nutshell; the abundance of apples on stage highlighting the notion that we are all susceptible to temptation. Equally symbolic and effectively employed was the length of rope, with its connotations of constraint, and its doom-suggesting noose, used variously as a telegram-line connecting Melchior and Wendla during their separation, and for a tug of war as Ilse attempts to haul Moritz away from the abyss of his inevitable demise.

Subtle, creative and atmospheric was the lighting design of Gavin Coll, and as impressively choreographed as the rest of the show, with players moving into special areas with perfect timing. The structure and texture of the building was highlighted to great effect, while the scene where each individual member of the cast carried on and employed their own tea-lights, placed on the floor, was a touch of atmospheric genius. The gentle use of colour washes perfectly framed each scene and captured the appropriate mood, while there was rarely a moment where a superfluous light illuminated an unused piece of the stage. Changes seemed to flow seamlessly together, enhancing the sense of a living, breathing piece of theatre.

Kathyann Murphy's set design was minimalist and super-effective, enhanced by the sheer simplicity of the boxes and benches that served as furniture throughout. The tree was an ever present and somewhat haunting piece of art which constantly kept one's mind alert to the central theme of the production. Stage Management under Kate Canavan, with Emma Louise Gregg, Laoise Grennan and Chloe Murphy Foley, was never evident as it was absorbed into the continual movement of the flow of the action. Vinny Osborne's sound management was flawless.

Various actors took their turns on musical instruments and integrated with the action, creating beautiful pictures and uniting the music with the drama. Led by Musical Director, Roisin Heenan, the band musicians were superb, always in tune and in touch with the mood and atmosphere of their pieces. Violinist, Cliodhna Heenan, especially, had a gypsy-like quality as she played and sauntered through the action. The principals and ensemble alike were vocally strong and secure, giving energy and passion especially to the Totally Fucked number, and the most enchanting and stirring emotion to the haunting harmonious Song of Purple Summer. Leah Meagher, who joined the dancers on stage as a replacement for a performer injured during rehearsals, presented choreography that ranged from grotesque contemporary ballet to Fosse-like terpsichorean style and modern hip-hop energy, in a display that hardly rested throughout the entire production, due to the fact that the changes of settings and furniture were all danced to perfection. The result of these three creative ladies working as a single unit was a cast infused with that same singular sense of purpose, drawing from them strong dramatic performances, vibrant, perfectly pitched musical delivery and sometimes explosive, sometimes serenely gentle displays of dance and energy.

As Melchior, Ruairí Nicholl displayed the required level of bravado to be a believable provocateur to his peers, and a perfect level of confusion and passion about the society he was attempting to understand and influence. It was the balance between innocence and his bravado that made his characterisation so believable. His vocal delivery was always excellent and passionate.

Hannah McNicholas Roche, as Wendla, gave a sublime performance of naïve vulnerability, gentle and sincere, confused yet passionate for education, and ultimately the sad victim of her own innocence. Her numbness, her passions and her heart-ache were perfectly pitched, and the strength and tenderness of her vocals completely complemented her persona.

Cian Gallagher, as Moritz, fretted and fumed with teenage angst as he lived in fear of failure in the eyes of his unrelenting father, and struggled equally with the guilt of his sexual urges. This was a compelling performance that perhaps wanted a few moments of calm to balance against the constant edginess of his conflicts, and thus would have made his demise less inevitable and even more tragic. His vocals had a strong rock-ballad feel and were delivered with style.

As Ilse, Caoimhe Tyndall spoke as precisely with her body-language and movement as she did with her words. The pains of abuse, rejection and confusion were translated into a virtual ballet of emotion, and her intensity and sincerity were abundant in her reaction to the death of Moritz. Beautifully sung, acted and danced.

Damien Sweeney as Herr and Anna Bergin as Frau represented all the adult and authoritative figures throughout the show and did so with comical menace as the school masters, and with disturbing disconnection as the various parental figures. Both achieved their comedic and dramatic goals with variety and distinction. Their vocal contributions were equally convincing and consistent.

Gavin Murphy gave a delightfully sincere and comical performance of Hanschen, joyous in the expression of love for Brandon Wright's more restrained and naïve Ernst. Both delivered all that was asked of them, with Gavin's overt sexuality being well counter-balanced by Brandon's sincere but courageous innocence.

Lisa Lyons gave depth and passion to the character of Martha, youthful and resilient even in the face of the abuse she has had to endure. This was another well-measured performance, and securely supported and enhanced by her talented comrades, Grace Nolan as Anna and Hannah Franchetti as Thea. The male cast was similarly enhanced by solid and reliable performances from Rory Sheehy as Georg and Dan Whelan as Otto, both of whom also contributed as performance musicians.

The chorus/ensemble may have been small in number, but their contribution to the acting, singing and dancing was mammoth. Appearing much more as a collective of supporting individuals than as a chorus, each should be proud of the way they enhanced and boosted the overall impact of the music and the movement. I must give a special mention to Morgan Moore who stepped in with just a day's notice to replace an injured cast member. It was not evident at all from the audience.Great attention to detail was a mark of Aoife Barron's costuming of the show, from appropriate school uniforms and the beautifully selected era-evoking dresses right down to socks, knickers and footwear, nothing looked out of place. Similarly, much attention was given to hairstyles, with Rachel Murphy ensuring that the boys, not just the girls, were appropriately styled. Make-up was even and natural looking, and the required signs of beating and bruising were subtle and effective and not over-done.

It was very pleasant to be greeted on arrival at the Smock Alley Theatre by ex- AIMS Youth Summer School attendee, Bryan Mulry, whose hospitality was abundant. It was equally pleasant to encounter show Producer, Kate Canavan at the interval and after the show, and to learn more about the company.

According to the programme notes, it was the intention of the company "to present the narrative in a manner which highlights the power of physical and authentic storytelling."  They achieved their goal, and so much more, and it was a privilege to be there to enjoy the fruits of their endeavours. Sincere thanks to all concerned for an incredibly moving theatrical experience.

Boyle Musical Society embarked upon their post-Covid theatrical endeavours with the ever-popular musical comedy, Guys and Dolls, and were richly rewarded with big audiences of people starved of good entertainment. This was a good choice, offering, as it does, lots of comedy gold and an easily identifiable musical score. It's also a show that is comfortably stage-able, doesn't break the bank costume-wise, and gives a director plenty of scope for putting a personal stamp on it.

Vivienne Moran, as director, sensibly played to the strength of her performers, putting good emphasis on the comedic side of the show. Guys and Dolls is a good vehicle for a young company acquiring experience, and it definitely paid off. There was good use of the chorus to keep ever changing patterns in the crowd scenes, and from a choreographic point of view, Vivienne again played to the ability of her dancers, keeping routines clean and not over-complicated. The Crapshooter's Ballet was particularly well designed, highlighting the best movers and using simple and effective gestures and steps to give the strongest impact. The Hot-Box ladies were tidy in all that they did.

Musical Director, Anne Kielty, got the show off to a good start with a lively and well-paced overture and Runyonland. The musicians provided a good bit of punch when it was required, but also handled the mellow moments with good sensitivity. Vocally, much good work was done to produce a full sound from an industrious chorus, and principals seemed well rehearsed in all their music. If there was an area that needed a bit of attention, both musically and dramatically, it was the pace of the show. I did feel that some of the dialogue, particularly in the long opening Mission scene, and some of the music, particularly the slower songs, needed an injection of pace to keep the action a bit more fluid.

Tom Nolan displayed a mellow and secure singing voice in the role of Sky Masterson, with 'My Time of Day' and 'Never Been in Love Before' being most memorable, and there was confidence in his rendition of 'Luck Be a Lady'. I felt that perhaps he didn't have quite the same confidence in his dialogue, which on occasions seemed a little hesitant. He needed a bit more self- belief to establish himself as the leader of the pack. Nevertheless, he did cut a fine figure in the role and worked well alongside Sarah Brown.

That lady was played delightfully and with a plentiful range of emotions, by the very capable Karen Gordon. She established her strait-laced persona from the get-go, and maintained it perfectly, until alcohol took a hold of her. Then she comically allowed her guard to drop and believably succumbed to Sky's advances. This was a nicely judged acting performance, and vocally, while there was a slightly obvious switch her chest voice to her head voice, she performed her duets with good emotion, with 'Marry the Man Today' being a particularly excellent number. Brimming with confidence and a very fine sense of comic timing was Darragh Beirne in the role of Nathan Detroit. He had a good understanding of his character, playing the reluctant romantic as comfortably as the fixer with the weight of the world on his shoulders. His relationship with Adelaide was strong, as was his comedy and his delivery of his musical numbers. Janet Feeney gave the performance of the night in her role as Miss Adelaide, effervescent in her comedy, extremely assured in her vocals and totally at ease as the star of the Hot Box. She used good and well-varied facial expressions, and exaggerated tones of anger very effectively to enhance her comedy. Her Lament was well-delivered, but 'Sue Me' and 'Marry the Man Today' were two of the highlights of the show. Diarmuid Beirne, Matt Burke and Gavin Ward combined successfully as Nicely- Nicely, Benny Southstreet and Rusty Charlie to provide comedic back-up to Nathan. All three men displayed good vocal ability, with Diarmuid making a particularly good job of 'Sit Down You're Rockin' the Boat', and their Guys and Dolls trio was very impressive, with Gavin showing the most adept combination of singing and dancing. Enda Ryan gave a thuggish quality to Harry the Horse, using his stature to be intimidating, where perhaps he could have eased back and relied more on his well scripted lines. Skyler O'Flaherty as Big Jule had a great appearance and just about the right level of menace to make a good impact.

John Reynolds was a gentle and caring Arvide who rendered his 'More I Cannot Wish You' song with sincerity. His movement and body language were a tad uncomfortable during this, and he might have benefitted from having somewhere to sit and give Sarah a good cuddle. Deborah Kehoe was an appropriately severe. Gen Cartwright, and Catherine Bolger a good gullible and nervous Agatha. As Lieutenant Brannigan, Cathal Tiernan went for a rather comical grumpy character and delivered his lines with the ferocity of an angry Jack Russell. He had a tendency to turn his back on the audience, but he gave a consistent performance. There was great enthusiasm from the chorus in all of their scenes, filling the stage with life and energy. Their enjoyment was very apparent, and their involvement added greatly to the ambiance of the various scenes. Their vocal prowess was shown at its best during 'Sit Down You're Rockin' the Boat', and the men gave good account of themselves in 'Luck Be a Lady'. The Hot Box girls did all that was asked of them with good discipline. 'Havana' was fast-moving and varied and performed with confidence.

Much thought went into the design of the set to give as many varied and interesting locations as the script demanded. The street scenes had a good skyline, attractive signage, and useful rotating pieces, and the sewer scene with its clever manhole entrance and nicely painted background was particularly effective. A star curtain and a decent set piece sufficed for the Hot Box scenes and the interior of the Mission was well presented. The only disappointment was the use, on a couple of occasions of a black curtain as a background, which particularly for the final scene of Act One, might have been better played against the empty set with the New York skyline. Props throughout were well selected and employed, and Stage Manager, Enda Commons, with his team, managed to keep the scene changes fairly brisk. Lighting was a good feature of the show, creating good atmosphere and usually highlighting the action very well. Only once or twice did principals wander out of their specials and got temporarily lost in shadows. Sound quality was good, with sharp cuing and a good balance throughout. A bit of an echo or interference might have made Joey Biltmore's voice sound more like he was on the other end of a telephone, but that's a minor point. For the most part, the show was very nicely costumed, with the street people in good styles, and the gamblers looking sharp and snappy. Havana was delightfully colourful, and the Mission uniforms were neat and tidy. The 'Take Back Your Mink' costumes were very decent, but a uniformity in the mink stoles would have enhanced their appearance, and I'm not at all sure how the costumes for 'A Bushel and A Peck' related to the song, even though they were attractive. Principal costumes were very good and well worn. Make-up was natural looking, and hairstyles all seemed appropriate, particularly Miss Adelaide's.

All in all, Boyle Musical Society rose to the challenges of this most enjoyable show with a high level of success. There was a wealth of rising talent on display, and in the experienced hands of Vivienne and Anne, the future looks very healthy. The audience left the theatre filled with laughter and compliments, and I'm grateful to have had the opportunity to join them in thoroughly enjoying your production. Sincere thanks for your warm hospitality, and I wish you continued growth and success in future productions.

With an attractive set, incorporating good technical standards, an energetic and enthusiastic cast brought good fun and bubbly entertainment from this production of the Dolly Parton Musical, 9 to 5. Donna Ruane's direction leaned heavily on accentuating the comedy of the show, which she did to good effect. Characters were well-realised, each with their own quirky tendencies and never going too over the top.

There was a slight tendency for the chorus to be cluttered upstage which could have been avoided had the principals moved further forward on occasions. Apart from that, the stage was well used, with good pictures created and plenty of energy and involvement from the chorus. . The dream sequences were very well played and again, very comical.

The show was played against a well- painted and functional, neutral set with props, furniture and projected images added to differentiate various scenes. Props and furniture were generally very good, but a little more care needed to be taken with some details. For example, when Franklin was first tied up, he needed assistance to remove the gag from his mouth, despite the fact that his hands were completely free. Some of the on-screen images didn't quite fit the screen, and for the main office scene, an image without people frozen in suspended animation would have been better. However, it was a good set, and the stage team, under Dave Keane's management, manoeuvred the numerous props and furniture pieces with a good degree of efficiency. The car boot was very good. Lighting was colourful and captured well the atmosphere of each scene, the venetian side-flats being particularly well used. Sound quality was very good throughout the show.

Musical Director, Deirdre Lee, led a well- tuned orchestra who seemed to enjoy the musical score and played with good rhythm and tempi throughout. She had also done a good job on vocal harmonies, creating a capable and confident choral sound from the stage. She was blessed with principals who were all very secure in their vocals. The show was musically strong. Claudia O'Sullivan brought good variety to her routines, most effectively during the dream sequences and the One of the Boys number. She had a willing and able chorus to work with, and with the exception of that occasional overcrowding towards the up-stage area, they performed extremely well.

A strong and capable female-dominated cast made their mark and hit the right notes in promoting equality in the workplace. In the central role of Violet Newstead, Vivienne Lee displayed a versatility that ranged from begrudgery to triumphant feminism, passing through loving motherhood, inspirational team leader, casual drug abuser and fairy tale dreamer on the way. At each phase of the journey she conveyed strong comedy, sincere emotions and a more than delightful vocal quality, making her a natural leading lady. Joining her on her journey was Elizabeth Murphy's backwoods Barbie, Doralee Rhodes, played with just the right amount of feisty effervescence. With strong vocals and equally impressive comedic timing, she fulfilled the "Dolly" role without resorting to an attempt at impersonation. Good work.

Nicole Scott played Judy Bernley with a melancholy that won the hearts of the audience, and then the most delightfully ditzy comedic characterisation. This was a beautiful performance that culminated in a strong and resolute rendition of Get Out and Stay Out.

I'm quite sure Maria McNulty was hoping that none of her primary school pupils were in the audience as she ripped open her blouse and performed the vampish "Hart to Heart", in a very capable and comedic interpretation of Roz Keith. She drooled most effectively over her boss, and we felt her pain at being constantly over-looked by him.

That boss, Franklin Hart Jnr. was played with disturbing but hilarious vulgarity and misogyny by David Alexander, whose cheesy wig and moustache added to the creepiness of his character and rendered him almost unrecognisable. This was a good performance with a very funny and totally tacky rendition of Here For You. Mike Flaherty was a warm and likeable Joe, sincere in his affection for Violet, secure in his comedy, and tender in tone in the well-delivered "Love Can Grow" duet.

Josie Gallagher stuttered and slurred her way through a highly amusing performance as Margaret, the office lush who finally comes clean after rehab, while Emma Gallagher impressed as the unfairly dismissed and then reinstated secretary, Maria Delgado. Completing the strong female line-up was Angela Prenty as the gullible and much cheated wife, Missy Hart. Very good support came from Mervyn Fahy as Doralee's supportive husband, Dwane, Gearóid Herraghty as Judy's love-rat ex-husband, Dick Bernley, Gerard Scott as Chairman of the Board, Mr Tinsworthy and particularly young Paddy O'Brien who made a very good impression as Violet's teenage son, Josh. The chorus were well rehearsed in their harmonies and made a good vocal contribution to the show. They acted and reacted well to the action on stage and danced with good energy and ability. Principal costumes were well chosen to suit the personality of the characters, and the chorus costumes were colourful and appropriate, with nice sets for the various special numbers. Hairstyles were generally very good and make-up was natural.

This was a good, clear and thoroughly entertaining production. Sincere thanks to all concerned, and for the generous hospitality on the night.

It is abundantly clear why The Sound of Music remains such a popular choice on the musical circuit. The story is timeless, and the music is wonderful, and who doesn't love to see those little marching children growing in confidence and finding the loving heart of their father. It has all the ingredients to fill an audience with warmth and appreciation. One of the keys to a successful production of the show is the performance of the Von Trapp children and their relationship with Maria. In this production, directors Philippa Alford and Stephen Fagan ensured that this bond was strong and secure. The children were well-disciplined, and each child had a good individual identity.

The pace of the show was excellent, and scene changes were quite well handled, but the Von Trapp mansion could have done with a bit of dressing. Similarly, the concert scene at the end needed some flags or banners to give a stronger indication of the alternative setting. The best feature of the set was the Abbey, which was well-painted and intimate, the bedroom was nicely achieved, and the terrace was tidy enough, but for Maria's entrance amid the hills, and for the finale as the family climb to the safety of Switzerland, a mountain backdrop, or even just a hillside cut out to cover the stairs would have added so much to those scenes. Furniture and props were good, and efficiently handled by the industrious stage crew, under John Dooley. The lighting of the show was fairly clean, and everyone could always be seen, although perhaps more mood lighting might have enhanced the concert and the more romantic scenes. Sound throughout was very satisfactory.

Costumes were good throughout, with the nuns being tidy and presentable, and the children looking spic and span in their sailor suits. The matching curtains and play clothes were delightful. Rolf looked a tad too 'gestapo' in attire and might have looked more comfortable in the sandy youth movement uniform. The captain and his guests were always well-dressed and elegantly turned out.

Emer Hartnett led a very competent band of musicians in a well-played and expressive rendition of the score. She also kept well in contact with her on-stage performers, ensuring their discipline and keeping them together even as they made their way through the hall. There was evidence of well-rehearsed harmonies from the nun's chorus, and the children and other principals seemed confident in all that they sang.

Choreographer Imelda Winters had few bodies to work with in the ballroom scene, but still managed to create a nice Landler for Kurt, Maria and the Captain. Her choreography of the children's routines was delightful and inventive and Sixteen Going on Seventeen had a good shape and was well danced by Liesl and Rolf. Thoroughly delightful in the central role of Maria was the talented Orla Williams, who not only acted with great natural ability, but whose speaking voice was refined and articulate and whose singing voice was crystal clear and quite sublime. She ran the gamut of her emotions most successfully. Damien Donegan was a most affable and charming Captain Von Trapp, who handled his affection for Maria and his children with sincerity. Perhaps he could have been a little sterner and introvert in the early scenes to accentuate his eventual relaxing, but he cut a fine figure nonetheless, and his rendition of his songs, particularly Edelweiss, was most affecting.

Tom McCarthy displayed very secure comedic timing in the role of Uncle Max, likeably roguish in his dealings with the Captain and Elsa, and comfortable when engaging with the children. His musicality complemented Elsa's in a well delivered How Can Love Survive. Patricia Voon, as the aforementioned Elsa, was appropriately flirtatious with the captain, relaxed with Uncle Max, suitably uncomfortable with the children and acerbic and dry witted towards Maria, achieving all that her character demanded. Angela O'Toole made an authoritative yet sympathetic Mother Abbess and gave an uplifting rendition of Climb Every Mountain. She even seemed tolerant of that world-weary nun who kept knocking back the communion wine!

Alanna Keane captured the impetuous innocence of Liesl most effectively, singing and performing with confidence and being an inspiration to the rest of the Von Trapp children. Sean Maguire as Friedrich, Ceola Cathcart as Louisa, Finn O'Shea as Kurt, Ciara Wynne as Brigitta, Aoife Cathcart as Marta and little Lucy Heywood as Gretl, did all that was required of them to present a perfect family unit. They managed their harmonies quite comfortably and always looked as if they were enjoying their contribution to the show.

Daragh Conneff, as Rolf, was charming and impulsive in his early flirting with Liesl and performed Sixteen Going on Seventeen delightfully, and he progressed effectively into the more unpleasant young Nazi of the second act and redeeming himself in the final scene.

There were good variations in the characters of effervescent, fun-loving Sister Margareta, played by Teresa Lynch, stern and severe Sister Bertha, played by Marie O'Neill and the more homely and wholesome Sister Sophia of Rossagh Cusack, each maintaining their characters effectively and making a good vocal contribution in How Do You Solve a Problem like Maria.

There was a particularly lovely performance from Laura Sheehan as Frau Schmidt, capturing all the frustration of her position within the household, and reacting with sincere indignation when intimidated by Herr Zeller. Very nicely played. There was an equally mature and confident performance from Brian McCabe as the turn-coat butler, Franz. Adam Pamplin's Zeller was suitably cold and threatening, and Tony Victory was a capable and competent Admiral Von Schriber. There were commendable performances too from Karen Fogarty as Ursula, Caroline Kane Montague as Baroness Von Schriber and the young postulants.

The Nuns Chorus contributed securely to the success of the show with good harmonies and a comfortable presence on the stage. While I was quite tickled by the comedy of the wine guzzling nun and the irreverent comedic behaviour of the young postulants, it came close to crossing the line into farce, but the chorus clearly enjoyed themselves and so did a very appreciative audience.

This show is cropping up quite a lot this year. Thank goodness it's one for which I have a great fondness, and I'm indebted to Kill Musical and Dramatic Society for a thoroughly entertaining production.

As with many companies this season, Dun Laoghaire decided to go for a popular "feel-good" show to lure the audiences back after lockdown, and The Wedding Singer proved to be a good choice, filled with lively up-beat music, a good range of comical characters and a plot that entertains enormously without taxing the brain too much. Just what the doctor ordered.

It has to be said that the final scene of the movie is considerably better written than the stage version, which is somewhat cheesy and disjointed, but fair play to director, Brian Dennison, for trying to make the most of it, with good comedic effect. He did a particularly good job of injecting pace and flow into a show that can often suffer from being rather piecemeal in design. Characters were generally well- developed, and he achieved good, varied atmospheres at the different weddings. While the story was well told, I think that more variety in the set might have helped to suggest different locations more obviously.

Any variety there was in the technical presentation of the show, came from good lighting and a quite well-used upper walk- way, with a cyclorama that varied with good effects. The main stage, however, was a curtained background that became a bit monotonous, despite being dressed with good props and furniture, and being well-managed by Nola Lambert and her team. It worked well for the various weddings, but less so for the offices and outdoor scenes. Perhaps the use of a few sliding/folding or revolving panels at the outer edges of the curtains might have added a little to variations in the visual impact of the scenery. As mentioned, the lighting was good, with good use of colours, starlight and disco effects, and the sound quality, apart from a few feedback issues, was good throughout the show.

Costumes for the show were very good, era appropriate and well-coordinated. A lot of attention was given to hairstyles and wigs, most of which were excellent, as was the make-up. Great job on "Kiss" star, Gene Simmons.

Musical Director, Des Cox had a very good band under his control, who played with precision and good balance throughout. Principals were most tuneful and well- prepared, and the chorus had good vocal quality and energy. All-in-all, a very pleasing musical presentation, which was often enhanced visually by well-conceived and varied choreography, in the hands of Laura Lambert. The various wedding routines, and the Bar mitzvah dance were particularly enjoyable, although Right in Front of Your Eyes and Move That Thang perhaps needed a bit more substance. Generally, the dances were well performed by an energetic chorus.

Playing the title role of Robbie Hart, David Hynes' greatest asset was a silky smooth vocal quality which was very good during the pop/rock numbers, but excellent in rendering the shows nicest ballads, "If I Told You" and "Grow Old With You".  He maintained a good, likeable character throughout the show, even if a tad over the top in the drunk scene, but this was a quality performance. Loveable, too, was Leonna Condron in the role of Julia, so loveable indeed that one wonders why she would ever have fallen for a schmuck like Glen. Her acting was innocent and sincere, and her vocals were quite beautiful. Her comedy was well-timed too. Laila McDonald had the perfect look for Hollie and she sang very well, but on occasions, she seemed a little self- conscious in her acting and movement. She did display good attitude in dealing with Sammy and was suitably sympathetic towards Robbie. Alan Lau's Sammy was a well-achieved un-cool, wannabe cool guy, giving energy to all his numbers, although he too seemed a little self-conscious of his abilities. Full of arrogance and narcissism was John May's Glen Guglia, very capably achieving the persona of a philandering love-rat. This role was confidently acted and very well-sung.

Oisin Casey got plenty of camp comedy from the role of George without ever taking it too far. A nicely balanced comical role, with good vocals and very comfortable movement. Deliciously crass and vulgar was Robbie's fiancée Linda, played as close to the knuckle as was reasonable by scantily-clad Laura Lambert. This was a very comical and well-delivered character, making the most of her few opportunities to shine.

The beautifully genteel portrayal of Rosie, by Marlene Connolly, resulted in her frequent outbursts of inappropriate commentary being completely hilarious. Everyone ought to have such a sassy, yet sophisticated granny. Very well played. Julia's waitress friends were played with confidence and a lot of fun by Hannah Sheehy, Steffi Rogers, Laura Charleton, Julianne Hurley and Ruth Crowley, all of whom added personality, comedy and great vocal back-up to the action, each displaying good individuality. Hannah was also a good Marilyn Munroe and Steffi convinced as Cher, alongside Jillian Fitzpatrick as a believable Dolly Parton, Ruairi Boland as a very well painted Gene Simmons, and Denis Sherlock had great fun pretending to be Elvis.

The chorus were really a collective of cameo supporting roles, from best man to brides, to parents, to secretaries and barflies. So many of them had their moment in the limelight and made the most of it. As a group, they responded very well and always appropriately to the central action. Their vocal prowess was of a very good standard and they all moved well.

Marian Holden and her team were delightful and efficient in their duties. Hospitality was generous and it was a pleasure to meet the Director before the show. Aside from the few small criticisms above, this was a thoroughly enjoyable presentation of a show that represents entertainment for entertainments sake. Very nicely done. Thank you for a lively and colourful night of musical fun.

Me and My Girl is a musical that follows the trials and tribulations of a Cockney man, Bill Snibson, after he learns he has inherited an earl's title.  It premiered at the Victoria Palace in December 1937. The production was a star vehicle for English comedian Lupino Lane, who also served as producer and director. The show has been revived in London multiple times, notably in 1985 at the Adelphi in a production starring Emma Thompson and Robert Lindsay. That production featured a revised book by Stephen Fry and Mike Ockrent and won the Olivier Award for Musical of the Year. This is the version I attended on Valentine's Night at Ballinrobe Community School.

Produced by Ballinrobe Musical Society and directed by AIMS colleague, Peter Kennedy, I was really looking forward to seeing their take on this classic gender- switched Cinderella story. I last saw them in 2019 when they produced a super 'Chitty Chitty Bang Bang', which was very popular. The Society was founded in 1944 and has produced 'Me and My Girl' before, in 2002.

This rags to riches story features Bill Snibson, a Lambeth costermonger, who is revealed to be the new Earl of Hareford and of course his newly discovered aristocratic relations are horrified. Bringing him to Hareford Hall, they attempt to educate Bill into the ways of the gentry and separate him from his cockney girlfriend Sally. So, it's 'Cinderella' with a dash of 'My Fair Lady'!

The success of the show firmly rests on the performer playing Bill Snibson and here we had the very enthusiastic John Byrne. Mr Byrne's Bill Snibson was full of energy, twitches and stage business. He ran around the stage, falling over, making witty remarks to the toffs and at times was exhausting to watch! His quieter scenes with Sally were lovely and showed a nice depth of characterisation. His singing was good too, particularly on "Leaning on the Lamppost" and "Hold My Hand" with Sally. Playing Sally was the wonderful Helena Brosnan. Ms Brosnan brought a classiness to the role which was refreshing. Her singing was exquisite, especially on "Once You Lose Your Heart" in a delicately played scene in a pub, and her duets with Bill were heartfelt. She really engaged with her other fellow performers too, reacting to their lines with thoughtful expressions and actions, which is somewhat rare in musical theatre!

The executers of the will of the former Earl of Hareford, Maria, Duchess of Dene played by Siobhan Campbell and Sir John Tremayne played by Niall Conway, summon Bill to them to break the news that he will be the new Earl. Ms Campbell played Maria as a domineering matriarch who was a stickler for tradition. She sported a fine RP and sang and danced with skill. Her love/hate relationship with Sir John was nicely played out too. Niall Conway as Sir John gave a masterclass on truthfulness in a role. He played his scenes with Maria with a gorgeous delicacy and was superbly empathetic with Sally. His drunk scene with Bill was the stand-out scene of the show and his comic timing was perfect. His singing was fine on the few numbers he was in too! Of course, for the drama to work there must be an antagonist and in this show we had two: Lady Jacqueline Carstone, a self- centred gold digger and Maria's daughter who's engaged to The Hon Gerald Bolingbroke a pompous fop. He's Maria's nephew, entitled and quite the simpering fool. Lady Jacqueline was played with great fervour by Kate McDonnell her attempts to seduce Bill were some of the funnier scenes in the production and she sang quite well, especially on "The Sun Has Got His Hat On" with Gerald and Company and "Thinking of No-one but Me" again with Gerald. As Gerald, Walter Donoghue had a super physicality and a good singing voice particularly on "The Sun Has Got His Hat On", where he stole the number! They were both very good characterisations and when Lady Jacqueline broke off her engagement with Gerald, he spent the rest of the show trying to woo her back whilst she went after Bill, for his new fortune not because she liked him. Other characters relevant to the plot were the family solicitor, Herbert Parchester played by Richard Crumlish in a scene stealing performance where he sang "The Family Solicitor" one of the show's best numbers; Des Treacy as Charles the butler, his performance of "An English Gentleman" with the staff of the house was excellent and he had superb comic timing; Gerry Hughes who played Sir Jasper Tring, a nonagenarian charismatic old relic, with a fine avuncular touch and Michael Sweeney and Gemma Gannon who played the dipso Lord Battersby and his domineering wife with nice comic timing. Suffice to say, Bill became an Earl and Sally married him and they all lived happily ever after.

Some of the songs in this show are immediately recognisable to patrons of a certain age such as "Leaning on the Lamppost", "The Sun Has Got It's Hat On" and of course "The Lambeth Walk". Musical Director, Finola Higgins, conducted a nine-piece band of rather excellent players.

The percussion drove the entire show and was perfect, with a great use of the slide whistle to accentuate the humour. The piano and violin were excellent on "Once You Lose Your Heart" and the brass and woodwind were all spot on. The harmonies on "Love Makes the World Go Round (reprise)" were excellent as was her work with the principals and it all bounced along like a day at the seaside. Choreography by Aoife McClafferty was very effective. The "Lambeth Walk" was ingenuously easy and yet looked great, especially when the cast exited through the audience at the end of the first act. The various pas de deux between Sally and Bill were great, they were like Fred & Ginger and both performers excelled especially on the reprises. The tap dances were also super, particularly on the title song.

It was all nicely stage managed by the Society's Chairperson, Kenneth McCarthy, brightly lit by Derek Bauman with energetic sound by Derek Recks. Costumes were excellent and of the era, especially the Pearly Kings and Queens and make-up and hair looked good. A nice set design by director Peter Kennedy was effectively painted by Sile Hughes and local students.

Peter Kennedy directed with a light touch, eliciting some lovely performances from some of his cast. Mr Kennedy accentuated the slapstick and farcical nature of the piece, especially on the brilliantly executed drunk scene between Bill and John. Some of the comic timing in the show was a bit off and some of the gags didn't quite land and we lost some of Stephen Fry's more subtle witticisms, but the physical comedy was very good. Generally, the direction was smooth the show was solid with good production values and the audience loved it!

Curtain Up Curtains is a musical comedy whodunnit, written by 'Cabaret' and 'Chicago' creators Kander and Ebb, with book by Rupert Holmes. It's an oddity for sure, light, and easy as it lampoons 'show people' and the Agatha Christie and Sherlock Holms locked room mysteries. It's a play within a play à la 'Hamlet' but without the ghosts or fine writing but with the body count. The trick to producing 'Curtains' is to not take it too seriously and too mine the text for the humour.

The show is set in 1959 Boston, where a troupe of actors is trying out a musical called 'Robbin' Hood of the Old West'. During the opening night curtain call, the supremely untalented star, Jessica Cranshaw, drops dead. Lt. Frank Cioffi, a closet musical theatre fan, is sent to the theatre to investigate what has been determined to be a murder, declaring no one is allowed to leave the building. The list of suspects includes pretty much everybody, as no one liked Jessica and her underserved fame. Cioffi falls for one of the actresses, Niki, and this attraction is not unrequited. Meanwhile, the body count rises and Cioffi realises a long- standing ambition to appear in a musical. Produced and staged by Malahide Musical and Dramatic Society in their local Community School, the show was directed by Emma Jane Reilly with musical direction by Emer Hartnett and choreography by Julianne McNamara. Emma Jane Reilly directed a fast-paced homage to theatre with a good eye for the comedy and farce. Ms Reilly also knew when to bring it all down to focus on specific relationships, giving time and space for these to develop. Some lovely little touches like the over emoting warm up for "The Woman's Dead" and the MD singing "The Man is Dead"; Joannie doing the fire speech; reversing the action for the "Robin Hood…" curtain call; the Cabaret homage on "Thataway!" and the blue material for "In the Same Boat -Complete". The timing of the gags and the dance numbers were great, and everything flowed beautifully especially the music. Emer Hartnett conducted a ten-piece band of horns, woodwind, keys, double-bass, guitar, and drums, with Ms Hartnett on keys and, surprisingly, vocals at the start of Act II when she sang "The Man is Dead" from the conductor's stand! I was captivated by the drummer who was so focused on what he was doing he really shone. He was stoic in his appearance and was the backbone of the production. The double-bass was equally responsible for driving the pace. Ms Hartnett's work with the ensemble was super. The harmonising on "He Did It" and "Show People" was gorgeous. The principals were all vocally very good and I loved Lynda O'Neill's dreadful tuning!

The dance numbers in the show are mostly in the play within the play and choreographer Julianne McNamara injected fun and energy into proceedings. "Wide Open Spaces" was a traditional hoedown where some performers were out of sync, not just Jessica, which was great. "Show People" was a throwback to the old MGM Musicals and worked a treat and we had elements of Fred & Ginger in Frank & Niki's pas de deux. "Thataway!" evoked earlier Kander & Ebb musicals like 'Cabaret' and 'Chicago', with the sexy, sleazy Fosse style choreography, which Georgia and the ensemble performed with loads of energy and panache.

Acting in a pastiche can be great fun as you get to lampoon your own calling. In 'Curtains' most of the performers are encouraged to go over the top, overact and generally behave like spoilt children. The only ones who don't do this are the cop, Lt. Cioffi and the stage manager, Joannie. They are more like parents to a rowdy bunch of kids sequestered in a theatre.

Playing Lt. Cioffi we were blessed to have Gavin Molony, who had a soft naturalism which morphed at times into excitement and glee that he was with his 'heroes' as he was a great admirer of theatre. He had great timing and was always present and in the moment on stage, totally focused on his fellow performers throughout. He had good energy also, exploding on to stage at times in his entrances which revitalised the cast. Mr Molony had a great voice too with a lovely tone and expression, especially on "Coffee Shop Nights" and "A Tough Act to Follow" with Niki the girl he falls for during his investigation. Kristin Keegan's Niki was demure and self-effacing yet clearly had something to hide. Ms Keegan played her as a wistful character in the flush of her attraction of Frank and this worked for this show. Her timing on the frequent red herrings she had to deliver was excellent as was her chemistry with Frank. She had a lovely voice and danced well particularly on "A Tough Act to Follow". They were perfect together and bounced well off each other. Playing one half of the writing duo, Georgia, who created the play within the play 'Robin Hood of the Old West', was Rebecca Gamble. Ms Gamble had a great stage presence and a wonderful voice with a marvellous silky tone. Her stage focus was particularly notable, and she was clearly fully invested in the role. Her onstage love/hate relationship with Aaron was very believable and the dénouement of their sub-plot was really pleasing for the audience. Her singing on "Thinking of Him" was lovely and "Thataway!" was brilliant. The other half of the duo was Aaron Fox, played by Daire Kelly. He gave us the sarcasm, the songwriter's excitement of getting to re-write some of the songs and the sadness of losing Georgia. He portrayed Aaron as a petulant yet quite lovable artist, which really worked for the character. His singing on "I Miss the Music" was gorgeous and the reprise with Georgia was touching. They were very well cast and like Frank and Niki quite believable as a couple.

The money-grabbing, tough producer of 'Robin Hood of the Old West', Carmen, was played with scenery chewing relish by Jennifer McGuire Noirant. Ms McGuire Noirant had an incredible voice, every time she sang was a masterclass on how to deliver a song. Reminiscent of Ethel Merman in her heyday, her timing, pace, expression, and dexterity was second to none. Her characterisation of Carmen as the brash and no-nonsense producer was excellent. Her tough love relationship with Bambi/Elaine was finely drawn and she showed the character's every thought in real time on her face. Lovely performance and I particularly enjoyed her "It's a Business" and of course "Show People". Bambi, her daughter was portrayed by Áine Murray, who had a great deer-in-the- headlights look, which she used to good effect in this show. Playing the understudy who wants her big break and being denied it exacerbated her ire, as did her mother's dismissal of her, which was palpable. She danced well and sang with aplomb and was brilliantly cast in the role and was great at the splits! Carmen's philandering husband and Bambi's stepfather, Sidney, was Mark Keegan. He had a great gravelly voice and an amazing moustache! He embodied the predatory producer with alacrity and zeal. Perhaps taking his cue from a famous Hollywood producer who is now incarcerated, he was all eyes and hands as he ogled the dancers, including his own stepdaughter. His comeuppance was expected and delighted in by the audience which is a testament to Mr Kelly's performance.

The director of the group was Englishman Christopher Belling here played by the deadpan Dave Clark. He was superb when delivering the brilliantly written one-liners of which his character had the lion's share. Belling is a role that's often played with a lot of camp, but Mr Clark didn't flounce around. He played him more as a harassed has been director, reduced to working on drivel, which was I think the right decision. The lynchpin of this production was Mary Gamble who played stage manager, Joannie. She was the personification of a pressured stage manager. She had all of the patter and the gestures and gave off that "I'll just mop up after your self-expression, shall I?" cynicism that some stage managers revel in. The constant setting and striking of the piano by her was very funny as were her expressions and general attitude. She also opened the show by giving the Fire speech to the audience, which was a great touch by Ms Reilly.

Other notable actors in the production were; Malcolm Bolton as Daryl Grady, theatre critic of the Boston Globe newspaper who was sarcastic, and clearly hated 'show people'; Pauline McGuire as Annie Shapiro, the money woman who bankrolled the production, she was on stage for much of the time with very few lines, but she was always on point, reacting to events and dialogue; Nathan Durkin as Bobby Pepper, the lead actor in 'Robin Hood…' where he excelled; Lynda O'Neill as Jessica Cranshaw who had to sing and dance badly, which she did!; Darren O'Reilly as Randy Dexter and James Sullivan as Harv Freemont, who played company members who shone in the 'Robin Hood…' play, both actors are new to the stage and I hope we will see them again as they were great.

The cool thing about this show is that the main set is actually a theatre stage, the play within a play set should look terribly amateur too, so it shouldn't cost a lot to get the right look! Designed by EJ Reilly, Stewart Bourke, and Teresa Farrell the set was garish and very effective and I loved the scaff tower on the apron. Sound by Jason Fallon was very band heavy, so they drowned out a lot of the vocals from the stage which was a pity. Lighting by Cathal O'Donoghue was good, and I liked the use of torches in Act II and the shell footlights. Andrew Reddy's costumes were super. Effectively costuming two shows in one, his 'Robin Hood…' costumes were perfect all yee haw and hoedown and the sailor's costumes and Cabaret Basques & red shorts were fab. The street clothes of the performers were also very good with a great range of furs!! Bairbre NíBhróin's wigs were excellent, very natural looking. Make Up by Catherine Fox, Lesley Nugent and Evelyn Lambe was also very good, and it was all perfectly stage managed by Caoimhe Farrell and her crew.

It was a great night of theatre, full of lovely theatrical business that the initiated in the audience clearly enjoyed, often seeing themselves up there in situations they may have experienced (minus the murders I hope). For the non- 'show people', it was a rip-roaring murder mystery whodunnit about people with massive egos.

Plant Based Musical Loosely based on Goethe's 'Faust' and a low budget Roger Corman film from 1960, 'Little Shop of Horrors' was turned into a musical by Alan Menken and Howard Ashman in 1982. Like Richard O'Brien's 1973 'Rocky Horror Picture Show', it's a comedy take on schlock horror B-movies of the '50's. Most audiences today will be aware of the Frank Oz film from 1986, which was very popular and made an unlikely star of its lead, Rick Moranis. Set in New York in the 1960's, it's about an orphan, Seymour, who is indentured to a flower shop owner, Mr Mushnik, who 'lets' him work in his failing shop in exchange for food and board. Seymour is secretly in love with his co-worker Audrey, who is the girlfriend of a sadistic misogynist dentist, Orin. Seymour buys an unusual plant that appears to be dying and inadvertently feeds it his own blood. Naming the plant Audrey II, he soon realises that the plant has become sentient and demands more flesh and blood. Mushnik notices that the plant has grown and is attracting good attention for the shop, so 'adopts' Seymour to keep the plant. However, Audrey II reveals that it wants to take over the world, so Seymour must make some difficult decisions.

It's a great plot, like an Ed Wood film or a pulp science fiction novel and has a super doo-wop score. I saw it produced by Shannon Musical Society in their local Comprehensive School in February this year and I loved it. It had charm and talent and didn't take itself too seriously.

Directed by Aódan Fox, with musical direction by Shane Farrell and choreography by Karen Barrett the production leaped off the stage with passion and energy and sheer joy. The Society constructed a revolve stage, which made for quick and easy scene transitions thus keeping the pace of the show fast and orderly. It had three wonderful leads in Tom Barrett as Seymour, Olivia Parkinson as Audrey and Eoin Sheedy as Mr Mushnik and fabulous Greek Chorus and the thunderous vocal of Colm McGuinness as the voice of Audrey II.

Aodán Fox directed with a real knowledge of the material and how he wanted it to look, feel and sound. The interpretation was excellent, not a direct copy as we often see but he added little touches, like the addition of an additional character to the Greek Chorus and played with the piece. The pacing was fast, aided by the revolve, yet he also allowed some quieter scenes room to breathe. Shane Farrell conducted a small band of seven players including himself on keys. They were tight and clearly fed off the energy of the cast, blending seamlessly into a rare synergy between the performers on stage and band. This rarely happens in my experience; in that they are usually two very separate entities who work together but remain aloof from each other. Here, Mr Farrell managed to blend the two together as one unit working in complete harmony and it worked so well, it gave us a complete experience.

It's not a big dance show but where we had dance Karen Barrett's choreography was full of energy. The Greek Chorus were perfectly in time with each other and were very well rehearsed. The bigger numbers like "Skid Row" were quite complex, given that most of the playing area was taken up with the revolve, yet wove in and around the structures. Even though she clearly had the dancers, Ms Barrett avoided making it too 'High School Musical', which was a good choice as all the choreography was there for a reason - to further the story and to expand on the characters' world rather than showcasing her or the performers talents. If more choreographers and MD's were as tuned into the director's vision as Ms Barrett and Mr Farrell were on this show; we'd rule the musical theatre world!

The ensemble was mostly quite young in age but seasoned in talent. They populated the streets of Skid Row with a grounded belonging, sang and danced with effortless ability and generally fleshed out the exterior scenes. They also provided excellent harmonies on the bigger numbers and subtle backing on some of the solo ballads. Joyful and present, these performers were very well cast and rehearsed.

Seymour is quite a difficult role as the character's journey from nervous nerdy orphan to murderer is tricky to pull off. However, Tom Barrett managed this with aplomb. Mr Barrett looked the part too; geeky and nerdy and clearly the last one to be picked for teams in school. His quirky dysmorphic physicality, glasses and costume helped too. His singing was good, his tuning first-rate, and his tone suited the character. "Suddenly Seymour" was excellent as was "Grow for Me". Seymour's journey from bookish shop boy to genocidal alien's apprentice was nicely plotted and we empathised with his exasperation and desperation. We also empathised with Audrey, his crush. Played by Olivia Parkinson who reminded me of the amazing Bernadette Peters, one of Sondheim's muses, in that she portrayed Audrey's vulnerability with such truth. Her singing was exceptional, on "Somewhere That's Green", a deceptively difficult song to do well, where she bared the emotion of the notes and on "Suddenly Seymour" where she lived the budding romantic connection with Seymour and got across the emotion of the song. A fabulous NYC accent, eccentric physicality, and a lovely vulnerability - Ms Parkinson was Audrey, and we could see why Seymour was smitten with her.

Another superb performance was Eoin Sheedy as Mr Mushnik. I loved his character; pure NYC complete with accent and Jewish mannerisms. He sang well on "Ya Never Know" and with great funny subtext on "Mushnik and Son". His Mushnik was quite caring, despite him being a bit of a monster towards Seymour, and the audience loved him. Audrey's egotistical misogynist boyfriend, Oran, was played by Ciarán Collins. He was uber-misogynist, snarky, full of himself and I suspect gave Audrey II indigestion! Oran can be overplayed, like a panto or cartoon-baddie, but Mr Collins played him with a smoothness rather than an over-the-top caricature. "Dentist" was a highlight of the production as was his various cameos later in the show!

Many shows are written with a Greek Chorus, it's a great narrative device that goes back to the dawn of theatre.
