Olivia Parkinson gave a warm and resolute performance as Kath, Joe's widowed mother. There was great strength in her determination to survive her hardships and great passion in her relationship with Joe. Her songs were delivered with clarity and sincerity.

Sally Fox as Billie, and Alanna Willets as Angie provided the comedic back-up to Sarah, and did so with a great sense of fun, and often a caustic sense of humour. These were strong performers who, given that the show is very much a drama with music, perhaps played just a little too obviously to the audience rather than to their fellow performers. They were, nonetheless, delightfully funny and crass, and both were very capable of belting out their lyrics. On Joe's side of the table, comedy support came from Cillian Fahy as Emmo and Ciarán O'Keefe as Lewis. Both made the most of their opportunities, with Cillian in particular, acting out the required immaturity to present himself as the twit of the group.

As the bad apple, irresponsible delinquent of the piece, Sean McInerney was a strong and repugnant Reecey, as was required of him. It's not always easy to play the bully, but he did so with conviction.

There was a note-worthy performance from old-timer, Aodan Fox, as the corrupt businessman, Mr Pressman, and it's fair to assume that the many younger performers on the stage have learned a lot from his self-assured, always considered and highly professional approach to every part he plays. Completing the younger cast were good solid performances from Tara Monaghan as Julie and Richard Germaine as Callum, while Dara O'Callaghan, Ian Collins, Laura O'Brien, Michelle Kelly, Sarah Allen and Kim O'Dea filled a vast array of supporting cameo roles with credibility and confidence. A special mention too, for the delightful cameo performances of Cormac Ross as Elvis and Cooper.

Sheer energy was the key to the success of the chorus, whether it was the vocal energy of their strong choral contributions, or the physical energy of their wonderfully performed dance routines. They were never on stage looking lost or being passive. They always contributed to the atmosphere and ambiance of their scenes. Visually, the show was also most successful. The black suit and white track-suit of Joe worked brilliantly in facilitating those numerous and essential fast changes. Similarly, Sarah's costumes were well selected to blend with each scene.

Costumes generally were attractive, era-appropriate and worn well by the company. From hairstyles, to make up, to footwear, the cast looked correct from head to toe. The extra-speedy on-stage costume change for Joe was amazingly slick!

There's no such thing as a flawless or perfect production, but it's an awesome experience when a show comes close. Not for the first time this season, I'm feeling that awe. Well done, Muse, on something pretty spectacular.

There was something nostalgic and wonderful about seeing Director Ronan Lardner and Musical Director, Shane Farrell working side-by-side in the very venue where they both cut their musical teeth, under the guidance of the late, great Joe O'Donoghue and the late, great Noel Kirrane. How proud their past masters would have been to see how both of their students have established themselves in musical theatre. They would most certainly have been impressed with this wonderfully joyful production of Sister Act. Boasting a highly talented front line and an energetic and enthusiastic chorus, this was entertainment of the highest order. An excellent comedian himself, director Ronan Lardner managed to wring every ounce of comedy out of the very funny script, and added many little individual touches, but he was just as thorough about playing up the sentimental side of the story.

The set for the show was as simple as possible, given a stage that has no room at all for massive pieces or storage, but it was clean, effective and well-painted. Only essential items of props and furniture were apparent, and it was more than enough. The centre piece of the set was an excellent circular stained-glass window, which, combined with really effective lighting, looked superb. The confessional boxes were very good, and the rest of the props were appropriate and acceptable. A centre stage black gauze was well used both for isolating the forward scenes but also as a bleed-through to create some nice effects. Lighting was generally very good, with atmospheric use of colours and back light. Sound quality throughout was just about perfect.

The band, under the direction of Shane Farrell, obviously enjoyed every note of this excellent musical score, playing with a vibrant and precise energy, always on point, and always sympathetic to the vocalists on stage. Tempi throughout were just perfect. Shane had gone to town on the choral vocals, as evidenced by secure harmonies, excellent diction and a certain joie de vivre in performance. This was a top drawer choral display. Musically and physically, they performed out of their skins, adding a secure backbone to the whole production. Their sheer sense of enjoyment was contagious.

Commanding the stage from the get-go, Emma Brady proved to be the perfect casting for the demanding role of Deloris Van Cartier. Her acting and her comedy were on point, her movement was fluid, and when she sang… Wow! With a voice like a finely tuned instrument, she raised the roof in every number. Whether with the gentle, dulcet and emotional tones of 'Sister Act' or unleashing the inner beast in 'Take Me to Heaven' and 'Raise Your Voice', the vocal quality was simply awesome. It almost converted me!

There was a sublime quality to the voice and performance of Frieda McGrath as the Mother Superior, dignity and decorum epitomized, until the strain of coping with Deloris eventually cracked her outer shell. Then she delighted us with a very funny and slightly demented rendition of 'I Haven't Got A Prayer'. Frieda and Emma played off each other absolutely beautifully.

A young and endearing Alana Mullins made a big impact as the shy and reserved Sr Mary Robert, then floored us all with her feisty power when she unleashed 'The Life I Never Led'. Such talent from one so young, and a very well-played role.

Who can resist a nun with attitude? With a voice that could shatter concrete, a presence that would ward of the devil, and an abundance of comedic talent, Clodagh Ruane rocked and rapped her way into our hearts with a superb performance as Sr Mary Lazarus.

Olivia McNama was filled with fun and religious fervour as the highly animated and extremely funny Sr Mary Patrick, making the most of all her opportunities to shine. There were equally accomplished performances from Eimear McGovern as Sr Mary Theresa and Sinead Whelan as Sr Mary Martin-of-Tours.

Congratulations to the very talented Declan Kelly for playing Monsignor O'Hara with great empathy, understanding, excellent comedic timing and a modicum of irreverent humour.

Norman Quinn presented us with a very sweaty and very loveable Eddie, playing the love-struck, weak-willed cop to perfection. He realised his comedy most effectively and sang like a nervous bird until he found himself being suddenly manly. A lovely performance.

Niall Conway was a strong and believable gang-leader in the role of mafia-style hoodlum, Curtis.

His stature made him imposing but it was his menacing demeanour and his confident acting that made him such a convincing character. The man can sing a bit too. He was ably assisted in his nefarious endeavours by a trio of comically inept bad-guys, Stuart Barrows as Joey, as smooth as he was stylish, Thomas Edwards, as TJ, the very funny idiot relation that everyone denies knowing, and Michael Cooney, the ludicrous Latino who represents the strongest argument for tighter border controls. Very good performances from this whole team of desperados.

As Deloris's night-club sidekicks, Michelle and Tina, Emer Kelly and Sinead Murphy sang and danced delightfully and handled their dialogue with assured comedic ability. It's a pity these parts aren't bigger, but very nicely played.

There was good support, too, from Sean King as the 'disposable' Ernie, who also doubled as an altar boy alongside Ruadhan Gormally. Feargal MacMeanmain made a delightful cameo appearance as the Pope, even kneeling down to kiss the floor of the school hall. A nice touch.

From a visual point of view, you can't go too far wrong with nuns habits, and in this case, they were worn well, and increased delightfully in glitz and glamour as the show progressed through to a dazzling finale. Principal costumes were all appropriate, although you could have been a little more flamboyant with the hoodlums outfits. Curtis was delightfully dapper as the gang-leader. Eddie's triple costume was very good, and not at all obvious before he was disrobed. Wigs/ hairstyles were fine, although Deloris might have had a slightly tidier corkscrew, but it didn't impede the quality of her performance. Make up seemed natural, with no glaring eye-liners or polished nails on the nuns. Good work.

Sister Act isn't the most challenging show to stage or to perform, but it is most certainly one of the best feel-good shows of the modern era, and when it is performed to such a high standard, it is easy to get carried along by the euphoria and the heavenly goodness of the piece. This wasn't a very good production, it was a very excellent production, and it was a privilege to see Marian Choral Society reaching such heights of achievement. Thank you for a truly wonderful night.

Tralee's Siamsa Tíre is a beautiful venue, and one that I always enjoy visiting, and when the standard of production and performance is as high as was presented by LOST, it makes the journey south seem somehow shorter and so worthwhile. "Evita" is a wonderful biographical musical, with a superb score and an intriguing story, but it can be very demanding, which makes the success of this production all the sweeter. From sets and costumes to direction and choreography and magical musicianship, all the elements came together beautifully to frame and accentuate a cast of excellent performers. Director Grainne O'Carroll's passion for this show was clearly evident in her disciplined and beautifully stylised production. The attention to detail was excellent, from the eye-catching set to the costumes, the lighting, the groupings on stage and the right tone and mood of each scene. With a very well-constructed and painted set, featuring nice little playing areas on the front aprons, and a stunning Casa Rosada centrepiece, the stage was beautifully and atmospherically lit throughout, with good use of colours and nicely defined special areas. Props were generally very good, although I'd like to have seen maybe more bunting or national flags for the countries on the Rainbow Tour. The projected footage of the cinema, and then the newsreel of the actual Eva Peron funeral was of very good quality. The production was streamlined, with little or no superfluous dressing or action, which saw the focal point of the action always clearly apparent, and it helped to maintain a very good pace. If she had felt so inclined, Grainne might have added another dimension visually by being a bit more flamboyant and carnival minded in the costuming of the 'Buenos Aires' number. However, chorus costumes had good variety between the street people and the sophisticates, and the men's uniforms were, by and large, appropriate and well-worn. Eva Peron's gowns were fabulous and flattering, her red outfit being wonderful in allowing her the freedom for the stylised dancing, and the white balcony dress was exquisite. Peron was sharp and elegant, and Che was cool and casual.

Ranging from precise military style routines to flamboyant street dances, including very well-devised choreographed fights and an elegant tango and waltz, a great amount of thought and care went into the work of choreographer, Tara Dore. It was vibrant, fluent and mostly extremely well executed by the chorus and dancers. Dancing on chairs is never easy, but in the 'Art of the Possible' routine, the cast were meticulously well-drilled. This was a most varied and exciting dance show.

A very strong orchestra, under the guidance and leadership of Musical Director, Anna Connolly, played the beautiful musical score with tone, balance and wonderful expression. Rhythms and pace were pretty much perfect. Chorus Mistress, Caitriona Fitzmaurice, had her singers well-drilled and full of expression and articulation. The quality of the music, throughout, was extremely high.

There can be few female roles as demanding as that of Eva Peron, requiring powerful vocals and a wide range of emotions, and in Clodagh Harrington, this production has found the perfect performer for the role. From the flirtatious social climber to the manipulative power behind Peron, she infused her character with style and dynamism, most often expressed through a pitch perfect and commanding vocal display.

Clodagh played this role several years ago as a very promising up-and-coming artiste, but now she has come of age with a quite brilliant performance.

There was a stirring performance too from Marcus Nolan as Peron, strong in stature, secure in his vocals, highly believable in his acting and also fleet of foot as he fought his way into power. This was a sincere and well-rounded characterisation.

Sean McElligot, as the narrator, Che, despite the annoyance of a dodgy radio- mic for his early scenes, never lost his composure and kept the story moving with a strong and confident personality, and an excellent voice.

Owen Rua Herlihy established himself as the crooner Magaldi with a fine rendition of 'On This Night of a Thousand Stars'. Perhaps we needed to see more obviously his flirting with Eva at the start, but his frustration at her behaviour as the show progressed was well-registered.

In the most thankless role of the Mistress, Lauren Glennon did all you really can do, which is to sell the beautiful 'Another Suitcase in Another Hall' with conviction. She displayed nice vocal quality and expression.

All the cameo supporting roles, like officers, ministers, sisters, servants and townsfolk, were played with conviction, and a special mention for little Kate Roche, who was the delightful solo voice in 'Santa Evita'.

If I was to be very critical, I could say that one or two performers were a tad behind the beat or stuttered in the execution of some of their steps, but to be honest, the overall impact of the very slick and disciplined choreography washed away any negative thoughts, as the chorus and dancers gave 100% commitment to every routine. They were vocally extremely secure and their involvement in the various scenes always had a purpose. They were poignantly stiff and upright as the pretentious Buenos Aires elite, and strong and revolutionary as street people. Very good work.

Giving that I attended this show on opening night, I'm reluctant to be too critical of minor technical issues, and I'm prepared to believe that the glitches with the radio-mics will be quickly eliminated. Indeed, as the night progressed, it was already being dealt with. However, the sound quality was a little bit patchy and uneven on occasions and did need some attention.

No production achieves perfection, if such a thing even exists, but when so many aspects of a show reach such a high level, it is fair to say that it was perfectly stunning, as was most definitely the case with this production. When the overall effect is powerful enough to blur out the small weaknesses, it says a lot about talent and quality and sheer entertainment value. This show was excellent. Thank you for an amazing night and for your hospitality and kindness.

Made in Dagenham, at its heart, is a socially conscious, gritty dramatic musical, peppered with good humour to bring levity to often heart-breaking situations. Its characters are strong and well-written, and the central romantic stories work hand in hand with the strong commentary on social injustice. It is, in many ways, as inspirational as it is entertaining. On the dramatic level, it works brilliantly, supported by an ample hand-full of poignant laments and anthems that make a powerful impact. It certainly inspired a high-quality standard of production and performance from the dedicated cast of Kilmainham and Inchicore, who delivered their goods with conviction and no shortage of talent. In the very safe hands of Director Art McGauran, the potential of this piece was fully realised, with good attention given to aesthetically assimilating the settings and the costumes to the era. On a set that was appropriately industrial, good set pieces were used to add colour and location, while space was well used, even when the stage was fairly full of bodies. My only gripe with the technical presentation of the show was over-amplification, which I believe was the result of an over-exuberant orchestra. A very confident and capable band of players, under the leadership of Musical Director, Barry Power, produced quality accompaniment to the production, albeit with a heavy handedness that, on occasions, competed with the sung and spoken words of a few characters on stage. As a result, I felt that much of the on-stage work was over-amplified to be certain of being heard. No such problems occurred, however, when the full chorus let vent, with strong voices and precise harmonies, indicating that they were vocally very well prepared.

Lighting was varied and atmospheric, with good use of pools of area lighting, and the more vibrant show-biz numbers were enhanced by an abundance of colour and contrast. That industrial and versatile stage was very well handled and manipulated by a very industrious stage crew, under the guidance of Stage Manager, designer and builder, Colum McDaid. With so many wonderful props and furniture to negotiate, the scene changes were surprisingly tidy and efficient.

Siobhan Ryan put plenty of aggression into the choreography of the shows torch- songs, correlating the steps and body language with the strength of the lyrics, and making the numbers all the more powerful. This was very good work. She also provided energetic, showy routines when the music demanded it, with style and variety enhancing such numbers as 'Pay Day', 'This is America', 'Cortina!' and 'Viva Eastbourne'. She was also blessed to have a company who gave 100% to their movement.

Amy Penston played Rita O'Grady, the reluctant hero of the story, with great credibility and warmth.

There was sincerity in her heart-wrenching choices between motherly responsibility and being a pioneer of social change, and she handled the conflict with her husband with a touching balance of love and exasperation. She also played the lighter side of her character with good comedic awareness, and when she opened up her vocal chords, she excelled.

As her husband Eddie, Gavin Molony was warm and affectionate in the home and delightfully roguish as one of the lads in his place of work, but it was during the conflicted scenes with his wife, and in his final realization of her true worth that his talents as an actor really shone through. A compassionate and moving performance. His singing was also remarkably good. The O'Grady children, Megan Lynch as Sharon and Evan Roberts as Graham, did all that was required of them, and played their emotional scenes particularly well. Very nice work.

Yvonne McCarthy was a strong and robust Connie Riley as the part required, yet she portrayed her more vulnerable self, and indeed her faded self in hospital, with dignity and sincerity. This was a lovely warm performance, and 'Same Old Story' was very well delivered. Sean Hendley, as Monty, gave a great and often comedic character to the ineffectual and easily rebuffed rep of his female workers. But it was the moment when he heart-breakingly declared his love for the departed Connie that we saw his acting at its finest. I don't believe there were many dry eyes in the theatre. Beautifully performed.

The most appalling string of expletives rolled naturally off the tongue of Sophia Daly, in a deliciously crass and amusing performance as potty-mouthed Beryl. What does it say about us, as an audience, that the utterance of the 'F' word can reduce us to fits of hysterical laughter? Well, perhaps it was the perfect, often caustic, delivery of the word from a very accomplished character actress/ comedienne that made it work so well without offending.

Lisa Younge, as Cass, Nikki Johnston as the addled-brained Clare and Louise O'Connor as the flighty glamour girl Sandra all added strong characterisations to the Dagenham workforce and performed with energy and commitment. Brian Carroll played Harold Wilson very much as a caricature of the famous Prime Minister, making him both crass and likeable all at once. This was a good comedy performance with a well- delivered rendition of 'Always A Problem'. It takes a powerhouse of a performer to play the powerhouse of a politician that was Barbara Castle, and there was no better a woman for the task than Naoimh Penston, who looked and acted the character with great reality, although I doubt if the real Barbara had a set of lungs like Naoimh, whose 'Ideal World' deservedly raised the roof. A brilliant vocal performance. David Supple proved to be a delightfully pompous, upper-class twit in the role of executive, Jeremy Hopkins, even if he was upstaged and out-smarted by his equally convincing and dignified wife, Lisa, beautifully played by Vanessa Murphy. Rogue of the story, American chief executive, Mr. Tooley, was played with unrestrained unpleasantness by the very capable Terry Martin, who was also well up to the vocal demands of 'This is America'. Good vocals, and an amusing cheesiness, were also presented by Kevin Macken-Tierney as the Cortina Man. Jack Halpin as Ron Macey and Darragh Carroll as Gregory Hubble added good comedy and character to their management roles, and Brian Dennison as Stan competently led an accomplished team of lads at the Ford Factory. A veritable myriad of supporting roles were all played with conviction by a cast who worked very well together as a team.

When they opened up in their anthems, the chorus made a powerful vocal contribution to the show, and their physical presence was highlighted by precise dance and movement and good acting and reacting to the circumstances in which they found themselves. Again, the team effort was very focused, strongly delivered and appreciated.

Wigs and hairstyles were notably excellent throughout the show, and costumes were perfect, from work overalls down to casual daywear. Nothing looked out of place. Outfits for This is America and Cortina added a smattering of razzle-dazzle to the proceedings. Make-up looked appropriate and natural, and an excellent job was done on visually realising the sickness of the ailing Connie.

With a company so secure in their characterisations, and a production team that high-lighted both the comedy and the poignant drama of the piece, I'm delighted that my first experience of Made in Dagenham was in such safe and talented hands. Thank you sincerely for such an enjoyable and worthwhile musical experience.

For audiences who have been starved of live theatre throughout the Covid pandemic, this was exactly the kind of comedy-driven, rib-tickling, finger-clicking entertainment that was required to warm their hearts and to lift their spirits. 'All Shook Up', possibly the best of the juke- box musicals, is all about comedy and fun, coupled with the ever-popular hits of the late, great Elvis, and an appreciative Fermoy audience enjoyed every minute of it.

In the safe hands of director Valerie O'Leary, this was a production that cruised along at a good pace throughout. There was good definition of characters, and good emphasis on the comedy of the piece, both the verbal and the physical, and for those musical numbers that weren't dominated by dance, good pictures were painted on the stage. A somewhat abstract set, at first sight, proved to be both functional and adaptable, with well selected set pieces and furniture helping to create the various scenes. The added fairground silhouette on the back wall completely changed the look of the set for act two. Scene changes, under the guidance of Stage Manager, Jacqui Creed, were smooth and sufficiently speedy as to not interrupt the flow of the show. The motorbike, the petrol pump, the juke-box were among the very good props. Lighting was generally very impressive, with particularly good back lighting and very good transitions from state to state. The sound was so good that I didn't even really notice it, except the few sound effects, which were good and well timed. All in all, this was a show that seemed effortless technically, due to well-directed efficiency. Very nice work. Niamh Twomey's choreography was vibrant and varied and added so much to the overall production. Some of the more energetic routines tested her dancers and chorus, who managed to achieve a high level of proficiency, with the ladies generally outshining the men, but no- one was lacking in energy or enthusiasm. Niamh also injected good comedy into many of the routines, particularly 'Teddy Bear/Hound Dog', 'Let Yourself Go' and 'You're the Devil in Disguise'.

Between them, Musical Directors Robbie Pender and Deirdre Foley presented a good well-balanced sound from the orchestra pit and some very accomplished choral singing from the folks on-stage. 'Heartbreak Hotel', 'Can't Help Falling in Love' and 'If I Can Dream' were particularly vocally inspiring. Both chorus and principals seemed well-rehearsed in their music, and the overall quality of the music was very good indeed. Rhythms and tempi were secure throughout.

Michael-Anthony Greene was an energetic, hip-swivelling, and extremely cool Chad who seemed to thoroughly enjoy his role. His singing was very suited to the rock'n'roll genre, and his ballads were nicely handled. He also had a fine sense of comedy.

More than a match for him was Alison McCormack's Natalie, who was fiery and feisty when required to be, but also delightfully vulnerable and insecure. She played her assumed character Ed with very good comedy. Vocally she was very confident throughout.

Michelle Smith gave a very good performance in the role of Sylvia, striking a good balance between concerned mother, lethargic café owner and empathetic friend and love-interest of Jim. She achieved all of these with good humour and with a most pleasant singing voice.

Rory Ward played Dennis the nerd with a wonderful sense of nerdiness and fun and easily won over the audience with great vocal and physical comedy. This was a most assured performance from a very fine character comedian, who also knows how to sell a song.

Equally assured and competent was Colette Daly as the feisty vamp Miss Sandra.

She handled Chad with dismissive authority and made the most of her comical love for Ed and did it all with impressive vocal quality.

Jack Fitzgerald gave some fancy footwork and a remarkably fine voice to his characterisation of Dean and played the pampered mummy's boy to a tee. This was a good comedy performance, with believable romantic notions for Lorraine, who was played most convincingly be Michelle Cooke. Here is another vibrant young performer who made a fine job of her singing, her comedy and her romance. Rebecca Beausang maintained a strong and comedic sense of authority as Mayor Matilda Hyde, and then melted delightfully under the amorous attentions of Diarmuid AIMS National President Rob Donnelly with Michael Greene  (Chad) and Ali McCormack (Natalie) Vaughan's Sheriff Earl. The timing between these two was very good, and Diarmuid managed to speak volumes with his body language. When he eventually got to speak, he won over his woman with self- assured authority and very good comedy. Good acting and vocal support came from Lisa Feerick as Henrietta, Orla O'Dwyer as Amorous, Hugh Mulqueen as Brad, and Stephen Niland impressed as the prison warden and the bus driver.

Energy and enthusiasm were the order of the day from a chorus who sang very well, acted their socks off and danced with a good degree of competence. Some of the dancers were better than others, but no- one let themselves down, and the overall contribution of the chorus to the show was of a very good standard.

Costume-wise, all was proper and correct, with good prison outfits at the start, colourful yet not over-glamorous outfits for the townsfolk, and then deliciously over-the-top fantasy costumes for Devil in Disguise. Make-up was generally good, but Natalie's stubble when she became Ed could have been a bit more pronounced. From where I sat, it wasn't too noticeable. The ladies all had hairstyles appropriate to the era, and the men were well-groomed. The Front of House display for this show was absolutely brilliant, with a highly appropriately decorated foyer, featuring a 'Tunnel of Love', memorabilia about Elvis, bunting everywhere, and so much more, all related to the show. Excellent and enjoyable work, combined by a friendly and informative front of house staff.

Musically, this show hit all the right notes, while visually and technically, it was colourful and slick. Performances were universally of a high order and the company on stage seemed to enjoy themselves as much as the audience did. That kind of feel-good is infectious, and Fermoy Musical Society produced it in bucket-loads. Congratulations to all and thank you for the fun.

A very fine sense of musicality was my first impression of this production, led by a delightfully mellow and tuneful orchestra, comprised of very capable soloists, particularly the violin and the woodwind. Musical Director/Conductor, Jimmy Brockie, did an excellent job, leading from the piano. The quality, tone and volume of the music was always extremely good, and he gave good leadership to the on- stage performers too. The three credited Chorus Mistresses, Lorraine Crowley, Denise Crowley and Aoibheann Carey- Philpott, should all be very pleased by the strong vocal performances of the chorus and the children.

Director, Jacinta McBride's greatest achievement with this production was to cast two completely inexperienced leads and to ensure that they reached a level of confidence and ability to carry the show so successfully. Inspirational leadership is a great quality in a director. There was no question that she put much thought into every aspect of the performance, from good use of the available space to the fine discipline of the Von Trapp children. The only area which possibly needed a bit more attention was the pace of the dialogue, which on several occasions was hampered by overly-long dramatic pauses. But most commendable was the performances she drew out of the delightfully natural and competent children. This was very good work.

Technically, I always appreciate when a company makes good use of very limited facilities, as was the case here. A great piece of work was done on creating the Von Trapp mansion with a nice white staircase and dome topped pillars and an attractive set of French doors with a pleasing mountainous back piece. Almost as good was the quickly erected pillars and railings for the convent cemetery. Less successful was the black curtains used for the convent, with 2 rather small and tawdry stained-glass windows. It was enough to suggest the location, but a bit of tidier artwork could have made it much more substantial. I commend the stage crew for keeping things moving at a good pace, and for managing the good selection of props and furniture. The only scene change that didn't really work was going from the terrace back into the house interior which occurred while "No Way To Stop It" was ongoing, and necessitated the principals leaving the stage while they were still singing.

Lighting throughout was very satisfactory, even if one or two black-outs seemed to happen slightly early. Sound quality was impressive, and well-balanced with the band.

In a show that doesn't demand too much from a choreographer, Chloe O'Leary managed to make her mark with good and varied routines for the children, and a particularly nicely choreographed 'Landler' for Maria and the Captain, which they performed very well.

Playing her first leading role, Maeve Murphy was very impressive as Maria. Her relationship with the Von Trapp children was warm and endearing and she handled her realisation of being in love with the Captain very nicely. She possessed a most pleasant singing voice, and her only flaw, musically, was to occasionally be slightly behind the beat, causing the MD to pull back the orchestra. This was, however, a very commendable first lead. Likewise, Robert J. Cogan was on his first theatrical outing as Captain Von Trapp. He had very good stature and presence, and delivered his lines very well, and he proved, in 'Edelweiss', to have a very pleasant singing voice. One wonders why he took so long to become involved in musical theatre, and I predict that he will play many roles in the future as he grows in confidence.

Angela Tanner was a gentle and motherly Mother Abbess, firm but compassionate in her dealings with Maria and the other nuns. She gave a fine rendition of 'Climb Every Mountain'.

There was more than a hint of Groucho Marx about Glen Barton in the role of Uncle Max, not only in appearance but also in his comedic antics. He was a firm favourite with the audience, and while I found his interpretation of the character a tad pantomimic for a minister for culture, it was an enjoyable and well-sustained characterisation.

Lorna Hughes brought a good level of elegance to Baroness Elsa, yet she was delightfully catty in her encounters with Maria, very nicely realising the comedic element of her nature. Both she and Max performed well in their musical numbers. As Liesl, Clodagh Tanner performed very comfortably and set a fine example for her junior siblings, showing confidence and understanding of her character. She looked well, alongside Fionn Mehigan in the role of Rolf, who was a believable suitor, and transformed competently into a misguided and confused Nazi. Both made a very good job of 'Sixteen Going on Seventeen'.

All of the Von Trapp children were delightful and very well disciplined. Andrei Macanovic was a charming Kurt, and Aidan Crowley was a good typical boy about to become a man. Orla Noonan was a cute and enchanting little Gretl, Lexi Costin's Marta was quirky and inquisitive, Ella Hughes Curtin was deliciously roguish as Louisa and most impressive was the clever clogs Brigitta, perfectly portrayed by Róisin Noonan.

Olive Vaughan was a very believable harassed house-keeper, and Fred Ryan Spengeman was a credible butler turned Nazi. Sisters Berthe, Sophia and Margaretta, as played by Liz Hesse- O'Sullivan, Mairead Hayes and Ava Crowley Costin respectively, gave a tuneful rendition of 'How Do You Solve a Problem', and more impressively, they managed to be very individual in creating their characters. Herr Zeller was as vicious as a rottweiller and impressively obnoxious, as played by a very capable Jerry Fitzgerald. There was good support, too, from Kevin O'Keeffe, doubling as Admiral Von Schreiber and Baron Elberfeld, Mary O'Flynn as Baroness Elberfeld, Marian O'Mahony as Frau Zeller and Aimee Manning as Ursula. Betty Brosnan, who greeted me so delightfully in Front of House, made a very worthwhile cameo appearance as the runner-up in the Kaltzberg Festival.

The evening got off to a wonderful start with a beautifully tuneful and articulate Nuns Chorus, led by Lorna Hughes as the soloist. Indeed, throughout the show, these ladies gave an excellent exhibition of choral singing. They were also very well turned out, and principals were always appropriately attired.

The children's costumes were neat and tidily worn. Good work here from the wardrobe team, and make up throughout looked completely natural.

The community spirit of this group is so strong and obviously the key to creating a wonderful atmosphere in the hall, and it filtered through to myself and the whole audience. My most sincere thanks for your warm hospitality, and for a most enjoyable performance of a show that I love dearly.

BOSCO captured the atmosphere of Halloween from the get-go with their production of 'The Addams Family', introducing us to the weirdest of weird families, and their deceased ancestors, in a vibrant and engaging opening chorus, played against an attractively eerie set. The main structure of the set was well- conceived and nicely painted, and props and furniture throughout were nicely made, or acquired. The torture "chair" was impressively dangerous, and Pugsley's rack was a thoughtful creepy piece of punishment apparatus. The representation of the moon was well-achieved, but not particularly magical, even if the scene was nicely played. Lighting was generally at a good level, with all the action clearly visible, and there were some nice effects using gobos, although they were perhaps a little over-used. Spotlights were well directed, and effects, (lightening, etc.) were very satisfactory. Sound quality was good throughout, with good cueing and good balance. Stage managers, Olivia Pentony and Maria Rafferty, assisted by an industrious stage team, had many pieces of furniture to move, and worked hard to achieve good variation in the settings, but the often lengthy scene changes, sometimes with musical accompaniment, but sometimes with silence, did affect the flow of the action.  While directors Corinna McCaughey and Jim McGuigan presented us with a good, polished production, I did feel that visually, the comedy of the piece could have been more exaggerated. In the role of Gomez, Kyle Emerson was a suitably authoritative figure, except, of course, when confronted by his wife. Kyle managed to convey both his love and his fear of Morticia convincingly and he had the vocal quality required for the role. I did feel that on occasions he could have played his comedy with a greater sense of the ridiculous, but this was, nevertheless, a good portrayal. As Morticia, Lauren Galway was deliciously vampish and I'm not surprised she frightened the wits out of Gomez. She had a pleasant and confident voice and played the cold- blooded matron to a tee.

Anna-Maria Boyle's Wednesday maintained a convincing dead-pan expression for most of the show, which worked perfectly in highlighting her weirdness. Her singing was very good, with 'Pulled' being a high point of musicality. Her relationship with Lucas was also very believable.

Nicole McCann-Finegan made a strong impression in the role of Pugsley, playing her comedy very well and singing delightfully. Daryll Galloghly was a very alternative Fester, playing him with a kind of impish sense of mischief, and it worked extremely well. He was very capable as a comedian, and used his physicality to gain additional laughs. A genuinely funny performance.

Grandma Addams was disgusting, and brilliant all at once, played so adeptly by Anne-Marie McAleenan, who squeezed every last drop of comedy out of her character. Of all the stage  characters, she was perhaps the one who best captured the exaggerated essence of the story. Brian Leavy was a suitably dull spirited Lurch, if a tad too young for the role, but he performed with confidence. Shane O'Keefe was a spirited Lucas Beineke and played extremely well opposite Wednesday. He got both the gormless and the determined sides of the character just right. As the straight-laced father, Mal, Damien Lavery was suitably austere and enjoyed lightening up when he discovered his old self, much as Helena Hughes achieved the transition from nervous, dissatisfied wife to hot-blooded vamp in the role of Alice. Her Waiting was competently performed, although both she and Mal seemed less secure in the difficult 'Crazier Than You' quartet.

It was a lovely touch to introduce "Young Wednesday" into Gomez's memories during 'Happy/Sad', and Aoife Jennings performed it beautifully.

Ann Marie Morgan's choreography was varied, energetic and always appropriate to the scene. There was good use of talented acrobats and ballet dancers which keep everything interesting and engaging. As befitted the nature of the show, there was a good comedic, surreal feel to her numbers. I wasn't overly impressed with the impact of The Moon and Me, but did appreciate the novelty of its choreography. Overall, the dancing was uplifting and made a very positive impact on the production. The pace of the show, apart from the lengthy scene changes, was good, but I did feel that had the production gone for the same level of outrage that the choreography achieved, it would have been more comical.

Good in their appearance, good in their dancing and movement and good in their vocal contribution to the show, the chorus and dancers worked hard all night. There were one or two stand out dancers, but everyone made a good impression.

Hats off  to the cast and the wardrobe team who, between them, came up with a very original and impressive set of costumes. All of the principals looked impressive and in-character, while the ghostly ancestors were a fabulous spectacle. Wigs were equally impressive and make-up was weird and wonderful. Visually, the whole piece had a lovely feeling of Halloween. Well done.

Very much thrown in to the position of Musical Director at the eleventh hour, Elizabeth Freeburn acquitted herself very respectably, keeping good control of the small band. There were perhaps a few occasions when the chorus had too much free rein with cut-offs, and 'Crazier Than You' seemed to give a few problems to the singers, but in general, the show was musically sound, and well balanced. Even with the usual heightened sense of community involvement and high spirits, I did feel that perhaps the production team needed to throw caution a little more to the wind and present this show with an even greater sense of the ridiculous. It was there, particularly in the choreography, and even at the level at which it was pitched, it proved to be a most enjoyable theatrical experience. Thank you to all involved for your dedication and enthusiasm, and sincere thanks to Jim McGuigan and the front of house team for the wonderful hospitality and refreshments.

Revenge of the Nostalgist UCD Musical Society has been around for some time and usually produce quirky works like 'Urinetown' or 'The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee' or they revive a Sondheim or a Kander & Ebb with a knowing and somewhat revisionist slant and a fierce originality. So, it was a bit of a surprise when they chose Dolly Parton's hit show '9 to 5' as their first musical this season. I mean there's not a lot a director can do with it apart from follow what the countless other versions out there do and create a feel-good romp. Bearing in mind the New York Times described it in 2009 as "an overinflated whoopee cushion" and a "gaudy, empty musical", so it is a bit of a challenge to make it work in 2022, given the rise of the #metoo movement and so on! Anyway, I went along with an optimistic curiosity to see UCD's take on this classic nostalgic crowd-pleaser. UCD Astra Hall is not really a theatre in the traditional sense in that it doesn't have flying or tabs or a platform stage. It's a general-purpose auditorium, often used for lectures and gigs and the occasional play or musical. We could see the set on entry, and it was a wide representation of a 'modern' office, complete with upstage windows and the doors of an elevator. It was quite impressive in its detail, more like a TV studio set or a film set. There was a wooden framed bed at centre stage, which looked out of place, and I thought maybe they work them so hard that the boss makes them sleep there! But no, it was set for the first number, "9 to 5", where the ensemble went through the motions of waking up, dressing etc. and going to work.

It started very well, great harmonies on the title song by chorus mistress Ava Barry and super big sound from the large orchestra expertly driven by Amber Dixon, with nice tight choreography by Niamh O'Brien of a large energetic ensemble. We eventually arrived at the office proper, complete with desks etc. Here we met the three female leads; Violet Newstead played by Jennifer Byrne, Doralee Rhodes (basically Dolly Parton) played by Lia Mullan and Judy Bernly played by Chloe Burke. The whole plot is about how they try to change the hearts and minds of big business and destroy misogyny.

Ms Byrne played widowed Violet as quite high-status, fuming over not getting promoted, when she believed she deserved it. Her singing was very good, particularly on "Around Here" and with Joe on "Let Love Grow" and on "One of the Boys" she excelled both vocally and in the dance. Violet introduced newbie, Judy, around the office and took her under her wing. Chloe Burke who played Judy, a mousey and embittered stay-at- home wife thrust into the big bad world by her ex-husband, had this haunting PTSD- like quality to her performance which really worked here. Judy is usually played as a comic relief character, but Ms Burke didn't push the comedy at all. It was still there, but it was more like pathos than farce. Her voice was stunning on "Get Out and Stay Out" the big power ballad of the show and she mapped Judy's journey from mouse to lion with skill. The final character of the trio was Doralee, who was the boss's secretary. Lia Mullan played the misunderstood Texan with a 'homespun' freshness that was enjoyable to watch. Wrongly accused of being the boss's mistress, she set the record straight and joined the other two on a quest to serve him his just desserts. Ms Mullan had a good grasp of the Country & Western genre that most of her songs were written in, and she had a cheekiness that enlivened the character.

All three had their own reasons for hating the boss, Franklin J Hart Jr, here played by Gearoid Riordan. Mr Riordan had the unenviable task of portraying a despicable, chauvinistic misogynist. But he did it well! His singing was on point, especially on "Here for You", where he graphically fantasised about seducing Doralee. His wife Missy, clearly oblivious to his philandering ways, was played by a fur-clad Aoife Blake, who in this version became gay by the end of the show. Hart's office manager, Roz Keith - in a brilliant performance by Alice Morgan, was obsessively in love with him. Ms Morgan captured the character of the repressed, nerdish fantasist perfectly. Her song, "Heart to Hart" had the audience whooping with joy and her second song, the sad "5 to 9" had them in the palm of her hand. Lovely, nuanced performance from Ms Morgan.

These were the principal roles in the show, and they were well cast I believe, and each performer was quite good. However, there was a disconnect between the characters here. They didn't blend. There was very little dynamism between Violet, Doralee and Judy - we didn't believe that they were united. Hart and Roz did have a good chemistry and worked well the couple of times they were on together. But the three amigos didn't really gel for me. It didn't help that the scene changes and transitions took so long, thus ruining the pace and the lighting was badly miscued and the sound was patchy. I'm sure stage managers, Clodagh Cullen and Aoife O'Sullivan speeded things up during the run, but the real problem was not them, they had to deal with an unwieldy set, which was clearly not designed for theatre.

Directors, yes there were two, Michael Bergin and Cormac Gilligan, seemed to pay very little attention to detail both in the set and in some of the performer's actions, which made the production seem quite ill-thought-out. For example: when they tied up Hart in the office, they didn't actually tie him up - they just draped the cord around him, so his lines about being unable to move were met with giggles from the audience; similarly, when they placed him on the bed, they just draped the rope around his neck and didn't tie him to the bed, yet this is referred to in the book. We could see the stagehand in the 'photocopy' machine feeding the A4 paper through the slot; there was nothing written on the paper on Joe's clipboard but yet it's referred to by Violet and Joe; when Violet was 'fixing' the garage opener, she didn't actually do anything to it; no liquid in cups or kettle; the size of the 'corpse' on the hospital trolley was too small - I could go on with many more examples, but this is what I mean about lack of attention to details. Details matter as you are asking your audience to suspend their disbelief and they want to, and the details help the illusion and our engagement with the production. I believe that details also help the performer believe in their character and their actions.

Anyway, back to the performers. In a rather underwritten role, Joe was the nerdy junior accountant who fell for Violet. Played by Patrick Mac Fhionnlaoich, he made the most of the role and his song with Violet "Let Love Grow" was quite sweet. The office lush, Margaret, was a great role to get the teeth into, and Alice O'Loughlin Kennedy did just that! She didn't go over the top with the drunk act, which was the right decision, choosing to play her as mildly inebriated. The reveal at the end of the show, where she has sobered up, was very well done. The CEO of the organisation, Mr Tinsworthy, was played by Alan Markey, he oozed that CEO confidence and his exchange with Violet towards the end of the show was rather good. Other roles of note were Violet's son Josh, well played by Eoin Ó'Dúinín; Doralee's husband Dwayne also well played by Luke Byrne, complete with Texan drawl and Judy's oily ex, Dick, played with simpering misogyny by Owen Finnegan. It should be said that I enjoyed the energy of the entire cast on this show, they played it for all they were worth, especially the ensemble. What they lacked in direction I feel they more than made up for with liveliness, due in no small part to the choreographer and chorus mistress. It struck me as I was watching the show that it didn't seem to have benefitted from much rehearsal, which may have explained the holes. Whilst the performers were clearly well-rehearsed in the choreography and the music/singing, lack of acting rehearsals may have accounted for some of the problems I saw in the performers. It also appeared to have been somewhat busked in terms of set moving and lighting and sound operation, possibly indicating few technical rehearsals.

As I mentioned at the start, UCD are renowned for presenting quirky, off-beat entertaining and imaginative shows.

Sadly, this was not one of them.

Family Plot Staged in the National Opera House in Wexford for just four performances in late November and early December, this show produced by Oyster Lane Theatre Group was fast and furious with wonderful orchestrations by Patrick Clancy and slick choreography by Jonny Smith all held together by director Thomas O'Leary. His interpretation, whilst not adding anything new, was solid and there were some stand out moments of theatre where everything just came together. He was blessed with a few excellent performers who added their own idiosyncratic takes on their characters which the director wisely left in.

It ran very smoothly and whilst it looked good at times, the set, by Mark Redmond didn't work for me and some of the lighting states failed to light the actors. It started with a very low energy, but when the Ancestors entered, it picked up and didn't let up until the end. This was helped by Stage Manager Colin Murphy, who kept the scene changes smooth.

And so, to the actors: the success of this show depends on the character of Gomez to keep the energy going, so it is imperative that the performer playing Ruth Donegan's kooky Grandma Addams scares the daylights out of Ami Stahlut's Alice Beineke him has energy, charm, wit and above all else excellent comic timing. The director wisely chose long time member Neal O'Leary to play Gomez. Mr O'Leary had superb comic timing in this role. He created a kind-hearted but very weird Gomez, which is exactly how he should be played. Gomez isn't normal and many actors seem to forget this, but Mr O'Leary didn't. He had a Robin Williams quickness and timing mixed with early Steve Martin and Peter Sellers mannerisms to create a brilliant character. His singing was good, going for expression rather than vocal dexterity. His scenes with Morticia and Wednesday really convinced and he delivered "Happy/Sad" with a gorgeous emotional intensity. Morticia was played with a haughty imperiousness by Niamh Bolger.

She had this lovely vibrato in her voice, which gave a new resonance to Morticia's songs particularly "Just Around the Corner" and "Secrets" with Alice. Her characterisation of Morticia was super, physically quite domineering with a biting sarcasm yet quite maternal to Pugsley. She played the rivalry with Wednesday with a quiet sub-text and had a great dynamic with Gomez. They bounced off each other very well.

Niamh Cullen's Wednesday was a petulant, spoilt teenager used to getting her own way and she oozed danger. Her singing was first-rate, the highlight for me being "Crazier Than You" with Lucas and "Pulled" where she really showed off her range. A very good performance. Playing her Uncle Fester was Michael O'Gorman who had great energy in the role. He leapt around the stage with the ancestors like he was possessed. His asides and direct address to the audience was spot-on and his singing was very good especially on "The Moon and Me", which was staged beautifully. Her brother Pugsley was played by the young Sam Bolger, who absolutely nailed Pugsley's character. He was cheeky, precocious, and quite evil at times. His dead-eyed stare was very effective, and he sang "What If" with a lovely emotion. Playing his Grandma was Ruth Donegan with a cackle and a hiss and a mad hairdo and very heavy make- up.

Her voice was great, she had just the right amount of rasp and her slowness worked well. She was very funny in "Full Disclosure" and had a nice dynamic with Pugsley. The family butler, Lurch, was played by Seán Hendley in a masterclass of physical comedy. His pace throughout the show never wavered and in the dance numbers he was always a step behind as he should be.

Excellent timing and a glum demeanour made him one of the funniest characters on stage.

The plot is all about Wednesday falling in love with a 'normal' person, Lucas, getting engaged and inviting him and his family over to hers for dinner so that they can tell the folks. Lucas Beineke, the all-American boy-next-door type, was played by Thomas Furlong. At first glance, he's the last person you would think Wednesday would be interested in. Or indeed that he would fall for her as she's so dour and pessimistic, but they did fall in love and that's the main plot of the whole show. Their incompatibility. Mr Furlong played him with a lovely energy and a sort of innocence that worked. His singing on "Crazier Than You" with Wednesday was excellent and they sounded great together. Accompanied by his parents, Alice and Mal, who were played by Ami Stahlut and Brian Kelly, he shows up for dinner. Ami Stahlut had an amazing voice, and she sang "Waiting" with such energy and feeling and emotion that the audience erupted into unrestrained applause and cheering. Her portrayal of Alice was just right, the stay-at-home wife and mother who wants to feel wanted again, wants to matter. Mal is a great role show as the character has a very recognisable journey; from stuffy accountant to ageing rocker. Brian Kelly did this very well, initially he portrayed Mal as an uptight ordinary guy appalled at Gomez and his family. But when he believed that he might lose Alice, he found his inner hippy.

Anyway, as you can imagine things don't go according to plan, but it all ended up unhappily ever after as they wouldn't have wanted it any other way. The show featured some marvellous set pieces such as the whole "Moon and Me" sequence, which was beautifully choreographed and lit, topped off with Greg O'Leary's descending moon projections. There was also a swing which was flown in for Gomez and Wednesday's "Happy/Sad" song, but they didn't use it, they just sat on it! The "Full Disclosure" scene was also a highlight, especially Ami Stahlut's cavorting Alice who got Lurch so excited that he smiled and covered up his excitement. Greg O'Leary's animations of Fester flying to and becoming one with the moon was something I hadn't seen done before and it worked brilliantly. Another highlight for me was Musical Director Patrick Clancy's orchestration, it was excellent particularly on some of the underscore. I know this show quite well but I heard things in the music I'd never heard before, there was a spookiness added to some of the songs, a discordant ambience which worked very well.

The job of the director is to interpret the source material for the medium you are working in, and I believe that Mr O'Leary did justice to the material here. He gave us a funny, irreverent piece of theatre that resonated with its audience and enabled his performers to explore their roles and worked with them to breathe life into their characters. Or should that be death? The choreography and music from the other creatives added another marvellous layer to a show that was a resounding success for Oyster Lane.

Habit Forming Based on the successful 1992 film starring Whoppi Goldberg as a wise- cracking lounge singer forced to go on the lam after witnessing her boyfriend murder a fellow hood, the musical was created in 2006 with music by Alan Menken and lyrics by Glenn Slater and was a hit around the world. I saw it in the Civic Theatre in Tallaght produced by Harold's Cross Tallaght Musical Society on opening night, Henchmen TJ (Jamie Place), Pablo (Paolo Garau) and Joey (Alan Duffy) in Lady in the Long Black Dress_ which was packed.

The show opened in a convent, 'Queen of Angels' where a group of nuns were attempting to sing, it was painful and thankfully we moved quickly to the Moonlight Lounge where Jenny McCabe as Deloris, flanked by Abba'esque backing singers, the 'Delorettes' were auditioning to sing in the club, run by Deloris' boyfriend Curtis, played with a subdued menace by Eddie Brady. The songs, 'Take Me to Heaven' and 'Fabulous, Baby!' were high- octane disco numbers performed with a wonderful panache and the 'Delorettes'; Leonna Condron, Kim Doran, Sarah McGauran, Laura Medbury, Sally Sheerin and Georgia Spooner produced some great harmonies and subtle dance moves. Told that she didn't get the gig, Deloris decides to leave Curtis but witnesses him murder one of his henchmen and runs to her old school friend, policeman 'Sweaty' Eddie, nicely played by Eoin Salley, for help. Eddie places her in a witness protection programme and brings her to the 'Queen of Angels' convent. Here we meet the Mother Superior, Julie Donnelly, who sings the beautiful 'Here Within These Walls'. Deloris sets out to win the hearts and minds of the nuns she's boarding with through a series of upbeat numbers infused with ecclesiastical choral openings.  She teaches the nuns how to sing and harmonise much to the displeasure of the Mother Superior who believes the devil may be at work through the disco beats and soul singing.

Meanwhile, Deloris' boyfriend, Curtis discovers where Deloris is holing up and sets out to capture and 'dispose' of her. Curtis' other henchmen, the hilarious TJ, played by Jamie Place; the Latino 'lover' Pablo, perfectly played by Paolo Garau and self-styled "ladies' man" Joey, played by Alan Duffy are like a cross between the Bee Gees and the Three Stooges. They infiltrate the convent but not before they treat us to one of the shows' best numbers 'The Lady in The Long Black Dress' a fabulous R&B tune redolent of 70's group Tavares mixed with Barry White.

But it's the nuns who blessed this show with pitch perfect singing and superb characterisations.

Delightful performances from Charlene Masterson as the hyper-active Sr Mary Patrick, Rosaleen Nolan as the dour Sr Mary Lazarus and Aoife Small as the demure Sr Mary Robert - who's touching rendition of 'The Life I Never Led' was lovely and Mary Galligan and Joan Kelly played Sr Mary Theresa and Sr Mary Martin-of-Tours with apostolic assurance.

Suffice to say, Deloris leads the nuns in a series of wonderful numbers, appearing on television and eventually singing for the Pope. Curtis and his dastardly incompetent flunkies get their comeuppance and Eddie gets his girl.

The musical direction by Dermot O'Callaghan was excellent, lovely work with the harmonies on "Raise Your Voice" and the other nun-led numbers and on "Take Me to Heaven" and "Fabulous Baby!" by Deloris and her backing singers. The band were cloistered backstage, but they sounded great with instrumentation from Wah Guitar to splendid horns, it was a musical trip through the '70s. Choreography by Lea Carroll, clearly working to her cast's strengths. It's not a big dance show, there are just too many nuns! But what she did do with them was well-rehearsed and simple enough to look good.

Wayne Handy created the set which was all stained-glass window effects upstage and on the side flats, with some other set pieces trucked on an off to represent other locations. Lighting by Tomás Fitzgerald was very front of house heavy, more side lighting would have added an extra dimension to scenes. Sound by Vinny Osborne was full range with each singer's voice nicely reverbed, with pulsing bottom end for the disco beats. Costumes by Andrew Reddy were exceptional. The range of colourful Nun's tabards was fabulous. Deloris's club costume was of the era and there was a lot of lame and sequins throughout the show!

I attended the first performance and I thought some of the scene changes were a tad slow, I felt that the crew were not well rehearsed. Miscuing in the lighting department didn't help as some transitions were in full lights.

Director Ciarán Mooney gave us a fairly solid show, little artistic touches like the Pope entering through the audience and beefing up Deloris's backing singers and adding a quirky slow-motion segment during "Bless Our Show", elevated it. However, it was Jenny McCabe's performance as Deloris that raised the show. She didn't try to emulate Whoppi but made the character her own. Her wise- cracking gangster's moll was straight out of an MGM Musical and her comic timing was delicious. Her naturalism midst a cast of over-the-top caricatures was refreshing and we were really rooting for her to overcome her challenges. Ms. McCabe also has a great voice with a superbly broad range. She shone in the big disco numbers and brought it down with skill on the title song, which is one of the better songs in the show. Ms. McCabe was Deloris Van Cartier, not just a sister act but a class act.

Hello Dolly!

Coolmine Musical Society (CMS) has been around since 1981 and has won many AIMS awards since then and played to many thousands of Dublin theatregoers with their innovative takes on modern and classical musicals. Their latest offering was Dolly Parton's "9 to 5" which took to the Draíocht stage in November of this year. Directed by Pat McElwain with Nicole McDonald on dance duty and Dave McGauran looking after the music, I was curious as to what these three award- winning creatives would do with the material.

Written in 2009 and based on a film made and set in the late '70's early '80's about office politics and a misogynist boss vs his rebelling staff. It is an engagingly old fashioned, simple story full of Dolly songs and lewd slapstick, with a cartoon thin plot and corny comedy; but with great roles for female performers, which is a nice change.  The plot follows the chaotic adventures of three downtrodden women struggling under the chauvinistic oppression of the good ole boy network of business and office politics. The three musketeers take their revenge not only on their sexist, misogynist boss, but also on global sexism and prejudice infecting office culture of the '80s.

John O'Donoghue's set was full of clean lines, sharp colours and was built by Jim Whelan and painted by Ben Hennessy, it looked great. Incorporating a video screen upstage, which showed the Dolly welcome video, plus the occasional image and a ticking clock. The side flats and headers and the gobos on the floor all worked together to create a corporate image where time was of the essence. The desks on castors were smooth and fabulously mobile and Hart's office, complete with his portrait was perfect. It was into this no-nonsense corporate environment we met our three heroines: Violet, a struggling widow played by Bronwyn Andrews; Doralee, the boss's PA played by Serena Salmon; and newcomer to the firm, the nervous Judy played by Nicole Lamb. Ms Andrews as Violet had poise and grace and a wonderfully expressive voice; Nicole Lamb's Judy was all nervous twitches and low self-worth, her character's journey to independence was marvellously done and her voice on "Get Out and Stay Out" brought the house down. But it was Serena Salmon's Doralee who stole the show for me. The more difficult role of the three in that it is clearly modelled on Dolly, and often played as an impersonation rather that a character. Ms Salmon did not fall into that trap and gave us a superbly nuanced performance of a Doralee who was 'mad as hell and not going to take it anymore'. Her scene with Hart where she attacks him was pure drama and her singing on "Backwoods Barbie" was tender, wistful, and powerful.

As the "sexist, egotistical, lying, hypocritical bigot", Kevin Hartnett played Franklin Hart (the nameplate on his desk read: F Hart) with outrageous misogyny. His performance of "Here for You" was so sleazy it went beyond humour and ventured into Weinstein territory, which was very difficult to watch but served to justify the three ladies' extreme retaliation. Mr Hartnett's performance was excellent. Hart totally ignored the person who was really in love with him (except to bully her into doing his dirty work), office manager Roz Keith. Played here with unfettered glee by Jenny Seery. Ms Seery was by far the funniest character on stage, yet she also got across the sad pathos of Roz. Her performance of "Heart to Hart" was hilarious and on "5 to 9" quite mournful. The love interests of our three amigos were very different to each other; Joe the office junior accountant was sweet on Violet, played by Daire Kelly in Clark Kent mode with the glasses and stoic demeanour and a fine singing voice; Doralee's husband, Dwayne played with Texan assurance by Ciarán Lenehan and Judy's ex-husband Dick played with a distasteful oiliness by Liam Egan. Whilst the three male characters are pure stereotypes, all three actors played them with a total sincerity, which was refreshing. Violet's other male in her life was her teenage son, Josh, played here by Eoin Kenny in a nicely tuned performance.

The office had its share of quirky characters such as Maureen, the office drunk. Liberally sipping from her hip flask, Maureen was played by Kathryn Gibbons with a nice restraint. Michelle Harris played Maria Delgado, who is curious about the running of the company and gets fired and rehired. Ms Harris spoke some of her lines in Spanish, which was very effective. Valerie Andrews played Kathy, one of the more no-nonsense characters with assurance. When Russell Tinsworthy the CEO of the Company, played with an avuncular calmness by Justin Parkes, visits he promotes and demotes with a modern political correctness I feel was absent back in the early '80s. But it served as a happy ever after.

Director Pat McElwain's attention to detail was so meticulous it permeated the entire production: from Dave McGauran's wonderful arrangement of both orchestra and chorus to Nicole McDonald's clever, innovative at times, choreography; Gerry McCann's excellent stage management team; Denis Twomey's pin-sharp lighting; Jody Trehy's well-balanced sound and Ali Murphy's excellent make-up and wigs. But he's right to be so meticulous and I wish more directors were as conscientious about their craft as Mr McElwain is. The attention to detail on this show was wonderful. From the clean lines of the set to the accuracy of the props and the smoothness of the transitions to the commitment of the performers - the show jumped off the stage bright and cheery like a newly minted penny.

The production had some nice ideas too, such as: the flying sequence where Hart was suspended at the end of Act I (most societies don't do this because of cost or resources); the multiple Roz characters; a projection of Violet on the cover of 'Time' magazine and so on. The production values were high on this show, from costuming to set painting and lighting - the show looked brilliant, all colour- matched and blended and very classy. Mr McElwain did push the more ribald elements of the story to the fore at times e.g. Hart's footballs, Roz's antics on the floor in front of him and on the sofa, but it was all done in the "worst" possible taste, which the audience absolutely loved!

Divorced, Beheaded, Died, Divorced, Beheaded, Survived. The famous rhyme takes on a new life as the basis of "Six," a musical reimagining of the six wives of King Henry VIII as they battle to emerge as the leader of a new pop girl group. While the show is really more of an 80-minute concert piece, it certainly packs a punch. The performers immediately break the fourth wall, informing the audience that they will be tasked with determining which one of them has the most tragic backstory and will therefore be named leader of the new girl group. From there, they take turns performing musical numbers telling their tragic backstories and making their case to become the group's star. Many esteemed critics of professional theatre were harsh in their estimation of this show, branding it, "a pale attempt to do for British history what Hamilton had done for American history", and "a vacuous attempt at feminism, which fails miserably because the whole central concept, (women competing against each other to win a popularity contest) was, in itself, a total contradiction of feminism."  Well frankly, I don't know what they were talking about. I viewed it purely as a creative piece of fun and entertainment based on a popular period of history, with identifiable and well-drawn characters. As such, in my own humble opinion, this production was a resounding and highly entertaining success.

Putting this piece together required a good awareness of aesthetic content on the part of director, Martina Lynch. With very little script to play with, the focus had to be on the costumes, the lights, the setting and of course, presenting six unique and individual characters. In most respects, all of this was achieved successfully. Lighting was excellent and costumes were good and inventive, and the establishment of individual characterisations was achieved through a strong opening number, "Ex- Wives", in a style reminiscent of Cell Block Tango from 'Chicago', where the ladies introduce themselves and recount their demise; hence, Divorced, Beheaded, Died, Divorced, Beheaded, Survived. Where Martina really made her mark was in the choreography of this, and indeed every number in the show. In an amazingly tight, disciplined and high-energy display, with a range of rock, pop, hip-hop and funk, this was an outstanding achievement of non- stop gyrations and gesticulations that left the audience even more breathless than the dancers themselves.

With no band to direct, Amy Penston's entire focus, as Musical Director, was to ensure that her charges were note perfect, tight in their harmonies, accurate in their timing and totally tuned into the backing tracks and filled with vocal energy. She did not fail them. This was a job extremely well done.

Roisin Vigors, as Catherine of Aragon, Henry's first wife, made great arrogant play of the fact that she was the wife who kept the King's interest the longest. Strong on vocal quality, excellent in "No Way", and a great mover, her whole performance had a wonderful air of smug superiority.

Leah O'Hare, as Anne Boleyn, initially worried me, with a couple of fragile notes in the opening number, but my worry soon dissipated when she gave vent to "Don't Lose Your Head" with vim and vigor and a very strong sense of comedy. Indeed, her frequent whinging that "I had my head chopped off" became a central running joke of the show. Very well-portrayed. Leah Byrne played Jane Seymour, arguably the most sedate and dignified wife of Henry. Her tragedy was that having given the King his much-desired son, she died shortly after his birth. Leah's portrayal captured that dignity, with a touch of gloating at being the provider of a son, and her vocal delivery of "Heart of Stone" was beautiful and sincere.

Doireann Hurley, as Anne of Cleves, brought the house down with her witty, quirky rendition of "Get Down". This was a combination of vocal dexterity, superb body language and a wink and a smile that couldn't help but woo the audience. Her charm and all-round ability were remarkably fine.

Holly Prestage, as Katherine Howard, despite her youth, gave a super- convincing sensuality to the most flirtatious and provocative of the King's wives, and her rendition of the "All You Wanna Do" number, captured the essence of her character perfectly. Very well sung and acted.

Last but not least, Bri-Elle Finn, as Catherine Parr, performed "I Don't Need Your Love" (seen as the feminist anthem of the show) with a stirring passion and beautiful vocal quality, but she was equally as accomplished in her funkier contributions.

But it was when the six girls performed as a unit that the magic really occurred, perfectly in sync in all their routines and perfectly in tune with all their harmonies. What a team!

Costumes were cute and quirky, modern in design but with a few appropriate hints of historical garb. Wigs and/or hairstyles were funky and fun, and make-up was great, giving the girls a super overall appearance. Loved the mock mics as well.

The set for the show was the only aspect of the production that could have been more elaborate. While the flats containing portraits of the six wives were fine, and the cyc at the rear of the stage allowed for nice lighting effects, it was a tad empty. Maybe a period, palace décor would have suited the historical nature of the story, or a modern studio set, to capture the contest element of the whole scenario. (Or maybe six large gilt-edged portrait frames, each with a throne, and the wives in frozen poses as the audience enter?) Thankfully, though, an excellent pop-concert style of lighting design meant that the background was never that important. And while the effects and flashing, moving lights were awesome, care was taken that focus was always on the right person at the right time, which showed great attention to detail. Sound quality was excellent throughout.

I was delighted and excited when this show popped onto my adjudication list, and I travelled to Arklow filled with anticipation. I was not to be disappointed. Studio 55 didn't just meet my expectations, they surpassed them, with a sparkling and scintillating show. Thank you, ladies, for a fabulous night.

Co-directors, Elizabeth Gregan and Yvonne Prendergast, on behalf of Bray Musical Society, presented us with an Oklahoma that was note perfect, word perfect and appeared to be very thoroughly rehearsed. An orchestra of very capable musicians, under Musical Director Elizabeth Gregan, treated us to an overture played to perfection. The choreography of Yvonne Prendergast gave us a good, lively Farmer and the Cowman and a well-presented Dream Ballet, and the females were tidy in their execution of Many a new day and Out of my Dreams. Kansas City, while fairly uncomplicated, was well performed. The costumes for the show were colourful and well selected, particularly the female dresses, and completing the overall look of the performers, hairstyles and make- up, with the exception of a couple of characters who needed to be better aged, were appropriate and pretty good.

The staging, while fairly simple in design, was effective enough in providing a good framework for the action, and while the lighting was straightforward in design, good use of colours and effective pools of light allowed for variety in the look and atmosphere of the different scenes. Scene changes, under the guidance of Greg Egan, were carried out with a minimum of fuss, and there was a very decent display of props appropriate to the show.

Performance wise, there was a very good characterization of Ado Annie, played with a delightful deadpan comedic style by Sarah O'Hanlon, with a nicely rendered Cain't Say No. Aunt Eller, played by Bairbre Murphy was the most comfortable and relaxed performer on stage and supported her good acting with safe and secure singing.

Stephen Carvill had a good look and a good voice for Will Parker, and he worked very hard, especially in his scenes with Ado Annie. He did need more direction to fully realize the comedy potential of his role. The same would have to be said for Nick Russell as Ali Hakim, who despite some good character acting, needed to be much larger than life to exploit the good comedy of the script.

Eoin Martin was very young to play Ado Annie's father, Andrew Carnes, despite making a good job of the character. Had he been more successfully aged with good make-up; he might have been more believable. Gertie Cummins was well- played by Grainne Shortt, with a laugh and a grunt that were very amusing. The Jud Fry of Peter Manning was quite menacing, but not really in a subtle manner. He did play the smoke house scene with Curly very well and delivered "Poor Jud is Dead" and "Lonely Room" in a satisfactory manner.

There were decent supporting performances from Kevin Rockett as Cord Elam, Tom Gallagher as Ike Skidmore, Dylan Anderson as Slim and Raven Gabriel as Fred.

Michelle Murray as Ellen, Catherine Gregan as Kate and Niamh Webbley- O'Gorman as Vivienne, led the female chorus in the very nicely sung "Out of My Dreams" and "Many a New Day".

The chorus generally brightened the atmosphere of all their scenes and impressed with their harmonies. They also moved well and were probably capable of much more than they were given.

Laurey, played by Orlaith Dunne, had a most delightful operatic quality and excellent diction, and some of her scenes were strongly acted, especially the confrontation with Jud, but a lack of chemistry between herself and Curly, played by Conor Martin, diminished the central romantic story line. With a very pleasant tenor voice, Curly seemed to lack the confidence to fully realize the lighter side of his character, and perhaps needed more direction to achieve his full potential. The overall tone and atmosphere of the show didn't seem to sparkle and was somewhat uninspired. Principals generally needed much more guidance in the development and delivery of their lines, and in achieving a more natural presence on the stage.

Romance was lacking, and verbal and visual comedy was missed on many occasions. While the music was note perfect, constant pedantic rhythms did little to inspire flair or flow in the delivery of the lyrics. Despite some very good voices and a hard-working chorus, many of the songs needed more joy and expression. I do appreciate that the whole company worked hard in presenting a show that was very clean and tidy and musically well-rehearsed, but I just longed for more natural flow and spontaneity.
