She worked well with the Players in the 'Kathleen Ni Houlihan' play within the play predicting doom and peril and generally 'haunted' the set, urging the young men to rebel against their oppressors.

This was a significant production in that all of the elements worked in tandem and complimented each other; from Wayne Handy's marvellous stage management and set design to Ronan Kenny's super lighting design to Derek Reck's powerful sound aided by Ultan Keena's costuming, hair and make-up designs. Everything dovetailed beautifully within Pat McElwain's artistic vision. But above all the production showed us the heart and soul of the show, it gave us what Mr Flynn wanted us to experience and for that it more than deserved its standing ovations.

Back to the '80's Leixlip Musical and Variety Group produced the comedy retro musical 'The Wedding Singer' written in 2006, with music by Mathew Sklar, lyrics by Chad Beguein and book by Tim Herlihy and based on the 1998 Adam Sandler / Drew Barrymore film of the same name. Directed and choreographed by Claire Tighe, with musical direction by Dermot O'Callaghan this was a fabulous high camp version of this ode to the '80's. It was fast and furious with great tongue in cheekiness and marvellous singing.

The plot is thin but fun. Wedding singer Robbie Hart and waitress Julia Sullivan have a DMC and bond the night before Robbie is jilted at the altar by Linda, his fiancée. Julia gets engaged to her Wall Street boyfriend Glen, who cheats on her, reveres money, and becomes the antagonist. But Robbie and Julia's bond becomes stronger, and this puts her wedding in jeopardy. Throw in a funny best friend, a rapping granny, frustrated bandmates, a synthy derivative score, a bunch of look-a-like performers in Vegas into the mix and you have a sure-fire formula for a hit show, which this was. Claire Tighe's production had great attention to detail. It's a comedy musical and Ms Tighe focused on delivering the laughs through her at times over the top cast. Most of it landed although some was a bit wide of the mark and incongruous. The musical is relentlessly derivative of 1980's music videos, pop songs and dance numbers and the director must embrace this as there is little else within the wispy plot. Thankfully Ms Tighe donned her legwarmers and sweat band and got physical. Her cast had a great chemistry together and their onstage relationships were well defined. The show had high quality production values in the set, lighting and sound and the band were electric and the choreography excellent. 1980's fashion, make-up and hairstyling was on full display and the experience was like being transported back to the days of MTV in a DeLorean. Her choreography reworked many famous MTV dances of the era. Most notable were "Flashdance", "Material Girl" and a very vibrant "Thriller". Her dancers were well-drilled and together with the wedding dances, of which there were quite a few, the show was a dance spectacular. The Hora dance during "Today You are a Man" was nicely executed but "Saturday Night in the City", which closed the first act, was the standout routine with the "Flashdance" trappings including the real shower over the brave Ms Brunton.

Musical director Dermot O'Callaghan's interpretation of the score was excellent. Fulling incorporating the gods of synth and moog, his sound was straight out of the eighties, with lots of brass. This is not a jukebox musical, but you'd be excused for thinking it was as Matthew Sklar's music is so redolent of the genre. Pat Benatar, Spandau Ballet, Irene Cara, Billy Idol, MJ, and Duran Duran came to mind during the show as did many other big- haired musical artists. His band veered between '80's disco, Jewish Klezmer and MOR rock to deliver a big sound. Mr O'Callaghan's work with the ensemble was also excellent, nice harmonies and power, especially on "Single" which popped and "Saturday Night in the City", which brought the interval curtain and the house down.

To do justice to this show you need to have two charismatic leads in Robbie and Julia, so the right casting is essential. The characters are uncomplicated, winsome, guy/girl next door types with excellent singing and dance skills. They must also have a flair for comedy. Ms Tighe cast Jamie Hennessy as Robbie and Orla Jennings as Julia. From the beginning of the show these two performers showed they had a wonderful chemistry together and as the musical progressed it just got better. Wonderful tender scenes like the dumpster scene where they connected and the scene where they wrote a song together and the kiss in the store that went on forever were very well directed and acted. There was a lovely momentum to their developing romantic relationship. Mr Hennessy's Robbie was quite charismatic on stage and had a good grasp of his character. His singing was first-class on all of his numbers, quite funny on "Somebody Kill Me" and hilarious on "Casualty of Love" at the wedding where he insulted everyone in a kinda stand-up comedy routine. Plus, he played guitar! Ms Jennings played Julia as a little bit ditzy, blind to her fiancé's real nature. She had a gorgeous tone to her voice, what we used to call a recording voice back in the day. Her voice on "Someday" and the solo reprise was very pure and dazzling. She was great with Holly and Angie on "Pop" and with Robbie on "Not That Kind of Thing", but it was their songs "If I told You", and especially "Grow Old with You" where their chemistry really glowed.

Julia's funny best friend, Holly was played by Jacqueline Brunton with a Madonna'esque sassiness. Her singing, comic timing and dance were first- class, and she had a lovely chemistry with Julia and a nice delicacy with Robbie. The 'funny best friend' role always requires a fine balance to perform, but Ms Brunton aced it. The shower scene during "Saturday Night in the City" at the end of Act I, was the lasting image from this production and Ms Brunton excelled in it as she did in "Pop" and "Right in Front of Your Eyes". She also had a good dynamic with Brian Dalton's Sammy, her on/off/ on again boyfriend. Mr Dalton, the bass player in the wedding band with his flock of Seagulls hair and creative physical comedy, was the most grounded character in the show and played his desire for Holly with subtlety. He can clearly play bass as his 'bass syncing' was excellent. "It's Your Wedding Day" was admirable as was all of his singing in the Wedding Band with the other two, and he was great on "Single", with the male ensemble. He had a lovely moment with George, the keyboard player of the band, when he realised that George was gay where he showed his sensitive side. George was played by Kevin Sherwin channelling Karma Chameleon era Boy George with the dreads and ribbons. Mr Sherwin gave us a low-key George, which was perfect. The character is quite sensitive, and he didn't go over the top with the campness. He blended well with Sammy and Robbie and had a great duet/ dance with Rosie on "Move That Thang". His singing was hilarious on the Spandau Ballet inspired "George's Prayer", and he had nice timing.

Robbie lived with his grandmother, who occasionally dispensed hilarious advice based on her own colourful past. Played with a lovely energy by Jenny McCabe, her performance as septuagenarian Rosie was perfect. "A Note from Grandma" was brilliant especially the timing on the last line! Her rap song "Move That Thang" with George was super, especially the acrobatic dance bits. Julia's mother, Angie, was another character prone to dispensing advice. Nicely played by Judy Miller with a slightly bitter edge, Ms Miller sang well on "Pop".

Robbie and Julia had emotional baggage, in the form of a crazy ex-girlfriend and a current sleazy fiancé. Robbie's ex, Linda, who jilted him at the alter was given the rock chick treatment by Aoife Masterson. Her performance of "A Note from Linda" was perfectly pitched but her standout moment was the riotous performance of "Let Me Come Home", a mixture of Pat Benatar and Joan Jett, where she tried to re-seduce Robbie. Excellent work. Julia's fiancé, Glen, was smarmily played by Ciaran Tighe. Mr Tighe epitomised the "Greed is Good" Gordon Gekko vibe with this womanising, slimy performance. He performed "All About the Green", a paean to the American Dream and love of the dollar quite well and showed high status, especially with Robbie. All of these characterisations were excellent, there wasn't one weak link here and this extended into the ensemble who were committed and strong. The look-a-likes at the end of the show in Vegas were all wonderful too, especially Elvis and Marilyn.

Claire Tighe, Aidan Mannion & Eileen Fagan designed the set, Darren Kelleher gave us a great light show, Jason Fallon gave us a full range sound with good sound effects and Rita Tighe, Judy Miller, Carol Byrne & Collette Conway designed the costumes. Lace and denim ruled the catwalk here, throw in a number of wedding dresses, sharp 'new romantic' suits and wall street braces and we were back to the '80's. Kevin Hynes looked after the make-up and hair. George's wig was perfect, looking like a flock of birds nested in it, as was the Tina Turner wig. The Cyndi Lauper, Madonna and Rock Chic looks both in hair and make-up were faultless. It was all perfectly stage managed by Mary Purcell and her crew.

'The Wedding Singer' was a wonderful nostalgic trip back to a time when we who lived in it were lucky to have such a range of styles of music, dance, and fashion. Leixlip's version was brim full of feel-good moments that put a smile on our faces, with a wonderful cast, scintillating music and dance this musical was excellent.

The Power of Love Clane Musical and Dramatic Society staged Joe DiPietro's homage to Americana and the birth of the teenager. 'All Shook Up' was written in 2004 by DiPetro and is an unusual jukebox musical in that it features music made popular by Elvis Presley and a plot straight out of Shakespearian comedies. Strange bedfellows indeed. The story centres around a roustabout (basically an unskilled labourer) called Chad who turns up in a sleepy small town on his busted motorcycle looking for a mechanic. He introduces the townsfolk to sex, and drugs and rock'n'roll, well not the drugs but certainly the other two, and sparks off a series of love affairs that radically change the town. The plot is a mash-up of; 'Footloose', Shakespeare's 'Twelfth Night' and 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', Edmond Rostand's 'Cyrano de Bergerac' and Benedek's outlaw biker film 'The Wild One', starring a leather jacketed Marlon Brando. Chad meets the mechanic, Natalie the local tomboy and she falls for his impish charms. Chad however falls for Miss Sandra, the curator of the local museum. Natalie dresses as a guy and becomes Ed, believing that he'll fall for her if she is more like him, and soon after the other townsfolk start to fall for each other, until everybody is mainlining sildenafil and they all live happily ever after.

We first met Chad, the cool but cerebrally challenged hero of the show, as he was released from jail. He was played by Robert Gallagher, who had a wonderful comprehension of the role. He had marvellous energy throughout the show, running from one situation to another, bouncing in and out of scenes, dispensing advice to Dean and Lorraine and everything revolved around him. His singing was also brilliant, injecting pathos into the songs where needed, lampooning them in others. He had good chemistry with Jim, Natalie and especially Dennis and danced with skill. Natalie, the mechanic who agreed to repair his bike and fell for him was played winningly by Niamh O'Carroll. She captured the tomboy aspect of Natalie's character, using the dress as an oil rag and acting quite cocky. When she became 'Ed', she lowered her voice and moved with less grace, which worked well. Her singing on "Blue Suede Shoes" as Ed was great as was her "Follow That Dream" both with Chad. They had a good dynamic together, particularly during "A Little Less Conversation", where they kissed and at the end of the show where they... well, no spoilers.

This small town in nowheresville was home to a diverse collection of people, some of who we got to meet. Natalie's father, widower Jim, was nicely played by Seán Lennon who also fell for Miss Sandra and ended up being mentored by Chad on how to woo. He had a good dynamic with Natalie and Sylvia and his scenes with Chad were excellent. He sang well on "Don't Be Cruel" and had a good stage presence. His friend, world- weary Sylvia, who runs the local bar and is sweet on him, was played by Grainne Ui Lúing who gave a lovely still performance. Her on stage relationship with Mr Lennon was great, we really wanted them to hook up. Her chemistry with onstage rebellious daughter Lorraine was excellent and she sang with passion on "There's Always Me" and energy on "Heartbreak Hotel". Charming performance from Sarah O'Flaherty as the feisty Lorraine. She had a good dynamic with Sylvia and her singing was good on "It's Now or Never" and "If I Can Dream" with new boyfriend Dean who was played by Kevin Macken as an innocent Mummy's boy who decides to rebel against his domineering mother, who is also the conservative mayor. These two characters were inspired to throw caution to the wind and hook up by Chad who believed you should act on your desires and hang the consequences.

Dean's mother, Mayor Matilda ruled the town with a pink-clad iron fist. Forbidding music and dancing and public displays of affection, Edel Marron O'Flaherty's mayor was a real cartoon baddie in this show, like something out of a Scooby Do cartoon. She shouted her way through the show believing her view should be slavishly adhered to, demanding Earl, the sheriff, shoot any dissenters, especially Chad. Her scenes with Earl were perfectly timed and she sang well on "(You're the) Devil in Disguise". The silent Earl was superbly played by Eric Nolan. His expressions and body language were perfect. When he eventually spoke, he wowed everyone in the theatre and his singing on "Can't Help Falling in Love" was super. Every roustabout must have a sidekick and Chad chose nerdy Dennis, played with high energy by Philip Darragh. Mr Darragh's physicality as Dennis was great. He rarely stood still but moved around the stage like a dervish. His speech was rapid and high pitched at times and his singing on "It Hurts Me" was full of emotion. The other outsider in town was big city girl Miss Sandra, who ran the museum. Obviously dismayed to be stranded in a cultural wasteland, Sarah McGauran played Sandra with a fine skill. Her singing was good on "Let Yourself Go" and on "Teddy Bear / Hound Dog" and her scenes with Ed were great.

This was a fun-filled romp of a production with a clever set, designed by the director, of sliding panels showing us the various locales including a garage, bar, and a fairground with a 'tunnel' of love car. Set painting and the use of giant prints helped to site the show accordingly. The surprise moment came with the reveal of the framed 'living' portraits in the museum, very Harry Potter, and they really looked like the famous paintings. Actors playing Mona Lisa, Beethoven, Frieda Kahlo and others stared out at the audience and joined in on Miss Sandra's song along with moving statues. Art McGauran literally putting the art on stage! Nomac, Naas MD & CMDS Wardrobe gave us a real 1950's look with great dresses. Amanda Lister looked after make-up, which was great and hair/wigs which were also suitable. Natalie's transformation into Ed was very well done. Cathal Donohue's lighting was excellent. Good use of movers which helped to add a vibrancy to the show. His cuing was perfect on the "One Night with You" breakout scenes and Wilkins Sound System delivered a crisp warm sound with good balance between band and singers. Siobhan Keogh had the hard task of stage managing this show. The stage is tiny, yet we must visit lots of locations. Ms Keogh handled it all with finesse with quick transitions and scene changes that helped the smooth running.

Grace McGrath's choreography was full of energy and an engaging lightness. From the superb opening "Jailhouse Rock", right up to the end. Her use of the small stage was clever, and I loved the flashlights in "All Shook Up", a huge number, that had multiple entrances and exits. Her cast were well-drilled on hip- thrusting and dances from the 1950's. The angels and devils were really original, and every dancer had a lovely nimbleness and precision. Dave McGauran's band were great, even though they were isolated away from us backstage, they were tight and strong. Guitar was very prevalent on most of the numbers and was faultless as was the driving drums and bass. Horns were also super, particularly on "There's Always Me". His work with the ensemble was excellent eliciting superb harmonies and power at times. I liked the arrangement and harmonies on "Heartbreak Hotel" and how characters would break into "One Night with You" as the others froze. Lovely work.

I was never a big fan of Elvis Presley's music back in the day, but this show reminded me of how good it really is. So, it was lovely to sit back and let it all wash over me. Art McGauran's interpretation of the musical was quite inspiring, he nailed the humour without forcing it, he had a great cast who knew what they were doing, and the music and choreography was top-notch. Great work.

The Phantom of the Strand 'The Phantom of the Opera' is a musical by Andrew Lloyd Webber that premiered in London in 1986. It is based on Gaston Leroux's Gothic horror novel 'The Phantom of the Opera'. In the 19th century, an ugly, vengeful but musically gifted ghost lived deep beneath the Paris Opera House. He secretly helps opera singer Christine become famous and falls in love with her. When he learns that Christine is in love with her childhood friend Raoul, the "Phantom" is heartbroken and channels his pain to seek revenge. Many theatregoers have seen the musical since 1986 and it has played and is playing all over the world. It is truly a modern classic and Carrick- On-Suir presented the Irish Adult Amateur Premiere in the Strand Theatre this April. Directed by Martin McNelis with musical direction by Fergal Carroll and choreography by Edel Quinlan, this was a big show on a small stage. Martin McNelis managed to tell the story quite well through the production. His direction of the actors worked best in the more light- hearted scenes with Firman and Andre and with Carlotta and Piangi, the comic timing in these scenes was nicely wrought and paced.

The 'love triangle' between Phantom, Christine, and Raoul, was more of the Victorian melodrama school requiring the performers to over emote at times but these three performers were quite compelling to watch for all that. Playing the Phantom was Neill Bourke who captured the innate sadness of the character. His singing on "All I Ask of You (Reprise)" on top of the Opera House was full of longing. His infatuation with Christine was delicately played and his duet with her "The Phantom of the Opera" was good, however "The Music of the Night" was excellent and soared. Mr Bourke had strong vocals and an empathetic performance style, but he pulled back on the evil, the vengeful killer driven mad by his deformity and his love for the beauty that he could not have, making the character pathetic rather than psychotic. As Christine, Ashley Cooke created a rather fragile Christine, more victim than heroine, controlled by the men around her. She didn't show much of Christine's gumption but was more timid and almost ambivalent both with Raoul and with the Phantom. "All I ask of You" with Raoul was perfect and she managed that famous high note on the title song. Keith Dwyer-Greene's Raoul was probably the most successful character interpretation. He was very believable and confident as Raoul, the strong hero type. He had an equitable dynamic with Ms Cooke, as the alpha male to her damsel in distress. His vocals were perfect, "Think of Me" and "All I Ask of You" were superb. These three performers are to be lauded for taking on such massive roles and they all shone in different aspects of the show. Phantom brooding at the organ in his lair, Christine distressed in the graveyard and Raoul trying to rescue Christine form the clutches of the Phantom. However, there was very little tension among them, we never felt fearful for their fates, which was a pity because it is a gothic horror and there should have been some elements of the genre on show.

The new owners, Firman and André, of the Paris Opera House where the story takes place were played with a light touch by Caolán Deehy-Power and Alan Hearne. Mr Deehy-Power played Firman, the money obsessed one with good timing and singing. Putting a positive spin on disaster, 'there's no such thing as bad publicity', he was a little overblown at times but did convince. Mr Hearne nailed the sarcasm of this character. He played André as a bit more 'devil may care', which was a nice contrast to Firman. He too was a tad overstated, but I liked his performance. They made a good double-act and were often quite funny, especially when working with Louise Russell's Carlotta and Eoin Sheedy's Piangi. These two characters were the divas of the Opera Company. They had a great funny dynamic together and had excellent comic timing. They were required to sing rather badly, and they didn't disappoint!

The resident Ballet Mistress, Madame Giry, was played with a beautiful stillness by Sandra Power. She exuded mystery and was, we suspect, the Phantom's confidant. Her accent was perfect, and she sang well, especially on "Down Once More / Track Down this Murderer". Playing her daughter, Meg, who was Christine's friend was Camille Walsh. Ms Walsh played her as a gentle yet fearless soul. Her dance was excellent as was her solo parts of "Think of Me". Other performers of note were Seamus Power who played con man Lefevre who sells the theatre knowing it's haunted; Padraig Sheehan played Reyer the company's repetiteur with good comic timing and authority; Chris Hanlon played the ill-fated Joseph Buquet was good on "Magical Lasso" and Jim Kennedy who played the Auctioneer in the Prologue and the Chief of Police later in the show had good presence. They were ably supported by a large ensemble who played members of the company and party guests on "Masquerade".

Edel Quinlan's choreography worked best in the ballet sequences. Her corps looked great, the ballerinas flanking her male dancer. The Masquerade Ball dances were good initially but became quite contemporary towards the end as the cast pointed at the audience. Ms Quinlan helped to create some of the nicer stage pictures and visuals in the show through the positioning of her dancers and also cleverly masked scene changes by moving them to the stage line at times. The choreography added another dimension to the staging, at times a subtle animation, at others an explosion of movement. Fergal Carroll was musical director on the show with Eamon O'Malley employed as Chorus Master.

The medium-sized band, sequestered in a room backstage, of players were good. Powerful horns at times and lovely violins. The percussion owned the show as did the keyboards, particularly the massive organ sound. Mr O'Malley's work with the chorus was good, they were very present on the bigger numbers. Some of the principals were beginning to sound tired by the time I saw the show, but Raoul was consistently good as was Phantom, Madam Giry and the majority of the chorus.

The original Phantom show was a feast for the eyes with an amazing set and costumes. This production did well in recreating some of this spectacle. John O'Donoghue's set design was excellent. The reveal of the pros and the red boxes was superb and a lovely moment. The Phantom's lair was well dressed with the candles, organ etc., and the boat journey was short but good. The chandelier looked a bit ramshackle but the dressing on the Opera's within the musical looked first-rate. The roof and the graveyard looked stunning with the angels and massive tombstone. The "Masquerade" costumes looked opulent and really lifted the scene. The other costumes were fine and of the era. The Commedia masks were good too as was Phantom's. Make up and hair styling also looked superb as did DBL's lighting, with their blues and star cloth. Sound by Star Systems got some powerful bass sounds out of the synths which resonated. The Phantom's voice was not reverbed enough though and wasn't loud and chilling as it should. The reverb on "Track Down This Murderer" was excellent, as it echoed around the theatre. Stage manager Michael O'Hara is to be commended for his sterling work on this show. It was a massive production on a relatively small stage and he and his crew handled it with dexterity.

This was a massive undertaking for a relatively small society to take on and they did well to fit it on the stage and for it to look and sound so good. But it did lack tension, both in the performers and the piece as a whole. We never felt that fearfulness for the characters and the momentum of the arc was constantly slowed down. It looked great though, the set and lighting worked nicely in tandem with the costuming and make-up. Some scenes were quite difficult to see however due to the vast amount of haze pumped onto the stage, but it added to the spookiness of the Phantom's underground lair. The cast were good and clearly loved the piece and I think this affection for the piece spilled out into the audience who gave it a rapturous standing ovation. Well done, Carrick.

'Little Shop of Horrors' was adapted into a musical by Alan Menken and Howard Ashman in 1982. Roughly based on Goethe's 'Faust' and a fun low budget Roger Corman film from 1960 staring Jack Nicholson, it's a comedy take on awful horror B-movies of the '50's.

Set in New York in the 1960's, it's about an orphan, Seymour, who is indentured to a flower shop owner, Mr Mushnik, who 'lets' him work in his failing shop in exchange for food and board. Seymour is secretly in love with his co-worker Audrey, who is the girlfriend of a sadistic misogynist dentist, Oran. Seymour buys an unusual plant that appears to be dying and inadvertently feeds it his own blood. Naming the plant Audrey II, he soon realises that the plant has become sentient and demands more flesh and blood. Mushnik notices that the plant has grown and is attracting good attention for the shop, so 'adopts' Seymour to keep the plant. However, Audrey II reveals that it wants to take over the world, so Seymour must make some difficult decisions.

I saw it produced by St Mary's Choral Society in the White Memorial Theatre in Clonmel in May this year. Directed by Des Henn with musical direction by Niall Kelly and choral direction by Robbie Pender and choreography by Barbara Meaney. Des Henn helmed a straightforward take on the show, his cast sang well and most of the obvious humour landed. The plant's puppeteer and voice stole the show, but Audrey and Mr Mushnik also impressed. The set was cleverly dressed with graffiti and other New York trappings and the music was excellent. The six Ronettes sang with good harmonies and effectively executed their simple well- rehearsed 'backing singer' style dance moves. The shop looked great but the frequent scene transitions seemed to take an age and slowed the pace of the show, however the band's playing covered well here. Costumes and make-up were okay, and the sound and lighting design lifted the show.

An excellent eight-piece band in the pit, two keys, bass, drums, guitar, trumpet and two reeds was conducted with vigour by musical director Niall Kelly. I loved the sax on the title song and the drums and bass throughout and the keys on "Somewhere That's Green" were lovely. Robbie Pender's work with the singers was proficient. The Ronettes had some lovely harmonies, and the leads sang well. Barbara Meaney choreographed the show, but there wasn't a lot of dance numbers as such. The Ronettes did have some choreography as they sang but it was very low energy and relaxed. "Skid Row" was a bit bigger involving more performers and worked quite well.

Joe Sheehan gave us a nice Seymour and had a good dynamic with Mr Bolger's Mushnik. His singing was very good especially on "Suddenly Seymour" with Audrey and "Feed Me (Git it)" with Audrey II and with Mushnik on "Mushnik and Son". He played Seymour's innocence and the character's descent into crime quite well. We had a nice gentle performance from Diarmuid Bolger as Mushnik who sounded uncannily like US comedian Rodney Dangerfield. His NYC accent was perfect, and I liked his unfussy performance. He sang well on "Ya Never Know" and he played Mushnik's duplicitous nature and sub-text with a fine ability. Playing Seymour's crush, Audrey was Emma Sunderland who I last saw as Natalie/Ed in St. Mary's 'All Shook Up', where she was brilliant. She didn't disappoint here either and sang brilliantly as Audrey. Her "Somewhere That's Green" was gorgeous as was "Suddenly Seymour" with Seymour. She played the victim of Cormac Maher's Orin skilfully, and we felt empathy with her plight.

Cormac Maher had oodles of energy but I feel this energy was misdirected. His Orin was more pantomime villain, as he mugged at the audience, than sadistic psychopath. He went too over the top with Orin becoming quite cartoonish. His singing on "Dentist!" was good, but again more subtlety would have sold the song better. His cameos as other characters were good, but his Orin was too big for this subdued production.

Of course, the real star of 'Little Shop of Horrors' is always the plant, Audrey II. Voiced by the wonderful Darragh Johnson, who had a superb voice, deep and expressive and pitched perfectly for each song. His "Feed Me (Git it)" was one of the best songs on the night I attended, and "Suppertime" was excellent. Jason Ryan operated the various plant-puppets and his timing or 'plant-syncing' to Mr Johnson's singing was perfect.

The musical is narrated by a voice over at the beginning and end and in between we have the Ronettes, six urchin girls played by Rachel Browne, Nicole Butler, Aisling Corbett, Caitlin Fanning, Grace Hogan and Eve Whelan. These performers sang with lovely harmonies and had good dance skills, but little energy or soul. As a sort of Greek Chorus, they told us what was going on. Referred to as urchins by Mushnik, they also played other characters and interacted with Seymour and with Audrey and Mushnik. At times, they would stand and stare blankly out at the audience as scenes were happening around them and seemed a little lost and inactive with no inner tension or energy, which was a pity as these characters are the heart of the story.

The set was designed by Stagewright in Galway, the shop set looked good although needed more dressing as there was very few flowers or plants on show initially, just the bunch of roses. There were more added in Act II as the shop became more prosperous, but still, it looked like an empty store that could have sold anything initially. The floor looked great, with the flagstones blending into tiles in the shop as did the graffiti on the walls and the stoop. The dentist's chair was quite authentic, but Orin's gas contraption was a poor design and broke during the show. The main design flaw was the flats that came in and out during the show. They took an age to bring in and set up. The plant puppets were fabulous though. Jimmy Trehy stage managed the show. The scene changes took from the pace of the show as the flats had to be wheeled on and offstage each transition. This was clearly not ideal as it did disrupt the flow. Creative Scene Productions looked after costumes on the show. Orin's leather jacket was too big for him and the green costumes on the Ronettes were also quite ill-fitting, but everything else looked good. Make up was good all around, especially Audrey's bruising and I loved the bad wigs on Mr Maher when he played the media characters. Alan McCormack's lighting design was good with a great use of foot lights and colour, especially green. Pat Marnane's sound was initially a bit mushy on the first song, but it improved once the show got going. A good range of sound effects and excellent reverb and depth on the Audrey II voice plus a good balance between band and singers.

'Little Shop of Horrors' is a great romp; it should be scary at times as there is some tension built into the story, the humour is dark and should be played seriously but tongue in cheek and there's lots of room for innovative set pieces and routines with the Ronettes and the front line. But we didn't really get any of that on this production, but the singing was excellent!

Addams Family Tree St Agnes' Choral Society haunted the Grand Opera House with their new production of the comedy musical 'The Addams Family' in May of this year. Based on comic book characters created by Charles Addams back in 1938, the family are a satirical transposition of the ideal American family; an eccentric, wealthy bunch who take pleasure in the ghoulish and are oblivious that people find them weird or fearsome. Directed by Laura Kerr with musical direction by Andrew Robinson and choreography by Ann Marie Morgan, this show was fast and funny in a lively production of song, dance, death and damnation. The plot is all about the Addams' eldest child, Wednesday falling in love with a 'normal' person, Lucas Beineke, getting engaged and inviting him and his family over to hers for dinner so that they can tell the folks.

Director Laura Kerr was a perfect choice to direct this show. She is an excellent director of comedy, knowing how far to push a gag and when to let it settle and wait for the audience to catch up. The comic timing in the show was masterful, and her work on the characterisations of the wonderful cast was excellent. Adding in Thing and Cousin It to the family was inspired and her Ancestors were plentiful, scary and had superb dance skills. Ms Kerr also added another character, Young Wednesday, played beautifully by Kate McClean. She appeared in the "Happy/ Sad" scene where Gomez is lamenting the fact that Wednesday is growing up. It was a poignant, heart-warming scene that served to deepen his and Wednesday's characterisations.

The set, by UK Productions, loomed over proceedings like another character and Andrew Reddy's costumes and Lisa Cunningham Black's make-up was stunning. The technical aspects were also super, great sound by the McCuskers and fantastic lighting and projection by ACK Productions and an unexpected bit of Fester flying by Adam Searle all helped to create the world of Charles Addams, a 19th century Gothic palette infiltrated by brash contemporary American life. This dichotomy was perfectly shown when the Beinekes came to dinner, thereafter the show really found its feet and the resultant madcap series of scenes were perfectly paced like a frenetic farce right up to the curtain of Act I. Act II was more sedate when the three sets of couples; Gomez and Morticia, Wednesday and Lucas and Lucas's parents Alice and Mal, were in danger of separating. It was slower, leaving room for exposition and further character development plus some outstanding dance numbers, choreographed by Ann Marie Morgan. Gradually it moved towards the darkness again and ended with a vocally huge song that showcased the society's choral prowess under musical director Andrew Robinson's astute guidance.

St Agnes' Choral Society were blessed with their cast. From the front line to the ensemble of Ancestors, this cast were one hundred percent focused on their roles. Leading the pack was Allen Gordon's Gomez. Looking a bit like Basil Fawlty, with great comic timing, Mr Gordon's Gomez had a lovely stillness and played him with a heavy dose of irony, the death-related puns; their first date to the play "Death of a Salesman" and longing to see Paris, the sewers of Paris, were delivered with just the right amount of self-awareness to land beautifully. His onstage relationship with Wednesday was very believable, "Happy/ Sad" was full of paternal pride and sorrow that she's grown up and will leave them soon, especially when Young Wednesday showed up. It was quite moving. He had a good voice and sang well on all of his numbers especially "Trapped" and "Not Today" and his dance on "Tango De Amor" was perfect. Playing his beloved wife, Morticia was Lorraine Jackson, gliding along the floor, with great arm and hand movements, Ms Jackson with her Vampiella styling was perfectly cast. Her little comic throw away lines were natural and perfectly pitched, whereas her one gag "Coroner, get it?" was overlaboured as it should have been. A character that is unknowingly funny, trying to be funny is hilarious. Her singing was excellent, "Secrets" and "Just Around the Corner" were superb as was her duet with Gomez, "Live Before We Die". They had a lovely chemistry and bounced beautifully off each other.

Aideen Fox played Wednesday with a great range of petulant expressions and was super at mimicking Morticia and at deadpanning. Her singing was amazing, with a superb range especially on "Pulled" and she eclipsed all in "Crazier than You". She had exceptional chemistry with Gomez, theirs was the most natural relationship on stage. Her brother Pugsley was played with irascibility and good comic timing by Jude Forsythe. He really captured the 'annoying little brother' trope and had a lovely energy. He sang well on "What If", not an easy song but he nailed it, pardon the pun. He also had a good dynamic with Grandma, they dovetailed nicely in performance as the youngest and oldest characters. She was played by a very heavily made up Gemma Duffy. Her physicality; hunched over yet spry, was terrific and must have hurt after the show. Suffering for her art, Ms Duffy was also helped by the other cast members with their reactions to her 'smell'. I loved how she would just turn up and watch the action, like Fester and she was great on "Full Disclosure". Martin McDowell's Fester had excellent direct to audience banter and was winningly camp. His physicality was great too, as he bounded around the stage. His American Footballer persona, lifting his wig to Alice was a great moment as was his flying. "The Moon and Me" was brilliantly staged and he sang it with a charming delicacy and focus. There was also Liam Nugent as Cousin It, as he shuffled around the stage, turning up unexpectedly, totally hirsute and wearing glasses completing the family along with Thing, a remote controlled 'hand' that dashed around the stage. They were all looked after by the butler, Lurch who was not as tall as most Lurches but had a lovely slow movement and superb vocal on "Move Towards the Darkness" and his comic timing especially with the Beinekes, was superb.

Playing Wednesday's fiancé soon to be in-laws was Josh Clarke as Lucas and his parents, Alice, played by Fiona Keegan and Mal played by Mark Tilley. Mr Clarke's Lucas showed real 'boy-next-door' mannerisms and epitomised the modern All mid-west American teen and was a great contrast to Wednesday. He sang well on "Crazier than You" and played the exasperated sensible boyfriend with good stage craft. Ms Keegan played Alice as quite ditzy but with a strong maternal instinct. Her "Waiting" was excellent, especially her choreography where she ended up flat out on the table. Her section with Lurch was hilarious and I loved her rhyming. Finally, Mr Tilley gave us a very uptight Mal, his scenes with Gomez were great, not understanding this weird creepy family and a bit scared of them. He had a great scene with Alice when he ripped off his shirt showing he was a real rocker underneath the stiff businessman, and he sang with passion on "Crazier than You" with Alice, Lucas and Wednesday.

Ms Kerr breathed new life into this show by not just sticking to the formulaic presentation but adding her own vision to it. It wasn't just page to stage and blocked like many directors are happy to do with musicals, but she expanded on the characters and their relationships, especially Gomez and Wednesday. This gave a realism to what is frankly a weird otherworldly family unit, which made us understand and empathise with them. The whole production reeked of quality and attention to detail and most importantly I think Charles Addams would have approved.

Wild Wild West The last time I saw Roscrea Musical Society was in 2019 when I attended their 'My Fair Lady", which was a superb show with an unconventional ending that I really liked. This year I was back to see their take on Rogers and Hammerstein's 'Oklahoma!' at the Abbey Hall in Roscrea. A classic musical, 'Oklahoma!' was written in 1943 and based on Lyn Riggs' 1930 play 'Green Grow the Lilacs'. The musical's plot is fairly similar to the play, but the play's ending is different in that Curly's fate for killing the farmhand is left undecided. 'Oklahoma!' tells a story of a frontier community in the 1800's banding together against an outsider, Judd Fry and follows the fledgling love affair between two sets of couples; Curly & Laurey and Annie & Will. Rodgers & Hammerstein reinvented the American musical with this show in that all of the songs actually further the plot and if features a fifteen- minute ballet sequence in the first act that foreshadows the action in Act II.

Directed by Paul Norton with musical direction by Mary Rose McNally and choreography by Stephanie Browne, this was very good production of this classic show, which jumped off the stage with considered acting performances, excellent choreography and singing. Paul Norton didn't reinvent the wheel with this one but did inject much tension into the production. His cast's acting was excellent, stand outs were Curly, Laurey, Judd and Ali. They owned their roles and performed with clear intentions and truth. In this well-known musical, the character development is often overlooked in favour of delivering the famous songs, so it's sometimes directed as a concert with bits of pesky acting that gets in the way of the music. But thankfully that didn't happen here. We actually got to know the characters and their dreams and so became involved and empathised with their lives.

The first character we saw on stage was Judd Fry, the antagonist of the story, as he delivered logs to his boss's cabin. Whilst he didn't give us much cause for concern at that point, his presence cast a pall over the brightly lit scene as if a cloud had appeared in the ever blue skies of Oklahoma. This was a small bit of direction but an important one as, for those that know the show, Fry is a harbinger of doom. Once he exited, we weren't sure if he was still lurking about during the rest of the scene, which straight away gave some tension. We heard Curly start to sing, and Aunt Eller entered to churn butter in the midday sun. Curly was played by Adam Skeffington, who portrayed him with an intense likability. Curly is often portrayed as a silly lovesick puppy, but Mr Skeffington gave us a considered performance of a character who is clever and protective and has reached the point in his life where he wants to settle down and leave his unstructured life behind. He had a lovely chemistry with Ms Rohan's Laurey, and their scenes were excellent. Mr Skeffington's scenes with Judd were full of tension and we could see a real battle of wills going on between them. His "Oh What a Beautiful Mornin'" was nicely paced and sung and was "The Surrey with the Fringe on Top" with Eller and his duet with Laurey, the love of his life who was playing hard to get, "People Will Say We're in Love", was warm and adorable. Laurey was played by Aishling Rohan. I really liked Ms Rohan's characterisation of Laurey. She didn't play her as bitchy and self-serving as is often the case in this musical. Her Laurey was warm and caring, unsure of where she was in life, and she played her journey through the story with skill.

There was a definite change in Laurey post dream, she heeded the warnings in the dream and became surer of herself and what she wanted, that is, a relationship with Curly. They had a super dynamic together and it was satisfying to see the power shift from Laurey to Curly after the dream as this is I'm sure what the writers intended. Her singing was excellent too. Her duet with Curly was exceptional as was "Many a New Day" with the female ensemble and through her sections in "The Surrey with the Fringe on Top" we caught a glimpse of real Laurey early on. Laurey lived with her Aunt Eller on the farm and paid Judd Fry to help with the manual labouring. Eller was given a lovely, warm kind portrayal by Siobhán Bowe. Ms Bowe's Eller was maternal towards not just Laurey but everyone! Her singing on "The Surrey with the Fringe on Top" with Curly was sweet and she controlled "The Farmer and the Cowman" once she entered the song. She was quietly dominant and wore her high status with assuredness. As Judd Fry, we had an intense performance from Prionnsias Loughnane. Judd Fry is the main antagonist in this show and should be played as the outsider. Clearly beset with mental health issues and possible a serial killer, the character is not easy to play as he lusts after Laurey. Mr Loughnane's Judd was quite psychotic, he had that narcissistic persistence that he would get what he believed he deserved, which was Laurey. The scene in the smokehouse with Curly was quite chilling and it was here their antipathy bloomed and altered the course of the story.

These were the main characters in the story, and they all played with super attention to detail and believability. Curly, Laurey and Eller had a great dynamic between them, they were very alike in that they seemed to want to see the best in people and we were in no doubt that they'd all live happily ever after. The fly in the ointment was Judd Fry, who clearly wanted what they had, a camaraderie and gentle humour and affection for each other, but didn't have the humility or social language to be able to integrate into pleasant society. His narcissism and psychotic nature contributed to his being the outsider who would rather burn everything if he couldn't have his way. Mr Norton focused on these elements of the story through his direction of these four performers and it gave a fabulous tension to the show.

The other love story was between Ado Annie Carnes and Will Parker. Played by Bríd Delaney and Dylan Hogan, they had a great dynamic too with Ado Annie exasperating Will because she couldn't decide whether to marry him or to go off into the wild blue yonder with travelling snake oil salesman Ali Hakim, wonderfully played by John Lynch. Ms Delaney had great comic timing and played Annie's indecision and fickle nature with proficiency. Her singing on "I Cain't Say No" was good and her responses to Ali's wooing were great as was her dynamic with Will. Mr Hogan's portrayal of Will was interesting. He seemed to pitch his voice quite high to possibly show the youthfulness of the character. He played Will's idiocy with good comic timing, particularly in his $50 scene with Ali, where he 'persuaded' Ali to buy his jumble. His trip to Kansas City didn't seem to mature him any and he presented as very genial and sweet, and his "Kansas City" was very good. Mr Lynch played Ali's penchant for getting into trouble with great timing and expression. His scenes with Annie were excellent and they bounced nicely off each other. His performance on "It's a Scandal! It's an Outrage!", which I'm happy to say was left in as it's often cut, was declaimed as it should be as the male ensemble filled in the melodies. Annie's father, Andrew, was played by Paul Spencer. Mr Spencer gave him a twinkle in the eye and a light touch which really worked. Carnes doesn't want his daughter to hook up with Will as he's a Cowman, so sets a high price, $50, for her hand. His dance on "The Farmer and the Cowman" was comic gold, like something you'd see in an old horse opera from the forties or 'Blazing Saddles'.

Obviously, there were many other performers on stage in the show in the ensemble and they all gave one hundred per cent and seemed to really get this interpretation. Mary Rose McNally was musical director, and her nine-band were sited in front of stage and were great. Ms McNally's work with the chorus was excellent, their "Kansas City" was punchy and "Many a New Day" with Laurey and the female chorus was great but the stand out was "The Farmer and the Cowman" and the title number, which had marvellous harmonies. Choreographer Stephanie Browne excelled on the "Dream Ballet" it was superb. This multi-character prophetic dance was our window into Laurey's dream/nightmare and featured many different styles of dance including a wonderful ballerina, four burlesque dancers, a hoedown and a strobe lit slow motion contemporary routine. Her work on "The Farmer and the Cowman" was equally as impressive, and "Kansas City" with the tap dance was also moved well as was "It's a Scandal! It's an Outrage!" with Ali and the male ensemble.

It all looked good too with set design by Ian Hanrahan, Paul Norton & Noel Ryan. The corn upstage looked great as did Eller's cabin. The old windmill down stage left, looked super. Judd's smokehouse also looked good, with the stove and the dirty animal skins. Events Lighting Solutions gave us a simple lighting design. Most of the show takes place in the same location with few lighting changes. Sound by Itech Productions, Joe Murphy. He achieved a good balance between band and singers. Costume by Pat McGann was supervised by Trish Delaney and Josie Kean. Lots of hats and chaps and denim. Ian Hanrahan stage managed the show with his crew. There's not a lot of scene changes here but they were quick and accurate and his marshalling of the large cast on a small stage was great.

It was a thoughtful production of an old classic, that gave a new insight to the themes of mental illness, prejudice, and murder contained within the plot and showed that 'Oklahoma!' is not just a pretty musical with hummable songs but is a really good story about love and lust and integrity in the wild west.

Sunshine On Laois!

Portlaoise Musical Society have been around since 1999, when they first hit the stage with 'Oklahoma' and since then have given the people of Portlaoise offerings such as 'Fiddler on the Roof', 'Singin' in the Rain' and other classics right up to their award winning 'Titanic' and in 2019, 'Ragtime'. Starring as Jud Fry in their first production was Paul Norton, who has gone on to direct many of their shows and he helmed their latest production, the Irish Premiere of 'Sunshine on Leith' in November at the Dunamaise Arts Centre. Many of you won't know much about this show, it being an Irish Premiere, so a few words on the origins I feel is needed. This Jukebox musical started out as a project by Dundee Rep in Scotland and was staged by them in 2007 and was made into a film in 2013. Playwright Stephen Greenhorn, who created the Scottish soap opera 'River City', wrote the book which is woven around songs written by Craig and Charlie Reid, known as The Proclaimers. Named after the band's second multi- selling album, the musical also contains songs from some of their other albums. It seemed like a winner when first mooted as their music, and there is a lot of it, is so catchy and the band rarely strayed far from their Scottish roots, so that would give the book provenance.

The plot centres around three couples. Army buddies Davy and Ally are back from the war in Afghanistan and trying to settle into civilian life. Ally takes up again with nurse girlfriend Liz while Davy, her brother, embarks on a relationship with Yvonne, her co-worker. Davy and Liz's parents, Rab and Jean, are about to celebrate their 30th wedding anniversary when an unknown blast from the past steps into their lives. That's it. There is little exploration of PTSD, which one would expect with soldiers returning home nor is there any meaningful consideration given to the nature of family. It's a soap opera plot with a hint of rom-com.

'Sunshine on Leith' seems to fall into the Jukebox Musical trap that has snared many other contrived shows. What suffers is not the music but the veracity of the story. None of the three love stories in the plot rise above a soap opera depth. The cliff-hanger at the end of Act I, where all three relationships are in danger of fracturing at the same time is pure melodrama and shamelessly contrived. The characters, except for Rab, are mundane and paper thin. But I suspect that Mr Norton knew this, and it is to his credit that he managed to integrate his vision for the piece and create a feel-good love letter to Edinburgh, shown by the projection of countless photographs of the Athens of the North. His use of projections and the mobile treads to denote locations helped to ground the piece. However, the constant moving of the set pieces during the many scene transitions became tiresome to watch, and I suspect execute, and adversely affected the pace of the show.

It came alive during the big well-known songs, which often started out with just one or two singers and then the whole ensemble would enter, creating a big overblown version of the song, thereby entering concert mode. This happened a lot throughout the show. That said, Musical Director Emer Hartnett did wonderful work with the chorus, their harmonies and power were superb. Her band were sited up stage left under a platform and in full view of the audience. They were excellent and were often augmented by musicians on the main part of the stage, which helped integrate the music into the plot. Choreographer, Stephanie Browne also managed to incorporate the choreography into the story and at times there was a lot of performers on stage, but they were well drilled and rehearsed. The addition of some traditional Scottish dance was sweet and the Call Centre scene, "Throw the 'R' Away", was particularly effective as the performers made great use of the treads and the A4 laminates. However, I found the Hibs scene choreography very unfocused.

With an ensemble of about seventy performers on the Dunamaise stage, all singing and dancing, sound designer and operator Vinny Osborne had his work cut out for him! But he nailed it, lovely deep bass and delicate highs from the band and every voice was crystal clear. Lighting all of this was Nick Anton's wonderful design, although it was hampered somewhat by the projections. Many scenes were set upstage against the cyc on the platform but weren't lit because of potential spill onto the projection screen. This was a pity, because I think we would have preferred to see the actors rather than a nice projection. The audience blinders via open white pars on the explosion as we moved from Afghanistan to Edinburgh was an excellent effect as was the mirror ball during "Oh Jean".

Set design by Paul Norton was clever. The main set pieces were the treads upstage which were moved around the stage to create different locations. The boxes at the beginning of the show were great and created a contemporary look to the show as the audience entered. The projections, of which there were many, helped to set the locations as they were mostly photographs. But I couldn't help wondering if they were needed. They were quite distracting at times and some of the shots were of the interiors of rooms, which we didn't need to see as we can use our imagination!

The lead performers were all very good. Their acting was uniformly excellent, their accents impeccable and they really gelled as a 'family' group. Shane Kelly's Davy was quiet and thoughtful, and his singing was admirable especially with Aishling Rohan's Yvonne, who's acting, and singing was faultless. Ally was played by Eoghan Fingleton, who really captured the essence of a character who was lost. His singing was also first-rate and his onstage relationship with Sarah Troy's Liz was the most naturalistic of all. Ms Troy played Liz as a character with intelligence and great self-control. I was particularly impressed with her journey from 'hometown girl' to 'wanderer', determined to better herself no matter what the cost.

Davy and Liz's parents, Rab and Jean, were played by Andrew Docherty and Hillary Treacy. Mr Docherty stole the show for me. His languid style of performance helped to bring life to Rab more than any other character. Rab is a well-written role in comparison to the others as his backstory is explored and developed. When he first meets Eilidh, his daughter from a previous brief affair, his confusion, fear, and surreptitious delight was written on his face. Mr Docherty's performance of "Oh Jean" was perfect as was his fronting the 'band' that opened Act II as they sang "Sky Takes My Soul". His accent and character were steeped in naturalism, and he was a joy to watch. Ms. Treacy's acting was superb. She embodied the character of Jean, a hard-working woman who has been deceived and feels like she has been living a lie for 25years. Her scene with Rab where they argue over his long- ago affair was outstanding. Aoife Digan's Eilidh was the result of Rab's affair, and she gave very moving performance. Her first scene with Rab was a tour-de- force of an emotional performance as she gradually revealed who she was and spoke of the death of her mother. All of these performers really made the best of the material, they managed through their skill and Mr Norton's direction to flesh out the characters.

Bob O'Kelly stage managed the show with some skill and although the transitions were somewhat laboured and clunky, I'm sure they improved during the run. Andrew Reddy oversaw the costuming and assembled some nice pieces for the show. I liked Rab's kilt and the soldier's uniforms at the beginning looked perfect. The NHS outfits were great as was the cleaners' costumes and the Hibs jerseys and scarves.

I did enjoy what Portlaoise Musical Society tried to do with the material. Their primary research of traveling to Edinburgh to understand Leith and where the show emanated from stood to them as they took many photographs, many of which were projected during the show, and immersed themselves in the culture. However, the story is utterly deferential to the presentation of the songs, which is always a problem with Jukebox Musicals. I wanted to know more about the characters, I wanted to feel empathy with them, but that's not in the book and despite the skill of the creatives and the cast, and the rousing choruses, something was missing for me.

Guts is All Newcastle Glees Musical Society presented the Northern Irish Premiere of this riotous musical based on the infamous sewing machinists strike in the Ford factory in London in the 1968. The musical, spawned from Nigel Cole's 2010 film, was first staged in 2014 in Adelphi Theatre starring Gemma Arterton. It's a super piece, full of rousing choruses and poignant solos with a dramatic book that takes some liberties but is somewhat faithful to the historical events. The story follows factory worker, Rita who becomes a reluctant heroine and labour activist who fights for equal pay for women. This has some negative impacts on her family life as well as on the men who work in the plant. However, her actions and those of her fellow co-workers led to the creation of the Equal Pay Act in 1970.

The Society has been around since 1957, when they launched with 'Trial by Jury'. Since then, they have produced a mixture of classic and contemporary shows to great acclaim. I first saw them perform when I adjudicated their superb 'Curtains' in 2019 and then again in 2020 with their immersive 'Calamity Jane'. Like many other societies, they took a forced break due to Covid-19 but bounced back in 2022 with this London-based musical. They own and operate the Annesley Hall on the seafront in Newcastle and run workshops for kids and teens plus stage the occasional concert series, and this is where I saw 'Made in Dagenham' in November 2022.

The show's director, Laura Kerr, gave us something very special with this production. Unlike many other musicals 'Made in Dagenham' is written like a play. The characters are three dimensional, the plot has many layers and there is a sense of watching history unfold in real time as it's based on real events. I'm sure that Ms Kerr was aware of the very dramatic origins of the story, but she wisely eschewed melodrama, instead working with her cast on naturalism, realism, and character development. This paid dividends as the acting was very natural and the character's objectives were extremely clear, and their onstage relationships were fully realised. Ms Kerr also pushed the comedy and the performer's comic timing was excellent. Choreography by Clare Donnelly was superb, especially the second act opener "This is America". Musical Direction by Mark Tilley was spot-on, and his 'hidden' orchestra were impressive as was the imaginative set. The overall interpretation of the source material was admirable in this production, funny and poignant in equal measure.

The production values were set very high on this show. The production team managed to build a brilliantly representative set reminiscent of a factory, complete with realistic machinery and even a time clock that the workers clocked in and out of. Costumes were excellent as were the 1960s wigs and make-up. Sound and lighting by Geoff Clark were good and suited the show. Annesley Hall does not have a big stage, but the Society managed to fit everything in; from a house to a factory to an office, everything looked like it belonged, all competently marshalled by stage manager Clair Williams. But it was the performances that really shone in this production, and I would argue that they could have staged it on a bus, and it would have been just as good! Playing our protagonist Rita O'Grady, the busy working mother who is thrust into the spotlight to become the voice of disenfranchised women in the workplace, we had Orla Russell who was perfectly cast. Ms Russell handled the pathos very well and her singing on "I'm Sorry, I Love You" with Eddie and "Busy Woman" was lovely. Her husband, Eddie, was played by Allen Gordon who played him with a relaxed confidence. His main song, "The Letter" was a showstopper of emotional intensity and they had a lovely chemistry together, especially when paired with their two onstage children, Graham, nicely played by Caden Curran and Sharon played by a very focused Martha Pryce. In the Ford factory were they both work, Rita's friend group were played by a group of very talented and well directed performers. Mia Pobloth played Sandra, a tall aspiring model. She owned the stage in all her scenes. Her singing was exceptional, displaying a wonderful range and power, particularly on the opening of "This is What We Want". Her acting was also great, inhabiting the role as if born to it. Katy Keaveney played the well- meaning but totally inarticulate Clare. This was a perfect comedy performance. Ms Keaveney was always 'on', when she was onstage, with little gestures and reactions to other characters, she presented a highly nuanced character. Her singing of "Wossname" was brilliant, with a good voice and outstanding comic timing. The wonderful Orla McCrickard played the foul-mouthed Beryl, with just the right amount of funny lewdness. She didn't go over the top into 'Carry On" territory but was quite subtle with the coarseness! Her singing and dancing were first-rate, and finally Cass, the sensible one who wants to be a pilot, was played with consummate ease by Melissa Poland. These four actors (Ms McCrickard, Ms Pobloth, Ms Poland & Ms Keaveney) benefitted from a good well-written script, which gave them room to develop their quirky characters. They all had perfect comic timing and East End accents. They had a great collective dynamic and were the backbone of this production.

The shop steward, Monty, was a marvellous characterisation created by Dean Richman. A wonderful spiv-like invention, with his ever-present cigarette and quickness of gesture and walk, he was perfectly cast. Monty's old friend and fellow activist Connie Riley, who was the Labour Party representative, was delicately played by Fiona Keegan. Ms Keegan nailed Connie's passion for worker's rights and her disillusion that she hadn't done everything she wanted. She had a lovely sub-text with Monty, which she played extremely well and sang beautifully on "Connie's Song" and shone as Rita's mentor as she passed the baton to her due to her declining health. These two characters played their fondness for each other and past romantic liaison with skilful elegance that was a joy to watch. Factory boss, Mr Hopkins was played by Lowry Hodgett with a supercilious old-school-tie charm and his wife, Fiona Keane's Lisa Hopkins, was excellent as the Upper-Class turncoat who sided with the factory workers. Brian McElroy played Mr Tooley, a head honcho from the USA division of the Ford organisation who visits Dagenham in a blaze of pure Americana to sort them out. Mr McElroy encapsulated the ignorant, forceful executive with much pizzaz. His accent and mannerisms were spot-on and, with a knowing contemporary nod to a famous ex-President with difficult financial issues, he revelled in the character's crassness. His singing was also quite good on "This is America", a huge overblown number that was a highlight of the show.

A large ensemble played multiple roles throughout this production. They were energetic, tuneful and one hundred per cent committed. Notable performers playing named characters included: Josh Clarke as Sid, who had good comic timing and was quite forceful with Monty as was Francis McKinney's Bill. Mr McKinney also played and sang as the Cortina Man with just the right amount of cheese! Finbar Finnegan played Stan with a nice presence and Jacob Blue as Barry was notable. Diarmuid Taggart played Mr Buckton with authority, Campbell Evans as Hubble was perfect, and Gordon Donaldson as Macer was spot-on. Bethany McKinney and Louise Warnock who played Emma and Jo were also well-cast.

Politicians of the day were represented in the show, specifically the Prime Minister, Harold Wilson. Here, played by Tim Reynolds, the character is written as something of a caricature and Mr Reynolds embraced this and showed no vestige of the real person, apart from the accent and pipe smoking. He elicited a lot of laughs from the audience and sang with gusto on "Always A Problem". The other politician was Barbara Castle, played here by Emma Nugent. Ms Nugent gave lovely performance and portrayed the politician's dilemma extremely well. Her singing on "In an Ideal World" was excellent and she dominated the scene with the factory workers in her office. This wasn't an impersonation, but more of an interpretation of the character's conflict of being true to her working-class origins yet having to work within the Government to balance the books.

Newcastle Glees Musical Theatre Society represent a benchmark in nonprofessional musical theatre production. They seem to choose work only if they can bring something new to it. In this case they brought a delightful realism to the characters and their situations, which resounded with their audience. This success was due in no small part to the vision and hard work of their director, Laura Kerr, who should be proud of her cast and creatives for giving us an exceptional production.

Yippy-Kay-A Rogers and Hammerstein's 'Oklahoma!' is set in near Kansas in 1909. A dust bowl state newly forged by settlers with the occasional farm and not much else. It's a horse opera, a romantic comedy where Native Americans have been killed off and so don't appear and everyone is bored to death with their lives, looking forward to their next drunken dance so they can hook up with someone, anyone. There's a jealous rivalry between the settled farmers and the cowhands they employ; the farmers envying the cowhand's freedom and the cowhands envying the farmer's wealth. It's an interesting story with plenty for a director to get their teeth into - jealousy, mental illness, misogyny, and murder.

I've seen many versions of this show down through the years and most of them have been identical to each other; the same dances, same musical arrangements, same direction, with very few exploring the actual drama unfolding between the characters, focusing instead on the well- known music, and burying or ignoring the tragedy within the story. So, it was with anticipation that I attended a performance of The Cecilian Musical Society's production at The Lime Tree Theatre in Limerick in November 2022.

Directed by Des Henn with musical direction by Michael Young and choreography by Barbara Meany, this was a very clean-looking production where everyone looked immaculate and there was not a speck of dust or dirt on Wayne Handy's pristine set to mar the presentation.

On the surface, very little happens in 'Oklahoma!', but that's okay because there is an underlying sexual tension among the characters, that nourishes the story. The director's role here, I would argue, is to focus on building this tension among them, until it explodes towards the end of Act II with the murder of Jud Fry, which should have a huge effect on everyone. Sadly, we didn't get this in Cecilian's production. Scenes that should have leapt off the stage in nail biting suspense were played too lightly, which was a missed opportunity to inject that much needed tension. That said, we did get a glimpse of anticipation, thanks to Jud, during the highly dodgy auction scene, which was nicely paced, but it wasn't sustained and evaporated quickly. We didn't feel any empathy for any of the characters, apart from Ali Hakim, whose dilemmas were effectively played by Jason Ronan and Ado Annie, brilliantly played by Ailish O'Donovan. Their relationship was the most adult and there was a real sexual tension between them.

However, production values were high on this show, with fabulous lighting by Michael O'Brien and Star System's superb sound. The simple representative set worked, and the costumes and make-up were of the era, and it was all competently stage managed by Ray Burke. So, it looked good (apart from being too clean) and sounded great. The performers were individually splendid, but they didn't gel as a collective. It seemed that each scene was directed in isolation without any reference to other scenes or a super objective. So, when they were assembled, they didn't quite dovetail together into a whole. At times it went into concert mode when the ensemble stood facing out like a choir, which affected the pace and the continuity of the story and the character relationships.

Musical director, Michael Young's work with the large ensemble, was great. The harmonies on "Kansas City" and "Oklahoma" were excellent. The band were lavish, the violin was especially expertly played and beautiful, and the horns and winds were at times gentle and at others aggressive and bold. Dance throughout this production was exquisitely performed and developed the story thanks to Barbara Meany's lovely choreography. It was quite intricate and delicate at times and it's a credit to her that the performers executed it all with such skill. Of course, the big dance number is the "Dream Ballet", which foreshadowed the events to come, and I'm happy to say that this was the highlight of the show for me. It was just mesmerising to watch; I didn't want it to end. And it was here, during this dark dream fantasy, that the characters started to live for me; they had objectives, passion, and connection.

The performers were, as I mentioned, uniformly quite adept. Barry Danaher's Curly had a great presence on stage, he towered above others as he strode around like a lovesick puppy. His Curly was curious as he came across as quite dim and one dimensional most of the time, yet when he was with Jud trying to cajole him into committing suicide, he showed a cunning maliciousness, but sadly this more interesting side of the character wasn't carried through into other scenes. His singing was excellent, he had a wonderfully expressive voice on the opening song "Oh What a Beautiful Morning" and on his duet with Laurey on "People Will Say We're in Love". Hilary Phayer's Laurey had a good dynamic with Aunt Eller and their scenes were good. Her scenes with Curly were a bit cloying but her scenes with Jud were quite dramatic. Ms Phayer's singing was excellent on "People Will Say We're in Love" with Curly and with the ensemble on "Many a New Day".

Probably one of the more interesting characters in the musical theatre canon is Jud Fry, the ranch hand on Laurey's farm who lusts after her. He is unique and should be played as an outsider which Aidan O'Connell did quite well. His physicality, hunched over as if he had the weight of his crimes on his shoulders, was marvellous as was his voice, a gruff curt growl. He sang "Lonely Room" with a fantastic, repressed anger, full of longing and fretfulness and we saw through this scene that he was suffering. Laurey lived on the farm with her Aunt Eller played by Gráinne Hartnett. Her portrayal made her quite soft and maternal but with a will of iron. Her affectionate and tender relationship with Laurey convinced and her faux flirting with Curly was charming. She sang well with the others and her control of both the dance and the auction was terrific, showing her character's high status.

The secondary romantic storyline concerned the love triangle of Will Parker, Ado Annie, and Ali Hakim. Adam Stapleton gave us a young, fresh-faced Will. His sojourn in the big city did little to mature him and his Will Parker was quite funny in his ineptitude. His quest to hook back up with Ado Annie, was effectively journeyed and he had a good chemistry with her, although he was a child compared to her. His singing was good on "Kansas City", and he bounced well off Ali. Ailish O'Donovan played Ado Annie, the girl who can't say no, dangling Will and Ali, she was caught between two lovers. Ms O'Donovan's Annie was full of energy and lit up the stage each time she entered. Her singing on "I Cain't Say No" was full of expression and fun and she had a great dynamic with Ali, played by Jason Ronan. Mr Ronan's accent as Ali Hakim was faultless. He didn't go over the top into caricature, which often happens with this role, but played him as a real character. His comic timing was a highlight of the show, and the audience loved him. His relationship with Annie was very funny yet quite mature and his singing on the slightly misogynistic "It's a Scandal! It's An Outrage" with the ensemble was full of indignation and incredulity. Ultimately, Annie chose Will over Ali as dictated by her father as Will paid him off. The father, Andrew, was played by Brian Henry. His scenes with Ali were very funny and believable. Although he is a hideous character, demanding money from Will or anyone, for his daughter's hand in marriage, Mr Henry played him as more of a buffoon, which worked in the context of this production.

The other named characters in the show were all quite well cast and helped create the world of the musical: Jane Henry's Gertie nailed that awful laugh; Martin Pierce's Marshall Cord Elam played the character's frustration with the townsfolks disregard for justice and the rule of law very well; Brian Quinlivan's Ike was solid as the rancher and Amanda Leddin's Vivian had a good stage presence as Laurey's friend who told the girl's fortunes. Brian Curtin's Slim and Caoimhe Síochrú's Ellen were also notable.

I enjoyed Michael Young and Barbara Meany's work immensely and some of the performers were excellent, especially Ms O'Donovan, Mr Ronan, and Mr O'Connell. But this production didn't hang together for me, the sum of the parts didn't add up to a cohesive production.

Carry On Addams!

9 Arch Musical Society, based in Claregalway produced 'The Addams Family' at the town Hall Theatre in Galway in November of this year. Hot on the heels of their award-winning 'Little Shop of Horrors' last year, director Alan Greaney reunited with musical director Shane Farrell and choreographer Jay Molyneux to put their own spin on the popular musical.

'The Addams Family' is a black comedy musical, quite well written with some witty one-liners and some excellent songs. The whole premise is of course ludicrous and sort of goes against what made the Addams Family so popular for Charles Addams when he wrote about them as he celebrated their weirdness. But, hey it's a musical so we leave our intellectual reservations at the door on the way in. The show opened with Thing (the hand) in a box on stage and a man in a dress suit telling us where the fire exits were located and urging us to buy raffle tickets. The man exited the stage, and the overture began, conducted by Thing with a baton, from his box.

The overture sounded great though, as Musical Director Shane Farrell took his band through some of the tunes foreshadowing the songs to come. Musically, this show is quite good with lots of songs with great hooks so that even if you didn't know them before you came, your guaranteed to be humming them as you leave the theatre. Mr Farrell clearly worked his magic on this show, and it paid off as his chorus were marvellous, particularly on "When You're an Addams", and "Move Towards the Darkness" and the harmonies on "Full Disclosure" were riotously good.

So, a quick synopsis of the plot: The Addams family, led by the elegantly black-clad Morticia with the never- ending cleavage and her ever-devoted Latino husband Gomez is troubled. Their daughter Wednesday, now eighteen, has fallen in love and is engaged, which she is keeping from her mother but confesses to Gomez. When she invites her fiancé, Lucas Beineke and his family over for dinner, it turns out that the 'normal' family are even more disturbed than the Addams. As Gomez, Jay Hall played him rather low- key, playing the pathos sweetly which, I couldn't help feeling, masked an innate sadness in the character. His singing was heartfelt on "Happy / Sad" and strong on "Not Today". Mr Hall was a wonderful foil for Suzanne Garvey's vampiric Morticia. Ms Garvey's singing was excellent, especially on "Just Around the Corner" and "Secrets" with Alice and she had a sparky chemistry with Gomez. They both convinced as their characters, embracing the dark side yet showing their love for their kids as any parent would do. This relationship was the fulcrum of the show, and they played it with adroitness.

Playing their troubled daughter, Wednesday, was Síofra Ni Chonluain, whose make-up was so strongly applied that she looked a lot older than Morticia! This aside, Ms Ni Chonluain played the moody teenager with foot stomping petulance. She sang fabulously with Pugsley on "Pulled" and with Lucas on "Crazier than You" and generally embodied the rebellious teen with confidence. Wednesday's brother Pugsley was played by Sarah Brennan in a stand- out performance for one so young. Her singing was excellent, and she totally nailed the irascible Pugsley and was fully immersed in the role. Displaying nice emotion on "What if", she had a great chemistry with Grandma and Morticia and an infectious inner energy, which permeated all her scenes.

Another member of the Addams clan was Uncle Fester, brother of Gomez. Played by Richard Brown in a quietly confident performance, Mr Brown accentuated Fester's gentler nature rather than the zombie wrangling wisecracking narrator we often see.
