Played by an avuncular Seamus Feerick, who sang with gusto on "How Can Love Survive" and "No Way to Stop It" and was great at the opening of Act II with the children. He also held the stage well in the concert scene, as the MC. Servants, Frau Schmitt and Franz were played by Gretl Sullivan and Patrick Hanrahan. Both performers were good and held the stage well. Finally, we had Rolf, Liesl's paramour, played by David O'Grady who was great at the beginning when he was courting Liesl, he was gentle and was clearly besotted with her and sang well on "Sixteen Going on Seventeen" with her.

Musical direction by Shane Farrell was excellent. It was bouncy and full of life thanks to his interpretation and conducting. The nun's chorus sounded good on "Preludium" and his work with the children was superb. Aoife McClafferty gave us the dance routines on this show, however on "Sixteen Going on Seventeen" the dance between Rolf and Liesl seemed to be very short. "So Long, Farewell" was cute and nicely performed by the young performers as was "Do-Re-Mi", a highlight of the show. The Ländler was another nice bit of choreography, particularly between Maria and the Captain as they got physically closer. Set was provided by Tony Finnegan, Festival Productions. It was a simple affair; a permanent raised platform upstage with three sets of threads leading up to it. It was changed from the Abbey to the Von Trapp mansion quite quickly. Derek Recks looked after the sound on the show. It was good and we could hear everything quite well. Ronan Kenny from Roken Lighting designed the lighting, which was okay. The stage was well lit and there were some nice states. However, the wedding procession through the centre aisle in the auditorium wasn't lit at all, which was a shame. Pat McGann Productions provided the costumes overseen by Eithne Blackwell. The nun's habits were good and the adults in the Von Trapp house looked great. I liked Elsa's costumes, very elegant, and Georg's suit looked good. The kid's uniforms and play clothes looked perfect. Jacinta Keane looked after hair and make-up and did a splendid job here. The make-up was perfect throughout and the kid's hair was flawless - great plaits!

Director Declan Kelly's tight production was light and fluffy, focusing on the development of the romantic relationship between Maria and Georg - everything else in the show was delegated to a sub- plot. There was no sense of drama from Herr Zeller, or the Admiral or the few Hitler Youth in the audience. The Hitler salutes were more like Black Power salutes as they used a fist rather than the hand outstretched, this was not only inaccurate but diluted the impact of Franz and Rolf being turned towards fascism. We never felt fearful for the family, and we didn't get that contrast between good and evil. The scene in the garden when Rolf arrives looking for the family was very swift so there was no anxiety built in what is written as a very tense scene. That said, it was a very bouncy production with lovely vocals from most of the cast and it was different from the film, and I think that the good reaction of the audience on the night I attended attested to the success of the production.

show_raw: Joseph And The Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat
review_text:
Go, Go, Go Banbridge!

Banbridge Musical Society prides itself on nurturing new talent and giving every member a place in their shows. Their production of Lloyd-Webber's Joseph... was no exception. With a cast of over fifty performers on stage at the Market Place Theatre, the cast rocked the place, and their infectious energy made the audience dance, sing, clap, and cheer. It was a unique take on the biblical tale of Jacob and his many sons that shunned the fourth wall and the drama of the story in favour of showcasing the cast and their love for the music. It was a good choice from director Ian Milford, who was also musical director on the show, to play it for laughs and add in contemporary references and expose the absurdity of the book.

Mr Milford's musical direction was great. His band of ten players clearly enjoyed providing accompaniment to the singing and were clapping along and were really engaged with the music. Mr Milford's conducting was top notch, he even at times spoke and argued with the cast on stage. The children's choir were super and managed some tricky harmonies on "Close Every Door". Highlights for me included the three degree-like presentation of "A Pharaoh's Story" with the three narrators, "Benjamin Calypso" with the brothers, the Elvis inspired "Song of the King" and "Go, Go, Go Joseph" which was full of disco motivated energy that had the audience singing and clapping along into the interval. I could even hear some of the audience singing this during the interval as they snacked out on sugary drinks! Jordan Rosborough's choreography was very simple for the most part but managed to include a number of different styles. From the French Café tango-esque of "Those Canaan Days" to the Country and Western hoedown/line dancing of "One More Angel in Heaven" to the pure disco of "Go, Go, Go Joseph". Each dance was infused with a youthful energy and was brilliantly rehearsed, and I loved the simple hand gestures of the children's chorus during the songs.

Like many eponymously titled shows, the success of a show often rests on the portrayal of the hero. Daniel May is a very versatile performer as proven here in his portrayal of Joseph. He is the epitome of a triple-threat, good dance, singing and acting plus a winning charisma that shines out to the audience. His performance of Joseph was in keeping with the lampooned nature of the show and he never took it too seriously, which was perfect. His singing on "Close Every Door" was masterful, with a pristine final high note that soared around the theatre. But it was his charming smile and how he made everything he did look easy that made the audience empathise with his Joseph, despite the parodic nature of the show. Playing the narrators, we had Kayla Lennon and Claire Costello. Both performers sang with great passion and talent and owned the stage, as did Aimee McVeigh, who joined them in a Three Degrees like presentation of "A Pharoah's Story". This was the song of the night as all three are brilliant singers and know how to deliver a song. Classy stuff. Ms McVeigh also played the lustful Mrs Potiphar with a lovely abandon! Daryll Galloghly played her cuckold husband, Mr Potiphar, like a Wall Street banker, all sharp suit and tech savvy with his MacBook and as Gad, another of Joseph's brothers, he was a vital part of the ensemble.

Playing the above-mentioned Pharoah, who is written as an Elvis like character (this is early Lloyd-Webber, where he chucked all of his ideas into each show!), we had Ruairi McAlinden. Mr McAlinden is that rare breed of actor in that he is a chameleon and literally becomes the character as theatregoers in this area of the country know. He could easily take up a side line as an Elvis Presley impersonator as he absolutely nailed his portrayal of the Pharoah. His singing and movement during "Song of the King" was pure Elvis, even down to the arthritic knee and the white jumpsuit! As one of Joseph's brothers, Ruben he was notable for his stagecraft - he was always on point - and his singing. Great performance. Playing Joseph's father, Jacob, we had Jim McGuigan. Mr McGuigan had a gravitas as Jacob. He was just as mischievous as his sons early in the show, taking selfies and larking about with them. Then mourning the loss of Joseph, he showed a poignant sadness in the character. A nicely pitched performance from Mr McGuigan and very well cast.

An exuberant ensemble made up of adults, teenagers and children gave this production a vitality that bounced it off the stage. They were totally on point with their movement and singing and were exhausting to watch, but also a joy to behold! There was a wonderful sense of community about this show, everybody seemed to be having a great time on stage and this permeated into the audience. A big congratulations must go to stage manager, Andrew McKnight for his crowd control on such a large cast of all ages. Also, he and his crew were invisible on the transitions, which were quick and accurate as were the many fly cues. Both Mr McKnight and Ian Milford designed the set, which was great. Because of the large cast it wasn't a big production in terms of scenery, but I liked the painted floor and the various drops of pyramids, camels, jail bars etc and the nightclub sign 'PHAROAHS' was brilliant as a backdrop to "Song of the King". The treads upstage worked well for the children, who were always on stage, and to create another level when needed. Oh, and the stick puppet Jacob was inspired, where he travelled over the pyramids to reunite with Joseph. Rodney Ellis' lighting design pulled out all the stops on this show, with movers and shakers flashing and blasting out to the audience - it was a great light show with lovely tight focus when needed. Enda and Barry McCusker gave us a great sound with nice separation between band and singers. I don't know how they managed to amplify the children as they didn't seem to have radio mics, but they did it and we could hear every note! Rosemary Kelly excelled on the costume, especially the coat and the parachute attachment. The brother's costumes looked good, and I liked the additional accessories, e.g., the berets, that were added for each song. The Narrator's dresses in Act II looked great as did Pharoah's late-stage Elvis Presley look.

This was a great show, full of energy and idiosyncratic theatrical ideas, some of which were ludicrously funny. It was more like a concert than a musical with a plot and characters, but I would argue that it was the right way to go with this material. I mean it's not 'Evita' or 'Phantom', which relies on the story. It's an early work by an artist trying out his ideas and playing around with different genres of music. So, this production also played around with the work, taking some artistic liberties, and contemporising it to make it more palatable to a modern audience. But ultimately it was all about the music and the songs, which still sound good today, especially when produced and staged by this talented society.

Gorey Little Theatre is a hidden gem of a playhouse in North Wexford. Opened some years ago, it has been expanded with a larger foyer and is home to the annual South Leinster Drama Festival and is a receiving house for small to mid- scale touring productions and events. It was here that I saw one of the most riveting shows this season in March of this year from Gorey Musical Society. They swept the boards last year in the Sullivan section at the AIMS Awards with their production of 'The Sound of Music' and I was keen to see what all the fuss was about.

'West Side Story' is based on Shakespeare's 'Romeo and Juliet' and originally entitled 'East Side Story' and set in New York, with music by Leonard Bernstein and book by Arthur Laurents, it was reimagined and retitled, a young Stephen Sondheim was brought in as lyricist, and it was recited to Los Angeles. Centring around an illicit love story between members of opposing gangs, the production was made into a film in 1961 and again more recently in 2021. This is a controversial show and is regarded as being quite racist in its stereotyping of Puerto Ricans. Recent professional productions have also been accused of whitewashing the cast, using white actors to portray the Latino characters. So, it's a tricky one to get right.

When I entered the foyer there was a crackling in the air from the audience, an eagerness for what was to come, this continued into the auditorium as there was a palpable excitement and buzz of anticipation. This was opening night, so it wasn't like these punters had already seen or heard about the show and it was 'West Side Story' a 1950's musical they were here to see, not something new and exciting like 'Hamilton'. As I settled in, my only hope was that they wouldn't be disappointed.

They weren't. This was a fabulous production, from the innovative set and colour coordinated costumes to the incredible choreography and inspired direction and amazing orchestra topped off by a cast of committed talented performers, this show was that perfect storm of a production we are always hoping to see. There was a synergy between all aspects of the show, between the cast and creatives and ultimately between the production and the audience. This production blasted off the stage with fierce choreography, excellent singing, and astute direction by Stephen Acton. His attention to detail with the ensemble complimented his excellent work with the principals. This was a true ensemble piece, as it should be, where all players were important and given time and space to excel from the group scenes right up to the curtain call where all performers were equal. His breakneck pacing of the action ensured that the audience were always engaged, and the running time seemed a lot quicker than it actually was.

Musically it was spot on, and musical director Conor McCarthy conducted a fifteen-piece orchestra that clearly relished Bernstein's electrifying score. Mr McCarthy's orchestration and interpretation had a contemporary vibe to it, it was hard to believe this was written in the fifties. His work with the ensemble was also quite spectacular, eliciting some fabulous harmonies and especially power from them on "Jet Song", "America" and "Tonight (Quintet)". This is one of the most difficult shows to choreograph on the non- professional circuit. The dances are so high octane, dangerous and very intricate that professional dancers sometimes struggle.

But choreographer Megan McEvoy obviously worked her ensemble tirelessly as they were absolutely excellent. The athleticism of the cast, their energy and commitment to the process was all up there on the stage. The opening "Jet Song" exploded onto the stage and was relentless in its choreographic ingenuity, merging dance and violence seamlessly. "Gee, Officer Krupke" was one of the funniest and rudest dances I've seen recently - wonderful stuff! "America" was another triumph, with the Latino inspired steps and flounces as was "The Rumble". Just when we thought it couldn't get any better, Ms McEvoy wowed us with her "Procession and Nightmare" ballet sequence in Act II. This was sublime and beautifully orchestrated and danced, as indeed was the whole show - it all blended flawlessly.

The performers were mostly all very young, with a few exceptions, and this was perfect as it's about the rashness and impulsiveness of youth. Tony was played by a thoughtful Emmet Donlon. Mr Donlon has an incredibly expressive voice, his "Maria" was a highlight of the show as was "Something's Coming". His acting was good too, playing the reluctant fighter who is trying to leave his old life behind him, we could feel his conflicts. His onstage relationship with Maria was very sweet and a lovely reprieve from the bombastic street life. She was played by an equally still Karla Tracey, who has an incredible range and beautiful tone. Her "Tonight" with Tony was amazing in its emotion and joy. "I Feel Pretty" was fun and light and lovely and "A Boy Like That" with Anita was fierce and poignant. Ms Tracey's acting was also marvellous. She clearly had a deep emotional connection with Maria, she loved her, and it showed, particularly at the end when she was mourning Tony. These two performers had a lovely dynamic, we really believed they were in love. Maria's brother, Bernardo, was played by Puerto Rican native, Michael Cruz. He was perfect in the role, his singing and dance was excellent, but it was the intense smouldering pride and his sense of duty, protecting Maria, Anita and the other Sharks that really shone through in his acting. An exceptional performance. Playing his girlfriend, Anita, we had Margaret Masterson. From the moment Ms Masterson entered the stage she impressed and demonstrated a lively and spirited character that the audience loved. "America" was her song, and she sang it with great zest and zing. Ms Masterson's dance was also marvellous. The scene when she visits the Jets was painful to watch and superbly performed, she showed fear and anger in equal measure. The Jets were headed up by Riff, played by Richard O'Toole. Mr O'Toole embodied the partisan hothead in his every move and utterance. His physicality was pure aggression and antagonistic hostility. This worked vividly for Riff as he just wants to assert his racist dominance over the Sharks. He sang well on "Jet Song" and "Cool" and whilst not a likeable character, he managed to get the audience to empathise with him. His fellow gang members were played by Brian Cooney, Seán Timmons, John Donohue, Darragh Cox, Tommy Cox, Aaron Leonard, Paul Kehoe, and Alex Murphy. These performers excelled as the violent street hoods, with their excellent dance, singing and characterisations. Their "Gee, Officer Kupke" was a highlight of the show for me. One of the oddest characters in the show, Anybody's, is a courageous tomboy who is desperate to become a Jet. Hannah McNiven played her with superb attention to detail from her shuffle to her lightening quick aggression, yet she also showed her softer side when Riff died. Her singing and dancing were excellent particularly on "Cool". Two of the Jet girls, Lauren Glynn and Sophia McCarthy danced brilliantly in "Cool" and at "The Dance at the Gym". They were sassy and aggressive and along with Clarice, Pauline and Minnie added to the dominance of the Jets over the Sharks.

The Sharks under the governance of Bernardo were played by Brandon Cogley, Brian Harty, Nacho Lopez, Evan Ryan, Thomas Rush, Will Cooper, Tiernan Donohoe and Bobby O'Callaghan. All were equally as strong as the Jets with excellent dance and singing. The Shark girls had that Latino attitude down pat, especially Maria Forrest as Rosalia, but Natacha Kinsella, Fia Duffy, Fiona Walker, Méibh Fitzpatrick, and Aisling O'Dwyer also acquitted themselves with their attitude dancing and singing. Ronan P. Byrne played Schrank, the local police detective who was trying to stop the gang violence. Mr Byrne played him as unapologetically blunt, harsh, and racist. His pacing was excellent, never rushed and always in control of his scenes. He also showed his character's frustration with the gangs and the constant violence he witnesses and has to clean up after. His sidekick, Officer Kupke was played with assurance by Paudie Breen. Daniel J. Healy gave us a lovely emotional Doc, the wise owner of a local store where the Jets hang out. His scenes with Tony were fabulous and they had a great chemistry, and I loved his reaction to the Jets treatment of Anita, he was incandescent with rage and disappointment. Finally we had the ubiquitous James Dobbs playing Glad Hand, organiser of the school dance where Tony and Maria meet. He was played by Mr Dobbs as a nerdy, excessively gleeful dork in a suit and glasses. Ignorant of the gang conventions of conduct, he kept pushing the kids together often ending up in the centre of a ruck!

The set was designed by Stephen Acton, Paul Doran, Nigel May & Gabrielle Beesley, and what a great set! Platforms, hidden entrances and exits, different levels all wrapped in a stars and stripes paint job by Gabrielle Beesley and a mobile Juliet balcony. It really worked and was expertly lit by Mark Redmond. Sound by I-Tec Productions was loud and in-yer-face and Nomac's costumes and a vast crew of make-up artists and hair specialists completed a production team that clearly loved the show as much as the performers, who were expertly wrangled by stage manager Paul Doran.

Gorey Musical Society's 'West Side Story' was a triumph, it ticked all of the boxes needed to be a successful show. It had all of the bells and whistles in terms of production, it had a brilliantly energetic cast and talented creatives who worked together rather than in isolation and most importantly it had a huge beating heart at the centre. I wouldn't be surprised if it went on to play at a bigger theatre or on tour around the country, it was that good.

Wild West Karaoke Oklahoma! tells a story of a frontier community in the 1800's banding together against an outsider, Judd Fry and follows the fledgling love affair between two sets of couples. Rodgers & Hammerstein reinvented the American musical with this show in that all of the songs actually further the plot and if features a fifteen- minute ballet sequence in the first act that foreshadows the action in Act II.

Produced by Fortwilliam Musical Theatre Society and staged in the Theatre at the Mill in Newtownabbey, eight miles north of Belfast, the show was directed by Kerry Rooney MBE, with musical direction by Paul Masterson and choreography by Cheryl O'Dwyer. There was no live musical accompaniment to the show as it was all sung to backing tracks, sort of like a Wild West Karaoke, and this caused a disconnect between the singer and the song which made for a very rigid production.

There was much to like here though, Curly our hapless hero was played with a casual charm by Dessie Havelin. He was very likeable and sang brilliantly too, the opener "Oh What a Beautiful Mornin'" was light and sweet. His onstage relationship with Laurey was very naturally played and we were never in any doubt that they would end up together as they had an endearing dynamic. The pig shed scene with Judd didn't land for us though. This was a pity as this scene is so important as it tips Judd over the edge. Judd was played by the imposing Pearce McFall. He looked every inch the outsider, with his dirty scruffy appearance and growling voice. He delivered "Pore Judd is Daid" and "Lonely Room" with deep character. His physicalisation of Judd was excellent, especially in the Dream Ballet sequence and he exuded menace in the final scene with Curly.

There are two love triangles played out in 'Oklahoma!". The first concerns Curly who moons over farm girl Laurey. This was nicely played with the relentless Curly stalking and chasing the elusive Laurey, played with a wistfulness by Helena Hendron. This was a lovely performance from Ms Hendron who mostly played the softer side of Laurey rather than the strong hard-bitten side. It worked well and dovetailed nicely with Mr Havelin's Alpha Male Curly. She sang divinely and with passion and their duet "People Will Say We're in Love" was excellent as was "Many a New Day" which she sang with her girlfriends. She deftly showed Laurey's indecision as she juggled Judd and Curly's affections against her real objective which was probably to get away from all of them!

The second and more interesting love story centred around Ado Annie's puppeteering of the desires of Will Parker and Ali Hakim. One of the more interesting characters in this show, Ado Annie is very different to the other young women. Jenny Johnston played her as a free-spirited individual that revelled in the defying of convention. Her "I Cain't Say No" was one of the better songs of the show and her deft controling of Will and Ali's affections was effectively shown. Will was played by Adam Goudy who had a great energy on stage, he bounded off and on like a lovesick puppy. He delivered his songs with gusto. "Kansas City" was good and "All Er Nuthin'" with Ado Annie was cute. This relationship with Ado Annie was perfectly played as was his frustration with her father, Andrew, who wanted money for her hand. John McCrudden played Ali  Hakim and he eschewed the stereotype in favour of his own interpretation, which was an amalgamation of Stephen Fry and Oliver Hardy, more English cad than Persian snake oil salesman. This worked quite well here as the character came across like an educated sophisticate conning the rubes. His relationship with Ado Annie was good and he played the indecision of wanting her / not wanting her really well. This triangle was nicely played out by all three performers and was a joy to watch. The other main character in the show is Laurey's Aunt Eller, with whom she shares the farm, played here by Ditanya McKinty. Ms McKinty, like Ms Hendron, played more to Eller's soft side. Even though she was matriarchal and clearly of high status, she didn't push this aspect of the character. This worked beautifully and it was a great contrast when she used the gun during "The Farmer and the Cowman". Her singing was excellent all around, but I particularly liked her harmonies on "The Surrey with the Fringe on Top". Drew Reid played Ado Annie's father, Andrew, and captured Andrew's frustration with Annie, trying to get someone to buy her off him as she was so wild, very well. He denoted his high status too by his stillness during the more populated scenes and when he became the 'judge' at the trail. Charlotte Cautley played Gertie Cummins, and absolutely nailed the laugh. She also showed Gertie's bitchiness towards Laurey as she was sweet on Curly, which we don't often see in most productions of 'Oklahoma!'

Chorus master Paul Masterson worked with the ensemble and the chorus quite well, there was a nice power from them especially on the title song and the "Finale Ultimo" with good intricate harmonies. Mr Masterson also coaxed some charming vocal performances from his principals. Mr Havlin and Ms Hendron were particularly good on "People Will Say We're in Love" as was Ms McKinty on her numbers. But as the music wasn't live, there was a disengagement sometimes between singer and music and at times it was a bit karaoke. The choreography in 'Oklahoma!' lives or dies on the Dream Ballet and choreographer Cheryl O'Dwyer gave us a rather good one. It was quite elaborate and layered and featured a gorgeous pas de deux from Curly and Laurey, a strange courting ritual between the genders and a violent ending with Judd. The other numbers were typical C&W fare which were well rehearsed and looked good. John McConnell and Seamus Hughes looked after set design and it worked quite well. It was a mostly open stage with a hint of a cabin stage right and with two ominous gallows joined together to show Judd's room. John McKee designed the sound, and I did find the vocals sometimes painfully loud, particularly Curly's solos. I also thought that more reverb could have been used on the mics when the performers were singing, this would have blended the music with the vocals better and make it sound less karaoke. Lighting was very front of house heavy, but the cyc was pleasantly lit at times. But Judd Fry's room was too bright and didn't show the dinginess of his life as I felt it should. Costumes by Margaret Mehaffey were perfect for the era. A good range of long dresses and hats and Ali's jacket and bow tie worked. But everybody looked too clean!! Good stage management from Andrew Devonshire and his crew. It's not a busy show as there's only a few locations but they were set up fairly quickly and didn't alter the pace of the production. Kerry Rooney directed a good tight production that looked bright and sparkling clean. He managed to infuse a bit of tension here and there, but we never felt afraid for Laurey. Although Judd was quite menacing towards the end of the show, he was quite soft early on. This sort of worked as we felt he was possibly not playing with a full deck and could snap at any moment. This was, I think, Mr Rooney's intention. It was a good production that gave us a glimpse into the harshness of frontier life in the old West where men were men and women were there to be tamed.

Belfast Operatic Company has been active since 1961, when they produced 'Patience' and 'The Gondoliers'.

Since then, they have staged many G&S operettas plus some classic and contemporary shows including this year's "The Hunchback of Notre Dame". Based on a novel written by Victor Hugo in 1831, the stage production of the 1996 animated Disney film has been around since it was first produced in Germany in 1999. Although there have been changes from the film, some aspects of it remain in some of the characters and in some of the text, which I think permeated the Belfast Operatic Company's production of the show in the Grand Opera House as most of the performers adopted American accents. This was quite inharmonious for a story set in 15th century Paris.

The story explores love, lust and faith and focuses on Quasimodo, a deformed bellringer, his uncle the Archdeacon Frollo and a Romani girl called Esmerelda with whom they both fall in love and is set in and around the Notre Dame cathedral. The Captain of the Paris guard, Phoebus, also falls for Esmerelda, who is part of a band of reviled Gypsies that the Church wants to banish. The musical was written by James Lapine and Peter Parnell with music and lyrics by Alan Menken and Stephen Schwartz and originally produced in Germany then moved to California where it was restructured, and this is the version we see today.

Director Kerry Rogers, gave us a sumptuous looking show with a stunning set, good quality costumes and make- up, all lit by a splendid lighting design and was quite faithful to the book. The performance I attended wasn't helped by the sound imbalance between vocals and band, in favour of the band. We lost a lot of the dialogue and the softer songs. Most performers adopted an American accent as I mentioned, which contributed to us, the audience, being distanced from the production. I felt some performances came across as tired on the evening I attended, this in turn gave the impression that the performers didn't connect and this came across to the audience.

Musically it was superb though and Adam Darcy conducted a fifteen-piece band with drive in the pit. His conducting was excellent, and I loved his interpretation of the score. The pace was good, and I liked the strings, they brought an elegance to the show. The chorus was excellent, their "Olim" was superb as was "The Bells of Notre Dame" and "Agnus Dei". They added a much-needed spirit to this show, and we could see them too in their robes, which added to the ecclesiastical look of the production. Some of the principals struggled a bit with some numbers, but I felt that Quasimodo and Phoebus had excellent voices as did Florika, especially in Act II, where she blew everyone away singing from the platform upstage left. It's not a big dance show obviously, but Timothy Bell choreographed some interesting moves, mostly on "Tavern Song", "Rhythm of the Tambourine" and "The Court of Miracles" for the Gypsies. The tambourine song was particularly well done and leapt all over the stage, it was clever and accurate and helped to liven up the show.

As Quasimodo, Conor Anderson's singing was sweet and sombre as he sang about his plight. "Heaven's Light" was beautifully sung as was "Out There". His physicality in the role was good too, hunkered down throughout with bent knees and a sideways shuffle, he expressed the deformities with a quiet nobility. His chemistry with Esmerelda was nicely played but I didn't see much dynamic with Frollo, played by Boyd Rodgers. Mr Rodgers played Claude with a restraint that at times worked, but generally he didn't have the gravitas to get across Claude Frollo's high status, menace, and eminence. His singing was good, but it was hard to hear him at times. "Hellfire" was a bit diluted by the dance activity on stage and very hard to hear the words, so we didn't really get the importance of the song. However, he worked well with Naomi Smyth's Esmerelda. They had a couple of good scenes, particularly in the church when he tried to convince her to be with him. Ms Smyth was one of the more energetic performers on stage on the show I saw. Her singing was good, especially on "God Help the Outcasts" but we missed a lot of her dialogue as her mic seemed to be turned right down. Her dance was great, she sashayed around the stage during the Gypsy numbers with great abandon. Esmerelda fell for the Captain of the Guard, Phoebus, played by David McCrossan who was easily the Quasimodo (played by Conor Anderson) and Esmeralda (played by Naomi Smyth) looking down from the top of the world most believable character on stage. His singing was excellent, and his acting was top notch. "Someday" with Esmerelda was one of the better songs of the evening. Again, it was hard to hear him at times, but generally his performance was superb, and he didn't force the American accent. His friend, Frederic, was played with assurance by Daniel Clarke, who gave a lovely soft performance.

The leader of the Gypsy gang, Clopin, was played by Corey Magee who didn't really convince. Clopin is an enigmatic magical character, and we didn't really get these qualities from Mr Magee. He seemed to disappear into the ensemble rather than being prominent and didn't exude the high energy nor danger required of this character. However, he sang well on "Topsy Turvy" and was a good dancer. One of this band of Romani was a girl called Florika, wonderfully played by Lauren Turner who sang with an amazing voice in Act II. In the opening scenes of the show, she hooked up with Claude's brother, Jehan and they ran away together, had a baby (Quasimodo) and died, leaving Claude to bring up the baby. Jehan was played by David Baillie, who had a good energy and was also quite prominent in the ensemble.

Quasimodo, up in the belfry, didn't really engage with anyone other than his Uncle Claude and the gargoyles. The animated gargoyles were played by a range of different performers, and they were good, but it was all very Disney with their chatter and pretending to be inanimate when Claude Frollo was there and mugging behind his back. A highlight of the show was the arrival of St. Aphrodisus, played by a puppet and voiced by Darryl Bowden. He sang "Flight into Egypt" with lovely sincerity and his fellow puppeteer was excellent. Other roles of note were the Madam played by the sneeringly good Sarah McLoughlin and Kevin McIlhennon as Father Dupin, who had gravitas and good stage presence.

Lighting by ACK Productions was lovely with accurate follow spots and vibrant colour; costumes by Triple C were good for the era, if a bit clean looking on the Gypsies; make-up and hair was also quite good, and it was all run very well by stage manager Maree Cusack and her crew. There were elements of this production that really worked; I liked the use of candles and fire in the show, it's not something we see much anymore; the star cloth and bell ropes looked great; the multiple uses for the benches were clever. I didn't like the production being muted at one point, where the dancers kept dancing, to represent what Quasimodo is experiencing - as we could hear the audience mentioning a certain TV Dance competition, which used the same device. There was a bit of a clash of styles in the show which I think confused and perhaps contributed to the sense of disassociation between audience and performance.

'Ghost' is a musical based on the 1990 film of the same name that made stars of Patrick Swayze and Demi Moore and won Whoopi Goldberg an Oscar. Following in the footsteps of other screen to stage adaptations, 'Ghost' relies heavily on the recognisability of its story to get bums on seats. Book by Bruce Joel Rubin and music and lyrics by Dave Stewart and Glen Ballard adds meat to the bones of what is a good story. The plot centres around a loving couple, Sam and Molly who move into a New York apartment helped by their friend Carl. Not long after, Sam is shot and killed in what seems like an arbitrary mugging. Like in the film, Sam appears as a ghost instantly after being shot, watching as his wife seeks help. He begins to investigate and learns that he was assassinated over a drug dealing money laundering operation at the bank where he worked with Carl. He finds his killer, Willie Lopez, and then seeks out psychic Oda Mae Brown who can hear him and thus gives him the means to communicate with Molly and tell her that she's in danger from Lopez who is attempting to recover Sam's address book for the bank access codes it contains. Along the way he meets other ghosts, and they help him to come to terms with his situation. It's a good plot, the book is well written, and the basics are all there to create a thrilling evening of ghostly entertainment.

Tralee Musical Theatre Society took on the challenge of staging the musical in Siamse Tire Theatre in April, under the direction and choreography of Oliver Hurley and musical direction of Michael Young with Laura Crowley as chorus mistress. Tralee, no stranger to high tech, decided to go down the video projection route, as many productions of this musical do, and assembled a huge collection of still and video imagery, some bespoke of the performers, that were shown throughout the show. Initially, this was quite interesting and a spectacle but as the show progressed the projections started to take over from the live action on stage and the performers became swamped by the swirling visual cacophony of visual information.

The production featured some nice performances from a good cast, who all sang with passion and power. Molly was played with a light touch by Janna Foley whose beautiful rendition of "With You", which is I think the best song in the show, was heart-breaking. Ms Foley had superb emotion and expression on this song as she did on most of her numbers. Her acting was good too, she captured Molly's loss very well. She had a very good dynamic with Sam early on and with Carl later in the show. But it was in her portrayal of Molly's vulnerability and bereavement that she excelled, you just wanted to hug her. Sam was played by Gary Murphy. It's a difficult role for sure and as alive Sam, he was quite good and very engaging and likable. As ghost Sam, he had very little energy on stage except for the fight scenes, but he did portray emotion quite well. I loved his "Unchained Melody" with the guitar early in the show, this was great and his scene with the Subway Ghost was excellent, he really got across Sam's frustration to us. As his friend and colleague at the bank, Carl, we had a powerhouse performance from Sean McElligott. He captured Carl's desperation and his guilt very well. He sang brilliantly throughout the show too, especially on "More" and "I Had a Life". The scene where he comforted Molly was excellent and they had a great dynamic. The reveal in the scene with Lopez was also splendid as he showed the darker side of Carl.

The other main character in the show was Oda Mae Brown, a sham psychic and charlatan, with a business designed to con grieving people out of their money. Played in the film by Whoopi Goldberg and written for a black actor with African American idioms of speech in the musical, this role is quite comic as Oda Mae discovers that she can in fact converse with the dead when Sam visits her asking her to help. Oda Mae was played by Jackie O'Mahoney and her characterisation fully embraced using the African American idioms, yet she is Caucasian. I feel that the idioms should have been toned down in rehearsal by the director lest it be mistaken as parodic, but they weren't. The audience seemed to find the performance very amusing which only seemed to embolden this interpretation. Her singing was excellent though, especially on "I'm Outta Here" and her performance in the scene with Sam and Molly towards the end of the show was quite nuanced and restrained.

Oda Mae had two assistants in her scam operation, Louise and Clara, whose job was to herald the rubes, protect Oda Mae from any dissent and create atmospherics through quasi-Gospel song and dance routines.

Brilliantly played by Amy Naughton and Sarah Brett, whose singing on "Are You a Believer?" and "Talkin' 'Bout a Miracle" was excellent. Sam's killer, Willie Lopez, was played by Tim Landers. Mr Landers had a great stage presence and made Lopez a very three-dimensional character, he made the role his own. He had a naturalism on stage, particularly on his telephone call scenes.

Two other ghosts are specifically featured in the show, and they are there to help Sam make sense of what has happened and to teach him how to interact with the living by using psychokinesis, like a poltergeist. He followed his corpse to the hospital after the shooting and met Hospital Ghost, played by Marcus Nolan. This ghost was flanked by many others, but he was clearly the leader. Mr Nolan had a wonderful voice on "Ball of Wax", a bluesy jazzy quality and equally on "Talkin' 'Bout a Miracle". He had a fine presence on stage and effortlessly portrayed the character's high status and was quite good at the dance sequences too. The other ghost known as Subway Ghost, was played with scenery chewing intensity by Aaron McLarnon. He was one of the most interesting characters on stage in the show and had wonderful energy in the role. His voice was quite brilliant and he almost rapped "Focus" in a sprechgesang or parlando delivery, and I loved his physicality. He taught Sam how to have a physical impact on the living world, which allowed him to save Molly and ascend to a better place.

Musical direction was by Michael Young who played keyboards and conducted a tight knit band of cello, violin, woodwind, brass, guitar, bass, and drums plus another keyboard.

They produced some lovely moments of underscore and accompaniment for the singers. Mr Hurley choreographed the musical. Some of the routines worked, like the robotic "More" but there were some dances put in that seemed unnecessary such as in "Suspend My Disbelief" and were actually distracting from the singing performances. Lighting design was by John Hurley who wisely used follow spots on the show, to save washing out the projections. Shane Murphy's sound design was very good, with a good range of well-cued sound effects. Lovely reverb, particularly on Molly's singing, enhanced the overall sound quality.

Oliver Hurley designed the set. It seemed to take many hands to move and fly flats and furniture, which detracted from the action of the show. Some of the images were quite nice but the sheer amount of video projection took the focus from the real-life action. Costume was good, particularly the ghost looks of muted colours and make up and hair was very good, again particularly on the ghosts. There is a sad little love story at the centre of this musical and I feel it was lost amidst the technical presentation. There was just so much visual information coming at the audience, we didn't know where to look. So, the actors were fighting against the production in a way. I would argue that, in theatre the production elements should support the performers rather than be grandstanded as they were in this show.

Urine Good Company In Teachers' Musical Society's latest show one of the leads says that nothing can kill a show like too much exposition. Another suggests that bad subject matter and a bad title could also kill a show. And this is indeed often true as we have all seen down through our years of theatregoing. Except for Greg Kotis and Mark Hoffman's 'Urinetown' where these qualities actually enhance the production. The Society staged the satirical musical comedy, written in 2001, in DCU St. Patrick's Campus in March this year and it was hilarious. It's a Brechtian socio-political satire that revelled in taking pot-shots at other musicals. At its heart though it is a satire of the legal system, capitalism, social irresponsibility, populism, bureaucracy, corporate mismanagement, and municipal politics. That's a lot to put into a musical theatre production, but 'Urinetown' manages it and a lot more. Directed by Ciarán Mooney, with musical direction by Dermot O'Callaghan and choreography by Nicole McDonald, the comedy was on point and most of the gags landed. Ben Hennessy's set was unpretentious yet efficient with excellent scenic painting and build quality. Lighting and sound were spot on, and Andrew Reddy's costumes were deliciously filthy for the poor and lavish for the rich.

Ciarán Mooney created some lovely little touches in this show like every time someone said the word 'musical' the cast did the 'jazz hands' gesture. This of course was perfectly in keeping with the tone of the show, which blatantly mocks other musical theatre shows like Les Mis, Cabaret, West Side Story and so on. His deft marshalling of the comedy was excellent, all of the cast had perfect comic timing and seemed to relish the jokes and the, sometimes, terrible puns. Mr Mooney's pacing was thrilling, each scene built on the previous one to create an exhilarating momentum. The choreography, by Ms McDonald was clever and was a tongue in cheek reference to other shows, like in "Cop Song" and the Les Mis inspired "Look at the Sky". Dermot O'Callaghan and his small band of excellent players sounded wonderful and his conducting and playing was brilliant. His work with the ensemble was also splendid, especially the Gospel style "Run, Freedom Run" where Bobby conducts the cast in a fabulous acapella and on "Why Did I Listen to that Man". The show was wonderfully cast, and each performer clearly got the humour, hamming it up when necessary and hilariously attempting pathos in a show that revels in its dark comedy. Leading the poor, we had reluctant hero Bobby Strong a toilet attendant played with ease in comedy, singing and vulnerability by Jordan Bass. His arch nemesis, Mr Cladwell, a menacing Eddie Brady and his lackies, Mr McQueen, a highly camped Rory Dignam and Ms Millennium a prim Sinéad Coughlan were supported by a paid off Senator Fipp, a wonderfully arch John Furlong. Cladwell ran the Urine Good Company who controlled the water in the town. Bobby worked with Penelope Pennywise, a standout performance of stillness and great vocals by Grace Kinirons, taking money from the poor for the privilege to pee. Bobby's Dad, Old Man Strong, a fabulous Fergal Sweeney, decided to pee in the street and was immediately arrested and sent to Urinetown by Officer Lockstock - a wonderfully deadpan Stuart Pollock, who also narrated the show and his sidekick, Officer Barrell played with pent-up aggression by Paul Breen. Thus started the revolution by the poor against Cladwell.

However, to make things even more interesting we were introduced to Cladwell's daughter wide eyed and innocent Hope, a superb Nicole Lamb, who falls for the heroic Bobby and empathises with the rebels. Their scenes and songs were brilliantly sung and acted. Bobby's penniless revolutionaries were a bunch of misfits who were mad as hell and wanted revenge. Chief among them were Little Sally, who frequently questioned the veracity of the show, played with infantile curiosity by Emmagene Cook and Two Blades Harry, a vicious idiotic thug given life by Garrett Rogers. Other notable poor included Eva Kelly's lame and pregnant Little Becky Two Shoes, Kevin Sheerin's Robbie the Stockfish, Nicole Kelly's Soupy Sue, and Michael Flynn's Tiny Tom. Together with the ensemble, these performers were the backbone of the production, their singing, choreography, and characterisations were knowing, very funny and perfectly on point throughout. Mr Mooney's world building was aided and abetted by a sterling high quality production team who created a wonderful atmospheric look to the production. Ben Hennessy's set was dirty, flexible, and referenced Andy Warhol in some of its design. Denis Twomey's lighting gave an eerie quality through footlights and blues and Jason Fallon's sound was perfectly balanced. Andrew Reddy's costumes went from filthy to ostentatious and Ali Murphy's hair and make-up was perfect. Gerry McCann stage managed it all with absolute ease.

It's a clever, existential musical that rolls along at a brisk pace that speaks to the current climate crisis, the inaction of governments and the growing divide between the rich and the poor. The jokes are, for the most part, puerile and the musical theatre references would possibly be lost on the uninitiated. But it does have a lot to say about climate change and capitalism and the last words uttered are "Hail Malthus!", referencing Thomas Malthus who is best known for his theory that population growth will always tend to outrun the food supply or in this case water supply.

Ciarán Mooney's direction was sharp, and he steered his cast expertly through the mayhem. The comedy was mostly verbal with a little bit of slapstick thrown in, but all expertly delivered. The singing was excellent, and we had some lovely harmonies floating about the grubby set, together with quite intricate choreography. A great evening's entertainment!

Let's Dance!

Written by Tom Snow, Dean Pitchford & Walter Bobbie and based on the hit film from 1984, 'Footloose The Musical' was originally penned in 1998, one of a number of classic films that were made into stage shows like 'Flashdance', 'Fame', 'The Producers', 'Hairspray' and Disney's 'Beauty and the Beast' and 'Aladdin' thus proving that nostalgia never goes out of style. It received a mixed critical reception, but the script was tweaked in 2005 to allow for more naturalism, which improved it considerably.

The audience at St Mel's College where St Mel's Musical Society staged the show consisted of some who would have remembered seeing the film when it came out, but the majority were young people and children! An open stage with the Society's logo and show title projected centre stage was soon filled with the young ensemble dancing and singing to a DJ set upstage with his decks.

The story is that Ren McCormack, a high school student from Chicago, moves with his mother to a small conservative rural town after his father walks out on them. However, Ren finds himself clashing with most of the town, including the Reverend Shaw Moore who has convinced the town to prohibit dancing. This, Ren finds preposterous and upsetting as it's the only thing he's good at. With the help of Ariel (the Reverend's daughter) and her school friends, Ren convinces the Reverend and the Town Council to let the teenagers be teenagers and dance.

Ren was skilfully played by Brian Dalton, he depicted the frustration of a city slicker being relocated to Bomont, Hicksville in rural America. His singing was strong and animated on "Footloose" and on "I Can't Stand Still". Mr Dalton had good vocal control on all of his songs and produced a fine falsetto in his duet with Ariel at the bridge on "Almost Paradise". His scenes with Ariel were quite sweetly done but it was his scene with the Reverend Shaw Moore in the second act where he really impressed. His emotional connection to the character was solid and his relationship with Shaw was quite touching. As Moore, Paul Hennessy portrayed the inner torment of a father who has lost a child quite movingly. He had a wonderful stage presence and control and sang "Can You Find It In Your Heart (Reprise)" and on "Heaven Help Me" with a delicate tenderness.

Ariel, Shaw's daughter and Ren's love interest, was played by Natasha Brady. She sang well and her scenes with Shaw were quite powerful and she had a nice chemistry with Ren. Ariel's mother, Vi, here played by Joanne Sexton was impressive on "Can You Find It In Your Heart", her voice was beautifully pitched and full of anguish. She was also extremely convincing and gave a deeply engaging performance and I loved how she kept creeping out to the back garden for a sneaky cigarette, even passing it to Chuck at one point to hide it from Shaw. The role of Ren's mother, Ethel, was taken by Louise Walsh. It is a rather underwritten role, but she did well with what she was given and impressed on "Learning to be Silent" with Vi and Ariel.

The ditzy friend of Ariel (there's always a ditzy friend) Wendy-Jo, was perfectly played by Caoimhe Hennessy.

Her attention to character was excellent and she had great comic timing. Alisha Manning played Urleen, the sensible one, quite well and Katie Gallagher's Rusty really impressed with her energetic and nuanced performance and her singing on "Let's Hear It For The Boy". The trio, a sort of Greek Chorus at times, all sang brightly on "Holding Out For a Hero" and softly on "Somebody's Eyes". Ren's friend Willard, a typical hick in dungarees and cowboy hat, was nicely played with genial comedy by Jessie Kersh. His budding romance with Rusty was cute and he performed "Mama Says" with hilarious conviction. Oisin Dowling played bad boy Chuck with a hint of misogynist menace and sang well on "The Girl Gets Around". The ensemble were split between the adult townsfolk and Ren's school buddies. They all had a superb energy and great singing and dance ability.

Vincent Tully conducted and was Chorus Master on this production. His band, The Urban Day Spa Orchestra, were great. Two guitars, two keyboards, reed & flute, drum, and bass. They made a huge sound on some of the numbers, "Holding Out for a Hero" was massive and had the audience rocking as was "Let's Hear it for the Boy". The quieter ballads such as "Somebody's Eyes" and "Learning to be Silent" were delicate and sounded beautiful. The ensemble were full of harmony on the ecclesiastical "On Any Sunday" (lovely woodwind here too) and on the bigger numbers above. Vi, Ethel and Ariel sounded lovely together on "Learning to be Silent" and I liked the zip lips at the end. Choreographer Niamh O'Brien had a busy show as you would imagine as it's called 'Footloose'. Her choreography was sharp, vibrant, and brilliantly executed by the ridiculously energetic cast. The opening dance to the title song was full of energy and fun and went on forever, which was a good thing! I loved the cheerleader inspired dance on "Holding Out for a Hero". The line dancing on "Still Rockin'" was good as was "Mama Says", which was cleverly done and the "Footloose (Finale)" was like a trip down choreographer's lane. Excellent work. Robert Belton and Eddie Kiernan designed the set and it suited the production. The kitchen worked well as did the diner with the guitar image on the flat. The gas pump looked good as did the chapel. The projections really worked too as they set the locations. I liked the scaffold tower in the audience used as the bridge, very clever. Shane Byrne's lighting design was bright and cheery, and he used the movers to great effect in all of the big bouncy numbers. He lit the bridge scene very well and didn't wash out any of the projections. Pat Marnane's sound design was also good. Great balance between band and singers and a good range of sound effects including a brilliantly loud train! Tracey Carty costumed the cast in street clothes of the era, and I liked the red robes in the chapel scenes. The cheerleader uniforms looked great as did the Diner uniforms. There was a lot of denim on show which was perfect! A 'Team of Dedicated People' looked after the make-up and hair, which all looked excellent. Ariel's bruising and black eye looked very realistic. Eddie Kiernan stage managed everything and everybody with accuracy and speed.

Alan Greaney directed with a light touch, empowering the young performers to create a very charming production with him that had a love of dance and song at its heart. The acting performances were very good by both young and experienced performers who were absorbed by and immersed in their characters and their character's journeys. The book is full of corny dialogue and even cornier gags, but the actors delivered with conviction and didn't lampoon or shy away from the cheesiness. This engaged the audience who were fully engrossed in the story. A wonderful production that highlighted the abilities of the young performers on show and underscored the Society's inclusivity and commitment to nurturing emerging talent.

show_raw: Joseph And The Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat
review_text:
Band of Brothers The show is basically about Jacob and his twelve sons, He clearly favoured Joseph, unwittingly causing friction between Joseph and his brothers. They decide to get rid of him and sell him into slavery, telling Jacob that he died. Thus began Joseph's adventures in Egypt. It's a well-known Bible story, outlined in many children's books and a very popular musical, produced hundreds of times a year world-wide. Lloyd Webber wrote it in 1968, when the then twenty-minute 'pop cantata' was staged at Wallace High School. Over the years that twenty- minute cantata has been expanded by Lloyd Webber and Rice into a full two- act musical and this is the version I saw in Solstice Arts Centre produced by St Mary's Musical Society. Directed by Tony Finnegan and with choral direction by Paul Byrne and choreography by Sinead Lightley, this youthful production was full of energy and fun.

The production team decided to use backing tracks instead of an orchestra on this show, which was a pity because there was a disconnect between the singer and the song and some of the singers timing was a bit off. That said, musical director Paul Byrne's work with the chorus and individual singers was good, with some nice harmonies and power coming off the stage. The children's chorus was sweet, and the principals were terrific, especially Narrator, Joseph and Pharoah. Sinead Lightley's choreography was inventive with some nice moves. "One More Angel in Heaven" was a nice line danced hoedown and "Those Canaan Days" featured a tango pas de deux, which was quite thrilling. The disco inspired "Go, Go, Go, Joseph" bounced along with great syncopated movement, but I didn't get the American reference with the cheerleaders and football players! And the backing dancers for "Song of the King" were good as were the children's actions.

In the show the Narrator's role is to deliver the exposition, the story. Originally written for a male voice but changed some time ago to a female voice, the Narrator role is often split between two performers as it's such a big sing. In this production we had just the one, Suzan McDonagh Fitzsimons. Her voice was wonderfully expressive, full of reverence and power. It's a massive feat of endurance and stamina to sing the many, many songs but she was superb. The wonderful Shane Lavelle played Joseph and demonstrated a fine voice, good acting skills, and exquisite dance. A true triple-threat, he was a perfect Joseph. His sense of timing and physicality was excellent. His "Close Every Door" was superb as was "Any Dream will Do". He had a beatific demeanour which was quite compelling to watch, and we really felt empathy for his Joseph. Once the brothers got rid of him, they sang "One More Angel in Heaven/ Hoedown" where Cian Blake-Lynch as Naphtali took the lead. His accent and posturing was perfect in this Country and Western number.

Joseph was eventually bought by a Mr and Mrs Potiphar. Mr Potiphar was a rich businessman played by Alex Hill, he was money mad, counting his loot and ignoring his wife (Nicole Smyth), until he caught her in flagrante delicto. Ms Smyth played the femme fatal with all her scheming on display. Potiphar got him thrown in prison, but he ingratiated himself to the Pharoah through demonstrating precognition and reading dreams and became his trusted advisor. The Pharoah is written as a latter years Elvis Presley, complete with Vegas costuming and pompadour. Played by Sean Flanagan, this was inspired lunacy and Mr Flanagan gave us a great Pharoah, his "Song of the King" was superb, with the Elvis sneer and hip thrusts.

Meanwhile, Joseph's family back home was now starving and poor, having lost their farm and living off crumbs. Joseph's brothers bemoaned what they did to him and how they lied to their father Jacob - played with gravitas by Alex Hill. They sang "Those Canaan Days", a sort of French lament led by Ciaran Dunne's Issachar. He nailed the French accent and mannerisms and had a good stage presence and sang well with the brothers on this quite funny pastiche. They travelled to Egypt believing there was plenty of food there and met Joseph but didn't recognise him in all of his finery. He decided to teach them a lesson and accuses them of stealing. The brothers deny this and sing "Benjamin Calypso", a strange Caribbean song led by Louis McGlinchey's Judah. Mr McGlinchey led it with a good energy and a fine voice. Joseph revealed himself; they all made up and lived happily ever after. The show looked good, with a clever set by Enda Nugent. It was pre-made and just about fit on the stage. The light panels looked great and the treads coming on and off were done with accuracy. Tricky co-ordination was controlled by stage manager Tracy Fitzsimons, who also managed the large cast. Lighting by Ronan Kenny was vibrant. The star cloth looked beautiful, and each scene had a distinctive look, and the stage units were nicely sculpted with light. Alan John White Sound was also solid. As they were playing backing tracks, good balance was relatively easy to achieve I'd suggest, and it was good. Excellent period costumes especially the Egyptian garb and Joseph's coat plus a massive multicoloured cloak that descended from the grid and covered the whole stage. Aisling Quinn looked after the make-up and she had a good range of looks for all of the characters, Mrs Potiphar and Pharoah looked great, especially Pharoah's wig.

Tony Finnegan helmed this fun production of 'Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat'. It opened in a Sunday School, which was quite clever especially when the kids came running in. The adults playing teachers worked well and eventually Joseph entered. It was a cute opener and thereafter it was quite a traditional production with period costume and even a camel. There was a nice vibe to this show, it didn't take itself too seriously which is, I think, the right way to tackle it now as it's so dated. The set was interesting, with the pyramid structure and the movable treads. The young kids in the cast were great, full of energy and life with good voices and they stole the show.

Dolly Parton (on video) opened this show by Londonderry Musical Society at the Millennium Forum Theatre by telling the audience it was watching a musical set back when there was no cell phones and when women couldn't be promoted to positions of power. She popped up again at the end wishing us well and singing a bar or two of the titular number and the audience loved it, as they did the whole show which was a feelgood romp, with excellent production values and a good cast. Written in 2009 and based on a film made and set in the late '70's and early '80's about office politics and a misogynist boss vs his rebelling staff. It is an engagingly old fashioned, simple story full of Dolly songs, a bit of slapstick, with a Rom Com thin plot and, in this version, some wonderful performances.

Directed by Michael Poole with Vanessa Chapman choreographing and Peter Doherty on musical direction duties, it started out with the ensemble behind the gauze, waking up and getting ready for work whilst Dolly told us who they were. This was a good theatrical device as straight away we know who everyone is without too much exposition because you know what that can do to a show. They all woke up to and sang the opening number "9 to 5" and quite literally performed the actions of the song. This segued into a very well-choreographed, by Vanessa Chapman, dance routine. The opening number can be a bit chaotic, but she managed to keep them tight and in line and even had Josh skateboarding across the stage. Dance-wise "Around Here" was also good as was "One of the Boys". I found the fantasy sequence less assured with "Potion Notion" being the untidiest. But Roz's "Heart to Hart" was excellent with the additional dancers making it really zing. Peter Doherty's twelve-piece orchestra was big and powerful. His arrangements worked particularly well on Doralee's C&W number "Backwoods Barbie" and on Judy's big song "Get Out and Stay Out". Chorally, the ensemble were well-rehearsed, and he got some lovely harmonies from them. "Shine Like the Sun" was perfect as was "Around Here" and "Change It" - they all featured a very competent chorus, who nailed the harmonies and timing. The principals were all excellent, especially Doralee, Violet and Judy, who had a beautiful voice.

This was a well-cast show, especially the three female leads. Lorraine Roddy's Violet was a charming, homely portrayal of a woman who becomes empowered through her own efforts and not because she's one of the boys. Ms Roddy had a fine voice, most notable on "Let Love Grow" with Joe and on "Change It". She sounded best when singing with Doralee and Judy - "Shine Like the Sun" was a showstopper. Leon Cullen played her teenage son, Josh and impressed with his laid-back performance. Sophie Doran gave a lovely unpretentious performance. Her Doralee, veered away from Dolly-clone and she made the character her own. Her singing and dance skills were certainly to the fore here as she nailed each song and dance number. "Backwoods Barbie" was a superb pean to being misjudged by her looks and she sang it very well. She opened "Shine Like the Sun" brilliantly and her accent was perfect. Doralee's husband Dwayne was played with 'good 'ol boy' Texan charm by Simon Quigg. The final musketeer of this feminist rebellion was the astonishingly good Cora Early who played Judy. The role is written for an older actor, yet she managed to portray Judy's situation with truth and honesty. It helped that Dick, a cocky Matthew Irwin, was a younger actor to match. She plotted Judy's journey from dowdy housewife to high-ranking executive with skill, yet still showed Judy's gentleness with the creche visits. Her singing on all of the songs was excellent, but especially on "Get Out and Stay Out" this was full of emotion and expression and was the song of the night. These three actors were super individually, but when together they became more than the sum of their parts. Their archenemy was Franklin Hart Jr, the CEO of the company where they all worked. Terrifically acted by Colin Ash, who got across Hart's misogyny and sexism with good ability. His singing was less assured but that didn't matter on "Here for You" as it's all about the actions, which were lewd, crude and very funny. He was great in the scene with Tinsworthy and was just hilarious to watch, knowing he'd get his comeuppance. Hart's long- suffering wife Missy was played with assurance by Christine Baggley and his office manager, Roz, by Una Culkin. Roz was the saddest character in the show, and she was beautifully played by Ms Culkin. Her yearning for Hart was painful to watch, particularly as he used and abused her affections. Her singing on "Heart to Hart" and "5 to 9" was good and her movement on the former was very brave and funny. The office had a collection of regular and weird workers! Joe, played by Kieran Connor, was keen on Violet and spent the show wooing her and their song, "Let Love Grow" was lovely. Margaret was the office lush and was played perfectly by Judith O'Hare, not too drunk and not too sober. Holly Deane was Maria, a sort of wannabe shop steward, who was fired and hired, and Aoife Lennon played office gossip Kathy. Chair of the Board Mr Tinsworthy was played with a twinkling solemnness by David Keown. A lovely cast all stage managed by Christine Deane and her crew.

This show looked expensive, high quality production values don't come cheap! The set was hired in from Proscenium Set Hire. It was big and detailed, and filled the wide expansive stage of the Millennium Forum. Martin McDonald's lighting was fab, with lovely colours and good use of movers. Michael Kielty's sound design achieved a lovely balance, between band and stage. The reverb on Judy's "Get Out and Stay Out" was excellent and helped make the song quite epic. Costumes were supplied by Utopia and Addis Blair, there was a good 1980's look on all characters. Costumes on the fantasy sequences were brilliant, especially "Potion Notion". Make- up and Hair was good too and of the era. Director Michael Poole did a good job on this show. Of course, it is hammy and creaky and out of date already, but he had such a good focus and made it work. The staging was quite good in places, especially the office scenes and Hart's house. The pacing of the production was quite fast as it should be, and it ran accurately along the rails like a commuter train. Well done!

A Year in the Life 'Rent' was written by Jonathan Larson in the early 90's and was based on Puccini's opera 'La Bohème'. It's is about a year in the life of a group of friends living in a building in New York City. Like in 'La Bohème', these friends are all struggling artists, but some are HIV Positive. The title refers to their inability to pay the rent as the area becomes more gentrified. As the show's creator sadly died just before the Off-Broadway premiere, the show has now become a homage to his memory, as has the recent film of 'tick tick... BOOM!'. Produced by Galway Musical Society and directed by Paul Norton, with musical direction by John Roe and choreography by Jay Molyneux, 'Rent' ran in the Town Hall Theatre in Galway for five sold out performances.

The whole show is sung-through and narrated by Mark, an aspiring filmmaker. He was given a solid characterisation by Brandon Collier, who with his ubiquitous video camera, drove the show. Their relationship with Roger was well- established and he came across as a warm, caring figure. He sang with passion and energy throughout, but especially on "Tango: Maureen" with Joanne and "Living in America" with Roger, their roommate, who was played by Keith Hanley, who also played guitar onstage. Mr Hanley really got across Roger's hopelessness in the face of being HIV positive. His was a very melancholic Roger, pining after his dead girlfriend and initially resistant to Mimi's charms. He established a warm relationship with Mark and with Mimi and Collins. His vocals on "Rent", "One Song Glory" and 'Living in America" showed a fine rock voice. His duet with Hannah Wright's Mimi, "Light My Candle" was excellent as was their "Without You" and "I Should Tell You". Ms Wright was believable in her addiction scenes and seductive in her scenes with Roger. She played the character with a hard edge that worked and was super in "La Vie Bohème". Her singing on "Out Tonight" was fabulous as was her "Light My Candle" where her timing was spot on. "Without You" was full of poignancy and longing and she played Mimi's decent back into addiction with skill.

Mimi's ex-partner and former roommate of Marks, Benny, who married into money and now owns a lot of real estate in the neighbourhood including the building where Mark, Mimi and Roger live, was very well played by Jay Hall. He captured the conflict of being a landlord to his friends. His singing was good too on "You'll See" and his sections of "La Vie Bohème A" and he took a lead on "Seasons of Love", which he nailed. Another ex-roommate, Tom Collins was played by Niall Conway. As the anarchic university professor, Mr Conway really convinced particularly in his relationship with Angel. His voice was exquisite, a fine baritone. He handled "Santa Fe" and "I'll Cover You" with ease but it was on the slow-tempo "I'll Cover You (Reprise)" with the ensemble where he shone. His emotional connection with this song was palpable. A very fine performance. Collins love interest was Angel, a drag queen with AIDS, who tended to him when he was mugged, here performed by Jay Molyneux. Mr Molyneux's performance was quite heartfelt and he resisted the impulse to overplay Angel, he wasn't overtly affected and this gave an affability and mellowness to the character. His relationship with Collins was well-defined and quite enchanting. Mr Molyneux's singing on "Today 4 U" was good and his sections in "La Vie Bohème" were full of energy. He also managed the really high notes on "Contact", it's a difficult sing, but he did it well.

The final two friends, who are also in a relationship were Joanne, played by Gabrielle Reid and Maureen (Mark's ex) here played by Helena Brosnan. Both were very believable in their onstage relationship and were dazzling when they sang the duet "Take Me or Leave Me". Ms Reid's "We're Okay" as Joanne was also good as was her duet with Mark, "Tango: Maureen". But it was Ms Brosnan who brought the house down with a very well performed live art 'performance piece' "Over The Moon". This song included the audience mooing, some very funny deadpan reluctant backing singers and a cowbell! Her characterisation of free- spirited artist Maureen was a highlight of the show.

In addition to the brilliantly dynamic cast above we also had featured performers who played many other roles. Aoife Kilroy, Sarah Jenkins, Éanna Marren, Catherine Ryan, David Alexander, Aisling Carrol, Jessica McDonagh, Michael Healy, Jane Patterson, and Niamh McSweeney were great. Ms McDonagh was superb on "Seasons of Love" especially and as the Waiter and Mr Alexander was quite menacing as The Man, but gentle in "Life Support". The "Voice Mail" sections were all very well sung with great timing by the various performers, in particular the Alexi Darling character and "Voice Mail #5" with the parents. They added lovely harmonies to the bigger numbers as did the Ensemble, particularly on "Rent", "La Vie Bohème" and "I'll Cover You (Reprise)". John Roe's musical direction was excellent. His small band sounded much bigger than the sum of their parts and I was particularly impressed with the guitars. His work with the ensemble was superb, strong harmonies on "Rent", "Seasons..." and "I'll Cover You (Reprise)" with delicate harmonies on "Will I" and "Life Support". Jay Molyneux (Angel) created some nice choreography in what is not a typical musical in that many of the characters are quite ill and on the verge of death! However, the erotic "Contact" was great, and the movement on the title song was strong.

John Wright designed a great set. The loft style apartment was full of 'stuff'. The brick effect on the flats was perfect as were the windows. The massive white material was perfect for "Contact" and the painting of the 'Christmas Tree' was clever and I loved the framed photo of Angel seen during the eulogies. Sound to Light designed the lighting on this show and it was perfect. The focus was excellent, and the full-stage bigger numbers were vibrantly lit. They also looked after the sound with a good balance between band and singers. Costume and make-up all worked a treat and it was all superbly stage managed by Chontelle Kenny. Producing 'Rent' is an exercise in reverence and a company feels compelled to do it justice, to realise Larson's concept. Many of the characters are based on people he knew, and it is incumbent on a director Dunboyne Musical Society LEGALLY BLONDE Blondes Have More Fun!

The original 'Legally Blonde - The Musical' has been described as "high- energy, empty-calories, and expensive-looking hymn to the glories of girlishness", an "ingratiating trifle" and "it should be entitled 'Irredeemably Bland'". It is true that the plot is not exactly Shakespearean in its' complexity (girl loves boy, girl loses boy, boy wants girl back, girl has moved on) nor are the characters anything more than two- dimensional. However, one knows this in advance of attending and indeed, I would argue that this is part of its charm. But there is an important message hidden away in there too, if you care to look.

Based on the novel by Amanda Brown and the 2001 film starring Reese Witherspoon, 'Legally Blonde' is about lovelorn Elle Woods whose boyfriend, Warner, dumps her because she's not serious enough, and moves away to attend Harvard. Elle follows him to college and whilst there grows up, gets an education, and ultimately finds her true vocation whilst staying true to herself. She also falls in love again. The writing, by Heather Hatch, Laurence O'Keefe and Neil Benjamin is clever, as the songs propel the action forward, incorporating elements of explanation, character development, and their cast to be true to his vision and to his legacy. Mr Norton's production was faithful to Larson's work, his interpretation was fresh yet still retained the style Larson envisioned. The show is a homage to Larson's genius and humanity and Mr Norton's production properly focused on the characters and their interactions, building empathy with the audience as they followed their paths during the course of a year. This was a brilliantly affecting show, some of the audience were in tears as indeed were the cast - that's the power of "Rent" and Mr Norton and his collaborators should be proud to have given us a beautiful production.

Blondes Have More Fun!

It is true that the plot is not exactly Shakespearean in its' complexity (girl loves boy, girl loses boy, boy wants girl back, girl has moved on) nor are the characters anything more than two-dimensional. However, one knows this in advance of attending and indeed, I would argue that this is part of its charm. But there is an important message hidden away in there too, if you care to look.

storytelling, choreography, set and costume changes. So much happens in "What You Want" that the location even moves from LA to Harvard as the number progresses. "Bend and Snap" seems like a dopey song but provides a fundamental plot point in the next scene. So, it may be fluff but its well-written fluff.

Directed by Orla Mulreid Deane in her directorial debut, with Emer Hartnett on musical direction duties and Grainne Kennedy choreographing, the musical was produced by Dunboyne Musical Society and staged in the local Community Centre in April to great public acclaim. It looked great with a set designed by Aidan Mannion. There was mobile rotating central door flat which was used a lot during the show and was very smooth. I liked the hair salon on the stage right apron with old school hair dryers and Elle's college room on the stage left apron. The window flats upstage were also quite good and really worked when the Greek Chorus popped through. Oh, and his use of pink was great and there was a lot of pink.

Lighting by Cathal Donohue was big, and colourful for the up-tempo full stage numbers, yet moody and focused for the slower ballads. The neon in the clothing store was a nice touch as was the backlight in the windows. The look of this show is particularly distinctive and also quite contrasting, pink LA vs brown Harvard. Costume design by Aoife O'Rourke, Lauryn McLeod and Ciara Rooney gave some fabulous costumes for the show, from Cheerleading Majorettes to the tweedy stuffy academic look and with super make-up and hair it all combined into a precise presentation.

This is a modern fairy-tale of a show, it's joyfully silly and enormously engaging. The music is irritating at times "Omigod You Guys" is an ear worm of a song and "Ireland" is just dire, but musical director Emer Hartnett's superb orchestrations of the mostly strong score, and work with the chorus and principals lifted the music to higher level. Grainne Kennedy's choreography was great and the real backbone of this show. Her 'Riverdance' was cheesy but brilliant, very syncopated! "Whipped into Shape" was excellent as was "Bend and Snap". But the winner for me was the fantastic "What You Want.", it was big and bold and crazy and went on forever.

Shona Delaney's Elle drew us into her character's journey from Valley girl to strong independent woman with an eye for fashion. She had a great singing voice especially on "Serious" where she had good comic timing with Warner and on "Legally Blonde" and "Chip on My Shoulder" with Emmett. Her dance was also good, and she had an infectious energy. Her Delta Nu Greek Chorus were played by Emma Dalton, Aoife O'Rourke and Grainne Dolan, each had great dance and singing skills and excelled with their comic timing and energetic performances.
